question: Cut the lights in a grotto at Waitomo, on New Zealand's North Island, and the ceiling blazes with thousands of tiny blue-green sparks, like a galaxy hung in the rock. What living things make this underground night sky?
context: New Zealand's glowworms (Arachnocampa luminosa) cling to the ceiling of Waitomo's Glowworm Grotto by the thousand; in the pitch dark their blue-green points look exactly like a starry sky. It is one of New Zealand's most-visited natural wonders — about 500,000 people came each year before the pandemic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: The tunnels of Waitomo were never dug out. Faintly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved them from limestone that formed on a seabed 30 million years ago and lies over 200 metres thick. What is a geographer's name for such cave-riddled, sinkhole-pocked limestone country?
context: Karst is landscape dissolved out of soluble rock — usually limestone — leaving caves, sinkholes, and underground rivers. Waitomo's limestone formed under the sea about 30 million years ago (the Oligocene) and is studded with fossilized corals and seashells; over 1,300 m of passages wind through it on two levels. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: Visitors drift through the Waitomo Glowworm Grotto by boat, in total darkness and silence — no talking, no lamps allowed. The reason is the glowworms themselves: a burst of noise or light provokes a swift reaction in their blue-green lights. How do the lights react?
choices: they flash from blue to red
context: Boats glide along the underground Waitomo Stream through the Glowworm Grotto while guides keep everyone silent; noise and light make the glowworms' glow fade, so darkness and quiet keep the living constellation bright. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: For generations, local Māori knew the mouth of the Waitomo cave but never ventured inside — until 1887, when chief Tāne Tinorau and English surveyor Fred Mace poled in together on a raft of flax stems, lit only by a candle. In Māori tradition, what did that dark cave-mouth mark?
choices: the lair of a taniwha, a water-monster
a place made tapu, or forbidden
a path for the spirits of the dead
context: Māori had known the Waitomo cave-mouth for generations but treated it as an entrance to the underworld and left it unexplored. In December 1887 the local chief Tāne Tinorau and English surveyor Fred Mace built a flax raft and poled inside by candlelight, following the Waitomo Stream where it vanishes underground — their first find was the glittering Glowworm Grotto. (Māori tradition.) Source: explorersweb.com/natural-wonders-waitomo-glowworm-caves; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave  (Legend.)

question: Chief Tāne Tinorau and his wife Huti opened the Waitomo caves to travelers in 1889, guiding visitors by candlelight themselves. For most of the next century the government ran the caves — until a landmark 1989 decision changed who owned them. What did that decision do?
answer: returned the caves to the founding family's heirs
choices: returned the caves to the founding family's heirs
sold the caves to a private tourism company
declared the caves a protected national park
handed the caves to a university for research
context: By 1889 Tāne Tinorau and his wife Huti were guiding travelers through the caves for a small fee — about 500 visitors came in the first two years, one of the earliest Māori-run tourism ventures. In 1989 the caves were returned to their descendants, who own and run them today; a 1990 Deed of Settlement grants the family a share of the revenue. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: The glowworm that lights the Waitomo ceiling, Arachnocampa luminosa, shines here and through New Zealand's wet forests — and on no other land on Earth. Even the glow in Australian caves like Tasmania's Marakoopa comes from separate cousin species that never crossed the Tasman. What do biologists call a species like this one?
context: Endemic means a species lives naturally in one region and nowhere else on Earth. Arachnocampa luminosa glows only in the caves and wet forests of New Zealand; its nearest relatives are themselves endemic to Australian karst caves — for example Arachnocampa tasmaniensis in Tasmania's Marakoopa and Gunns Plains caves — but they are separate species that never crossed the Tasman. (How the larva actually makes its light belongs to biology, not geography.) Source: inaturalist.org/taxa/125921-Arachnocampa-luminosa; caveanimals.com.au/glow-worms

question: On 20 February 1943, near the village of Paricutin in Michoacan, Mexico, a farmer named Dionisio Pulido watched the ground of his own cornfield crack open and start spitting ash -- a brand-new volcano being born at his feet. You'd think a mountain needs centuries to rise. How tall was Pulido's volcano by the end of that first day?
context: Within 24 hours the new cone stood about 50 m (160 ft) tall; it kept climbing to its final 424 m by 1952, then fell silent forever. Dionisio Pulido had witnessed something almost no human ever has -- a volcano's birth from its very first minute. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'; IUGS Geoheritage, 'Paricutin Volcano'.

question: For nine years after it burst from the ground in 1943, Paricutin's lava crept across the Mexican countryside and slowly swallowed the whole town of San Juan Parangaricutiro. Today the town lies gone beneath a frozen sea of black rock -- all except one structure that still juts up out of the hardened lava. What is it?
choices: The roof of the town hall
context: Only the church of San Juan Parangaricutiro survived, its bell tower and altar rising out of the black rock. Locals call the surviving altar a miracle; it is still used for occasional services, and pilgrims walk out across the lava to reach it. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'Viejo San Juan Parangaricutiro'; Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'.

question: Between 1963 and 1967 an undersea volcano built a brand-new island, Surtsey, off the southern coast of Iceland. It became a rare natural laboratory, closed to the public and watched over by scientists studying how life first reaches brand-new land. One year they found a healthy tomato plant growing there -- sprouted, they realized, from a researcher's own improperly buried waste. What did the scientists do about their surprise tomato?
answer: Pulled it up, to keep the island pristine
choices: Pulled it up, to keep the island pristine
Fenced it off and studied its growth
Celebrated it as Surtsey's first crop
Left it alone as a natural experiment
context: The tomato was pulled up at once to keep Surtsey pristine. Only scientists may land there; the first plant to arrive on its own, sea rocket, sprouted in 1965. Surtsey is a UNESCO-protected natural laboratory for watching how life colonizes new land. Source: Wikipedia, 'Surtsey'.

question: In Indonesia's Sunda Strait, between the islands of Java and Sumatra, the volcano Krakatoa blew itself to pieces in the colossal eruption of 1883. But the strait did not stay quiet: a new volcano has since risen from the same waters and still smokes and grows there today. Indonesians call it Anak Krakatau. What does that name mean?
context: 'Anak' means 'child' -- Anak Krakatau, the Child of Krakatoa, first rose permanently above the waves in 1930 and grew 7-9 m taller each year. In 2018 one flank slid into the sea and it lost most of its height, but it is rebuilding still. Source: Wikipedia, 'Anak Krakatoa'.

question: In nine years of eruption, the slow lava of Paricutin, in Michoacan, Mexico, killed no one at all -- it crept too slowly to catch anyone. Yet the volcano did take three lives. They died not from lava or falling rock, but from a violent weather-hazard that the volcano's own churning ash cloud brewed up in the sky overhead. What killed those three people?
context: Volcanic ash clouds build up enormous static charge and crackle with lightning. Three people near Paricutin were killed by that lightning, even though the creeping lava itself claimed no lives in nine years of eruption. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'.

question: About 1,000 kilometers south of Tokyo, in the Pacific, an undersea eruption in 2013 shoved a small new islet up out of the water beside the existing island of Nishinoshima. Eruption after eruption, the lava kept piling up -- the islet merged with the old island and swelled to some twenty times its former size. Japanese officials watched each new eruption with quiet delight. What did Nishinoshima's eruptions do for Japan?
answer: Added brand-new national territory to its map
choices: Added brand-new national territory to its map
Opened a rich new deep-sea fishing ground
Built a natural harbor for its navy
Raised a sunken island back above the sea
context: The new lava enlarged Nishinoshima to roughly 4.1 sq km -- about twenty times its old size -- literally adding fresh land, and the surrounding waters, to Japan's territory. Undersea eruptions are still redrawing the map today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nishinoshima (Ogasawara)'.

question: Abu Simbel, in far southern Egypt, guards its entrance with four seated giants of the pharaoh Ramesses II, sitting shoulder to shoulder across the temple front -- each rising about 20 m, as tall as a six-story building. What is most unusual about how the whole temple was made?
answer: Cut directly into a solid sandstone cliff
choices: Cut directly into a solid sandstone cliff
Built up from sun-dried mud brick
context: Abu Simbel is entirely rock-cut: instead of stacking blocks, workers under Ramesses II chiseled the whole temple -- facade, halls, and the four 20-m colossi -- straight into a living sandstone cliff, so it is really one carved mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel; egymonuments.gov.eg/archaeological-sites/abu-simbel.

question: In the 1960s the reservoir Lake Nasser was rising to drown Abu Simbel forever. To save the 3,200-year-old temple, an international team pulled off one of history's boldest rescues. What did they do?
answer: Sawed it into over a thousand blocks and moved it uphill
choices: Sawed it into over a thousand blocks and moved it uphill
Raised the whole temple straight up on hydraulic jacks
Floated it whole on giant sealed pontoons to safety
Ringed it with a new dam to hold the lake back
context: Behind the new Aswan High Dam, Lake Nasser was rising to swallow the temple. From 1964-1968 an international team sawed Abu Simbel into 1,036 numbered blocks (807 for the Great Temple, 235 for the Small) and rebuilt it on higher ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: Right beside the giant Great Temple at Abu Simbel stands a second, smaller temple that Ramesses II carved for his queen, Nefertari. Unusually, her statues on its front rise as tall as the pharaoh's own. To which goddess did he dedicate the queen's temple?
context: Hathor was the Egyptian goddess of love, joy, and music. Nefertari's temple is one of very few where the queen's statues on the facade stand as tall as the pharaoh's -- and she is shown as Hathor herself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: One of the four giant Ramesses statues at Abu Simbel had lost its head and shoulders to an earthquake in ancient times. When the temple was rescued and rebuilt in the 1960s, the engineers made a deliberate choice about that broken colossus. What did they do with the fallen head?
answer: Left it lying at the statue's feet
choices: Left it lying at the statue's feet
Rebuilt it from fresh matching sandstone
Sent it to a museum in Cairo
Replaced it with a copy in concrete
context: An ancient earthquake toppled the head and torso of the second colossus. When they rebuilt the temple in the 1960s, the restorers deliberately left the broken pieces lying at its feet, exactly as they had fallen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: To save Abu Simbel, the rescue team lifted the whole temple 65 m up the cliff and set it back about 208 m from the rising lake, then pieced the blocks back together. Fitting a 3,200-year-old mountain of rock back into place, how closely did they match the original?
choices: To within about half a meter
context: The team raised Abu Simbel 65 m and moved it about 208 m back from the water, reassembling the blocks to a tolerance of only about 5 mm so the ancient sunrise alignment would still work. The seams are almost invisible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: Deep inside Abu Simbel, four gods sit carved into the very back wall, about 60 m down a pitch-dark corridor. Twice a year -- around February 22 and October 22 -- the rising sun spears straight down the passage at dawn and lights three of the four faces, while one god alone stays in shadow. Which one?
context: The three lit figures are Ra-Horakhty, Amun-Ra, and the deified Ramesses; Ptah, linked to the underworld, is the one left in darkness. Many hold that the ancient builders designed the alignment deliberately. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel; corroborated egymonuments.gov.eg and worldhistory.org/image/15453.

question: When Abu Simbel was cut apart and rebuilt on higher ground in the 1960s, engineers labored to preserve its famous sunrise alignment. The sun still floods the sanctuary and lights the gods twice a year -- but it is often said the modern builders couldn't quite match the original. What is the small imperfection?
answer: The sunlit days shifted by about one day
choices: The sunlit days shifted by about one day
The beam now lights all four gods, not three
The sunbeam reaches only halfway down the hall
The sunrise now misses the sanctuary in winter
context: It is widely reported that the original illumination fell on about February 21 and October 21, and that after the 1960s move the dates slipped by roughly a day -- a reminder that modern engineers couldn't perfectly reproduce 3,200-year-old astronomy. Source: egiptoexclusivo.com/en/blog/solar-alignment-at-abu-simbel; suryatara.com/abu-simbel-sun-festival.  (Legend.)

question: Above a bend of the Waghora river gorge in Maharashtra, India, a steep cliff curves in a horseshoe nearly 76 m high. Along that wall lie about 30 ancient Buddhist halls and monasteries, complete with rows of pillars, shrines, and sculpted ceilings. How was this whole complex at Ajanta created?
answer: carved directly out of the solid cliff
choices: carved directly out of the solid cliff
built up course by course in fired brick
assembled from precisely fitted stone blocks
framed and roofed in carved teak beams
context: Not one block was stacked at Ajanta: every pillar, doorway, and ceiling was cut away from the living basalt of the gorge, so the finished halls stand inside the hollowed rock. The horseshoe cliff bends about 76 m above the Waghora river in Maharashtra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; worldhistory.org/article/849/the-ajanta-caves/

question: Inside the Ajanta caves, dim walls suddenly blaze with color: processions of princes, dark-eyed queens, elephants, and dancers, painted in ochre and deep blue and still glowing after some 1,500 years. It is the largest surviving body of ancient Indian painting, and nearly every scene retells one of the Jataka tales. What do these Jataka stories recount?
choices: the ten avatars of the god Vishnu
the daily rituals of the resident monks
context: Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's earlier births -- as princes, animals, even a great six-tusked elephant -- each life teaching a virtue such as generosity or patience. Nowhere else on earth survives so much ancient Indian painting as on these cave walls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: Beside the shrine of Cave 1 glows the most beloved image at Ajanta: a tall prince with lowered eyes and a jeweled crown, his head tilted in quiet compassion, holding a single blue lotus. He is a bodhisattva -- an enlightened being who lingers in the world to help others toward release. What is this gentle Cave 1 bodhisattva called?
context: Padmapani means 'the lotus-bearer,' a form of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. On the opposite side of Cave 1's shrine stands his sterner companion, Vajrapani, 'the thunderbolt-bearer.' The Padmapani mural is the single most reproduced image of Ajanta. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: For over a thousand years after its monks departed, Ajanta lay swallowed by jungle and forgotten by the outside world. Then in April 1819 a British army officer, out hunting across the Deccan hills, glimpsed a dark cave mouth through the trees, and a local boy led him inside to the painted halls. What had the officer been chasing when he stumbled onto the lost caves?
context: The officer was Captain John Smith of the Madras army, and the date was 28 April 1819. Inside Cave 10 he scratched his own name and the date over a 1,500-year-old painting -- graffiti that can still be read on the pillar today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; livehistoryindia.com/story/monuments/how-ajanta-caves-were-rediscovered

question: The roughly 30 caves at Ajanta were hollowed for two different uses. Most are square halls ringed by small cells, where monks slept, studied, and gathered. A handful are tall worship-halls with an aisle running around a domed shrine, so pilgrims could circle it in prayer. What are these two kinds of Buddhist cave called?
context: A vihara is a monastery of living-cells; a chaitya-griha is a worship-hall built around a stupa for circling in prayer. Five of Ajanta's caves are chaityas (9, 10, 19, 26, and 29) and the rest viharas; Cave 10, the oldest, is a chaitya. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: Ajanta was carved in two bursts six centuries apart. A first cluster of caves was cut around the 2nd-1st century BCE; then, after roughly 600 silent years, the site's grandest halls and most glorious murals were carved in a single dazzling wave under the Vakataka emperor Harishena, around 460-480 CE. What surprising fact is true of many of Harishena's second-phase caves?
choices: they were each carved by a single monk
they copied the plan of the early caves
they were meant as palaces, not temples
context: When Harishena's Vakataka dynasty collapsed soon after his death, the carvers downed their tools mid-work. Several of the grand later caves still stand half-made -- roughed-out pillars, blank plastered walls, and figures only partly cut from the living rock, frozen at the moment the carving stopped. The first, far smaller phase belongs to the Satavahana era around the 2nd-1st century BCE, when Cave 10, the oldest, was cut. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; worldhistory.org/article/849/the-ajanta-caves/

question: Sailing into Santorini, ships pass between sheer cliffs about 300 m high curving for miles around a ring of deep water. This is no ordinary bay: after a giant Bronze Age eruption emptied the magma beneath, the volcano's whole summit sank and the sea flooded in. What do geologists call this kind of feature?
context: Santorini's bay is a caldera -- the basin a volcano leaves when its emptied magma chamber collapses. This drowned crater is about 12 by 7 km across, ringed by cliffs near 300 m high and up to about 385 m deep. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini_caldera

question: Dig down through Santorini's volcanic ash and you reach Akrotiri, a town of the Minoan world so complete that its stone houses still stand two and three storeys tall, with paved lanes and clay drainpipes. People nickname it 'a second Pompeii' -- but one fact staggers visitors: compared with Pompeii, when was Akrotiri buried?
context: The buried town is Akrotiri, part of the Minoan world. It was sealed roughly 1,600 years before Pompeii (destroyed 79 CE) -- back in the Bronze Age -- yet its houses still stand two and three storeys high with paved streets and clay drains, so visitors can walk through their upper floors. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city)

question: Pompeii's ash preserved thousands of bodies frozen where they fell. But at Akrotiri on Santorini, buried the same way under volcanic ash, archaeologists found almost none -- no crowds of the dead at all. What is the leading explanation for this eerie emptiness?
answer: the townspeople felt earthquakes and fled in time
choices: the townspeople felt earthquakes and fled in time
the acidic ash slowly dissolved the bones away
the survivors came back and buried their dead
floods later washed the bodies out to sea
context: Archaeologists report 'no uninterred human skeletal remains' at Akrotiri. Warning earthquakes seem to have driven the townspeople out in good order before the blast -- and they carried their valuables with them, which is why the houses were found nearly bare. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city)

question: Akrotiri's houses were stripped almost bare -- its people had carried their wealth away. But in 1999, tucked inside a wooden box within a clay chest, excavators lifted out the one object of solid gold ever found in the whole town. What was this lone treasure?
context: The lone gold object is a small ibex (wild goat) figurine, found in 1999 inside a wooden box within a clay chest, beside a pile of animal horns. That the whole town yielded just this single precious piece is itself the clue that its people left in an orderly evacuation, taking their wealth. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/image/1358/gold-ibex-akrotiri/

question: In 1970, diggers at Akrotiri on Santorini uncovered the 'Spring Fresco' -- swallows swooping over clusters of red lilies on rocky volcanic ground. Artists had finished it well before 1600 BCE, yet it instantly became a landmark in the study of Aegean art. What set it apart from every earlier fresco find?
answer: it was the first fresco found still on its original wall
choices: it was the first fresco found still on its original wall
it was the oldest fresco ever dug up in the Aegean
it was rebuilt from thousands of tiny scattered fragments
it was the first fresco ever hung whole in a museum
context: Uncovered in 1970, the Spring Fresco -- swallows swooping over red lilies on a rocky volcanic landscape -- was the first Aegean wall-painting ever found perfectly preserved on the very wall where it was painted, not pieced together from fallen fragments. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/673/akrotiri-frescoes/

question: The eruption that buried Akrotiri erased an entire advanced society -- swallowed by sea and ash, as one ancient phrase put it, in a single day and night. Struck by that image, some scholars have wondered whether the memory of Thera's fate inspired a famous ancient story of a great civilization that vanished beneath the sea. Which story?
choices: the myth of the lost city of Ys
context: Because a whole advanced society here vanished under sea and ash, some scholars have linked Thera to Plato's story of Atlantis, the drowned island empire. It is a real and popular scholarly hypothesis -- but it stays SPECULATIVE and unproven, never established as fact. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Minoan_eruption  (Legend.)

question: At Aksum in northern Ethiopia, a field of giant pillars rises from the ground, each cut from a single stone and carved with rows of blind 'windows' and a false 'door' at its foot, floor stacked upon floor. Each Aksum stele was carved to imitate what?
context: Aksum's stelae are single blocks of stone carved to look like the tall, multi-storey tower-houses that Aksumites actually built -- complete with rows of false windows on every 'floor' and false doors detailed right down to imitation door-locks. The Obelisk of Axum shows nine storeys; the fallen Great Stele depicts thirteen. Source: Wikipedia, 'Obelisk of Axum.'

question: The giant carved stones at Aksum were not statues of gods or victory monuments. Beneath the largest of them, archaeologists dug down and found stone-lined chambers cut deep into the rock. What did each towering Aksum stele mark the spot of?
context: Each towering stele was a grave-marker, standing over the underground burial chamber of an Aksumite king. The biggest stones were reserved for royalty, so the whole field is really a royal cemetery -- a skyline of stone 'skyscrapers' marking the tombs of a kingdom's rulers. Source: Wikipedia, 'King Ezana's Stele' and 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: In 1937, Italian troops occupying Ethiopia on Mussolini's orders sawed the 24-metre, 160-tonne Obelisk of Axum into three pieces, took it to Rome, and set it up near the Circus Maximus. Almost 70 years later, in 2005, Italy at last returned the giant stele to Aksum. How did Italy move the massive obelisk back to Ethiopia?
answer: by a giant Antonov cargo plane
choices: by a giant Antonov cargo plane
by a Red Sea cargo ship
by a convoy of heavy trucks
context: The Obelisk of Axum -- 24 m and 160 tonnes of a single phonolite block -- was looted in 1937 during Mussolini's occupation of Ethiopia and re-erected in Rome, where it stood about 68 years. In April 2005 Italy finally flew the three sections home aboard a giant Antonov An-124, one of the world's largest cargo planes; the operation cost $7.7 million. The obelisk was re-erected at Aksum and unveiled in 2008. Source: Wikipedia, 'Obelisk of Axum.'

question: The empire of Aksum grew rich as the great middleman between inland Africa and the Roman Mediterranean. From its Red Sea ports, Aksumite merchants exported ivory, tortoise-shell, and gold, and in exchange imported costly luxuries carried by sea. Which luxuries did Aksum bring in?
context: Aksum was the principal supplier of African goods to the Roman world: ivory, tortoise-shell, and gold went out, while silk and spices came in from as far away as India. Sitting between inland Africa and the Red Sea, this middleman trade made Aksum one of the great commercial powers of the ancient world. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: The Aksum stelae were quarried as single blocks from Gobedra Hill, 4 km west of the city -- but the biggest weigh hundreds of tonnes, and the builders had no saws big enough to cut them out. How did Aksum's quarry workers crack these colossal blocks free from the bedrock?
answer: soaked wooden wedges until they swelled and split it
choices: soaked wooden wedges until they swelled and split it
heated the rock, then cracked it with cold water
drilled it out with hardened iron chisels
levered it free with long bronze bars
context: The stelae were quarried as single blocks from nepheline-syenite at Gobedra Hill, about 4 km west of Aksum. Workers cut grooves into the rock, drove in wooden wedges, and soaked them with water; as the wood swelled it split the giant block free. Teams of laborers then dragged the colossal stones to the burial field. Source: Metropolitan Museum and archaeological sources on the Gobedra quarry.

question: The Great Stele of Aksum -- 33 metres and roughly 520 tonnes, cut from one block -- is very likely the largest single stone that people anywhere have ever tried to stand upright on end. Today it does not tower over the stele field; it lies in enormous broken pieces on the ground. What most likely brought the Great Stele down?
answer: it collapsed during the very attempt to raise it
choices: it collapsed during the very attempt to raise it
it was shaken down by a powerful earthquake
it was cracked apart by repeated lightning
it was toppled by treasure-hunters digging beneath
context: The Great Stele -- about 33 m and 520 tonnes -- is arguably the largest single block of stone humans anywhere have ever attempted to raise on end. Scholars believe it fell and broke during the very attempt to erect it, and it has lain shattered ever since. As it toppled, it is thought to have crashed onto the massive roof stone of an underground tomb known as Nefas Mawcha, collapsing the chamber below (per UNESCO). Source: SFU Museum of Archaeology; UNESCO; Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'  (Legend.)

question: Around 270 AD, King Endybis of Aksum began doing something that ancient rulers treated as a mark of true sovereignty -- a sign that a kingdom stood as a power in its own right, beholden to no greater ruler. What did Endybis begin producing at Aksum?
context: Around 270 AD, King Endybis of Aksum began minting coins in gold, silver, and bronze. Minting one's own coinage was one of the ancient world's classic marks of a sovereign power, and Aksum was one of the few kingdoms of its age -- and one of the very few in Africa -- to do so. Aksumite coins circulated across the Red Sea trade world. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: In the ancient city of Aksum stands the Church of St Mary of Zion, first built under King Ezana in the 4th century AD and one of the oldest churches in Ethiopia. For many centuries this church held a unique privilege in the Ethiopian empire: one great ceremony could take place lawfully only here. What ceremony?
context: For centuries, an Ethiopian ruler could be crowned legitimate emperor only at Aksum, in a service tied to the Church of St Mary of Zion. The original church, founded under King Ezana in the 4th century AD, is among the oldest in Ethiopia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion.'

question: Aksum minted its own coins for centuries, and those little metal discs quietly record one of the great turning points in the kingdom's history. Around 340 AD, under King Ezana, the images stamped on Aksum's coins changed: the old royal symbols were dropped, and a new emblem appeared that makes Aksumite money some of the earliest anywhere to carry it. What new symbol appeared on the coins?
context: Under King Ezana in the 330s-340s AD, Aksum became one of the first kingdoms anywhere to adopt Christianity -- and you can watch it happen on the money. Around 340 the coins' older pagan crescent-and-disc gives way to the cross, making Aksumite coinage some of the earliest in the world to bear a Christian cross. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: Beside the Church of St Mary of Zion at Aksum stands a small, closely guarded chapel. Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that inside rests a most sacred object, said to have been carried long ago from King Solomon's Jerusalem by Prince Menelik; a single monk, chosen for life and never allowed to leave the grounds, is its only keeper. Held on faith, what does Aksum claim to guard here?
context: The Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion claims to guard the Ark of the Covenant -- in the Hebrew Bible, the chest that held the tablets of the Ten Commandments. By Ethiopian tradition, Prince Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought it from Jerusalem; only a single guardian monk, appointed for life and forbidden ever to leave, may see it. This is a sacred belief, held on faith -- neither proven nor disproven. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion.'  (Legend.)

question: The Pharos, Alexandria's great lighthouse and one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, burned a fire at its summit to guide ships through the night. But sailors could catch its signal even in full daylight, centuries before electricity. How did the Pharos warn ships by day?
answer: It flashed sunlight from a huge polished mirror.
choices: It flashed sunlight from a huge polished mirror.
It sent up a tall column of black smoke.
It rang an enormous bronze harbor bell.
It raised bright banners along the tower.
context: By day a polished mirror at the top of the Pharos threw the sun's light out to sea; the flash was said to be visible nearly 47 km from shore, from a tower rising perhaps 100-130 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria; britannica.com 'Lighthouse of Alexandria'.

question: In 331 BC Alexander the Great chose the spot for Alexandria, laid out its broad avenues and its harbor, and named the new city after himself. Alexandria would grow into the greatest city of the ancient Mediterranean world. What became of Alexander and the city that carries his name?
answer: He never returned to see the city finished.
choices: He was crowned Egypt's pharaoh in the city's temple.
He never returned to see the city finished.
He personally dug the city's first harbor channel.
He raised his statue at the city's main crossroads.
context: Alexander's architect Dinocrates laid the city out on a grid of broad avenues crossing at right angles, but Alexander himself marched off to Persia within months and never saw the finished city that carries his name. Source: worldhistory.org/alexandria/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Alexandria.

question: The Library of Alexandria wanted to be more than large. Its royal keepers set it one relentless mission and chased it for centuries, filling hall after hall with papyrus scrolls. What did the Library of Alexandria set out to collect?
answer: A copy of every book in the world.
choices: A copy of every book in the world.
The holy scriptures of every religion.
A map of every land ever charted.
The verses of every Greek poet.
context: Chasing a copy of every book in existence, the Library gathered tens of thousands of scrolls (ancient estimates range wildly, from 40,000 to several hundred thousand) to become the greatest library of the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria.

question: As Alexander the Great marked out Alexandria's walls in 331 BC, the story goes that he had no chalk to draw the lines on the dark Egyptian soil, so he traced the whole city outline in pale barley-meal instead. Then something happened that frightened him badly, until his seers talked him back to calm. According to the legend told by Plutarch, what happened to Alexander's barley-meal outline?
answer: Flocks of birds swooped down and ate every grain.
choices: Flocks of birds swooped down and ate every grain.
A sudden desert wind scattered it to nothing.
A night rainstorm washed the pale lines away.
Stray dogs trampled the outline into mud.
context: Plutarch (Life of Alexander 26) tells it: the birds terrified Alexander, but his seers read a good omen in it, saying the city would feed and nourish peoples from many nations. Framed here as legend. Source: livius.org (Plutarch, Life of Alexander 26).

question: On the rocky point at the mouth of Alexandria's harbor stands Fort Qaitbay, a squat stone fortress the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay raised around 1480; it still guards the water today. What did the sultan build his fort from?
answer: Salvaged from the fallen ruins of the ancient Pharos.
choices: Salvaged from the fallen ruins of the ancient Pharos.
Shipped up the Nile from the Aswan quarries.
Hauled across the sea from the isle of Cyprus.
Cut fresh from the cliffs of the western desert.
context: Earthquakes in AD 956, 1303, and 1323 brought the Pharos down; around 1477-1480 Sultan Qaitbay reused its fallen stones to raise Fort Qaitbay on the exact spot, and the fort still stands there today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria; britannica.com 'Lighthouse of Alexandria'.

question: Alexandria's hunger for scrolls turned ruthless: by royal decree, every ship that docked in the harbor was searched, and any books aboard were carried up to the Library, where scribes copied them out by hand. Once the scribes finished, what did the Library do with the borrowed scrolls?
answer: It kept the original scrolls and gave owners the copies.
choices: It kept the original scrolls and gave owners the copies.
It kept the copies and gave owners the original scrolls.
It kept both versions and paid the owners in silver.
It kept neither, returning every scroll untouched.
context: These were catalogued as 'books of the ships'; the Library kept the originals and gave owners the copies. Its great book-collecting rival was the Library of Pergamon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria (citing Galen).

question: Beneath the streets of modern Alexandria wind the Catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa, Roman-era burial halls cut deep into the rock and then lost and forgotten for more than a thousand years. In 1900 they were stumbled upon entirely by accident. How were the catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa found again?
answer: A donkey fell through the ground into the shaft.
choices: A donkey fell through the ground into the shaft.
A well-digger's bucket dropped into the void.
A flood tore open a long-sealed doorway.
A farmer's plough snagged on a buried statue.
context: Inside, three cultures meet in one carved tomb: the Egyptian god Anubis stands in Roman legionary armor, a wall shows the Greek myth of Persephone's abduction, and statues wear Egyptian poses in Roman dress. 'Kom el Shoqafa' means 'Mound of Shards,' after the broken feast-pottery mourners left behind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Kom_El_Shoqafa.

question: Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, chief scholar of Alexandria's great Library, learned that at noon on the longest day of the year the sun shone straight down a deep well at Syene, far to the south, throwing no shadow at all, yet at that same moment in Alexandria an upright pole DID cast a short shadow. From nothing but that difference in shadows and the distance between the two cities, Eratosthenes worked out a single number and got it right to within about 1 percent. What did Eratosthenes measure?
answer: The distance around the whole Earth.
choices: The distance around the whole Earth.
The distance from the Earth to the sun.
The width of the Moon's grey disc.
The height of the dome of the sky.
context: The Alexandria shadow measured about 7.2 degrees, exactly 1/50 of a circle; multiplying the Syene-to-Alexandria distance by 50 gave Earth's circumference within roughly 1% of the true value. Jealous rivals nicknamed the brilliant Eratosthenes 'Beta,' the second letter, sneering that he was second-best at everything. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eratosthenes.

question: In the Punjab city of Amritsar, the shrine of Harmandir Sahib sits on a small island in the middle of a vast square pool. Rich or poor, every pilgrim reaches it the very same way. What forms the single link between the shore and the island shrine?
context: The one crossing is the marble Guru's Bridge (Guru da Pul), about 202 feet long and 21 feet wide, the sole way in and out, so the shrine seems to float alone on the water. Source: SGPC (sgpc.net/sri-harmandir-sahib); Wikipedia (Golden Temple).

question: At dawn in Amritsar, the great pool around the Harmandir Sahib blazes as though the water itself had caught fire, a spreading sheet of molten light. What gives the shrine's reflection this burning glow at sunrise?
answer: its dome and towers are covered in real gold
choices: its dome and towers are covered in real gold
its walls are faced with polished brass
its roof is laid with sheets of copper
its surface is coated in gold-colored paint
context: Maharaja Ranjit Singh had the sanctum overlaid, marble and copper around 1809, then gilded with roughly 400 kg of gold leaf about 1830. The low sun strikes that gold and pours its fire down into the pool, the Amrit Sarovar, below. Source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple); Incredible India (Sri Harmandir Sahib).

question: At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, pilgrims from every land wade down the steps into the great square tank at dawn and cup the water to their lips. They come not merely to wash, but because of what this particular water is held to be. What do the faithful believe the pool holds?
answer: nectar that heals body and soul
choices: nectar that heals body and soul
the tears of a grieving saint
context: The pool is the Amrit Sarovar, 'amrit' meaning nectar and 'sar' a pool, and the city of Amritsar takes its very name from it. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru, had the great tank completed around 1577; its water is revered as amrit, nectar believed to heal body and soul. Source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple / Amrit Sarovar).  (Legend.)

question: In Guru Arjan's day the great temples and mosques of India rose high above the streets, their worshippers climbing long flights of steps up to the holy place. At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the fifth Sikh Guru built the very opposite: he set the shrine's entrance below the surrounding ground, so that everyone walks down a flight of steps to go in. What did Guru Arjan intend this downward entrance to teach the pilgrim?
answer: that God is found with the humble, not the proud
choices: that God is found with the humble, not the proud
that all who enter shed their rank at the door
that the shrine must bow before its sacred pool
that the way to God sinks low before it climbs
context: Guru Arjan also gave the Harmandir Sahib a door on each of its four sides, open to every caste and faith, from every direction, while other shrines faced only one way. Asked why he built low when others built high, he is remembered as replying that God is found with the humble, those who bow, and not with the proud. Source: sikhism.net.in (Golden Temple); SGPC (sri-harmandir-sahib).

question: Beside the Golden Temple in Amritsar stands a vast dining hall, the langar, that feeds around 100,000 people a day, for free, and to anyone at all, of any faith or caste, prince or pauper. To make plain that all who eat there are equals, the langar keeps one firm rule at every meal. What is that rule?
answer: everyone sits together on the floor to eat
choices: everyone sits together on the floor to eat
everyone eats standing, in a single line
context: The langar (Guru Ka Langar) is called the world's largest free kitchen: around 50,000 meals on an ordinary day, well over 100,000 on festivals, cooked by roughly 500 volunteer sevadaars working nearly around the clock, about 12,000 kg of flour and 13,000 kg of lentils daily, with a machine turning out some 200,000 rotis. All sit on the floor as equals, so that no one who comes to the Guru's door is turned away hungry. Source: The National (2023); goldentempleamritsar.org (langar).

question: Venice wears the world's crown as the city of canals and bridges — yet Amsterdam quietly outdoes it. Amsterdam's centre is sliced by 100-plus kilometres of water into some 90 islands, and to knit them into one walkable town it is crossed by more bridges than Venice — more than almost any city in Europe. Roughly how many bridges span its canals?
context: Over 1,200 bridges span Amsterdam's 100-plus kilometres of canals, linking its roughly 90 islands — a denser web of bridges than Venice itself. The showpiece is the 17th-century 'canal ring' (grachtengordel) around the old core, dug in planned phases and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — Geography; Canals of Amsterdam / grachtengordel; UNESCO WHC 1349).

question: Around the year 1270, fishermen settled at the boggy mouth of a small tidal river called the Amstel, but the North Sea kept surging up the river and drowning the marsh they meant to farm. To shut the tide out, they threw a single great water-work clean across the river's mouth, and the town that grew behind it swelled into a mighty city. What kind of water-work was it?
context: Here is the delight the question kept back: 'Amstel-dam' — a dam across the little River Amstel — is exactly what the name 'Amsterdam' records. Historians date the dam to about 1264–1275, and Amsterdam first appears in an official record in 1275. Dam Square, the busy plaza at the city's heart, still stands on the spot where that first dam held back the tide. Source: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — Etymology/History; Dam Square).

question: The Royal Palace of Amsterdam is a giant of solid sandstone, yet it stands on ground so soft — soaked peat and clay — that by rights it should sink slowly into the mud. It hasn't, because the builders first drove 13,659 tall poles straight down through the muck to a firm bed of sand far below, then stood the whole palace on their tops. What, exactly, are those 13,659 poles?
context: The 13,659 piles are whole softwood tree trunks — fir and spruce shipped from Scandinavia — driven about 12 metres down to the first firm layer of sand beneath the peat. A mountain of stone floating on a buried forest: the poet Constantijn Huygens called the building 'the world's Eighth Wonder.' It opened in 1655 as Amsterdam's city hall and became a royal palace only in 1808. Sources: Wikipedia (Royal Palace of Amsterdam — 13,659 wooden piles); dutchamsterdam.nl.

question: Parts of Amsterdam and vast stretches of the Netherlands lie BELOW the level of the sea, so water constantly seeps up into the fields and streets and must be lifted out and flung over the dikes — a task that never ends. For hundreds of years, long before electric pumps, the Dutch did this endless lifting with tens of thousands of one kind of machine. Which machines pumped the Netherlands dry?
context: The classic Dutch windmill was often a water pump, not a flour mill: its sails turned an Archimedes' screw or scoop-wheel that lifted seepage up and over the dikes, tirelessly. Electric and diesel pumping stations later took over the job. Much of Amsterdam's centre sits about 2 metres below sea level, kept dry only by this constant pumping. Sources: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — elevation about −2 m below sea level; polders); incredibleamsterdam.com.

question: After a devastating flood in 1675, Amsterdam's mayor Johannes Hudde ordered careful water-level readings that hardened into a single fixed zero mark — the reference point from which the height of land above or below the sea is measured. Called the 'Amsterdam Ordnance Datum,' or NAP, this one city's flood benchmark became the official 'zero height' for how large an area?
context: Mayor Johannes Hudde's benchmark grew into the NAP (Normaal Amsterdams Peil), which became the reference 'zero' for elevation across much of Western Europe — so a mountain's height in several countries is still measured up from a mark first set in flood-prone Amsterdam. Source: Wikipedia (Normaal Amsterdams Peil; Amsterdam — polders).

question: Along Amsterdam's canals, the tall, narrow brick houses famously lean — and much of that leaning was done on purpose. Many were built tilting FORWARD, their top edge jutting out over the water beyond the base, a style the Dutch call 'op de vlucht.' Why did their builders purposely tip the whole front wall out over the canal?
answer: so goods hoisted up the front wouldn't scrape the wall
choices: so goods hoisted up the front wouldn't scrape the wall
so rain would run off the front instead of the windows
so the top-floor rooms would catch more sun
so the tall house would look grander from below
context: Because the staircases were too tight for big furniture, Amsterdammers hauled loads up the OUTSIDE, using a hoisting hook and beam — the hijsbalk — still seen at the top of many gables; the forward tilt kept the swinging load from scraping the facade. Not every lean is intentional, though: houses that tilt SIDEWAYS, leaning unevenly into their neighbours, are usually truly sinking — their wooden piles have begun to rot where a falling groundwater level let air reach the wood. Sources: expatica.com, dutchreview.com (Amsterdam canal houses); amsterdamian.com (hijsbalk); commonedge.org (rotting piles).

question: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall on Earth: a 979-metre drop, over half a mile of it a single unbroken free fall off a sheer cliff. The plunge is so long that, in the dry season, the falling water does something astonishing on the way down. What?
answer: it breaks apart into a drifting mist and blows away
choices: it breaks apart into a drifting mist and blows away
it freezes into a hanging sheet of ice
it splits into a braid of smaller streams
it doubles back and sprays upward in the wind
context: Angel Falls is the tallest waterfall on Earth: 979 m in all, with a single uninterrupted plunge of 807 m, more than half a mile of free fall. The drop is so vast that much of the water vaporizes into mist and swirls away in the turbulent air, especially in the dry season, before it ever reaches the valley floor. Source: geology.com highest-waterfall; simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: Angel Falls doesn't spill from between hills — it pours straight off the sheer vertical edge of a flat-topped mountain that rises like a giant stone table out of the Venezuelan rainforest, walled off from the world by cliffs on every side. The Pemón call these sky-islands the 'houses of the gods.' What do geographers call such a steep-sided table mountain?
context: The mountain is Auyán-tepui, and 'tepui' is the Pemón word for these sheer-sided table mountains — the 'houses of the gods.' Their flat summits are marooned islands in the sky, cut off by cliffs on every side, in Canaima National Park, Bolívar State, Venezuela. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls; Slate/Atlas Obscura on the tepuis.

question: At the foot of Angel Falls, the water gathers into the small Churún River, which flows on into the wider Carrao. In the end these streams carry the great waterfall's water into one of South America's mightiest rivers. Which one?
context: Angel Falls drops from Auyán-tepui in Canaima National Park; the water that survives the plunge flows out as the Churún, into the Carrao, and finally into the mighty Orinoco — not the Amazon, whose basin lies to the south. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: The Pemón people have lived below Angel Falls for centuries, and never called it 'Angel Falls.' In 2009 Venezuela's government officially adopted their own name for it, Kerepakupai Merú. What does that Pemón name mean?
answer: the waterfall of the deepest place
choices: the waterfall of the deepest place
context: The Pemón name Kerepakupai Merú (also rendered Parakupá Vená) means 'waterfall of the deepest place.' Venezuela formally adopted the Pemón name in 2009, after President Hugo Chávez championed it. The English name honors bush pilot Jimmie Angel, who made the falls famous abroad — but the Pemón had always known them; he did not 'discover' them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls; simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: Angel Falls carries the name of Jimmie Angel, an American bush pilot who first flew over it in 1933 while hunting a rumored bed of gold. In 1937 Angel tried to land his little plane right on the mountain's flat summit — but the wheels sank into the boggy ground and stuck fast, and he and his companions had to climb back down the cliffs on foot. What became of the plane he left behind?
answer: it stayed stranded on the summit for 33 years
choices: it stayed stranded on the summit for 33 years
it was hauled down for scrap within a year
it slid over the cliff edge in the next storm
it was carried off piece by piece by looters
context: Angel's plane, named 'El Río Caroní,' sat marooned on the summit of Auyán-tepui for 33 years. In 1970 the Venezuelan Air Force lifted it off in sections by helicopter; it was restored and is now displayed at the airport in Ciudad Bolívar. Angel's climb down after the crash took 11 days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls; jimmieangel.org 'Operation Auyantepui 1970'; countryreports.org.

question: Venezuela's flat-topped table mountains are so cut off — sheer cliffs on every side, sealing strange plants and creatures on their summits like islands in the sky — that in 1912 the writer Arthur Conan Doyle, famous for Sherlock Holmes, dreamed up a remote plateau where prehistoric monsters still survived. What novel did he set on such a mountaintop?
context: Doyle drew on explorers' accounts of Mount Roraima, a neighboring tepui with its own sheer walls and marooned summit life. His 1912 novel 'The Lost World' — in which dinosaurs still survive atop a remote plateau — helped launch the whole 'lost world' genre of adventure fiction. Source: Slate/Atlas Obscura, 'Mount Roraima inspired The Lost World.'

question: Scattered across southern Venezuela stand dozens of sheer-walled table mountains, flat tops standing high and lonely above the rainforest, built of some of the oldest rock exposed anywhere on Earth. How do geologists explain these isolated flat-topped giants?
answer: erosion wore away a vast highland, leaving these hard stumps
choices: erosion wore away a vast highland, leaving these hard stumps
lava flows piled up and cooled into flat sheets
an ancient seabed was thrust up and planed flat
desert sand dunes hardened and were lifted high
context: The tepuis are the eroded stumps of a once-continuous sandstone plateau. Their layered quartzite and sandstone — the Roraima Supergroup, roughly 1.7-1.9 billion years old — sit on the Precambrian Guiana Shield, among the oldest exposed rock on Earth. Source: geologyscience.com on Roraima geology; Grokipedia Auyán-tepui (Roraima Supergroup ~1.87 Ga).

question: Cambodia's national flag is unique among all the world's flags — it is the only one that pictures a building. At its center rise the five stone towers of a single, world-famous temple. Which temple is pictured on the flag of Cambodia?
context: The five lotus-bud towers on the flag are the silhouette of Angkor Wat, the vast Khmer temple on the plain north of Siem Reap. It has appeared on Cambodian flags since 1863, and no other nation's flag depicts a building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

question: Angkor Wat spreads its moat, walls and towers across about 400 acres — roughly 160 hectares — all as a single unbroken complex, so vast that Guinness World Records gives it an official world title. Which title does Angkor Wat hold?
answer: the largest religious monument in the world
choices: the largest religious monument in the world
the largest building in the world
the largest fortress in the world
the largest palace in the world
context: Guinness lists Angkor Wat as the largest religious structure on Earth — note the word 'religious': it is not the largest building overall, but no house of worship anywhere covers more ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

question: Almost every temple at Angkor was cleared of jungle and rebuilt stone by stone. Ta Prohm looks utterly different: giant strangler figs still pour over its walls, their pale roots swallowing the doorways and cracking the sandstone. Why does Ta Prohm alone remain locked in the grip of the forest?
answer: restorers chose to leave it as they found it
choices: restorers chose to leave it as they found it
its stone is too soft to cut the roots from
villagers guard its trees as sacred
it lies too deep in the jungle to reach
context: Unlike its neighbors, Ta Prohm was deliberately never cleared: 20th-century restorers left it as explorers had found it, its walls still locked in the roots of towering strangler figs, so visitors could see a temple exactly as the jungle had reclaimed it. A bird drops a fig's seed high in a host tree's canopy; the seedling sends roots down the trunk until it engulfs the stone — holding Ta Prohm's walls together and prying them apart at once. The 2001 film shot among the roots earned it the nickname the 'Tomb Raider temple.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: The five great towers of Angkor Wat were not arranged by accident: the Khmer raised them as a stone model of a sacred five-peaked mountain, the mythical home of the gods, while the broad moat stands for the cosmic ocean that rings that mountain. Which mythical mountain does Angkor Wat's five-towered shape represent?
context: In Hindu and Buddhist cosmology, Mount Meru is the five-peaked mountain at the center of the universe and the home of the gods. Angkor Wat is a 'temple-mountain' — its towers are Meru's peaks, its moat the surrounding ocean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

question: Nearly every temple the Khmer ever built opens toward the east, to greet the rising sun. Angkor Wat is the great exception: its main gateway faces the opposite way, toward the west and the setting sun. Scholars such as George Coedes read this reversal as a clue that King Suryavarman II meant his temple to serve a second purpose besides worship. What second purpose does the westward orientation suggest?
context: This is a scholarly interpretation, not settled fact: George Coedes and Maurice Glaize argued that the west-facing gate — west being the direction of the setting sun and, in Hindu tradition, the dead — points to Angkor Wat doubling as the funerary temple of Suryavarman II, who commissioned it around 1113-1150 CE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat  (Legend.)

question: At the very center of the walled city of Angkor Thom rises the Bayon, a temple built from dozens of stone towers. Its towers bear about 200 giant, identical carvings, the same one repeated over and over. What is carved, some 200 times over, across the towers of the Bayon?
context: The Bayon's roughly 200 huge, serene, faintly smiling faces are thought to portray the compassionate bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara — or King Jayavarman VII himself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon

question: Banteay Srei is a miniature jewel-box temple built of deep pink-red sandstone, and its carvings are the finest at Angkor — so crisp, deep and delicate that they seem impossible to cut in hard stone by hand. Uniquely among the great Angkor temples, no king built it; a royal advisor did. What does its Khmer name, 'Banteay Srei,' mean?
context: Consecrated in 967 CE and built by the courtier Yajnavaraha rather than a king, Banteay Srei ('Citadel of the Women') is famed for carving so fine it is compared to goldsmith's work or woodcarving. In 1923 the future French writer Andre Malraux was arrested for stealing statues from it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banteay_Srei

question: A stone inscription still standing at Ta Prohm records, in careful detail, how many people were assigned just to serve and supply this one temple-monastery — the priests, dancers, cooks and laborers who kept it running. The figure is staggering for a single temple. Roughly how many people?
context: King Jayavarman VII founded Ta Prohm as a Buddhist monastery (originally Rajavihara, 'Royal Monastery') by its stele of 1186 CE; the inscription lists nearly 80,000 people attached to it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Along Angkor Wat's eastern gallery runs a carved scene about 49 metres long — the largest stone version of this Hindu myth found anywhere on Earth. In it, a long row of gods and a long row of demons grip a giant serpent and haul it back and forth, spinning the Sea of Milk like a butter churn. In the myth, what magical prize were they struggling to churn up from the ocean?
choices: the first rays of the sun
context: The 'Churning of the Sea of Milk' (Samudra Manthan): gods and demons use the serpent Vasuki as a rope to spin Mount Mandara and churn the ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality. Angkor Wat's is the largest carved telling in the world. Source: https://www.wmf.org/news/churning-sea-milk-gallery-angkor-cambodia  (Legend.)

question: The Khmer turned Angkor into a hydraulic city. To survive the long dry season, they hand-dug colossal rectangular reservoirs — the greatest about 8 kilometres long — to hoard the monsoon rains and feed water to their rice fields for months on end. What is such a giant Khmer reservoir called?
context: The West Baray, about 7.8 km by 2.1 km, is one of the largest hand-dug reservoirs on Earth, with a small island temple — the West Mebon — at its center. Barays stored monsoon water to irrigate rice through the dry months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Baray

question: For centuries people pictured Angkor as a lost scatter of temples drowned in jungle. Then archaeologists flew planes over the forest firing millions of laser pulses at the ground and timing each echo to map the surface hidden beneath the tree canopy — a technique called LiDAR. Stripped of its trees, the map revealed what Angkor truly had been. What did the LiDAR survey show Angkor to be?
answer: the largest city of the pre-industrial world
choices: the largest city of the pre-industrial world
the oldest walled city in all of Asia
a chain of forts guarding a gold route
a ring of tombs around a sacred lake
context: LiDAR fires laser pulses from a plane and times their return to map ground hidden under vegetation. The 2013 surveys revealed not a lone temple but a planned grid of roads, canals and neighborhoods stretching for miles — the largest city of the entire pre-industrial world. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1306539110

question: Angkor grew into a sprawling megacity of perhaps 700,000 people — then, across the 1300s and 1400s, it slowly emptied until the jungle swallowed it. Reading the growth rings of ancient trees, scientists traced its fall to the breakdown of the one vast engineered system that Angkor, unlike any other medieval city, had been built entirely around. Which of Angkor's systems failed, bringing the megacity down?
context: Angkor was a 'hydraulic city' utterly dependent on its canals and reservoirs. Tree-ring evidence shows severe droughts and destructive floods in the 14th-15th centuries, as the climate shifted toward the Little Ice Age, wrecking the water network and forcing the city's gradual abandonment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor

question: At the exact center of Angkor Thom, the walled capital of the Khmer Empire, stands the temple called the Bayon: a mountain of more than fifty stone towers packed close together. One feature is carved onto those towers over two hundred times, each turned toward a different point of the compass, and it is the sight that made the Bayon world-famous. What is carved, again and again, across the Bayon's towers?
context: These are the famous smiling faces of the Bayon, nicknamed 'the smile of Angkor.' More than 200 survive on the roughly three dozen towers still standing (sources disagree on the original tower count, citing about 49, 54, or 59). When the French writer Pierre Loti reached the temple the faces unnerved him: 'all of a sudden my blood curdled as I saw an enormous smile looking down on me... then three, then five, then ten, appearing in every direction.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon; smarthistory.org/bayon-temple-angkor-thom; cambodgemag.com (quoting Pierre Loti, 'Un pelerin d'Angkor').

question: Most temple walls of the ancient world show gods, kings, and great battles. But the lower galleries of the Bayon are covered instead with the everyday life of the Khmer people: cooks at open-air fires, hunters, a woman giving birth, even people picking lice from one another's hair. One crowded scene shows a ring of men leaning in, shouting and placing bets. What contest are they gambling on?
context: The Bayon's outer galleries are famous for carving daily life rather than only gods: a market with women selling fish, a game of chess, and bookies taking bets at a cockfight. They are one of the richest windows we have into how ordinary people actually lived in the medieval Khmer Empire. Sources: factsanddetails.com/southeast-asia/Cambodia (Bayon reliefs); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon.

question: No one can say for certain whom the Bayon's giant faces portray. Many scholars read them as a single holy being repeated hundreds of times across the towers; others believe they are the face of the god-king Jayavarman VII himself, gazing out over every corner of his realm, and some say they are both at once. Which Buddhist figure do scholars most often see in the serene, smiling faces?
choices: Maitreya, the Buddha yet to come
context: The faces are usually identified with Avalokiteshvara (Lokeshvara), the Mahayana bodhisattva of compassion, but because there is no clear inscription, scholars still debate whether they also portray Jayavarman VII as a god-king, his face broadcast in every direction. The Bayon was the last great state temple built at Angkor, and Jayavarman VII made it Mahayana Buddhist, where Angkor Wat had begun as a Hindu temple. Sources: smarthistory.org/bayon-temple-angkor-thom; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon.

question: The five great gate-towers into Angkor Thom rise nearly 23 m above the moat, and at the foot of each one, on either side of the passage, a huge stone beast rears up with a god riding on its back, its head lowered toward a pool of lotus blossoms. Which of the gods' mounts stands watch over the gateways of the city?
context: The beast is Airavata, the three-headed elephant of the god Indra, its trunks reaching down to pluck lotus flowers while Indra rides on its back. Each of the five gates rises about 23 m and is crowned with four faces pointed to the cardinal directions, so the whole 9-square-km walled city is watched over from its edges inward. Sources: helloangkor.com (Angkor Thom gates); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Thom.

question: Not every carving at the Bayon is myth. One of its longest panels records a real war: fleets of crowded war-canoes ramming one another, warriors pitching overboard into water thick with fish and crocodiles, and a victory feast carved beneath the fighting. On which body of water did the Khmer fight this great naval battle?
context: The battle is the Khmers' war against the Chams (from the kingdom of Champa, in what is now central Vietnam), fought on the Tonle Sap, the vast lake at the heart of Cambodia. The Cham warriors can be picked out by their distinctive head coverings. The Bayon carves this real history on the same walls as its gods and myths. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon; lonelyplanet.com (Bayon).

question: To reach the gates of Angkor Thom you cross a causeway over the moat, and it is lined with two long rows of stone giants: gods on one side, demons on the other, each row gripping the body of an enormous serpent and leaning back as if in a colossal tug-of-war. The whole bridge is built to retell one famous Hindu myth. Which story is frozen into the causeway?
answer: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
choices: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
the Descent of the River Ganges
the Burning of the Three Cities
the Rescue of Sita from Lanka
context: In the myth, the gods and demons wrap the serpent Vasuki around a mountain and churn the Ocean of Milk together to produce amrita, the elixir of immortality, which is why they are frozen mid-heave on the bridge. There are 54 gods on one side and 54 demons on the other, 108 figures in all. You can tell them apart by their faces: the gods have calm oval faces, the demons bulging round eyes and grimacing scowls. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Thom; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samudra_manthan.  (Legend.)

question: The largest religious monument on Earth, Angkor Wat lifts five stone towers above the Cambodian jungle. The towers were arranged to model one sacred mountain -- the peak that Hindu myth calls the home of the gods and the fixed center of the whole universe. Which sacred mountain do Angkor Wat's towers picture?
context: Mount Meru is the golden world-mountain at the heart of Hindu and Buddhist cosmology, imagined as the axis of the universe ringed by seas and continents. Angkor Wat's five towers rise in a quincunx -- four around one taller central peak -- turning the whole temple into a stone model of the cosmos with Meru at its center. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (five towers in quincunx modelling Mount Meru); worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat.  (Legend.)

question: The white silhouette of Angkor Wat has ridden on Cambodia's flag since 1863, staying there through kingdom, republic, and revolution alike. On the flag itself, where does the temple sit?
context: Angkor Wat sits at the very center of Cambodia's national flag -- a white temple silhouette on a broad red band -- and has appeared on Cambodian flags since 1863. Buildings turn up on a handful of the world's flags, but Cambodia is the only nation to place one at its flag's center, an honor no other monument on Earth holds. The temple stayed at the heart of Cambodian identity even as the empire that raised it faded into the jungle. Source: britannica.com/topic/flag-of-Cambodia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Cambodia (Angkor Wat central on Cambodia's flag, on Khmer flags since 1863).

question: A moat 190 metres wide and more than five kilometres around encircles Angkor Wat. It helped defend the temple -- but on Angkor Wat's stone map of the Hindu universe, this great ring of water was built to stand for something far vaster at the rim of the world. What does the moat of Angkor Wat represent?
context: In Hindu cosmology Mount Meru stands at the center of creation, surrounded by a vast cosmic ocean. Angkor Wat's builders recreated that image: the central towers are Meru and the broad moat is the primordial ocean encircling it. The moat is about 190 m wide and over 5 km around. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (moat 190 m wide, ~5 km perimeter, representing the cosmic ocean around Meru).

question: Most of Angkor's temples were swallowed by the jungle after the empire faded -- split apart by strangler-fig roots and left in ruins -- yet Angkor Wat itself stayed nearly whole. Historians credit one community that never left, keeping up their worship inside its walls without a break for some 800 years. Who kept Angkor Wat alive?
context: After the Khmer court shifted toward Phnom Penh in the 1400s, Angkor's other temples were abandoned to the forest, but Theravada Buddhist monks kept living and worshipping at Angkor Wat unbroken for roughly 800 years. That continuous care is a key reason the temple survived far more intact than its neighbours. Source: worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat (continuous Buddhist worship preserved the temple).

question: Along a 49-metre gallery in Angkor Wat runs one of the most famous carvings in all of Asia: 88 gods grip the head of a giant serpent while 92 demons haul on its tail, the two lines straining against each other in a colossal tug-of-war with the snake stretched between them like a living rope. Which Hindu myth is carved here?
answer: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
choices: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
the Descent of the River Ganges
the Burning of the Three Cities
the Slaying of the Buffalo Demon
context: This is the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan). To win amrita, the nectar of immortality, gods (devas) and demons (asuras) churn the cosmic sea, using the serpent Vasuki as their rope wound around Mount Mandara. Angkor Wat's relief shows 88 devas and 92 asuras -- and in the story, the moment they succeed they fall to fighting over the prize. Source: penang-traveltips.com (49 m relief, 88 devas / 92 asuras); britannica.com/topic/churning-of-the-ocean-of-milk.  (Legend.)

question: Almost every Khmer temple opens toward the sunrise, but Angkor Wat alone faces west -- and its long wall-carvings are meant to be read counter-clockwise, the reverse of the usual order. These two unusual choices have led most scholars to favour a single purpose for the temple. What was Angkor Wat most likely built to be?
context: West is the direction of the setting sun and, in Hindu belief, of death and the god Yama. Angkor Wat's westward orientation and its counter-clockwise (prasavya) reliefs -- the reverse of the auspicious order -- lead many scholars to conclude that Suryavarman II built it as his own funerary temple and mausoleum. He was known after death as Paramavishnuloka, 'he who has gone to the supreme world of Vishnu.' Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Angkor_Wat (west = death, funerary temple, prasavya reliefs).  (Legend.)

question: In Angkor Wat's great carving of the gods and demons churning the sea, the mountain they are spinning as a churning-rod begins to sink into the ocean, threatening to ruin everything. To rescue it, the god Vishnu plunges beneath the waves and takes the shape of a giant animal that bears the mountain up from the depths. Into what creature does Vishnu transform?
context: The turtle is Kurma, the second avatar of Vishnu. As the churning drags Mount Mandara down into the Ocean of Milk, Vishnu becomes the great turtle Kurma and supports the mountain on his shell from the sea-floor; at the very center of Angkor Wat's relief he appears again in human form, steadying it. Source: penang-traveltips.com (Vishnu's turtle avatar Kurma supporting Mount Mandara).  (Legend.)

question: Angkor Wat was raised from as many as ten million blocks of sandstone, some weighing a tonne and a half apiece. No stone like it lies near the temple, so the Khmer quarried every block from a single holy mountain about 50 kilometres away and floated them to the site along a network of canals. From which mountain did all that sandstone come?
context: The sandstone came from Phnom Kulen (Mount Kulen), a plateau some 40-50 km to the northeast that the Khmer revered as the birthplace of their empire. Workers cut 5-10 million blocks and floated them to Angkor along purpose-built canals -- one of the great logistical feats of the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (Kulen sandstone, 5-10 million blocks up to 1.5 t, canal transport).

question: Angkor sat in a land of drenching monsoons and long dry seasons, so its engineers stored water on a titanic scale. Their largest hand-dug reservoir still holds water 900 years on -- a rectangle of water 7.8 kilometres long, one of the biggest reservoirs ever cut by hand. What is this giant Khmer reservoir called?
context: This is the West Baray, a man-made reservoir about 7.8 by 2.1 km and part of Angkor's immense water grid of canals, moats and embankments spread over roughly 1,000 sq km. Reservoirs like it caught the monsoon rains to irrigate rice and supply a city of hundreds of thousands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Baray (7.8 x 2.1 km, one of the largest hand-cut reservoirs on Earth).

question: For centuries only Angkor's stone temples rose above the trees; the wooden city that once surrounded them had rotted away, so no one knew how large Angkor had truly been. Then in 2012 archaeologists mounted an instrument beneath a helicopter and flew a tight grid over the jungle, mapping the ground surface hidden beneath the canopy. Their survey exposed a lost metropolis of roughly 1,000 sq km -- among the largest cities of the pre-industrial world. What technology finally revealed the true extent of Angkor?
context: The tool was LIDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), which fires laser pulses from the air and times their reflection to build a 3-D map of the bare ground beneath vegetation. In 2012 Damian Evans's Greater Angkor Project scanned the region in about 20 hours of flying, revealing a low-density city of an estimated 750,000-900,000 people across ~1,000 sq km. Source: sydney.edu.au (Damian Evans, Greater Angkor Project, LIDAR); pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1306539110.

question: Angkor's population of nearly a million depended entirely on a colossal grid of reservoirs and canals to carry them through the long months between monsoons. When scientists read the growth rings of Angkor's ancient cypress trees, they found the 1300s and 1400s brought violent, decades-long swings of climate the water network could not survive. Which climate disaster do those tree rings blame most for Angkor's fall?
context: Tree-ring studies of old cypress trees revealed two prolonged megadroughts in the mid-1300s and early 1400s, broken by unusually fierce monsoons. The droughts starved Angkor's reservoirs while the violent rains that followed choked its canals with debris -- damage the vast water system never recovered from, hastening the city's decline as the court moved toward Phnom Penh. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1111282109; livescience.com/17702 (megadrought and Angkor's collapse).

question: One place on Earth is so relentlessly windy that its yearly AVERAGE wind speed -- not the rare gust, the everyday average -- is already a gale of about 80 km/h, and its blizzards have torn past 240 km/h. Guinness World Records calls it the windiest place on the planet. Which place is it?
context: Commonwealth Bay, on the coast of East Antarctica -- and Cape Denison on its shore, where Douglas Mawson built his hut -- is listed by Guinness World Records and the National Geographic Atlas as the windiest place at sea level on Earth. The cause isn't a passing storm: freezing air pours off the high inland ice sheet and funnels down to this exact stretch of coast almost without pause, so the yearly AVERAGE wind speed is already a gale. Death Valley is the hottest place, the Atacama the driest non-polar desert, and Vostok the coldest -- each holds a different record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Bay

question: At Cape Denison the wind almost never rests. Freezing, dense air pools on the high inland ice sheet, then slides seaward under its own weight, funnelling and accelerating as it drops toward the coast. Meteorologists have a special name for this kind of cold wind pouring off the ice. What is it called?
context: The word comes from the Greek katabatikos, 'going down.' Cold air is heavy, so where it collects on a high ice plateau it acts like an invisible flood -- spilling downhill under gravity and gathering speed, funnelled faster as the land narrows toward the coast. Chinook winds also blow downslope but WARM as they fall; trade winds and monsoons are driven by heat and the planet's rotation, not by cold air draining off ice. Antarctica's katabatic winds are the fiercest on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Bay

question: In 1912 Douglas Mawson and his Australasian Antarctic Expedition wintered in a hut at Cape Denison, on what turned out to be the windiest coast on Earth. When Mawson later wrote the story of those brutal years, he gave the book a title that has clung to the place ever since. What did he call it?
choices: The Worst Journey in the World
context: Mawson published The Home of the Blizzard in 1915, and the name stuck to Cape Denison. His Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911-14 had pitched camp, without knowing it, on the windiest coast on Earth. The other choices are real polar memoirs too: The Heart of the Antarctic (Ernest Shackleton), The Great White South (photographer Herbert Ponting), and The Worst Journey in the World (Apsley Cherry-Garrard). Source: antarctica.gov.au -- 'Home of the Blizzard' book

question: High on the frozen East Antarctic plateau, far from any coast, one lonely research station logged -89.2 C (-128.6 F) on 21 July 1983 -- the coldest air temperature ever recorded at a weather station anywhere on Earth. Which station holds that record?
context: Vostok Station, a Russian base, sits about 3,488 m (11,444 ft) up on the East Antarctic ice sheet, roughly 1,300 km from the South Pole -- the great height and the distance from any warming ocean are why the air there turns so brutally cold. One careful detail: -89.2 C is the coldest AIR temperature ever measured at a weather station. Satellites later spotted even colder ICE-SURFACE patches on the plateau (about -94.7 C in 2010), but those are surface readings, not official air records, so both facts stay true. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_Station

question: Two miles down through the East Antarctic ice sheet, drills reached a shock: a liquid freshwater lake about 250 km long and 50 km wide, sealed away from sunlight for roughly 15 million years -- the largest of some 675 lakes now known to hide beneath the continent's ice. What is this buried lake called?
