context: Bryggen -- literally 'the wharf' -- is Bergen's old Hanseatic quarter, and its leaning colorful gables are the emblem of the city, drawing visitors to Vagen bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryggen ; grokipedia.com/page/Bergen

question: Behind the colorful gables of Bergen's Bryggen wharf, foreign merchants ran a walled trading post for some four centuries, holding a tight grip on Norway's most valuable export -- the dried cod called stockfish. Which merchant power controlled this wharf?
context: German merchants of the Hanseatic League held their Bergen privileges from the mid-1300s until 1754, trading grain and goods for the stockfish that fed much of Catholic Europe on fast days. Their walled post was called a Kontor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bergen ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryggen

question: From Bergen's harbor, boats set out into Norway's grandest scenery: immense arms of the sea reaching up to 200 km inland between vertical rock walls, with Sognefjord running deeper than the ocean just offshore. Bergen is famed as the gateway to these dramatic inlets. What is this kind of deep coastal sea inlet called?
context: Fjords are valleys that Ice-Age glaciers gouged far below sea level; when the ice melted, the sea flooded in. Sognefjord is the world's longest and deepest at 1,308 m. Sitting between it and Hardangerfjord, Bergen is Norway's 'gateway to the fjords.' Source: en.visitbergen.com/about-bergen/facts-about-bergen ; grokipedia.com/page/Bergen

question: In Bergen, rain falls on roughly 230 to 240 days out of every year -- so relentlessly that locals joke a true Bergener never bothers with an umbrella, just flips up a hood and waits the shower out. This soaking earns Bergen which title?
choices: the rainiest city in the Alps
context: Bergen gets about 2,250 mm of rain a year across some 240 wet days -- widely reckoned the rainiest in Europe, though the world's crown belongs to Mawsynram in India. The umbrella joke is genuine local lore. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bergen ; WebSearch (visitbergen, Forbes / David Nikel)

question: Bergen sits in a bowl ringed by mountains, and the 18th-century playwright Ludvig Holberg fixed its fond nickname, 'the city of seven mountains.' He chose seven on purpose, to make his rainy home echo a far grander city celebrated for its seven hills. Which city was Bergen made to imitate?
context: Ludvig Holberg -- Bergen-born and a leading writer of the Dano-Norwegian Enlightenment -- modeled the nickname on Rome, the classical 'city of seven hills.' To this day Bergeners cheerfully argue over exactly which seven of their peaks should count. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen ; planetware.com  (Legend.)

question: Bergen's endless rain has a cause you can see on the skyline: moist Atlantic winds sweep in off the sea, slam into the city's ring of mountains, are forced upward, cool as they climb, and wring their water out over the town below. What is this kind of mountain-made rainfall called?
context: Orographic rainfall (from Greek oros, 'mountain') happens wherever moist air is forced up over high ground, cools, and releases its water -- it is exactly why Bergen's seaward mountains keep the city under some 240 rainy days a year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bergen ; gofjords.com

question: The Hanseatic League ran four great overseas trading posts -- its 'Kontors' -- at Novgorod, London, Bruges, and Bergen. In 1979 UNESCO placed Bergen's Bryggen on its World Heritage list for something none of the League's other three Kontors could offer. What was it?
answer: it alone kept its original medieval buildings
choices: it alone kept its original medieval buildings
it alone was the birthplace of the whole League
it alone was the largest of the four Kontors
it alone traded in Russian furs and wax
context: Of the League's four Kontors -- Novgorod, London (the Steelyard), Bruges, and Bergen -- only Bryggen's medieval buildings survive, rebuilt on their old footprints after fires in 1476, 1702 and 1955. UNESCO listed it in 1979 as the last preserved Hanseatic Kontor in the world. Source: hanse.org/en/the-medieval-hanseatic-league/die-kontore ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryggen

question: In a quiet town in the Indian state of Bihar, pilgrims gather beneath a single fig tree where, tradition holds, a wandering prince sat until he awakened and became the Buddha. What is this town called?
context: Bodh Gaya sits in Bihar, India, on the bank of the Falgu River (also called the Niranjana or Lilajan). In the Buddha's own day the place was known as Uruvela. Pilgrims come from across the Buddhist world to the single sacred fig that marks the spot of his enlightenment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodh_Gaya  (Legend.)

question: Right beside the sacred tree at Bodh Gaya stands a polished stone slab that the emperor Ashoka set in place around 250 BCE to mark the exact spot the Buddha is said to have sat. By what name is this ancient stone seat known?
context: The stone seat is the Vajrasana, Sanskrit for 'Diamond Throne.' Emperor Ashoka set it beside the tree around 250 BCE and built the first shrine at the site — the earliest known royal monument marking the spot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabodhi_Temple

question: Rising directly over the sacred tree at Bodh Gaya is the Mahabodhi Temple, a soaring tower 55 metres (180 ft) high, first raised in the Gupta era around the 5th-6th century CE and standing ever since as one of the oldest towers in India made almost entirely from a single material. Which material is it?
context: The Mahabodhi Temple rises 55 metres (180 ft) and dates to the Gupta era (5th-6th century CE) — one of the oldest and most imposing structures in India built entirely of brick, and still standing. Its complex was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabodhi_Temple

question: The oldest human-planted tree in the world with a known planting date does not grow at Bodh Gaya at all. Around 288 BCE a Buddhist nun carried a cutting of the Bodh Gaya tree across the sea to Sri Lanka, where a king planted it in his royal capital and monks have guarded it ever since. In which ancient city does this tree, the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, still grow?
context: The tree is the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi. Its planting date is 'known' because it was recorded in the Sri Lankan chronicle the Mahavamsa; Ashoka's daughter, the nun Sanghamitta, is said to have carried the cutting, planted by King Devanampiya Tissa around 288 BCE. Now over 2,300 years old, it stands raised on terraces and was ringed by a golden fence in 1969. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaya_Sri_Maha_Bodhi

question: By 1876 the last ancient tree at Bodh Gaya had died in a storm, leaving the site of the Buddha's enlightenment without its tree. To restore it in 1881, the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham planted a new sapling drawn from a remarkable source. What did he plant?
answer: a cutting from the tree's own descendant in Sri Lanka
choices: a cutting from the tree's own descendant in Sri Lanka
a wild fig dug from the banks of the Falgu River
a sapling raised from seeds of the original dead tree
a young fig sent as a gift by a Nepalese monastery
context: The original Bodh Gaya tree had been destroyed and regrown several times over the centuries, and the last old tree died in an 1876 storm. In 1881 Alexander Cunningham replanted the site from the Sri Lankan lineage — so the tree at the world's most famous enlightenment site is a descendant of a cutting once sent abroad. The parent survives through its own child. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodhi_Tree

question: Seen from high above, Borobudur on the island of Java isn't shaped like a tower or a pyramid: its square base and stacked terraces form one enormous symmetrical diagram of the entire Buddhist cosmos -- a sacred pattern that pilgrims physically walk through. What is this kind of symbolic cosmic diagram called?
context: A mandala is a symbolic map of the cosmos used in Buddhist and Hindu meditation -- and Borobudur is a mandala you can climb. Its square base runs about 123 m (404 ft) on each side, rising through nine stacked platforms (six square, then three round) to a central dome about 35 m (115 ft) high. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Unlike a cathedral or mosque, Borobudur has no interior at all -- no rooms, no inner hall to gather in. The Javanese monument is meant to be experienced by moving through it from the base all the way to the summit. How does a pilgrim make the journey?
answer: by spiraling clockwise up its open-air terraces
choices: by spiraling clockwise up its open-air terraces
by climbing a single staircase straight to the top
by ascending ladders fixed to its outer walls
by riding a ramp built for royal processions
context: Following every gallery to the summit means walking more than 5 km (3 miles), always clockwise, with the monument on your right. There is no shortcut and no shrine to reach -- the long climb is itself the pilgrimage, a slow rise from the everyday world at the base toward enlightenment at the peak. Source: sacredsites.com; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: Ringing the three round terraces at the crown of Borobudur stand 72 bell-shaped structures of grey stone, their surfaces pierced all over with a lattice of small openings. Peer through the gaps and you can just glimpse something in the shadows within. What is hidden inside each stone bell?
context: These 72 latticework shells are called perforated stupas, and each cradles a seated Buddha making the 'turning the wheel of dharma' gesture -- teachings you glimpse but never fully see. Counting these plus 432 Buddhas in open niches on the terraces below, Borobudur was built with 504 Buddha statues in all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: For centuries Borobudur was one of the wonders of the world; then it fell silent and vanished from memory, unknown to the outside world for hundreds of years. Yet the giant monument on Java still stood, essentially whole, the entire time. What had hidden it so completely?
context: After centuries of use the monument was abandoned; layer by layer, eruptions of the surrounding volcanoes dusted it in ash while tropical jungle grew over the mound until it looked like an ordinary forested hill. It lay lost to the wider world for hundreds of years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Borobudur is built in three stacked tiers, and each one is named for a plane of the Buddhist cosmos that a climbing pilgrim passes through in turn on the way up. The three circular terraces at the very crown -- the final stage of the whole ascent -- carry which name?
choices: Svarga, the heaven of the gods
context: The three worlds are Kamadhatu (desire) at the hidden base, Rupadhatu (form) on the square terraces carved with gods and stories, and Arupadhatu (formlessness) on the round summit, where the carvings stop and only the stupas remain. The climb dramatizes the soul's rise from worldly craving toward release. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: Borobudur rises from the fertile Kedu Plain of Central Java, a landscape crowded with volcanoes -- the same eruptions that once helped bury the monument in ash. It stands in full view of one particular smoking peak, among the most active volcanoes on all of Earth. Which volcano looms over Borobudur?
context: Mount Merapi is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. The volcanic ash that once buried Borobudur, the fertile Kedu Plain it sits in, and the andesite stone the temple is built from all come from this restless volcanic landscape; Merapi's 2010 eruption dusted the temple in acidic ash once more. Source: britannica.com/topic/Borobudur; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Borobudur hides a secret storey. Its lowest level was encased inside a thick outer wall of stone, burying 160 carved panels that no visitor ever sees -- found by chance in 1885, photographed, then walled up again, with only one corner left exposed today. What do these buried carvings illustrate?
answer: how good and evil deeds are repaid
choices: how good and evil deeds are repaid
how the Sailendra kings were crowned
how the great monument was built
context: The hidden base holds the Karmawibhangga reliefs, carvings of the Buddhist law of karma -- good deeds and their rewards, cruel deeds and their punishments. Buried when the base was encased in stone, they were discovered in 1885 and photographed in 1890, then covered again; only the southeast corner is left visible. Source: photodharma.net; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karmawibhangga_Museum

question: The 72 latticed stone stupas crowning Borobudur don't all look the same up close. As a pilgrim climbs from the lower circular terraces to the highest one, the little openings in the stone shift in a deliberate pattern, making the Buddha within harder and harder to see. How do the openings change?
answer: from diamond-shaped holes to square holes
choices: from diamond-shaped holes to square holes
from square holes to round holes
from wide holes to no holes at all
from few holes to many small holes
context: On the two lower circular terraces the openings are diamond-shaped (rhombic); on the highest terrace they become square. The change is symbolic: as the pilgrim nears the formless summit, the Buddha grows harder to glimpse -- form itself dissolving as enlightenment approaches. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: At the very peak of Borobudur sits one great central stupa, larger than the 72 latticed ones around it and sealed shut with solid stone. Each of those 72 cradles a finished, seated Buddha -- but when restorers opened this crowning stupa, they found something strange and unexpected inside. What was in it?
choices: a golden reliquary of the Buddha's tooth
a chamber of gold and jeweled offerings
nothing at all, only empty air
context: Unlike its 72 neighbors, the main stupa held no visible Buddha -- only a single unfinished, rough-hewn statue, now kept in the site museum. Some scholars think it was a discarded mistake; others believe the roughness was intentional, an image of a formless enlightenment that words and shapes cannot capture. The meaning is still debated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unfinished_Buddha

question: By the 1900s Borobudur was crumbling -- its terraces bulging and sliding as rainwater rotted the earthen hill inside. To save it, a huge UNESCO-led rescue in the 1970s and 80s took the most drastic step imaginable for a 1,100-year-old monument. What did the engineers do to Borobudur?
answer: took it entirely apart and rebuilt it block by block
choices: took it entirely apart and rebuilt it block by block
sealed the whole monument inside a glass dome
moved it stone by stone to higher, drier ground
injected the inner hill with concrete to freeze it
context: Between 1975 and 1982, more than a million stone blocks were numbered, lifted off, cleaned, and set back in place on a new hidden foundation of concrete and drainage layers to stop the terraces collapsing -- a technique called anastylosis. The rescue cost about US$6.9 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Brazil's capital used to be Rio de Janeiro, packed onto the crowded Atlantic coast. To pull the whole nation inland, the government marked out bare highland scrub and raised an entire new capital, Brasilia, from empty ground to its 1960 inauguration. How long did building the whole city take?
context: Rio de Janeiro handed over the role of capital in 1960. Ground was broken in the mid-1950s and the whole city rose from bare cerrado scrub in just 41 months, inaugurated on April 21, 1960 -- a national capital conjured from empty ground to opening day in under four years. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; clickpetroleoegas.com.br, 'Brasilia was born in just 41 months')

question: Brasilia wasn't left to sprawl at random like older cities -- the planner Lucio Costa laid the whole capital out to one master design, the Plano Piloto, before a single brick was set. Seen from high overhead, the finished city famously resembles one big object. What is Brasilia most often said to look like?
context: The master plan, the Plano Piloto, was designed by urban planner Lucio Costa, who won a national competition for it in 1957. From the air the layout reads like a giant airplane (some also say a bird or dragonfly): two gently curved 'wings' hold the housing while a long straight 'fuselage' holds the government buildings. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; free-map.org, 'Brasilia: The Airplane-Shaped Capital')

question: The Cathedral of Brasilia looks nothing like an old stone church. Oscar Niemeyer built it from sixteen curved white concrete columns -- each weighing about 90 tons -- that swoop down near the ground and then soar back up toward the sky, lifting a glass roof open to the heavens. Brazilians nicknamed the soaring white structure after one of the objects from the crucifixion of Jesus. What is this cathedral's famous nickname?
context: Oscar Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasilia is a hyperboloid of 16 curved concrete columns, each about 90 tons, dedicated on May 31, 1970. Niemeyer said they were like two hands reaching toward heaven; Brazilians dubbed the soaring white ring a 'crown of thorns.' The glass roof opens the interior to the sky. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_Brasilia; en.wikiarquitectura.com)

question: Many people picture Brazil as endless Amazon rainforest, but Brasilia sits nowhere near the jungle. It was planted far inland on a high plateau about 1,170 metres up, chosen as neutral central ground far from the crowded coast, in a wild region Brazilians call the cerrado. What kind of biome is the cerrado?
context: The cerrado is Brazil's vast tropical savanna. Brasilia sits on it at roughly 1,172 m on a high plateau of the Brazilian Highlands -- deliberately chosen as neutral central ground, far inland from the established coastal cities, so no existing city would dominate the new capital. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia)

question: People love to guess what Brasilia's outline resembles from above, but its planner, Lucio Costa, insisted the design carried one deliberate meaning. He said the plan grew from an ancient, simple gesture -- the mark a person scratches on bare ground to claim a place as their own. What did Costa say the shape of Brasilia truly stood for?
context: Lucio Costa wrote that the plan was 'born of a primary gesture of one who marks or takes possession of a place, two axes crossing at right angles, the very sign of the Cross.' The east-west Monumental Axis holds the government; the curved north-south Residential Axis holds the housing -- so the famous 'airplane' is, by its designer's own account, really a cross. (Costa's Pilot Plan proposal, via wiki.acervolima.com and archdaily.com/1041821)

question: Brasilia sits on high, dry plateau with no coast for hundreds of miles, yet the capital curves around a wide blue lake -- Lake Paranoa -- dotted with sailboats and lined with lakeside palaces. This is no natural lake; planners built it on purpose to give their inland city a waterfront. How did engineers conjure the lake out of the dry plateau?
answer: they dammed a river and flooded the valley
choices: they dammed a river and flooded the valley
they lined a huge basin with concrete and filled it
they piped rainwater down from distant mountains
they pumped up groundwater to fill a hollow
context: Engineers dammed the Paranoa River to flood the artificial Lake Paranoa, wrapping the dry inland capital in water. The dam opened on September 12, 1959 -- President Kubitschek's birthday -- and Niemeyer shaped the lake's edge as a 'dynamic curve, like the ocean waves.' (artsandculture.google.com, 'The History of Lake Paranoa'; e-geos.it, 'Brasilia, Paranoa Lake')

question: Brasilia's most photographed landmark is a study in matched opposites: two identical slim towers standing side by side, flanked by a pair of giant white concrete bowls -- one a shallow saucer opening up to the sky, the other flipped over into a solid dome. Which of Brasilia's famous landmarks is this?
context: The National Congress sets two twin towers between two great concrete bowls: the upturned, open bowl (opening to the sky) shelters the Chamber of Deputies -- 'open to the people' -- while the domed, upside-down bowl covers the Senate, symbolizing reflection and deliberation. It stands at the tip of the plan's 'fuselage' on the Praca dos Tres Poderes. Brasilia became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist architecture and urban design. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_Brazil; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; whc.unesco.org/en/list/445)

question: Above Bruges' great market square, the Markt, rises the 83-metre brick Belfry; near its top hang 47 tuned bronze bells, and one musician can set them all ringing across the city at once. What is this instrument called?
context: The Belfry (Belfort) climbs 83 metres over the Markt, and 366 steps reach the carillon of 47 tuned bells — about 27.5 tonnes of bronze, the great bourdon alone near 11,000 pounds — still played by a carillonneur from a hand-and-fist keyboard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfry_of_Bruges

question: Bruges grew rich as one of medieval Europe's greatest ports, its ships reaching the North Sea through a tidal channel called the Zwin. Over the 1400s the Zwin silted shut with sand and mud, stranding Bruges inland with no way to the sea. Which nearby city seized the sea-trade and rose to lead the Low Countries in its place?
context: The Zwin, a tidal channel torn open by a great storm in 1134, had made inland Bruges one of medieval Europe's foremost ports. When it choked with silt around 1500, the sea-trade and prosperity passed to Antwerp, which became the economic flagship of the Low Countries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwin

question: Bruges today looks almost untouched by time — a maze of canals, cobbled lanes, and stepped-gable brick houses — while other trading cities long ago tore their medieval quarters down and rebuilt in grander styles. What kept Bruges' old city whole when they lost theirs?
answer: It grew too poor to tear down and rebuild, so the medieval city simply survived.
choices: It grew too poor to tear down and rebuild, so the medieval city simply survived.
A ruling duke decreed that its medieval streets be preserved forever.
It was carefully rebuilt as a replica after being flattened in wartime.
The townsfolk restored the old quarter on purpose to draw in pilgrims.
context: At its height around 1350 Bruges held some 46,000 people and the richest money-market in the Low Countries; once the Zwin closed, the impoverished city could not afford to demolish and rebuild, so its medieval streets survived almost whole. The historic centre became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruges

question: At sunrise the Bryce Amphitheater in southern Utah blazes with thousands of glowing stone spires, crowded closer together here than anywhere else on Earth. What are these iconic Bryce rock formations called?
context: Bryce holds the largest concentration of hoodoos found anywhere on Earth, crowded densest inside the Bryce Amphitheater. Hoodoos are tall, thin rock spires that rise from arid basins, bulging thicker and thinner along their height like totem poles. (NPS 'Geologic Formations', nps.gov/brca; brycecanyoncountry.com)

question: Of the thousands of stone spires crowding Bryce Canyon, one 150-foot pinnacle is the park's single most photographed landmark, an icon printed on postcards and trail signs. What is this most famous Bryce spire named?
context: Thor's Hammer -- a slab of harder rock perched on a slender stone neck, standing roughly 150 feet tall -- is Bryce's most famous single hoodoo. (Wildland Trekking 'Hoodoos of Bryce'; desertusa.com 'Hoodoos of Bryce Canyon')

question: Bryce Canyon takes its name from Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon pioneer who built a cabin below these cliffs in 1875 and grazed cattle in the tangle of spires. Asked what he made of the bewildering stone maze on his land, he gave a dry reply now quoted on park signs. What did he reportedly say?
answer: A hell of a place to lose a cow.
choices: A hell of a place to lose a cow.
A garden the Lord left half-finished.
The finest cattle range in all Utah.
A cathedral no man's hand could build.
context: The park is named for Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon pioneer who homesteaded below the cliffs in 1875. He reportedly called the maze of spires 'a hell of a place to lose a cow.' (Wikipedia 'Ebenezer Bryce'; brycecanyoncountry.com 'The History of Bryce Canyon's Namesake')

question: At dawn the spires of Bryce Canyon blaze in shades of rose, orange, and deep red, a band of stone so vivid that early mappers labelled it the 'Pink Cliffs.' The rock itself is a pale limestone. What paints Bryce's stone all those warm colours?
choices: red desert sand blown onto it
context: The rock is the pink Claron Formation limestone, about 50-60 million years old. Iron oxide staining the stone gives it its rose, orange, and red glow -- the band early mappers named the 'Pink Cliffs.' (Grand Canyon Trust 'Steps of Grand Staircase-Escalante'; geology.utah.gov 'The Pink Cliffs')

question: Bryce Canyon's name is misleading. A true canyon is a valley cut downward by a river slicing through rock, the way the Colorado River sawed out the Grand Canyon. But at Bryce there is no such river, and there never was one. So what is Bryce, in geological terms, really?
answer: a set of amphitheatres eroded into a plateau's edge
choices: a set of amphitheatres eroded into a plateau's edge
a deep basin scooped out by a moving glacier
a wide crater blasted out by a meteor strike
a rift valley where the earth's crust pulled apart
context: Bryce isn't a true canyon: no central river carved it. Its bowl-shaped amphitheatres were eaten backward (headward erosion) into the eastern edge of the high Paunsaugunt Plateau. (Wikipedia 'Bryce Canyon National Park'; brycecanyoncountry.com 'Erosion in Bryce Canyon')

question: Everyone assumes wind carved Bryce Canyon's delicate spires, but the real sculptor is ice. On more than 200 nights a year the temperature drops below freezing; water trickles into hairline cracks, freezes, expands, and pries the rock apart, flake by flake, over centuries. Geologists have a precise name for this freeze-and-thaw rock-breaking. What is it called?
context: The real sculptor is frost, not wind: temperatures dip below freezing more than 200 nights a year, and water seeping into cracks freezes and expands about 9%, prying the rock apart -- the process called frost wedging. Slightly acidic rain then dissolves the limestone's cement, thinning the spires between freezes. The hoodoos don't line up with the prevailing winds, and crusted, plant-anchored soil gives wind no loose grains to blast with. (desertusa.com 'Hoodoos of Bryce Canyon'; NPS 'Hoodoos', nps.gov/brca; Wildland Trekking)

question: At Bryce, two neighbouring hoodoos can crumble at wildly different speeds -- one may still stand tall centuries after the other has melted into a slope. The difference is a matter of what armour each spire wears. What gives a long-lasting hoodoo its staying power?
answer: a hard caprock shielding the softer stone beneath it
choices: a hard caprock shielding the softer stone beneath it
a core of solid granite running up its centre
a hard iron shell coating its entire surface
a dense slab of rock anchoring it at the base
context: Each hoodoo owes its totem-pole shape to a caprock -- a layer of harder dolomite or limestone on top that shelters the softer mudstone beneath, so the protected column erodes far slower than the rock around it. (Wildland Trekking 'Hoodoos of Bryce'; desertusa.com)

question: Long before geologists studied Bryce, the Paiute people had their own account of the crowd of red spires. They called the rocks the 'Legend People' -- birds, lizards, and animals that looked like people -- and told how a trickster froze them into stone as punishment for their greed and misdeeds. In Paiute stories, which trickster turned the Legend People to stone?
context: To the Paiute the hoodoos are the Legend People (To-when-an-ung-wa) -- beings who 'looked like people' but were birds, animals, and lizards -- turned to stone by the trickster Coyote for their misdeeds; the Paiute call the rocks Anka-ku-was-a-wits, 'red painted faces.' In one telling Coyote invited the greedy Legend People to a grand banquet and, as they sat down in their finest paint and clothing, cast the spell that froze every one of them into stone before a single bite was taken. (NPR 'A Paiute Take On Bryce Canyon's Hoodoos', Paiute elder Indian Dick, 1936; brycecanyoncountry.com 'Native American Lore')

question: Bryce Canyon sits at the very top of a colossal landform called the Grand Staircase -- a series of giant cliff 'steps' that climb more than 6,000 feet over 100-plus miles of Utah and northern Arizona, each step a different band of coloured rock. Bryce's Pink Cliffs form the top step. Far to the south, what world-famous landform forms the very bottom step of this staircase?
context: Bryce sits at the very top of the Grand Staircase -- a giant flight of cliffs climbing more than 6,000 vertical feet over 100-plus miles -- whose lowest step, far to the south, is the Grand Canyon (its north-rim Kaibab Limestone is the bottom tread). Zion, a middle step, sits between them. (Grand Canyon Trust 'Geology Rocks: Steps of Grand Staircase-Escalante'; Wikipedia 'Grand Staircase')

question: Hungary's capital straddles the Danube: hilly, castle-topped Buda on the west bank and flat, bustling Pest on the east. For centuries the two towns had no permanent link -- until one great span finally joined them in 1849. What is Budapest's first fixed bridge across the Danube called?
context: Buda (hilly, crowned by the royal castle) and Pest (flat and commercial) were separate towns until the Szechenyi Chain Bridge -- the first permanent bridge over the Hungarian Danube -- opened on 20 November 1849; the two sides formally united into 'Budapest' in 1873. The Liberty, Margaret, and Elisabeth Bridges are all real Budapest crossings built later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szechenyi_Chain_Bridge

question: Budapest holds an official title no other capital can claim -- the 'City of Spas,' granted in 1934. Its warmth isn't pumped from any plant; it wells up on its own, as more than 100 thermal springs seep through the rock beneath the streets. Together, how much warm mineral water do they pour out every day?
context: Budapest sits over 100-plus natural thermal springs -- said to be more than under any other capital -- which yield roughly 70 million litres (about 40,000 cubic metres) of warm mineral water a day; this underground abundance earned it the official 'City of Spas' title in 1934. The other figures are plausible-sounding but well off the real daily flow of about 70 million litres. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spas_in_Budapest

question: On a snowy Budapest winter's day, thick steam rolls off a grand outdoor pool where bathers soak chest-deep -- some hunched over chessboards that float on the water between them -- as snow settles in their hair. This lemon-yellow, palace-like bathhouse, fed by a spring drilled 1,256 metres down that surfaces at a scalding 77C, is the largest medicinal bath in Europe. Which Budapest bathhouse is it?
context: The Szechenyi Baths (opened 1913), a neo-Baroque bath-palace, is called Europe's largest medicinal bath -- 3 outdoor and 15 indoor pools fed by a spring drilled 1,256 m down that surfaces near 77C. The winter chess matches on floating boards in the steaming outdoor pool are a real, much-photographed tradition, not a legend. The Gellert, Rudas, and Kiraly are other famous Budapest baths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szechenyi_thermal_bath

question: Budapest's hot springs puzzle first-time visitors -- there's no volcano for hundreds of kilometres, yet warm water rises all over the city. The reason lies underground, along the sharp boundary where the wooded Buda hills drop to the flat Pest plain: the Danube follows this line, and deep, Earth-heated water climbs to the surface here. This boundary is a famous example of what geological feature?
context: Budapest's heat is not volcanic: the city lies on the Buda thermal fault zone, where the Buda hills meet the Pest plain and the karst rock is dropped about 1,000 m under the Pest side. Rainwater sinks deep, is warmed by the Earth's inner heat, and rises back to the surface along the fault. A rift valley, an escarpment, and a continental divide are different boundary features. Source: pangea.stanford.edu (Geothermal Budapest, Toth 2020)

question: More than 200 caves riddle the limestone beneath Budapest's Buda hills -- one of the largest cave systems of its kind anywhere on Earth. Caves like these can be dissolved out of limestone in several very different ways. What carved the maze of caves under Buda?
answer: hot mineral water rising from below
choices: hot mineral water rising from below
the surf of an ancient sea
context: Warm, mineral-rich water rising from deep below dissolves limestone into caves from the bottom up -- the reverse of ordinary rain-fed caves, which form from the top down as rainwater seeps in from the surface. This bottom-up 'thermal karst' has produced over 200 caves under the Buda hills, one of Earth's largest thermal-water cave systems, fed by the same deep water that surfaces in the city's baths. River caves, sea caves, and glacier caves are all real cave types, but none of them carved the Buda caves. Source: vilagorokseg.e-epites.hu (Caves of the Buda Thermal Karst); atlasobscura.com

question: Beneath Buda Castle hill lies a labyrinth of caves where, during the brutal 1945 siege of Budapest, a secret hospital built for just 60 patients took in more than 600 wounded. Decades later, at the height of the Cold War, the Hungarian state quietly rebuilt these same rock tunnels to serve a chilling new purpose. What was the cave-hospital secretly converted into?
context: This is the 'Hospital in the Rock' (Sziklakorhaz), part of a roughly 3.3 km cave-and-cellar labyrinth cut into the soft limestone under Buda Castle hill. Built for 60-70 patients, it took in more than 600 wounded during the 1945 siege of Budapest, and was later secretly refitted as a Cold War nuclear-fallout bunker; it is a museum today. A radio post, a police prison, and a fuel depot are the kinds of hidden facilities Cold War states really did build underground, but not what this one became. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_in_the_Rock

question: The neo-Gothic Hungarian Parliament stretches 268 metres along the Pest bank of the Danube, its spires mirrored in the dark water at night. It rises exactly 96 metres -- a coded tribute to 896, the year the Magyars founded Hungary -- and by old custom no building in Budapest was allowed to stand any taller. One other great Budapest landmark was deliberately built to that very same 96-metre height. Which is it?
context: Both the Hungarian Parliament and St. Stephen's Basilica rise to exactly 96 metres -- a matched height often said to symbolise that worldly and spiritual power stand equal in Hungary -- and 96 nods to 896, the traditional date the Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin. By long custom no building in central Budapest rises above 96 m. Matthias Church, Buda Castle, and Fisherman's Bastion are other real Budapest landmarks, none built to that height. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Parliament_Building; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Stephen's_Basilica_(Budapest)

question: Deep under Budapest's Jozsef Hill hides a cave, discovered in 1984, whose walls bristle with glittering, needle-like aragonite crystals -- the crown jewel of the city's underground. It didn't form like its neighbours: here a gas rising with the thermal water turned into a powerful acid that slowly ate the cavern out of the solid limestone. Which acid carved the Jozsef-hegy Cave?
context: The Jozsef-hegy Cave (found 1984) is famed for its needle-like aragonite crystals. It formed by 'sulfuric-acid speleogenesis': hydrogen-sulfide gas (the rotten-egg smell) rising with the thermal water oxidised into sulfuric acid, which dissolved the limestone -- the same rare process that carved Carlsbad and Lechuguilla Caverns in the USA. Ordinary caves are carved by weak carbonic acid from rainwater. Source: researchgate.net (Minerals and speleothems of the Jozsef-hegy Cave, Budapest)

question: A smoldering partnered dance now performed in grand ballrooms from Paris to Tokyo was actually born in the 1880s among poor immigrants, dockworkers and sailors crowded into the riverside tenements of Buenos Aires's La Boca barrio. What is this dance?
context: Tango grew up in La Boca's port arrabales -- the tenement courtyards, cantinas and dance halls of Buenos Aires's poorest immigrant districts -- in the 1880s, danced by dockworkers and sailors long before it conquered the ballrooms of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango

question: No boulevard on Earth is broader than the one slicing through downtown Buenos Aires: roughly 110 metres from kerb to kerb, with up to seven lanes of traffic each way, so wide that crossing on foot often takes two or three green lights. What is this record-holding avenue called?
context: Avenida 9 de Julio is recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's widest avenue. Its name honours the 9th of July, 1816 -- the day Argentina declared its independence from Spain -- so the broadest avenue on Earth is essentially a boulevard named after a birthday. The white Obelisco stands at its centre. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenida_9_de_Julio

question: In Buenos Aires's dockside La Boca barrio, a short lane called Caminito is famous for tin-walled houses splashed in clashing blues, reds, greens and yellows, no two walls alike. The poor workers who built these shacks could not afford proper house paint, so where did all this colour come from?
answer: leftover paint scraped from the harbour ships
choices: leftover paint scraped from the harbour ships
coloured clay dug from the riverbank
reject batches from a paint factory
old tiles shipped over from Italy
context: La Boca's shipyard workers finished their corrugated-tin homes with whatever paint was left over from the boats in the harbour, so each wall ended up a different colour. The dockside painter Benito Quinquela Martin later turned the barrio into a deliberate open-air canvas, and Caminito became one of Buenos Aires's most photographed streets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Boca

question: In one wealthy Buenos Aires district, thousands of marble mausoleums stand shoulder to shoulder above the ground, arranged in blocks along named lanes and little plazas, so that visitors stroll it exactly like wandering a miniature stone city -- and Eva 'Evita' Peron lies buried among the elite here. What is this famous walk-through burial ground called?
context: La Recoleta Cemetery holds 4,691 above-ground mausoleums laid out in blocks like a small city of the dead, and is regularly ranked among the most beautiful cemeteries in the world. Eva Peron -- 'Evita,' Argentina's famous first lady -- rests in her family's tomb here, one of its most visited graves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Recoleta_Cemetery

question: In the La Boca barrio, the football club Boca Juniors plays in a stadium built with three steeply stacked tiers on three sides and one oddly flat wall on the fourth. Its fans boast that it 'does not shake, it beats,' because the packed concrete stands visibly pulse up and down when tens of thousands of supporters leap in unison. By what affectionate nickname is this stadium known?
context: La Bombonera -- 'the chocolate box' -- earned its nickname from its unusual shape: three steep tiers and one flat vertical stand make it look like an open box of bonbons. Its close, steep walls trap and amplify the roar of Boca Juniors' fans, and the stands really do flex when the crowd jumps, giving rise to the saying 'La Bombonera no tiembla, late' -- it does not shake, it beats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Bombonera

question: Tango's aching, breathing melodies pour from its signature instrument -- a small button-and-bellows squeezebox pushed and pulled on the player's knees. Strangely, this most Argentine of sounds is not Argentine at all: the instrument was invented in 1840s Germany to give poor village churches a cheap substitute for a pipe organ, and German immigrants carried it to Buenos Aires around 1870. What is this instrument called?
context: The bandoneon was invented around 1840 by Heinrich Band in Germany as an affordable instrument for small churches that could not afford an organ. German immigrants brought it to the Rio de la Plata around 1870, where it became the very voice and soul of tango -- no tango orchestra is complete without its plaintive, breathing tone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandoneon

question: The Rio de la Plata beside Buenos Aires never runs blue or green: from one bank clear to the other it stays a steady, murky brown the whole year round. What gives this enormous river its permanent brown colour?
context: The Rio de la Plata's brown comes from the immense load of fine sediment -- silt and mud -- that it carries and holds in suspension, staining the whole estuary the colour of milky coffee from one bank to the other. Tannins, algae or dissolved minerals turn other rivers brown, but here the cause is plain suspended sediment washed down off the land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_la_Plata

question: Stand on the Buenos Aires waterfront and look out over the Rio de la Plata: there is no far shore at all, only muddy brown water running flat to the horizon like an open sea. So enormous is this expanse where it meets the Atlantic that people have long argued whether it can even be called a river at all. Among the world superlatives claimed for it, which one does the Rio de la Plata actually hold?
answer: the widest river in the world
choices: the widest river in the world
the muddiest river in the world
the widest freshwater river in the world
the widest river delta in the world
context: Near Buenos Aires the Rio de la Plata already spans more than 40 km, and it flares to roughly 220 km wide where it meets the Atlantic -- so vast it looks like a muddy brown sea with no far shore. Counted as a river it is the widest in the world, though geographers debate whether so broad a brackish body should count as a river or an estuary at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_la_Plata

question: In the heart of Bukhara, Uzbekistan, a slender brick tower has risen over the old city since the year 1127. Five times a day for nearly nine centuries, Muslims have been called to prayer from the gallery at its top. A tall tower built onto a mosque for the call to prayer goes by which name?
context: This is the Kalyan ('Great') Minaret, about 45.6 m tall (nearly 48 m to the tip), completed in 1127. A minaret is the tower from which a mosque sounds the call to prayer; the Kalyan has done so for close to 900 years. A belfry is a Christian bell-tower, a pagoda a tiered East Asian temple tower, and a ziggurat an ancient Mesopotamian stepped temple. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret

question: Legend says that when Genghis Khan rode into Bukhara in 1220 to raze it, he tilted his head so far back to see the top of the towering Kalyan minaret that his hat tumbled off. As he bent to pick it up, the conqueror — who boasted he had never once bowed to any man — was so struck by the tower that he made a surprising choice. In this beloved but unproven tale, what did he do?
answer: He ordered the minaret spared as the city burned.
choices: He ordered the minaret spared as the city burned.
He had the minaret pulled down before all else.
He made his archers shoot down from its gallery.
He renamed the towering minaret after himself.
context: The tale is a favourite of Bukhara guides but is historically unverified. What is real: the Kalyan minaret did survive the Mongol sack of 1220, when much of the city was destroyed. Genghis Khan (c. 1162–1227) led the Mongol conquest of Central Asia. Sources: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/kalyan-minaret ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret  (Legend.)

question: The Samanid Mausoleum in Bukhara, raised for the Samanid dynasty in the 900s, is a near-perfect cube about nine metres on each side. Its whole surface is woven into 'basketweave' and checkerboard bands that seem to shift and shimmer as the sun crosses the sky — the same wall looking different at dawn and at dusk. From what single material is the entire tomb built and patterned?
context: Each side is about 9.4 m. The tomb's beauty is famous precisely because it is achieved in plain baked brick alone — no coloured tile — laid so that raised and angled bricks throw shifting shadows through the day. It is one of the oldest surviving monuments of Central Asian Islamic architecture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samanid_Mausoleum

question: Bukhara stood at a great crossroads of the Silk Road, and camel caravans hauling silk, spices, and silver streamed in from across Asia. To house them, the city filled with special walled inns — each a ring of rooms around a big central courtyard, where traders could stable their camels, lock away their bales, and sleep safely before travelling on. What was a Silk Road inn of this kind called?
context: A caravanserai (from Persian) was the roadside inn of the Silk Road, its courtyard big enough for camels and cargo. Bukhara also roofed its crossroads with domed trading bazaars grouped by trade — the Jewelers' Dome (Toqi Zargaron, 1569) alone once held 36 goldsmiths' workshops. A bazaar is a market, a madrasa a religious school, a hammam a bathhouse. Sources: https://people-travels.com/sights/trading-domes-of-bukhara ; https://visitworldheritage.com/en/silk-road/browse-bukharas-bazaars/d167d600-e417-4dce-9d3b-dc41cc314bac

question: When Genghis Khan's Mongols stormed Bukhara in 1220, they smashed nearly every great building in the city — yet the exquisite Samanid Mausoleum came through untouched, to be admired a thousand years later. It escaped the raiders for one surprising reason. Why did the Mongols leave this tomb standing?
answer: Flood silt and sand had long buried it, so they never found it.
choices: Flood silt and sand had long buried it, so they never found it.
They honoured it as the tomb of their own ancestors.
A wide belt of marsh made it impossible to reach.
Its keepers paid the raiders richly to pass it by.
context: The Samanid Mausoleum survived the Mongol sack because, over the centuries before 1220, floods had heaped mud and sand over it until it was hidden from view; the raiders simply never saw it. It was dug back out much later. The tomb, in effect, was saved by being lost. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samanid_Mausoleum

question: For nearly 900 years Bukhara's Kalyan minaret has soared over the old city — but it also carries a chilling nickname, kept alive by a grim custom that lasted right into the early twentieth century: the 'Tower of Death.' What did the emirs of Bukhara do at the tower to earn it that name?
answer: Flung condemned prisoners from its top gallery to the square below.
choices: Flung condemned prisoners from its top gallery to the square below.
Chained rebels in iron cages to starve high above the crowd.
Burned executed enemies on a pyre built atop its roof.
Sealed plague victims inside its shaft until the sickness passed.
context: The custom is real: for centuries, and into the early 1900s, the condemned in Bukhara were led to the minaret's high gallery and thrown to their deaths on the pavement below. The Scottish traveller Fitzroy Maclean, who visited in 1938, recorded that men were cast down from 'the delicately ornamented gallery which crowns it.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret ; Fitzroy Maclean, 'Eastern Approaches' (1949).

question: The Ark of Bukhara is a huge mud-brick citadel — its walls run nearly 800 metres around and rise up to 20 metres high — and it served as the fortress-palace of Bukhara's rulers for over a thousand years. Oddly, the entire citadel stands lifted about 20 metres above the plain, on a vast mound. What is that great mound beneath it made of?
answer: The rubble of its own earlier forts, rebuilt again and again.
choices: The rubble of its own earlier forts, rebuilt again and again.
A natural outcrop of bedrock rising from the plain.
An artificial hill of packed clay hauled in by hand.
The buried ruins of an ancient Greek fortress-town.
context: Each time the citadel was destroyed or decayed, its rulers levelled the ruins and built again on top — so the Ark literally sits on roughly 20 m of its own former selves. Its walls run about 790 m around and rise 16–20 m; it was the seat of Bukhara's emirs for over a thousand years, until 1920. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_Bukhara

question: Chor Minor, a small gatehouse in a Bukhara back lane, is crowned with four sky-blue domed turrets — and strikingly, no two of the four are alike: each bears a different carved emblem. Some scholars believe the four mismatched designs were meant as deliberate symbols. According to that reading, what do Chor Minor's four turrets represent?
choices: the four seasons of the year
the four winds of the desert
context: Chor Minor — Persian for 'four minarets' — was built in 1807 by a wealthy merchant, Khalif Niyaz-kul, as the gateway to a madrasa (an Islamic school) that has since vanished, leaving only the gate. Some scholars read the four differing motifs on its turrets as hints of different faiths — seeing suggestions of a cross, a fish, and other symbols. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chor_Minor

question: Bukhara's old town is no dead ruin: people still live, pray, and trade among some 140 mosques, tombs, madrasas, and 16th-century domed bazaars crowded into its old streets — a historic core UNESCO added to its World Heritage List in 1993. For all that old architecture packed into one living town, Bukhara carries a two-word nickname. What is Bukhara often called?
context: About 140 monuments crowd Bukhara's historic centre, yet it stays a lived-in, working town — which is what makes its nickname a small surprise: it is called a 'museum city.' UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Bukhara as a World Heritage Site in 1993. The rival nicknames belong to other cities: the 'Eternal City' is Rome, the 'Forbidden City' is Beijing's imperial palace complex, and the 'Golden City' is Prague. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukhara ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/602/

question: On the coast of Lebanon, about 40 km north of Beirut, the ancient harbor of Byblos and its Phoenician sailors gave the world a tool so powerful that nearly every nation on Earth still relies on it -- you are using it to read this very sentence. What did Byblos give us?
context: Byblos -- called Gebal by the Phoenicians -- has been lived in without a break since about 5000 BCE, one of the oldest cities on Earth. Its Phoenician traders carried the 22-letter alphabet by sea, and nearly every alphabet in use today descends from it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos; /Phoenician_alphabet)

question: The little stone harbor of Byblos, on the coast of Lebanon, has been lived in without a single break since around 5000 BCE -- one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns on Earth. Long before the Greeks renamed it Byblos, the Phoenicians who built it called their city by another name. What did the Phoenicians call Byblos?
context: 'Gebal' is thought to mean 'mountain town' or 'frontier town.' Excavations begun in 1860 revealed settlement layers running from the Neolithic all the way to the Ottoman era, plus five Byblian royal inscriptions dated roughly 1150-950 BCE. (worldhistory.org/Byblos; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos)

question: The Phoenician alphabet of Byblos used only 22 signs, far fewer than the hundreds in Egyptian hieroglyphs. It managed this by refusing to write one of the two basic kinds of speech-sound at all, leaving readers to fill them in from memory -- a trick that works because Semitic languages pack their meaning into the OTHER kind. Which kind of sound did Phoenician leave unwritten?
context: A script that writes only consonants and leaves the vowels to the reader is called an abjad -- Semitic languages carry their meaning mostly in the consonants, so it works. Centuries later the Greeks would borrow this alphabet and add signs for the vowels. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: The Phoenicians of Byblos, Tyre, and Sidon ruled the ancient Mediterranean as its finest seafarers, and their 22-letter alphabet turned up in ports from the Levant to Spain. The Romans would later plant THEIR letters by conquering with legions -- but the Phoenicians spread theirs through the everyday activity their ships were built for. What was that activity?
context: With only a couple dozen signs to learn -- versus years of training for hieroglyphs or cuneiform -- a merchant could master the alphabet, not just a priest. Phoenician ships carried it across North Africa and southern Europe, so it spread by trade rather than conquest. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: In 1923, a landslide on the hillside at Byblos tore open a set of royal tombs. Ten meters down one shaft, French archaeologists found a carved stone coffin covered in writing -- the oldest long inscription in the Phoenician alphabet yet discovered, a 38-word text from about 1000 BCE. Whose coffin carried this earliest full witness of the alphabet?
context: French archaeologist Pierre Montet found the coffin in 1923 after the landslide exposed the royal tombs; the burial shaft ran ten meters deep. The Ahiram sarcophagus now rests in the National Museum of Beirut, and UNESCO listed Byblos's Phoenician alphabet inscriptions in its 'Memory of the World' register in 2005. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahiram_sarcophagus)

question: The oldest long text in the whole Phoenician alphabet is not a hymn or a king's brag -- it is a curse carved around the lid of a royal coffin at Byblos, calling down doom on any later king who would drag the coffin from its tomb. Which specific fate did the curse promise the tomb-robber?
answer: his own royal scepter would snap in two
choices: his own royal scepter would snap in two
his firstborn son would die before him
his name would be chiseled off every stone
his bones would lie unburied on the shore
context: The inscription warns that if any king disturbs the coffin, 'his imperial scepter shall break... the throne of his kingship shall overturn, and peace shall depart from Byblos.' It is the oldest substantial Phoenician text known -- a 38-word warning from about 1000 BCE. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahiram_sarcophagus)

question: Byblos was the ancient world's great port for Egyptian papyrus -- the paper the Greeks wrote and read on. The Greeks so tied their scrolls to this one Lebanese harbor that they named the paper 'byblos' after it, a single scroll a 'biblion,' and a whole collection of scrolls 'ta biblia,' 'the books.' Say 'ta biblia' aloud: which famous sacred book takes its very name from that phrase?
context: The same root gives us 'biblio-' words -- a bibliophile is a book-lover, a bibliography a list of books -- all tracing back to a Lebanese harbor's papyrus trade. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos; etymonline.com/word/Byblos)

question: Every letter of the Phoenician alphabet of Byblos began as a tiny picture of some everyday thing, and the letter's name was simply that thing's name. The very first letter, 'aleph,' was a little drawing of a horned farm animal's head. Flip our capital 'A' upside-down and you can still make out its two horns. What animal was 'aleph'?
context: This is called acrophony: a letter's picture was named for a thing, and the first sound of that thing's name became the letter's sound -- 'aleph' (ox) gave the 'a' sound. Aleph became Greek alpha and then our A. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet; ancient-hebrew.org/ancient-alphabet/aleph.htm)

question: Keep hunting the pictures hidden in our letters. In the alphabet of Byblos, the sign 'mem' became our zig-zag capital 'M,' and -- like every Phoenician letter -- its name was the plain word for what it once drew. That name survives almost unchanged as the Hebrew word 'mayim.' What everyday thing did 'mem' first picture?
context: Other letters still hide their pictures too: 'bet' was a house (Hebrew 'bayit'), 'dalet' a door, 'ayin' an eye (Hebrew 'ayin' still means eye), 'kaph' a palm of the hand, and 'resh' a head. Each letter's name was the thing it once drew. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: The alphabet born in Phoenician Byblos crossed to Greece, then sailed on to Italy. There a mysterious people -- famous for the painted tombs they left in the hills north of Rome -- took the Greek letters, reshaped them, and passed them to the Romans around the 600s BCE, giving us the Latin ABCs on this page. Which people handed the alphabet to Rome?
context: The full trail runs Phoenician -> Greek -> Etruscan -> Latin, so the ABCs of English are great-great-grandchildren of a Lebanese trading script. The Romans borrowed the letters from the Etruscans around the 7th century BCE. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet)

question: The letters of Byblos have cousins far to the east and south. One branch of the family became Aramaic, then Hebrew; another passed to a desert-trading nation that cut the rose-red temples and tombs of the city of Petra into a canyon in Jordan -- and from that nation's flowing script grew the Arabic writing used across the world today. Which people carried the alphabet's family line toward Arabic?
context: The same Phoenician root branched east into Aramaic, and from Aramaic into Hebrew and -- by way of the Nabataean script -- Arabic. Scholars say nearly every alphabet on Earth either descends from this first Semitic alphabet or was inspired by one of its descendants. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet)

question: A thousand years ago the largest city in what is now the United States rose on the Mississippi floodplain across from St. Louis -- a city we call Cahokia, crowned by over a hundred flat-topped mounds, the tallest as tall as a ten-story building. Its people raised these giants without quarrying a single block of stone. What did they pile up, load by load, to build them?
context: The greatest were 'platform mounds' -- flat-topped earthen pyramids that served as raised bases for temples and the halls of chiefs. Basket by basket, Cahokia's builders moved an estimated 55 million cubic feet of soil, in about 120 mounds all told. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: Cahokia's centerpiece, Monks Mound, climbs in four broad terraces to about 30 m (100 ft) -- a colossal artificial hill of some 22 million cubic feet, all carried up by hand. Its rectangular base is so vast -- roughly 13 acres -- that it covers nearly the same ground as one of the ancient world's most celebrated monuments. Which monument does Monks Mound's footprint rival?
context: Its base -- about 291 by 236 m -- rivals the Great Pyramid's ~13-acre footprint, making Monks Mound the largest earthwork in the Americas and the largest pyramid north of Mexico. It only matches Giza at the base: the stone pyramid still rises more than four times higher. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monks_Mound.

question: Everyone knows this ancient metropolis as 'Cahokia' -- yet the people who raised its hundred mounds and then vanished never used that word, and their own name for their city is lost forever. Where does the name we use today actually come from?
answer: a neighboring people who arrived long after
choices: a neighboring people who arrived long after
the French explorers who found the ruins
a river that flows past the site
an old Spanish word for the mounds
context: When French explorers reached the area in the 1600s, they named the long-abandoned ruins after the Cahokia, an Illiniwek people then living nearby -- who had not built the city and arrived centuries after it emptied. The builders left no writing, so their own name for their metropolis is unknown. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: In Cahokia's vast Grand Plaza, huge crowds gathered to watch the city's favorite sport: a player would roll a smooth, disc-shaped stone across the packed earth, then hurl a wooden lance to land on the very spot where the rolling stone would finally stop. What was this wildly popular Cahokian game called?
context: The game was chunkey, and it mattered so much that beautifully polished chunkey stones were buried as elite treasures. Crowds packed the Grand Plaza to cheer these contests of skill. Source: Gilder Lehrman / World History Commons Cahokia essays; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72.

question: Around 1100 CE, at its dazzling peak, Cahokia may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people -- for that moment likely making it more crowded than a certain great European capital of the very same century. No settlement in what became the United States would pass Cahokia's size until Philadelphia topped 40,000 in the 1780s. Which European capital of the 1100s did Cahokia probably outnumber?
context: The population is an estimate -- 'may have held' 10,000-20,000 at its ~1100 CE peak -- but that likely put Cahokia ahead of the London of the same century. That no U.S. city surpassed it until Philadelphia passed ~40,000 in the 1780s shows Cahokia was a true metropolis, not a scattered village. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia.

question: The graves and workshops of Cahokia brim with exotic goods hauled astonishing distances: hammered ornaments of copper carried down from the Great Lakes, and glossy sea-shells -- some as broad as a man's hand -- found hundreds of miles from any coast. From which distant shoreline did Cahokia's traders bring those great marine shells?
context: Cahokia sat at the hub of a continent-spanning trade web: lightning-whelk and conch shells came up the Mississippi from the Gulf of Mexico, copper from the Great Lakes, and Mill Creek chert hoes from quarries in southern Illinois. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia.

question: At the height of its power, Cahokia walled off its sacred heart -- Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza -- behind a defensive barrier running two miles around, studded with jutting guard towers and rebuilt three or four times across two centuries. What was this enormous city wall built of?
context: This was a palisade -- a two-mile stockade of 15,000-20,000 oak and hickory logs, each about a foot thick and 20 feet tall, with guard-tower 'bastions' roughly every 85 feet, rebuilt several times over about two centuries. Source: gilderlehrman.org Cahokia essay; cahokiamounds.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: Just west of Monks Mound, postholes reveal that Cahokians raised great rings of upright red-cedar posts -- a 'Woodhenge,' a wooden cousin of Britain's Stonehenge -- carefully aligned with the sunrises of the seasons. Stand at the center of this ring at the spring or fall equinox, watch the dawn, and one striking thing appears to happen. What does the rising sun seem to do?
answer: rise straight out of Monks Mound itself
choices: rise straight out of Monks Mound itself
set Monks Mound's summit ablaze with light
split into twin beams above the plaza
cast a long shadow across the whole ring
context: The circle is nicknamed 'Woodhenge' -- the best-studied ring (~1000 CE) had 48 red-cedar posts and spanned about 410 feet. At the equinox the rising sun appears to emerge from the front of Monks Mound half a mile away, as if the mound itself gives birth to the dawn -- a striking effect of careful alignment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge.  (Legend.)

question: Deep inside the mound archaeologists labeled Mound 72, they uncovered the grave of a powerful young man laid out upon a glittering bed of some 20,000 polished shell beads. The beads had not been scattered -- they were painstakingly arranged into the outline of a single animal, its head set beneath the man's head and its long form spreading out beneath his arms and legs. Which creature did those thousands of beads take the shape of?
context: This is the 'Birdman' burial: the beads formed a falcon, its head beneath his head and wings and tail beneath his limbs -- a falcon-warrior symbol of a powerful ranked society. Bead counts vary in the sources (Wikipedia ~10,000; Grokipedia and popular accounts ~20,000). He did not lie alone: Mound 72 held over 270 burials, many of them sacrificed attendants -- evidence of rulers who held power of life and death. Radiocarbon dates it to about 1030 CE. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mound_72; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72.  (Legend.)

question: By about 1350 CE, mighty Cahokia stood silent and all but empty, and scholars still argue over why its thousands drifted away. One long-popular theory blamed the Cahokians themselves -- claiming they cut down so many trees for building and fuel that they stripped the land and triggered the very floods that ruined their farms. When researchers recently studied the ancient flood layers around Cahokia, what did they find about this 'self-inflicted collapse' story?
context: A 2021 Washington University study of the flood layers found scant evidence that local logging caused the flooding, challenging the old self-destruction idea. The real cause is still genuinely debated: a great Mississippi flood around 1200 buried farmland in silt, and Little Ice Age drought and resource stress are also blamed. Cahokia became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 -- one of only a handful in the U.S. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1501904112; source.washu.edu (2021).

question: The ancient Greeks named Seven Wonders of the World -- awe-inspiring marvels every traveler longed to see. Over the centuries, six of the seven crumbled into ruins or vanished without a trace. Only ONE still stands today, more than 4,500 years after it was built. Which of the Seven Wonders is the sole survivor?
context: Six of the Seven Wonders -- the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus, the Temple of Artemis, and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus -- are long gone. Only the Great Pyramid of Giza, on the desert edge of Cairo, still stands after about 4,500 years -- the last survivor of the ancient world's Seven Wonders. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: Around 2600 BC the pharaoh Khufu ordered the Great Pyramid raised at Giza -- a mountain of 2.3 million stone blocks that took some 26 years to build. For all its size and mystery, the Great Pyramid was built to serve one main purpose. What was it built to be?
context: The Great Pyramid was the tomb of Pharaoh Khufu (Greek name Cheops), built in Egypt's Old Kingdom around 2600 BC over roughly 26 years from some 2.3 million stone blocks -- the grandest royal tomb ever raised. Later stories reimagined it as a granary or a temple, but it was always a tomb. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: When the Great Pyramid was finished around 2600 BC, it became the tallest structure humans had ever built -- and it kept that title for a jaw-droppingly long time, until Lincoln Cathedral in England finally overtook it. For roughly how long did the Great Pyramid reign as the tallest building on Earth?
context: The Great Pyramid rose 146.6 m and stayed the tallest human-made structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years -- not surpassed until Lincoln Cathedral's spire around 1311 AD. Erosion has since lowered it to about 138.5 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: A famous story claims that Napoleon's soldiers blasted the nose off the Great Sphinx of Giza with a cannon in 1798. Historians are certain this tale is FALSE. What is the strongest evidence that Napoleon's troops did NOT destroy the Sphinx's nose?
answer: a sketch made before Napoleon shows the nose gone
choices: a sketch made before Napoleon shows the nose gone
Napoleon's army never actually reached Egypt
the Sphinx's nose was carved separately and later lost
cannon fire cannot damage such hard limestone
context: The Sphinx's nose was already gone long before Napoleon: a sketch from 1737 -- decades before French troops reached Egypt in 1798 -- shows it missing. The nose was most likely chiseled off deliberately centuries earlier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Sphinx_of_Giza  (Legend.)

question: The Giza pyramids and nearly every grand royal tomb of ancient Egypt were deliberately built on the WEST bank of the Nile, never the east. To the Egyptians, the west was the land of the dead -- the fitting side for a grave. What made the west the side of death in their eyes?
answer: it was where the sun died each evening
choices: it was where the sun died each evening
it was where the Nile's flood began each year
it was where the desert winds blew hottest
it was where their enemies' lands lay
context: Egyptians watched the sun set and 'die' in the west each evening, then be reborn in the east at dawn, so they made the west bank the realm of the dead and placed their royal tombs -- including the Giza pyramids -- there. Source: egypttoursportal.com; inside-egypt.com

question: Digging beside Khufu's pyramid at Giza, archaeologists uncovered a large cemetery of the pyramid-builders themselves, along with the remains of a whole town built to house and feed thousands of them. Who does this evidence show actually built the Great Pyramid?
answer: paid Egyptian workers, free and proud
choices: paid Egyptian workers, free and proud
enslaved captives seized in foreign wars
prisoners condemned to years of hard labor
foreign engineers hired from distant lands
context: The builders were skilled, paid Egyptians, not slaves: their tombs sat honorably beside the king's pyramid, their work-gangs bore proud names like 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure,' and about 10,000 workers were fed some 21 cattle and 23 sheep every single day. Source: guardians.net/hawass; cbc.ca

question: In the heart of medieval 'Islamic Cairo,' a mosque founded in the year 972 AD grew into a school that has taught students without a break ever since -- over a thousand years, making it one of the oldest continuously running universities on Earth. Which Cairo mosque is this ancient university?
context: Al-Azhar's mosque was founded by the Fatimids between 970 and 972 AD; the teaching that grew around it makes al-Azhar one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world. It stands in the medieval quarter of 'Islamic Cairo,' near the Citadel of Saladin (begun 1176 AD). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azhar_University

question: Stretching about 6 kilometers through Cairo is one of the world's most extraordinary neighborhoods: a vast, ancient cemetery where thousands of living families have made their homes AMONG the tombs -- cooking, sleeping and sending children to school in buildings shared with the graves, wired for electricity and running water. What is this inhabited necropolis called?
context: Cairo's City of the Dead (al-Qarafa) is a necropolis roughly 6.4 km (4 miles) long where families live among the tombs, some for generations -- a working neighborhood of graves and homes with schools, water and electricity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_the_Dead_(Cairo)

question: Around the year 1382 an emir built a grand caravanserai -- a walled inn for traveling merchants -- in the middle of Cairo. Over the centuries it swelled into a maze of covered alleys packed with lantern-makers, spice sellers, goldsmiths and coppersmiths, and it has traded non-stop for more than 600 years. What is Cairo's famous medieval bazaar called?
context: Khan el-Khalili was founded around 1382, when the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili built a large khan (a merchants' caravanserai) here; it grew into one of Cairo's greatest bazaars and still bustles today in the medieval heart of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_el-Khalili

question: When the Great Pyramid was new, it did not have the rough, stepped surface we see today -- it gleamed, sheathed in a smooth outer skin of polished white limestone so bright it dazzled in the sun. After a huge earthquake in 1303 shook this casing loose, where did most of that beautiful white stone end up?
answer: carted off to build medieval Cairo
choices: carted off to build medieval Cairo
buried beneath the drifting desert sand
ground up to make builders' cement
context: A massive earthquake in 1303 loosened the Great Pyramid's smooth white Tura-limestone casing, and medieval Cairenes carted it away to build the city -- into structures such as Sultan al-Hasan's mosque (1356) and, later, Muhammad Ali's Alabaster Mosque -- leaving the stepped stone core we see today. Source: thevintagenews.com; scienceinsights.org

question: When the Fatimid general Jawhar founded a brand-new royal capital in Egypt in 969 AD, he named it after a planet that was rising in the sky at that very moment -- a planet the Arabs called al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star.' From that name comes Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira, 'the Victorious.' After which planet was Cairo named?
context: Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira ('the Victorious' or 'the Vanquisher'), comes from al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star' -- the planet Mars -- which was rising in the sky as the Fatimid general Jawhar founded the city in 969 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo  (Legend.)

question: The ancient Egyptians called their country Kemet, 'the Black Land,' after the dark, rich soil that fed their whole civilization -- set against the barren 'Red Land' desert stretching away on either side. What natural event laid down this fertile black soil, year after year?
answer: the Nile's yearly flood, dropping fresh silt
choices: the Nile's yearly flood, dropping fresh silt
ash blown in from distant volcanoes
rotting reeds from the river marshes
fine dust carried on the desert winds
context: The Nile's yearly flood spread a fresh layer of black silt across the valley, making Egypt astonishingly fertile; Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the Black Land,' set against Deshret, 'the Red Land' of the surrounding desert. Source: historycollection.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deshret

question: Table Mountain rises straight up behind Cape Town, its summit a broad, level plateau rather than a peak. On many days a low white cloud forms along the top and pours slowly over the mountain's front edge, hanging there for hours before it burns off in the sun. Capetonians long ago gave this recurring cloud an affectionate nickname. What do they call it?
context: That draping cloud is Cape Town's beloved 'tablecloth,' formed when moist sea air is forced up the slope and cools into cloud right at the rim, then spills over and vanishes in the warmer air below. Locals say the mountain has 'laid its tablecloth.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; hiketablemountain.co.za.

question: Cape Town has a playful old legend to explain Table Mountain's cloud. Long ago, they say, a retired Dutch pirate named Jan van Hunks sat smoking his pipe on the mountain when a mysterious stranger appeared and dared him to a pipe-smoking contest. For days the two puffed furiously, their smoke piling higher into a vast white cloud, until van Hunks realised, too late, the terrifying identity of his rival. In the legend, who had van Hunks been smoking against?
context: In the folktale the stranger was the Devil, and a lightning bolt ended their duel; when the 'tablecloth' pours over Table Mountain, Capetonians joke that Jan van Hunks and the Devil are at it again. It is legend, not history. Source: awoltours.co.za; the-legends.fandom.com/wiki/Jan_van_Hunks.

question: Ride to the flat top of Table Mountain and, scrambling over the warm summit rocks, you will almost certainly meet its commonest little mammal: a plump, round, tail-less creature about the size of a large guinea-pig, basking lazily in the sun. Locals have a friendly name for this cheerful rock-dweller. What do they call it?
context: The dassie, or rock hyrax, is a plump, tail-less little mammal that lives in colonies among the warm summit rocks and is the animal visitors spot most often on top of Table Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; awoltours.co.za.

question: Most visitors reach Table Mountain's summit on the cableway, first opened in 1929, whose cars glide up the sheer cliff in under five minutes and carry up to 65 people at a time. These particular cars are famous as one of only a handful of their kind in the world, thanks to one unusual thing they do on every trip up and down. What is unusual about Table Mountain's cable cars?
answer: the floor rotates a full turn
choices: the floor rotates a full turn
the two cars pass midway up
the roof opens for the view
the cabin is walled in glass
context: Since 1997 the cableway's 'Rotair' cars have a floor that spins a full 360 degrees during the climb, so all 65 passengers see the whole panorama without moving — one of only a handful of rotating cableways on Earth. The cableway first opened on 4 October 1929. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain_Aerial_Cableway.

question: The cableway sets visitors down near one end of Table Mountain's flat top, but that spot is not quite the mountain's highest. The true summit lies a little higher, out across the broad plateau, and reaching it means a walk of a few kilometres over the level rock. By what name is this true high point of Table Mountain known?
context: Maclear's Beacon, a stone cairn about 1,086 m (3,563 ft) high, is the true summit of Table Mountain — a little higher than the upper cableway station. Sir Thomas Maclear built it in 1865 as a trigonometrical survey station. Devil's Peak, Lion's Head and Signal Hill are the neighbouring heights around the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain.

question: Table Mountain is not cloaked in forest but in a low, wiry, wind-hardened shrubland — dense with tough little bushes and dazzling wildflowers that hug the rocky slopes. This distinctive Cape vegetation carpets most of the mountain and the surrounding peninsula, and it carries its own Afrikaans name. What is this kind of Cape shrubland called?
context: Fynbos — Afrikaans for 'fine bush' — is the fine-leaved, flower-rich shrubland that makes up about 80% of the Cape Floral Kingdom and cloaks most of Table Mountain. Chaparral, maquis and matorral are its cousins in California, the Mediterranean and Chile. Source: wwf.panda.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fynbos.

question: Botanists have counted the wild flowering plants of Table Mountain and its national park: around 2,200 different species, all packed onto one flat-topped mountain. They often set this figure against the entire native flora of Great Britain — an island many hundreds of times larger than the mountain. How does Table Mountain's plant tally compare with all of Britain's?
answer: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
choices: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
it holds about half of Britain's flora
it holds about a tenth of Britain's flora
