context: Kelp only looks like a plant. A giant kelp is a brown alga (a seaweed); its body is called a thallus, not a plant with true roots, stems, and leaves. The Great African Sea Forest fringes Cape Town and runs over 1,000 km up the cold coast toward Namibia -- said to be the only forest of giant 'sea bamboo' (Ecklonia maxima) on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelp_forest ; seachangeproject.com/great-african-seaforest/

question: In the giant-kelp forests off the Pacific coast of California, each frond is rooted to the seabed in dim light far below and must race upward through the water to reach the sunlight -- and giant kelp is one of the fastest-growing living things on the whole planet. On a good day, how much taller can a single frond grow between one sunrise and the next?
context: Giant kelp can shoot up 30-60 cm -- up to about two feet -- in a single day, among the fastest growth of any living thing, as it races sunlight to the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelp_forest

question: Off California's Monterey coast a single giant kelp can raise a swaying tower 45 metres tall -- as high as a fifteen-storey building -- straight up from the seabed to the sunlit surface. Down below, it grips bare rock with a root-like tangle called a 'holdfast'. But a holdfast only anchors the bottom; what keeps the towering frond standing upright all the way to the top?
choices: The steady pull of the tide.
context: A giant kelp grips bare rock with a root-like 'holdfast' and floats upright on rows of gas-filled bladders called pneumatocysts. Macrocystis pyrifera off California is the largest of all algae, reaching 45 m (150 ft) and sometimes 60 m -- and it grows only in cool water below about 21 C (70 F), which is why kelp forests cling to cold-current coasts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrocystis

question: The mangroves of the Sundarbans do something a tropical rainforest cannot: instead of holding their carbon in wood and leaves that rot and release it within a few years, they sink it down into deep, waterlogged, airless mud where it stays locked away for centuries -- burying several times more carbon, acre for acre, than a rainforest. Scientists have a special name for the carbon that coastal forests like this lock into their drowned, oxygen-starved soils. What do they call it?
context: Mangroves are 'blue carbon' powerhouses: by burying carbon in deep, airless, waterlogged mud they lock it away for centuries and store several times more per hectare than tropical rainforest (one commonly cited estimate is up to ~1,000 tonnes per hectare versus ~200 for rainforest), sequestering it 2-4x faster. 'Blue carbon' is the name for carbon captured by the ocean's coastal ecosystems -- mangroves, seagrasses, and salt marshes -- as opposed to the 'green carbon' held by forests on land. Source: marinebiodiversity.ca/mangroves-the-unsung-heroes-of-blue-carbon-storage/

question: Northern Chile's Atacama Desert runs right down to the ocean's edge, yet it is the driest place on Earth outside the poles — some weather stations have gone years without a single drop of rain. The sea is right there, but the current sweeping past just offshore is a main reason the land stays bone-dry. Which current is it?
context: Cold water chills the air just above it, and cold air cannot rise to form rain — so the Humboldt breeds fog but almost never a downpour. The sea off this coast sits near 16°C (61°F) when tropical seas usually top 25°C. The current is a MAIN cause of the aridity, working alongside the sinking air of the subtropical high and the Andes rain shadow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current.

question: In the Atacama's hyper-arid core, some riverbeds have lain bone-dry for 120,000 years and a few weather stations have never once recorded rain. The ground is so lifeless and parched that NASA hauls its rovers and instruments there to rehearse missions — treating this stretch of Chilean desert as a practice stand-in for which world?
context: The Atacama doubles as Mars. Its core averages only about 15 mm of rain a year, and one station logged just 0.5 mm a year from 1964 to 2001; evidence suggests parts saw no significant rain from 1570 to 1971. That Mars-like dryness makes it NASA's favorite rehearsal ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert; history.com/articles/driest-place-earth-atacama-desert.

question: Rain almost never falls on the Atacama coast, so the little water that keeps this shore from being utterly barren arrives another way: a thick sea-fog that climbs the coastal cliffs at dawn off the cold current offshore, then vanishes as the sun burns through. Chileans have their own name for this life-giving mist. What is it called?
context: The mist is the camanchaca, and the Atacama is the largest fog desert on Earth. In a land with almost no rain, that dawn fog rolling off the cold sea IS the water. (The cassimbo is its Angolan cousin, the garúa the coastal fog of Peru, and the haar a cold sea-fog off Britain.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert.

question: In the rainless hills above Chungungo, Chile, villagers hang huge nylon mesh screens — atrapanieblas, or 'fog catchers' — across the ridgetops to comb drinking water out of the drifting sea-mist. It sounds like it should yield a mere trickle, yet the largest fog-catching arrays near Huasco proved astonishingly productive. Roughly how much water can such a fog farm wring from the mist on a good day?
context: Tens of thousands of liters. Large fog-catching towers near Huasco were reported to yield 10,000–50,000 liters of water a day, and the village of Chungungo once ran 94 nylon-mesh atrapanieblas to supply about 300 people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_collection.

question: Along southern Africa's Atlantic shore, the cold Benguela Current chills the coast into the Namib Desert — a place where dunes hundreds of meters tall pour straight down into the pounding surf, and with almost no rain the morning sea-fog is the only dependable water. The Namib has stayed arid for something like 55 to 80 million years, a stretch of time that, by many accounts, makes it the world's ___?
context: By many accounts the world's oldest desert — a rival to the Atacama for both age and dryness. The cold Benguela Current, running from Cape Point up to about 16°S, breeds the fog that on more than 180 days a year is the Namib's main water. Its Sossusvlei dunes, up to about 300 m, are among the tallest on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benguela_Current.

question: Fog off the cold Benguela Current cloaks Namibia's northern Atlantic shore so thickly that sailing ships lost their bearings and ran aground in the murk. Their rusting hulks still lie half-buried in the sand as the dunes slowly swallow them. Portuguese sailors called this shore 'The Gates of Hell'; the local San people named it 'The Land God Made in Anger.' By what name is this coast known today?
context: The Skeleton Coast — named both for the whale and seal bones that once littered it and for the skeletal hulks of wrecked ships. The dunes still hold named wrecks: the Eduard Bohlen (now stranded far inland as the sand advanced), the Otavi (1945), the Dunedin Star, and the Portuguese Bom Jesus, aground since the 1530s and one of the oldest shipwrecks ever found in sub-Saharan Africa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeleton_Coast.

question: In the heart of the Namib stands Deadvlei, a blinding-white clay pan ringed by some of the tallest dunes on Earth. Scattered across it are the black, twisted remains of camel-thorn trees that died roughly 600 to 700 years ago, when shifting dunes choked off the river that once fed them. Yet the trees still stand, whole and unbroken, after all those centuries. Why has the dead wood never decayed away?
answer: it was too dry to rot away
choices: it was too dry to rot away
salt from the pan preserved it
context: Too dry to rot. With almost no moisture, the fungi and bacteria that drive decay cannot survive, so the camel-thorn wood never rotted — the desert sun has simply scorched it black. The trees died around 1340–1430, when drought and encroaching dunes cut off the Tsauchab river. Deadvlei is ringed by Sossusvlei's giant dunes, the tallest nicknamed 'Big Daddy' at about 325 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadvlei; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sossusvlei.

question: On a world map, slide South America east across the Atlantic and Brazil's bulge tucks almost perfectly into the notch of West Africa's Gulf of Guinea -- even along the deep-water edge the coastlines miss by under 130 km. What best explains so snug a fit?
answer: The two continents were once joined as a single landmass.
choices: The two continents were once joined as a single landmass.
An ancient land bridge once linked the two facing coasts.
Ocean currents carved the two coasts into matching curves.
The two continents are drifting toward a future collision.
context: This coastline 'fit' was the first great clue to continental drift. Alfred Wegener pointed it out in 1912, matching not just the visible shores but the edges of the continental shelves: along the 500-fathom (about 900 m) contour, the Americas and Africa/Europe line up with less than 130 km of mismatch -- like torn halves of one sheet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea

question: In 1912 the German scientist and polar explorer Alfred Wegener argued that all of today's continents had once been fused into one giant landmass, ringed by a single world-ocean. What name did Wegener give that lost supercontinent?
context: Pangaea is Greek for 'all Earth', and the single ocean surrounding it was Panthalassa, 'all sea'. It assembled about 335 million years ago and began breaking apart about 200 million years ago, first splitting into a northern half, Laurasia, and a southern half, Gondwana. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea

question: Critics dismissed Wegener's matching coastlines as coincidence, so he turned to Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived only in freshwater ponds and lakes and could never have crossed the open salt sea. Where its fossils lie became his hardest proof. Where do Mesosaurus fossils actually turn up?
answer: On the facing shores of Brazil and West Africa.
choices: On the facing shores of Brazil and West Africa.
On the facing shores of India and East Africa.
On the facing shores of Australia and Antarctica.
On the facing shores of Arabia and the Horn of Africa.
context: A freshwater animal could never have swum across a salt ocean, so identical Mesosaurus fossils in matching Permian rocks on the Brazilian AND West African coasts -- and nowhere in between -- meant the two shores were once joined. Wegener found the same pattern in the seed-fern Glossopteris and the reptile Lystrosaurus, smeared across South America, Africa, India and Antarctica. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/Mesosaurus

question: Just below the 8,849 m summit of Mount Everest -- Earth's highest point -- the pale Qomolangma limestone is studded with fossils of trilobites and crinoids. Since those animals lived in only one kind of habitat, what was Everest's summit rock originally?
answer: The floor of a warm, shallow sea.
choices: The floor of a warm, shallow sea.
The bed of a cold mountain lake.
The mud of a wide river delta.
The soil of a swampy forest.
context: Trilobites and crinoids (the 'sea lilies') lived only in the ocean, so their fossils prove this pale summit rock -- the Qomolangma Formation -- formed on a sea floor. It is Ordovician marine limestone laid down about 450 million years ago; fragments of trilobites, crinoids and ostracods turn up in rock just about 6 m below the 8,849 m summit. How that old ocean floor reached the roof of the world is the next question -- the plates did it. Source: https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/summit-limestone.html

question: Thingvellir in Iceland draws visitors to Almannagja, a rift canyon where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge -- the seam that runs down the middle of the Atlantic -- breaks above the ocean onto dry land. Here you can do something possible on almost no other dry land on Earth. What can a visitor do standing in this rift?
answer: Stand in the gap between two great plates as they pull apart.
choices: Stand in the gap between two great plates as they pull apart.
Watch two plates crash together and heave up a mountain.
See one great plate dive beneath another into the mantle.
Feel two plates grind sideways as they scrape past.
context: The two plates are the North American and the Eurasian, separating about 2 cm a year; over the last 10,000 years the Thingvellir rift has widened about 70 m and dropped about 40 m. As they part, magma wells up to make fresh crust -- this is seafloor spreading, normally hidden kilometres under the ocean but here walkable on land. Source: https://www.thingvellir.is/en/education/nature/tectonic-movements/

question: A loop of volcanoes and earthquakes about 40,000 km long circles the entire Pacific Ocean -- the 'Ring of Fire' -- holding about 90% of the world's earthquakes and two-thirds of its active volcanoes. What is happening all around the Pacific's rim to build such a violent ring?
answer: The ocean floor is diving down beneath the surrounding plates.
choices: The ocean floor is diving down beneath the surrounding plates.
The plates are pulling apart to open brand-new seafloor.
The continents are sliding sideways along the ocean's edge.
A single giant hotspot is melting the whole Pacific rim.
context: This diving-down is called subduction: the dense Pacific seafloor plunges into trenches beneath the lighter plates around it, melting and feeding the volcanoes above. About 90% of the world's earthquakes and roughly two-thirds of its active volcanoes ring this boundary. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: Mount Everest and the whole Himalayan range are still growing -- Everest rises roughly 4 mm every year at a deep boundary called the Main Himalayan Thrust. Something enormous keeps shoving this range higher into the sky. What is driving the Himalayas upward?
answer: The Indian plate is ramming north into the rest of Asia.
choices: The Indian plate is ramming north into the rest of Asia.
A hotspot of rising magma is punching up through Tibet.
The Pacific plate is sinking into a trench beneath Asia.
Two plates are pulling apart and stretching the crust thin.
context: India, once part of the southern supercontinent Gondwana, drifted north and collided with Asia; the crust had nowhere to go but up, crumpling into the highest mountains on Earth. The range still rises about 4 mm a year at the Main Himalayan Thrust, the boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest

question: In September 2005, near Ethiopia's Dabbahu volcano in the Afar desert, more than 160 earthquakes struck and then the ground tore open along a crack 60 km long and up to 8 m wide -- in just ten days. Geologists realised they were watching, live, the start of something that usually takes millions of years. What was being born in the desert?
answer: The floor of a brand-new ocean tearing open.
choices: The floor of a brand-new ocean tearing open.
A chain of new volcanoes rising from a hotspot.
A giant crater left by a volcano's collapse.
A canyon carved by sudden desert flash floods.
context: The Afar sits on the East African Rift, where the African plate is splitting into the Nubian and Somali plates at about 8-9 mm a year. The low, hot Afar Depression is a baby ocean basin; one day the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden will pour in. The 2005 Dabbahu event let scientists watch a continent begin to break apart in real time. Source: https://earthlymission.com/new-ocean-forming-africa-35-mile-crack-ethiopia-2005-dabbahu-fissure-afar-rift/

question: California's San Andreas Fault runs about 1,200 km along a 'transform' boundary, where the Pacific and North American plates grind horizontally past each other. The Pacific side, carrying Los Angeles, creeps steadily northwest a few centimetres a year. If that motion just keeps up for about 20 million years, what becomes of Los Angeles?
answer: It slides north to sit right beside San Francisco.
choices: It slides north to sit right beside San Francisco.
It slides north and rams into the Oregon coast.
It slides north and drifts out into the open Pacific.
It slides north to be swallowed at Alaska's trench.
context: Because the plates grind horizontally past each other (a right-lateral transform boundary) at about 3-4 cm a year, Los Angeles isn't rising or sinking -- it is travelling north. When the fault lurched on 18 April 1906, it tore about 430 km at magnitude ~7.8 and jolted roads and fences sideways by up to about 6 m, wrecking much of San Francisco. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault

question: The Challenger Deep, in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is the lowest point on Earth's surface -- a subduction trench where the Pacific plate plunges beneath the smaller Mariana plate. In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste all the way to its bottom. How does the depth of Challenger Deep compare with the height of Mount Everest?
answer: It is deeper than Everest is tall.
choices: It is deeper than Everest is tall.
It is about as deep as Everest is tall.
It is about half as deep as Everest is tall.
It is about twice as deep as Everest is tall.
context: Challenger Deep reaches about 10,935 m down -- nearly 11 km -- while Everest rises 8,849 m, so Everest could sink into the trench and still leave roughly 2 km of water overhead. This is subduction at its extreme: the old, dense Pacific seafloor bends and dives into the deepest gash on the planet. The Trieste descent came on 23 January 1960. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench

question: The Hawaiian islands grow steadily older toward the northwest, because a fixed 'hotspot' -- a plume of hot rock deep in the mantle -- keeps punching fresh volcanoes up through the drifting Pacific plate above it. Far out to sea, the trail of old volcanoes makes a sharp bend of about 120 degrees. What single event does that kink in the volcano chain record?
answer: The moment the Pacific plate changed the direction it moved.
choices: The moment the Pacific plate changed the direction it moved.
A time when the hotspot's eruptions grew far more violent.
The place where the chain rams into the Aleutian Trench.
The spot where two separate hotspot trails once crossed.
context: The bend, dated to about 47 million years ago, marks when the Pacific plate swung from heading nearly north to heading northwest; the hotspot stayed put while the plate above it turned, so the older Emperor seamounts point one way and the younger Hawaiian chain another. The whole Hawaiian-Emperor chain runs about 6,200 km with over 80 volcanoes; its newest, Kamaehuakanaloa (once called Loihi), is still growing underwater off Hawaii island. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: Wegener's drifting continents sat unproven for decades because no one could show the 'engine'. Then, after World War II, Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen mapped a deep rift down the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and in 1963 Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews found the seafloor's magnetism recorded in matching, mirror-image stripes on either side of that ridge. What did those symmetrical stripes finally prove was happening?
answer: New seafloor forms at the ridge and spreads out both sides.
choices: New seafloor forms at the ridge and spreads out both sides.
The whole Earth is slowly swelling and cracking its crust.
The continents plough forward through the solid ocean floor.
Meteor strikes shattered the crust into the moving plates.
context: The mirror-image magnetic stripes showed that fresh crust forms at the ridge, records Earth's magnetic field as it hardens, and is carried away on both sides as the seafloor spreads -- Harry Hess's idea, now confirmed. This finally gave Wegener's continents their engine (heat-driven mantle convection), and the unified theory took its modern name, plate tectonics, in the 1960s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading

question: The Indian subcontinent is far from standing still — it is still ploughing north into the rest of Asia, and geologists love to point out that it creeps forward at almost exactly the speed of one familiar thing that grows. What grows at about the same pace as India's slow northward march?
context: India drifts north at roughly 5 cm a year — about the rate fingernails grow — and because the collision is unfinished, the Himalayas are still being pushed upward today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_plate

question: North of the Himalayas spreads the Tibetan Plateau — a cold, thin-aired highland larger than all of Western Europe, its whole mass thickened and heaved up by the India-Asia collision. What sweeping nickname has this vast tableland long carried?
choices: the Land of the Thunder Dragon
the Land of the Morning Calm
context: The Tibetan Plateau covers about 2.5 million km2 — larger than Western Europe — at an average height near 4,500 m, all thickened and lifted by the same India-Asia collision; its nickname is 'the Roof of the World.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Plateau

question: Mountaineers dream of the 'eight-thousanders' — the 14 peaks on Earth that rise above 8,000 m. You might picture them scattered across the continents. In reality, how many of the 14 stand in the single Himalaya-Karakoram belt raised by India's crash into Asia?
context: Every one of Earth's 14 peaks above 8,000 m stands in the Himalaya or the neighbouring Karakoram — the entire roster of the planet's tallest mountains, all raised by this single continental pile-up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander

question: Nanga Parbat soars 8,126 m over the mountains of northern Pakistan, standing at the sharp western corner of the Himalayan arc where India's plate drives hardest into the crust. Guinness World Records lists this single peak for one geological superlative. Which is it?
choices: the most isolated mountain on Earth
context: Guinness World Records lists Nanga Parbat as the fastest-rising mountain; thermochronology puts its uplift near 7 mm a year, concentrated at the western Himalayan syntaxis where India's push is squeezed into a knot. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/fastest-rising-mountain  (Legend.)

question: Just below the very summit of Mount Everest, 8,849 m up, climbers have chipped out pale limestone and split it open to reveal fossils of little animals that lived on a shallow sea floor about 450 million years ago. Which creatures lay sealed in the roof of the world?
context: The summit stone is the Ordovician Qomolangma Formation — marine limestone bearing trilobites, crinoids (sea lilies) and brachiopods laid down on a tropical seafloor ~450 million years ago. The famous Himalayan ammonites come from lower rock, not the summit. Source: https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/summit-limestone.html

question: The sea-floor rock now perched at the top of the Himalayas was once the bed of a real ocean — the great sea that lay between India and Asia until the two continents slammed together and squeezed it shut around 50 million years ago. What was this vanished ocean called?
context: The seafloor now atop the Himalayas was the bed of the Tethys Ocean, the sea that once separated India from Asia; as India rammed north the Tethys closed (final closure ~50-60 million years ago) and its floor crumpled into the peaks. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012821X16306707

question: In the folded ranges of western Iran, the same kind of continent-against-continent collision that raised the Himalayas is unfolding today — a whole plate grinds north into Eurasia at about 25 mm a year, crumpling up the Zagros Mountains. Which plate is doing the pushing?
context: The Arabian plate drives into Eurasia at about 25 mm a year, still crumpling up Iran's Zagros Mountains — a live continent-continent collision, the same engine that built the Himalayas and the Alps. Source: https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/science-and-policy/plate-tectonic-stories/zagros-ramge/

question: When ocean floor collides with a continent it dives down into the mantle and is destroyed. But India is a slab of light continental rock, and for 50 million years it has kept ramming into Asia without vanishing. What has India's leading edge been doing all that time?
answer: forcing its way in under Asia
choices: forcing its way in under Asia
piling up as a coastal range
context: Because India is thick, buoyant continental crust it could not subduct like ocean floor; it forced partway under Asia, roughly doubling the crust's thickness there and buckling the surface up into the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayan peaks. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/why-mount-everest-can-grow-and-shrink-plate-tectonics

question: The Matterhorn rises like a stone fang above Zermatt, Switzerland, deep in the heart of the European Alps. Yet geologists found that the rock making up its very summit does not belong to Europe at all — it was hauled here from a different continental plate when the Alps were crushed upward. Which plate does the Matterhorn's peak come from?
context: The Matterhorn's summit is the Dent Blanche nappe — a fragment of the African (Adriatic) plate stranded on European rock, carried at least ~500 km from the African margin as Africa closed the Tethys and crushed up the Alps. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dent_Blanche_nappe

question: The Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States are soft, green, forest-covered ridges today. Yet they are ancient — heaved up 300 million years ago when the supercontinent Pangaea assembled — and geologists' models suggest that in their towering youth these worn-down hills once stood as tall as which range?
context: Raised in the Alleghanian orogeny ~300 million years ago as Pangaea assembled, the Appalachians once towered — models suggest peaks near 20,000-30,000 ft, rivalling today's Himalayas — before hundreds of millions of years of erosion wore them to green stubs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alleghanian_orogeny  (Legend.)

question: Long before the Atlantic Ocean existed, the Appalachian Mountains did not stop at the coast — they ran on unbroken into what is now Europe, part of one gigantic mountain chain across Pangaea. When the Atlantic tore open and widened, it ripped that chain in two. Where does the Appalachians' severed other half rise today?
context: Before the Atlantic opened, the Appalachians and the Caledonian mountains of Scotland, Scandinavia and eastern Greenland were one continuous chain (the Central Pangaean Mountains), later split apart as the ocean widened. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caledonian_orogeny

question: Mount Everest is still rising about 2 millimetres a year — but a 2024 study delivered a surprise: nearly half of that lift has nothing to do with India shoving into Asia. Some other force close by has been lightening the crust and letting the peak spring up higher. What is giving Everest this extra push skyward?
answer: a river carving away nearby rock
choices: a river carving away nearby rock
context: About 89,000 years ago the Arun River was captured by the Kosi system; the combined rivers gouged out billions of tonnes of rock, and the lightened crust springs upward (isostatic rebound), adding roughly half of Everest's ~2 mm-a-year rise (Nature Geoscience, 2024, UCL). Source: https://www.sci.news/othersciences/geoscience/mount-everest-river-13304.html

question: Off Australia's northeast coast, in the warm Coral Sea, tiny coral animals have piled limestone into a chain about 2,300 km long over millions of years — a single living thing so vast that astronauts can pick it out from orbit. Which reef is this?
context: The Great Barrier Reef, off Queensland in the Coral Sea, runs about 2,300 km (1,430 miles) — the largest structure ever built by living creatures, the work of countless tiny coral polyps over millions of years, and so vast it can be seen from space. (NOAA — oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gbrlargeststructure.html)

question: Divers describe a living reef as glowing gold, green, and pink — but strip away its tenants and the coral itself is a pale, almost see-through animal. Those vivid colors actually come from millions of tiny partners crowded inside the coral's own tissue. What are these hidden lodgers?
context: Those partners are microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. They live inside the coral's tissue and use sunlight to make food, feeding the coral and painting it its brilliant colors; the coral animal itself is nearly colorless. (Wikipedia, 'Coral bleaching')

question: During a marine heatwave, stressed corals across an entire reef drive out the tiny partners that live inside their tissue and feed them, all at once. Scientists have a one-word name for this heat-triggered event that can sweep a whole reef in a single hot summer. What is it?
context: This is coral bleaching. When the water gets too warm the stressed coral expels its zooxanthellae; with the algae gone, the clear tissue reveals the white limestone skeleton beneath, and the reef turns bone-white. A bleached coral is not dead yet — if the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and it recovers. (Wikipedia, 'Coral bleaching')

question: You might think a reef the size of Italy is far too vast to be badly harmed in a single hot summer. Yet when a marine heatwave struck the northern Great Barrier Reef in 2016, later surveys measured how much of that region's coral had died in that single event. What share did they find?
context: Back-to-back marine heatwaves in 2016 and 2017 caused the most severe and widespread bleaching ever recorded on the Great Barrier Reef; the 2016 event alone killed an estimated 29-50% of the coral in the northern section. Reefs can recover from a hot year — but not when struck again before they heal. (Wikipedia, 'Coral bleaching'; NOAA)

question: Off the coast of Belize, the Great Blue Hole is a startlingly perfect dark-blue circle punched into the pale ring of Lighthouse Reef — about 300 m across and 125 m deep, far deeper than the shallow reef around it. Geologists have worked out how such a deep, round pit came to sit inside a reef. What was it originally?
answer: a cave on dry land, later drowned by the sea
choices: a cave on dry land, later drowned by the sea
a crater blasted out by a falling meteorite
the throat of an ancient undersea volcano
a pit bored by a giant ocean whirlpool
context: The Great Blue Hole began as a limestone cave on dry land during the ice ages, when the sea was far lower; when the oceans rose it flooded and its roof collapsed, leaving a near-circular pit about 318 m across and 124 m deep. Stalactites recovered from inside prove it was once a dry cavern above the waterline. Jacques Cousteau charted it from his ship Calypso in 1971 and made it world-famous. (Wikipedia, 'Great Blue Hole')

question: In the Pacific Ocean, Enewetak is a near-perfect ring of low coral islands enclosing a calm turquoise lagoon, with open ocean on every side and no larger island anywhere in the middle. Coral slowly built this circular reef around a volcanic island that has since disappeared. What is a formation like this called?
context: This is an atoll — a ring of coral reef enclosing a lagoon where a volcanic island once stood, like Enewetak in the Pacific. Most of the world's roughly 440 atolls lie in the Pacific Ocean. (Wikipedia, 'Atoll')

question: Charles Darwin, sailing the Pacific aboard the Beagle, knew that reef-building coral can only grow in warm, sunlit water near the surface. So how could a living coral ring end up alone in the deep open ocean, with only a lagoon inside and no island to grow on? Darwin's bold answer explained why the coral had kept building steadily upward for ages. What did Darwin realize was slowly taking place?
answer: the volcanic island was slowly sinking
choices: the volcanic island was slowly sinking
the volcanic island was slowly eroding away
the ocean floor was slowly rising
the sea level was slowly climbing
context: Darwin's subsidence theory: coral first fringes a volcanic island; as the volcano slowly sinks, the coral grows upward to stay in the sunlit shallows — passing through fringing reef, then barrier reef, then atoll — until only a ring of reef and a lagoon remain. He was proven right in 1952, when geologists drilling through Enewetak Atoll hit volcanic basalt about 1,400 m down, and the delighted team put up a sign reading 'Darwin was right.' (Wikipedia, 'Atoll'; Britannica; Smithsonian / ScienceBlogs on the 1952 Enewetak drilling)

question: The Maldives is a nation of nearly 1,200 islands strung across 26 coral atoll rings in the Indian Ocean, each island built entirely of coral rather than solid rock. Among all the world's nations, what record does the Maldives hold?
choices: the most crowded country on Earth
context: The Maldives, built entirely of coral across 26 atoll rings and about 1,192 islands, is the lowest and flattest country on Earth — its highest natural point is only about 2.4 m (under 8 feet) above the sea. (Wikipedia, 'Geography of the Maldives')

question: Mount Mazama once towered over Oregon's Cascade Range until, about 7,700 years ago, it blew its top in a colossal eruption and its summit crashed downward. The vast bowl left behind slowly filled with rain and snowmelt to become Crater Lake. What do geologists call the giant basin it left?
context: A caldera forms when a volcano empties its underground magma chamber and its summit collapses into the void -- far larger than a crater, the smaller pit around a volcano's vent. Mount Mazama's collapse about 7,700 years ago left the caldera that Crater Lake now fills. Source: USGS, Geology and History Summary of Mount Mazama and Crater Lake (usgs.gov).

question: Crater Lake is huge and remarkably deep, yet its water is among the purest on Earth -- a vivid, clear sapphire blue with barely any sediment. Its entire volume is naturally replaced only about once every 150 years. What fills this high Cascade lake?
context: With no muddy river flowing in, sunlight sinks deep into the clear water and the blue wavelengths scatter back to your eye -- the source of that intense color. Crater Lake's whole volume renews only about every 150 years, kept full by the deep winter snows of the Cascades. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Crater Lake sits nearly 6,200 feet up in Oregon's Cascade Range, a broad blue sheet some 20 square miles across, filling the caldera left when Mount Mazama fell. Its clear sapphire water is famous the world over. Which United States record does Crater Lake hold?
answer: the deepest lake in the United States
choices: the deepest lake in the United States
the oldest lake in the United States
the largest lake in the United States
the highest lake in the United States
context: At 1,949 feet (594 m) deep, Crater Lake is the deepest lake in the United States -- and among the ten deepest on Earth. It sits high in the Cascades, spreads about 20 square miles, and fills a young caldera, yet it is not the highest, largest, or oldest U.S. lake -- only the deepest. Lake Baikal and Lake Tanganyika plunge far deeper elsewhere in the world, so the 'in the United States' qualifier keeps the claim true. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: In an ordinary lake, a white dinner plate lowered on a rope vanishes into the murk within a few feet. Scientists tried exactly this on Crater Lake -- and the plate stayed clearly visible as it sank down, and down. About how far down could they still see it?
context: The white disk is called a Secchi disk. In 1997, researchers measured clarity of 142 feet (43 m) at Crater Lake -- among the clearest freshwater ever recorded. With almost no sediment or algae to cloud it, sunlight drives deep, feeding the lake's legendary blue. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Crater Lake's caldera was not the end of the story: after Mount Mazama fell, fresh eruptions built a brand-new volcano on the sunken caldera floor, and its cinder cone grew tall enough to poke above the water. What did Crater Lake champion William Gladstone Steel name this small young cone in 1885?
context: Wizard Island is a small cinder cone that grew inside the caldera AFTER Mount Mazama collapsed -- a young volcano rising from the floor of the ruined old one. Early Crater Lake champion William Gladstone Steel named it in 1885 because its cone reminded him of a sorcerer's (wizard's) pointed hat. Source: William Gladstone Steel (en.wikipedia.org).

question: For well over a century, a full-size hemlock log nicknamed the 'Old Man of the Lake' has ridden the waters of Crater Lake -- first recorded in 1896, and preserved so perfectly by the cold, pure water that the tree is centuries old. What is so strange about the way this log rides the water?
answer: It floats upright, standing straight up like a post.
choices: It floats upright, standing straight up like a post.
It floats fully submerged, gliding just below the surface.
It spins slowly in place, turning like a compass needle.
It freezes into the winter ice and thaws free each spring.
context: The 'Old Man of the Lake' stands about 1.2 m (4 ft) proud of the surface and has bobbed vertically since it was first noted in 1896 -- over 130 years upright. The frigid, mineral-poor water preserves the wood so well that carbon dating puts the tree at 450+ years old. In a 1938 study, John Doerr found it wandered at least 62 miles (100 km) around the lake in a single summer, moving most on windy days. Source: Old Man of the Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: The eruption that destroyed Mount Mazama and carved Crater Lake's caldera about 7,700 years ago was the largest the Cascade Range has produced in a million years. Set beside the famous 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens -- which flattened whole forests -- Mazama's climactic blast was roughly how many times more powerful?
context: Mazama disgorged roughly 50 cubic km of magma -- about 40 times what St. Helens produced in 1980. Its pale 'Mazama ash' settled across the Pacific Northwest and beyond, and geologists still dig up that single bright layer as a natural time-stamp; traces have been found as far away as Greenland. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org); Mazama ash, Crater Lake Institute (craterlakeinstitute.com).

question: The Klamath people were living in this land when Mount Mazama erupted, and their oral tradition may preserve an eyewitness memory of it. In the story, Llao, spirit of the underworld, dwelt beneath the mountain, while Skell ruled the sky; the two waged a furious battle. How does the Klamath account say it ended?
answer: Skell hurled the mountaintop down onto Llao, sealing him deep below.
choices: Skell hurled the mountaintop down onto Llao, sealing him deep below.
Llao buried Skell's people under a river of fire and ash.
The two spirits made peace and agreed to share the mountain.
Skell fled across the western sea and never returned.
context: This is Klamath ORAL TRADITION, not written history -- but because the Klamath lived in this land when Mazama fell about 7,700 years ago, many regard the story as a genuine memory of the eruption, carried down across thousands of years. In the tale, the mountain's collapse seals Llao in the underworld beneath what is now Crater Lake. Source: The Creation of Crater Lake, Klamath tradition (traveloregon.com).  (Legend.)

question: In the small northern-Italian town of Cremona, around the year 1700, Antonio Stradivari built stringed instruments so perfect that a single one now sells for millions and is called the finest ever made. Cremona is famous above all for making which instrument?
context: Antonio Stradivari (c.1644-1737) spent almost his whole long life in Cremona, and any instrument he made is called a 'Stradivarius.' He built violas and cellos too, but it is his violins the world calls the finest ever made. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.

question: Antonio Stradivari signed every instrument that left his Cremona workshop with the same mark - one naming himself and carrying the Latin word 'Cremonensis,' meaning 'of Cremona.' What did he use to sign his work?
context: The label read, in Latin, 'Antonius Stradivarius Cremonensis Faciebat Anno' and the year - 'Antonio Stradivari of Cremona made this in the year ___.' He glued one inside every instrument that left his house on Cremona's Piazza San Domenico (today Piazza Roma). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Stradivari.

question: Antonio Stradivari built more than a thousand instruments over 75 years in his Cremona workshop. Three centuries have passed since - full of wars, fires, and hard everyday use. Surprisingly, about how many of his instruments still survive today?
context: Over roughly 75 years Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments (scholars count near 1,116). Around 650 survive today, and a single violin can now sell for millions of dollars. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.

question: In 2011 the pristine 1721 'Lady Blunt' Stradivarius, made in Cremona, sold for $15.9 million - the most ever paid for a violin at auction. Yet the sale is remembered for something else entirely. What became of all that money?
answer: it all went to Japanese tsunami relief
choices: it all went to Japanese tsunami relief
it endowed a violin museum in Cremona
it was divided among the seller's heirs
it funded a search for lost Stradivari violins
context: The 'Lady Blunt' - named for Lord Byron's granddaughter, Lady Anne Blunt - sold for a record $15.9 million in a 2011 online auction. Its owner, the Nippon Music Foundation, gave every penny to relief for Japan's 2011 earthquake and tsunami. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Blunt_Stradivarius; bloomberg.com 2011-06-20.

question: The most celebrated Stradivarius of all, the 1716 'Messiah' from Cremona, now rests in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum looking almost brand-new after three centuries - its varnish unworn, its carved edges still crisp and sharp. Why does this violin still look untouched?
answer: it has been played almost never
choices: it has been played almost never
it was restored just a few years ago
it was kept locked in a bank vault
it is a careful modern copy
context: The 'Messiah' got its name from a violinist's joke: because everyone talked about it but no one ever saw it, Jean-Delphin Alard quipped it was 'like the Messiah of the Jews: one always expects him but he never appears.' Barely played, it now sits in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum as a yardstick for future makers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiah_Stradivarius.

question: No one has ever fully proven why Antonio Stradivari's Cremona violins sound so glorious, but here is one leading theory. During his lifetime a long cold spell gripped Europe - the 'Little Ice Age,' roughly 1645 to 1750. According to this idea, how did the cold help create such perfect violin wood?
answer: Alpine trees grew slowly, making dense spruce
choices: Alpine trees grew slowly, making dense spruce
frost split the logs into thin, light panels
the cold thickened the varnish as it dried
snowmelt soaked the wood and softened its tone
context: It's only a theory. Tree-ring study traces Stradivari's spruce to the high forests of Val di Fiemme in Trentino, Italy, and the cold 'Maunder Minimum' would have made those trees grow slowly and evenly, giving dense, even-grained wood. A rival theory points to chemistry instead - traces of aluminum, copper and calcium hint at treatments like borax (to kill woodworm) or sodium silicate. Neither is proven. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.  (Legend.)

question: The legendary violin virtuoso Niccolo Paganini prized one instrument above all others - and it was not a Stradivarius but a violin by Stradivari's great Cremona rival, Giuseppe Guarneri. Paganini nicknamed it for the huge, overpowering force of its sound. What did he call it?
context: Paganini's favorite was a 1743 violin by Giuseppe Guarneri 'del Gesu' - a nickname from the sacred 'IHS' Christogram Guarneri stamped on his labels. Paganini called the violin 'Il Cannone,' the Cannon, for its powerful tone. Fewer than 200 Guarneris survive; one, the 'Vieuxtemps,' later sold for about $18 million (2013). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Guarneri.

question: For 300 years people have believed a Stradivarius from Cremona simply sounds better than any violin made today. So in a 2012 experiment in Paris, ten world-class soloists put on welder's goggles - unable to see what they were holding - and compared priceless old Strads against brand-new violins. What did the players decide?
answer: most of them preferred a brand-new violin
choices: most of them preferred a brand-new violin
every soloist singled out a Stradivarius
they judged all the violins identical
they refused to trust their own ears
context: In the 2012 Paris test, run by Claudia Fritz and Joseph Curtin, 6 of the 10 soloists picked a new violin as their favorite, and the new violins outscored the old Italians overall. A 2017 listening study found audiences also couldn't reliably tell old from new - and judged the new violins to project better across a hall. The Stradivarius 'secret' has never actually been proven. Sources: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1619443114; theviolinchannel.com 'The Paris Experiment.'

question: Writing did not begin with poems or prayers. The oldest tablets from the Sumerian city of Uruk, dating to about 3300 BC, are account-books from the temple storehouse, tallying grain, sheep, and cattle. Among the very first things ever written down were daily rations of bread and jugs of what?
context: Beer and bread were the twin staples of Sumer, both brewed and baked from barley, and the temple paid its workers in both. The earliest Uruk tablets are ration lists and receipts -- writing was invented for accounting, not literature. Source: worldhistory.org/cuneiform/

question: The world's oldest writing comes from the Sumerian city of Uruk. Mesopotamia was a flat land with almost no stone to carve and almost no timber, so its scribes could not record their words the way the peoples around them did. What did the Sumerians write on instead?
context: Mesopotamia had almost no stone or timber, but endless river mud. Scribes shaped clay into a tablet, wrote while it was damp, then let it dry in the sun or baked it hard. Clay is the reason so much Sumerian writing survives today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: Around 3300 BC, Sumerian scribes at Uruk pressed the world's oldest writing into wet clay with a cut reed. Modern scholars named the script 'cuneiform,' after the Latin word 'cuneus' -- the very word that names the shape every one of its marks takes. What does 'cuneus' mean?
context: 'Cuneiform' literally means 'wedge-shaped.' Every sign, however complex, is built entirely from little triangular wedge impressions -- no curves, no pen-strokes. Press a reed's corner into clay and you get a wedge; that single mark, repeated, became the world's first writing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: Half a million cuneiform tablets survive today, while almost all the paper and papyrus of the ancient world has crumbled and rotted to dust. The clay tablets of Mesopotamia owe their survival to a violent accident that struck city after city -- one you would expect to have destroyed the writing, not preserved it. What accident saved so many tablets?
context: Fire destroys paper but bakes clay: a burning city fired its clay tablets exactly like a kiln fires pottery, turning soft mud into near-indestructible ceramic. The greatest cuneiform libraries -- like Nineveh's -- survived precisely because they were put to the torch. Source: britishmuseum.org/blog/how-write-cuneiform

question: For thousands of years before the first tablet, the accountants of Mesopotamia tracked debts in three dimensions: each sheep, jar, or measure of grain was a small molded clay token, and the tokens for one deal were sealed inside a hollow clay ball called a bulla. Scholars think writing was born when someone did what to the tokens?
answer: stamped their shapes on the outside
choices: stamped their shapes on the outside
strung them onto a knotted cord
context: Instead of breaking open a sealed bulla to check the count, accountants began stamping each token's shape onto the outside of the ball -- and eventually skipped the tokens entirely, drawing the shapes straight onto a flat tablet. Three-dimensional counters had become two-dimensional signs. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/the-origins-of-writing

question: Here is a fact that surprises people: cuneiform was never one language. Over roughly 3,000 years, dozens of completely unrelated peoples across the Near East borrowed the very same wedge-signs to write down their own speech. But the script was first invented at Uruk, around 3300 BC, to record just one people's everyday tongue. Whose language did cuneiform first write?
context: Cuneiform began at Uruk around 3300 BC as a way to write Sumerian, but a script is only a set of signs -- so unrelated peoples could borrow it for their own tongues. Over three millennia Akkadians, Babylonians, Elamites, and Hittites all wrote their completely different languages in the same wedges, exactly the way the same alphabet today writes English, Spanish, and Vietnamese. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: A full circle has exactly 360 degrees, and a clock runs in strange counts instead of clean hundreds. Both habits are inheritances from the scribes of ancient Sumer, who over 4,000 years ago counted not in tens, the way we do, but by a much larger base number. Which number did Sumerian arithmetic count by?
context: The Sumerians counted in base-60 (sexagesimal), probably because 60 divides so evenly -- by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and more. By long tradition we still owe the 60-second minute, the 60-minute hour, and the 360-degree circle to their clay-tablet math. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexagesimal  (Legend.)

question: The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled the ancient world's greatest library at Nineveh -- over 30,000 clay tablets -- sending scribes across his empire to hunt down and copy texts. Ashurbanipal took special pride in one personal accomplishment that set him apart from nearly every other king of his age. What was it?
answer: he could read the ancient scripts himself
choices: he could read the ancient scripts himself
he had killed a lion on foot
he could recite long poems from memory
he never lost a single battle
context: In an age when literacy was a scribe's specialized craft and most kings kept scribes to read for them, Ashurbanipal could personally read both Akkadian and the already-ancient Sumerian. His Nineveh library, dug up in the 1850s, preserved the fullest surviving copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Buried in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, on twelve clay tablets, lay the oldest great story humanity has ever recovered: the Epic of Gilgamesh. When scholars finally read the eleventh tablet in the 1870s, they got a shock -- it told a tale that Jewish and Christian readers thought began in the Book of Genesis, only written centuries earlier. What ancient story does that tablet tell?
context: Tablet XI describes a god-sent flood that drowns the world, survived by one man in a great boat -- matching Noah's flood, but recorded before Genesis was written. The discovery stunned Victorian Britain and made cuneiform tablets front-page news. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh  (Legend.)

question: In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught engraver turned British Museum assistant, was hunched over a fire-blackened tablet from Nineveh when the wedge-signs suddenly resolved into a lost tale no one had read in over 2,000 years -- a discovery that would make him instantly famous. According to his astonished colleagues, the normally reserved Smith then did something wildly out of character. What did he do?
context: Smith reportedly grew so excited that he 'began to remove articles of his clothing' and ran round the room shouting in delight. He had taught himself cuneiform on his lunch breaks and was the first modern person to read the tablet after more than two millennia of oblivion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)  (Legend.)

question: High on a limestone cliff at Behistun in western Iran, about 100 metres up, King Darius the Great had a giant cuneiform inscription carved around 500 BC. In the 1830s and 40s the scholar Henry Rawlinson spent years copying it sign by sign -- a dangerous feat, since the carving sits on a sheer rock face far above the ground. How did Rawlinson reach it to copy it?
answer: he hung from ropes on the cliff
choices: he hung from ropes on the cliff
he cut a stairway in the rock
he copied it through a telescope
context: Rawlinson began scaling the Behistun cliff in 1835 and had accurate copies in Europe by 1847, at one point using an agile local boy to cross the most dangerous stretch. His years of perilous work made Behistun the single most important source for reading the lost script -- cuneiform's 'Rosetta Stone.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behistun_Inscription

question: The Behistun cliff did more than record Darius the Great's victories -- it became the master key to cuneiform. Darius had ordered his boast of crushing nineteen rebellions carved not once but three times side by side, each in a different language of his empire. Why did that triple carving finally let scholars read cuneiform?
answer: one script was nearly an alphabet
choices: one script was nearly an alphabet
one version was carved in Greek letters
the tablet came with a scribe's dictionary
the signs were labeled with small pictures
context: The three scripts were Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian. Old Persian was by far the simplest -- almost an alphabet, and close to later Persian -- so scholars deciphered it first, then used that reading to unlock the far more complex Elamite and Babylonian. Nothing at Behistun could be read in advance; the key was that one text appeared in three scripts, and one of them was simple enough to break into. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behistun_Inscription

question: On the tablets of Babylon and Nineveh, cuneiform is riddled with signs that were written but never spoken aloud -- silent helpers with no sound at all. Before the name of a city, a god, or a wooden object, a scribe placed a little mark to tell the reader what kind of thing the next word was, so a place would not be confused with a person of the same name. What are these silent category-flags called?
context: These silent signs are called determinatives. Cuneiform signs juggle three jobs -- a logogram (a whole word), a syllabogram (a unit of sound), or a determinative (a silent category-tag) -- and one sign can serve as any of them depending on context. That triple duty is exactly why the script took scholars decades to crack. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: High in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca called their capital Qosqo -- 'the navel of the world.' Chroniclers say the whole city was laid out to trace the body of a single sacred animal, with the hilltop fort of Sacsayhuaman as its head. Which animal was the city of Cusco shaped like?
context: The puma, condor, and serpent were the Inca's three sacred creatures, but the plan of the capital itself took the shape of a crouching puma, with the hilltop stronghold of Sacsayhuaman crowning the hill as its head. 'Qosqo' meant 'the navel of the world.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco

question: Sacsayhuaman's mortarless limestone walls fit so perfectly that guides still prove it to tourists with a simple test -- they try to slide a thin everyday object down into the seam between two giant blocks, and it will not go in. Which thin object is famously used to show how tight these joints are?
context: The chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon wrote in 1553 that not even a rial -- a Spanish silver coin -- could be slipped between two of Sacsayhuaman's stones. The Inca cut and re-cut each block until it hugged its neighbours exactly, with no mortar of any kind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: In the puma-shaped plan of Cusco, the hilltop stronghold of Sacsayhuaman forms the great cat's head, its three mighty terrace walls climbing the ridge one behind another above the city. Inca tradition reads these great walls as one part of the puma's head in particular. Which part of the puma are Sacsayhuaman's walls said to be?
context: Sacsayhuaman's terraces climb the hillside in three great walls of sharp saw-tooth angles -- its most striking feature -- long imagined as the bared teeth of the puma whose head the fortress forms above Cusco. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: Every 24 June, tens of thousands of people crowd onto the great grassy esplanade below Sacsayhuaman's walls to watch a spectacular costumed reenactment of an ancient Inca ceremony, complete with a royal procession. Which Inca festival is staged here each year?
context: The festival is Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun. Once the empire's grandest ceremony, it is reenacted every 24 June on the esplanade below Sacsayhuaman, drawing tens of thousands of spectators. Source: intiraymiticket.com/blog/inti-raymi-sacsayhuaman/

question: On a narrow lane in Cusco called Hatunrumiyoc, visitors crowd around one grey Inca block set into an old palace wall. It is celebrated because its edges were carved to interlock with the surrounding stones on a startling number of separate sides. On how many sides does this famous stone lock into its neighbours?
context: This is the famous Twelve-Angled Stone (Piedra de los Doce Angulos), part of a wall from the palace of Inca Roca -- now the Archbishop's Palace. Each of its twelve corners was cut to lock against a neighbouring block exactly, without mortar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatun_Rumiyoc

question: From the central square of Cusco, the Inca built the hub of the greatest road network in the ancient Americas -- the Qhapaq Nan. Its paved royal roads climbed over snow peaks, crossed coastal deserts, and pushed into rainforest, tying the whole empire together. Roughly how many kilometres of road did this network cover?
context: Four great royal roads radiated from Cusco's central square across roughly 40,000 km of paved track, linking snow peaks, deserts and rainforests in what are now six countries -- Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Colombia. The Qhapaq Nan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/1459/

question: When a powerful earthquake wrecked more than a third of Cusco's buildings in 1950, the Spanish colonial churches and houses crumbled -- yet the Inca walls beneath them stood perfectly intact. Inca masons had shaped their stonework with a distinctive design that lets it flex and settle during a quake instead of toppling. What is that earthquake-proof feature of Inca walls?
choices: blocks set on beds of sand
context: The great earthquake of 21 May 1950 destroyed more than a third of Cusco, yet the Inca foundations came through untouched. Inca walls use trapezoidal doorways (wider at the base) and inward-leaning, interlocked blocks, so the stones lock tighter as the ground shakes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco

question: The perfect-fit stones of Sacsayhuaman so amaze visitors that some claim aliens or a lost super-technology must have raised them. Archaeologists disagree, pointing to the marks that the real Inca tools left across every block face. How did Inca workers actually shape these giant limestone blocks?
answer: by pounding them with harder hammerstones
choices: by pounding them with harder hammerstones
by grinding them with wet sand
by cracking them with fire and cold water
by carving them with bronze chisels
context: Inca workers pounded the blocks into shape with jiwayas -- dense, harder river cobbles used as hammerstones -- using no iron tools at all. The faces still carry thousands of tiny impact dimples from the hammering. No aliens or lost technology were involved. Source: machupicchualtitude.com

question: The largest block in Sacsayhuaman's walls is a limestone monster estimated at well over a hundred tonnes -- heavier than a fully loaded lorry. The Inca quarried it about 35 km away and somehow brought it all the way to the hilltop fort. How did Inca crews move such a colossal stone across the mountains?
answer: dragged by teams of workers on log rollers
choices: dragged by teams of workers on log rollers
floated on a raft down a river
hoisted by a tall wooden crane
rolled along on giant stone wheels
context: The largest limestone block is estimated at anywhere from about 128 to 200 tonnes (the weights are estimates, not exact measurements). Inca crews dragged it roughly 35 km from the quarry at Rumicolca on ramps and log rollers, hauled by hundreds of workers -- without wheels or draft animals. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: Before the Spanish came, the holiest building in Cusco was the Qorikancha, the Inca Temple of the Sun. Spanish chroniclers described a sacred garden inside it where the corn stalks, flowers, and a whole herd of life-size llamas were not living things at all, but models crafted by the empire's finest artisans. What were the models of this ceremonial garden made of?
context: Chroniclers such as Garcilaso de la Vega described the Qorikancha's walls sheathed in sheets of gold and a garden holding golden corn, flowers, and about twenty llamas with their herders, all worked in gold and silver. The Spanish stripped the temple -- much of the gold went into the ransom of the captured emperor Atahualpa -- and built the church of Santo Domingo on its Inca foundations, where the Inca walls still outlast the earthquakes that crack the church above. (The golden garden is known from Spanish chronicles.) Source: smarthistory.org/maize-cobs/  (Legend.)

question: High in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca ruled their whole empire from Cusco, and its Quechua name, Qosqo, comes from a part of the human body. In the Inca tongue, Cusco was the ___ of the world. Which body part?
context: Qosqo is traditionally translated 'the navel' -- the still center from which the empire's four quarters radiated. The half-Inca chronicler Garcilaso de la Vega popularized 'navel of the world' in his Royal Commentaries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco; studycountry.com.

question: Cusco sits so high in the Peruvian Andes -- about 3,400 meters up -- that visitors arriving from the coast often feel dizzy and breathless in the thin mountain air. For centuries, Andean people have chewed the leaves of one local plant to ease this. Which plant's leaves?
context: The coca leaf is the traditional Andean remedy for soroche (altitude sickness), chewed or brewed as tea for thousands of years. Cusco stands about 3,400 m (11,200 ft) up, near the Sacred Valley and the Urubamba River. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco.

question: From the great central plaza of Cusco, four royal roads shot outward, one to each of the four quarters of the realm -- and the Inca named their entire empire after this fourfold shape, all four parts meeting at the capital. By what name did the Inca know their empire?
context: Tawantinsuyu means 'the four parts together' (tawa = four). Four great roads split from Cusco to the quarters -- Chinchaysuyu, Antisuyu, Qullasuyu, and Kuntisuyu -- all meeting at the capital. Chachapoyas, Chinchorro, and Tiwanaku were other real Andean cultures. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawantinsuyu.

question: A striking tradition about Cusco holds that the emperor Pachacuti, rebuilding the city in the 1400s, laid out its whole core in the shape of one sacred Andean animal -- the great hilltop fortress Sacsayhuaman forming its head, and the meeting of two rivers its tail. Which animal was the city said to be modeled on?
context: Scholars treat the puma layout as a tradition, not settled fact: Sacsayhuaman is said to form the puma's head and the meeting of the Saphi and Tullumayo rivers its tail, from Pachacuti's 1400s rebuild. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuaman; terandes.com.  (Legend.)

question: The Inca raised the fortress of Sacsayhuaman above Cusco from limestone blocks so enormous that some weigh well over 100 tons, fitted together without mortar and standing solid for five centuries. With what did the Inca shape and haul these giant stones into place?
context: The Inca had no iron tools, no wheel, and no draft animals -- Sacsayhuaman's zig-zag ramparts (longest ~400 m) were raised with hammerstones and manpower alone. The joints are so tight the Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon wrote that not even a coin could be slipped between two blocks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuaman.

question: On Hatun Rumiyoc street in Cusco stands a single greenish block, set without mortar into the wall of the Inca ruler Inca Roca's old palace, that Peru treats as the emblem of all Inca stonework. What remarkable feature makes this one famous stone so celebrated?
context: The Twelve-Angled Stone is a single greenish-diorite block cut with twelve corners that lock into its neighbors without mortar, set in Inca Roca's old palace wall (now the Archbishop's Palace). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_angle_stone.

question: Across the Inca empire's vast web of mountain roads, an urgent message could travel from Cusco to a frontier a thousand miles away in only a few days -- faster than any horse could have carried it. How did the Inca move news so quickly across the Andes?
context: These relay runners were the chasquis, posted at short intervals along the royal roads; each sprinted his own stretch at full speed and handed off to the next, so news crossed the empire in days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system.

question: For nearly four centuries the Spanish banned it, but every June 24th now, costumed crowds pack the ancient ramparts of Sacsayhuaman above Cusco to re-stage Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of their supreme god Inti. Which heavenly body did this reborn festival honor?
context: Inti Raymi is the Inca winter New Year, festival of the sun god Inti, established by the emperor Pachacuti and last held before the Inca emperor in 1535. The Spanish banned it; it was reborn in 1944 as a pageant staged at Sacsayhuaman each June 24. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inti_Raymi.

question: When a powerful earthquake struck Cusco in 1950, the Spanish colonial church of Santo Domingo cracked and collapsed -- yet the ancient Inca walls it had been built directly on top of stood completely unharmed, even shrugging off the wreckage to reveal the old Inca temple beneath. What lets Inca stonework ride out earthquakes that flatten the buildings stacked above it?
answer: the fitted stones shift, then settle back
choices: the fitted stones shift, then settle back
the walls are simply too thick to crack
a deep bed of sand cushions the shaking
flexible mortar bends with the ground
context: Inca blocks are trapezoidal and lean slightly inward, and because they are dry-fitted without mortar they can shift during a tremor and resettle rather than shatter. The 1950 quake wrecked the Santo Domingo church and laid bare the undamaged Inca masonry of Coricancha beneath. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qorikancha; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco.

question: Cusco's holiest temple, Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, so dazzled the arriving Spanish that they wrote home in disbelief: its courtyard held a garden where the corn stalks, llamas, and flowers were all life-size models cast in gleaming metal, and the temple's walls were faced with shining sheets of the same. Which metal sheathed Coricancha's walls?
context: Coricancha (Quri Kancha, 'the golden enclosure') had gold-sheathed walls and a garden of gold-and-silver plants and animals. The gold is gone because the Spanish stripped it -- much went to the 1533 ransom of the captured emperor Atahualpa, and the Dominicans built the Church of Santo Domingo on the temple's Inca walls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qorikancha.

question: The Inca laced the Andes with some 40,000 km of stone highway radiating from Cusco, and where a road met a deep canyon they slung a swaying suspension bridge across the gorge. The last of these still in use, Q'eswachaka over the Apurimac River, is torn down and rebuilt entirely by hand each year by the local Quechua families. What are the great cables of this Inca bridge twisted from?
context: Q'eswachaka spans about 45 m over the Apurimac River and is the last surviving Inca rope bridge, rebuilt each year from braided ichu grass by the Quechua communities who keep it. The Inca road network, the Qhapaq Nan, ran without the wheel or horses, its cargo carried by llama caravans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system.

question: The Inca ran their vast Andean empire -- collecting taxes, counting people, tracking storehouses of grain -- from Cusco with no written language at all. How did Inca officials keep the empire's accounts and records straight without any writing?
context: These were the quipu -- bundles of knotted colored cords read in a base-10 place system, where the knot type and its position gave units, tens, and hundreds. Specialists called quipucamayocs recorded census, taxes, and stores from Cusco -- a whole empire's accounts kept without a single written word. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu.

question: More than a quarter of a billion people today write in the Cyrillic alphabet, from Moscow to Belgrade. Yet the two brothers who gave the Slavs their first letters -- Cyril and Methodius -- were Greeks, sons of a Byzantine army officer, raised together in one great city of the 800s. Which city was the brothers' childhood home?
context: The brothers grew up in Thessalonica (Thessaloniki), the Greek port where their father Leo served as a Byzantine military officer (a droungarios) of the theme of Thessalonica. Cyril was born Constantine (826/827) and Methodius born Michael (815-820); together the two are honored as the 'Apostles to the Slavs.' Reputable estimates put Cyrillic's readers today at roughly 250-350 million across 50-plus languages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius

question: When Cyril and Methodius reached Great Moravia in 862, they found a Slavic people who had never possessed an alphabet of their own. One later account describes how these Slavs had kept their records in the days before the brothers came -- not with letters, but by a rougher, older method. What did the Slavs use?
context: The account came from a monk who signed himself Chernorizets Hrabar ('Hrabar the Brave'), whose treatise 'On the Letters' (O pismeneh) defended the new Slavic alphabet. He recorded that before Christianity 'the Slavs did not have their own letters, but read and communicated by means of strokes and incisions' -- tallies and rough sketches. He credited Saint Constantine (Cyril) with later composing 'thirty-eight letters ... suitable to express Slavic sounds.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernorizets_Hrabar  (Legend.)

question: In Great Moravia, Cyril and Methodius discovered that no Greek or Latin letter could spell many Slavic sounds -- so around 863 they built a brand-new alphabet of loops, circles, and crosses. They named it 'Glagolitic,' from the Old Church Slavonic word 'glagol.' What does 'glagol' mean?
context: 'Glagol' means 'word' or 'utterance,' so the alphabet's name means, roughly, 'speech itself.' Glagolitic -- around 41 letters of loops, circles, crosses, and triangles -- was the first alphabet ever used for Slavic manuscripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_script

question: The alphabet is named Cyrillic in honor of Saint Cyril of Thessaloniki -- yet Cyril himself never made it. He and Methodius had created Glagolitic, and Cyril died in Rome in 869. The streamlined script we now call Cyrillic was assembled a generation later, by his followers at the Preslav Literary School. In which realm did those scholars work?
context: Constantine took the monastic name 'Cyril' only weeks before he died in Rome on 14 February 869 -- so the alphabet honors a name he held only at the very end of his life, and one he never made. His disciples, taken in by Tsar Boris I of Bulgaria, adapted it at the Preslav Literary School (founded 886, later moved to Veliki Preslav under Tsar Simeon I the Great). The oldest dated Cyrillic inscription (921) was found near Krepcha, Bulgaria. As one summary puts it, the name Cyrillic 'denotes homage rather than authorship.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script

question: Open a Russian newspaper and the letters look almost Greek -- because the scholars who built Cyrillic took most of its shapes straight from Greek formal book-script. But Greek had no signs for certain Slavic sounds like 'sh', 'zh', and 'ch'. Where did they find letters for those missing sounds?
context: The Preslav scholars adapted Greek uncial (formal book-script) for most letters, but borrowed shapes from the brothers' earlier Glagolitic for sounds Greek lacked: Zh, Sh, Shch, Ts, Ch, and Yu. So Glagolitic quietly survives inside every page of modern Cyrillic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script

question: Across most of the Slavic world, the newer Cyrillic quickly swept the older Glagolitic script aside. Yet in one country priests and notaries kept writing the swirling loops of Glagolitic in their everyday documents as late as the early 1800s -- nearly a thousand years after it was born. Where did this last stronghold of Glagolitic survive?
context: The surprise is the direction: Glagolitic clung on longest not in the Slavic east but in Croatia and Dalmatia, where priests and notaries on Adriatic islands like Krk kept writing the old script into the early 1800s -- alongside Latin and Cyrillic. Its swirl of loops, circles, and triangles had first been shaped in Great Moravia nearly a thousand years before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glagolitic_script

question: In the Afar desert of Ethiopia, the summit of Dallol steams with pools glowing neon-green, canary-yellow and orange over a crust of twisted salt cones -- a scene so unlike anywhere on Earth that scientists visit it to rehearse missions to another world. Which planet does Dallol stand in for?
context: Dallol's alien, acidic, sulphur-and-iron landscape is studied as a stand-in for Mars -- a 'planetary field analog' scientists use to practice how they'd hunt for life on other worlds. The Danakil around it is also the hottest place on Earth by year-round average temperature (near 35 C), and its floor lies about 120 m below sea level. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; PMC 'The Dallol Geothermal Area ... Planetary Field Analog'; Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)

question: Dallol's crust isn't painted by any artist, yet it blazes in bands of neon-green, golden-yellow and fiery orange. As the hot brine wells up and dries on the surface, what actually paints these unearthly colors?
context: As the hot brine cools and evaporates, dissolved iron, copper and sulphur crystallize out and crust the salt in greens, yellows, oranges and whites -- the ground is literally painted by minerals, not by living things. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; Wikipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'.)

question: For centuries, Afar miners have hand-cut the salt crust of the Danakil into flat slabs called amole, then loaded them onto camel caravans -- about forty slabs a camel -- to carry deep into the Ethiopian highlands. For hundreds of years, Ethiopians used these salt slabs directly as what?
context: The slabs are called amole, and for centuries they served as actual currency across Ethiopia -- 'white gold.' Afar miners still cut the flats of Lake Karum (Lake Asale, about 120 m below sea level) by hand and load roughly forty blocks per camel. (Great Ethiopian Tours 'Lake Asale Salt Flats & Camel Caravans'; IBTimes UK 'white gold'.)

question: Dallol's summit pools glow in bands of green and gold, yet rainwater that sinks into the crater is superheated by magma only a few kilometres down and comes welling back up as a scalding, mineral-loaded brine. That leaves Dallol's water roughly as acidic as which liquid?
context: One of the most fiercely acidic natural waters ever measured: the pools are hydrothermal -- groundwater heated by shallow magma and so saturated with sulphur that their pH plunges near 0, measured as low as about -1.7, roughly the acidity of battery acid. That is far beyond the ordinary sour bite of lemon juice or vinegar. (Grokipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)'; ACS Earth & Space Chemistry, 'A Polyextreme Hydrothermal System Controlled by Iron', pH 0.1 to -1.7.)

question: Beneath the Danakil lie almost unbelievable layers of salt -- in places up to two kilometres thick. This salt didn't fall from the sky; it piled up over ages because an arm of one nearby sea kept flooding the sinking basin and then drying out under the desert sun. Which sea kept pouring in and evaporating away?
context: An arm of the Red Sea repeatedly flooded the sinking basin and then dried out, each cycle leaving salt behind. The evaporite deposits run over 500 m thick and reach as much as 2 km (some estimates ~2,500 m). (Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'; Grokipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)

question: The Danakil sits over the Afar Triple Junction, where three great plates of the Earth's crust -- the African, Arabian and Somali -- are slowly rifting apart, splitting the continent open at a centimetre or two a year. Geologists predict that if this widening keeps up for millions of years, the whole basin will grow into what?
context: This is the Afar Triple Junction, where the Nubian (African), Arabian and Somali plates pull apart at roughly 1-2 cm a year -- the continent is being torn open, and geologists expect the sea to eventually flood in and form new oceanic crust here. Framed as a far-future prediction. (Grokipedia 'Danakil Depression'; Wikipedia 'Danakil Depression'.)  (Legend.)

question: A short trek from Dallol, the volcano Erta Ale holds a lake of molten lava whose churning surface has never fully hardened since at least 1906 -- the longest-lived on Earth. Our planet counts well over a thousand active volcanoes, yet open lava lakes are so rare that in 2019 the whole world held only about how many at once?
context: Erta Ale means 'smoking mountain' in the Afar language, and locals call its southernmost pit 'the gateway to hell.' Its lava lake has been present since at least 1906, the longest-lived on Earth; in 2019 only about eight volcanoes worldwide had a lava lake at all. (Wikipedia 'Erta Ale'; Grokipedia 'Erta Ale'.)

question: Blades sold in the markets of Damascus were prized for a strange beauty: across the bright steel ran a rippling, flowing pattern of wavy bands, unlike any plain sword. How did the smiths give the blades this rippling pattern?
answer: It was forged into the steel itself.
choices: It was forged into the steel itself.
It was painted on with dark dye.
It was etched in with acid later.
It was inlaid with silver wire.
