context: The decree granted the 13-year-old Ptolemy V a divine cult and tax relief for the temples, and ordered that a copy be set up in hard stone, in all three scripts, in every first-, second-, and third-rank temple. That command is why more than one such decree stone survives — and why the text was carved so durably. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone.

question: Champollion had one edge his rival Thomas Young lacked. Since boyhood he had mastered a language still chanted in the old churches of the Nile valley, and knowing how its words sounded let him hear the ancient language behind the pictures. Which language had he mastered?
context: Coptic is the final stage of the Egyptian language, written in Greek letters and still used in the Coptic Christian liturgy — the last living descendant of the tongue the pharaohs spoke. Champollion was so steeped in it he wrote, 'I dream in Coptic.' A prodigy, he had reportedly mastered Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac and more by age 16. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-François_Champollion.

question: At a temple beside the Nile near Egypt's southern frontier, a priest named Nesmeterakhem cut a short inscription to the god Mandulis on 24 August 394 CE. Though no one knew it then, it was the very last hieroglyph anyone would ever carve — after it, the script fell silent. At which southern temple was this final hieroglyph made?
context: The 'Graffito of Esmet-Akhom,' carved by the priest Nesmeterakhem for the god Mandulis on 24 August 394 CE, is the last securely dated hieroglyphic inscription. It survives on the island temple of Philae, near Aswan. Soon after, no one alive could read the script, and it stayed dark for some fourteen centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffito_of_Esmet-Akhom.

question: On a temple wall at Karnak, one line of hieroglyphs runs left-to-right and the next runs right-to-left — the Egyptians carved them in whichever direction the wall's design demanded, and sometimes top-to-bottom. Yet a reader is never lost about where a line begins. Looking at the owls, hawks, and striding human figures in the carving, how do you tell which way to read the line?
answer: Read toward the direction the figures face
choices: Read toward the direction the figures face
Read away from the figures, at their backs
Read from the largest figure to the smallest
Read starting from the crowned or seated figure
context: As a rule, the human and animal signs face the START of the line, so you read toward their faces — walking into the line of birds and figures. The word 'hieroglyph' is itself Greek, hieroglyphikos, 'sacred carving'; the Egyptians called their own script medu netjer, 'the words of the gods.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_hieroglyphs.

question: For generations, fishermen along the coast of Peru watched a warm ocean current push in almost every year as the year drew to a close. They named the warm current in Spanish, and that name is now used worldwide for this whole climate pattern. What did the fishermen call it?
context: The warm current peaked right around Christmas, so the Peruvian fishermen called it El Nino de Navidad -- the Christ Child, after the newborn Jesus whose birth the season celebrates. Today 'El Nino' names the warm phase of the whole tropical-Pacific cycle. Source: NOAA PMEL, 'What is El Nino?'  (Legend.)

question: Sea level is not truly level. Near Indonesia, in the western Pacific, the sea surface stands about half a meter higher than it does off the coast of Peru -- a great mound of warm water heaped up on the ocean's western side. Steady winds blowing across the tropical Pacific pile that warm water up in the west. What are these winds called?
context: The easterly trade winds blow steadily from the Americas toward Asia, dragging warm surface water westward until it heaps up near Indonesia about half a meter higher than off Peru, at 28-30C versus a cool ~20C in the east. When the trades slacken, that piled-up warm water is free to slide back east -- the start of an El Nino. Source: Wikipedia, El Nino-Southern Oscillation; Grokipedia, ENSO.

question: Most years the trade winds keep the Pacific's warm water pooled far to the west near Indonesia, while cold, deep water rises along Peru's coast. But every few years the trade winds go slack, and the vast warm pool slides back eastward until it reaches South America. When that warm water arrives off the Peruvian coast, what happens to the cold, deep water that normally rises there?
answer: The cold upwelling shuts off entirely
choices: The cold upwelling shuts off entirely
The cold upwelling grows even stronger
The cold water rushes west to Indonesia
The cold water sinks into a trench
context: This is El Nino's core: warm water spreading east caps the ocean like a lid and shuts down the cold upwelling off Peru. The eastern Pacific, normally near 20C, warms toward the 28-30C of the west -- the warm eastern-Pacific phase that defines an El Nino. Source: NOAA PMEL; Grokipedia, ENSO.

question: The cold water welling up off Peru carries nutrients that feed vast schools of anchoveta, supporting what has long been the largest single-species fishery on Earth. Then the great El Nino of 1972 arrived and its warm water rolled in along the coast. What became of Peru's giant anchovy catch that year?
answer: It collapsed, and the catch crashed
choices: It collapsed, and the catch crashed
It doubled as anchovy crowded the shore
It shifted north into El Nino's warm water
It held steady, saved by deep-sea fishing
context: Without the nutrient-rich upwelling, the anchoveta starve and scatter, and the fishery collapses. The 1972 El Nino crashed the catch from about 12 million tons toward roughly 4 million; it collapsed again in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16. This is a place-economy fact -- El Nino can wreck the livelihood of a whole coast. Source: Wikipedia, 1972 Peruvian anchoveta crisis; Oceana; Grokipedia.

question: El Nino has an opposite twin. Sometimes the Pacific trade winds, instead of slackening, blow even HARDER than usual -- driving the cold upwelling off South America into overdrive and chilling the eastern Pacific far below its normal temperature. What do scientists call this cold, super-charged opposite of El Nino?
context: La Nina -- Spanish for 'the little girl' -- is El Nino's cold mirror image: stronger trade winds, fiercer upwelling, an extra-cold eastern Pacific. Note that this is the Pacific's natural back-and-forth, not the same thing as long-term global warming. Source: NOAA PMEL; Grokipedia, ENSO.

question: High above the tropical Pacific runs a giant overturning loop of air: it rises over the warm western pool near Indonesia, drifts eastward high in the atmosphere, sinks over the cool eastern Pacific off South America, and returns westward along the surface as the trade winds. This vast east-west air loop is the atmospheric engine that El Nino throws into reverse. What is this Pacific air loop called?
context: British scientist Gilbert Walker first mapped it in the 1920s, so it carries his name. He also charted the see-saw of air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia -- the Southern Oscillation -- which is why the whole warm-and-cold cycle is called ENSO, the El Nino-Southern Oscillation. Source: Wikipedia, El Nino-Southern Oscillation; Grokipedia, ENSO.

question: Through teleconnections, a single strong El Nino reshuffles weather around the whole planet at once. In the same season that the warm water pools off South America, El Nino reaches clear across the ocean to Australia and Indonesia. What kind of weather does a strong El Nino typically bring to Australia and Indonesia?
context: This is the dinner-table wonder of El Nino: a single warm patch of Pacific water can, in the same season, parch Australia and Indonesia with drought, failed monsoon, and bushfire while drowning Peru and the southern United States in floods -- one ocean, opposite disasters half a world apart. Source: NOAA PMEL; Grokipedia, ENSO teleconnections.

question: El Nino's warm Pacific reaches clear across the Americas and stirs the air over the Atlantic Ocean during hurricane season, ramping up the wind shear there -- a sharp difference between the fast winds high in the sky and the slower winds near the sea surface. What does an El Nino year usually do to the Atlantic hurricane season?
choices: Pushes the storms far out to sea
context: You might expect a giant climate event to whip up storms everywhere, but El Nino does the opposite in the Atlantic: its wind shear -- fast upper-level winds that rip the tops off growing storms and keep them from organizing -- makes Atlantic hurricane seasons quieter. In the Pacific it does the reverse, boosting hurricanes and typhoons. Source: NOAA PMEL; Grokipedia, ENSO.

question: Once an El Nino begins, it tends to feed itself and grow: as the eastern Pacific warms, the trade winds weaken; and weaker trade winds let even more warm water spread east, warming the ocean still more, which weakens the winds further still. In 1969 a Norwegian-American meteorologist worked out this self-reinforcing coupling of ocean and atmosphere, one of the engines that makes an El Nino swell. What is this ocean-atmosphere loop called?
context: The meteorologist was Jacob Bjerknes, and the loop is named the Bjerknes feedback: a warm ocean weakens the winds, and weaker winds warm the ocean, on and on -- so a small nudge can snowball into a full El Nino. Source: Grokipedia, ENSO (Bjerknes Feedback Mechanism).

question: One of the deadliest disasters in human history unfolded in 1876-1878, when a monster El Nino gripped the Pacific and famine spread at once across India, China, and Brazil, killing an estimated 19 to 50 million people. Scientists and historians link the catastrophe to one thing that El Nino did to the weather over India and Asia. What did that El Nino do to help trigger the famine?
answer: It caused the monsoon rains to fail
choices: It caused the monsoon rains to fail
It drowned the fields in endless floods
It battered the coast with destructive cyclones
It scorched the fields with fierce heat
context: The great El Nino of 1877-78 shut down the monsoon across India and disrupted rains in China and Brazil; crops failed and an estimated 19-50 million people died -- among the deadliest famines ever recorded, chronicled in Mike Davis's 'Late Victorian Holocausts.' The death-toll estimates are wide and the human causes are debated by historians; what is settled is the El Nino climate trigger. Source: Wikipedia, Great Famine of 1876-1878.  (Legend.)

question: El Nino has switched on and off for thousands of years, long before anyone kept written weather records. To reconstruct those ancient El Ninos, scientists sailed to the reefs and shallow lagoons ringing remote Palmyra and Kiritimati, in the central Pacific, and drilled out cores banded with fine yearly layers -- each one locking in the chemical fingerprint of that year's ocean warmth and rainfall. Which natural archive did they read to trace El Nino back thousands of years?
context: Fossil coral is the atoll's weather diary: a coral colony grows a fresh layer each year and locks the surrounding sea's temperature and rainfall into the oxygen-isotope chemistry of its limestone skeleton -- and warm, rainy El Nino water leaves a distinct signature. By drilling old coral heads on Palmyra, Fanning, and Kiritimati, scientists read El Ninos going back thousands of years; lake-bed mud and tree rings on other continents preserve the same long story. Source: Eos, 'Corals Make Reliable Recorders of El Nino'; MDPI paleo-ENSO review.

question: The Kailasa temple at Ellora in India was never built up from stacked blocks. Instead, its makers freed the entire three-storey temple from a single basalt cliff, cutting away every scrap of rock that was not part of it. To carve a whole temple out of solid stone this way, where did the workers have to begin?
answer: They started at the top and cut straight down.
choices: They started at the top and cut straight down.
They started at the base and cut straight up.
They tunnelled in from the side of the hill.
They cleared the courtyard and worked outward.
context: Kailasa is a 'rock-cut' monument -- carved from living stone rather than stacked from quarried blocks. The carvers began at the very top of the cliff and chiselled downward, freeing the temple from the mountain, the exact reverse of ordinary building. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora; mymodernmet.com/kailasa-temple-ellora-caves.

question: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was cut whole from a basalt cliff over roughly twenty years in the 8th century. Every wall, pillar and carving on it was shaped using only the simple technology of that age. What kind of tools freed this giant temple from the living rock?
context: Iron hammers, chisels, picks and wedges -- basic hand tools -- were the only technology used; there were no cranes, no machines and no explosives. Source: mymodernmet.com/kailasa-temple-ellora-caves; indialegacy.in.

question: To build a temple you normally carry stone TO the site. The Kailasa temple at Ellora demanded the reverse: the temple was hidden inside a solid cliff, and the only way to reveal it was to chisel away and haul off everything that was not temple. Over about two decades of cutting, roughly how much basalt did the workers remove by hand?
context: An estimated 200,000 tonnes of basalt (some estimates run higher) were chiselled out and carried away over roughly twenty years. Because it is one continuous piece of stone, a single wrong cut could never be patched or replaced. Source: mymodernmet.com/kailasa-temple-ellora-caves; artnet.com.

question: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved as a full-size stone replica of one sacred mountain: Mount Kailash, the remote Himalayan peak that Hindu tradition names as a god's earthly home. Which god does this mountain-temple enshrine as the lord of that peak?
context: Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak, is revered by Hindus as the abode of the god Shiva; the Ellora temple is a symbolic stone image of that mountain, dedicated to Shiva -- and its very name, Kailasa, is the mountain's own. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora.

question: On one particular measure, the Kailasa temple at Ellora outdoes every other monument on Earth -- it holds a genuine world record. For what distinction is it most often celebrated?
answer: the biggest thing ever cut from one rock
choices: the biggest thing ever cut from one rock
the oldest surviving temple on Earth
the tallest stone temple in the world
the first monument freed from living rock
context: Ellora's Cave 16, the Kailasa, is described as the largest single monolithic rock excavation in the world -- the biggest structure ever cut from one continuous piece of stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellora_Caves.

question: The long cliff at Ellora that holds the Kailasa temple is honeycombed with dozens of temples and monasteries -- and, remarkably, they were not all cut by followers of a single religion. Carved side by side into the same rock face, in relative harmony, are the sacred caves of which three faiths?
context: The cliff holds 34 caves -- 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain -- carved as the three faiths shared the region; the site is often cited to illustrate ancient India's religious harmony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellora_Caves.

question: Carved into an outer wall of the Kailasa temple is one of the most admired sculptures in all Indian art: the ten-headed demon-king Ravana, trapped beneath Mount Kailash, straining with every arm to shake the sacred mountain loose. Seated calmly above him, the mountain's own god presses it back into place. In the carving, what is all it takes to pin the whole mountain down?
answer: the press of a single toe
choices: the press of a single toe
context: The panel of Ravana shaking Kailasa is considered one of the finest sculptures in Indian art. In the Hindu story, Shiva calmly presses the mountain down with a single toe, trapping the demon-king beneath it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora.  (Legend.)

question: The Kailasa temple at Ellora appears to be lifted into the air on a carved plinth of full-size beasts that ring its base, as though a living herd were bearing the whole mountain-temple aloft. Life-size elephants fill much of this stone menagerie -- but striding among them, helping to shoulder the temple, is which other great beast?
context: Full-size elephants and lions, columned galleries, the gateway (gopuram) and two free-standing victory pillars were all left standing from the living rock as the quarry was cut away around them -- nothing was ever assembled or added. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora; mymodernmet.com.

question: Within the Kailasa complex at Ellora, cut from the very same rock as the temple, stand five small detached shrines. Three of them are dedicated together to a trio of goddesses whom Hindus honour as the living spirits of India's most sacred rivers. Which three river goddesses are enshrined there?
context: Of the five detached shrines carved from the rock, three honour the river goddesses Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati -- the personified spirits of India's holiest rivers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora.

question: The Jordan River empties into the Dead Sea, but no stream flows out again, so evaporation has left it about ten times saltier than the ocean. A first-time bather wades in expecting to swim — but the water does something startling. What happens?
answer: It pushes them up to bob on the surface like a cork.
choices: It pushes them up to bob on the surface like a cork.
It drags them straight down to the muddy floor.
It coats their skin in a slick grey mineral mud.
It tugs swimmers toward the centre in a current.
context: Ten times ocean saltiness makes the Dead Sea's water so dense — about 1.24 kg per litre — that a bather floats high on the surface, famously able to lie back and read a newspaper without sinking. The Dead Sea is a closed, 'endorheic' lake: water flows in but only evaporation takes it out, so the salt keeps building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: High in the Bolivian Andes lies the Salar de Uyuni, a blinding-white salt flat left when ancient lakes dried up — over ten thousand square kilometres of dead-level crust. When a thin sheet of rainwater settles across it, the whole plain transforms. Into what?
answer: the world's largest mirror, reflecting the sky
choices: the world's largest mirror, reflecting the sky
the world's largest ice rink, frozen glass-smooth
the world's largest sand dune, rippling white
the world's largest geyser field, hissing steam
context: The rain-mirror is so flawless that sky and ground merge and visitors seem to walk on clouds. Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat, about 10,582 km², left where prehistoric lakes dried up; beneath its crust lies brine holding roughly a fifth of the world's known lithium. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: Point to the biggest lake on your classroom map and you might pick one of the Great Lakes. But one closed body of water, ringed by five countries and cut off from every ocean, dwarfs them — it holds about three and a half times as much water as all five Great Lakes put together. Which body of water is it?
context: The Caspian Sea covers about 371,000 km², making it the largest lake on Earth — it holds roughly three and a half times the water of all five Great Lakes combined. Despite its size it is endorheic: no outlet reaches the ocean, so it loses water only to evaporation, which leaves it brackish. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea

question: The Dead Sea has no outlet: everything the Jordan River delivers stays until it evaporates. Landlocked and shrinking, its shore has ended up holding a distinction that belongs to nowhere else on the planet. What distinction is it?
answer: the lowest dry land on Earth
choices: the lowest dry land on Earth
the widest tidal flat on Earth
context: With no outlet, the Dead Sea's shore has sunk to about 430 metres below sea level — the lowest exposed dry land on Earth. Nearly all the water the Jordan delivers is lost straight back to the sky, since the region gets less than 50 mm of rain a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: When Ice-Age Lake Bonneville dried away in Utah, it left the Bonneville Salt Flats — a dead-level plain of blinding-white salt crust stretching about 40 square miles. Since 1914 this flat has drawn a very particular crowd year after year. What do they come to do?
answer: set world land-speed records in racing cars
choices: set world land-speed records in racing cars
shoot sweeping scenes for desert movies
hold vast open-air electronic music festivals
launch high-altitude weather balloons at dawn
context: On the Bonneville Speedway, the salt is so hard and flat that jet-powered cars have topped 600 mph; racers have chased land-speed records here since 1914. The crust — almost 1.5 m thick at its centre — is the dried floor of Ice-Age Lake Bonneville, left behind when the lake evaporated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonneville_Salt_Flats

question: Lake Chad sits in Africa's Sahel, shared by Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon. Between the 1960s and the 1980s a run of dry years wiped out about 95% of its area — from roughly 25,000 down to about 2,000 square kilometres. What is it about Lake Chad that left it so easily drained?
answer: It is so shallow that a person could nearly wade across it.
choices: It is so shallow that a person could nearly wade across it.
High mountains ring it and block the rains from ever reaching it.
It has no river feeding it — only the desert's rare rains.
It lies far below sea level, where fierce heat boils it away.
context: Only about 2 m deep at most — barely deeper than a person is tall — Lake Chad had almost no reserve to lose, so a run of dry years and water drawn off upstream for irrigation shrank it by roughly 95% between the 1960s and 1980s, from about 25,000 down to some 2,000 km². Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Chad

question: Across nearly all of Nevada and much of Utah spreads a region so distinctive that the explorer John C. Frémont gave it a sweeping name in the 1840s. He named it for one strange thing every valley within it shares. What do all these lands have in common?
answer: no drop of their water ever reaches the ocean
choices: no drop of their water ever reaches the ocean
no rain has fallen on them within living memory
no tree there grows taller than a grown person
no river within them freezes, even in winter
context: Frémont named it the Great Basin — about 209,000 sq mi of internal drainage across Nevada and Utah, the largest region in North America where no water reaches the sea. Rain there evaporates, sinks into the ground, or gathers in closed lakes like Great Salt Lake. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basin

question: In 1960 the Aral Sea in Central Asia was the world's fourth-largest lake. Then it began to die — and no drought was to blame. Human hands cut off the two great rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. Who cut off those rivers, and for what?
answer: Soviet planners diverted them to irrigate cotton fields
choices: Soviet planners diverted them to irrigate cotton fields
Ottoman engineers diverted them to power flour mills
British firms diverted them to float log rafts downstream
Persian kings diverted them to fill palace gardens
context: From the early 1960s, Soviet central planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton across the Central Asian desert. Cut off from its only water, the endorheic Aral Sea — then the world's fourth-largest lake at about 68,000 km² — began to collapse. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: As the Aral Sea shrank, the fishing town of Moynaq — once home to some 30,000 people who lived by fishing — watched the water retreat tens of kilometres, leaving its harbour stranded far inland. Moynaq's idled fishing fleet then met a fate that made the town world-famous. What became of the boats?
answer: They were left to rust, marooned across the bare desert.
choices: They were left to rust, marooned across the bare desert.
They were hauled off and stacked in a scrap boneyard.
They were swallowed and buried by drifting sand dunes.
They were sawn up for scrap along the old harbour quay.
context: The Aral's exposed bed became the toxic Aralkum Desert, and Moynaq's rusting trawlers, stranded 30 to 90 km from any water, became the world's iconic image of a vanished sea. By 2007 the Aral had shrunk to about a tenth of its 1960 size, and in 2014 its eastern basin dried up completely. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: The Okavango Delta in Botswana pulls off a backwards trick: it flushes greenest not during the rains, but in the depths of the dry season, when the surrounding Kalahari is at its most parched and brown. What accounts for this upside-down timing?
answer: floodwater from Angola's rains arrives months late
choices: floodwater from Angola's rains arrives months late
underground springs well up only when the air dries
thick fog rolls off the desert and soaks the reeds
night frost melts and trickles across the flats by day
context: The surge from Angola's summer rains travels about 1,200 km down the Okavango over roughly a month, then spreads across the floodplains in the dry season — greening the desert when it is driest. The river never reaches the sea: it fans into the Kalahari as an inland delta, where 96–98% of the water vanishes to evaporation and sand. It became UNESCO's 1000th World Heritage Site in 2014. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okavango_Delta

question: For most of the Ice Age, Utah's Lake Bonneville was a closed basin with no outlet, and meltwater kept filling it higher and higher. About 17,500 years ago its rising surface reached a low pass on its northern rim and began to spill over. What did that overflow turn into?
answer: a colossal flood that roared toward the Snake River
choices: a colossal flood that roared toward the Snake River
a slow trickle that drained it over many centuries
a deep freeze that locked it solid to the floor
a quiet seepage that emptied it into hidden caves
context: The Bonneville Flood sent almost 5,000 km³ of water toward the Snake River in under a year and dropped the lake's level by roughly 410 feet — among the largest floods known in Earth's history. It happened because a closed, overfilled basin finally found an escape over its rim. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bonneville

question: Chesapeake Bay reaches 200 miles up the eastern U.S. coast — not a slice of open ocean, but the drowned mouth of the Susquehanna River, where its prized blue crabs and oysters flourish as the river's flow meets the incoming Atlantic tide. Geographers give this kind of coastal feature its own name. What is it?
context: An estuary is a partly enclosed coastal body where a river's fresh water blends with the salty tide into a half-and-half mix called 'brackish' water (the word traces to Latin aestuarium, 'tidal inlet'). Because the two waters mix and pile up nutrients there, estuaries rank among the most productive natural habitats on Earth. A delta, by contrast, is the fan of sediment a river drops at its mouth — a landform, not a mixing zone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estuary

question: Twice every single day, the tide in one bay on Canada's Atlantic coast climbs about 16 m (52 ft) — roughly the height of a five-storey building — then drains away again, leaving boats that floated beside the docks at high tide stranded on bare mud far below. These are the highest tides in the world. Which bay is it?
context: The Bay of Fundy's funnel shape sets the water sloshing at just the right rhythm (tidal resonance), amplifying the range to a mean of 11.7 m (38.4 ft) at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia, with rare extremes near 17 m. It holds the famous record for the highest AVERAGE tidal range — essentially tied with Ungava Bay's Leaf Basin in Quebec (about 9.75 m) — so geographers credit Fundy with the highest mean range rather than over-claiming a single global number. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_range

question: Chesapeake Bay, a 200-mile inlet on the U.S. Atlantic coast, looks like an ordinary bay — but before the last ice age ended it was no bay at all, only the dry valley of the Susquehanna River winding toward a far-off shore. One great change at the close of the ice age turned that dry valley into today's bay. What was it?
answer: the sea rose and drowned the valley
choices: the sea rose and drowned the valley
a glacier gouged out the valley
a river carved a deep canyon
context: As the last ice age ended, melting ice sheets raised the sea, and around 10,000 years ago the rising Atlantic flooded the Susquehanna's old river valley, 'drowning' it into a 200-mile bay. A coastline drowned this way keeps the branching, tree-like outline of the original river channels, each old streambed now an arm of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesapeake_Bay

question: Along Spain's Galician coast the sea reaches deep inland up a cluster of long, flooded valleys; seen from above, each one branches like the bare limbs of a tree — every side-valley now a calm, sheltered finger of the sea. Geographers give this kind of drowned coastal valley its own name. What is it?
context: A ria is a drowned river valley — river-carved, so it keeps the branching, tree-like shape of the old streams. That is what sets it apart from a fjord, which is glacier-carved and steep U-shaped. The word 'ria' comes from the Galician río ('river'); Galicia's celebrated Rías Baixas are the classic example, and Chesapeake Bay is a ria too. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria

question: Each autumn, huge crowds gather on the banks of China's Qiantang River to watch a startling sight: a single wall of water up to 9 m (30 ft) high sweeps in from the sea and charges UP the river at 40 km/h, straight against the current, going the wrong way. Nicknamed the 'Silver Dragon,' it is the world's largest example of one particular river phenomenon. What is that phenomenon called?
context: A tidal bore is the leading edge of an incoming tide squeezed into a wave (or a train of waves) that races upstream against a river's normal flow. The Qiantang 'Silver Dragon' is the biggest on Earth; crowds have watched it for centuries, though its power has also swept away onlookers who stood too close. A tsunami, by contrast, is set off by an undersea quake or landslide, not by the tide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_bore

question: On the Amazon River, a wave called the pororoca charges tens of kilometres upstream, rolling up to 4 m (13 ft) high, and surfers paddle out to ride it — not for the few seconds an ocean wave allows, but for as long as the wave keeps rolling inland; in 2003 one surfer stayed up for 37 minutes on a single wave. The wave's name comes from Brazil's indigenous Tupi language. What does that Tupi name mean?
context: The Tupi name pororoca is often taken to mean 'great roar' — because along the Amazon you HEAR the wave minutes before you see it. It peaks at the September and March equinox spring tides, when the Sun and Moon pull together, and can travel up to 800 km inland. Surfers prize its length: in 2003 Picuruta Salazar rode a single pororoca wave about 12.5 km (7.8 mi), staying up for 37 minutes — a record — and an annual championship has run at São Domingos do Capim since 1999. But the wave is dangerous, carrying debris that can include whole uprooted trees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca

question: England's Severn River and China's Qiantang both send a roaring wave charging upstream against the current each year, yet thousands of other rivers with equally strong tides never do. That upstream wave forms only when two conditions come together. Besides a very large tidal range, what shape must the river's channel have for the wave to build?
context: The recipe for a tidal bore is a big tidal range (usually over about 6 m) PLUS a shallow channel that narrows and shoals upstream: the funnel squeezes the rising tide until it rears into a wave. Without the funnel the same tide just rises quietly. England's gentler Severn bore (up to about 2 m, a favourite of river surfers) shows the same recipe at a smaller scale. Human meddling can switch a bore off, too — a 1960s causeway nearly killed the once-huge bore on Canada's Petitcodiac River. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_bore

question: The height printed on a map for most mountains never changes. Mount Etna, the great volcano above Catania on Sicily's east coast, is different: surveyors keep re-measuring its summit because the number keeps shifting. What keeps changing Etna's height?
answer: Each summit eruption builds it up or tears it down
choices: Each summit eruption builds it up or tears it down
The whole cone is slowly sinking into the sea
Summit glaciers melt and reform every year
Wind strips ash from the peak each winter
context: Etna is the largest and most active volcano in Europe, standing about 3,400 m (11,000+ ft) tall. It erupts so often -- 16 times in the single year 2001 -- that fresh lava and ash keep rebuilding or blasting away its summit, so its official height genuinely rises and falls over time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Etna

question: Just north of Sicily, the small island of Stromboli has tossed up glowing bursts of lava every few minutes for thousands of years, never fully stopping. Its red glow is so steady after dark that sailors have steered by it for centuries, and they gave the island a fitting nickname. What is it?
context: Stromboli has erupted almost non-stop for roughly 2,000-5,000 years, its bursts flaring at intervals from minutes to hours. Because that glow is visible far out to sea night after night, sailors long used it as a natural beacon and dubbed the island the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strombolian_eruption

question: Stromboli's cone rises only about 926 m above the sea, small enough to climb in a single morning. When scientists mapped the seafloor all around the island, what did they find?
answer: The island is only the peak of a huge undersea mountain
choices: The island is only the peak of a huge undersea mountain
A second active crater lies hidden beneath the waves
An older, buried volcano sits under the island
The island is slowly drifting toward Sicily
context: Stromboli plunges more than 2,700 m below the waves -- the sunlit island is just the exposed tip of a giant undersea mountain. A huge horseshoe-shaped scar on its flank, the Sciara del Fuoco ('Stream of Fire'), funnels erupted lava and rock straight down into the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromboli

question: One family of volcanic eruptions runs almost like clockwork: every few minutes a vent burps a burst of pasty, glowing scoria blobs and molten bombs that arc tens to a few hundred meters up, then rain back down. It is only a mild blast -- level 1 or 2 on the explosivity scale -- and the lava is sticky rather than runny, so onlookers can safely watch the show from a nearby ridge night after night. Volcanologists file every eruption of this kind under one named style. What is that style called?
context: Those brief, rhythmic bursts (Volcanic Explosivity Index 1-2) are so characteristic of Stromboli that the entire style is called 'Strombolian' -- gentler than an ash-rich Vulcanian blast, far smaller than a towering Plinian column, and stickier than a fluid Hawaiian eruption. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strombolian_eruption

question: In the Aeolian Islands off Sicily, one smoking island so struck the ancient Romans that they pictured it as the chimney of a god's underground forge -- the rumble was his hammer shaping weapons and armor, and the sparks were the fire it belched. They named the island for that fire-god, and from that one island's name grew a word now used the world over. Which god was it?
context: The Romans named the island Vulcano for Vulcan, their god of fire and the forge, and imagined it as the chimney of his workshop -- earthquakes were Vulcan hammering weapons for the war-god Mars. From that one island's name came the English word 'volcano' and its cousins across Europe. (The Greeks had called it Thermessa, 'source of heat,' the private foundry of Hephaestus.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcano

question: In 1669, as Mount Etna's lava ground slowly toward the city of Catania, a priest named Diego Pappalardo and about fifty men dug a trench and pulled off the first recorded diversion of a lava flow -- the molten stream really did turn aside. Yet within days the lava swung back and destroyed part of Catania anyway. What undid their success?
answer: A nearby town, fearing the diverted lava, chased the diggers off
choices: A nearby town, fearing the diverted lava, chased the diggers off
A stronger summit burst simply overwhelmed the trench
The diverted lava cooled and dammed its own channel
Days of heavy rain collapsed the fresh trench walls
context: Pappalardo's roughly 50 men made the first recorded attempt to divert a lava flow. But people from a town toward Paterno, seeing the diverted lava now heading their way, chased the diggers off -- so the flow returned to its path toward Catania and buried part of the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1669_eruption_of_Mount_Etna

question: Long before anyone understood geology, the ancient Greeks told a story to explain why Mount Etna shook the ground and belched fire. After Zeus defeated a hundred-headed, fire-breathing monster, they said, he pinned it forever beneath the mountain, and its endless writhing was what made Etna roar and smoke. Which monster lies trapped under Etna in the myth?
context: In the myth, Zeus buried the hundred-headed monster Typhon beneath Etna, and its struggles shook the earth and spat flame -- flames the smith-god Hephaestus was sometimes said to use at his forge below the mountain. It is a story invented to explain a real, restless place. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhon  (Legend.)

question: In the candlelit taverns of Lisbon's oldest quarters — Alfama and Mouraria — a lone singer closes her eyes and pours out a slow song of heartbreak and longing over a crying, plucked guitar, while the whole room holds its breath. What is this Lisbon song called?
context: Fado — from the Latin 'fatum,' meaning fate — was born in the early 1800s in Lisbon's poorest, oldest quarters: Alfama, Mouraria and Bairro Alto, first sung by sailors, bohemians and tavern singers by candlelight. The music is literally named after fate itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fado

question: At the heart of every Lisbon fado is a single feeling: the bittersweet ache of longing for someone or something loved and lost, a sorrow so tender it turns almost sweet. There is one word for this exact feeling, and English has no true translation for it. What is the word?
context: 'Saudade' is the untranslatable Portuguese ache — a bittersweet yearning for someone or something loved and lost — and it is the single feeling every fado circles around. English has no one word to match it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fado ; https://aeon.co/ideas/saudade-the-untranslateable-word-for-the-presence-of-absence

question: Lisbon's fado floats on the shimmering, weeping voice of the guitarra portuguesa, a small pear-shaped guitar. Its tuning head is unlike any ordinary guitar's: the strings run to a gleaming metal fan of screws instead of a row of pegs, and each one is tightened by turning a screw with one small key. Which key is it?
context: The guitarra portuguesa is tuned with a small watch key: its twelve steel strings, arranged in six doubled pairs, run to a distinctive fan-shaped mechanism of screws that the player turns with the same kind of key once used to wind a pocket watch. The modern instrument descends from the 1750s English guitar, and comes in two models — the Lisbon guitar, tuned in D for a brighter, more resonant sound, and the Coimbra guitar, tuned in C for a darker one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitarra_portuguesa

question: Portugal has a second kind of fado, even stricter than Lisbon's. In the old city of Coimbra it is performed only after dark, out in the stone squares, by singers wrapped in flowing black capes — and by tradition only one group of people is allowed to sing it. Who?
context: Coimbra's fado, tied to its ancient university, is sung only by men — students and graduates in flowing black academic capes — at night in the city's squares, following an old troubadour tradition. Lisbon's fado, by contrast, rose up from sailors and tavern singers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fado

question: Amália Rodrigues, remembered as the 'Queen of Fado,' grew up poor in Lisbon, selling fruit down on the city's docks before her voice carried Lisbon's song across the world. What distinction does she still hold?
choices: the most-played voice on European radio
the first Portuguese star in Hollywood
context: Amália Rodrigues, the 'Rainha do Fado' (Queen of Fado), became the best-selling Portuguese artist in the history of recorded music. When she died on 6 October 1999, Portugal declared three days of national mourning, and in 2001 she became the first woman moved to the National Pantheon among Portugal's greatest figures. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A1lia_Rodrigues

question: Legend traces Lisbon fado all the way back to Maria Severa, a fiery half-Romani singer of the Mouraria whose doomed love affair scandalized the city and who died of tuberculosis at just 26, buried in a common grave. Ever since, fadistas have honored her by always performing in one black garment — the very kind she wore while singing of her broken heart. What is it?
context: Legend — not documented history — traces fado to Maria Severa Onofriana (1820–1846), a half-Romani singer of the Mouraria famous for her affair with the Count of Vimioso; she died of tuberculosis at 26 and was buried in a common grave. Fadistas are said to wear a black shawl in mourning for her, the costume echoed by every singer since. In 2011 UNESCO added Lisbon fado to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Severa_Onofriana ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fado

question: Emperor Akbar raised the imperial city of Fatehpur Sikri near Agra in the 1570s — its palaces, gateways and great mosque were all cut from a single local stone, giving the whole capital one dramatic, unbroken colour. What stone is Fatehpur Sikri built from?
context: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri on a rocky ridge near Agra in the 1570s, and its uniform red sandstone earned it the nickname 'the red city.' Occupied only from about 1571 to 1585, it survives today as one of the world's best-preserved 'ghost capitals.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Fatehpur_Sikri

question: Emperor Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri as a flawless new capital near Agra, then walked away from it within about fifteen years, leaving a perfect ghost city behind. The bare rocky ridge it stood on could never keep the fast-growing court supplied with one basic thing, and that shortage finally emptied the city. Which necessity ran short?
context: A brand-new capital emptied out mainly because its rocky ridge and the shallow, drying Sikri lake could not supply enough water for the growing city — the classic 'why abandon a new capital?' answer. Some historians add that Akbar also left around 1585 to run frontier campaigns and moved his court to Lahore. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Fatehpur_Sikri  (Legend.)

question: At Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar built the Buland Darwaza, a monumental gateway inlaid with white and black marble and reached by a broad flight of steps. Among all the great gates of the world, what record does the Buland Darwaza hold?
context: Built around 1575 to mark Akbar's conquest of Gujarat, the Buland Darwaza ('Exalted Gate') rises about 54 metres (176 feet), climbed by 42 steps, and is often called the highest gateway in the world. Across its arch runs a Persian line attributed to Jesus: 'The world is a bridge, pass over it, but build no houses on it' — an eerie motto for a city soon abandoned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buland_Darwaza  (Legend.)

question: In the fierce summer heat of Fatehpur Sikri, the royal women retreated to the Panch Mahal, an airy five-storey pavilion of open columns that shrinks floor by floor toward a tiny rooftop dome. Look closely at the columns holding it up and you notice a deliberate choice the carvers made. What did they do?
choices: every column bears the same design
every column hides a carved verse
context: The Panch Mahal ('Five Palace') is a badgir, a wind-catcher whose open storeys trapped the breeze to cool the royal women in the summer heat. Its 176 columns dwindle from 84 on the ground floor to just 4 holding the rooftop kiosk — and famously no two of them are carved alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panch_Mahal,_Fatehpur_Sikri

question: Emperor Akbar built his magnificent new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, on a rocky ridge beside the village of Sikri, near Agra, in the 1570s. Why did Akbar choose that exact spot for his imperial city?
answer: because a Sufi holy man there had promised him a son
choices: because a Sufi holy man there had promised him a son
because the high ridge could be easily defended
because it lay at the very center of his empire
because great caravan routes crossed there
context: Akbar, still without an heir, was told by the Sufi (Muslim mystic) saint Sheikh Salim Chishti that he would finally have a son. The boy, born at Sikri in 1569, was named Salim in the saint's honour and grew up to become the emperor Jahangir — so the whole red city rose as an act of gratitude. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salim_Chishti  (Legend.)

question: In the great mosque courtyard at Fatehpur Sikri stands the small white marble tomb of the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, carved so delicately that light pours right through its walls. To this day, women who long for a child come to the tomb and do one particular thing there. What do they do?
answer: tie a thread onto the tomb
choices: tie a thread onto the tomb
leave a coin at the tomb
light a lamp by the tomb
context: The tomb's walls are carved into lace-like jali (lattice) screens. Women hoping for a child tie a thread to the screen and return to untie it once the wish comes true — echoing the very prayer for a son that founded the whole city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Salim_Chishti  (Legend.)

question: In the old Moroccan city of Fes stands a mosque-school that Guinness and UNESCO recognize as the oldest continually operating university on Earth — founded back in 859 AD by a woman, the merchant's daughter Fatima al-Fihri. What is this school called?
context: Al-Qarawiyyin has taught continuously since 859 AD and is recognized by Guinness World Records and UNESCO as the oldest still-operating university on Earth. Its founder, Fatima al-Fihri, vowed to pour her entire inheritance into building it. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_al-Qarawiyyin)

question: Fes el-Bali, the walled old town of Fes, is one of the largest car-free areas of any city on Earth — a medieval maze of thousands of lanes, many barely wide enough for two people to squeeze past. With no room for a single car, how do heavy loads still get delivered across it today?
context: Fes el-Bali is one of the world's largest car-free urban zones: roughly 9,000 lanes, most only 1.5-3 meters wide, so donkeys and handcarts still handle the deliveries cars never could. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fez,_Morocco)

question: At the Chouara Tannery in Fes, workers have cured leather by hand in stone vats for a thousand years. The pits reek so violently — hides steep for days in a brew of pigeon droppings, cow urine, and quicklime — that guides press one small thing into each visitor's hand to hold under the nose. What is it?
context: The Chouara Tannery has worked leather by hand for about a thousand years. Hides first soak for days in white vats of pigeon droppings, cow urine, and quicklime to soften them; the mint helps visitors bear the reek before the hides are dyed with poppy, indigo, and henna and laid out to dry in the sun. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouara_Tannery)

question: Tucked inside al-Qarawiyyin in Fes is one of the oldest working libraries on Earth. Among its guarded treasures lies a Quran from the 9th century, its verses inked not on paper but on a far older writing surface. What is it?
context: Al-Qarawiyyin's library is among the oldest working libraries on Earth. Its treasures include a 9th-century Quran written on gazelle parchment and the original manuscript of Ibn Khaldun's history, which the author himself donated in 1396. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_al-Qarawiyyin)

question: Across the lane from a grand madrasa in Fes hangs Dar al-Magana, finished in 1357: a wall of thirteen little windows fronting a water clock whose inner floats and weights still aren't fully understood. To mark each passing hour, the hidden machine performed one small action at a window. What did it do?
answer: dropped a metal ball into a bowl
choices: dropped a metal ball into a bowl
context: Dar al-Magana, finished on 6 May 1357, faces the Bou Inania Madrasa. Each hour a hidden mechanism of floats and weights released a metal ball into one of thirteen brass bowls — and its exact workings are still not fully understood today. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar_al-Magana)

question: The whole old city of Fes runs on a single modest river, the Oued Fes — one stream made to serve a dense, thirsty medieval city. Long ago the city's builders re-engineered the river itself to pull this off. What did they do to it?
answer: split it into many small canals
choices: split it into many small canals
pumped it up to rooftop tanks
context: The Oued Fes is deliberately split into a web of small canals threaded through the medina, feeding its fountains, turning its mills, and filling the tannery vats — a single river engineered to serve the whole old city. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fez,_Morocco)

question: Geirangerfjord in western Norway is the postcard fjord: cliffs over 1,000 m rise straight from a 15-km arm of the sea, and down one wall spills the Seven Sisters, a waterfall of seven slender streams. On the cliff directly opposite stands one lone waterfall facing them. What does Norwegian legend say this solitary fall is forever trying to do?
context: The lone waterfall is the Suitor (Friaren); legend says his endless courtship of the seven sisters across Geirangerfjord will never succeed. The Seven Sisters (De syv soestrene) tumble down the opposite wall, the tallest stream free-falling about 250 m. The whole scene joined UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2005 as part of the 'West Norwegian Fjords.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Sisters_Waterfall_(Norway)

question: High on the near-vertical walls of Geirangerfjord in Norway, hundreds of metres above the water, cling the ruins of Skageflaa, Knivsflaa and Blomberg, reachable today only by boat and then a steep, punishing climb. What clung to these dizzying ledges, where people once lived cut off from the world?
context: Skageflaa, Knivsflaa and Blomberg are abandoned mountain farms perched hundreds of metres up Geirangerfjord's near-vertical walls; most can be reached only by boat and then a steep climb. Families once farmed these ledges in near-total isolation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geirangerfjord

question: One Norwegian fjord runs 205 km inland, farther into the country than any other, and plunges to 1,308 m below the surface, while sheer cliffs tower another 1,000 m overhead. Norwegians crown this longest and deepest giant the 'King of the Fjords.' Which fjord is it?
context: Sognefjord ('Fjordenes konge,' King of the Fjords) is Norway's longest fjord at 205 km and its deepest at 1,308 m, yet near its mouth the seafloor rises to a shallow sill only about 100 m down. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sognefjord

question: In New Zealand's Fiordland, one dark mountain rises in a single sharp spire straight out of the water of Milford Sound, climbing 1,692 m from the surface, so overwhelming that Rudyard Kipling called the place the 'eighth Wonder of the World.' What is this peak called?
context: Mitre Peak rises 1,692 m almost straight from Milford Sound; Rudyard Kipling dubbed the fiord the 'eighth Wonder of the World.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: The word 'fjord' sailed into English straight from Old Norse fjoerdr, the tongue of Norway's Viking seafarers, meaning a waterway you cross over. From that very same ancient root, English gets one of these everyday words. Which one?
context: 'Fjord' comes from Old Norse fjoerdr, a passage or crossing over water, the same root that gives English 'ferry.' A ford (a shallow river crossing) comes from a related but distinct Germanic root. https://grokipedia.com/page/Fjord

question: Milford Sound in New Zealand's Fiordland is one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth: a single day can dump 250 mm of rain, and the yearly total tops 6,000 mm. Right after a heavy downpour, the sheer fiord walls put on a show that fades away once the sun returns and the rock dries. What suddenly appears all across the cliffs?
choices: fog rolling thick along the walls
clouds pooling low in the valley
context: With about 6,412 mm of rain a year, and up to 250 mm in a single day, Milford Sound is one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Each downpour spawns hundreds of temporary waterfalls that streak the fiord walls, then dry up within a day or two of clear weather. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: New Zealand's Milford Sound is famous for being misnamed: geographers insist it is really a fiord, not a sound at all. The two words look alike and both name a valley the sea has drowned, but a fiord and a sound are drowned for different reasons. What makes a fiord a fiord, and not a sound?
answer: its valley was cut by ice, not water
choices: its valley was cut by ice, not water
its water is salt, not fresh
its walls are granite, not slate
its tide runs fast, not slow
context: A true 'sound' is a drowned RIVER valley, but Milford's trough was gouged by glaciers over millions of years, making it, strictly, a fiord. The name 'Sound' is a geographic mistake that stuck; the surrounding region is even called Fiordland. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: Sail into Norway's Sognefjord and the depth-sounder does something odd: the water is shallowest right at the mouth, only about 100 m deep, then the seabed drops away to a basin over 1,300 m deep locked behind it. What forms the shallow lip that bars this deep fjord's entrance?
answer: a bank of rubble the ice bulldozed there
choices: a bank of rubble the ice bulldozed there
a delta of silt the river dumped there
a bar of sand the tide swept in
a reef the cold-water coral built up
context: A glacier erodes less near its snout and dumps a terminal moraine there, leaving a shallow bedrock-and-rubble sill across a fjord's mouth. Behind the sill the basin plunges far deeper: at Sognefjord the mouth sill is only ~100 m down while the inner trough exceeds 1,300 m. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord

question: Geologists call fjords 'drowned valleys,' and they mean it literally. A glacier carved a deep Norwegian valley clear down to the coast, then the ice age ended and the glacier melted away, leaving the valley empty. Over the thousands of years since, water crept back in and filled it, making a fjord. What flooded the empty glacier valley?
answer: the sea rose and crept up the valley
choices: the sea rose and crept up the valley
the valley floor sank beneath the waves
the glacier's meltwater pooled and stayed
a highland river swelled and filled it
context: A glacier ground the valley floor below sea level; when the ice melted, the rising sea flooded the trough. So a fjord is a 'drowned valley,' saltwater filling a valley the ice, not a river, carved. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord

question: During the last ice age, ice up to 3 km thick crept down Norway's valleys and gouged Sognefjord more than 1,300 m deep, far deeper than any river could cut. Besides grinding the bedrock smooth as it slid over it, how did the moving ice bite so deep into solid rock?
answer: it froze onto blocks and tore them loose
choices: it froze onto blocks and tore them loose
it melted and dissolved the stone away
its meltwater blasted the rock apart
it cracked the rock with its sheer weight
context: During the Pleistocene, ice up to about 3 km thick ground out Sognefjord to 1,308 m, far deeper and steeper than any river could, by abrasion (rock frozen into the ice polishing striations) and plucking (ice tearing loose whole blocks). https://grokipedia.com/page/Fjord

question: On the coast of East Greenland lies a fjord that is not one channel but a vast branching tree of arms, its longest limb reaching about 340 km inland and its waters spreading across some 38,000 km2, the largest fjord system on Earth. What is this giant called?
context: Scoresby Sund (Kangertittivaq) in East Greenland is the largest fjord system on Earth, a tree of branching arms whose longest reaches ~340-350 km inland over a basin of ~38,000 km2. Its inner arms drop to ~1,450 m, and glaciers at its head calve icebergs that drift down the branches to the sea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoresby_Sound

question: Plot the world's fjord coasts on a map, Norway's thousand inlets, New Zealand's Fiordland, Alaska, Chilean Patagonia, Greenland, Scotland's sea lochs, and the scattered dots snap into one clear pattern, clustering along cold, high-latitude coasts and never in the warm tropics. This map of fjords is secretly a map of what vanished thing?
answer: where Ice Age glaciers reached the sea
choices: where Ice Age glaciers reached the sea
where great rivers met the sea
where old volcanoes ringed the sea
context: Fjords form only where Pleistocene ice sheets flowed all the way to the sea, so mapping the world's fjords traces the reach of the last ice age's glaciers, Norway alone has over 1,000. https://grokipedia.com/page/Fjord

question: Flamenco — Spain's fiery art of wailing song, driving guitar, and thunderous stamping dance — was born in the hot southern region around the cities of Seville, Cádiz, and Granada. What is this Spanish region called?
context: Andalusia (Andalucía), in Spain's deep south, is flamenco's homeland. From the 15th century, Roma families — the gitanos — settling here fused their music with the Moorish sounds of Al-Andalus, North African rhythm, Sephardic Jewish song, and local Andalusian folk. Wikipedia calls this centuries-long cultural intermingling the root of flamenco. Source: Wikipedia, 'Flamenco'.

question: At a flamenco night in a Seville courtyard, the audience is no mere crowd — they drive the beat with sharp cracking claps, soft cupped-hand pops, and crisp finger-snaps timed to the music. What are these flamenco hand-claps called?
context: Palmas — rhythmic hand-clapping — turn the whole room into a percussion section. They come in two kinds: palmas sordas, soft muffled pops made with cupped hands under the quiet singing, and palmas fuertes (or claras), sharp cracks made by snapping two or three fingers into the flat palm for loud, fast footwork. Source: Wikipedia, 'Palmas (music)'.

question: The gitanos — the Roma families who forged flamenco in the courtyards of Seville — were not native to Spain. They arrived in the 15th century as wanderers from a homeland far to the east, carrying music they would fuse with Moorish and Jewish Spain. Where did the Roma originally come from?
context: The Roma reached Spain from northern India in the 15th century and settled largely in Andalusia as the gitanos. There they fused their music with the Arab-Andalusian sounds of Al-Andalus, North African rhythm, and Sephardic Jewish song — the cultural intermingling that gave rise to flamenco. Source: Wikipedia, 'Flamenco'.

question: In a late-night Jerez flamenco session, the guitar, the hand-claps, and the dancer's stamping heels all lock together into one relentless twelve-beat cycle. Lose your place in it and the whole performance collapses. Flamenco has one word for this all-governing cycle — what is it?
context: The compás is flamenco's rhythmic heartbeat — most styles ride a demanding twelve-beat cycle, and the clapping, guitar, and heel-stamps must all lock into it. Wikipedia notes that compás 'is most often translated as rhythm but it demands far more precise interpretation than any other Western style of music.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Palo (flamenco)'.

question: Flamenco's many styles are called palos, each with its own mood. Near midnight in Jerez de la Frontera comes the fastest and most explosive palo of all — born right there in Jerez and traditionally saved to close the show in a whirlwind of clapping and stamping feet. Which palo is it?
context: The bulerías is flamenco's fastest, most exuberant palo, born in Jerez de la Frontera, and by tradition it closes the show — everyone joins a final storm of palmas and footwork. Its cousins riding the same twelve-beat cycle include the deep, foundational soleá, the most tragic seguiriya, and the joyful alegrías of Cádiz. Source: Wikipedia, 'Palo (flamenco)'.

question: On a Seville stage, a flamenco dancer wears a floor-length gown ending in an enormous ruffled train that pours out for meters behind her. As she spins, she whips and kicks that heavy train into sweeping arcs with her feet. What is this signature piece of flamenco costume called?
context: The bata de cola is flamenco's dramatic long-tailed dress, its ruffled train weighted so the dancer can hurl and sculpt it in the air with kicks and turns — a virtuoso skill in itself. Its partner move is the zapateado, the machine-gun heel-and-toe footwork that turns the stage floor into a drum. Source: Wikipedia, 'Flamenco'.

question: The poet Federico García Lorca gave a name to the mysterious force that seizes an Andalusian flamenco singer only when they perform on the very edge of danger — a dark, shivering, goosebump-raising spirit that, Lorca said, 'won't appear if he can't see the possibility of death.' What did Lorca call this spirit?
context: In a famous 1933 lecture in Buenos Aires, 'Play and Theory of the Duende,' Federico García Lorca called duende 'a power, not a work... a struggle, not a thought' — the soul that arrives only when an artist risks everything. He said, 'All that has dark sounds has duende,' and quoted an old Andalusian singer: 'The duende surges up, inside, from the soles of the feet.' Source: Lorca, 'Play and Theory of the Duende' (poetryintranslation.com).  (Legend.)

question: In a Seville tablao, a flamenco player sits astride a plain wooden box and drums the beat out of its front face with bare hands — yet the instrument isn't Spanish at all. Enslaved Afro-Peruvians built it on the coast near Lima from old shipping crates, and guitarist Paco de Lucía carried one home from Peru in 1977, where it became a staple of flamenco percussion. What is this instrument called?
context: The cajón — literally 'box' or 'crate' — was invented by enslaved Afro-Peruvians on Peru's coast, often from a plain shipping crate or fruit box. Paco de Lucía met the instrument in Lima in 1977 through Peruvian percussionist Caitro Soto, took one back to Spain, and it became flamenco's main drum. Peru declared the cajón part of its National Heritage in 2001. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cajón'.

question: Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, is crowned by an enormous dome finished in 1436. Almost six hundred years later, no one has ever built a larger dome out of the one building material that Filippo Brunelleschi used for its great shell. Which material was it?
context: Brunelleschi's dome used about four million bricks and is still the largest brick-and-masonry dome ever built. Rome's ancient Pantheon has a slightly wider dome, but it was poured in concrete rather than laid in brick; Brunelleschi's was also the first octagonal dome of its size raised since antiquity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Cathedral

question: When Filippo Brunelleschi raised the great dome over Florence's cathedral, the shell grew so wide that rival masters and the watching crowds could not fathom how the unfinished dome kept from caving in before it was closed at the top. What about his method left them unable to explain it?
answer: he raised it with no supporting frame beneath it at all
choices: he raised it with no supporting frame beneath it at all
he cast it as one solid shell of poured liquid stone
he hung it from great iron chains off the bell tower
he shaped it over a vast mound of packed earth
context: No forest could supply enough timber to prop a span that wide, so the dome had to hold itself up as it climbed higher and higher — the feat that stunned Florence. Source: https://science.howstuffworks.com/engineering/architecture/brunelleschis-dome.htm

question: Florence sits on the River Arno, crossed by several ancient bridges. On the night of 3–4 August 1944, the retreating German army blew up every one of them but one — sparing a single medieval bridge still crammed with tiny goldsmiths' and jewelers' shops. Which bridge did they leave standing?
context: The Ponte Vecchio, the shop-lined medieval bridge over the Arno, was the only Florence bridge the retreating Germans did not destroy that night. Why it was spared is debated — some accounts credit German consul Gerhard Wolf, others Hitler's fondness for the city. Source: https://www.historyhit.com/the-detonation-of-the-bridges-of-florence-and-german-atrocities-in-wartime-italy-during-world-war-two/

question: The real secret that let Brunelleschi's dome climb ever higher without collapsing lay in how its bricks were laid. Rather than stacking them in plain flat rings, which would have slid off the steepening, inward-leaning wall, he set them in a self-gripping pattern that locked each new ring to the one below and passed the weight down onto the stone ribs. What pattern did he use?
context: The herringbone pattern (Italian spina-pesce, 'fish-spine') locked each new ring in place and channeled the weight onto the ribs, so the spiral of brickwork reinforced itself as the masons climbed instead of sliding off the wall. Source: https://engineering.princeton.edu/news/2020/05/18/double-helix-masonry-researchers-uncover-secret-italian-renaissance-domes

question: A dome this heavy strains outward at its base, trying to burst apart like a barrel with no hoops. A Gothic cathedral would have braced that outward push with flying buttresses — the stone arms that lean against a church's outer walls — but Florence's proud officials had banned that 'foreign' style outright. So Brunelleschi buried his defenses inside the masonry, out of sight. What did he sink around the dome's base to bind it together?
answer: concealed rings of stone, iron, and wood
choices: concealed rings of stone, iron, and wood
concealed hoops of bronze and molten lead
concealed straps of forged steel plate
concealed bands of oak and twisted rope
context: Brunelleschi wrapped hidden 'chains' — rings of stone clamped with iron, plus a ring of wood — around the dome to squeeze it inward and stop it splaying apart, doing the job of the flying buttresses Florence's officials had forbidden. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Brunelleschi

question: Brunelleschi's dome is not one shell of brick but two — a heavier inner dome with a lighter outer dome built over it, with a narrow gap running between the two skins. Because of that hidden cavity, visitors to Florence today can do one particular thing inside the dome. What is it?
answer: climb a stairway that rises through the gap to the very top
choices: climb a stairway that rises through the gap to the very top
ride a lift installed in the gap between the two shells
walk out onto a gallery ringing the inner shell in the gap
look down into the shadowy gap between the two shells
context: The double shell cut the dome's weight, and about 463 steps climb up in the gap between the two walls, letting visitors walk up inside the dome to the lantern at the very top. Source: https://duomo.firenze.it/en/discover/dome

question: The painter Giorgio Vasari tells a story of how Brunelleschi beat his rivals to the commission. Refusing to show anyone his plans, he set the other masters a challenge: whoever could perform one simple feat deserved the job. Each rival tried and failed — then Brunelleschi did it in an instant, and it looked easy only because he had just shown them how. According to Vasari, what was the feat?
answer: standing an egg upright by tapping its base flat
choices: standing an egg upright by tapping its base flat
drawing a perfect circle freehand, with no compass
lifting a marble block using only a length of rope
balancing a gold coin on the edge of a blade
context: By Vasari's account, Brunelleschi challenged his rivals to stand an egg on end on a marble slab; when they all failed, he tapped its base flat so it stood — the answer looks obvious only once he shows you. The tale is likely embellished: his friend Manetti's earlier biography never mentions it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Brunelleschi  (Legend.)

question: Every winter on the plains of Alberta, a warm, dry wind comes pouring down the eastern side of the Rocky Mountains and can make a foot of snow vanish in a single afternoon -- some of it melting, some evaporating straight into the bone-dry air. The Blackfoot named it the 'snow-eater.' What do people there call this wind today?
context: The chinook ('snow-eater') is the North American name for a warm, dry downslope wind off the Rockies; a good one can raise the temperature many degrees in hours and strip a snowy field bare. The distractors are real winds too -- but the mistral, bora and sirocco all blow in the Old World, and the first two are cold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_wind

question: As a chinook climbs the western slopes of the Rockies, its moisture condenses and falls as rain and snow, so the air that spills down the eastern side into Alberta is bone-dry -- yet it arrives hotter than the air it shoves aside. What heats this dry wind as it sinks down the mountain's far side?
answer: sinking into thicker air below, it is squeezed and heats up
choices: sinking into thicker air below, it is squeezed and heats up
sliding down the slope, it is heated by friction with the rock
crossing the sunlit valley, it soaks up the day's heat
sweeping over bare ground, it draws warmth from the soil
context: This is the foehn effect. On the way up, the air loses its moisture and releases latent heat; on the way down, the denser air below compresses it, so it warms at the faster 'dry' rate and ends up hotter than it started -- a foehn can lift temperatures by as much as 14C (25F) in a few hours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_wind

question: On the morning of January 22, 1943, a chinook came roaring down off the mountains onto a town on the northern Great Plains and drove the thermometer from -4F all the way to +45F in just two minutes. Plate-glass storefront windows cracked from the sudden thermal shock. To this day it is the fastest temperature change ever recorded on Earth. In which town?
context: Spearfish, South Dakota holds the Guinness record: a 49F leap in 120 seconds as the chinook rolled off the Black Hills. By about 9:30 that morning it had plunged back to -4F. The other three are real chinook-belt towns on the plains east of the Rockies. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_wind

question: Each autumn a hot, bone-dry wind squeezes through Southern California mountain passes like Cajon and San Gorgonio, drops the humidity below 10%, gusts past 80 mph, and drives wildfires downslope toward Los Angeles. What is this wind called?
context: The Santa Ana winds are the same warm, dry downslope wind as the chinook and foehn. Southern Californians call them the 'devil winds,' and writers from Raymond Chandler ('Red Wind') to Joan Didion built stories around the edge they put on everyone's nerves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Ana_winds

question: Off the high Alps pours a warm, dry wind that can melt the winter snow in a day. Alpine folklore blames it for headaches, restlessness and dark moods, and the belief ran so deep that some old Swiss and Austrian courts once accepted 'a day of this wind' as a mitigating circumstance for a crime -- though doctors have never confirmed any such effect. What is this original Alpine wind called?
context: The foehn is the original wind of this whole family; the North American chinook and California's Santa Ana are the same beast under other names. The mood-and-health belief ('Foehnkrankheit'), first reviewed by the physician Anton Czermak in the 1800s, remains unproven folklore -- but the old courtroom custom really did exist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_wind  (Legend.)

question: Down the eastern face of the Argentine Andes a warm, dry wind roars onto the vineyards of Mendoza and San Juan, sometimes topping 240 km/h (150 mph) and stripping the humidity from the air. What is this wind called?
context: The zonda is the Argentine cousin of the chinook and foehn, and its fierce reputation lent its name to the Pagani Zonda supercar. The pampero, by contrast, is the cold wind that blows the other way -- up off the Argentine pampas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zonda_wind

question: Warm foehn winds spilling down the eastern slopes of the Antarctic Peninsula can lift the air temperature by up to 17C (30F) and melt the surface of ice shelves like Larsen C -- dotting the ice with ponds of meltwater even in the depths of winter. On the neighboring Larsen B shelf, that same surface melting helped trigger what event in 2002?
answer: its sudden collapse and shattering into the sea
choices: its sudden collapse and shattering into the sea
a huge single iceberg calving off its front
a fast retreat of its edge back toward land
a swarm of new crevasses splitting its center
context: In 2002 the Larsen B ice shelf disintegrated in a matter of weeks -- meltwater ponds like these had wedged into cracks and helped break it apart. Foehn winds keep warming and melting the surface of neighboring Larsen C in the same way, even through the polar winter. Source: https://www.carbonbrief.org/foehn-winds-causing-antarcticas-larsen-c-ice-shelf-to-melt-in-winter/

question: The Red Sea looks like a settled, permanent body of water on any map, but geologists insist it is only half-finished. Arabia is tearing away from the Horn of Africa along the Red Sea Rift, and the salt-water gap between them creeps wider year after year. Given millions of years more of this slow split, what do geologists expect the Red Sea to eventually become?
context: The Red Sea is a genuine baby ocean. It began opening in the Eocene and sped up in the Oligocene as the Arabian Peninsula split from the Horn of Africa along the Red Sea Rift; geologists say that, given millions of years more, it is on track to widen into a full-sized ocean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea (Grokipedia checked first, fetch blocked 403).

question: Continents normally drift apart no faster than a fingernail grows -- a couple of centimetres across a whole year. So geologists were astonished by what happened along the Red Sea rift in Ethiopia's Afar region in 2005: in a single burst of tectonic activity lasting only about three weeks, the ground yanked itself apart all at once. About how far did the rift pull open in those three weeks?
context: In 2005 the Afar rift widened by roughly 8 metres (26 ft) in about three weeks -- you can genuinely watch this sea grow. This was the Dabbahu rifting episode: a roughly 60-km-long dyke injected about 2.5 cubic km of magma into the crust in weeks, and it was the first such event ever captured by satellites. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea and https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04978.

question: A mid-ocean ridge -- the great seam where two plates pull apart and fresh crust wells up between them -- normally hides two miles down on the pitch-black deep-sea floor, where no one can walk. Ethiopia's Afar Depression is one of only two spots on Earth where that ocean-making seam has risen right up onto dry land you can stroll across. Which other place lets you walk on a spreading ridge above the waves?
context: Afar is one of only two places on Earth -- the other is Iceland -- where a mid-ocean-ridge spreading centre sits on dry land instead of being hidden about two miles under the sea. Iceland straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Hawaii, the Galápagos and Yellowstone are volcanic hotspots, not spreading ridges. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Afar_Depression (corroborated https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Triangle).

question: As the Afar crust stretches and thins, whole stretches of its floor have sagged far below the level of the distant ocean. The Danakil Depression lies roughly 125 metres down, and just over the border in Djibouti glitters a blinding-white, super-salty lake cradled in the rift -- the single lowest patch of dry ground anywhere on the African continent. Which lake sits at that lowest point of Africa?
context: Lake Assal in Djibouti is the lowest point in all of Africa, about 155 metres (509 ft) below sea level, ringed by salt where the Afar rift has dropped the crust. The nearby Danakil Depression floor lies roughly 125 metres below sea level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danakil_Depression.

question: Rising straight from the baking Danakil floor is Erta Ale -- 'smoking mountain' in the Afar language -- one of the most restless volcanoes on the planet. Since at least 1906 its summit pit has never once sealed over or fallen still, cradling a feature so rare that only a handful of volcanoes anywhere on Earth manage to hold one for so long. What has Erta Ale kept churning in its summit pit for more than a century?
context: Erta Ale holds one of Earth's very few long-lived lava lakes -- a churning pool of molten rock around 1,100-1,200 C that has persisted since at least 1906. Its southernmost pit has earned the grim nickname 'the gateway to hell,' though the summit stands just 613 m high. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erta_Ale (corroborated Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program).

question: Nowhere else on Earth stays as hot, averaged across the whole year, as Ethiopia's Danakil. At its blistering heart once sat a tiny salt-mining settlement where the heat almost never let up: from 1960 to 1966 it averaged a punishing 34.6 C (94 F) across every day and night of the year, taking the official world record as the hottest inhabited place on the planet. Which settlement holds that record?
