Freshwater ice barely floats in heavier seawater, so a berg rides very low, hiding most of itself beneath the surface. This is the picture behind 'the tip of the iceberg.' About how much of an iceberg lies hidden below the waterline?
context: Freshwater ice weighs about 920 kg per cubic meter and seawater about 1,025, so a berg must sink roughly nine-tenths of its bulk just to float — only about a tenth shows above the surface. That hidden mass is why 'the tip of the iceberg' came to mean the small visible piece of a much bigger problem. Source: NOAA / US Coast Guard Navigation Center (navcen.uscg.gov); Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: Two kinds of ice float in the waters off Greenland: thin 'sea ice' that forms when the ocean's surface freezes each winter, and towering icebergs that drifted down from the glaciers. A thirsty sailor soon learns the two are not the same. What is surprisingly true of an iceberg's ice, but not of sea ice?
answer: It's fresh water you could drink
choices: It's fresh water you could drink
It's saltier than the sea around it
It is barely a year old
It never melts, even in warm water
context: An iceberg is glacier ice — snow pressed down over thousands of years on land — that 'calved' (broke off) from the end of a glacier or ice shelf and floated away, which makes it fresh water. Sea ice is completely different: it's the ocean's own surface frozen into a salty crust each winter. The word 'iceberg' even comes from the Dutch ijsberg, 'ice mountain.' Source: NOAA (oceanservice.noaa.gov); Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: The ice spotters watching the shipping lanes off Newfoundland don't call every chunk of floating ice an 'iceberg' — a piece must be more than about 15 meters long to earn the name. The most dangerous small ones ride barely a meter above the water, about the size of a truck, and hide from radar in rough seas. What nickname do sailors give these little truck-sized chunks?
context: To count as a true 'iceberg,' floating ice must be more than about 15 meters long. Smaller pieces have their own names: a 'bergy bit' stands about 1-5 meters out of the water, and a 'growler' — named for the growling sound of air hissing out of the melting ice — rises less than a meter, about the size of a truck or a piano. Low and dark, growlers are notoriously hard for ships' radar to catch. Source: International Ice Patrol size classes; Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: The iceberg that sank the Titanic in the North Atlantic in 1912 didn't form anywhere nearby. Researchers trace it back years and hundreds of miles: it was born on a glacier, then rode the cold Labrador Current south through 'Iceberg Alley' off Newfoundland and into the shipping lanes. On whose glaciers was the Titanic's iceberg born?
context: The Titanic's iceberg was born on Greenland's glaciers — researchers point to the Jakobshavn Glacier near Disko Bay — then drifted south down 'Iceberg Alley' on the cold Labrador Current, into the North Atlantic shipping lanes off Newfoundland. After the 1912 disaster, more than a dozen nations founded the International Ice Patrol (run by the US Coast Guard) in 1914 to track drifting bergs and warn ships. Source: Wikipedia, 'Iceberg that sank the Titanic'; International Ice Patrol.  (Legend.)

question: The largest icebergs ever measured aren't Arctic at all — they're flat-topped 'tabular' giants that calve off (break away from) Antarctica's floating ice shelves. When B-15 broke from the Ross Ice Shelf in 2000, it was so vast that scientists reached for an island to describe its size. Which island was the Antarctic berg B-15 as big as?
context: B-15 calved from Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf in March 2000, measuring roughly 295 by 37 km — about 11,000 square kilometers, the size of Jamaica. Antarctica's flat-topped 'tabular' bergs, wider than they are tall, calve off floating ice shelves and dwarf Arctic bergs. Another giant, A23a, broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986, grounded on the seabed for about 30 years, then finally drifted free in 2020. Source: Wikipedia, 'Iceberg B-15' and 'A23a'; British Antarctic Survey.

question: Most icebergs look white or pale, but sailors off Antarctica sometimes meet one that glows an eerie, deep sapphire blue all the way through — like a floating jewel. That color is a clue to the ice's history: it tells you the berg is something surprising. What does a deep-blue iceberg reveal about its ice?
answer: It is thousands of years old
choices: It is thousands of years old
It is barely a year old
It is still full of trapped air
It is really salty sea ice
context: Fresh glacier ice is full of tiny trapped air bubbles that scatter light and look white. But after thousands of years, the sheer weight of the ice squeezes those bubbles out; with nothing left to scatter the light, the dense ice absorbs the red and yellow wavelengths and reflects deep blue back to your eye — so a blue berg is old ice. Rarer still, a few Antarctic bergs glow jade green, colored by iron-rich dust frozen into the ice. Source: NOAA (oceanservice.noaa.gov); National Geographic.

question: Over the last 500 years, one tiny north-Atlantic island has erupted a jaw-dropping share of ALL the lava that has poured out anywhere on the whole planet. Roughly what fraction of Earth's total erupted lava has come from Iceland alone?
context: Over the past 500 years Iceland's volcanoes have produced roughly a third of all the lava erupted on the whole planet -- astonishing for one small island that packs in around 30 active volcanic systems. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: In 2021, a volcano called Fagradalsfjall woke up on Iceland's Reykjanes peninsula after roughly 800 years of silence. Strangely, it caused no panic -- instead about 700,000 visits were logged over three years. What did the crowds hike across the lava fields to do?
choices: Soak in the warm ash pools
context: Fagradalsfjall began erupting on March 19, 2021 -- the area's first eruption in about 800 years. Rather than forcing evacuations, it became a spectacle: roughly 700,000 visits were logged across the 2021-2023 eruptions as people hiked out to watch fresh lava. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagradalsfjall

question: Almost the entire length of the world's longest mountain range hides deep beneath the oceans, marking where the sea floor splits and spreads apart. Iceland is the rare place where this undersea range rises high enough to break the surface and become dry land. Which spreading ridge surfaces in Iceland?
context: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent boundary -- the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart along it. Almost everywhere it lies deep undersea, but in Iceland it rises onto dry land, so the country is literally splitting. Iceland also sits over a hotspot; both feed its volcanoes, and the plates here diverge -- they never collide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: The rift running through Iceland is the actual seam between two of Earth's great tectonic plates, and the island is slowly splitting in two along it as they crawl apart. Which two plates meet and pull apart beneath Iceland?
answer: The North American and Eurasian plates
choices: The North American and Eurasian plates
context: Iceland straddles the seam between the North American and Eurasian plates. They drift apart about 2 cm a year, so Iceland grows a little wider annually -- the western half riding with North America, the eastern half with Eurasia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: Nearly everywhere on Earth, the boundary between two tectonic plates lies hidden far beneath the sea. But at one national park in Iceland you can walk down into the open rift itself, along a gorge with a cliff of North America rising on one side and a cliff of Eurasia on the other. What is this rift-valley park called?
context: At Thingvellir National Park you can walk into the Almannagja gorge -- the largest fault crossing the rift -- with a wall of the North American plate on one side and Eurasia on the other. Thingvellir also hosted the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, founded in 930 AD, but the geological wonder is the rift itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thingvellir

question: The Silfra fissure, a flooded crack in Iceland's rift zone, is the one spot on Earth where divers can drop into the gap between two tectonic plates and glide with North America on one side and Eurasia on the other. Beyond that unique dive, Silfra draws divers from around the world for one more superlative. What is Silfra famous for?
context: Silfra sits in the Thingvellir rift and is the only place on Earth where you can dive or snorkel directly in the crack between two tectonic plates. Its glacial meltwater is filtered for decades through porous lava rock, giving over 100 meters (328 ft) of visibility -- said to be the clearest water on Earth. Source: https://www.padi.com/dive-site/iceland/silfra/  (Legend.)

question: One of Iceland's strangest dangers is born where fire meets ice: a volcano hidden under a glacier, like Grimsvotn beneath the vast Vatnajokull ice cap, quietly melts the ice from below. Meltwater pools in a hidden lake under the glacier until it suddenly bursts free in a violent flood. Icelanders have their own word for this glacier-burst flood. What is it?
context: A jokulhlaup (Icelandic for 'glacier run') bursts out when a volcano melts a glacier from below until the trapped meltwater breaks free. Grimsvotn, under the Vatnajokull ice cap, is a jokulhlaup factory: its 1996 Gjalp eruption unleashed a flood peaking around 500,000 cubic meters per second -- many times the flow of a great river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6kulhlaup

question: In April 2010 a volcano erupted through the ice of Iceland's Eyjafjallajokull glacier, throwing up a cloud of fine, glassy ash. A steady jet-stream wind carried it southeast over Europe, and because such ash can wreck jet engines, authorities grounded flights across the continent -- cancelling over 100,000 flights and stranding around 10 million passengers. This was the worst shutdown of European air travel since which event?
context: The 2010 Eyjafjallajokull ash plume rose about 9 km and, blown southeast by a steady jet stream, blanketed Europe. Most European airspace closed April 15-20; over 300 airports in about 20 countries stopped flights, more than 100,000 flights were cancelled and roughly 10 million passengers were stranded -- the worst air-travel disruption since World War II. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_eruptions_of_Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull

question: Just after midnight on January 23, 1973, the Eldfell volcano ripped a glowing fissure across the little Icelandic island of Heimaey, barely a kilometer from the sleeping town. Nearly all 5,300 residents were carried to safety within about six hours -- remarkable for a small island in the middle of a winter night. How were the townspeople evacuated so fast?
choices: On planes from the island airstrip
context: When Eldfell's fissure tore open barely a kilometer from Heimaey's town center in the early hours of January 23, 1973, nearly all ~5,300 residents were evacuated by the island's fishing boats within about six hours -- much of the fleet happened to be in the harbor that night. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell

question: The Eldfell eruption on Heimaey dragged on for months, and a slow wall of black lava crept toward the mouth of the island's harbor -- the lifeline of this fishing town. If it sealed the harbor, the town was finished. So for weeks the islanders and their helpers battled the advancing lava head-on, fighting to chill it solid before it could seal them off. What did they blast onto the lava to freeze it in place and save the harbor?
context: To stop Eldfell's lava from sealing off the harbor, townspeople and crews pumped about 7.3 million cubic meters of seawater onto the flow -- up to 1,000 liters per second through 32 pumps -- cooling it solid. They saved the harbor, and the hardened lava even improved it by forming a new breakwater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell

question: Everyone arrives at Iguazú expecting one enormous waterfall, but the river splits around forested islands and spills over a 2.7-km arc as a long row of separate falls. Guides quote a headline number for how many that adds up to — a total most first-timers never guess. About how many falls is it?
context: Iguazú isn't one waterfall but a system of roughly 275 cascades strung along a 2.7-km (1.7-mile) arc — and the count actually shifts with the water, from about 150 in the dry season toward 300 in flood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: When U.S. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt first laid eyes on Iguazú — an arc nearly three times wider than Niagara Falls — she reportedly summed it up in one tart remark. What did she gasp?
context: Iguazú's arc is nearly three times as wide as Niagara, and Niagara is the shorter drop too — so the pity was earned. 'Poor Niagara!' is the line everyone repeats about Eleanor Roosevelt's first visit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls (width corroborated by https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/iguazu-falls-bucket-list)

question: Along Iguazú's 2.7-km arc, one feature dwarfs every other: a U-shaped chasm where about fourteen separate falls converge and crash together into one ~82-metre plunge, hurling up a permanent tower of mist. This most violent part of the whole system carries a fittingly sinister name. What is it called?
context: In Spanish it's the Garganta del Diablo — the Devil's Throat. About fourteen cascades pour together into this one U-shaped chasm and drop roughly 82 metres, the tallest and loudest part of the whole falls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil%27s_Throat,_Iguazu_Falls

question: Of Iguazú's couple-hundred cascades, a single deep gorge swallows a shockingly outsized share of the whole river by itself. Standing on the catwalk at its rim, about how much of the entire Iguazú River are you watching pour into that one gorge?
context: That gorge is the Devil's Throat, and it hogs about half of the Iguazú River's entire flow — funnelling it into a chasm roughly 82 m high, 150 m wide, and 700 m long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil%27s_Throat,_Iguazu_Falls

question: Long before Europeans came, the Guaraní people lived along this river and gave it the name still used today: Iguazú. In their language they joined two everyday words — 'y' and 'ûasú' — to capture what towered in front of them. What does 'Iguazú' mean?
context: In Guaraní, 'y' means water and 'ûasú' means big — Iguazú is simply 'big water.' The Guaraní named the river for the obvious long before any European saw it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Guaraní oral tradition explains Iguazú with a tale of jealous rage: a forest serpent-god meant to take a girl named Naipí for himself, but she fled downriver by canoe with her mortal love, Tarobá. In the legend, what did the furious god do that created the falls in an instant?
answer: he sliced the river in two
choices: he sliced the river in two
he turned their canoe to stone
context: This is told as legend, not history. In the Guaraní tale the serpent-god, robbed of Naipí, slashed the river into a cliff so the fleeing canoe would plunge — condemning Naipí and Tarobá to fall forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Iguazú has been a movie star, too. A Palme d'Or-winning 1986 epic about Jesuit priests among the Guaraní opens with a captured father lashed to a wooden cross and sent tumbling over the falls — an image so breathtaking it helped win the film an Oscar for its cinematography. What is this movie called?
context: The film is The Mission (1986), which took the Palme d'Or at Cannes and an Oscar for cinematography — much of it shot at Iguazú, including the martyred priest sent over the cataracts lashed to a cross. Source: https://about.new7wonders.com/2011/05/30/the-mission-at-iguazu-falls/

question: Great dusky swifts spend the daylight hours snatching insects from the mist above Iguazú's cascades. At dusk the whole flock streams back to a single, astonishing roost — a place so hard to reach that few predators dare follow. Where does this little bird tuck its nests?
answer: on ledges behind the falling water
choices: on ledges behind the falling water
on cliff shelves above the gorge
on rock stacks amid the rapids
in crevices deep in the canyon wall
context: Great dusky swifts really do fly straight through the curtain of falling water to reach ledges on the bare rock behind it — the sheet of water walls their nests off from predators. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/great-dusky-swift

question: The hard black rock that Iguazú's water leaps off isn't ordinary bedrock: it's the top of a colossal stack of ancient lava flows, piled up to a kilometre thick across the whole Paraná Plateau when this corner of South America was buried under erupting lava. Geologists have a term for such a vast sheet of stacked, hardened lava. What is it?
context: It's flood basalt — the Serra Geral formation of the Paraná Plateau, a stack of old lava flows up to about 1,000 m thick. The whole river simply tumbles off the edge of that ancient lava sheet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Iguazú will not stay put. Just as Niagara does, the falls are slowly gnawing their way upstream: beneath the tough basalt lip the softer rock washes out, the overhang cracks and drops away, and the whole cliff-line creeps a couple of centimetres farther upriver every year. Geographers have a specific name for this slow migration of an entire waterfall. What is it?
context: It's headward erosion. Undercutting strips the soft rock from beneath the hard basalt cap, the ledge collapses backward — and so the whole waterfall slowly migrates toward the river's source, about 1.4 to 2.1 cm a year, the same slow retreat that is dragging Niagara upstream too. Undercutting, plunge-pool scour and hydraulic action are the mechanisms doing the work; 'headward erosion' is the name for the migration itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: A 17th-century Persian saying boasts that the Safavid capital of Isfahan -- with its blue domes, its enormous square, and its painted palaces -- is so dazzling that to see this one city is to have seen a huge share of everything on Earth worth seeing. How much of the world does the proverb claim Isfahan equals?
context: The proverb runs 'Isfahan nesf-e jahan ast' -- 'Isfahan is half the world.' Shah Abbas the Great made Isfahan his capital around 1600 and packed it with wonders to earn the boast. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan)  (Legend.)

question: At the center of Isfahan, Shah Abbas the Great laid out a rectangular plaza around 1600 that runs some 560 m end to end -- big enough to rank among the largest public squares anywhere on Earth, framed on all four sides by mosques, a palace, and a bazaar gate. What is this vast plaza called?
context: Naqsh-e Jahan means 'Image of the World.' About 160 x 560 m (~89,600 m2), it was built 1598-1629 and is protected by UNESCO as 'Meidan Emam, Esfahan.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqsh-e_Jahan_Square)

question: Isfahan's great central square was not only a marketplace and a parade ground -- the Safavid shahs also used the whole plaza as a royal polo field, galloping after the ball while the court watched from a palace terrace. Four hundred years on, what from those matches still stands at each end of the square?
context: The marble goalposts said to date from the Safavid games still stand at the square's north and south ends, some 400 years later. The shah watched from the terrace of the Ali Qapu Palace on the west side. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqsh-e_Jahan_Square)  (Legend.)

question: On the east side of Isfahan's great square sits the small, jewel-like Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque -- and unlike almost every other grand mosque, it has no towering minaret and no open courtyard at all. What explains these missing features?
answer: it was the shah's private family mosque
choices: it was the shah's private family mosque
it was left unfinished when Shah Abbas died
it was originally a royal library
it was meant only for winter use
context: Because it was the shah's private family mosque rather than a public one, it needed no minaret to summon crowds and no courtyard to hold them. It was named in 1622 after Sheikh Lotfollah, Shah Abbas's revered father-in-law. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Lotfollah_Mosque)

question: Isfahan's Si-o-se-pol, a nearly 300-m Safavid span of 33 stone arches across the Zayanderud river, was more than a bridge and more than the city's favorite gathering spot. Its builders gave the structure a clever second purpose that a plain bridge could never serve. What was it?
answer: it held the river back as a dam
choices: it held the river back as a dam
it cooled the palace with piped water
context: The 33-arch Si-o-se-pol ('bridge of 33 arches') was built 1599-1602 under the Safavid commander Allahverdi Khan; it could pond the Zayanderud upstream like a dam, and its arcades are still where people of Isfahan meet at dusk. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si-o-se-pol)

question: Shah Abbas II built a garden pavilion in Isfahan around 1647 and named it Chehel Sotoun -- 'Forty Columns.' Yet a visitor who counts the slender wooden columns holding up its porch finds only twenty. Where are the other twenty columns?
answer: mirrored in the pool out front
choices: mirrored in the pool out front
painted as a trick on the back wall
context: By tradition the twenty columns double to 'forty' in the long reflecting pool laid before the pavilion -- the name is a poetic count, not a literal one. Chehel Sotoun was finished under Shah Abbas II around 1647. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chehel_Sotoun)  (Legend.)

question: The great blue dome of Isfahan's Shah Mosque glows across the square in turquoise and cobalt, its whole surface a skin of glazed tiles. To cover so vast a dome quickly, its Safavid craftsmen perfected a faster tile-glazing method that broke with the older, painstaking mosaic style. What was their shortcut?
answer: painting many colors onto each tile before firing
choices: painting many colors onto each tile before firing
firing each tile once for every color
pressing gold leaf over the glaze
carving the design into wet plaster
context: The method is called haft-rangi -- 'seven colors' -- because up to seven glaze colors were painted onto a single square tile and fired together, far faster than cutting and fitting single-color mosaic pieces. It gave Isfahan's domes their glowing skin. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Mosque_(Isfahan))

question: Sweden's High Coast, on the Gulf of Bothnia, is the fastest-rising land known on Earth: it has climbed about 300 metres over the past ten thousand years, and it still rises roughly 8 mm every year. What is lifting this whole coastline?
answer: An ice-age glacier that pressed the crust down has now melted away
choices: An ice-age glacier that pressed the crust down has now melted away
A plume of hot magma is slowly rising beneath the whole region
Two tectonic plates are colliding and crumpling the coast here
Ages of river sediment have piled up along the whole shore
context: The crust floats on the soft, dense mantle below. A great ice sheet — here about two miles thick — pressed the land down like a hand pushing into a mattress; now that the ice has melted, the land is slowly springing back up. This is 'isostatic rebound.' Sweden's High Coast (Hoega Kusten) has risen about 300 m since the ice melted and still rises ~8 mm a year — Wikipedia calls it the highest known isostatic rebound on Earth. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2000, joined in 2006 with Finland's Kvarken archipelago) precisely because it shows the process live, and it is where post-glacial rebound was first recognised and studied. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Coast ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/898/

question: Around Hudson Bay in Canada — the very heart of the old Laurentide Ice Sheet, whose ice vanished only about 8,000 years ago — sensitive instruments pick up a genuine anomaly: one everyday measurement comes out noticeably lower there than almost anywhere else on Earth. Which one?
answer: Gravity — a scale shows you weigh a hair less
choices: Gravity — a scale shows you weigh a hair less
Air pressure — a barometer reads a touch lower
The magnetic field — a compass pulls a bit weaker
The temperature — a thermometer runs a shade colder
context: Where the ice pressed hardest, the crust is still slightly 'dented' and has not fully risen back, so there is a little less mass beneath you — and gravity reads measurably weaker: about 0.3 milligals below normal, meaning you would weigh roughly 0.005% (about a tenth of an ounce) less at Hudson Bay than elsewhere. Honest caveat: incomplete rebound explains only about a quarter to a half of this gravity low; the rest comes from slow, deep mantle flow, not the vanished ice. The Laurentide Ice Sheet was about 3.2 km thick (up to ~3.7 km over the bay) and weighed on the order of 10 trillion tons; the land there still rises about 1 cm a year and has roughly 650 more feet to rebound over the next ~5,000 years. Sources: https://earthlymission.com/hudson-bay-quebec-gravity-anomaly-explained/ ; https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/92GL00687

question: At Finland's Kvarken archipelago, on the Gulf of Bothnia, the maps go out of date within a single human lifetime: the coastline visibly moves from one decade to the next. What is happening to this shore?
answer: Fresh land keeps rising from the sea, gaining new meadows each year
choices: Fresh land keeps rising from the sea, gaining new meadows each year
The coast is steadily sinking, drowning its old fishing villages
Fierce storms are tearing the shoreline back a little each year
Great tides scour the flat shores bare twice every single day
context: The land at Kvarken rises about 8-9 mm a year, so the shallow sea keeps turning into ground: roughly 700 hectares of fresh land — about twice the size of New York's Central Park — surface every year (around one square kilometre annually). New islands and meadows appear within a human lifetime, and old harbours are left stranded far inland: Vaasa's harbour grew too shallow to use, and after the town burned in 1852 it was rebuilt 6-7 km closer to the sea (the fire triggered the move, but the retreating shoreline is why they rebuilt seaward). Geologists expect the shallow Kvarken seabed to surface within about 2,000 years, pinching the Gulf of Bothnia into a southern gulf and a northern lake. (The Baltic here is nearly tideless, so the 'great tides' option was a red herring.) Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/uplift-underway-in-finlands-kvarken-archipelago-153740/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kvarken

question: Istanbul is the only great city on Earth that sits on two continents at once — half of it in Europe, half in Asia — divided down the middle by a narrow saltwater channel busy with ferries. What is the name of that channel splitting the city?
context: The Bosphorus is about 31 km long and pinches to just ~700 m at its narrowest — a saltwater strait, not a river. Istanbul is the only major city built across two continents, and ferries and bridges knit its European and Asian halves together. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosphorus

question: Around the year 537 AD, the emperor Justinian finished a colossal domed monument in just under six years — its dome so wide and ringed with windows that it seemed to float on light. Which Istanbul landmark, still standing after nearly 1,500 years, is this?
context: Justinian I ordered Hagia Sophia raised after riots destroyed the earlier church; it went up in just 5 years and 10 months (532–537 AD), designed by two scholars — the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer Isidore of Miletus. It remained the largest cathedral on Earth for nearly a thousand years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: In the heart of old Istanbul sprawls one of the oldest and biggest covered markets on Earth — a roofed maze of around sixty streets and over four thousand shops, first built under Mehmed the Conqueror in the 1450s, where a quarter-million people bargain every single day. What is this vast covered market called?
context: The Grand Bazaar has around 61 covered streets and over 4,000 shops, begun under Mehmed II in the 1450s–60s. Between 250,000 and 400,000 people pass through it every day — one of the oldest and largest covered markets anywhere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bazaar,_Istanbul

question: Beneath Istanbul's busy streets lies a dim, echoing reservoir built 1,500 years ago under the emperor Justinian — the Basilica Cistern, a forest of 336 marble columns rising from shallow water. Two of those columns don't rest on plain stone bases, but on two enormous carved faces hauled there from some far older ruin. Whose face is carved at the base of those two columns?
context: The Basilica Cistern (Turkish Yerebatan Sarayı, 'Sunken Palace') was built under Justinian in the 6th century, about 138 m by 65 m, its 336 columns standing over the shallow water. Two columns rest on huge carved Medusa heads dragged from an older Roman building — one set upside down, the other on its side. No one knows for certain why they were placed that way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_Cistern

question: Hagia Sophia has switched roles again and again across 1,500 years: an Orthodox Christian cathedral, then a mosque after Mehmed II took the city in 1453, and today a mosque once more. But in 1935, Turkey's new secular republic reopened the ancient building as something belonging to no single faith. What did Hagia Sophia become in 1935?
context: Hagia Sophia lived four lives: an Orthodox cathedral from 537, a mosque after Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, a museum from 1935 under the secular Turkish Republic, and a working mosque again from 2020. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: Istanbul is one of the few cities to have carried three great names. Constantine the Great made it the Roman Empire's capital in 330 AD, and it took the name Constantinople for the next thousand years. But it had already existed for centuries as a small Greek town, founded by settlers from Megara around 660 BC. What was that first Greek town called?
context: Settlers from Megara founded Byzantium around 660 BC. Constantine the Great refounded it as the Roman capital in 330 AD, and it became Constantinople; the name 'Istanbul' — from the Greek phrase 'stin poli,' 'to the City' — became official only in 1930. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Istanbul

question: The Galata Tower, a stout stone cylinder built by Genoese settlers in 1348, still rises above Istanbul's northern shore. A famous legend from 1638 tells of Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi, who crossed the entire Bosphorus in one astonishing feat — from the European side clear to the Asian shore. How does the legend say he made the crossing?
answer: he glided across on home-made wings
choices: he glided across on home-made wings
he swam the whole way across
he crossed on a single tightrope
he rowed over in a tiny skiff
context: The Galata Tower (~67 m) was raised by Genoese settlers in 1348 and called the 'Tower of Christ,' once the tallest building in the city. The 1638 tale of Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi gliding on home-made wings across the Bosphorus is a beloved legend, not documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galata_Tower

question: For a thousand years Constantinople turned back every army behind its triple Theodosian Walls — a deep moat backed by two towering lines of stone ramparts. Then in 1453 the young sultan Mehmed II finally broke through with a single fearsome weapon, built specially for the siege and so massive that teams of oxen had to haul it into position. What was this siege weapon?
context: Mehmed II's Hungarian founder Orban cast a giant bronze bombard, the 'Basilic,' about 9 m long, which hurled stone balls of roughly 500 kg; accounts say teams of oxen dragged it to the walls. The 5.7-km triple Theodosian Walls had guarded the city for a thousand years before falling on 29 May 1453. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1180/1453-the-fall-of-constantinople/ ; https://worldhistoryedu.com/walls-of-constantinople/

question: The Bosphorus curls through Istanbul like a river, but it is really a strait — a narrow saltwater channel joining two seas, only about 700 metres wide at its tightest pinch. One great sea has no other natural passage out to the wider Mediterranean except through this single gap. Which sea is bottled up behind the Bosphorus?
context: The Bosphorus is the only sea-gate out of the Black Sea, linking it through the Sea of Marmara to the Mediterranean. About 31 km long and only ~700 m wide at its narrowest, it is a true strait, not a river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosphorus

question: For nearly four hundred years the Ottoman sultans ruled a vast empire from one sprawling palace in Istanbul, set on a wooded point of land where the Bosphorus flows into the Sea of Marmara. Mehmed the Conqueror began building it in 1459, and it stayed the seat of Ottoman power until the mid-1800s. Which palace was that centre of the empire?
context: Mehmed the Conqueror began Topkapı Palace in 1459 on Seraglio Point, where the Bosphorus meets the Sea of Marmara. It housed the sultans for about 400 years, until they moved to the new Dolmabahçe Palace in 1853. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topkap%C4%B1_Palace

question: Sultan Ahmed I raised his great mosque facing Hagia Sophia between 1609 and 1616, and gave it six slender minarets. This set off a scandal: the holiest mosque in all Islam, the Great Mosque of Mecca, also had exactly six minarets — and nothing was supposed to rival Mecca. According to legend, how did the Sultan settle the uproar?
answer: he funded a seventh minaret added at Mecca
choices: he funded a seventh minaret added at Mecca
he had one of his six minarets torn down
he left his sixth minaret unfinished
he renamed his mosque to honour Mecca
context: The six-minaret Sultan Ahmed Mosque (1609–1616), nicknamed the 'Blue Mosque' for its tens of thousands of blue İznik tiles, faces Hagia Sophia across a square. Legend says Ahmed I paid for a seventh minaret at Mecca's Great Mosque to settle the rivalry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Ahmed_Mosque

question: Jaipur is one of Rajasthan's four most famous cities, and each of the four is known by a vivid nickname earned from its own signature look. Step through the gates into Jaipur's old walled town and the reason for its nickname surrounds you at once. What is Jaipur nicknamed?
context: The whole walled old town of Jaipur is washed a single terracotta pink — the traditional colour of welcome — which earned it the name the 'Pink City.' Its Rajasthan neighbours wear their own nicknames: Jodhpur is the Blue City, Jaisalmer the Golden City, and Udaipur the City of Lakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Jaipur's old town was not always its famous single colour. In 1876, Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II ordered every building painted that one shade — the traditional colour of welcome and hospitality — as a vast gesture to honour one important visitor then arriving in the city. Whom was Jaipur dressed up to greet?
answer: the visiting Prince of Wales, Britain's future king
choices: the visiting Prince of Wales, Britain's future king
Queen Victoria, newly proclaimed Empress of India
the Viceroy of India, the Queen's deputy in Delhi
the Nizam of Hyderabad, a great Indian prince
context: The guest was Albert Edward, the Prince of Wales, on his 1875–76 royal tour of India; he would later be crowned King Edward VII. Pink was the colour of hospitality, so Ram Singh II had the whole old town washed in it to welcome him — and Jaipur has stayed pink ever since. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Jaipur was founded in 1727 as a brand-new capital by Sawai Jai Singh II, a Kachhwaha Rajput ruler remembered as much for one consuming personal passion as for the city he built. What was Jai Singh II's ruling passion?
context: Jai Singh II was a serious astronomer who built great stone observatories in Jaipur, Delhi, and other cities. He named his capital 'Jaipur' — the City of Jai — and founded it on 18 November 1727. His love of the sky shaped the city, from its careful plan to its climbable observatory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Most of India's old cities grew over centuries into tangled mazes of winding lanes. Jaipur was different: in 1727 its planner Vidyadhar Bhattacharya drew the entire city on paper before a single house was built, then laid it over the ground in one bold geometric design. What overall shape did he give Jaipur?
answer: a rectangular grid of nine blocks
choices: a rectangular grid of nine blocks
a star of eight avenues from the palace
a cross of four great roads
context: Vidyadhar Bhattacharya's grid split Jaipur into nine rectangular blocks — two reserved for the palace and state buildings, seven for the public — cut by broad main streets about 34 metres wide. It made Jaipur one of India's first fully planned cities, and in 2019 UNESCO listed the walled city for its blend of Hindu, Mughal, and Western planning. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1605/

question: At the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, the open-air observatory Sawai Jai Singh II completed in 1734, an astronomer taking a reading of the sun or a star did something visitors still find astonishing today. How did he read Jai Singh's 19 instruments?
choices: by peering through a brass telescope
by floating a magnetic needle in water
by reading a printed star almanac
context: Instead of small handheld tools, Jai Singh built his 19 astronomy instruments as huge masonry structures — ramps, bowls, and towers you climb — all for naked-eye observation of the sky. The Jantar Mantar was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jantar_Mantar,_Jaipur

question: The largest single instrument at Jaipur's Jantar Mantar is the Samrat Yantra, which soars about 27 metres — the height of a nine-storey building — yet is precise enough to tell the local time to within roughly two seconds. Among the world's great time-telling devices, what does that make the Samrat Yantra?
context: The Samrat Yantra ('Supreme Instrument') is the world's largest stone sundial, about 27 metres (88–90 feet) tall. Its shadow is so big it visibly creeps along at roughly 1 mm per second — about a hand's breadth every minute — so you can actually watch the sun's motion with your naked eye. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jantar_Mantar,_Jaipur

question: Jaipur's rose-pink Hawa Mahal, the 'Palace of Winds,' is a five-storey honeycomb facade pierced by 953 tiny latticed windows, built in 1799 so the palace's royal women could watch the busy street below unseen. The palace earned its airy name from a trick of physics: force a breeze through hundreds of such tiny gaps and the air does something that keeps the rooms cool behind them. What does the breeze do?
answer: it speeds up into a brisk, rushing draft
choices: it speeds up into a brisk, rushing draft
it slows into a soft, gentle drift
it splits into many fine, criss-crossing streams
it swirls into slow, circling eddies
context: Those 953 tiny openings work like a natural air-conditioner: squeezing a breeze through so many small gaps speeds the air up — a Venturi (or chimney) effect — and the faster draft cools the rooms behind, which is exactly how the 'Palace of Winds' got its name. The Hawa Mahal was built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawa_Mahal ; https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/india-hawa-mahal-palace-of-the-winds/index.html

question: The Hawa Mahal in Jaipur, designed in 1799 by the architect Lal Chand Ustad, rises in a tall, tapering tier of pink screens that grows narrower toward the top. Lal Chand shaped this pyramid-like profile on purpose, to echo the crown worn by one beloved Hindu god. Whose crown does the Palace of Winds imitate?
context: The Hawa Mahal's tapering, pyramid-like shape was designed to resemble the mukut — the tall crown — of Lord Krishna. It was commissioned by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh and built in 1799. Source: https://www.yatrapur.com/hawa-mahal/

question: Inside Amber Fort, the great hilltop palace-fortress of red sandstone and marble above Jaipur, lies a hall called the Sheesh Mahal, its walls and ceiling encrusted with thousands of tiny convex mirrors backed with coloured foil. Shut the doors, light just one small candle, and the dark hall transforms. What does that single flame do?
answer: the whole hall blooms into a sky of stars
choices: the whole hall blooms into a sky of stars
the room seems to stretch on forever
your reflection splinters into a thousand faces
the walls shimmer with a shifting rainbow
context: The Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace) is covered in thousands of tiny convex mirror pieces set with coloured foil, so the light of a single candle flame reflects and glitters across the whole hall like a starlit sky. Amber Fort, begun by Raja Man Singh I, mirrors itself in Maota Lake below — the palace's main water source — and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 as part of the 'Hill Forts of Rajasthan.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amer_Fort

question: In New Orleans, when a brass band comes swinging down the street, a crowd of strangers falls in behind it — twirling parasols and waving handkerchiefs, dancing along, and anyone at all is welcome to join. What is this dancing crowd that follows the band called?
context: The band and family up front are the 'main line'; the crowd of dancers who fall in behind — parasols twirling, handkerchiefs waving — are the 'second line,' and anyone can join. Second lines roll at both street parades and jazz funerals, and it is one of New Orleans's most beloved traditions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funeral

question: A New Orleans jazz funeral has two halves. Marching to the cemetery, the brass band plays slow, mournful dirges; but once the body is laid to rest, the band 'cuts the body loose' and bursts into hot, joyful music for the dance back home. Which up-tempo song most famously erupts on that jubilant march home?
choices: "Just a Little While to Stay Here"
context: On the way to the grave the band plays dirges like 'Nearer My God to Thee' and 'Just a Closer Walk With Thee.' Once the body is entombed, it 'cuts the body loose' and swings into joyous numbers — most famously 'When the Saints Go Marching In' (or 'Oh, Didn't He Ramble') — for the dancing march home. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funeral

question: In New Orleans stood the one public square in all of America where enslaved people could gather on Sundays — their single day of rest — to drum, sing, and dance in the open, keeping alive rhythms that would later grow into jazz. What was this square called?
context: Under the French slave code, the Code Noir, Sunday was a day of rest, and Congo Square became effectively the only place in the United States where open African drumming survived. Those rhythms seeded jazz; the square now sits inside Louis Armstrong Park in the Tremé neighborhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Square

question: On New Year's Eve in 1912, an eleven-year-old New Orleans boy named Louis Armstrong fired his stepfather's pistol into the air to celebrate — and was promptly arrested and shipped off to a home for wayward boys. There a teacher, Peter Davis, put an instrument in his hands and made him the band's leader, setting him on the road to becoming the most famous jazzman alive. What instrument did young Armstrong first learn to play in that reform school?
context: The reform school was the Colored Waif's Home. Instructor Peter Davis handed Armstrong a cornet — the trumpet's stubbier cousin — and made him bandleader. 'Satchmo' would go on to remake jazz around the improvising soloist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: From 1897 to 1917, New Orleans set aside a legal red-light district where early jazz pianists found their steadiest work, playing the brothels and saloons night after night. When the U.S. Navy forced the district shut in 1917, those musicians packed up, rode the riverboats up the Mississippi, and carried jazz north to Chicago. What was this district — jazz's first paying home — called?
context: Storyville was named for alderman Sidney Story, who wrote the ordinance creating it and was mortified that the vice quarter forever bore his name. Secretary of War Newton Baker had the Navy close it at midnight on November 12, 1917, to clear vice from near military bases — and the musicians' exodus helped carry New Orleans jazz up the Mississippi. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storyville,_New_Orleans

question: In old New Orleans, on their one free day, enslaved Africans gathered in a public square to dance to pounding drums, gourds, and banjos, alongside European fiddles and tambourines. Their most celebrated dance shook the whole crowd stamping in unison — and its name still echoes in New Orleans music today. What was this signature dance called?
context: The bamboula — named for the bamboo-headed drum that drove it — along with dances like the Calinda and Juba, filled Congo Square on Sundays. That blend of African drums with European strings still surfaces in New Orleans second lines and Mardi Gras Indian parades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Square

question: During a 1926 recording session, New Orleans-born Louis Armstrong's lyric sheet fluttered to the floor mid-take, as the story goes. Rather than stop the band, he kept the tune rolling by improvising made-up sounds where the words should have been — and the record, 'Heebie Jeebies,' became a surprise hit that spread a whole new style of jazz vocals. What is this wordless, improvised vocal style called?
context: Armstrong didn't invent scat, but 'Heebie Jeebies' helped make it famous. The dropped-sheet-music tale is likely a legend Armstrong enjoyed telling; either way, scat means singing improvised nonsense syllables as if the voice were a horn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: Louis Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, is often called the single most important figure jazz ever produced. His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the 1920s so reshaped the music that one part of a jazz performance became its beating heart — the very art of the music, and the standard by which every jazz musician after him would be measured. What did Armstrong make the centerpiece and soul of jazz?
context: Critics say Armstrong 'almost single-handedly created the role of the jazz soloist,' building his lines on the song's chords rather than just its melody. From his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings on, the improvised solo became the art at the heart of jazz. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: A New Orleans pianist who got his start playing the brothels of the city boasted, to widespread mockery, that he had personally 'invented jazz' back in 1902. The critics scoffed at his bragging — yet in 1915 he really did publish one of the very first jazz compositions ever put into print. What was this landmark published tune called?
context: The braggart was Jelly Roll Morton, who started playing piano in Storyville brothels at fourteen. Critics mocked him for 'exaggerating his worth,' but his 'Jelly Roll Blues' (1915) truly was among the first jazz compositions ever published. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton

question: On February 26, 1917, a New Orleans group cut the very first jazz record ever released — and it was pure novelty: the cornet, clarinet, and trombone deliberately honked, squealed, and hollered, imitating the racket of animals purely for laughs. Marketed as a gimmick, it became a runaway national hit. What was this first-ever jazz record called?
context: The band was the Original Dixieland Jass Band — note the early spelling 'Jass' — a white New Orleans group, even though Black New Orleans musicians had been creating the music for years. Their barnyard-noise novelty introduced jazz to a national audience. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_Dixieland_Jass_Band

question: Around 1900, before anyone had ever recorded jazz, one New Orleans cornet player blew so loud and so wild that people swore his horn could be heard clear across the city on a still night. Fans crowned him the very first 'King' of the new music. Yet today we can only imagine his playing — because not one single recording of him is known to survive. Who was this first king of jazz, now more legend than history?
context: Buddy Bolden's career ended in 1907, at age 30, when he suffered a mental collapse and was committed to the state asylum in Jackson, Louisiana, where he died in 1931. His signature tune, 'Buddy Bolden's Blues' — once the scandalous 'Funky Butt' — was so wild that clarinetist Sidney Bechet remembered 'the police put you in jail if they heard you singing that song.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Bolden  (Legend.)

question: Jerusalem's Old City is a walled square of pale golden stone barely 0.9 square kilometres across, small enough to walk from end to end in an hour. Inside its walls it is divided into four named neighborhoods, each with its own community and holy places. What are these four quarters called?
answer: the Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian Quarters
choices: the Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian Quarters
the Jaffa, Damascus, Zion, and Herod Quarters
the Greek, Latin, Coptic, and Syriac Quarters
the Roman, Crusader, Ottoman, and British Quarters
context: The whole walled Old City fits inside about 0.9 square kilometres — smaller than many city parks — yet it is split into the Muslim Quarter (the largest and most crowded), the Christian Quarter, the Jewish Quarter, and the Armenian Quarter (the smallest, roughly 0.13 sq km). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_City_(Jerusalem)

question: In Jerusalem's Old City, worshippers fold tiny slips of paper carrying written prayers and press them into the cracks between the massive weathered stone blocks of one revered structure — a custom families have kept up for centuries. Which sacred site is filled with these paper prayers?
context: Jews call it simply the Kotel — 'the Wall.' It is the holiest place where Jews gather to pray, and for centuries visitors have tucked folded prayers into the gaps between its ancient stones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Wall

question: The honey-colored stone walls that ring Jerusalem's Old City look ancient, and visitors often assume some Israelite or Roman king raised them in antiquity. In truth they are barely 500 years old, built within a single decade by one determined ruler. Which ruler built the walls that still stand today?
context: The walls you see today were raised in just five years, from 1537 to 1541, by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent — about 4 km around and some 12 metres high. Herod, Hadrian, and Saladin all shaped Jerusalem in far earlier centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walls_of_Jerusalem

question: Through the narrow, twisting lanes of Jerusalem's Old City runs a roughly 600-metre route that Christian tradition marks as the path Jesus walked, carrying his cross, toward his crucifixion. Pilgrims still follow it on foot, pausing to pray at 14 marked stations along the way. What is this route through the city called?
context: Via Dolorosa means 'the Way of Sorrows.' The route is marked by 14 Stations of the Cross, each recalling a moment of the Passion; the final five stations lie inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where the route ends. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Dolorosa

question: The shrine crowning Jerusalem's central raised platform was completed around 691 CE on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. Its brilliant gilded cap has become the visual symbol of the entire city, and scholars regard it as the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture anywhere in the world. What is this monument called?
context: The Dome of the Rock was built around 691 CE by the caliph Abd al-Malik, making it the oldest surviving Islamic building in the world. Its golden dome shelters the Foundation Stone, an exposed slab of bedrock that Jews, Christians, and Muslims all hold sacred. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock

question: Just east of Jerusalem's walls, across the deep Kidron Valley, rises a long ridge whose Jerusalem-facing slope has served as a Jewish burial ground for roughly 3,000 years — around 150,000 graves stepping down the hillside, making it one of the oldest cemeteries on earth still in use. What is this ridge called?
context: The Mount of Olives faces the Old City across the Kidron Valley. Its western slope holds roughly 150,000 graves and has been a Jewish cemetery for about 3,000 years. At its foot lies the Garden of Gethsemane, where some gnarled olive trees are believed to be many centuries old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_of_Olives

question: In the eastern wall of Jerusalem's Old City, facing the Kidron Valley, stands a double-arched gate that was deliberately bricked up in 1541 and has stayed sealed ever since — in part because Jewish tradition holds that the Messiah will one day enter the city through this very gate. Which sealed gate is this?
context: The Golden Gate (also called the Gate of Mercy) was sealed in 1541 and has stayed bricked up ever since. Jewish tradition teaches that the Messiah will enter Jerusalem through this eastern gate, coming from the Mount of Olives across the valley. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_(Jerusalem)  (Legend.)

question: The Western Wall, where Jews gather to pray, is not a wall of the Jewish Temple at all — a fact that surprises many visitors. Its giant lower stones survive from a massive building project the Judean king Herod the Great carried out around 19 BCE. What is the Western Wall a surviving side of?
answer: the huge platform Herod built to enlarge the Temple Mount
choices: the huge platform Herod built to enlarge the Temple Mount
the fortress Herod built to guard the Temple courts
the aqueduct Herod built to carry water to the city
the royal palace Herod built on the western hill
context: Herod the Great didn't rebuild only the Temple — around 19 BCE he raised an enormous artificial platform around the sacred hill to enlarge it, and the Western Wall is a surviving retaining wall holding up one side of that platform. The Temple building itself was later destroyed; the exposed prayer section of the retaining wall rises about 19 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Wall

question: Ancient Jerusalem drew its water from a single spring, the Gihon, sitting just outside the city's defenses. Facing an Assyrian siege, King Hezekiah's workers cut a tunnel more than 500 metres through solid rock to bring that water safely inside the walls. An inscription discovered in 1880 — carved by the workers themselves — boasts of one astonishing feat. What did the diggers achieve?
answer: they cut from opposite ends and met in the middle
choices: they cut from opposite ends and met in the middle
they finished the entire tunnel in a single night
they carved it in a perfectly straight underground line
they cut it wide enough to march soldiers through
context: The Gihon Spring was ancient Jerusalem's only reliable water source. Around 700 BCE, with the Assyrians advancing, King Hezekiah's engineers tunneled over 500 metres through bedrock. The Siloam inscription, found in 1880, was carved by the workers to record the moment the two teams — digging toward each other from opposite ends — broke through and met underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gihon_Spring

question: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre — the traditional site of Jesus's crucifixion and tomb — is shared by six rival Christian communities who agree on almost nothing, and their disputes over the building can turn bitter. Yet the single key to the church's front door, and the daily task of unlocking and locking it, has belonged to the same guardians for centuries. Who holds the key to Christianity's holiest church?
context: For centuries, two Muslim families have safeguarded the door so that no single Christian group can control it: the Joudeh family keeps the roughly 30-centimetre iron key, and the Nuseibeh family unlocks and locks the door each day. Tradition traces the arrangement to Saladin, who granted it in 1187. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Holy_Sepulchre

question: High on the front façade of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem — the traditional site of Jesus's crucifixion and tomb — a plain wooden ladder rests on a stone ledge beneath an upper window, above the main doors. Visitors have puzzled over this curious object for generations, and it has become one of the church's most famous sights, known around the world by a single nickname. What is this ladder called?
context: The 'Status Quo,' fixed in 1757, governs the six Christian communities that share the church; because nothing can change without all of them agreeing, a wooden ladder propped on a façade ledge has not moved for roughly 300 years — earning it the name the 'Immovable Ladder.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Holy_Sepulchre  (Legend.)

question: In Jiangxi, China, one town packed with porcelain kilns glowed so fiercely at night that travelers said the whole place looked ablaze, as if lit by fire at midnight. For over a thousand years it has fired the world's most prized porcelain. Which town is it?
context: Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province, has produced porcelain for over 1,000 years and is called China's 'Porcelain Capital.' The French Jesuit Pere d'Entrecolles wrote in 1712 that arriving at night, 'one thinks that the whole city is on fire, or that it is one large furnace with many vent holes.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen; gotheborg.com (Letters of Pere d'Entrecolles).  (Legend.)

question: So much fine porcelain sailed to Europe from Jingdezhen and the other kilns of one Asian country that Europeans stopped saying 'porcelain' altogether and named the ware after that country itself. Which everyday word for porcelain is the result?
context: English called porcelain 'China dishes' in the 1570s, 'China-ware' by the 1630s, and simply 'china' by the 1650s -- the ware named for the land it came from. Source: etymonline.com/word/china; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain.

question: When Jingdezhen's porcelain reached Europe, Italians gave it the second name we still use today -- 'porcelain' -- from their word porcellana, their name for a certain glossy seashell that the shiny glaze called to mind. Which shell gave porcelain its name?
context: In Italian, porcellana meant a cowrie shell; the smooth, glassy surface of the new ware resembled the shell, so the glossy porcelain borrowed its name. Source: etymonline.com/word/porcelain; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain.

question: Jingdezhen's porcelain owes its pure white color to a special clay dug from a nearby hill the Chinese called 'High Ridge.' Potters worldwide now call this white porcelain clay by a word taken straight from that hill's own name. Which clay is it?
context: The clay is kaolin, and its name comes straight from the hill: the Chinese called it Gaoling -- gaolingtu, 'High Ridge earth' -- a hill and village near Jingdezhen. The word reached English in 1727 through Pere d'Entrecolles' 1712 report, and the mineral kaolinite was later named from it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite.  (Legend.)

question: Jingdezhen had everything porcelain needs in one spot -- fine clay, porcelain-stone, and pine forests for kiln fuel. But the finished ware was too brittle to survive a jolting overland cart ride, so the town shipped it out by boat instead. On which river did Jingdezhen float its porcelain to the world?
context: Jingdezhen sits on the Chang River, whose boats carried the brittle porcelain far more safely than jolting carts could. The town also lay beside China's finest porcelain-stone deposits and was ringed by pine forests for kiln fuel -- clay, stone, fuel, and a river, all in one place. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: For decades European potters tried and failed to copy Jingdezhen porcelain -- without the right white clay, their pieces slumped and cracked in the kiln. A Jingdezhen merchant told the French priest d'Entrecolles they had left out half of what porcelain needs, comparing its two raw materials to two parts of a living body. Which pair?
context: Chinese potters called kaolin clay the 'bones' of porcelain and the ground porcelain-stone its 'flesh.' The merchant said Europeans failed because they tried to make 'a body in which the flesh would be supported without bones' -- plenty of stone, but no kaolin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen; gotheborg.com (d'Entrecolles).  (Legend.)

question: At Jingdezhen the emperor kept his own private 'imperial kiln,' and one painted design belonged to him alone. It is said that under the Qing dynasty, a Jingdezhen painter who put this forbidden image on porcelain for anyone else could be executed together with his whole family. What was the emperor's reserved design?
context: The five-clawed dragon signified the emperor himself: under the Yuan, five claws marked the emperor and four marked princes, and by the Ming, using the five-clawed dragon outside the imperial circle counted as treason. The tale of a painter executed with his family is a traditional account. Source: sothebys.com (Enter the Dragon); taliesinantiques.com.  (Legend.)

question: Kaolin clay gives porcelain its white body, but on its own it won't hold together in the fire. Jingdezhen potters mixed it with a second local rock that, fired at scorching heat, fuses everything into glassy 'hard-paste' porcelain -- and the town sat right beside China's finest deposits of it. What is this second rock called?
context: The second ingredient is petuntse, also called China stone or porcelain stone; fired with kaolin at very high heat, it supplies what the clay lacks to form true hard-paste porcelain. Jingdezhen's nearby deposits were the finest in China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: In 1433 the Ming court sent Jingdezhen a single order for porcelain painted with dragons and phoenixes -- not to sell, but purely to give away as gifts to officials and foreign envoys. The number of pieces demanded in that one order is staggering. About how many was it?
context: A single 1433 imperial order called for 443,500 pieces of Jingdezhen porcelain in dragon-and-phoenix designs, all destined as court and diplomatic gifts -- a glimpse of the imperial kilns' astonishing output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: Most Chinese towns take their names from a river, a mountain, or a compass direction. Jingdezhen is a rare exception. Around 1004, Song Emperor Zhenzong so loved the town's thin white porcelain that he had each piece stamped with something of his own and renamed the whole town after it. After what did he name the town?
context: Emperor Zhenzong's 'Jingde' era ran 1004-1007. Enchanted by the local ware, he ordered pieces marked 'made in the Jingde period' and changed the town's name from Changnanzhen to Jingde-zhen -- 'Jingde town' -- a rare Chinese city named for an emperor's reign-title. Source: kupi.com (Jingdezhen history); chano-yu.com.  (Legend.)

question: For two centuries European kings spent fortunes trying to uncover how the Chinese made porcelain, giving the guarded formula a mysterious, alchemical-sounding name as if it were a wizard's secret. In 1712 the French Jesuit Pere d'Entrecolles, living beside Jingdezhen, finally described the recipe in letters home. What did Europeans call this coveted secret?
context: Europe called the porcelain secret the 'Arcanum.' d'Entrecolles mailed the first detailed Western account of Jingdezhen's methods in 1712 (a second letter followed in 1722), spreading the recipe and later helping found France's Sevres works. Germany's Meissen had in fact already achieved hard-paste porcelain around 1708-10 using local kaolin, so the letters did not give Europe its first porcelain -- they revealed the recipe to the wider West. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francois_Xavier_d'Entrecolles; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain.

question: Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, but climbers fear K2 — the world's SECOND-highest peak, rising on the China–Pakistan border — far more, because it kills far more often than Everest ever has. What chilling nickname have mountaineers pinned on K2?
context: American climber George Bell coined the 'Savage Mountain' nickname after the 1953 expedition, saying, 'It's a savage mountain that tries to kill you.' At 8,611 m (28,251 ft), K2 stands second only to Everest's 8,849 m, rising in the Karakoram range on the China–Pakistan border. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Everest, Annapurna, Nanga Parbat — the great Asian peaks nearly all wear ancient local names passed down for centuries. 'K2' is the odd one out: it isn't a word in any language, and it means nothing in the tongues of the people who live nearest it. This lonely peak on the China–Pakistan border was simply too remote to have earned a common local name. Where, then, did the strange label 'K2' actually come from?
context: In 1856 the British surveyor Thomas Montgomerie, working on the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, labelled the Karakoram peaks K1, K2, K3 and so on — the 'K' standing for Karakoram. K1 later reverted to its local Balti name, Masherbrum, but K2 sat so deep in the range that no common local name reached the mapmakers, so the survey code stuck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Everest, though far taller than K2, is now climbed by hundreds each year, and fewer than one in fifty climbers lose their lives on it. K2 is a different beast: no peak of its fame has a darker reputation, and for years its terror rested on a single grim statistic. Historically, of the climbers who reached K2's summit, roughly what share never made it back down alive?
context: K2's fatality rate has historically run above 20% — roughly one death for every four climbers who reached the top — which is why the peak, not taller Everest, earns its dread. By comparison, Annapurna is usually ranked the single deadliest 8,000er by death-to-summit ratio, historically closer to one in three. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Near the very top of K2 lies the most feared stretch in all of mountaineering: a short, brutally steep gully of snow and ice that every summit climber must cross. Worse, it runs directly beneath a towering wall of overhanging ice cliffs — called seracs — that can break loose and scour the slope without warning. What is this dreaded passage on K2 called?
context: The Bottleneck, a couloir around 8,200 m, funnels climbers directly under a band of hanging seracs. On 1–2 August 2008, a serac collapse there sheared the fixed ropes and eleven climbers died — K2's worst single disaster. Lower on the mountain lie other named cruxes like House's Chimney and the Black Pyramid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: K2 threw back climber after climber until 31 July 1954, when an Italian expedition led by the geologist Ardito Desio finally put two men on the summit. The route they forged that day proved so reliable that most climbers have followed the very same line up K2 ever since. What is this classic route called?
context: Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli reached the summit on 31 July 1954 via the Abruzzi Spur, on the expedition led by geologist Ardito Desio. The ascent stayed controversial because support climber Walter Bonatti and porter Amir Mehdi were forced to bivouac in the open above 8,000 m. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: During a ferocious storm high on K2 in 1953, an American team was struggling to lower a desperately sick teammate when six roped-together climbers suddenly slipped at once and began sliding toward a deadly plunge. In a heartbeat, one of them — Pete Schoening — stopped the whole falling chain with a single split-second move that mountaineers still speak of simply as 'The Belay.' How did Schoening save all six?
answer: wedged his ice axe behind a rock
choices: looped the rope around his shoulders
wedged his ice axe behind a rock
caught the rope with his bare hands
anchored them with a tent stake
context: Pete Schoening braced a single ice axe behind a boulder and held all six of his roped teammates during the 1953 American expedition's storm-battered retreat — a save mountaineers still simply call 'The Belay.' The sick climber they were lowering, Art Gilkey, was later swept away and died. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2  (Legend.)

question: By 2021, thirteen of the world's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks had been climbed in the dead of winter — all except K2, which had thrown back every winter attempt for decades in cold near −40 °C and hurricane-force winds. Then, on 16 January 2021, ten climbers finally stood together on its frozen summit, completing what many call the last great 'first' in high-altitude mountaineering. Whose team achieved this historic first winter ascent of K2?
context: The ten Nepali climbers deliberately regrouped about ten metres below the top so that no one would be first, then stepped onto the summit together while singing Nepal's national anthem. The team was led by Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja and Mingma Gyalje Sherpa; of the ten, only Purja climbed without supplemental oxygen. Sources: https://www.planetmountain.com/en/news/alpinism/k2-nepalese-mountaineers-claim-historic-first-winter-ascent.html ; https://www.ukclimbing.com/news/2021/01/first_winter_ascent_of_k2_made_by_all-nepali_team-72688

question: Kabuki — Japan's dazzling theatre of painted faces and frozen poses — began not in a grand hall but out in the open air. Around 1603, a former shrine dancer, Izumo no Okuni, led an all-female troupe in a wild new dance-drama, performing on the dry, pebbled bed of a river running through Kyoto. On which river's dry bed did kabuki first take shape?
context: The river is the Kamo (Kamo-gawa), and the exact spot — its wide, dry, pebbled bed in central Kyoto — is remembered as the Shijogawara. There, around 1603, Izumo no Okuni, a former miko (shrine maiden) by tradition linked to the great Izumo Taisha shrine, drew crowds with a flashy, avant-garde dance-drama that grew into kabuki. In a famous irony, the theatre a woman founded on this riverbed would ban women within a generation and become entirely male. The other choices are real rivers of the Kyoto region: the Kamo, Katsura, and Uji all feed the Yodo River system. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Kabuki takes its name from the kabukimono — flashy young rebels in the streets of early-1600s Kyoto and Edo who wore outrageous, mismatched clothes and swaggered against every custom. Their nickname came from the old Japanese verb kabuku. In its original, literal sense, what did kabuku mean?
context: The verb kabuku literally meant to tilt or lean off-center, and from it came kabukimono — roughly 'the tilted, crooked ones' — a nickname for the outrageously dressed show-offs of the early 1600s who flouted every rule of proper dress. Only later were the three kanji 歌 (song), 舞 (dance), 伎 (skill) chosen to write 'kabuki' — a clever phonetic fit that also happens to describe the art. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: At the most thrilling moment of a kabuki play in Edo (old Tokyo), the hero suddenly slams to a halt — every muscle locked, one foot stamped down, both eyes crossed hard toward the nose — and holds the statue-still pose while a fan in the crowd bellows his stage-name. What is this frozen, cross-eyed climax pose called?
context: The frozen pose is the mie; the crossed-eye glare freezes a moment of peak emotion (and, by tradition, wards off evil). As the actor holds it, a devoted fan shouts his stage-name — a cry called kakegoe. The mie and the bold makeup style were pioneered by the great actor Ichikawa Danjuro I (1660–1704). keren are spectacular stage tricks and chunori is 'flying' on wires above the crowd; aragoto is Edo's bombastic superhuman-hero style. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Osaka's kabuki theatres were temples of spectacle, each forever outdoing the last with new stage machinery. Around 1758 the Osaka playwright Namiki Shozo built a bold new device into the theatre — an innovation Western stages would not copy for well over a century, and still used in playhouses worldwide today. What did Namiki Shozo add to the Osaka stage?
answer: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
choices: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
the hanamichi, a raised walkway into the crowd
the seri, a set of trapdoor stage elevators
the chunori, a rig for flying actors on wires
context: The device is the mawari-butai (revolving stage), a giant turntable set into the stage floor and credited to the Osaka playwright Namiki Shozo around 1758 — the world's oldest revolving stage, predating similar machinery in Western theatres by well over a century, and still standard in playhouses today. Kabuki loved such spectacle: seri trapdoors lifted actors and whole sets up through the floor, chunori ('riding in the sky') hoisted an actor over the audience on wires, and the hanamichi was a raised walkway that carried actors dramatically through the crowd. But the spinning stage was Osaka's own. Source: Wikipedia 'Namiki Shozo I' & 'Revolving stage'; Playbill 'History of the Theatrical Turntable'; KABUKI WEB.

question: Kano, one of the oldest cities of West Africa, guarded its trans-Saharan trade behind ramparts that ran some 11 miles around the town and rose up to 30 feet high, begun around 1100 by Sarki Gijimasu and raised higher by the kings who followed. What were Kano's mighty walls built from?
context: The walls, called the Ganuwa in Hausa, were begun by Sarki (King) Gijimasu around 1095-1134 and extended by his successors over the following centuries. By 1851 the explorer Heinrich Barth recorded them as roughly 10-11 miles around and up to 30 feet high; after the British conquest in 1903, General Frederick Lugard said he had 'never seen anything like it in Africa.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ancient Kano City Walls' & 'Kano (city).'

question: In one corner of Kano, deep clay pits brim with near-black indigo, and cotton cloth has been dipped and re-dipped there by hand since around 1498 - the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still worked anywhere in Africa. These pits sit beside one of Kano's old city gates and take its name. Which gate is it?
context: The Kofar Mata dye pits are the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still in use in Africa: cloth has been coloured in the same clay pits for more than five centuries. (Wikipedia says 'more than 500 years'; the specific date of about 1498 comes from Kohan Textile Journal and other textile-trade sources.) The dye uses just three natural ingredients - indigo-plant leaves, wood ash, and potash - left to ferment in the pits for weeks. In its prime Kano had some 270 pits; only a few dozen still work today. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kofar Mata Dye Pits'; Kohan Textile Journal.

question: Kano's Kurmi Market, founded in the 15th century by King Muhammad Rumfa, was one of the greatest markets on the southern edge of the Sahara, its wares loaded onto camel caravans bound for Timbuktu, Tripoli, and beyond. Across the whole desert, Kano was prized above all for one product. What was it?
context: By 1851 Kano was exporting on the order of 10 million pairs of leather sandals and 5 million tanned hides a year, and its indigo cloth and leather reached as far as Timbuktu, Tripoli, Lake Chad, Morocco, and Europe. The Kurmi Market itself was established by the reforming king Muhammad Rumfa (reigned about 1463-1499). Source: Wikipedia, 'Kano (city).'

question: At ancient Thebes — today the city of Luxor, on the Nile's east bank — pharaohs spent two thousand years enlarging a colossal temple complex. We call it Karnak, after a nearby village, but its own builders gave it the proud name 'Ipet-isut.' What did that name mean to them?
choices: the House of a Million Years
the Horizon of the Two Lands
the Throne of the Rising Sun
context: 'Ipet-isut' means 'the Most Select of Places' — the ancient Egyptians' own boast that Karnak was the finest, holiest ground in all of Egypt. It stood at Thebes (modern Luxor) on the Nile's east bank, dedicated above all to Amun-Re, king of the gods. Source: discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; Britannica /place/Karnak.

question: Karnak, on the Nile at Luxor, grew for two thousand years into the largest religious complex ever built. Egyptologists are so struck by its scale that they don't call it a temple at all — they give the whole sprawl a grander nickname. What is Karnak often called?
context: Karnak is the largest religious complex ever built — a whole 'city of temples' that grew for two thousand years until it sprawled across more than 2 square kilometres. It is not one building but a walled expanse of temples, chapels, pylons, courts, and its own sacred lake, so vast that the single word 'temple' no longer fits it. Guinness World Records lists Karnak as the largest ancient Egyptian temple site. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; britannica.com/place/Karnak.

question: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall is a forest of 134 stone columns. Down its central aisle stand twelve giants, each rising as high as a six-storey building — about 21 metres — their tops flaring open like blossoms. These pillars were all carved to imitate a single plant that grew along the Nile. Which plant?
context: The twelve central columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall stand about 21 m (69 ft) tall — a six- to seven-storey building — carved as papyrus stalks crowned with open-blossom tops. Papyrus was Egypt's own plant: it grew thick along the Nile, and its stalks were pressed into sheets to write on. The 122 shorter outer columns (roughly 10–15 m) wear closed papyrus-bud tops. At about 5,000 sq m, the hall is the largest room of any religious building in the ancient world. Source: memphis.edu/hypostyle; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnak.

question: Karnak was not built to one plan. Over nearly two thousand years its courts, pylons, and halls piled up in clashing styles, their walls out of line, each generation of builders adding onto the last. Who were the builders who kept enlarging Karnak across twenty centuries?
answer: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
choices: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
the temple's guild of master masons
