Its signature plants -- chamise, manzanita, and scrub oak -- are packed with flammable oils, and fire sweeps through every few decades as part of the natural cycle. It is one of only five Mediterranean-climate shrublands on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral

question: Central Chile is pinned into a narrow ribbon between the towering Andes and the cold Pacific -- the one slice of South America that shares California's wet-winter, dry-summer climate. Its silvery, drought-hardy scrubland is South America's answer to the fire-country hills of the north. What is central Chile's Mediterranean shrubland called?
context: Chile's matorral is walled off from the rest of the world -- the bone-dry Atacama Desert to the north, the Andes to the east, the Pacific to the west. That isolation makes about 95% of its plants grow nowhere else, including the towering Chilean wine palm, Jubaea chilensis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_matorral

question: California's chaparral burns down to black stubble in the autumn wildfires -- yet within a few weeks, fresh green shoots are already pushing up through the blackened ground. How do these shrubs come storming back so fast after the flames pass?
answer: they resprout from a fire-proof underground burl
choices: they resprout from a fire-proof underground burl
they regrow new leaves along their scorched stems
their seeds sprout quickly in the fresh warm ash
new plants blow in on the wind from unburned slopes
context: Many chaparral shrubs -- like chamise and toyon -- store energy in a woody, fire-resistant swelling at the root crown called a burl (or lignotuber). The branches burn away, but the burl survives underground and sends up new sprouts within days. Fire here is not the end of a plant's life; it is a reset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral

question: Line up all five Mediterranean-climate regions on a globe and a hidden rule appears: California, central Chile, the South African Cape, southwest Australia, and the Mediterranean Basin itself all sit at nearly the same latitude, each on the matching side of its continent. Where on their continents do all five lie?
answer: the west coast, in the mid-latitudes
choices: the west coast, in the mid-latitudes
the east coast, in the mid-latitudes
the west coast, deep in the tropics
the east coast, close to the poles
context: Each region hugs the western edge of its continent between about 30 and 40 degrees from the equator. There, cold ocean currents chill the coast and a belt of high pressure -- the subtropical ridge -- drifts poleward each summer, shoving the rain-bearing storms away. Only in winter, when the high slips back toward the equator, do the fronts break through. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_climate

question: Near the southern tip of Africa, around the Cape of Good Hope, a low evergreen shrubland crams roughly 9,000 plant species into one small corner of the country -- about two-thirds of them growing nowhere else on Earth. It forms the smallest, and by far the richest, of the world's six great plant kingdoms. What is this Cape shrubland called?
context: Fynbos (Afrikaans for 'fine bush') carpets the Cape Floristic Region -- at about 78,555 square kilometres, the smallest of Earth's six floral kingdoms, yet so rich it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. It holds over 600 species of Erica (heath) alone, against just two or three dozen across the entire rest of the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fynbos ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Floristic_Region

question: In the far southwest of Australia, a low sandy heath bursts each spring into one of the greatest wildflower shows on Earth -- more than 8,000 native plant species, half of them found on no other continent. What is this southwest Australian Mediterranean heath called?
context: Kwongan is the sand-plain heath of Southwest Australia, holding about 70% of the region's 8,000-plus plant species -- half of them endemic. Alongside the Cape's fynbos, it is one of the planet's supreme wildflower hotspots, ablaze with banksias, kangaroo paws, and orchids each spring. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwongan

question: In the world's five fire-prone Mediterranean shrublands, a wildfire can strip a whole hillside down to bare black earth -- and yet the same plants come roaring back thicker than before. Many of them lock their seeds inside hard, woody pods for years, sometimes decades. What finally cracks those pods open to reseed the burnt ground?
answer: the intense heat of the wildfire itself
choices: the intense heat of the wildfire itself
the first heavy rains of winter
years of slow rot and decay
context: This fire-triggered seed release is called serotiny (or pyriscence). Resin seals the woody pods shut until a fire's heat melts it, dropping seeds onto freshly cleared, nutrient-rich ash with no competitors. In Australia's Banksia, a tiny winged 'separator' inside each pod then doles the seeds out gradually over the wet and dry spells that follow. Fire, here, is not a disaster -- it is the trigger the whole shrubland waits for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotiny

question: Add up all five Mediterranean-climate regions -- the Mediterranean Basin, California, central Chile, the Cape, and southwest Australia -- and together they cover only about 2% of the Earth's land, five small scraps at the edges of five continents. For such a tiny sliver of the planet, how large is their share of the world's known plant species?
answer: nearly a fifth of all known plant species
choices: nearly a fifth of all known plant species
about one plant species in every fifty
roughly half of all known plant species
barely one plant species in a thousand
context: Just five small regions -- about 2% of the land surface -- hold close to 20% of all known plant species, an astonishingly outsized share of the planet's flora. Biologists link this explosion of diversity to the long summer drought and the regular fires, which together carve the land into countless micro-habitats where new species split off and specialize. Source: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6038726/

question: The Challenger Deep, at the southern end of the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is the deepest known point in any ocean -- the lowest spot on the whole solid face of the Earth. About how far below the waves is its floor?
context: The Challenger Deep bottoms out at about 10,935 m (35,876 ft) -- nearly 11 km straight down, the lowest point on the planet's solid surface. It is named for HMS Challenger, whose 1875 voyage first sounded these depths. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on land. If you could pick it up and drop it into the Challenger Deep -- the deepest point in any ocean -- what would happen to its peak?
answer: its summit would still lie about 2 km underwater
choices: its summit would still lie about 2 km underwater
its summit would rise about 2 km above the water
its summit would poke just above the surface
its summit would still lie about 6 km underwater
context: Everest rises 8,849 m above sea level; the Challenger Deep drops to about 10,935 m. Sink the whole mountain to the bottom and its summit would still lie roughly 2,086 m -- about 2 km -- beneath the waves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: In 2012, the film director James Cameron folded himself into a lime-green submersible called Deepsea Challenger and sank for hours to the floor of the Challenger Deep. What made his dive a world first?
answer: he reached the deepest point on Earth entirely on his own
choices: he reached the deepest point on Earth entirely on his own
he was the first human ever to reach that seafloor
he set a record for the longest time spent on the bottom
he collected the first rock samples from that depth
context: The first descent to the Challenger Deep, in 1960, carried two men. James Cameron's 2012 dive in the Deepsea Challenger was the first time anyone reached the deepest place on Earth alone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded by instruments struck off Valdivia, Chile in 1960, where the Nazca plate dives beneath South America; the ground shook for a full ten minutes. How big was it on the magnitude scale?
context: At about magnitude 9.5, the 1960 Valdivia earthquake is the strongest ever recorded. It ruptured some 800 km of the fault where the Nazca plate dives beneath South America, and its tsunami raced clean across the Pacific. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Valdivia_earthquake

question: The Mariana Trench plunges deeper than any other trench on Earth, and the secret lies in the slab of Pacific seafloor that dives down into it. What is unusual about this particular slab of ocean crust?
answer: it is some of the oldest, coldest, densest crust on Earth
choices: it is some of the oldest, coldest, densest crust on Earth
it is some of the newest, warmest, lightest crust on Earth
it is the thickest, driest continental crust on Earth
it is the softest, most crumbly crust on Earth
context: The Pacific plate diving here is up to about 170 million years old -- ancient for ocean floor. Old crust is cold and dense, so it sinks steeply and drags the trench down with it: the older and colder the slab, the deeper the trench. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench

question: At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the deepest water on Earth, the ocean presses on every surface with a crushing force. Roughly how much greater is that pressure than the pressure at the surface?
context: At the bottom the pressure is about 1,099 atmospheres -- roughly 16,000 pounds per square inch, over a thousand times what you feel at sea level. It would crush an unprotected human in an instant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: From Chile to Alaska to Japan, every earthquake of magnitude 9 or greater since 1900 has struck the same kind of place: a subduction zone, where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. Why do these boundaries unleash the very biggest quakes?
answer: the plates jam together, strain builds for centuries, then the fault suddenly lurches
choices: the plates jam together, strain builds for centuries, then the fault suddenly lurches
the plates slide past each other smoothly, so strain leaks away little by little
hot magma rises through the crust, then bursts out in one enormous blast
the crust slowly stretches and thins, until at last it rips itself apart
context: At a locked subduction boundary, friction pins the plates while they keep converging, storing centuries of strain. When the fault finally gives, it slips all at once over hundreds of kilometres -- a megathrust rupture. Every magnitude-9 quake on record has been one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megathrust_earthquake

question: Alaska's 'Good Friday' quake of 1964 struck the Aleutian megathrust -- where the Pacific plate dives beneath North America -- and did more than shake: at Montague Island the ground was thrust permanently upward, out of the sea. By roughly how much did it rise?
context: At Montague Island the ground was lifted 13-15 m (43-49 ft) relative to the sea, stranding beaches in the air, while other stretches of coast sank by up to about 2.4 m. The rupture tore roughly 600 miles of fault; at about magnitude 9.2 it was the second-strongest quake ever recorded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Alaska_earthquake

question: Japan's Tohoku megathrust quake of 2011 -- on the fault where the Pacific plate dives beneath Japan -- shoved the main island of Honshu about 2.4 m eastward and even nudged the planet's spin. What did it do to the length of a day?
answer: it shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
choices: it shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
it lengthened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
it shortened the day by a full second
it lengthened the day by a full minute
context: Redistributing that much mass tightened Earth's spin, like a skater pulling in her arms. The quake shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds and tipped Earth's axis by an estimated 10-25 cm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami

question: On 26 December 2004, a megathrust quake off Sumatra ripped along the Sunda fault, where one plate dives beneath another, tearing open the longest earthquake rupture ever observed and unleashing a catastrophic tsunami across the Indian Ocean. About how long was the tear in the seafloor?
context: The rupture ran about 1,300 km -- roughly the distance from London to Rome -- and faulting lasted nearly ten minutes. The quake was so vast it set the whole planet ringing, flexing the Earth by as much as 10 mm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami

question: The Cascadia fault off Washington and Oregon last ruptured in a great quake around the year 1700 -- but no European or American was there to write it down. Yet scientists know the date almost to the day. How did they pin it down?
answer: from Japanese records of a tsunami that struck with no local earthquake
choices: from Japanese records of a tsunami that struck with no local earthquake
from Spanish sailors' logs of a storm far out in the Pacific
from Russian fur-traders' diaries kept along the Alaskan coast
from Chinese court reports of strange tides in the South China Sea
context: Japanese villages logged a mysterious tsunami on 27-28 January 1700 -- big waves with no earthquake to explain them. Tracing this 'orphan tsunami' back across the Pacific, scientists matched it to a Cascadia rupture the evening before, about 9 p.m. on 26 January 1700. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1700_Cascadia_earthquake

question: Along the coast of Washington stand eerie 'ghost forests' -- groves of grey, long-dead red cedar, killed all at once when the great Cascadia quake struck around 1700. What did the megathrust do to wipe out a whole forest?
answer: it dropped the coastline, so the sea flooded in and drowned the trees
choices: it dropped the coastline, so the sea flooded in and drowned the trees
it buried the trees under a thick blanket of volcanic ash
it shook so hard the trees were torn out by their roots
it set the forest ablaze with sparks from the grinding rock
context: When the fault slipped, the coast suddenly dropped and salt water poured over the forest, killing the cedars where they stood. Their outermost tree rings all date to 1699 -- the last summer they grew before the flood -- independent proof that fixes the quake to the winter of 1700. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1700_Cascadia_earthquake

question: In the Saxon town of Meissen, Europe's first porcelain factory opened in 1710 inside a soaring medieval castle high on a bluff above the Elbe River — its thick walls chosen to help guard the precious recipe. Which castle sheltered Europe's first porcelain works?
context: Production of Europe's first true hard-paste porcelain began in 1710 inside the Albrechtsburg, a 15th-century castle in Meissen — its walled hilltop rooms perfect for hiding a jealously guarded secret. The royal manufactory had been founded that same year by Augustus the Strong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: The very first ware to make Meissen's fortune was not white at all. In 1710 Johann Friedrich Böttger put a dark-red stoneware on sale that was prized across Saxony's princely courts. How were the finest pieces of Böttger's red stoneware worked and decorated?
answer: cut and polished like a gemstone
choices: cut and polished like a gemstone
gilded all over with gold leaf
finished with a thick salt glaze
context: Before Meissen ever produced anything white, Böttger perfected this hard, dark-red stoneware — later called 'Böttger ware' — so dense and tough it could be cut, faceted, and polished like a gemstone. It went on sale in 1710, the first true product of Europe's first porcelain works. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger

question: By a favorite Meissen legend, Johann Friedrich Böttger searched for years for the pure white clay that could make true porcelain — then found it, the story goes, in the most ordinary thing imaginable. The 'white earth' was dug near Aue in the Saxon hills and sold dirt-cheap for pennies; Böttger had it close at hand the whole time. In what everyday item had his porcelain clay been hiding?
answer: the powder in his old wig
choices: the powder in his old wig
the flour in the castle kitchen
the chalk in his writing box
context: By a much-loved (if unprovable) Meissen legend, Böttger traced the porcelain clay to the powder in his own wig — 'Schnorr's white earth,' dug near Aue by the ironmaster Johann Schnorr and sold cheap to whiten wigs. Böttger noticed the wig powder felt oddly heavy, had it tested, and found the perfect white clay. Source: ceramicstoday.glazy.org/articles/schnorr.html

question: So few places on Earth could make true porcelain that in Böttger's day a single fine cup could cost a small fortune, and royalty across Europe locked their pieces away in guarded cabinets like chests of jewels. Under what glittering two-word nickname did the prized Meissen ware become known?
context: Porcelain was so precious it was nicknamed 'white gold' (weißes Gold). The breakthrough came around 1708, when Böttger, working with the scientist Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus, finally cracked the recipe that had eluded Europe for centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger

question: Böttger and the scientist Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus knew the Chinese blended a special white earth into their porcelain, but for years they hunted in vain for the right one. The secret that finally gave Meissen its porcelain was a soft, snow-white clay dug from the Saxon hills — the one ingredient that let the paste fire hard, white, and translucent. What is this porcelain clay called?
context: Kaolin — white 'china clay' — was the missing key. Fired past 1,300°C it turned white, glassy, and translucent, and rang like a bell when struck. Meissen guarded it fiercely, moving the clay in sealed barrels under sworn secrecy; even so the 'arcanum' leaked, and rival factories sprang up in Vienna, then at Sèvres and in England. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: To prove a piece was genuine and fend off copycats, the Meissen factory began painting a small blue emblem under the glaze of its porcelain around 1720 — a design borrowed from the coat of arms of Saxony and used almost without a break ever since, making it one of the world's oldest trademarks still in use. What is the famous Meissen mark?
context: The blue crossed swords, adapted from the arms of the Electorate of Saxony and introduced in 1720, are reportedly one of the oldest trademarks still in continuous use anywhere in the world. Two artists then made Meissen famous beyond its chemistry: painter Johann Gregor Höroldt brought brilliant enamel colours in the early 1720s, and sculptor Johann Joachim Kändler modelled the rococo figurines that rival factories scrambled to copy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: Melbourne hides its coolest life not on its grand boulevards but in the skinny passages threaded between them -- once delivery routes, now packed with hole-in-the-wall bars, cafes, and street art repainted so often, much of it overnight, that no two visits ever look the same. What does the city famously call these hidden passages?
context: Melbourne's laneways began as narrow service alleys behind its grand Victorian streets and are now the city's signature -- lined with tiny bars, cafes, and constantly repainted murals. Hosier Lane, opened as an official street-art gallery in 1998, is repainted so often (much of it overnight) that no two visits look the same. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosier_Lane

question: Melbourne is the only Australian city that never ripped out its tramlines -- its green-and-gold trams have rolled continuously since 1906, back when nearly every other city on Earth was tearing up its tracks for buses. Among all the world's cities, what distinction does Melbourne's tram network hold today?
context: Melbourne kept its trams when almost every other city tore its tramlines out -- spared by wide streets, union backing, and the cost of ripping up track. Today the network runs about 250 km of double track, roughly 24 routes and some 500 trams, and carried about 154.8 million passengers in 2023-24: the largest urban tram network in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trams_in_Melbourne

question: In central Melbourne, to keep cars from blocking the trams, drivers pull off a maneuver found in almost no other city: at certain intersections they turn RIGHT by first pulling into the far-LEFT lane, then waiting in the middle of the junction until the road clears. (Australians drive on the left, so a right turn normally starts from the right.) What is this tram-friendly maneuver called?
context: Australia drives on the left, so a right turn normally begins from the right-hand lane. Melbourne's 'hook turn' inverts that: at tram-crossed intersections, drivers turn right from the far-left lane and wait mid-junction until the way clears, so turning cars never block the trams. Written into Victoria's road rules by 1939, it is the only such rule that exists purely for the trams' sake. Source: https://www.racv.com.au/royalauto/transport/vic-road-rule-guides/what-are-hook-turns-how-to-do-one.html

question: At the peak of the 1850s boom, about two tonnes of gold a WEEK poured into Melbourne's Treasury from fields just inland -- wealth that paved the grand boulevards and planted the gardens of what admirers dubbed 'Marvellous Melbourne.' Which two towns were the great goldfields feeding this river of gold?
context: Gold was struck in Victoria in 1851, and strikes at Ballarat and Bendigo made it one of the world's great goldfields. In 1856 alone Victoria yielded over 3 million troy ounces (about 95 tonnes) of gold. The wealth built 'Marvellous Melbourne' -- a nickname coined by British journalist George Augustus Sala in 1885 -- whose population had leapt from about 29,000 in 1851 to 123,000 by 1854. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_gold_rush

question: Melbourne sits on a weather knife-edge, where cold fronts sweeping off the Southern Ocean slam into hot air from Australia's baking interior. On a summer afternoon the temperature can crash about 15C in under an hour, then climb again -- sometimes more than once in a day. What do locals call that abrupt southerly blast that ends a hot spell?
context: Melbourne's famous 'four seasons in one day' comes from its position on the boundary where cold fronts off the Southern Ocean collide with hot air from inland Australia. A 'cool change' -- the sudden arrival of that colder southerly air -- can drop the temperature by around 15C in under an hour before it swings back to sun, sometimes several times a day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Melbourne

question: Australia is often called the most geologically stable continent, so you might expect almost no volcanoes near a big southern city. Yet Melbourne is built on dark basalt plains dotted with the cones and craters of a geologically young volcanic field. How many separate eruption points dot the region around the city?
context: Melbourne sits on flat basalt plains at the head of Port Phillip Bay, where the Yarra River meets the sea. The plains to its west and north are Quaternary (geologically young) basalt from the Newer Volcanics Province -- with over 400 eruption centres, one of the world's largest young volcanic fields. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Geography_of_Melbourne

question: In southwestern Colorado, a high plateau called Mesa Verde -- Spanish for 'green table' -- rises above deep canyons. Instead of building their stone villages on the flat mesa top, the Ancestral Puebloans put them somewhere far more surprising. Where did they build them instead?
answer: Inside rock alcoves in the cliff faces
choices: Inside rock alcoves in the cliff faces
Up in the branches of tall trees
Down along the flat riverbanks below
context: The Ancestral Puebloans built their villages inside natural sandstone alcoves worn into the canyon walls, sheltered under the cliff overhangs -- which is why they are known as 'cliff dwellings.' The name 'Mesa Verde' is Spanish for 'green table,' for the tree-covered plateau above. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: Mesa Verde holds some 600 alcove dwellings, but most are tiny -- three out of four have only a room or two, little more than storage cubbies. One, called Cliff Palace, is the giant exception: the largest cliff dwelling in all of North America, with 23 round ceremonial chambers and once home to around 100 people. Set against those two-room cubbies, how many rooms does Cliff Palace hold?
context: Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America -- about 150 rooms and some 23 round ceremonial chambers, once home to roughly 100 people. Of Mesa Verde's ~600 dwellings, about three in four hold only one to five rooms, which is what makes this stone city so exceptional. Source: https://coloradoencyclopedia.org/article/cliff-palace

question: Deep inside Cliff Palace and the other Mesa Verde villages are round rooms sunk into the ground, each entered not by a door but by climbing down a ladder through a hole in the roof, past a central firepit. The Ancestral Puebloans gathered in these chambers for their ceremonies. What are such rooms called?
context: These round, sunken ceremonial rooms are called kivas -- reached by a ladder down through a hole in the roof, with a central firepit and a roof once carried on stone pillars. (A cenote is a Maya sinkhole, a kachina a Pueblo spirit being, a hogan a Navajo home.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: A popular myth says the people who built Mesa Verde's cliff cities mysteriously vanished around 1300 CE. In truth they did nothing of the kind -- they moved away, and their direct descendants are still here today, farming the same corner of the country as their ancestors did. Who are those living descendants?
choices: The Navajo of the high desert
The Apache of the southern mountains
The Comanche of the open plains
context: The builders did not vanish -- their direct descendants are today's Pueblo peoples, including the Hopi, the Zuni, and the Rio Grande pueblos such as Acoma and Taos; some 26 tribes and pueblos trace their ancestry to Mesa Verde. The old name 'Anasazi' is a Navajo word meaning roughly 'ancient enemies,' which is why scholars now say 'Ancestral Puebloans.' Source: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/swscience/ancestral-puebloan.htm

question: Almost every alcove village at Mesa Verde opens toward the south and southwest, and archaeologists say the Ancestral Puebloans chose that direction deliberately, not by chance. What did facing this way do for the people living inside the cliff?
answer: Let winter sun warm the rooms and summer shade cool them
choices: Let winter sun warm the rooms and summer shade cool them
Hid the homes and made them hard for raiders to storm
Drained the rains away and kept the rooms from flooding
Kept the river close and the daily climb short
context: The alcoves were chosen for what we now call passive-solar design: facing south and southwest, they let the low winter sun reach in and warm the stone, while the overhang shaded the rooms from the high summer sun and kept them cool. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: Around 1300 CE the Ancestral Puebloans abandoned Mesa Verde completely and migrated south, leaving the great cliff cities standing empty. For six centuries no one knew what had driven them out -- until scientists studied the tree-rings preserved in the builders' own cut roof-beams, each ring marking a single year of the tree's growth. Ring by ring, the beams recorded the slow calamity that had gripped the region for a generation. What was it?
answer: A long drought that emptied the streams
choices: A long drought that emptied the streams
A long freeze that killed the crops
A long chill that shortened the summers
A long wet spell that rotted the harvests
context: Reading dates from tree-rings is called dendrochronology. The beams record a 24-year 'Great Drought' from 1276 to 1299 -- among the driest stretches in 2,000 years -- the leading explanation for why the people left, though other pressures likely added to it. Astronomer A.E. Douglass published the first Mesa Verde tree-ring dates in 1929. Source: https://www.nps.gov/archeology/sites/npsites/mevetreerings.htm

question: The flag of Mexico shows, at its very center, a striking emblem: a fierce eagle perched on a spiny desert cactus. Aztec legend says their god sent this exact sign to mark where they should found Tenochtitlan — the island city that became Mexico City. In the flag's emblem, what is the eagle doing?
context: In Aztec legend the god Huitzilopochtli told his wandering people to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus devouring a snake; they spotted it on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there in 1325. The omen is legend, but that eagle-and-snake still sits at the very center of Mexico's flag today. Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan/

question: The Aztecs of Tenochtitlan had almost no dry ground to farm on their crowded island in Lake Texcoco, so they raised their crops on the water itself — heaping rich mud from the lakebed into long rectangular plots and lashing them fast with willow roots. In the canals of Xochimilco, on the edge of Mexico City, farmers still tend these water-gardens today. What are these Aztec lake-plots called?
context: Chinampas were artificial garden-plots raised from the lakebed and anchored by the roots of ahuejote willows — so productive they helped feed a city of 200,000. The canals of Xochimilco, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, are the last living fragment of the Aztec lake-city. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/412/

question: When Hernan Cortes and his soldiers reached Tenochtitlan in 1519, the sheer scale of the Aztec island-capital astonished them: perhaps 200,000 people lived among its causeways and canals, and Cortes wrote that it rivaled the greatest cities of Spain. In all of Europe, only a few cities could compare. How did Tenochtitlan's population stack up against Henry VIII's London, the England of that same year?
context: With roughly 200,000 people Tenochtitlan was about five times the size of Henry VIII's London; Cortes compared it to Seville and Cordoba, and only Paris, Venice, and Constantinople might have rivaled it. This was no primitive village but one of the largest and most engineered cities on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: Tenochtitlan was a genuine water-city, an island set in the wide lake of Texcoco. Its successor, modern Mexico City, is now sinking fast — in places the ground drops nearly half a metre a year, cracking pavements and snapping underground pipes. The sinking traces straight back to a drastic thing the Spanish colonists did to that lake. What did they do to it?
context: The Spanish drained Lake Texcoco to fight floods and build out onto the lakebed. Exposed to air, the old clay slowly dries and compacts, so Mexico City sinks — as much as 9 metres over the last century. You can watch it: the Angel of Independence, unveiled in 1910 with nine steps, has since had fourteen more added as the ground fell away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City

question: Late on 21 February 1978, electric-company workers digging a trench in the heart of downtown Mexico City, just off the great plaza, struck something enormous: a carved stone disk over three metres across, weighing eight and a half tons, showing a goddess hacked to pieces. Their trench had sliced into a monument buried under the modern streets for 450 years. What had the workers uncovered?
answer: the Templo Mayor, the Aztecs' great temple
choices: the Templo Mayor, the Aztecs' great temple
the palace of the emperor Moctezuma
the skull-rack of the sacred precinct
context: The disk showed Coyolxauhqui, the moon goddess dismembered in Aztec myth; it lay at the foot of the Templo Mayor, the twin-shrined great pyramid at the heart of Tenochtitlan. Archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma led the dig that followed, and the temple's excavated base can be visited beside the cathedral today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Templo_Mayor

question: Inside Mexico City rises Chapultepec, a rocky wooded hill the Aztec kings kept as a royal retreat, now crowned by a castle. The forest park spread around it is one of the largest city parks in all the Americas — at nearly 700 hectares it more than doubles the area of a world-famous park in the United States. Which celebrated park would fit inside Chapultepec more than twice over?
context: Chapultepec covers about 686 hectares — more than double New York's Central Park — and its Nahuatl name means 'grasshopper hill.' The Aztec kings prized the wooded hill both as a retreat and as the source of the fresh spring water piped into Tenochtitlan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec

question: The Metropolitan Cathedral on Mexico City's central plaza, begun in 1573, is among the oldest and grandest churches in the Americas — and by the 1990s it was in danger, one corner sagging far lower than the rest as the soft ground gave way unevenly beneath it. To save the leaning cathedral, engineers carried out a bold rescue below its floor. What did they do to stop it toppling?
answer: reshaped the soil beneath it to level it
choices: reshaped the soil beneath it to level it
drove deep steel piles under one side
encased the whole church in a steel frame
rebuilt it on higher, firmer land
context: Engineers drilled shafts and carefully removed soil from under the higher side so the cathedral would settle back toward level — a technique called underexcavation. The uneven tilt comes from the same soft, drained lakebed that troubles the whole city. Source: https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/05/climate/mexico-city-sinking-nasa-aquifer-water

question: For five hundred years, everyone who has ruled the Valley of Mexico — Aztec kings, Spanish viceroys, modern engineers — has battled the same stubborn curse: after heavy rain, water floods the basin and simply will not drain away by itself. In most great cities a river carries such water off to the sea. Why does the water have nowhere to go in the Valley of Mexico?
answer: no river flows out of the mountain-ringed basin
choices: no river flows out of the mountain-ringed basin
the ground stays frozen most of the year
the surrounding desert swallows every drop
the sea sits higher than the valley floor
context: The Valley of Mexico is endorheic — a closed basin with no natural river to the sea, cupped by mountains at 2,240 m (7,350 ft). Water can leave only by evaporation or by the drains people dig, which is why floods and drainage have shaped the city's entire history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City

question: On a clear day, from the higher parts of Mexico City, two snow-capped giants stand side by side on the horizon. Aztec legend tells of a warrior who came home from war to find his beloved princess dead, and knelt beside her forever until both turned to stone beneath the snow. The tragic romance is a legend — but the two towering white peaks looming over the valley are utterly real. What are these two landmarks?
choices: the peaks of Orizaba and La Malinche
context: Popocatepetl (5,426 m, Nahuatl for 'the smoking mountain') is an active volcano that still puffs ash; its neighbor Iztaccihuatl ('the white woman,' 5,230 m) is dormant, its snowy ridge said to look like a sleeping woman — the princess of the legend. Both loom over the Valley of Mexico. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popocat%C3%A9petl

question: The lake around Tenochtitlan was brackish — too salty and bitter to drink — so Aztec engineers ran a stone aqueduct several kilometres from the fresh springs of Chapultepec hill into the heart of the island city. Cleverly, they built it as two identical channels running side by side, not one large one. Why two channels instead of a single bigger one?
answer: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
so twice as much water would arrive at once
so two rival cities could each be served
so priests could bless one and use the other
context: With two parallel channels the Aztecs never had to leave the city dry: they could close and scrub one while the other kept flowing. It was maintenance engineering as shrewd as any in Europe at the time — one more sign that Tenochtitlan was a fully engineered metropolis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: A strange peril stalks Mexico City. In the great quakes of 1985 and 2017, the epicentres lay hundreds of kilometres away, yet both flattened buildings in the capital while barely rattling towns much closer to where the earth first broke. Seismologists blame one feature of the ground the modern city was built upon. What is Mexico City sitting on that makes far-off earthquakes so deadly there?
answer: a soft bed of old lake-clay
choices: a soft bed of old lake-clay
a deep nest of active faults
a hollow maze of lava tubes
a vast pocket of underground gas
context: The soft, water-logged lakebed clay traps earthquake waves and amplifies them 5 to 50 times, making the ground roll like jelly for long seconds while firm rock at the valley's edge barely moves. That is why the far-off 1985 and 2017 quakes struck the old lake-center so violently. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Mexico_City_earthquake

question: Draining the flood-prone Valley of Mexico has been a fight without end. Crews hacked out the first great channel, the Tajo de Nochistongo, by hand in 1607, and their successors were still at it four centuries later — in 2019 they finished a colossal bored tunnel over 60 kilometres long and as deep as 200 metres, among the longest drainage tunnels on Earth. What is this giant modern tunnel called?
context: The Tunel Emisor Oriente, 62.5 km long and up to 200 m deep, was completed in 2019 to carry stormwater and sewage out of the sinking basin — the newest move in a 400-year campaign the cosmographer Enrico Martinez began with the 1607 Nochistongo cut. As the city keeps sinking, moving water OUT only grows harder. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emisor_Oriente_Tunnel

question: Off the shore of Miyajima island in Hiroshima Bay stands a giant vermilion (bright red-orange) structure that rises straight out of the sea, so that at times it seems to float on the water, cut off from land -- one of the most famous sights in all of Japan. In Shinto, what is this kind of sacred structure called?
context: A 'torii' is the traditional Shinto gateway that marks the boundary between the everyday world and sacred ground; Miyajima's vermilion O-torii is one of the most iconic images of Japan. The island's popular name Miyajima means 'shrine island' (its formal name is Itsukushima), and it has been revered as an island of the gods since ancient times. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine; gltjp.com/en/article/item/20233/

question: The vermilion gate of Miyajima is famous the world over: it stands far out in Hiroshima Bay, ringed by seawater and mirrored on the calm surface, so that it seems to float free of the shore. What raises the water around the gate's base to create this 'floating' scene?
context: The 'floating' is a tidal illusion, not the gate moving. At low tide the sea drains away and the same gate that seemed to float now stands on walkable sand; to see it truly float, the tide must rise to about 250 cm to cover its base, so guides publish daily Miyajima tide tables. The O-torii stands about 16.5 m (50 ft) tall, roughly 160 m out in the bay. Source: japan-guide.com/e/e3450.html; japanactivity.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine

question: At Miyajima, even the shrine's great halls do not stand on the island's solid ground -- they are built out on wooden piers over the tidal shallows, so the whole shrine sits above the water. Why did its builders refuse to set it on the island itself?
answer: so no one would tread on the sacred island's soil
choices: so no one would tread on the sacred island's soil
so the sea gods could bless passing ships
so the halls would ride out the region's tsunamis
so pilgrim boats could dock beneath the shrine
context: The island itself was held so sacred that ordinary people were forbidden to set foot on its soil, so Itsukushima Shrine and its gate were built on wooden piers out over the tidal zone, technically never touching the holy ground; pilgrims once approached only by boat, passing through the torii from the sea. Ancient taboos even forbade births, deaths, and burials on Miyajima to guard its ritual purity, and there is no cemetery on the island. The chancellor Taira no Kiyomori had the shrine rebuilt into its grand present form in 1168, dedicating it to three sea goddesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine; travel.gaijinpot.com/itsukushima-shrine/; quiltripping.com

question: Around 2500 BCE -- more than 2,000 years before Greece or Rome -- Mohenjo-daro rose on the Indus River and may have held 40,000 people. Fly over its ruins today and one feature leaps out that almost no other Bronze Age city shares: its street plan. How were Mohenjo-daro's streets laid out?
answer: In a deliberate grid of right angles
choices: In a deliberate grid of right angles
In rings around a central palace
In a maze of winding lanes
context: Mohenjo-daro's grid -- laid out around 2500 BCE, more than two millennia before Greece or Rome -- covered roughly 300 hectares and may have housed about 40,000 people: a fully planned city on a scale the world would not match again for ages. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Every brick in Mohenjo-daro was baked to the same proportions, its sides in a fixed 1-to-2-to-4 ratio -- and the very same brick shape turns up in Indus cities hundreds of miles away. What does this identical brick-making, repeated across such distances, reveal about the Indus cities?
answer: They shared a single system of measurement
choices: They shared a single system of measurement
They were built by one traveling workforce
They were all governed by one king
context: The 1:2:4 brick (thickness:width:length) turns up in Indus cities hundreds of miles apart -- proof the whole civilization shared a system of measurement and planning, not merely a building fashion. (world-archaeology.com/great-discoveries/mohenjo-daro)

question: In a Mohenjo-daro house of 2500 BCE, a paved bathing floor drains through a chute built into the wall, carrying the wastewater out to a covered sewer beneath the street -- an indoor bathroom of a kind most of the ancient world reserved for kings alone. How common were such private bathrooms across the city?
choices: About half of all houses had one
Roughly one house in three had one
Only the grandest houses had one
context: Almost every Mohenjo-daro house -- not just the wealthy ones -- had its own bathing floor and latrine, wastewater running out through chutes in the walls. Private indoor bathrooms were essentially unknown elsewhere for thousands of years. (thearchaeologist.org/blog/sanitation-of-the-indus-valley-civilisation)

question: Rome's Cloaca Maxima, one of the ancient world's great sewers, was begun about 600 BCE. Mohenjo-daro, too, ran covered brick drains carrying waste from nearly every house beneath its streets. How much earlier than Rome's famous sewer were Mohenjo-daro's drains built?
context: Mohenjo-daro's covered street drains date to about 2500 BCE, while Rome's celebrated Cloaca Maxima began around 600 BCE -- so the Indus city had a citywide sewer roughly nineteen centuries before Rome. (humanprogress.org/centers-of-progress-pt-3-mohenjo-daro-2)

question: At the very heart of Mohenjo-daro sits the Great Bath -- a sunken brick basin about 12 metres long and 2.4 metres deep, its floor sealed watertight with a thick layer of natural tar and reached by a staircase at each end. Among all the structures of the ancient world, what distinction does the Great Bath hold?
answer: The world's oldest known public water tank
choices: The world's oldest known public water tank
The world's oldest known irrigation tank
The world's oldest known swimming pool
context: Sealed with bitumen over finely fitted bricks and gypsum plaster, the Great Bath (about 12 m by 7 m, 2.4 m deep) is the oldest known public water tank on Earth -- and many believe it may also be the world's oldest ritual bathing pool, though what ceremonies happened there is unknown. (worldatlas.com/articles/interesting-facts-about-the-great-bath-mohenjo-daro)

question: The Indus people who raised Mohenjo-daro pressed their writing onto more than four thousand small objects -- mostly stone seals -- using some 400 to 600 different signs. Scholars long ago learned to read Egypt's hieroglyphs and Sumer's cuneiform. What has become of the Indus script?
choices: It was decoded in the last century
It proved to be early Persian
It proved to be early Sanskrit
context: More than 4,000 inscribed Indus objects survive, using roughly 400-600 signs, yet no one knows the language or what a single seal says -- the great unread script of the ancient world, even as Egyptian and Sumerian were long ago deciphered. (worldhistory.org/Indus_Script)

question: In 1926, archaeologist John Marshall lifted from the Mohenjo-daro ruins a bronze figure barely 10 centimetres tall -- one hand set on the hip, bangles stacked the length of one arm, cast some four thousand years ago by the lost-wax method. By what nickname is this famous little bronze known today?
context: 'Dancing Girl' is only a modern nickname -- nothing proves she danced. Cast around 2000 BCE by the lost-wax method and found by John Marshall in 1926, the 10.5 cm bronze still astonishes people with how lifelike a 4,000-year-old figure can look. (smarthistory.org/dancing-girl-mohenjodaro)

question: We call the city Mohenjo-daro, but the people who built it four and a half thousand years ago never did. That word is modern Sindhi, given by local people long after the city lay dead, and it means 'Mound of the Dead Men.' What is known about the name the city's own people used?
answer: Its true ancient name is unknown
choices: Its true ancient name is unknown
Its name is carved on the Great Bath
Its name meant 'City of the River'
context: 'Mohenjo-daro' -- 'Mound of the Dead Men' -- is a modern Sindhi name for the ruins. Because the Indus script has never been read, the name the city's own people used for their home is lost completely. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Egypt and Sumer shouted the power of their rulers in stone -- pharaohs' pyramids, kings' palaces, gilded tombs. At Mohenjo-daro, archaeologists have found none of these: no royal tomb, no clear palace, no ruler's monument anywhere in the city. What do many scholars cautiously conclude from this absence?
answer: It may have been a strikingly equal society
choices: It may have been a strikingly equal society
A hidden priesthood may have ruled it
Merchant families may have held the wealth
Its kings may have shunned all display
context: Sir John Marshall first noted Mohenjo-daro's missing kings, and a 2026 University of York study found its houses actually grew more equal in size over time -- so many read it as an unusually egalitarian city, though whether it hid rulers is still debated. (york.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/2026/research/world-first-city-prospered-wealth-gap-shrank)  (Legend.)

question: At Lothal, a sister-city of the Indus world built near the sea, archaeologist S.R. Rao uncovered an enormous brick basin about 37 metres long, linked by channels to a tidal river. Marine fossils and crusts of salt prove that seawater once filled it. What is this great basin widely believed to have been?
choices: The world's oldest known public bath
context: Excavated by S.R. Rao between 1955 and 1960, the Lothal basin (about 37 by 22 m) is widely identified as the world's oldest known dockyard, where boats could load and unload on the tide -- though some scholars argue it was instead a giant water tank. Salt crusts and marine microfossils confirm seawater once filled it. (lothal.org/lothal-dockyard-history)  (Legend.)

question: Around 1900 BCE, the great cities of the Indus fell silent and their people drifted away -- one of archaeology's enduring mysteries, since no single cause is written plainly in the ruins. Several explanations have been argued over the years. Which one do most researchers today consider the leading theory?
answer: A drying of the region's climate
choices: A drying of the region's climate
context: The leading modern theory ties the Indus decline (around 1900 BCE) to a weakening monsoon -- perhaps a 20-30% drop -- and the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra / Sarasvati rivers during the global '4.2-kiloyear' drought. It remains the leading theory, not settled fact; the old idea of a violent conquest has largely been abandoned. (nature.com/articles/s43247-023-00763-z)  (Legend.)

question: At Meteora, in central Greece, Orthodox monks built monasteries on the flat tops of natural stone pillars that rise up to 400 metres straight out of the Thessaly plain. For hundreds of years, how did a monk or a visitor reach a monastery at the top?
answer: hoisted up in a rope net raised behind them
choices: hoisted up in a rope net raised behind them
carried up a stone stair cut into the pillar
led up a narrow ledge spiralling the rock
walked across a bridge from the cliffs behind
context: The nets stayed the main way up until stone staircases were finally cut in the 1920s. Asked how often they replaced the fraying ropes, the monks famously answered, 'When the Lord lets them break.' Of two dozen monasteries once built on these rocks, six are still lived in today. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteora)

question: Up close, the Meteora pillars in Greece are not solid granite but conglomerate -- thousands of rounded pebbles and sand cemented into stone. Pebbles get their rounded shape only from being tumbled by moving water, so about 60 million years ago this highland was no highland at all. What kind of place laid this rock down?
answer: the delta of an ancient river
choices: the delta of an ancient river
the beach of a vanished sea
the bed of a mountain torrent
the outwash of a melting glacier
context: Geologists read the rounded river gravel like a fingerprint: about 60 million years ago a great river dumped its load of pebbles here, building a delta that later hardened into rock. Uplift and erosion then carved that rock into the towers the monks would one day climb -- the landform came first, and without it there could be no monasteries. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteora)

question: Bhutan's Paro Taktsang monastery clings to a sheer granite cliff 900 metres above the valley floor, in a spot so wild that a legend grew up to explain how anyone first reached the cave up there. The story says the 8th-century master Guru Padmasambhava arrived on the back of a magical creature, then meditated in the cave to tame the local demons. What creature does the legend name?
context: The monastery's name, Paro Taktsang, means 'Tiger's Nest,' straight from this legend. The cave where Guru Padmasambhava is said to have meditated became sacred, and in 1692 a monastery was built around it, clinging to the granite 'like a gecko.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paro_Taktsang)

question: Mount Athos, a self-governing monastic peninsula in northern Greece, keeps a rule called the avaton that has held for roughly a thousand years and is upheld today by both Orthodox tradition and Greek law. Under this ancient rule, who is forbidden even to set foot on the peninsula?
context: The monks regard the whole mountain as the garden of the Virgin Mary, kept for her alone; by tradition not even most female animals may be brought onto it. Male pilgrims may visit, but only a limited number each day. Mount Athos has governed itself for over a thousand years and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Athos)

question: Mount Athos is a self-governing monastic peninsula jutting 50 kilometres into the Aegean Sea, with twenty monasteries and no road from the mainland -- the only way in is by boat from the town of Ouranoupoli. But turning up with a boat ticket is not enough. What else must every visitor obtain before being allowed to land?
answer: a special written permit to enter
choices: a special written permit to enter
a blessing from the mainland bishop
a promise to fast during the stay
a letter from a home parish priest
context: The document is called the diamonitirion, checked when the boat lands. From Ouranoupoli the vessel carries pilgrims down a coast lined with monasteries founded over a thousand years ago -- the oldest, the Great Lavra, back in the year 963. There is still no road: the sea is the only door. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Athos)

question: St Catherine's Monastery stands alone in the desert at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt. Through centuries of wars that swept the region, no army ever destroyed it -- and the monks credit a document they still guard, said to carry the personal pledge of a great leader that his people would forever protect them. Whose promise is that charter said to bear?
context: The charter is the Ashtiname, said to bear the handprint of the Prophet Muhammad himself and to grant the monks his protection. Whether or not the original was truly his, ruler after ruler honoured it, and the monastery survived unbroken where countless others fell. It is also built around what tradition holds is the biblical Burning Bush. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)  (Legend.)

question: In the 8th and 9th centuries, Byzantine emperors launched the iconoclasm -- ordering religious images across the empire smashed and burned. St Catherine's Monastery, alone in the Sinai desert, lay far beyond the reach of the image-breakers, and its ancient icons came through untouched. Which world-famous image is among the treasures it saved?
answer: the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator
choices: the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator
the earliest known icon of Archangel Michael
the earliest known icon of Apostle Paul
the earliest known icon of Prophet Elijah
context: Because St Catherine's lay in the Sinai desert, beyond the reach of the emperors' image-breakers, it kept its ancient icons when almost every early example elsewhere in the empire was destroyed -- among them the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator, Christ shown as 'ruler of all,' which survived the very iconoclasm that wiped out such images everywhere else. Never sacked and never rebuilt, the monastery also still holds the oldest wooden roof-truss in the world, from Justinian's original 6th-century church. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)

question: St Catherine's Monastery, alone in the Egyptian desert, guards a library so rich that only the Vatican's holds more precious manuscripts. In 1844 and again in 1859, the scholar Constantin von Tischendorf carried away from it pages of an astonishing find: a Bible hand-copied in the 4th century, among the oldest nearly complete Bibles on Earth. By what name is that ancient manuscript known today?
context: The manuscript is the Codex Sinaiticus, written in Greek in the 4th century -- one of the two oldest near-complete Bibles in existence. Its pages are now shared among four institutions, including the British Library, but it first came to light in this remote desert monastery, kept safe by the dry air for 1,500 years. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)

question: Around 500 BC the Zapotec began building their capital atop a ridge rising some 400 metres (1,300 ft) above the fertile Valley of Oaxaca in Mexico. Before a single building went up, they reshaped the mountain itself. What did they do to the mountaintop?
context: Archaeologists call this the artificial levelling of the mountaintop. On the flattened ridge -- about 1,940 m above sea level -- the Zapotec laid out a Main Plaza roughly 300 by 150 m and coated it in white plaster: a giant artificial platform in the sky, home to some 17,200 people at the city's height. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('created through artificial levelling of the mountaintop'; ridge rises 'some 400 m from the valley floor'; '~1,940 m above sea level'; population '~17,200').

question: Set into one wall at Monte Alban are more than 300 carved stone slabs showing naked men with bodies twisted into contorted poses. Nineteenth-century visitors named them 'los Danzantes' -- 'the dancers.' Modern archaeologists reject that reading. What do they now believe the figures actually are?
context: The twisted poses once suggested dancing, but the figures show wounds -- some genitally mutilated, some labelled by name -- and are now read as tortured, sacrificed war prisoners, displayed in stacked rows like a public gallery of the defeated. Carved early in the city's life (c. 500-200 BC), they are among Monte Alban's oldest monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('19th-century notion... now discredited'; 'tortured, sacrificed war prisoners, some identified by name'; 'genitally mutilated'); corroborated famsi.org/reports/93003/93003Orr01.pdf.

question: In 1932 the archaeologist Alfonso Caso tunnelled into Tomb 7 at Monte Alban and struck the richest single treasure ever found in ancient Mesoamerica -- over 300 objects, including some 121 pieces of worked gold. Among them was one find now famous above all the rest. What was it?
answer: a human skull covered in turquoise mosaic
choices: a human skull covered in turquoise mosaic
a jade mask inlaid with obsidian eyes
a gold breastplate shaped like the sun
a headdress of green quetzal feathers
context: Caso opened Tomb 7 on 9 January 1932. The turquoise-mosaic skull, its eye-sockets set with polished seashell disks, lay among about 121 gold items weighing some 3,598 g. The hoard was actually a later Mixtec burial that re-used the centuries-old Zapotec tomb -- not the work of Monte Alban's original builders. Source: eluniversal.com.mx (Caso, 9 Jan 1932; ~300 Mixtec objects; 121 gold items ~3,598 g; turquoise-mosaic skull); montealbanoaxaca.com/wiki/tomb-7/.

question: Every building at Monte Alban lines up with the great plaza -- except one. 'Building J' is shaped like an arrowhead and deliberately twisted to a different angle, its point aimed away from the plaza's grid entirely. What did the Zapotec build it to line up with?
answer: the rising of the star Capella
choices: the rising of the star Capella
the fixed point of the North Star
context: Building J's steps align with the heliacal rising of Capella -- the first dawn each year the star reappears -- which in that era fell within a day of the Sun passing directly overhead (the zenith) at Monte Alban's latitude. Its arrowhead footprint, set askew to everything else, still marks it out on the site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('unusual arrow-like shape'; 'steps... aligned... to the rising of the star of Capella... within a day of the Sun passing directly overhead over Monte Alban').

question: Set into the walls of Building J at Monte Alban are more than 40 carved slabs, each showing a place-name sign beneath an upside-down human head. Archaeologists read the whole gallery as a single claim Monte Alban's rulers made about dozens of other towns. What did they claim?
context: The place-signs sit beneath inverted heads -- a Mesoamerican sign for a defeated, sacrificed enemy. The slabs list towns Monte Alban's elite claimed to have conquered, and for at least one, the Canada de Cuicatlan region, archaeology confirms the conquest really happened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('more than 40 large, carved slabs... place-names... upside-down heads... places which the Monte Alban elites claimed to have conquered... confirmation in the Canada de Cuicatlan region').

question: Founded around 500 BC, Monte Alban gave the Zapotec more than a mountaintop capital. Its people are credited with one of the earliest examples, anywhere in ancient Mesoamerica, of a skill that would spread across the region in the centuries that followed. Which skill did the Zapotec help pioneer here?
context: Cut into the Danzantes and conquest slabs are dot-and-bar dates and hieroglyphic signs -- among the earliest writing and calendar notation known from Mesoamerica, and an early step toward true written language in the Americas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('the Zapotecs had writing and calendrical notation... among Mesoamerica's earliest writing traditions'); corroborated people.wku.edu (bars, dots, and hieroglyphs on the slabs).

question: Off California's Monterey Bay, divers rise through swaying underwater forests as tall as a 15-story building, anchored to the rocky sea floor and reaching toward the sunlit surface. These towering marine forests are built not from trees, but from vast stands of what?
context: Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) is the largest of all marine algae -- normally about 100 ft (30 m) tall and up to 175 ft (53 m) in ideal conditions, forming the tallest underwater forests on Earth. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 'Giant kelp.'

question: A giant-kelp forest off California's Monterey Bay grows in layers like a rainforest, its fronds climbing from the rocky floor to a canopy spread across the sunlit surface. Each frond is lifted toward that sunlit surface by a row of its own tiny gas-filled floats. What are these floats called?
context: Each giant-kelp frond is buoyed toward the sunlit canopy by its own gas-filled float called a pneumatocyst -- a tiny balloon at the base of every blade, filled with a mix of oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. (The kelp grips bare rock not with roots but with a claw-like holdfast, and its stemlike stipes carry the leaflike blades.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Pneumatocyst'; Wikipedia, 'Macrocystis pyrifera.'

question: Off California's Monterey Bay, giant-kelp forests survive only while one predator keeps the spiny sea urchins in check by eating them; biologists call it the classic 'keystone species.' Remove this one animal and the urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to naked rock. Which animal is this keystone guardian of the Monterey kelp forest?
context: The Monterey kelp forest stays standing only because sea otters -- the classic 'keystone species' -- eat the sea urchins that would otherwise mow the kelp down to bare rock. When otters vanish, urchins multiply and strip the seabed into an 'urchin barren'; since 2014 much of California's coast has flipped to barrens, with otters now guarding only the surviving kelp patches. Source: UC Santa Cruz News, 'Sea otters maintain remnants of healthy kelp forest amid sea urchin barrens' (2021).

question: Along about 1,000 km of South Africa's Cape coast spreads the Great African Sea Forest, a golden underwater wilderness of giant bamboo kelp found nowhere else on Earth. In the caves and on the shores beside it, archaeologists keep unearthing beads, stone tools, and painted art. For how long do these finds suggest people have lived beside this same kelp forest?
context: South Africa's Great African Sea Forest is the only forest of giant bamboo kelp (Ecklonia maxima) on Earth, running about 1,000 km along the Cape coast -- and the caves beside it hold art and tools suggesting people have lived alongside it for nearly 100,000 years. Source: Sea Change Project, 'Great African Seaforest'; Discover Wildlife, 'Great African Sea Forest.'

question: You might expect the warm, sunny tropics to grow the sea's greatest forests -- yet there are almost no kelp forests there. Instead, giant kelp rings the coasts of California, Chile, South Africa and Tasmania. What do all of these kelp coasts share that the warm tropics lack?
context: Giant kelp thrives only where the sea stays below about 21 C (70 F) and cold currents well up nutrients from the deep -- which is why kelp forests ring cool coasts like California, Chile, South Africa's Great African Sea Forest and Tasmania, but never the warm tropics. Source: Wikipedia, 'Macrocystis pyrifera.'

question: In 1535 the French explorer Jacques Cartier, guided by people from the Iroquoian village of Hochelaga, climbed the one forested hill that rises green out of the middle of what is now Montreal. That hill still crowns the city today. What is the hill called?
context: Cartier named it 'Mont Real,' the royal mountain, in honour of King Francis I of France, and the city's name 'Montreal' grew straight out of the hill's. Mount Royal's wooded slopes still tower over the downtown core. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: The sprawling park that covers the slopes of Montreal's Mount Royal was laid out in the 1870s by Frederick Law Olmsted, the founding master of American landscape architecture. Olmsted is most celebrated for co-designing which other city's most famous green space?
context: Olmsted and Calvert Vaux designed New York's Central Park in 1858; Olmsted then shaped Mount Royal Park, inaugurated on May 24, 1876, across about 280 hectares (692 acres). He believed a wild green mountain inside the city could rest a weary mind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: From a distance Mount Royal has the smooth, rounded profile of an old volcano, and for generations Montrealers assumed a fire-mountain had once stood here. But geologists studying its hard grey rock, formed about 125 million years ago, uncovered a stranger truth. What is Mount Royal actually the remains of?
answer: a mass of magma that hardened underground and never erupted
choices: a mass of magma that hardened underground and never erupted
the collapsed rim of a volcano that blew its own top off
a slope of lava that froze solid partway down a mountain
a mound of rubble left behind by a meteorite strike
context: Around 125 million years ago molten magma pushed up into soft sedimentary rock and cooled hard while still trapped underground - a magma intrusion. The softer rock around it slowly eroded away, leaving the tough igneous core standing as the hill. Mount Royal is one of the Monteregian Hills, a whole line of these bared intrusions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: Montreal's winters are so brutal that the city built a warm second city underground: the RESO, some 32 kilometres of climate-controlled tunnels linking malls, ten metro stations, offices, universities and hotels, where nearly half a million people a day walk, shop and commute without ever going outside. What record does the RESO hold?
answer: the largest underground pedestrian network in the world
choices: the largest underground pedestrian network in the world
the world's first fully underground shopping city
the longest indoor walkway in North America
context: The RESO - from reseau, French for 'network' - grew out of the 1962 Place Ville Marie tower into roughly 32 km of passages, the largest underground pedestrian network on Earth. Montrealers can cross downtown in shirtsleeves while the streets above sit far below freezing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_City,_Montreal

question: The explorer Rene-Robert Cavelier de La Salle was certain he could find a river shortcut clear across the continent to the silk and spice riches of Asia. He set out up the St. Lawrence from his estate just above Montreal - and came back years later with nothing. His neighbours mocked the broken dream by pinning a name on his land and the wild rapids beside it, a mocking name that has stuck for over 350 years. What did they name it?
context: La Salle's seigneury and the impassable rapids beside it have been called Lachine ('La Chine,' China) ever since, and his men were teased as 'les Chinois,' the Chinese. Those same Lachine Rapids, too violent for boats to run, forced every fur trader to stop and portage here - which is exactly what made Montreal the great hinge of the North American fur trade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lachine,_Quebec  (Legend.)

question: Five low, sandy places lie strung in a row along the coast of southern New England and New York: Long Island, Block Island, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket, and Cape Cod. All five are the same thing — rubble the last great ice sheet shoved to its southern edge and left behind in a line as it melted. Geographers gather these five glacier-built places under one collective name. What is it?
context: The Outer Lands are a chain of terminal moraine strung along the Laurentide Ice Sheet's farthest edge across southern New England and New York. The distractors are all real but not glacier-dump islands: the Outer Banks are barrier islands off North Carolina, the Sea Islands lie off Georgia and South Carolina, and the Thousand Islands dot the St. Lawrence River. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_moraine

question: High on the wall of an alpine valley, hundreds of feet above the floor, runs a long ridge of shattered rock. Frost cracked the rock off the cliffs above and dropped it onto the glacier that once filled the valley, and the ice carried it along as a ridge. When the glacier melted down, the ridge was left stranded up high like a bathtub ring marking the old ice level — some run 3 km long and 140 m tall. What is a stranded ridge like this called?
context: A lateral moraine lines the flank of a glacier's valley with frost-shattered debris fallen off the walls; when the ice shrinks, the ridge is left perched high and dry, its steep inner face — the side that once leaned against the ice — reaching slopes near 80 degrees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraine

question: Two dark stripes run straight down the middle of a great Swiss glacier, from Konkordiaplatz — where its feeder ice streams merge and the ice is over 900 m thick — all the way down to its toe, 23 km below. These medial moraines look like racing lines painted on the ice. This river of ice is the largest glacier in the Alps. Name it.
context: A medial moraine forms when two ice streams merge and their two inner side-ridges join into one dark band carried down the glacier's center. The Aletsch's two stripes even have names — the Kranzbergmoräne (west) and the Trugbergmoräne (east). At about 23 km long and 82 km², the Aletsch is the largest glacier in the Alps. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aletsch_Glacier

question: Lake Garda, the largest lake in Italy, fills a long valley at the southern foot of the Alps. A line of low hills runs clear across the valley's open end, penning the water in behind a natural dam. What kind of dam is it?
answer: a ridge of rubble a glacier dumped
choices: a ridge of rubble a glacier dumped
a flow of lava a volcano hardened
a heap of rock a landslide dropped
a slab of crust a fault dropped
context: The Garda glacier heaped concentric rings of rubble across the valley's mouth over successive ice ages, building the great horseshoe geologists call the Anfiteatro morenico del Garda — the 'morainic amphitheatre.' That arc of moraine dams Italy's largest lake (~370 km²). Lava flows, landslides, and fault movements dam other lakes, but Garda's dam is glacial rubble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Garda

question: Walk up one glacier-carved valley and you cross a dozen low ridges of till — the glacier's jumbled rubble — one behind the next, like rungs of a ladder climbing the valley floor. Geologists read the whole row in order to reconstruct the valley's ice-age history. What does each single ridge in the row record?
answer: a pause in the ice sheet's slow retreat
choices: a pause in the ice sheet's slow retreat
a separate, far older ice age's advance
a single hard winter's deep snowfall
an ancient meltwater river's buried channel
context: These are recessional moraines: each transverse ridge marks a spot where the melting glacier's front briefly stalled before shrinking further, so a single valley can hold ten or more — and some form on a yearly cycle (annual moraines). Read in order, they map the ice sheet's retreat like bookmarks in the melt. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/recessional-moraine

question: Everyone assumes Moscow's Red Square was named for the colour of communism or the red-brick Kremlin beside it. But its Russian name, Krasnaya Ploshchad, comes from an old word that has drifted in meaning over the centuries. When the square was first named, what did 'krasnaya' mean?
context: Krasnaya Ploshchad really means 'Beautiful Square'. In old Russian 'krasnaya' meant beautiful; over time it came to mean 'red', while a new word, 'krasivaya', took over 'beautiful' -- both growing from the same ancient Slavic root. So the name has nothing to do with communism or red bricks; it was simply 'the beautiful place'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Square

question: Down in Moscow's Ploshchad Revolyutsii station, 76 life-size bronze statues crouch along the platform, and one is a border guard kneeling beside his dog. For good luck -- especially before a big exam -- passengers rub the same spot on that bronze dog until it gleams like gold. Which part of the dog do they rub?
context: The station is Ploshchad Revolyutsii ('Revolution Square'), opened in 1938, lined with 76 life-size bronze figures by Matvey Manizer -- sailors, soldiers, students and farmers. Generations of hopeful passengers, students most of all, have rubbed the border dog's nose before exams, wearing the bronze to a bright polished gold. Source: https://www.rbth.com/multimedia/pictures/2016/11/22/metro-close-up_649969

question: From the outside, St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square looks like one gloriously chaotic building of swirling domes, thrown up for Ivan the Terrible after he stormed the city of Kazan in the 1550s. But the way it was actually put together surprises visitors who step inside. What is St Basil's, structurally?
answer: nine separate chapels fused into one
choices: nine separate chapels fused into one
one great hall beneath the tallest dome
a monastery of many linked cloisters
a fortress-church ringed by high walls
context: Ivan the Terrible had it built in 1555-1561 to celebrate taking Kazan (and Astrakhan). It is really eight smaller churches arranged around a taller ninth central chapel dedicated to the Intercession -- nine chapels fused into a single wildly beautiful whole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: The Moscow Kremlin's mighty red-brick walls and 20 towers -- a great triangle running over 2 km around -- went up in the 1480s and 1490s and still guard the seat of Russian power. Yet the master-builders who designed these most Russian of walls were foreigners, brought in from abroad for the job. Where did those architects come from?
context: The Kremlin -- a triangular fortress of red-brick walls about 2,235 m around and 5 to 19 m high, studded with 20 towers -- was raised by Italian master-builders in 1485-1495. It remains one of the largest active medieval fortresses in Europe and still houses Russia's government today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Kremlin

question: St Basil's Cathedral is famous worldwide for its onion domes swirled in candy-bright colours, no two of them alike. But that rainbow is a surprise: for its first century or more the cathedral looked nothing like the postcard we know, the swirls only being painted on much later. What did St Basil's look like when Ivan the Terrible first saw it finished?
context: When first finished under Ivan the Terrible, St Basil's was mostly plain red brick and white stone. The famous swirled rainbow was only added between the 17th and early 18th centuries -- so the candy-coloured domes everyone photographs are a later flourish, not the original look. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: Ivan the Terrible built the great cathedral on Red Square to trumpet his conquest of Kazan -- a monument to a mighty tsar's war. Yet Muscovites came to call it 'St Basil's', after a man honoured in a small chapel added in 1588. Who was this Basil that the cathedral took its everyday name from?
answer: the barefoot holy fool who wandered Moscow
choices: the barefoot holy fool who wandered Moscow
the tsar's warrior brother who died in war
the pilgrim monk who walked from Kiev
the architect who raised the great domes
context: The cathedral's formal name is the Cathedral of the Intercession, but its popular name comes from a chapel added in 1588 over the grave of Basil the Blessed -- a 'holy fool' who wandered Moscow barefoot and was deeply revered. So the church built to glorify a fearsome tsar is remembered by the name of a penniless beggar-saint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: A grisly old Moscow legend claims that when St Basil's Cathedral was finished, Ivan the Terrible had its architect blinded, so that no one could ever build anything so beautiful again. Historians say this dark tale is almost certainly a myth. What does the record actually suggest became of the builder, Postnik Yakovlev?
answer: he went on to build other cathedrals
choices: he went on to build other cathedrals
he was rewarded with a great estate
he died before the work was done
context: This is a popular tale, not history. Records show the builder, Postnik Yakovlev, went on to work on other cathedrals after St Basil's was finished -- so he plainly was not blinded. Historians treat the blinding story as a myth that grew up around Ivan the Terrible's dark reputation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral  (Legend.)

question: Moscow's Komsomolskaya station is no bare subway stop: a golden baroque ceiling rides on 68 white-marble columns, dripping with chandeliers, while eight great mosaics by the artist Pavel Korin blaze overhead. Korin filled that ceiling with a single, proud theme from Russia's past. What do his eight mosaics show?
choices: the saints of the Orthodox church
context: Komsomolskaya (opened 1952) crowns its golden ceiling with eight mosaics by Pavel Korin of Russia's great military figures -- Alexander Nevsky, Dmitry Donskoy, Suvorov, Kutuzov, and Soviet soldiers raising the flag over the Reichstag. The station won the Grand Prix at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komsomolskaya_(Koltsevaya_line)

question: The whole east side of Red Square, directly facing the Kremlin wall, is filled by one enormous building from the 1890s: a 242-metre stone front behind a soaring roof of iron and glass, sheltering long indoor streets below. Muscovites have poured through GUM for well over a century. What kind of place is it?
context: GUM (from the Russian for 'State Department Store') is a vast shopping arcade, built in 1890-1893 with a light iron-and-glass roof engineered by Vladimir Shukhov.
