Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Reiche; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kosok; worldhistory.org/article/665/nazca-lines.  (Legend.)

question: In New Orleans, earthen levees taller than a house hold the Mississippi back. Stand atop one out in Lakeview, a neighborhood built on drained swamp that lies below sea level, look out at the passing river, then turn and look back at the town behind you. What do you see?
answer: The river runs higher than the streets.
choices: The river runs higher than the streets.
The river flows straight through the streets.
The river drops over a waterfall downtown.
The river splits the town into islands.
context: New Orleans really does sit lower than the river beside it. About 65% of the city lies at or below mean sea level, while the Mississippi at its yearly high-water mark rises to roughly 14 feet above sea level, so behind the levees the river runs higher than the streets, and only those earthen walls and the pumps hold it out. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: When Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans in 2005, whole newer neighborhoods went under the flood, yet the French Quarter, the oldest part of town, stayed mostly dry. It comes down to where Bienville's settlers built back in 1718. In a delta this flat, where was the highest, safest ground?
answer: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
choices: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
On the shore of Lake Pontchartrain, to the north.
Far out on a sandy island in midstream.
Up on a low hill set a mile inland.
context: In a flat delta the highest ground is the strip of land right beside the river. Every flood, the Mississippi dropped its heaviest silt first at its own edge, building a 'natural levee' ridge 10-20 feet above sea level. Bienville's settlers laid the French Quarter (the Vieux Carre) on that ridge in 1718, which is why it stayed mostly dry in Hurricane Katrina while lower, drained-swamp neighborhoods flooded. Sources: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans'; SERC/Carleton coastlines module.

question: New Orleanians will tell you that in the old days a hard rain could raise the water table so high that airtight coffins popped up out of the wet ground and floated down the street. Whether that story is the whole reason or not, and the old French and Spanish Catholic custom played a part too, the city settled on one striking way of laying its dead to rest. What is it?
answer: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
choices: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
Deep graves sealed under heavy concrete slabs.
Graveyards set far off on high, dry ridges.
Cremation, the ashes kept inside the cathedral.
context: New Orleans buries much of its dead above ground in stone tombs, whole 'Cities of the Dead' laid out like little streets. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, opened in 1789 on Basin Street, is the oldest: a single square block holding thousands, including the voodoo priestess Marie Laveau, believed to lie in the Glapion family crypt. The high-water-table 'floating coffins' story is the reason locals give; the French-Spanish Catholic custom of wall vaults also shaped the tradition. Sources: experienceneworleans.com; Wikipedia, 'St. Louis Cemetery.'  (Legend.)

question: The old French Quarter of New Orleans, the Vieux Carre, was settled right on the bank of the Mississippi in 1718. As the great river reaches the old city, it does one dramatic thing plain to see from the levee. What does the Mississippi do as it passes the Vieux Carre?
answer: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
choices: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
It splits into two channels around a midstream island.
It tumbles over a line of rapids downtown.
It runs dead straight for miles past the docks.
context: The Mississippi curls around the old French Quarter in a huge sweeping bend, and it is from that great crescent-shaped curve that New Orleans takes its nickname, 'the Crescent City.' Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded the city in 1718 for the French Mississippi Company, naming it La Nouvelle-Orleans for Philippe II, Duke of Orleans. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: At Congo Square in New Orleans, a French colonial law of 1724 gave enslaved Africans their Sundays free. By the hundreds they gathered there to drum and to dance the Bamboula and the Calinda, keeping the rhythms of their African homelands alive. Over the next century those Sunday rhythms grew into a wholly new American music, born in this city. What music was it?
context: The Code Noir of 1724 gave enslaved Africans their Sundays free, and at Congo Square they gathered by the hundreds; the architect Benjamin Latrobe, visiting in 1819, counted 500 to 600 people dancing in tribal groups. The African rhythms they kept alive there fused, over generations, into jazz. The square is now inside Louis Armstrong Park in the Treme, and you can still hear those rhythms in New Orleans jazz funerals, second-line parades, and Mardi Gras Indian processions; the name 'Congo Square' was officially restored in 2011. Source: Wikipedia, 'Congo Square.'

question: In 1913 the New Orleans engineer A. Baldwin Wood built the most powerful water pumps on Earth, giant spinning screws that sucked the swamp dry and let the city drain its marshes and raise whole new neighborhoods like Lakeview on the reclaimed land. But that triumph hid a curse: draining the swamp is the very reason New Orleans keeps sinking today. How does pulling the water out drop the land itself?
answer: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
choices: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
The pumps crack the bedrock, which slumps down.
Lake water seeps in and hollows the earth.
The weight of new buildings presses the mud down.
context: Wood's 1913 screw pump was 12 feet across, the largest and most powerful in the world; his 1927 version could move a million gallons every five minutes, and some 1913 pumps still ran through Hurricane Katrina. But draining the swamp let the spongy organic soil dry out, decay, and compact, so the ground itself dropped: more than half the city is now below sea level. Geographer Richard Campanella said of the pump builders, 'Their intentions were good... Instead, they created a new and bigger one.' Wood's drainage designs were copied worldwide, even helping drain the Netherlands' Zuiderzee. Source: Historic New Orleans Collection, 'The Pumps That Built (and Sank) the City.'

question: For thousands of years the Mississippi has wandered across its delta, switching course again and again, and today it is straining to do so once more, to forsake its long, sluggish channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans for a shorter, steeper run to the Gulf. Since 1963 a single giant floodgate complex, the Old River Control Structure, has fought to hold it in place. Where is the river trying to go instead?
context: The Old River Control Structure, completed in 1963, holds roughly a 70/30 split, letting about 30% of the flow go to the Atchafalaya while the rest stays in the channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans. In the great flood of 1973 the river nearly tore the structure out and almost captured the Atchafalaya for good, which would have left both cities stranded on a stagnant backwater while the Mississippi built a whole new delta near Morgan City. The close call forced the Army Corps of Engineers to add an auxiliary structure. Source: Wikipedia, 'Old River Control Structure.'

question: Coastal Louisiana is drowning. Since the 1930s it has lost nearly 1,900 square miles of marsh, an area the size of Delaware, slipping into the Gulf at times as fast as a football field of wetland every hour. What main cause do scientists point to?
answer: Levees and dams upstream trap the river's mud.
choices: Levees and dams upstream trap the river's mud.
Salt water from the Gulf poisons the marsh grass.
Hurricanes have torn the wetlands away for good.
Drainage pumps have sucked the coastal marshes dry.
context: Because upstream levees and dams keep the Mississippi from spilling over and laying down fresh sediment, the delta marshes are no longer being rebuilt, and they are sinking and washing away. Coastal Louisiana has lost nearly 1,900 square miles of land since the 1930s, an area about the size of Delaware, at times vanishing as fast as a football field of wetland every hour, leaving New Orleans ever more exposed to storms. Sources: USGS via nola.com; mississippiriverdelta.org.

question: When France's gift, the Statue of Liberty, was dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886, she gleamed a shiny reddish-brown and stayed that way for years before slowly turning the pale green she wears today. What actually turned her green?
choices: Workers repainted her a protective green
Her bronze surface tarnished like an old coin
Salt spray bleached the dark metal pale
context: The statue's skin is copper only about 2.4 mm thick -- roughly two pennies stacked. Air, water, and pollution weathered it to a green layer of verdigris (copper patina) that now actually protects the metal underneath; the green is corrosion, not paint or bronze. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty

question: Central Park's 843 acres of meadows, lakes, and rocky woods sit right in the middle of Manhattan and look like a piece of wild countryside the city simply grew around. What is the surprising truth about that scenery?
answer: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
choices: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
It is the last untouched wilderness left on the island
It was once a royal hunting forest from colonial days
It formed in a glacier-carved valley long ago
context: Central Park only looks natural. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux's winning 'Greensward Plan' (chosen April 1858) landscaped the whole park from scratch in the 1850s-60s -- the 'natural' park is the most man-made thing in the city. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: Several great suspension bridges hang over the waters around New York City, but only one, when it opened in 1883, was the longest in the entire world -- its main span reaching nearly 1,600 feet. Which one was it?
context: The Brooklyn Bridge opened May 24, 1883; its 1,595.5-foot main span made it the world's longest suspension bridge, and it was among the first strung from bundled steel wire -- each of its four main cables holds 5,282 galvanized steel wires. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: High over the crowds in Grand Central Terminal, a vast turquoise ceiling shows the golden constellations of the zodiac. Two months after the station opened in 1913, a sharp-eyed commuter noticed something badly wrong with the star map. What was the mistake?
answer: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
choices: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
Two of the twelve zodiac signs are missing
The stars glow in the wrong seasonal colors
A thirteenth constellation was invented and added
context: A commuter spotted the reversed zodiac within two months of the 1913 opening. Officials floated a 'God's-eye view from outside the heavens' explanation; astronomer Harold Jacoby's leading theory is that the painter laid the flat sky-chart on the floor and projected it upward, flipping the image. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: When Grand Central Terminal's great ceiling was scrubbed clean in the 1990s, the restorers deliberately left one small rectangle near the constellation Cancer untouched and grimy. Why keep that one dirty patch?
answer: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
choices: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
To hide an old water stain they could not remove
To preserve the original artist's faded signature
To mark the center point of the painted sky
context: During the 1990s restoration, one dark rectangle near Cancer was deliberately left uncleaned -- a preserved patch showing how much tar and nicotine from decades of indoor tobacco smoking had blackened the whole ceiling. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: Central Park's peaceful meadows give no hint of the violence that built them: to clear the rocky ridges in the 1850s, workers set off enormous blasting charges. Just how much gunpowder did leveling the site take?
answer: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
choices: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
More than was fired at the Battle of Bunker Hill
More than was fired at the Battle of Yorktown
More than was fired at the siege of the Alamo
context: Building Central Park meant hauling out about 5 million cubic feet of soil and rock and trucking in over 18,500 cubic yards of topsoil from Long Island and New Jersey -- and blasting the rocky site used more gunpowder than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: To sink the Brooklyn Bridge's huge stone towers into the riverbed, workers dug inside giant air-pressurized underwater chambers called caissons. Many came up wracked with pain -- some paralyzed, some killed -- by an illness the doctors of the 1870s could not explain. What do we now call it?
context: Surfacing too fast from the pressurized caissons caused decompression sickness -- 'caisson disease,' the bends. Chief engineer John A. Roebling died of tetanus before construction began; his son Washington was left paralyzed by it and directed the work by telescope from his bedroom while Emily Warren Roebling ran the site for years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: Manhattan's streets lock into a strict rectangular grid -- except for one older road that slants diagonally across the whole island, and wherever it cuts the square blocks it opens a famous triangular plaza: Times Square, Herald Square, Madison Square. Which road is it?
context: Broadway is the one great diagonal breaking Manhattan's grid -- an older route following the island's natural lay of the land. It slices across the right-angle streets and carves out the triangular 'squares.' The rigid grid itself was set by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners%27_Plan_of_1811

question: The Hudson River sliding past Manhattan hides a secret: twice a day its current stops and runs backward as salty ocean water pushes upstream, as far as 150 miles north to Troy -- the Lenape called it 'the river that flows both ways.' Geographically, the lower Hudson is therefore not truly a river, but what?
context: The Hudson beside Manhattan is a tidal estuary -- an arm of the sea whose current reverses with the ocean tides all the way up to Troy, about 150 miles inland. The Lenape/Mahican name Muhheakantuck means 'the river that flows both ways.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River

question: New York's mightiest skyscrapers cluster in Midtown and the Financial District, and it is no accident: such towers must be anchored to extremely hard, ancient bedrock that happens to lie near the surface in exactly those spots. What is this tough foundation rock called?
context: Manhattan's skyscrapers stand on hard metamorphic bedrock -- chiefly Manhattan schist -- well suited to carrying enormous towers. Where that rock lies near the surface, in Midtown and the Financial District, is where the tallest clusters rise. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan

question: When the Empire State Building opened in 1931, the slender spire crowning its 102 stories was not mere decoration -- it was built for a strange, futuristic job that never once worked in practice. What was the spire originally meant to do?
answer: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
choices: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
Broadcast the world's first television signal
Serve as a giant lightning rod for the city
Hold a rotating searchlight for ships at sea
context: The Empire State Building's spire was designed as a mooring mast where zeppelins would dock and let passengers off -- but the plan was abandoned once it was clear the high winds swirling around the tower made airship docking impossible. Built in about 410 days during the Great Depression, the tower stayed the world's tallest for roughly 40 years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building

question: New York City drinks over a billion gallons of water a day, carried through tunnels from reservoirs in the Catskill Mountains more than 100 miles to the north. What is the astonishing thing about how nearly all of it reaches the city's taps?
answer: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
choices: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
It is filtered clean through the bedrock as it travels
It is pulled from the Atlantic and then desalinated
It is chilled inside mountain tunnels to stay fresh
context: About 95% of New York City's drinking water -- over a billion gallons a day -- arrives by gravity alone, no pumps, flowing downhill through aqueducts from Catskill and Delaware watershed reservoirs up to about 125 miles north. Part of it runs through the Delaware Aqueduct, at about 85 miles the world's longest continuous tunnel, carrying roughly half the city's water beneath the Hudson River without a single pump. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_water_supply_system

question: New Zealand's two main islands sit alone in the South Pacific, but seafloor mapping shows they are only the highest peaks of a single huge slab of continental crust -- nearly all of it sunk beneath the ocean, hidden from every ordinary world map. What did geologists name this drowned, almost-entirely-underwater continent?
context: About 94% of Zealandia lies underwater; only New Zealand, New Caledonia and a few smaller islands rise above the sea. Because it is genuine, continuous continental crust -- not scattered ocean islands -- geologists formally argued in 2017 that it counts as a true continent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: New Zealand is one of only two lands anywhere that rise above the waves from a vast, almost-entirely-drowned continent in the southwest Pacific. Its lone companion above water is a chain of islands lying well to the north. Which land is New Zealand's fellow survivor above water on this hidden continent?
context: New Caledonia and New Zealand are the only large pieces of the continent Zealandia to break the surface -- New Caledonia near its northern end, New Zealand toward the south. Everything between is drowned continental shelf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: The continent that New Zealand rides on is almost entirely drowned -- yet its single loftiest point stands far above the clouds, a snow-and-ice summit rising 3,724 m in the Southern Alps of the South Island. Which mountain is this highest point of the mostly-sunken continent?
context: Officially Aoraki / Mount Cook, keeping its Maori name Aoraki. At 3,724 m it is the highest point not only of New Zealand but of the whole continent of Zealandia -- nearly all of which lies drowned beneath the Pacific. Source: geosociety.org/gsa-today/march-april-2017/zealandia-earths-hidden-continent

question: New Zealand broke away from the other continents about 80 million years ago and drifted in isolation so complete that one whole class of land animals never took hold there -- only two tiny species ever crossed the open sea to settle. In their absence birds multiplied into every corner of the land, and several of them, with nothing on the ground to hunt them, gave up flight altogether. Which class of land animal is New Zealand's native fauna almost entirely without?
context: New Zealand's only native land mammals are two tiny bat species. With no cats, rats, deer or monkeys to hunt them or compete with them, birds and insects evolved to fill the empty roles -- several birds even lost the power of flight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna_of_New_Zealand

question: Trace your finger straight down New Zealand's South Island and you follow one of Earth's great cracks in the crust -- a nearly ruler-straight boundary, about 600 km long, where the Pacific and Australian plates grind past each other. Along it a young mountain range is still being shoved skyward. What is this plate-boundary fault called?
context: The Alpine Fault runs about 600 km up the spine of the South Island, where the Pacific and Australian plates slide past each other and heave up the Southern Alps. It ruptures in huge earthquakes roughly every few centuries; the last great one struck around 1717 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Fault

question: In the wild, roadless southwest of New Zealand's South Island, Ice Age glaciers ground out a maze of steep valleys that the rising sea later flooded, leaving long dark arms of ocean walled by cliffs. The most famous is Milford Sound, where Mitre Peak leaps 1,692 m straight from the water and over 6 metres of rain fall a year -- a scene Rudyard Kipling called the 'eighth Wonder of the World.' What is this whole drowned-valley region of New Zealand called?
context: The region is named for its fiords -- sea-drowned glacier valleys such as Milford Sound. Though early sailors called them 'sounds' (a word for river-carved inlets), they are technically fiords, gouged by ice and later flooded by the sea. Milford is one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: Lake Taupo, in the middle of New Zealand's North Island, looks like a calm holiday lake -- but its broad, rounded basin is really a colossal wound in the Earth. About 25,600 years ago this very spot erupted with such fury that it flung out roughly 1,170 cubic kilometres of rock and ash, then collapsed into the vast crater the lake now fills. Volcanoes capable of a blast this size are nicknamed 'supervolcanoes,' and only a handful are known anywhere on the planet. Compared with every other super-eruption in Earth's history, what is the Taupo blast?
context: The Oruanui eruption about 25,600 years ago was Earth's most recent VEI-8 event -- the very top of the volcanic explosivity scale, and no volcano anywhere has erupted on that scale since. Lake Taupo sits in the Taupo Volcanic Zone, fed by the Pacific plate diving beneath the North Island, the same engine behind Rotorua's geysers and boiling mud. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taup%C5%8D_Volcanic_Zone

question: In Ireland's Boyne Valley, the huge grass-topped mound of Newgrange was raised around 3200 BC -- making this Irish tomb about 500 years OLDER than two of the most famous monuments on Earth. Which two?
answer: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
choices: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
Petra and the Great Wall of China
context: Newgrange went up around 3200 BC -- roughly five centuries before either Stonehenge's great stone circle or Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza. Its Neolithic builders had no metal tools and no writing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: The front of Newgrange today gleams with a curved wall of bright white stone, studded with dark round cobbles -- rock that Stone Age builders hauled about 80 km from the Wicklow Mountains to the south, with no wheels and no metal. What is that white facing-stone?
context: The bright facade is white quartz carried from the Wicklow Mountains, set with dark granite cobbles from the Mourne Mountains to the north -- stone moved dozens of kilometres by people with no carts. (The gleaming wall is a modern reconstruction from quartz found scattered at the mound's foot.) Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Newgrange's builders, working around 3200 BC with no metal tools and no wheels, gathered and stacked a grass-topped stone dome about 85 metres across. Roughly how much stone and earth did they pile up by hand to build it?
context: The mound is about 85 metres wide, 12-13 metres high, and covers roughly an acre -- an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth, all gathered and stacked by hand in the Stone Age. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: The builders of Newgrange aimed their whole tomb at a single sunrise each year. Above the doorway they left a small stone opening, so that at dawn on that one morning a blade of sunlight shoots 19 metres straight down the passage and floods the pitch-dark inner chamber -- even with the great stone door shut. Which sunrise did they build it to catch?
context: For a few mornings around the winter solstice -- the shortest days of the year -- the rising sun threads the passage and lights the inner chamber for about 17 minutes before fading, a light show engineered over 5,000 years ago. Sources: https://www.newgrange.com/winter-solstice-newgrange.htm ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: At the entrance to Newgrange lies a massive 5-tonne slab carved with Ireland's most famous prehistoric emblem -- a bold pattern of coils winding into and out of one another, cut into the rock 5,000 years ago with only flint, since Neolithic Ireland had no metal at all. What is this ancient coiled emblem called?
context: The great entrance stone (Kerbstone K1) carries a bold triple spiral -- a 'triskele' -- about 3 metres long, cut with nothing but stone and flint tools. Another famous triskele hides deep inside the chamber. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Newgrange's inner chamber is roofed by corbelling -- flat stones stacked so each juts a little further inward than the one below, with no mortar anywhere, meeting in a dome nearly 6 metres up. Astonishingly, after more than 5,000 years that chamber is still bone-DRY. What clever trick did the builders use on the roof-stones to keep the rain out?
answer: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
choices: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
they sealed the joints with sticky river clay
they smeared the stones with black pine tar
they dug hidden drains beneath the chamber floor
context: The mortar-free corbelled vault has kept the chamber watertight for over 5,000 years -- partly because the builders cut grooves into the roof-stones to channel rainwater outward, away from the room below. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: At dawn on a December morning in 1967, archaeologist Michael J. O'Kelly stood alone in the black inner chamber of Newgrange and became the first person in modern times to watch the ancient sunbeam creep down the long passage and light up the tomb. Studying the small stone slot above the entrance that let the beam in, O'Kelly gave it the plain English name it still carries today. What did he call it?
context: On 21 December 1967, Michael J. O'Kelly watched the solstice beam creep in, 'lighting up everything as it came' -- the first recorded modern witness -- and coined the term 'roof-box' for the opening that channels the light. Source: https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2025/1220/1549633-newgrange-winter-solstice-light-show-sunrise-discovery-michael-j-okelly/

question: Newgrange does not stand alone. It rises in Bru na Boinne, a sacred bend of Ireland's River Boyne where Stone Age people raised a whole ritual landscape of tombs, built long before the age of the Egyptian pharaohs. Two other giant passage-tombs share this ground with Newgrange, each a grass-topped mound with its own carved stones and dark inner chamber. What are the names of these two great sister-tombs?
context: Newgrange, Knowth, and Dowth are the three great passage-tombs of Bru na Boinne -- a Neolithic ritual landscape of at least 90 monuments in a loop of the River Boyne, older than the pharaohs and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. Knowth alone holds more than a third of all the megalithic art in Western Europe. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BA_na_B%C3%B3inne ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowth

question: Niagara is really three waterfalls side by side: the giant Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, plus two smaller falls across the American border. Of all the water in the Niagara River, how much pours over the Horseshoe alone?
context: Niagara is really three waterfalls side by side: the giant Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, the wide American Falls, and the slender Bridal Veil Falls beside it. The Horseshoe crest curves about 670 m (2,200 ft) across, and its water drops an average of 57 m (188 ft) into a plunge pool roughly 35 m deep. Almost the whole river — close to nine-tenths of the flow — thunders over the Horseshoe alone, leaving only about a tenth for the American and Bridal Veil falls combined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: Right at the brink of Niagara sits a large wooded island called Goat Island, planted midstream exactly where the river tips over the edge. What does Goat Island do to the great waterfall?
answer: Splits it into two separate falls
choices: Splits it into two separate falls
Splits it into three separate falls
Separates the small Bridal Veil Falls off
Bends the flow into the Horseshoe's curve
context: Goat Island parts the river into the Canadian Horseshoe Falls and the American Falls. A second, much smaller scrap of rock — Luna Island — then splits the slender Bridal Veil Falls off from the American Falls, which is how Niagara ends up as three falls in all. Both big falls were already there when Europeans first described the site before 1678. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: Stand at Niagara and you'd swear the falls were fixed in place forever — but geologists have proved they are not. Over the roughly 12,000 years since the Ice Age, the falls have shifted about 11 km from the cliff near Queenston where they first began to thunder. What are the falls slowly doing?
choices: Sinking down into a deepening pit
Growing taller as fallen rock piles up
Drifting sideways toward the Canadian shore
context: A waterfall that walks: Niagara gnaws its way upstream, toward Lake Erie, leaving the long gorge behind it as its trail. It once retreated fast — up to about a metre a year — but since engineers diverted much of the flow, today's regulated erosion has slowed to roughly 0.3 m a year or less (some estimates near 0.1 m). Source: ijc.org/en/niagara-falls-moving

question: Niagara's cliff is built in two layers: a hard cap of Lockport dolostone resting on a bed of Rochester shale. This layering is the very reason the falls keep crumbling their way upstream. What is the plunging river actually doing to the cliff to make it retreat?
answer: Scooping out the shale bed from under the cap
choices: Scooping out the shale bed from under the cap
Grinding the dolostone cap thinner from above
Freezing in the shale and cracking it apart
Dissolving the dolostone cap in the river water
context: The river can't easily attack the tough Lockport dolostone cap, so instead it hollows out the weak Rochester shale underneath until the overhanging ledge, left unsupported, snaps off. Geologists call a waterfall that eats its way upstream like this a 'knickpoint.' Source: serc.carleton.edu/vignettes/collection/25474.html

question: In late March 1848, the water over Niagara's crest dwindled to a bare trickle and the great riverbed lay exposed and drying in the sun. Curious townsfolk clambered down onto the naked rock and, by many accounts, pried what long-buried objects out of the mud?
answer: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
choices: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
Spanish gold coins and jeweled crosses
Dinosaur bones and ancient fossil shells
Ship timbers and heavy iron anchors
context: With the falls stilled, people reportedly walked far out on the dry bed — some all the way to Goat Island, a few even driving buggies — and a cavalry troop is said to have paraded on the exposed rock. Treasure-hunters dug up weapons from the War of 1812, which had been fought along this very river. These colourful accounts are widely retold but not all independently verified. Source: smithsonianmag.com/travel/when-niagara-falls-ran-dry-180972198  (Legend.)

question: On March 29, 1848, people living near Niagara woke to an eerie silence: the thundering falls had all but stopped, and the riverbed was drying to mud. Something upstream had choked off almost the entire flow of the river. What had blocked it?
answer: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
choices: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
A sudden earthquake had shifted its channel
A landslide had buried the gorge in rock
A long drought had emptied Lake Erie
context: A warm spell cracked the winter ice on Lake Erie; then easterly winds shoved the floes into the mouth of the Niagara River, where they piled into a natural ice dam between Buffalo and Fort Erie. For roughly 30 to 40 hours barely a trickle went over the crest — the only near-total stoppage ever recorded. When the dam gave way, the river roared back to life. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: A few kilometres below the falls, the Niagara gorge makes a sharp right-angle turn and the whole river erupts into a huge, deep basin of spinning water — the Niagara Whirlpool. This strange spot exists because, about 5,500 years ago, the backward-eroding falls broke into something hidden underground. What did the retreating falls cut into?
answer: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
choices: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
A soft pocket of ash from an old volcano
A deep cavern carved by underground streams
A crack left open by a long-ago earthquake
context: The falls sliced into the St. David's Gorge, an ancient valley that an earlier river had carved and glaciers had then packed with loose debris, lying crosswise to Niagara's path. The whirlpool basin is about 518 m long, 365 m wide and up to 38 m deep, and it can even run backward — at full flow the water spins counter-clockwise, but the churning sometimes reverses and forces incoming water to dive beneath itself to reach the outlet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Whirlpool

question: In June 1969, engineers did something astonishing: they switched the American Falls OFF. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers dumped tens of thousands of tons of rock across the river, building a dam that shoved the entire flow over to the Horseshoe Falls and left the American Falls bone dry for months. Why did they deliberately shut the falls down?
answer: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
choices: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
To hunt the dry riverbed for sunken treasure
To film a blockbuster movie on the bare cliff
To lay the footings for a new stone bridge
context: Starting June 9, 1969, the Army Corps built a 600-foot cofferdam out of more than 28,000 tons of rock, steering the river toward the Horseshoe Falls and leaving the American Falls dry for about five months so scientists could study its unstable, crumbling face. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: The 1969 study of the dry American Falls turned up a surprise about the great heap of fallen boulders piled at its foot. What were those boulders actually doing?
answer: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
choices: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
Cementing into a solid new stone ledge
Making the cliff collapse even faster
Washing slowly downstream in the current
context: The talus — rubble from rockfalls in 1931 and 1954 — was actually propping up the fragile cliff. Clearing it away would only trigger MORE collapse, so in 1975 the International Joint Commission decided to leave the boulders in place and simply pin the rock face with bolts and cement. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: Niagara Falls is astonishingly young — it simply did not exist 13,000 years ago. At the close of the last Ice Age, the glaciers that had buried Southern Ontario under 2–3 km of ice finally melted back. What did that great melt do to give birth to the falls?
answer: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
choices: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
It cracked open a fault that split the land apart
It let the sea rush inland and flood a deep valley
It uncovered a volcano that blasted out a gorge
context: As the ice sheets melted about 12,500 years ago, the newly filled Great Lakes had to drain toward the sea — and their overflow began pouring over the edge of a long cliff-like ridge called the Niagara Escarpment, near Queenston. That first plunge was the birth of the falls, which have been marching upstream ever since. Source: niagaraparks.com/visit-niagara-parks/plan-your-visit/niagara-falls-geology-facts-figures

question: In Viking-age Scandinavia, someone who wanted to record a name or a boast owned no paper, no pen, and no ink -- none of it had reached the frozen North. Their whole alphabet was built from short, straight lines. So how did a Viking actually make these letters?
answer: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
choices: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
Pressed them into wet clay with a reed
Brushed them onto bark with berry dye
Wove them into cloth with coloured thread
context: Runes are an alphabet made to be knifed into wood and stone -- no paper or ink required. Being cut by hand is why they are all short, sharp strokes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: Our word 'alphabet' is stitched from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta. The Norse of Scandinavia named their own row of runes with the very same trick -- by running its first six letters together into one word. What did the Vikings call their set of runes?
context: The runic alphabet is the FUTHARK, named f-u-th-a-r-k after its first six runes -- the same naming trick behind 'alphabet' (alpha + beta). The 'aett' was a group of eight runes within it; ogham and Cyrillic are entirely separate scripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: At Jelling in Denmark stands a great royal runestone, raised around 965 CE by King Harald Bluetooth. Its runes spell out a boast: that Harald had 'won for himself all Denmark and Norway' -- and then done one more thing that changed his people forever. What else does the stone boast that Harald did?
context: The inscription calls him 'the Harald who won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.' Because it records the kingdom's conversion, the stone is nicknamed 'Denmark's baptismal certificate' -- though remember it is a king's own boast in stone, not neutral history. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/  (Legend.)

question: One face of the great Jelling stone in Denmark shows Christ with his arms flung wide -- but he isn't nailed to a wooden cross. Instead his body is wrapped and tangled in ribbon-like branches, as though held fast in a living tree. This carving, made around 965 CE, holds a famous record. What record is it?
answer: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
choices: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
The oldest human figure carved in the North
The only image of Christ on any runestone
The first Christian carving in Scandinavia
context: It is the oldest known image of Christ found in Scandinavia. Scholars think the carver posed Christ 'hanging in a tree' on purpose, to echo Odin, who in Norse myth hung nine nights on the world-tree Yggdrasil -- the old gods giving way to the new faith, frozen in stone. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/

question: Visitors to Jelling in Denmark today see the great runestone as bare grey granite -- rough, weathered, and plain. But when researchers studied microscopic traces caught deep in the carved grooves, they realised the stone looked utterly different the day King Harald first raised it. How did the Jelling stone originally look?
context: The bare grey stone was once painted in vivid colour. Denmark's National Museum used surviving specks of pigment to reconstruct the original hues -- a reminder that Viking monuments, like ancient Greek temples, once blazed with colour rather than standing plain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelling_stones

question: Every phone, headset, and speaker that pairs wirelessly carries a small blue 'Bluetooth' symbol. Engineers picked that name in 1997 after King Harald Bluetooth of Denmark, who had once united quarrelling Danish tribes -- just as the technology unites gadgets. And the story goes that the little symbol hides a secret about the king himself. What is the Bluetooth logo said to be?
answer: His two initials, joined into one rune
choices: His two initials, joined into one rune
A tiny map of his united kingdom
The shape of his blackened tooth
context: The Bluetooth NAME really was inspired by Harald Bluetooth -- proposed by Intel's Jim Kardach in 1997 because Harald united Denmark as the tech unites devices. The logo being his bind-rune (the runes Hagall/H and Bjarkan/B merged) is the popular, widely-repeated story rather than a documented fact. His own nickname likely came from a dark, dead tooth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth  (Legend.)

question: Denmark's Jelling stones are famous, but the most remarkable runestone of all stands in Sweden. Around 800 CE a father named Varinn raised the tall grey Rok stone in memory of his dead son Vamod. Among the many thousands of runestones known across Scandinavia, the Rok stone holds one celebrated record. What record does it hold?
answer: The longest runic inscription ever found
choices: The longest runic inscription ever found
The tallest runestone in all Sweden
context: The Rok stone carries about 760 runes -- the longest known runic inscription -- carved across all five faces of the slab. It is also a puzzle-box of cipher runes and riddles, and it even name-drops the Gothic king Theodoric the Great on his horse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B6k_runestone

question: Runes from Viking Scandinavia look sharp and angular -- built from diagonal and upright strokes, but almost never a flat horizontal line running across a letter. This was no style choice at all; it came straight from the physical way every rune was made. Why did rune-carvers avoid horizontal strokes?
answer: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
choices: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
It was the hardest stroke to cut cleanly
It took twice as long to carve
It needed a much longer knife to cut
context: Runes are angular on purpose. Cut by knife into wood, a horizontal stroke runs along the grain -- blurring the letter and threatening to split the plank -- so carvers used clean diagonal and upright cuts. Curves were dropped for the same reason: they are hard to slice cleanly. Runes also had no fixed direction, running left-to-right, right-to-left, or alternating line by line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: Wind and the spinning of the Earth bend the ocean's surface currents into five enormous, slow-turning whirlpools — two in the Pacific, two in the Atlantic, and one in the Indian Ocean — each wheeling across an entire ocean basin. What are these five ocean-spanning whirlpools called?
context: Each of the five subtropical gyres turns clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise to the south. Eddies are much smaller swirls, a maelstrom is one violent whirlpool, and vortices can be any size — only 'gyre' names an ocean-wide loop. Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gyre.html

question: Each of the five ocean gyres gathers drifting plastic into a patch of garbage in its calm center. One of these patches covers an area about twice the size of Texas, and it was the first one ever found — a yacht captain sailed into it by accident in 1997. Which ocean garbage patch is it?
context: It drifts in the calm heart of the North Pacific Gyre, halfway between California and Hawaii. Yacht captain Charles Moore sailed into it by accident in 1997, and oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer coined the name 'garbage patch.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch

question: One ocean whirlpool is the biggest on the planet — ringed by four mighty currents, about 20 million square kilometers of turning sea, so vast that a single drop of water needs roughly four and a half years to ride all the way around it once. Which of the ocean's five gyres is this giant?
context: The North Pacific Gyre spans roughly 20 million square kilometers, walled by the North Equatorial, Kuroshio, North Pacific, and California currents. A drop of water takes about 54 months to finish one loop. Source: grokipedia.com/page/North_Pacific_Gyre

question: Despite sprawling across a vast stretch of open ocean, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch has never been photographed from space — no satellite can see it at all. Why is something that enormous invisible from orbit?
answer: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
choices: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
It sinks far too deep below the ocean surface for any camera to spot
It stays hidden beneath a permanent, thick bank of ocean storm clouds
It drifts far too fast for any orbiting satellite to lock onto it
context: About 94% of the patch's estimated 1.8 trillion pieces are microplastics smaller than a fingernail — so diffuse the 'patch' is more a peppery soup than an island you could ever walk on. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: When the Ocean Cleanup team hauled up and weighed the plastic drifting in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, one type of debris outweighed every other kind — nearly half (about 46%) of the total mass. Which kind of debris makes up almost half the patch's weight?
context: The 2018 Ocean Cleanup study put the patch's plastic near 79,000 tonnes, and roughly 46% of that mass was discarded or lost fishing gear — 'ghost' nets that keep snaring sea life for years. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: The Sargasso Sea drifts in the middle of the North Atlantic, and in one striking way it is unlike every other named sea on Earth. What is it that makes the Sargasso Sea one of a kind?
answer: It is the only sea with no land coastline at all
choices: It is the only sea with no land coastline at all
It is the only sea that never freezes over in winter
It is the only sea lying entirely below global sea level
It is the only sea where no fish are able to live
context: The Sargasso has no land borders whatsoever — it is walled instead by four ocean currents: the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic, the Canary, and the North Equatorial. It is the only sea on Earth defined by moving water alone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: In 1492, Christopher Columbus's ships pushed west into the Sargasso Sea and found the water matted with mile after mile of thick golden weed. His sailors grew frightened — not of storms or monsters, but of the seaweed itself. What did Columbus's crew fear the Sargassum would do?
answer: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
choices: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
clog the hulls until the timbers rotted away
hide sea serpents coiled within the weed
grow thick enough to walk across to land
context: Columbus's 1492 crossing left the first written account of the Sargasso Sea. His crew's dread of being caught fast in the weed seeded centuries of legends about ships trapped forever in the Sargassum — though the weed never actually stops a vessel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: The Sargasso Sea is named for its golden Sargassum weed. Biologists give this seaweed a rare label — 'holopelagic' — for the remarkable way it lives out its entire life. What is true of Sargassum weed across its whole life cycle?
answer: It drifts on the open sea and even breeds there, never touching bottom
choices: It drifts on the open sea and even breeds there, never touching bottom
It dies back each winter, then regrows from spores when spring returns
It anchors to a reef to release its spores, then tears loose and floats off
It sinks to the seabed each night and rises to the surface each day
context: 'Holopelagic' means Sargassum completes its whole life — growing, drifting, and breeding — without ever attaching to the bottom. The Sargasso's water is so clear that divers can see down as far as 60 meters. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: Around 30° north, the belt of ocean surrounding the Sargasso Sea can go so windless that old sailing ships sat becalmed for weeks, their sails hanging dead, unable to move. Spanish crews gave this dead-calm zone a grim nickname: the 'horse latitudes.' Where did that strange name come from?
answer: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
choices: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
The glassy calm water mirrored the shape of a horse's head
Wild horses once swam across these waters between continents
The first ship to chart the zone was named the Sea Horse
context: Becalmed for weeks with drinking water running low, crews reportedly threw dead and dying horses overboard to save what water remained — the grim story behind the name 'horse latitudes.' Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/horse-latitudes.html  (Legend.)

question: Here is one of the ocean's oldest mysteries, unsolved from Aristotle's day until 1920: every freshwater eel in Europe and North America is born in one single patch of open ocean, then drifts and swims thousands of miles to far-apart rivers, returning only once — to breed where it began. In which sea are all of these eels born?
context: Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt cracked it in 1920 by chasing ever-smaller eel larvae across the Atlantic until the tiniest led him to the Sargasso Sea — a nursery with no shore where every Atlantic eel begins life. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1501694  (Legend.)

question: In the walled old city of Sanaa, high in the mountains of Yemen, more than 6,000 slender houses stand packed shoulder to shoulder, many of them five to nine stories tall and older than a thousand years. What are these ancient towers mostly built from?
context: Sanaa's tower houses are built of packed (rammed) earth and burnt mud brick, with only the lowest floor in stone -- yet they climb five to nine stories and have stood for centuries, earning old Sanaa its nickname as a city of ancient skyscrapers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a; UNESCO WHS 'Old City of Sana'a' (whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/).

question: Sanaa is so old that people have lived there without a break for more than 2,500 years -- and an old Islamic tradition pushes its origin back even further, to the family of Noah after the Great Flood. Legend says the city was first laid out at the foot of Mount Nuqum by whom?
context: In Islamic and biblical tradition, Shem (Sam) is a son of Noah, and Yemeni legend credits him with founding Sanaa below Jabal Nuqum, the mountain that overlooks the old city. Historians cannot confirm any founder, but the unbroken 2,500-year habitation is well established. This is legend, not verified history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: Climb to the top rooms of a Sanaa tower house and the afternoon sun pours in through semicircular fans of red, blue, and green glass set into lacy carved gypsum above each window, washing the whitewashed walls in colored light. What are these signature stained-glass fanlights of Sanaa called?
context: These are QAMARIYA windows -- the name comes from qamar, Arabic for 'moon,' for their crescent-fan shape. Panes of colored glass are set into fretted gypsum plaster. By contrast, a mashrabiya is a projecting latticed wooden window-screen, not a stained-glass fanlight. Qamariya windows are a hallmark of old Sanaa's tower houses. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: From a distance, Sanaa's brown mud towers look iced like gingerbread -- every floor outlined and swirled with bright white patterns. But the builders didn't paint those white gypsum friezes only to look beautiful. On a house made of mud brick, what practical job does the white gypsum coating do?
answer: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
choices: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
it reflects the sun to keep the rooms cool
it seals cracks against burrowing insects
it lets the family mark out their own house
context: Old Sanaa gets real rain, and unprotected mud brick would erode. The white gypsum (juss) friezes and copings act like a waterproof skin, channeling rainwater off the vulnerable earthen walls -- so Sanaa's famous 'gingerbread' decoration is also its raincoat. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/.

question: For more than a thousand years, anyone entering the old walled city of Sanaa has passed beneath a single towering fortified gateway in its high clay ramparts -- a landmark still thronged with traders and travelers today. What is this great gate called?
context: This is BAB AL-YEMEN, the 'Gate of the Yemen' -- the grand gate of old Sanaa, over a thousand years old and still the main way in through the city's high walls of packed clay. The other choices are famous gates of other Islamic cities: Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuweila in Cairo, Bab Boujeloud in Fez. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_al_Yemen; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: In 1972, workers repairing the attic of the Great Mosque of Sanaa -- among the oldest mosques on earth -- pulled a cache of ancient parchments from sacks hidden in the roof. Under ultraviolet light, one page revealed a faint second layer of writing beneath the visible text: long ago, someone had scraped the page clean and written over it. What did scholars find in that hidden, erased under-layer?
answer: an even older copy of the Quran
choices: an even older copy of the Quran
a merchant's tally of spice prices
a map of the caravan roads to Mecca
a Christian gospel in old Syriac
context: This is the SANAA PALIMPSEST (part of the 'Sanaa manuscript'). A palimpsest is a page whose original writing was scraped off and overwritten; here, ultraviolet imaging recovered a lower Quranic text older than the upper one. Radiocarbon dating placed the parchment at roughly 578-669 CE, ranking it among the very oldest Qur'anic manuscripts known -- a rare window into how the earliest copies were written. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a_manuscript.

question: The grandest building at Palenque, a Maya city on a jungle escarpment in Chiapas, Mexico, is a steep stepped pyramid crowned by a small summit temple, and it hides a rubble-choked stairway plunging deep into its heart. By what name is this famous pyramid-temple known today?
choices: the Temple of the Foliated Cross
context: The pyramid takes its name from three stone tablets in its summit temple carved with 617 Maya glyphs, one of the longest hieroglyphic texts in the ancient Americas, recording the life of the king buried within. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spotted the trapdoor-like floor slab that hid the stairway. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed that a floor slab in the summit temple of Palenque's great pyramid was pierced by a double row of stone-plugged holes, as if made to be lifted. Raising it opened a rubble-filled stairway; his crew dug downward for four seasons, and in June 1952, some 25 metres inside the pyramid, they broke through a sealed wall. What lay in the chamber beyond?
context: It was the first tomb ever found inside a Maya pyramid, overturning the old belief that these pyramids were only solid platforms for temples. In the anteroom lay the skeletons of six young attendants, apparently sacrificed to accompany their king. The king within was K'inich Janaab' Pakal. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Inside the tomb of the Maya king Pakal at Palenque, the royal skeleton lay wearing a mask built from some 200 small fitted pieces of a single precious stone, its eyes made of shell and gleaming obsidian. The Maya prized this green stone above gold itself. Of what stone was Pakal's death mask made?
context: Jade, carved and polished and set in mosaics, was the most treasured material of the Maya world, a symbol of breath, water, and life. Pakal's mosaic mask, about 200 pieces of jadeite with eyes of shell and obsidian, now rests in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: The coffin of the Maya king Pakal, deep inside Palenque's great pyramid, is sealed by a single carved limestone slab weighing about five tonnes, one of the masterworks of ancient American art. Its relief shows the king tipping backward at the instant of death. In his 1968 bestseller Chariots of the Gods?, Erich von Daniken insisted the carving showed Pakal at the controls of a rocket, blasting off like an astronaut. Maya scholars flatly reject this: the sacred image Pakal falls along stands at the very center of the Maya universe. What is Pakal actually shown falling along?
context: That sacred image is the Maya World Tree, a great cross-shaped ceiba whose roots reach the underworld and whose branches hold up the sky; von Daniken mistook its branching, cruciform form for a rocket. Pakal is carved at the instant of death, falling down the trunk into the underworld, as the scholar Linda Schele put it, 'down the Milky Way.' The ancient-astronaut reading ignores the Maya writing and symbols carved all around the figure, which name the scene plainly. Source: Wikipedia, K'inich Janaab' Pakal.  (Legend.)

question: When Alberto Ruz cleared the hidden stairway inside Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions, he found a hollow, serpent-shaped stone tube built along the steps, running from Pakal's sealed tomb far below all the way up to the temple floor 25 metres above. Archaeologists puzzled over why the Maya would run this narrow duct out of a sealed tomb. What did they build it to carry?
context: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier named this hollow stone tube the 'psychoduct.' Shaped like a serpent, it runs from Pakal's sarcophagus up the hidden stairway to the temple floor above, and the Maya are thought to have built it as a road for the dead king's soul to pass between his tomb and the living world. It is one of the eeriest features of any Maya pyramid. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Rising from the middle of Palenque's rambling royal palace is a structure found at no other Maya city in the world. From its upper rooms, whose walls carry carved glyphs of the planet Venus, Maya priests seem to have watched the jungle horizon and tracked the movements of the sky. What is this famous Palenque structure?
context: Palenque's four-storey palace tower is unique in the Maya world, its inner walls carved with glyphs of Venus, whose cycles the Maya followed closely. One striking claim: at sunset on the winter solstice, seen from the tower, the sun appears to drop straight into the Temple of the Inscriptions, the pyramid holding Pakal's tomb. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Beneath the plaza of Palenque, the Maya vaulted the Otulum stream inside a stone channel running nearly 300 metres. In one stretch, known as the Piedras Bolas aqueduct, they engineered a first for the entire ancient Americas, a feat of water control no other New World people is known to have managed. What did Palenque's builders achieve here?
context: By vaulting the stream and then sharply narrowing part of the channel, Palenque's engineers forced the water under pressure, able to spurt upward, perhaps to feed a fountain or basin. Penn State researchers call the Piedras Bolas aqueduct the earliest known pressurized water feature in the New World, centuries before the Spanish arrived. Source: Penn State News, 'Maya plumbing'; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Cross the empty Syrian desert and you suddenly reach Palmyra: a whole classical city of pale stone still standing in the sand, threaded down its heart by one grand avenue running more than a kilometre. What is Palmyra's famous main avenue called?
context: The Great Colonnade is Palmyra's spine -- a ceremonial street about 1.1 km long lined with columns roughly 9.5 m high, mostly raised in the 2nd century AD, and you can still walk between the standing pillars today. Palmyra's beauty earned it the nickname the 'Bride of the Desert.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Palmyra should not exist. It sits deep in the empty Syrian desert, far from any river -- yet a thriving city grew there, ringed by twenty kinds of date palm. The reason was one natural source of fresh water, the only reliable water for days in any direction. What is this famous desert water source called?
context: The Efqa spring was Palmyra's whole reason for being -- an oasis in a sea of sand, the one dependable water on the desert crossing, so every caravan crossing the wilderness HAD to stop there. That is exactly why a great city could rise in such an unlikely spot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Palmyra grew into one of the richest cities of the Roman East, though it sat in the middle of nowhere. Its position was everything: every caravan hauling silk and spices between the Mediterranean and Persia was funnelled through this one desert city. How did Palmyra turn that steady stream of caravans into a fortune?
answer: charged a toll on their goods
choices: charged a toll on their goods
context: Palmyra worked like a desert toll-booth on the Silk Road. It even carved its customs law onto a great stone slab -- the Palmyrene Tariff -- spelling out the tax on every kind of good passing through, and those profits paid for the city's grand monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Outside Palmyra, in a bleak desert gully now called the Valley of the Tombs, more than fifty grand monuments to the dead still stand -- some built to hold whole dynasties of a single family across a century or more. Palmyra's grandest tombs took a form rarely seen anywhere else in the ancient world. What shape did these distinctive family tombs take?
context: Palmyra's tower tombs rose as high as four storeys -- stone apartment blocks for the dead, with family members sealed in shelf-niches floor above floor. The most recent one dates to about AD 128. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Queen Zenobia, the rebel ruler of the desert caravan city of Palmyra, broke away from Rome and forged a short-lived desert empire. Around AD 272 the emperor Aurelian besieged Palmyra, crushed the revolt, and took Zenobia prisoner. By many accounts, what fate did Aurelian's captive queen then meet?
answer: paraded through Rome in golden chains
choices: paraded through Rome in golden chains
beheaded on the spot in the desert
ransomed back to the Persian court
died of fever on the road to Rome
context: By many accounts Aurelian spared his royal captive. After leading Zenobia through Rome in golden chains in his triumph of AD 274, he is said to have let her live out her days in a comfortable villa at Tibur (modern Tivoli). The ancient sources disagree about her end, so Zenobia's final fate is really legend as much as settled history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenobia

question: In 2015 the militants of ISIS deliberately dynamited Palmyra's greatest ancient monuments, among them the Temple of Bel and the Arch of Triumph, in a campaign of cultural destruction. Yet archaeologists are confident these ruins can be faithfully rebuilt, stone by stone. What made that possible?
choices: carved fragments buried in the sand
context: Detailed 3-D scans and photographs had been made before the war, so the 'New Palmyra' project (2015) -- built on work by the Syrian coder Bassel Khartabil -- created digital models to guide the rebuilding, and reconstruction of the Arch of Triumph began in October 2022. The scans mattered all the more because of what ISIS had done in August 2015: days before it began dynamiting the city's ancient temples, it publicly beheaded Palmyra's 83-year-old antiquities chief, Khaled al-Asaad, who had guarded the ruins for about half a century, for refusing to reveal where the city's treasures were hidden. He had said, 'I am from Palmyra, and I will stay here even if they kill me.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaled_al-Asaad

question: In southwestern Turkey a whole hillside gleams brilliant white, as if a waterfall of snow had frozen mid-tumble into hundreds of shallow terraced pools. Locals named the place 'Pamukkale.' What do those two Turkish words mean?
context: The soft, piled-up look of the white rock reminded people of mounds of cotton: pamuk means 'cotton' and kale means 'castle.' Pamukkale sits in Denizli Province in southwestern Turkey, in the valley of the Menderes -- the river the ancient Greeks called the Meander. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: Up close, Pamukkale's blinding-white cliff isn't snow and isn't salt -- it is solid rock, built up in smooth ledges as scalding, mineral-rich spring water spills down the slope and hardens in the sun. Geologists have a special name for this pale, hot-spring stone. What is it?
context: As the hot spring water cools at the surface, the dissolved lime (calcium carbonate) it carries hardens out and lays down another paper-thin layer -- the very same mineral recipe that grows a cave stalactite, except here it builds terraces in open sunlight instead of dripstone in the dark. Tufa is the softer cousin left by cool water; Pamukkale's dense, banded, hot-spring stone is travertine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: Pamukkale's white cliff is not a dead, finished fossil. As long as its hot springs keep bubbling up and spilling over the ledges, something is still happening to the stone itself, year after year. What is happening to the stone?
choices: the old stone is dissolving away
the terraces are turning to marble
the whole cliff is sliding downhill
context: The terraces are alive: as long as the seventeen hot springs flow, fresh travertine is laid down and the whole white formation -- already about 2,700 m long and 160 m high -- keeps growing. When pools grey with algae and grime, keepers rotate and re-flood clean water across them to keep the white bright; a hotel-driven greying in the late 20th century was reversed by closing the terraces to bathers and traffic. Source: https://www.naturalworldheritagesites.org/sites/hierapolis-pamukkale/

question: Pamukkale's shimmering terraces would be a marvel on their own -- but climb to the very top of the white cliff and you find something astonishing perched up there, its marble ruins still crowning the white stone today. What was built on the summit?
context: The city is Hierapolis, the 'holy city' -- a Greco-Roman spa resort with a theatre seating around 15,000, colonnaded streets, temples, and one of the ancient world's largest necropolises (a sprawling city of tombs) for pilgrims who came to 'take the waters.' In 1988 UNESCO listed Hierapolis-Pamukkale as a single World Heritage Site, honoured for BOTH its natural white terraces and its ancient ruins. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/485

question: At Hierapolis, one thermal pool nicknamed for Cleopatra stays a swimmable 36 degrees C year-round and draws swimmers from across the world for a startling reason found almost nowhere else on Earth. What can bathers do here?
answer: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
choices: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
drink the spring said to cure blindness
walk a glass floor above the ruins
float over a mosaic of the sea-god
context: The bath is nicknamed Cleopatra's Pool (the Antique Pool); legend even says Cleopatra herself once swam here -- a charming story, not history. Long ago an earthquake toppled the pool's marble portico straight into the thermal spring, and its fluted columns and carved blocks still rest across the bottom -- so bathers float in the roughly 36 degrees C mineral water directly above the fallen ancient stone. Source: https://visitingturkey.com/destinations/pamukkale/cleopatra-pool

question: At Hierapolis the priests would lead bulls and birds up to the mouth of one particular cave -- and within moments the animals would collapse dead, while the priests standing right beside them walked away unharmed. Having no science to explain it, the Greeks and Romans gave the killing cave a dreadful name and built a shrine over it. By what name did they know it?
context: They called it the Ploutonion -- 'Pluto's Gate' -- a doorway to the underworld of Pluto, god of the dead. The geographer Strabo wrote of it: 'I threw in sparrows and they immediately breathed their last and fell.' Long dismissed as a myth, the walled-up cave was rediscovered in 2013 by archaeologist Francesco D'Andria, together with an inscription to Pluto and Kore and a statue tied to Hades and the three-headed dog Cerberus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ploutonion_at_Hierapolis  (Legend.)

question: For centuries the eunuch Galli priests at Hierapolis seemed to carry divine protection: they could stride right up to the deadly Pluto's Gate -- where any animal dropped dead -- and stroll back out alive, every single time. Yet there was nothing miraculous about it at all. What was the simple, natural reason the priests survived?
answer: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
choices: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
the priests had slowly grown immune to it
the priests quietly held their breath inside
the gas only turned deadly after nightfall
context: The carbon dioxide seeping from the cave is heavier than air, so it collects in an invisible 'lake' along the ground -- lethal to a low animal (or one held down into it) but harmless to a tall priest whose head stayed up in the breathable air above. It looked like a miracle; it was simple physics. A 2018 study led by biologist Hardy Pfanz measured CO2 up to 91% deep in the grotto, with the gas layer about 40 cm deep and deadliest at dawn after building up overnight -- and researchers still found freshly killed birds, mice, and dozens of beetles at the site. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/roman-gate-hell-killed-its-victims-cloud-deadly-carbon-dioxide

question: Down the middle of the Atlantic runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a seam where fresh seafloor wells up and shoves Europe and North America apart by about 2.5 centimeters every year. That yearly creep almost exactly matches the growth rate of one part of your own body. Which?
context: Two and a half centimeters a year sounds like nothing, but over millions of years it pried open an entire ocean -- and it is still going, so the Atlantic is a little wider today than when you were born. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge (corroborated by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, https://www.whoi.edu/oceanus/feature/mid-atlantic-ridge-volcanic-processes/).

question: We do not have to reconstruct the drift only from ancient rocks. Since the space age, one modern technology has clocked North America and Europe pulling apart in real time -- measuring the widening gap to the millimeter, year after year. Which technology?
context: GPS was built to tell you where your car is, but it is precise enough to watch continents move -- fixed ground stations on either side of the Atlantic creep apart on the readouts by roughly 2.5 cm a year. It turned Wegener's century-old idea into something we now measure directly. Source: https://earthhow.com/continental-drift-plate-tectonics/.

question: Spread a world map flat and, across one ocean, two facing coasts look like torn halves of a single shape -- the outward bulge of one sliding neatly into the inward curve of the other. The mapmaker Abraham Ortelius remarked on the match back in 1596, long before anyone could explain it. Which two coastlines fit together like puzzle pieces?
answer: West Africa and eastern South America
choices: West Africa and eastern South America
eastern North America and northwest Europe
context: The resemblance is striking enough that people noticed it for centuries -- Abraham Ortelius pointed it out in 1596 -- yet it took until the 1900s and Alfred Wegener to argue the coasts really had been torn apart, not just coincidentally shaped alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift.

question: The Appalachian Mountains run up the eastern side of North America, worn down to green ridges. Their rock belt does not simply stop at the coast -- it was once continuous with a mountain chain now stranded on the far shore of the Atlantic, torn away when the ocean opened between them. Which range across the water is the Appalachians' severed other half?
context: Wegener pointed to matching mountain belts like this as evidence the continents had once been joined: the Appalachians of North America line up with the Scottish Highlands, and South Africa's Karroo rock beds match Brazil's Santa Catarina beds across the ocean. Tellingly, the man pressing these clues was no geologist -- Alfred Wegener was a meteorologist and polar explorer, an outsider whose profession his critics held against him. Sources: https://www.discovermagazine.com/planet-earth/continental-drift-a-revolutionary-theory-that-was-once-considered ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener.

question: Matching coastlines could be coincidence -- so the real jolt came when geologists dug the SAME fossil animal, a small reptile called Mesosaurus, out of rocks on both shores of the South Atlantic: in Brazil and in South Africa. This freshwater creature could never have swum across a salt ocean. Which explanation did the fossil evidence ultimately support?
answer: the two coasts were once a single joined land
choices: the two coasts were once a single joined land
an ancient land bridge later sank beneath the sea
the same species arose on each coast separately
river floods rafted the fossils across the ocean
context: Wegener stacked up more of these twin-continent clues: the Glossopteris fern turns up across South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica -- one flora scattered over five now-separate lands. The tidiest explanation was that the lands had once been joined. Yet geologists still resisted for decades, because Wegener could not name a force strong enough to move a continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift (Glossopteris: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener).

question: In 1970 the drilling ship Glomar Challenger hauled up long cores of rock from deep beneath the floor of the Mediterranean Sea. Scientists Kenneth Hsu and William Ryan studied the layers, which recorded conditions about 5.5 million years ago, and reached a startling conclusion about the entire Mediterranean. What had once happened to it?
answer: it had dried up into vast salt flats
choices: it had dried up into vast salt flats
it had frozen over into a thick ice shelf
it had drained away through the seafloor
it had boiled off in a volcanic upheaval
context: Cut off from the Atlantic when the Strait of Gibraltar sealed, the Mediterranean -- itself the shrinking remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean -- evaporated almost completely, dropping kilometers below sea level and leaving buried salt over 2 km thick. Around 5.33 million years ago the Atlantic burst back through Gibraltar and refilled it in the Zanclean flood, one of the largest floods Earth has ever seen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis.

question: The Atlantic was not the first ocean to sit in its place. Geologist J. Tuzo Wilson showed that oceans open wide and then slam shut again in the same belts of the globe, over and over. Right where the Atlantic now lies, an EARLIER ocean had already opened and closed hundreds of millions of years before it. What is that vanished predecessor ocean called?
context: This open-and-shut rhythm is called the Wilson cycle, after J. Tuzo Wilson, who described it in 1966. It runs on a slow conveyor of rock: fresh crust is shoved out at mid-ocean ridges while old, cold, heavy crust is dragged back down at deep trenches. Because of it the map never stops rearranging -- roughly 250 million years from now the Atlantic is expected to close and today's continents to crowd into a brand-new supercontinent. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_cycle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_Proxima.

question: Deep beneath the streets of Paris, mile after mile of tunnel is lined with human bones — skulls and thigh-bones stacked into neat walls and archways, the remains of an estimated six million people. By what name is this underground maze of bones known?
context: The bones were carted here in the 1780s from Paris's overflowing graveyards and later stacked into deliberate walls and archways; the famous count of about six million is only an estimate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Paris  (Legend.)

question: For centuries Paris buried its dead in crowded churchyards like the Cimetière des Innocents, until the ground itself rose into a mound higher than a man. In the spring of 1780, the overcrowding finally caused a disaster that forced the city to act. What happened?
answer: Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
choices: The flooding Seine washed loose bones into the streets.
A fire tore through the cemetery's wooden crosses.
Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
Grave-robbers tunnelled into the burial vaults.
context: In spring 1780 the pressure of the rotting dead burst a wall into a neighbouring cellar. The city closed the Cimetière des Innocents and, from 1785, moved the bones by torchlight into the empty tunnels beneath the city — so the Catacombs' dead were relocated there, not buried where they now lie. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: The tunnels that now hold Paris's bones were not dug as tombs at all. For centuries, workers had been hollowing out these galleries beneath the city for a completely different reason, leaving the ground honeycombed with passages. Why had the tunnels been dug in the first place?
answer: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
choices: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
To carry the city's sewage down to the river.
To move soldiers secretly during sieges.
To store and cool the city's wine.
context: Paris was largely built from limestone dug out from directly beneath itself, honeycombing the ground with tunnels. When the mines emptied, those same galleries later became the perfect place to store the dead. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: The Louvre, the Arc de Triomphe, and the very bone-walls of the Catacombs were all cut from a single pale, creamy building stone — laid down on a warm, shallow sea about 45 million years ago and quarried from directly beneath the city. Geologists gave this famous 'Paris stone' its own name. What is it called?
context: It is Lutetian limestone, named after Lutetia — the Roman name for Paris — and about 48–40 million years old. The Louvre, Les Invalides, Place de la Concorde and the Arc de Triomphe are all built from it.
