context: The legend is rich with detail: the town of Velvary is said to have boiled its eggs so they wouldn't smash on the road, and one village reportedly sent a wagon of cheese by mistake. Is it true? A 2008 Czech chemistry-institute test of the old mortar found protein traces that fit the tale, but a 2010 Charles University study found no organic additive -- so the egg legend is one that lab evidence only partly backs. Source: https://prague-now.com/history/charles-bridge-built-with-a-curve-and-with-egg/

question: One of Prague's most famous legends tells of Master Hanus, the clockmaker said to have built the Old Town's Astronomical Clock. The story goes that the town councillors, terrified he might build an even finer clock for a rival city, made sure he never could. According to the legend, what did they do to Master Hanus? (Historians say it never really happened.)
choices: they threw him in the river
context: The blinding of Master Hanus is Prague's most beloved clock legend: the tale says the councillors blinded him so he could never repeat his masterpiece, and that the ruined clockmaker climbed the tower and thrust his hand into the gears to stop the clock forever. In truth the Orloj was built in 1410 by Mikulas of Kadan with the scholar Jan Sindel; Hanus was a real later clockmaker who came to no such harm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: In 1393, King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia had the priest John of Nepomuk bound and hurled from Charles Bridge into the Vltava -- legend says because John refused to reveal what the queen had told him in confession. He drowned and was later made a saint, and today his is the most-touched statue on the bridge. In art, one distinctive halo sets St John of Nepomuk apart from every other saint. What does his halo contain?
context: The five stars recall the legend that five lights appeared on the Vltava where John of Nepomuk drowned in 1393, on the order of King Wenceslaus IV. His 1683 bronze is the oldest statue on Charles Bridge, and touching the plaque beneath it is the tradition said to bring you back to Prague. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Nepomuk

question: St Vitus Cathedral, rising inside Prague Castle, guards a treasure even more jealously than the tombs of the Bohemian kings buried within it: the ancient Crown Jewels of Bohemia, the golden crown of St Wenceslas among them. They are sealed in a chamber whose door was built so that no single official -- not even a king acting alone -- could ever open it. What secures the door to the Crown Jewels' chamber?
answer: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
choices: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
two locks, one key held by the king and one by the archbishop
three locks, opened only when the three chief lords of Bohemia agree
five locks, their keys shared among the cathedral's canons
context: The Crown Jewels of Bohemia -- including the crown of St Wenceslas, made in 1347 -- rest in a chamber inside St Vitus Cathedral behind a door with seven separate locks. Seven keys are held by seven different people (among them the president, the prime minister, and the Archbishop of Prague), and all seven must gather in person before the door can be opened. The cathedral, begun in 1344 under Charles IV and not consecrated until 1929, also glows with an Art Nouveau stained-glass window designed by the Czech painter Alfons Mucha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vitus_Cathedral

question: Prague Castle has been the seat of Bohemian kings, Holy Roman emperors, and -- to this day -- the Czech president, its palaces, gardens, and the towers of St Vitus Cathedral crowning the hill above the Vltava. Guinness World Records singles Prague Castle out with one worldwide superlative. What record does it hold?
answer: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
choices: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
the oldest stone castle in the world
the tallest castle towers in the world
the most-visited castle in the world
context: Prague Castle sprawls over roughly 70,000 square metres -- about 570 metres long and 130 wide -- which earns it a place in Guinness World Records as the largest ancient castle complex in the world. Founded around 880, it is still the official residence of the Czech president. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Castle

question: On 23 May 1618, a crowd of furious Bohemian Protestants stormed into Prague Castle, seized two Catholic royal officials and their secretary, and threw all three out of a high window -- a drop of some 21 metres to the ground below. To everyone's amazement, not one of the three men died. Catholics cried that angels had caught them in mid-air; the Protestants scoffed that something far humbler had broken their fall. What did the Protestants say saved the three men?
context: The 1618 Defenestration of Prague hurled two imperial regents -- Jaroslav Borita of Martinice and Vilem Slavata of Chlum -- and their secretary Philip Fabricius from a Prague Castle window; all three survived the ~21 m fall by landing in the refuse heaped in the moat below. The quarrel helped ignite the Thirty Years' War, and the lucky secretary was later ennobled as 'Baron von Hohenfall' -- Baron of Highfall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestrations_of_Prague  (Legend.)

question: On the same Javanese plain, a few miles from the up-spiking Hindu towers of Prambanan, stands its great near-contemporary: not a spire at all but a vast, low, terraced Buddhist mandala crowned with rows of bell-shaped stupas, one of the largest Buddhist monuments on Earth. What is that neighboring monument called?
context: The two masterpieces are near-contemporaries on the same plain: Borobudur, the broad Buddhist mandala, and Prambanan, whose central Hindu tower stabs 47 metres (about 154 ft) straight up -- the tallest Hindu temple in Indonesia. Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple site in the country and the second-largest in all Southeast Asia, after Angkor Wat in Cambodia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: A Javanese legend explains why so many shrines cluster at Prambanan. The spirit-summoning prince Bandung Bondowoso could marry Princess Roro Jonggrang only if he raised a thousand temples in a single night. His ghost-workers had finished 999 when the unwilling princess tricked them into fleeing before dawn. Cheated of his final temple and his bride, the furious prince took his revenge. What did he do to her? (Legend.)
context: The tale of Roro Jonggrang ('slender virgin') is folklore, not history. In the legend, the prince Bandung Bondowoso -- having killed her father, King Boko -- was told he could marry the princess only by building a thousand temples in one night; with summoned spirits he raised 999, but Roro Jonggrang lit fires and had her maids pound rice in the east to counterfeit the dawn. The roosters crowed, the spirits fled, and the enraged prince cursed her into stone as the missing final statue. Tradition still points to the statue of Durga slaying the buffalo demon, in the Shiva temple's north chamber, and calls it Rara Jonggrang -- the very princess turned to stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rara_Jonggrang

question: Prambanan's three tallest towers stand in a row, and the central one -- a 47-metre spire, higher than the two beside it -- is dedicated to the Hindu god of destruction and rebirth, the cosmic dancer whose steps whirl the universe into being and out again. Which god does that great central tower belong to?
context: The three tall central temples honor the Hindu Trimurti: the 47-metre central tower belongs to Shiva the destroyer, flanked by shorter temples for Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, each about 33 metres tall. The whole compound was raised around 850 CE by the Hindu Mataram (Sanjaya) dynasty, begun by Rakai Pikatan and dedicated to Shiva -- its original Sanskrit name was Shivagrha, 'House of Shiva,' recorded in the Shivagrha inscription of 856 CE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Walk the inner balustrades of Prambanan's main temple and the carved stone unfolds, panel by panel, into one of Hinduism's greatest stories: a virtuous prince whose bride is snatched away by a ten-headed demon-king, and the long war to win her back -- fought with the help of a whole army of monkeys and their leaping, flying general. Which tale is carved into these walls?
context: Panel after panel along the inner balustrades follows the Ramayana: Princess Sita, carried off by the demon-king Ravana, and her rescue by Prince Rama with the help of Hanuman and his monkey army. The epic still comes alive at Prambanan today -- performed as an open-air ballet on full-moon nights beneath the towers. Prambanan was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Climb Quebec City's old-town ramparts and you can walk the wall-top for kilometres, passing through massive stone gates with the St. Lawrence River far below — about 4.6 km of fortification in all. Among every town Europeans raised in North America north of Mexico, which claim belongs to Quebec alone?
answer: the only town still ringed by walls
choices: the only town still ringed by walls
the oldest walled town on the continent
the first town Europeans fortified here
the biggest town the French ever built
context: Old Quebec is the only intact fortified colonial town in North America north of Mexico — about 4.6 km of ramparts you can walk atop, pierced by old gates. Most walled cities elsewhere pulled their walls down for traffic; Quebec's survived, and in 1985 UNESCO named the old town a World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City' / 'Old Quebec.'

question: The name 'Quebec' comes straight from an Algonquin word, 'kebec.' Long before any fort stood there, the word already described this exact place on the great St. Lawrence River, where the French would later build atop the cliff. What does 'kebec' mean?
choices: where the cliff meets the water
context: 'Kebec' is Algonquin for 'where the river narrows.' Just below the city the wide St. Lawrence squeezes tight against the cliffs — so whoever held the high rock commanded the water gateway to the whole interior of the continent. Champlain planted his 1608 settlement on exactly that chokepoint. Source: Wikipedia, 'Quebec'; Musee de la civilisation, Trousse Premiers Peuples.

question: When the French explorer Jacques Cartier scrambled up the great cliff above the St. Lawrence, he spotted stones glittering in the rock and was sure he'd struck it rich. He named the height Cap Diamant — 'Cape Diamond' — and the name stuck. But when the glittering 'diamonds' were examined, what did they turn out to be?
context: Cartier's 'diamonds' were only quartz — the blunder gave French the old phrase 'faux comme un diamant du Canada' ('false as a Canadian diamond'). But the name held: Cap Diamant, the cliff rising about 100 m straight out of the St. Lawrence, still crowns Quebec City, a natural fortress that decided where the town would stand. Source: Britannica, 'Cape Diamond'; Wikipedia, 'Cap Diamant.'

question: Crowning the cliff above Quebec City sits the Citadelle, a 'star fort' — instead of plain straight walls, its ramparts zigzag out into sharp angled points called bastions. This shape was not for looks. What did those jutting, angled points let the defenders do to anyone attacking a wall?
answer: catch them in crossfire from two sides
choices: catch them in crossfire from two sides
pour boiling oil straight down on them
keep the cannon hidden from their view
flood the ditch below with river water
context: The Citadelle is the largest British-built fortress in North America — four bastions and three straight curtain walls set at angles so every stretch of wall could be swept by fire from the bastions on either side, leaving attackers no blind approach. It is still an active army base, home of the Royal 22e Regiment (the 'Van Doos') since 1920, and a cannon still booms from it every day at noon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Citadelle of Quebec.'

question: One building rears over Quebec City's old town like a medieval castle — turrets, steep copper roofs, perched on the cliff edge above the river. Yet the Chateau Frontenac has always been a hotel, opened to its first guests in 1893. Who built this fairy-tale castle?
context: The Chateau Frontenac was raised by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which opened it in 1893 to lure travelers onto its trains — a 'castle' built to sell railway tickets. It holds a Guinness World Record as the most photographed hotel on Earth, and takes its name from Louis de Buade, Count of Frontenac, the governor who defended New France against British and Iroquois attacks in the 1690s. Source: Britannica, 'Chateau Frontenac'; WorldAtlas.

question: By the 1870s the British soldiers had marched out of Quebec City, and many townsfolk wanted the old stone walls and gates gone — they choked the traffic and seemed a useless relic. The ramparts were nearly torn down for good. Why can you still walk them today?
answer: the Governor General intervened to save them
choices: the Governor General intervened to save them
a sudden war made the walls needed again
the demolition crews hit bedrock and gave up
the walls proved too costly to tear down
context: The walls standing today are the masonry ramparts an engineer, Gaspard-Joseph Chaussegros de Lery, raised in 1745. When the British garrison left in the 1870s, Quebec nearly demolished them for road traffic — until Governor General Lord Dufferin intervened around 1871, even having grand gates rebuilt, so the fortifications would survive. That rescue is why Old Quebec is a walled city at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City.'

question: Rain-soaked winds off the Pacific drench the coast of southern Chile, but they hit the high wall of the Andes, and the land on the far, sheltered side lies in the mountains' 'rain shadow' -- bone-dry desert, arid even within 200 miles of the ocean. Which South American desert is this?
context: Argentine Patagonia is a COLD winter desert -- average temperatures near 3 C with frequent frost -- and the largest desert in Argentina (about 673,000 sq km, roughly the 8th-largest on Earth). The Andes block the westerly Pacific winds so completely that much of it stays arid within about 200 miles of the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagonian_Desert

question: Moist Pacific wind sweeps in off the ocean and is driven up the windward slope of Washington's Cascade Range -- which is exactly why the sagebrush country behind the mountains stays dry. As that ocean air is forced up the wind-facing 'windward' side, what happens to nearly all its water?
answer: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
choices: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
the warm air sinking down the far side dries it back out
the peaks block the clouds and scrape them off the wind
the thin summit air simply lets the water escape upward
context: This is the heart of every rain shadow: moist air forced up the windward slope expands and cools, its vapour condenses, and it falls as rain on that side -- so the air clears the crest already 'wrung dry,' leaving desert behind the mountains. Western Washington soaks under Pacific rain on the Cascades' windward flank, while the Columbia Basin just east lies in their dry shadow. The common misconception is that the far side is dry because the sinking air warms; the real cause is that the rain already fell on the way up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow

question: Snow can dust the sand dunes and hard winter frost grips a vast COLD desert that sprawls across Mongolia and northern China. It stays bone-dry because it lies high and far inland, walled off from the ocean's moisture by great mountain ranges to its south. Which desert is this?
context: The Gobi covers about 1.3 million sq km (the 6th-largest desert) across Mongolia and northern China. Sitting high and deep in the continent's interior, cut off from the sea, it is a COLD desert -- frost and even snow can settle on its dunes -- with only about 194 mm of rain a year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobi_Desert

question: In the American West, four mountain ranges rise one behind another, and each strips more moisture from the Pacific storms rolling east -- the first is California's Sierra Nevada. Beyond them all lies a scorched trough that is at once the DRIEST and the LOWEST place in North America, its Badwater Basin sunk 282 feet below sea level. Name this valley.
context: Four successive mountain ranges, beginning with the Sierra Nevada, strip Pacific storms of their moisture before they reach the valley floor. Badwater Basin lies 282 ft (86 m) below sea level, and Death Valley averages under 2 inches of rain a year -- it recorded ZERO rainfall in 1929, 1953 and 1989. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Death_Valley; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Valley

question: The summit of Mount Waialeale, on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, is drenched by trade-wind rain almost every single day -- about 11,000 mm a year, among the wettest spots on Earth. Yet barely 15 miles away, on the island's sheltered leeward side, one sun-baked town collects only about 20 inches of rain a year. Name this dry town in the rain shadow of one of Earth's rainiest peaks.
context: Mount Waialeale's summit sees rain on about 289 days a year and averages roughly 11,430 mm (450 in) -- a record 666 inches fell in 1982. Yet leeward Waimea, only about 15 miles away on the same island, averages just ~20 inches. The wettest and driest places on Kauai almost touch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Wai%CA%BBale%CA%BBale

question: Down the eastern, leeward slope of the Rocky Mountains, a warm dry 'foehn' wind sometimes comes roaring off the peaks and can shoot the temperature up 25 F (14 C) in a matter of hours -- bare ground can appear where deep snow lay that morning. Ranchers named this snow-devouring wind. What do they call it?
context: As the dry air sinks down the leeward side it is compressed and warms -- a 'foehn' wind, which can raise the temperature by as much as 14 C (25 F) in hours. East of the Rockies this warm downslope wind is the chinook; 'snow eater' is the folk nickname it earned for how fast it strips the snow, while the rapid warming itself is well-documented meteorology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_wind

question: On the Himalaya's southern, windward slopes the summer monsoon unloads staggering rain -- the Indian village of Mawsynram catches over 11,000 mm a year, among the rainiest places anywhere on Earth. But the mountains wring that air dry, so the great highland just north of the crest gets under 200 mm and is itself a bleak, cold desert. Name this rain-starved highland.
context: The Himalaya cast the most dramatic rain shadow on Earth. On the windward south side, Mawsynram and neighbouring Cherrapunji take well over 11,000 mm of monsoon rain a year, while just across the crest the Tibetan Plateau gets under 200 mm -- one of the greatest wet-to-dry contrasts found anywhere. Source: earthdate.org/episodes/rain-shadow

question: On July 10, 1913, a weather station on the floor of Death Valley recorded 134 F (57 C) -- a reading that stood for a century as the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth, though scientists now doubt it was accurate. What is the name of that blistering outpost, still the valley's main visitor hub today?
context: The 134 F (57 C) logged at Furnace Creek on 10 July 1913 held the world heat record for a century, but scientists now dispute its accuracy; the highest reliable modern reading is 130 F (54.4 C) in 2020. Furnace Creek sits on the valley floor behind four moisture-stripping mountain ranges. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Death_Valley  (Legend.)

question: New Zealand's Southern Alps stand broadside to the roaring westerly winds off the Tasman Sea. On the West Coast the rain pours down -- up to 15 metres a year near the mountain spine, feeding dense temperate rainforest. But cross barely 30 km to the eastern, sheltered side of the crest and the yearly rain collapses about fifteen-fold to a single metre, leaving the country's driest, brownest land. Name this dry eastern region.
context: The Southern Alps meet the prevailing westerlies head-on. The West Coast drinks up to ~15,000 mm of rain a year near the Main Divide (coastal towns ~3,000 mm), but only about 30 km east of the crest rainfall collapses to roughly 1,000 mm -- a near fifteen-fold drop -- making Central Otago the driest land in New Zealand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Alps

question: The hills around Jerusalem are green in winter and catch about 600 mm of Mediterranean rain. But the city sits on a ridge, and its eastern flank is the dry lee: walk just a few miles east and downhill and the rain falls to barely 100 mm, the green vanishes, and the bare, folded land plunges toward the Dead Sea -- a full desert only miles from the green Mediterranean coast. Name this desert at Jerusalem's edge.
context: The Judaean Desert lies in the rain shadow of the hills of Jerusalem, immediately east of the city. Rainfall drops from about 600 mm on the western, Mediterranean-facing side to roughly 100 mm in the east, where the land falls steeply to the Dead Sea -- a full desert only a few miles from the green coast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaean_Desert

question: In 1950s Kingston, Jamaica, a DJ would haul a truckload of towering speaker stacks into an open dirt yard and throw an all-night street dance — and by mid-decade the loudest of these pulled a bigger crowd than any live band in town. What did Jamaicans call this whole traveling music institution, its wall of speakers and the crew who ran it?
context: The Jamaican 'sound system' — a mobile DJ outfit of huge speaker stacks and a generator — was the engine of the island's whole music culture, and the men who ran the biggest ones became stars. The first great commercial system belonged to Chinese-Jamaican businessman Tom Wong ('Tom the Great Sebastian'); rivals like Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd battled for the loudest bass and the rarest records. Every genre that followed — ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub — was built to be played on these speakers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound system (Jamaican).'

question: Around Jamaica's 1962 independence, Kingston musicians grabbed the American rhythm-and-blues records their sound systems loved, sped them up, and threw the guitar's accent onto the OFF-beat — the springy up-stroke between the beats. Guitarist Ernest Ranglin caught the flip perfectly: American R&B goes 'chink-ka,' he said, but this new Kingston sound goes 'ka-chink.' What was this bouncy homegrown genre called?
context: Ska was Jamaica's first homegrown pop genre — jumpy and brass-driven, born of American R&B sped up and flipped onto the off-beat. Its greatest band, the Skatalites, cut hard instrumental hits like 'Guns of Navarone,' while independence-year anthems such as Derrick Morgan's 'Forward March' (1962) caught the mood of a nation just cutting free from Britain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ska.'

question: In the sweltering Kingston summer of 1966, the island's musicians dragged ska's frantic, jumpy tempo way down to a slow, cool sway — and at that lazy new pace the electric bass line finally stepped out front to lead the whole song. What did Jamaicans name this slowed-down sound that ruled Kingston's dance yards for the next two years?
context: Rocksteady took its name from Alton Ellis's 1966 hit 'Rock Steady,' and bandleader Lynn Taitt summed it up: 'Rocksteady is really slow ska.' It lasted barely two years, but by slowing everything down it handed the spotlight to the bass — the deep, rolling foundation that reggae would soon build its entire sound upon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rocksteady.'

question: One down-at-heel Kingston neighborhood, its houses patched together from scrap timber and rubble, turned out an astonishing roll call of musicians in the 1960s — Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, and Bunny Wailer of the Wailers among them — and from its cramped government housing yards the new sound of reggae went out to conquer the world. What is this legendary Kingston district called?
context: Trench Town, a poor Kingston neighborhood built of timber-and-rubble 'knog' housing, was the cradle of reggae — home also to Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, and Toots. Bob Marley immortalized it in 'No Woman No Cry' (1974), singing of sitting 'in the government yard in Trenchtown,' the real public-housing yard on First Street where he grew up. In 2018, UNESCO honored the reggae music of Jamaica as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, praising its voice on 'injustice, resistance, love and humanity.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Trench Town'; UNESCO (2018).

question: Producer Clement Dodd — 'Coxsone' to everyone in Kingston — ran a hit factory on Brentford Road so central to the island's music that it earned the nickname 'the Motown of Jamaica': it launched Bob Marley and the Wailers, Toots and the Maytals, Burning Spear, and the Skatalites across ska, rocksteady, and reggae. What was Coxsone Dodd's legendary Kingston music house called?
context: Studio One was the beating heart of Jamaican recording — its house band and back catalogue shaped ska, rocksteady, and reggae, and its old rhythms are still sampled around the world. Coxsone Dodd's chief rivals each had a legendary room of their own, among them Lee 'Scratch' Perry's backyard Black Ark studio, built in 1973. Source: Wikipedia, 'Studio One (record label).'

question: In his cramped Kingston studio, a radio-and-television repairman named Osbourne Ruddock — known across the island as King Tubby — took finished reggae records, wiped the singer's voice clean off them, and rebuilt the bare bass-and-drum track into a spacey, echo-soaked instrumental. Hailed as the master of this new studio craft — the distant ancestor of every modern remix — King Tubby is the man most credited with pioneering which Jamaican style?
context: Dub — Jamaica's gift to the age of the remix — reportedly began by accident in 1968, when engineer Byron Smith left the vocals off a pressing of the Paragons' 'On the Beach' and the dance crowd went wild for the bare instrumental. King Tubby made dub an art, 'playing' his 12-channel mixing desk like an instrument in his tiny Waterhouse studio, riding echo and faders live. He was shot dead outside his Kingston home in 1989. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dub music' and 'King Tubby.'  (Legend.)

question: By the late 1960s, Kingston singles carried an instrumental 'version' on the flip side, the vocals gone and only the riddim left. At the dance, sound-system DJs stopped just spinning discs, grabbed the microphone, and rode the beat with their voices — hyping the crowd and trading rhymes live over the bare track. Pioneers like Count Machuki and U-Roy made it an art many historians now call a direct ancestor of American rap. What was this Jamaican vocal style called?
context: Toasting — the Jamaican DJ chanting rhythmically over an instrumental 'version' — is widely seen as one ancestor of rap. Its pioneers, Count Machuki and U-Roy, grabbed the mic at sound-system dances and 'chatted' over the bare riddims, turning the DJ from a record-spinner into a star performer in his own right. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toasting (Jamaican music).'

question: In 1985, a Kingston teenager named Wayne Smith and keyboardist Noel Davey punched up the 'rock' preset on a cheap Casio home keyboard, producer King Jammy polished it into a hit, and out came the first fully computer-made Jamaican beat — the 'Sleng Teng' riddim. It launched a brand-new, all-electronic era of the island's music, and that one robotic bassline was reused on something like 500 different records. What is this electronic era of Jamaican music called?
context: Here is the twist: the 'Sleng Teng' bassline that reshaped Jamaican music wasn't written in Kingston at all. It was a factory preset built in 1980 by a young Casio engineer in Japan, Hiroko Okuda, who had studied reggae for her thesis. She only learned years later that her little demo tune had sparked a whole genre — and was amazed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sleng Teng.'

question: Reykjavik, Iceland's capital, sits at about 64 degrees north, up near the Arctic Circle on the island's southwest coast. Among the world's national capitals, what record does that far-northern spot earn it?
answer: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
choices: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
the coldest capital of any country on Earth
the world's only capital inside the Arctic Circle
the world's northernmost city of any kind
context: Reykjavik sits at 64 degrees 08' north. Nuuk, the capital of Greenland, actually lies a touch farther north at 64 degrees 10' N -- but Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, not a sovereign state, so Reykjavik keeps the title of northernmost capital of a fully independent country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Through Reykjavik's long northern winters almost every home stays warm, yet the city burns virtually no oil or coal and its winter air stays clean. What heats the city instead?
answer: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
choices: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
rooftop solar panels across the city
heat pumps drawing warmth from the sea
context: Naturally hot water is pumped from volcanic rock and run through a district-heating network that warms nearly all of Reykjavik's buildings; about 90% of Iceland's homes are heated this way. Because the city burns almost no fuel for heat, greenhouse-gas emissions from space heating in the Reykjavik area fell from around 270,000 tonnes a year in 1960 to roughly 12,000 tonnes today. Iceland's first geothermal district-heating system opened in 1930, warming a school, a hospital, a pool and about 60 homes. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power_in_Iceland ; https://web.mit.edu/nature/archive/student_projects/2009/bjorn627/TheGeothermalCity/Reykjavik.html

question: The first Norse settlers to sail into the bay of what is now Reykjavik saw pale plumes rising from the shore -- steam venting from natural hot springs -- and named the place after that sight. What does the name 'Reykjavik' mean?
context: In Old Norse, reykr means 'smoke' and vik means 'bay,' so Reykjavik is 'Smoky Bay.' The settlers took the steam drifting off the hot springs for smoke and named their new home for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Hallgrimskirkja, the great pale church that towers over Reykjavik, was shaped by architect Gudjon Samuelsson to echo one of Iceland's iconic volcanic rock formations. Which formation did he build it to resemble?
choices: jagged fields of black volcanic ash
context: Basalt is the dark volcanic rock that covers much of Iceland; when a thick lava flow cools slowly it cracks into tall, many-sided (often hexagonal) columns, like those seen behind the Svartifoss waterfall. Gudjon Samuelsson drew Hallgrimskirkja's stepped, upward-sweeping shape from those columns. Designed in 1937 and built from 1945 to 1986, the church stands 74.5 m (244 ft) tall -- the tallest in Iceland. Source: https://guidetoiceland.is/travel-iceland/drive/hallgrimskirkja

question: Reykjavik sits near the Arctic Circle, yet its winters rarely fall below minus 15 degrees C -- often milder than cities hundreds of miles to its south. What keeps this far-north capital so surprisingly warm?
answer: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
choices: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
heat rising from Iceland's volcanoes and lava fields
tall mountains that block the cold Arctic winds
warm winds blowing up from mainland Europe
context: The warm water of the North Atlantic (an arm of the Gulf Stream system) washes Iceland's coast and keeps Reykjavik's winters mild -- rarely below minus 15 degrees C, sometimes milder than places far to its south. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: In Reykjavik's high summer the sun never fully sets -- people mow their lawns and play football late at night in plain daylight, the sky still glowing at 1 a.m. Around December, though, the city gets only four or five dim hours of light a day. What is this bright, near-endless summer daylight called?
context: Because Reykjavik lies so far north, from about May 20 to July 24 the sun never sinks more than 5 degrees below the horizon, so summer nights never go fully dark -- the 'midnight sun.' The flip side comes near midwinter (about Dec 2 to Jan 10), when the city gets fewer than five hours of daylight and the sun climbs only about 3 degrees above the horizon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Rio de Janeiro means 'River of January.' A Portuguese fleet reached this vast bay on 1 January 1502 and named the place for that day -- yet a traveler hunting Rio's shoreline for the river will search in vain. By the traditional story, why is there no river?
answer: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
choices: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
Mapmakers copied a mislabelled older chart
Settlers named it for a river back in Portugal
context: By the traditional account, a Portuguese fleet -- usually credited to Gaspar de Lemos and Goncalo Coelho -- sailed into the huge bay on 1 January 1502 and took its narrow, cliff-flanked entrance for the mouth of a great river, naming the spot 'River of January' for the month. There is no river: Rio in fact curls around a bay, Guanabara Bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro  (Legend.)

question: Arms flung open 28 metres wide, a 30-metre figure of pale soapstone has watched over Rio since 1931 from the 700-metre granite peak of Corcovado. In the worldwide 07/07/2007 vote it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Which monument is this?
context: Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) is 30 m tall with arms 28 m wide on an 8 m pedestal, built of reinforced concrete faced in pale soapstone atop the 700 m peak of Corcovado, and inaugurated on 12 October 1931 after nine years' work. On 7 July 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: Long ago, Portuguese traders boiled refined sugar down and sold it as a hard block molded into one distinctive shape. Rio's Pao de Acucar, the bare granite monolith standing at the mouth of Guanabara Bay, was nicknamed 'Sugarloaf' because it looked just like that block. What shape was the block of molded sugar?
context: Refined sugar in that era was boiled down and molded into a tall cone -- a 'sugarloaf' -- for storage and shipping. Portuguese traders thought the bare 396 m granite dome at the bay's mouth looked just like one, so they named it Pao de Acucar; in English, Sugarloaf Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Mountain

question: Christ the Redeemer stands atop a granite peak the Portuguese named Corcovado, reached since 1884 by a little cog railway that climbs 3.8 km through the Tijuca Forest. The name 'Corcovado' is a blunt, almost comical description of the mountain's shape. What does 'Corcovado' mean in Portuguese?
context: 'Corcovado' is Portuguese for 'hunchback,' after the peak's bent, humped profile. Since 1884 the Corcovado Rack Railway, a cog train, has climbed 3.8 km up through the Tijuca Forest to the summit that Christ the Redeemer now crowns. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corcovado; britannica.com/place/Mount-Corcovado

question: Since 1912 a small cable car nicknamed the Bondinho has carried passengers up Rio's Sugarloaf in two stages, pausing at Morro da Urca before rising to the 396-metre summit. Engineer Augusto Ferreira Ramos built it so early that it counts as only the ___ passenger cableway ever raised anywhere on Earth.
context: The Sugarloaf cable car -- the Bondinho -- opened in 1912, reportedly only the third cableway ever built anywhere in the world. Dreamed up by engineer Augusto Ferreira Ramos, it climbs in two stages, pausing at Morro da Urca (220 m) before rising to the 396 m summit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Cable_Car

question: Guanabara Bay, the inlet Rio wraps around, reaches 31 km inland, scatters more than 130 islands, yet pinches to a mouth just 1.5 km wide, guarded by Sugarloaf. It began as a river valley on dry land; when the last Ice Age's meltwater lifted the sea, saltwater climbed the valley and drowned it. What is the geographer's term for a coastal inlet drowned this way?
context: A drowned river valley like this is called a 'ria' -- an old river-carved valley flooded when seas rose after the last Ice Age (unlike a fjord, whose valley was carved by a glacier). Guanabara Bay runs about 31 km inland, up to 28 km wide, narrows to a ~1.5 km mouth guarded by Sugarloaf, and holds more than 130 islands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanabara_Bay

question: Sugarloaf and Corcovado are Rio's bald granite giants -- toughened cores of ancient rock left towering after ages of weathering stripped away the softer rock that once buried them. Geologists have one word for a lone hard-rock mass exhumed and left rising this way. Which term names it?
context: Such isolated bald domes are called bornhardts -- a dome-shaped kind of 'inselberg' (German for 'island mountain'). Geologist Wilhelm Bornhardt coined the idea in 1900 for the rock-islands he saw rising from African plains: a core of especially resistant granite is left standing as the softer rock around it weathers away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inselberg; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Mountain

question: The dark-green mountains rising inside Rio -- the Tijuca Forest, one of the largest forests inside any city on Earth -- look like untouched jungle. Yet in the 1800s coffee plantations had stripped these very slopes bare, and the springs feeding the city were drying up. From 1861, on the orders of Emperor Pedro II, the rainforest we see today was brought back. How was Rio's Tijuca Forest restored?
answer: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
choices: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
it grew back on its own once farming stopped
it was seeded from aircraft after a fire
it was transplanted whole from the Amazon
context: The Tijuca Forest (~3,958 hectares) is one of the world's largest urban forests -- and hand-made. After coffee plantations stripped the slopes and choked the streams supplying Rio, Emperor Pedro II placed the land under federal control in 1861 and ordered it replanted, overseen by Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: Rio gave the world samba, the swaying music-and-dance at the heart of its Carnival. It grew in the early 1900s among Afro-Brazilian families in the dockside district nicknamed 'Little Africa,' nurtured in the home of a revered Bahian host, Tia Ciata. In 1917 the very first samba ever recorded became the smash hit of Carnival. What was that landmark song called?
context: Samba was born in the early 1900s in the Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods near Rio's port, an area nicknamed 'Little Africa,' and incubated in the home of the Bahian matriarch Tia Ciata. The first recorded samba, 'Pelo Telefone,' was registered by the musician Donga in 1916 and became the hit of the 1917 Carnival. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba

question: One of the world's largest urban rainforests, Rio's Tijuca Forest, was replanted entirely by hand between 1861 and 1887 -- well over 100,000 trees pressed one by one into slopes that coffee plantations had scraped down to bare dirt. You might imagine an army of foresters. In fact, records credit most of that quarter-century of planting to a startlingly small crew. How many workers did the bulk of that planting?
context: Records credit most of that quarter-century of planting to just six enslaved workers -- Eleuterio, Constantino, Manuel, Mateus, Leopoldo, and Maria -- who set out more than 100,000 trees between 1861 and 1887, growing back an entire forest tree by tree under Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: High on its exposed 700-metre peak, Christ the Redeemer takes a beating from Rio's fierce summer storms. In February 2008 the statue's head, eyebrows, and fingers were chipped; in 2014 a fingertip broke clean off. Which storm hazard keeps scarring the figure this way?
context: Because it crowns an exposed ~700 m peak with its arms flung wide, Christ the Redeemer is struck by lightning often. A February 2008 strike chipped the head, eyebrows, and fingers; a 2014 strike broke off a fingertip. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: The steep granite that makes Rio beautiful also makes it deadly: torrential summer rain soaks the thin soil of its hillside favelas until whole slopes give way. After catastrophes in 2010 and 2011 -- the 2011 landslides in the mountains north of Rio killed more than 900 people -- the city rolled out a distinctive new safeguard across its most exposed favelas. What did Rio install to protect hillside residents?
context: In January 2011, extreme rain in the mountains north of Rio set off thousands of landslides that killed well over 900 people -- among the deadliest natural disasters in Brazil's history; an April 2010 downpour of 288 mm in 24 hours had already triggered some 300 slides. Rio responded by installing 'Sirenes Cariocas' -- sirens that sound in hillside favelas when rainfall reaches dangerous levels. Source: rioonwatch.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_2010_Rio_de_Janeiro_floods_and_mudslides

question: Where the Nile finally reaches the Mediterranean, it stops being a single river and splays across the coast into a broad green fan of new farmland. The ancient Greeks named this whole kind of landform after the one capital letter of their alphabet whose shape it matched. Which letter?
context: Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BCE of 'the Delta, as it is called by the Ionians.' The Greek capital delta, the letter shaped like a triangle, matches the Nile's fan of land almost perfectly. For centuries 'the Delta' meant only the Nile's mouth; only later did 'delta' become the word for any river-mouth fan of new land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_delta  (Legend.)

question: The Nile Delta was ancient Egypt's breadbasket — the deep, dark, endlessly fertile farmland at the river's mouth that fed the pharaohs for thousands of years. Even though this delta sits at the far NORTHERN top of Egypt on the map, the ancient Egyptians knew the whole region by what name?
context: It sounds backwards, but the Nile flows north, so the delta is DOWNstream — the 'lower' end of the river — even though it lies in the north. Its topsoil runs up to 21 m (70 ft) deep, and the fan stretches about 240 km along the coast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta

question: Most big rivers spread into a smooth fan where they meet the sea. The Mississippi does the opposite: it dumps mud into the Gulf of Mexico faster than the Gulf's gentle waves can sweep it aside, so it builds narrow lobes of land straight out into open water. Seen from above, this delta's shape is nicknamed after what?
context: The narrow lobes are called 'passes,' and the whole shape is the classic 'bird's-foot' delta. It forms because the river's sediment power overwhelms the Gulf's weak waves and tides, so the river builds the coastline on its own terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_Delta  (Legend.)

question: In the age of the pharaohs the Nile fanned out to the Mediterranean through SEVEN separate mouths — the Pelusiac, the Canopic, the Sebennytic and more, each a branch carving its own path to the sea. Silt and flood-control projects have sealed branches off over the centuries. How many of those seven still carry the Nile to the sea today?
context: Only two flowing branches survive: the Rosetta and the Damietta, which give the delta its two great arms. The others — the Pelusiac, the Canopic, the Sebennytic and more — silted up or were closed by flood management. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta

question: A river delta's shape is decided by a three-way tug-of-war. When the RIVER's mud-power wins, it pokes out long fingers like the Mississippi's bird's-foot. When the SEA's WAVES win, they smooth the mud into a curved fan like the Nile's. A third force, when it dominates, slices a delta into a branching maze of long sandbars and islands — the shape where the Ganges and Brahmaputra reach the sea. Which force is it?
context: Geographers sort deltas by which of three forces wins: river (fluvial), wave, or tidal. Tide-dominated deltas like the Ganges-Brahmaputra get combed into long, finger-like sandbars aligned with the rise and fall of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_delta

question: The Ganges and the Brahmaputra, two of Asia's mightiest rivers, join forces and pour so much crushed Himalayan rock and mud into the sea that together they raise the single LARGEST river delta on the whole planet — a green lowland that is home to more than 250 million people. What is this record-breaking delta called?
context: The Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna together build the Bengal (or Ganges-Brahmaputra) delta — over 105,000 km² across Bangladesh and India's West Bengal, the largest and most populous delta on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_Delta  (Legend.)

question: Along the seaward edge of the great Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, salt-tolerant trees stand rooted in brackish water, their tangled roots threaded through an endless maze of tidal channels — the largest tidal forest of its kind on Earth. What is this world-famous coastal wilderness called?
context: The Sundarbans covers about 20,400 km² of the delta's seaward fringe and takes its name from the sundri tree (Heritiera fomes) that dominates it. It is the world's largest tidal mangrove forest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_Delta  (Legend.)

question: In the far north of Siberia, the Lena River builds the greatest of all the Arctic's deltas — a fan nearly 250 miles (400 km) wide reaching into the frozen Laptev Sea. What happens to this vast delta over the course of a single year?
answer: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
choices: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
It stays locked beneath solid ice all year, never thawing even at the height of summer.
Its channels dry to cracked mud through the rainless season, then refill when the snowmelt returns.
It vanishes under deep snowdrifts each winter, then reappears as bare gravel flats in the short summer.
context: The Lena builds the largest delta in the Arctic, fanning about 400 km (250 mi) wide into the Laptev Sea off Siberia's north coast. It lies frozen as tundra for roughly seven months a year, then bursts into a lush wetland for a few short summer months when the thaw floods across its islands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Delta

question: The Okavango River tumbles out of the Angolan highlands but never makes it to any sea. Instead it fans across a huge sunken basin into a glittering maze of channels, islands and lagoons that swells to three times its size each flood — then simply sinks away and evaporates into the sand. Which great desert does the Okavango vanish into?
context: The Okavango spills into a tectonic trough in Botswana's Kalahari Desert, one of the world's great inland (endorheic) deltas — almost none of its water ever reaches an ocean. At flood it spreads up to 15,000 km²; in 2014 it became the 1,000th UNESCO World Heritage site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okavango_Delta  (Legend.)

question: A delta only grows while its river keeps feeding it fresh mud. Upstream dams have cut the Mississippi's sediment load nearly in half, and levees wall the river off from its own marshes — so the starved delta is sinking and drowning, handing Louisiana back to the Gulf of Mexico. At its worst, that coast was vanishing at a rate people described as losing how much?
context: USGS measured coastal Louisiana shrinking by about 2,006 square miles (5,197 km²) between 1932 and 2016. At its worst that was a football field of wetland lost every 34 minutes; even at slower recent rates it is roughly one every 100 minutes. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/news/national-news-release/usgs-louisianas-rate-coastal-wetland-loss-continues-slow  (Legend.)

question: Step inside Rome's Pantheon and the only daylight pours in from a single round hole at the very top of the dome — about 9 metres wide and open straight to the sky. What is this opening at the dome's crown called?
context: The Pantheon's opening is the oculus (Latin for 'eye'), about 9.1 m across, and it is the building's only source of daylight. As the sun crosses the sky, its shaft of light sweeps around the marble interior like a moving spotlight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: The round opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome is completely open, so when a storm blows over Rome the rain really does fall straight through it onto the marble floor below — yet the ancient temple never floods. How is the rainwater dealt with?
answer: small drain holes in the floor
choices: small drain holes in the floor
gutters along the base of the walls
a bed of sand beneath the paving
channels feeding a pool at the centre
context: The floor is very slightly domed (convex) and holds 22 nearly invisible drainage holes that carry the rainwater into an underground channel — a system that has kept the Pantheon dry for roughly 1,900 years. Source: https://thepantheonrome.com/pantheon-oculus/  (Legend.)

question: Rome's Colosseum sat around 50,000 spectators, who streamed in through 80 arched entrances around the outer wall. Above every one of those 80 arches, the Romans had carved the same kind of marking. What did they carve above each arch?
context: Each of the 80 entrances was carved with a number (I to LXXX); a spectator's ticket sent them to the right numbered arch and straight to their seat — crowd control that works exactly like a modern stadium. Capacity estimates range from about 50,000 to 80,000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum

question: The Pantheon's dome is 43.3 metres across, and the Romans set its height — from the floor up to the opening at the crown — to that exact same 43.3 metres. Because the width and height match so perfectly, one ideal solid would fit precisely inside the great rotunda. What solid fits exactly inside the Pantheon?
context: Because the dome's height to its crown equals its 43.3 m width, a full sphere 43.3 m across fits exactly inside the rotunda. It remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome — built with no steel reinforcement — after about 1,900 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome  (Legend.)

question: A dome as vast as the Pantheon's should crack or crush its own walls under its enormous weight, so as it curved toward the crown the Roman builders shifted the concrete recipe from heavy travertine at the base to ever-lighter stone higher up. Which stone did they pack into the mix near the very top?
context: Near the very top the Roman builders packed the concrete with pumice, a volcanic rock so full of air pockets it can float on water. The mix grades from heavy travertine near the base, to terracotta, then to light volcanic tufa and pumice near the top; the dome is also 6.4 m thick at its base but only 1.2 m thick around the crown. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: On blazing afternoons a huge retractable awning, the velarium, was spread over the Colosseum crowd from 240 tall wooden poles. Hauling it out and rolling it back across the seats was skilled, dangerous high work, so the Romans didn't use locals — they marched in a trained crew from a military base about 200 km away, near Naples. What kind of base did the awning crew come from?
context: The awning crew were sailors from the imperial fleet's base at Misenum, on the Bay of Naples — men who already knew how to handle sail and rigging in the wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velarium  (Legend.)

question: After Rome fell, most of its ancient buildings were slowly torn apart, their marble and stone hauled away to raise new palaces and towers. Yet the Pantheon still stands whole — the best-preserved building of ancient Rome. What spared it from being quarried for its stone?
answer: it was turned into a church
choices: it was turned into a church
it was made into a fortress
it was rebuilt by an emperor
it was buried by a flood
context: In AD 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, so it was protected and maintained instead of stripped for building stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: Begun in 312 BC by the official Appius Claudius Caecus, the Via Appia was the first of Rome's great paved highways, running dead straight out of the city on tightly-fitted blocks of volcanic stone you can still walk today. So prized was this road that the Romans gave it a grand royal nickname. What did they call the Via Appia?
context: Its Latin nickname was regina viarum, 'the queen of roads.' Its polygonal lava paving stones can still be walked about 2,300 years later. The road first ran ~212 km from Rome to Capua and was later extended to the port of Brundisium (modern Brindisi). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way  (Legend.)

question: Roman harbours and sea walls have stood in salt water for 2,000 years, and modern scientists traced that strength to one special ingredient the Romans dug from the ground near Pozzuoli, on the Bay of Naples. Mixed with lime and water it forms a mineral glue so tough it even sets hard underwater. What was this key ingredient?
context: The ash is called pozzolana, after Pozzuoli near Naples; blended with lime it makes a hydraulic cement that hardens even underwater, which is why Roman marine concrete has lasted 2,000 years in the sea. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/we-finally-know-why-ancient-roman-concrete-lasts-thousands-of-years

question: Modern concrete decays and weakens within decades, yet Roman concrete has stood for 2,000 years. In 2023 an MIT-led team traced its endurance to tiny white flecks of lime scattered through the ancient mix — flecks that give Roman concrete one remarkable ability modern concrete lacks. What can it do?
context: The lime flecks (lime clasts) form when the Romans 'hot-mixed' the concrete with reactive quicklime. When water seeps into a crack, the flecks dissolve and re-crystallize as calcium carbonate, gluing the crack shut before it can spread. In the MIT test (led by Prof. Admir Masic), cracked hot-mixed concrete sealed itself within two weeks, while concrete made without quicklime did not heal. Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106  (Legend.)

question: Rome's aqueducts carried water for tens of miles into the city with no pumps — just a channel sloping gently downhill the whole way, so gently that too little tilt would leave the water stalled and stagnant. The Roman writer Vitruvius even set a rule for the least slope a channel could have. Over each kilometre of its long run, how far did a typical aqueduct actually drop?
context: The channels ran gently downhill the entire way, often dropping just a few centimetres over a whole kilometre. The Roman engineer Vitruvius advised a minimum tilt of about 1 in 4,800 (roughly 20 cm per kilometre). With no pumps anywhere on the route, that barely-there slope still moved water for tens of miles across arches and through tunnels into Rome. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman_aqueduct

question: Long before Rome had an empire, its early kings faced a swampy, flood-prone valley where the Forum would later stand. In the 6th century BC they built the Cloaca Maxima, the 'Greatest Sewer' — a huge stone drain to carry the water away to the Tiber. What is most astonishing about the Cloaca Maxima now?
answer: it is still in use today
choices: it is still in use today
it was rebuilt three times over
it now carries a subway line
context: Begun under the Etruscan king Tarquinius Priscus in the 6th century BC, the Cloaca Maxima still carries rainwater down to the Tiber roughly 2,500 years later — one of the world's oldest sewers still in use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima  (Legend.)

question: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) is the most isolated inhabited island on Earth, some 3,700 km from Chile. Besides its giant stone moai, its people left a second riddle: rongorongo, rows of tiny glyphs carved into wooden tablets. What is rongorongo's remarkable place in the history of human writing?
answer: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
choices: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
The oldest writing system in the world
The largest writing system, with thousands of signs
The fastest writing ever to spread worldwide
context: Across the thousands of islands of Oceania, only Rapa Nui developed a glyph-script of its own -- which is why rongorongo is so often called the only writing ever invented anywhere in the Pacific. Scholars still debate whether it is true writing or a proto-writing 'memory aid' for chants, so its exact status is unsettled. Roughly 600 distinct signs are known: stylized people, plants, and seabirds like the frigatebird, most carved into Pacific rosewood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.  (Legend.)

question: Rongorongo, the tiny glyph-script of Easter Island, is read in a baffling style called 'reverse boustrophedon.' You begin at the bottom-left corner and read one line straight across. To read the very next line, what must you do with the whole wooden tablet?
answer: Flip the whole tablet upside down
choices: Flip the whole tablet upside down
Read the next line from right to left
Turn it over to read the back face
Rotate it a quarter-turn and read down
context: In reverse boustrophedon, every other line is carved upside down, so a reader flips the tablet a full 180 degrees at the end of each line and reads on. The glyphs stand only about a centimetre tall. The longest surviving text, the 'Santiago Staff,' carries roughly 2,920 of them; the Mamari tablet seems to hold a lunar calendar -- one of the very few passages scholars have even tentatively identified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.

question: Egyptian hieroglyphs and the Maya script both fell silent when their last native readers died -- yet scholars later learned to read them again. Easter Island's rongorongo also lost its trained scribe-chanters, the tangata rongorongo, in the 1862 Peruvian slave raids. Where does rongorongo stand today?
answer: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
choices: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
A bilingual tablet unlocked it, like the Rosetta Stone
It proved not to be real writing, just carved decoration
Computer analysis of its glyphs finally cracked the code
context: One islander later told Bishop Jaussen that 'there was nobody left on the island who knew how to read the characters, since the Peruvians had brought about the deaths of all the wise men.' Only about two dozen inscribed objects survive worldwide, and rongorongo remains completely undeciphered; scholars still argue over whether it was ever true writing at all. Egyptian hieroglyphs were also unreadable for centuries before the Rosetta Stone cracked them -- but rongorongo has no such key. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo; history.com/articles/easter-island-people-rapanui.

question: Rotorua, in New Zealand, carries a nickname no other city would want: 'Sulphur City.' A whiff of rotten eggs hangs over the whole town, because the hot rock deep underground constantly leaks one particular gas up through the soil. Which gas is it?
context: It is hydrogen sulphide (H2S) -- the very gas that gives rotten eggs their stink -- seeping up from Rotorua's geothermal ground. Locals wear the 'Sulphur City' nickname (and the joke name 'Rotten-rua') with a grin. Carbon dioxide and methane are odourless, and sulphur dioxide smells sharp and acrid rather than eggy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua

question: In the Whakarewarewa valley at Rotorua, one geyser puts on the region's greatest show, hurling boiling water as high as 30 m into the sky as often as twenty times a day -- the biggest active geyser anywhere in the Southern Hemisphere. What is this record-holding geyser's name?
context: Pohutu -- Maori for 'big splash' -- is the largest active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere (not the whole world; the tallest active geyser is Yellowstone's Steamboat). Old Faithful also erupts in Yellowstone, Strokkur in Iceland, and Lady Knox is a real geyser at nearby Wai-O-Tapu. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pohutu_Geyser

question: At the Whakarewarewa living village in Rotorua, Te Arawa families cook their meals the same way their ancestors did for centuries. How do they cook a basket of corn, seafood and vegetables?
answer: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
choices: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
they bake it on hot stones in an earth oven
they smoke it slowly over a driftwood fire
they dry it for days in the summer sun
context: The Te Arawa and Tuhourangi people lower flax baskets of food on cords into the boiling Parekohuru hot spring, and build wooden steam boxes over natural vents -- cooking corn, seafood and vegetables with the ground's own heat, no fire needed. (Hot stones in an earth oven is the hangi, the more familiar Maori method used where there is no geothermal spring.) Source: whakarewarewa.com / en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: At Rotorua's Whakarewarewa valley, one smaller geyser can be trusted to play first, spraying up 7 to 9 m a few minutes before the valley's famous giant geyser roars to life -- so guides watch it as a natural signal that the big eruption is about to begin. What is this 'indicator' geyser called?
answer: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
choices: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
context: The Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser got its name during a 1901 royal visit, because its triple plume resembled the three feathers of the Prince of Wales crest; it reliably plays just before Pohutu, so it earns the nickname 'the Indicator.' Kereru is another Whakarewarewa geyser, Lady Knox is at Wai-O-Tapu, and Waimangu was a famous New Zealand geyser (now dormant). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: The Champagne Pool at Wai-O-Tapu, near Rotorua, is one of New Zealand's most photographed wonders: a steaming turquoise pool ringed by a brilliant burnt-orange shelf where minerals crust out of the scalding water at its edge. Which two elements give that vivid orange rim its colour?
context: The orange rim is a crust of arsenic and antimony minerals -- orpiment and stibnite -- settling out of water that also carries faint traces of gold and silver. The pool fizzes like a glass of champagne because carbon dioxide bubbles rise through it. It is about 65 m across and 62 m deep; its surface sits near 74 C, while the water feeding it from below reaches roughly 260 C. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_Pool

question: Rotorua is not a lone hot spot. Its geysers, boiling mud and steaming ground are the northern end of a single vast volcanic system that runs down the middle of New Zealand's North Island, reaching south to the volcanoes of Tongariro. What is this whole volcanic belt called?
context: The Taupo Volcanic Zone stretches across the central North Island, where the crust is being slowly pulled apart and thinned, letting magma rise close to the surface and boil the groundwater. Rotorua sits at its northern end. The Auckland, Coromandel and Northland volcanic regions are all real, but they are separate systems. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: The volcanic region that powers Rotorua holds a planetary record. Over the last 350,000 years it has erupted more than 3,900 cubic km of lava from over 300 separate eruptions -- more than anywhere else on Earth. It is the world's most productive source of which volcanic rock?
context: Rhyolite is a pale, silica-rich lava that tends to erupt explosively rather than flow quietly. The Taupo Volcanic Zone is the most productive rhyolitic volcanic region on Earth, which is why the whole area -- Rotorua's geysers included -- sits over such shallow, restless heat. Basalt, andesite and obsidian are other real volcanic rocks, but the zone's record is for rhyolite. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: At Ryoan-ji in Kyoto, monks tend a dry-landscape garden — a karesansui — made of almost nothing: a low earthen wall, a flat rectangle of raked white gravel, and fifteen bare stones. Only one green, living thing is allowed to grow among them. What is it?
context: The only green at Ryoan-ji is a thin skirt of moss ringing the base of each stone — everything else is gravel and rock. Karesansui means 'dry landscape': a garden of stone and sand with no pond, no stream, and almost no plant life, built to be looked at rather than lived in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji.

question: Ryoan-ji is famous the world over for one thing: a bone-dry rectangle of gravel and stone, a garden with no water at all. Yet the temple grounds also cradle a large, peaceful pond older than the rock garden itself. For centuries people knew this pond by an affectionate name borrowed from the waterbirds that came to spend each winter on it. By what name was the pond long known?
context: Ryoan-ji is known everywhere for its waterless garden, yet the temple grounds hold a large old pond, Kyoyochi, dug long before the rock garden. People long called it the Oshidori-ike — the 'Mandarin Duck Pond' — for the mandarin ducks that came to winter there, a reminder that water and life surround the one bone-dry courtyard the temple is famous for. Source: discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: Each morning at Ryoan-ji, a monk rakes the white gravel into long straight furrows and curved lines that sweep around each of the fifteen stones. In a dry Zen garden like this, the combed gravel is meant to stand for one natural element, with the stones rising out of it. What does the raked gravel represent?
context: The classic reading of a karesansui: the raked gravel is water and the standing stones are islands or mountain peaks rising from it — an entire seascape conjured in a bone-dry courtyard. The furrows are recombed by hand every day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/ryoan-ji-rock-garden.

question: Ryoan-ji's garden holds exactly fifteen stones in five clusters, placed so cunningly that from anywhere on the wooden viewing veranda at least one stone always hides behind another — a visitor sees fourteen at most, never all fifteen at once. An old temple tradition names the single condition under which a person could finally behold every one of the fifteen. According to that tradition, what reveals all fifteen at once?
answer: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
choices: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
rowing a boat across the temple pond
waiting for the light of a full moon
climbing up to the abbot's private room
context: From every spot on Ryoan-ji's veranda at least one of the fifteen stones stays hidden behind another, so a visitor can only ever count fourteen. Temple tradition offers a single exception: it is said that only a person who has reached inner enlightenment could ever behold all fifteen at once. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; sacred-japan.net/guides/ryoanji/.  (Legend.)

question: Behind the fifteen stones runs a low wall, and part of Ryoan-ji's quiet beauty is the soft brown, cloud-like blotches that stain it. The monks did not paint those patterns, and no artist designed them. What slowly created the stains over the centuries?
answer: oil seeping out of the clay
choices: oil seeping out of the clay
rain washing rust from the tiles
context: When the wall was built, its clay was boiled together with rapeseed oil. Over the following centuries the oil slowly wept back out through the surface, leaving the soft brown, cloud-shaped stains prized today. The Japanese have a word for this kind of beauty found in age, weathering, and imperfection: wabi-sabi. Source: muza-chan.net/japan/index.php/blog/ryoanji-earthen-wall; najga.org/using-earthen-walls-for-japanese-gardens.

question: Near Ryoan-ji's stone garden in Kyoto sits a low stone water basin ringed by four Japanese characters. Read on their own, the four make no sense — each is only half a character. The empty center of the basin is itself meant to be read as a fifth character, one that all four share to become complete. Which character is the empty center?
context: The empty center reads as 口 (kuchi), the character for 'mouth' — a simple box shape that completes each of the four surrounding characters. Joined together they read 'ware tada taru wo shiru': 'I know only contentment,' a Zen teaching about needing no more than you already have. The basin is said to have been donated by Tokugawa Mitsukuni, a lord of the Tokugawa family. Source: traditionalkyoto.com/gardens/ryoan-ji/; discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: High on Bolivia's Altiplano spreads a single blinding-white plain so vast -- 10,582 square kilometres -- and so level that it runs to the horizon in every direction, with no hill, rock, or plant to break it. What geographic record does this Bolivian expanse hold?
context: The Salar de Uyuni sprawls across 10,582 km2 of the Bolivian Altiplano -- roughly 100 times the size of the USA's Bonneville Salt Flats -- making it the largest salt flat on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: A few centimetres of rain sometimes settle over the Salar de Uyuni in a thin sheet of dead-still water that stretches about 129 kilometres across the flat. For the few weeks before it dries away, this flooded plain earns a famous title. What is it?
context: After the rare rains, a thin sheet of dead-still water turns the Salar into a flawless reflector about 129 km (80 miles) across -- the world's largest natural mirror, where sky and salt blur into a single white void. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: The Salar de Uyuni is a treeless plain high in the Bolivian Andes, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest forest or quarry. With no wood or stone to build with, the little hotels that shelter travellers who cross it cut their walls, beds, and tables from the one material the plain offers without limit. What is that material?
context: With no rock or timber for hundreds of kilometres, hotels here -- the Palacio de Sal, Luna Salada, and Playa Blanca -- are built almost entirely of cut salt blocks: walls, beds, tables, and floors. Source: https://www.forbes.com/sites/jimdobson/2018/01/05/escape-to-the-last-jedi-battleground-in-bolivia-and-stay-in-a-hotel-made-entirely-out-of-salt/

question: When the Salar de Uyuni dries out, its hard salt crust splits into a vast tiled floor of repeating shapes -- thousands of them, each a metre or two across, fitting edge to edge all the way to the horizon. What shape are these repeating salt tiles?
context: As the crust dries it cracks into a honeycomb of polygons a metre or two wide, tiling to the horizon. A 2023 study by Lasser and Goehring showed the hexagons form as salty water sinks and fresher water rises in convection 'rolls' below the crust, piling salt into ridges where neighbouring rolls meet. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/03/230301101524.htm

question: Across all 10,582 km2 of the Salar de Uyuni the ground rises and falls by less than a single metre -- it is the flattest large surface on Earth. Space agencies like NASA prize this glass-smooth, dazzling-bright plain for one particular job. What do they use it for?
choices: to track the planet's slow wobble
context: Because the Salar is so flat and bright, satellites are calibrated against it about 5 times better than against the ocean surface; NASA's ICESat used it to verify its altitude measurements to within about 2 cm. Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20050071074 ; https://icesat.gsfc.nasa.gov/icesat/publications/GRL/fricker-2.pdf

question: Under the dry salt crust of the Salar de Uyuni lies a hidden lake of buried brine, and dissolved in it sits roughly a fifth of the world's known resources of one soft, silvery metal -- the metal at the heart of nearly every phone and electric-car battery. Which metal is trapped in the brine below?
context: The brine beneath the crust holds a huge share of the world's lithium RESOURCES -- Bolivia has roughly 22% of the known global total (about 23 of ~105 million tonnes). That figure is the store in the ground, not the amount actually mined. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: The Salar de Uyuni holds an estimated 10 billion tonnes of salt, sitting more than two miles up on the Andean high plain, nowhere near any ocean. Where did such a mountain of salt come from?
answer: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
choices: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
a cut-off ancient arm of the Pacific Ocean
mineral ash blasted out by nearby volcanoes
salt dust blown up from the Atacama Desert
context: The whole flat is the dried bed of Lake Tauca, an Ice-Age lake that filled the basin during the Pleistocene and then evaporated away roughly 12,000-13,000 years ago, leaving the salt behind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: Cross the blinding-white Salar de Uyuni toward its middle and a rocky hill suddenly breaks the emptiness -- Incahuasi, an 'island' marooned in a sea of salt. Its slopes bristle with thousands of a single strange plant, the tallest topping 12 metres and some over a thousand years old. What covers Incahuasi Island?
context: Incahuasi Island's giant cacti (Trichocereus/Echinopsis) reach up to 12 m and grow only about 1 cm a year, so the tallest are over a thousand years old. The 'island' itself is fossilized coral and stromatolites -- a petrified reef stranded at about 3,650 m, proof this white desert was once underwater. Source: https://www.machupicchu.org/isla-incahuasi-2026-the-cactus-island-in-the-uyuni-salt-flats.htm

question: Rivers run down off the Andes into the basin of the Salar de Uyuni, but the basin has no exit -- not one river carries its water onward to any sea. Cut off like this, a basin can only lose its water to evaporation, so its salt stays behind and piles up instead of washing away; geographers call such a sealed, outlet-less basin 'endorheic'. That same trait -- no drain to any ocean -- is what makes which other famous body of water so salty?
context: A basin with no outlet to the sea is 'endorheic' (from the Greek for 'flowing within'): its water can only leave by evaporating, so dissolved salts and minerals stay trapped and concentrate over time -- which is why salt and lithium pile up at Uyuni. The Dead Sea lies in the same kind of sealed, endorheic basin, with no river carrying its water out to any ocean, so evaporation has left it famously, extraordinarily salty. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: At the heart of Samarkand, in Uzbekistan, opens a vast paved square framed on three sides by towering madrasas — grand Islamic colleges. Its Persian name means, quite simply, 'sandy place.' What is Samarkand's celebrated central plaza called?
context: The Registan ('sandy place' in Persian) was Samarkand's medieval marketplace and the ceremonial heart of Timur's empire, framed by three great madrasas: the Ulugh Beg (1417-1420), the Sher-Dor (1619-1636), and the Tilya-Kori (1646-1660). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registan

question: Islamic religious buildings almost never show living beings, covering their walls instead with geometry and holy script. Yet the great portal of the Sher-Dor madrasa, on Samarkand's Registan, famously breaks that custom with a startling scene of animals. What does the Sher-Dor portal actually depict?
answer: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
choices: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
a phoenix and a dragon around a flowering tree
peacocks flanking a cypress under a crescent moon
context: 'Sher-Dor' means 'Lion-Bearing.' Two striped tiger-lions chase white does across the portal while sun-discs with human faces rise from the cats' backs — an echo of pre-Islamic Zoroastrian sun-symbolism. Such figural images are rare in Islamic sacred art, which is what makes the 1619-1636 mosaic so startling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher-Dor_Madrasa

question: In Samarkand stands the Gur-e-Amir, the tomb of the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane). Crowning it, and visible right across the city, is a huge bright-blue dome — deeply fluted with vertical ribs and bulging outward in a rounded shape. The dome is fondly nicknamed for an everyday object it resembles. What is the Gur-e-Amir's dome most often compared to?
context: The melon-shaped, ribbed azure dome of the Gur-e-Amir (built 1403-1404) is about 15 metres across and 12.5 metres high, its bright-blue tiles set with deep rosettes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: Climbing a Samarkand hillside is the Shah-i-Zinda, a narrow lane lined with more than twenty tombs tiled in every shade of blue. Its name means 'The Living King,' honoring Kusam ibn Abbas, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad. Legend says that when enemies beheaded Kusam as he prayed, he did something miraculous. What, in the legend, does Kusam do?
answer: carries his severed head down a deep well
choices: carries his severed head down a deep well
rises into the sky on a shaft of light
sleeps in a cave until the last day
steps from his tomb each night to pray
context: The Shah-i-Zinda ('The Living King') is an avenue of more than twenty blue-tiled mausoleums, among the finest tilework in Central Asia. By legend Kusam ibn Abbas, beheaded at prayer, took up his own head and descended a well where he lives to this day — an oral tradition, not history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah-i-Zinda

question: Timur commanded the Bibi-Khanym mosque in Samarkand (finished 1404) to be the largest in all Islam — its outer walls longer than a football field, its main dome some 40 metres high. But it had been thrown up at reckless speed. What happened to the enormous Bibi-Khanym soon after it was finished?
answer: bricks began falling from its great dome
choices: bricks began falling from its great dome
cracks split its huge entrance arch
its minarets leaned and had to be propped
its foundations sank into the soft ground
context: Raised in just 1399-1404 with the plunder of Timur's Indian campaign, the Bibi-Khanym mosque (outer walls 167x109 m, main dome ~40 m) was among the largest ever attempted — and so over-ambitious that masonry began dropping from its dome within a few years. Later earthquakes ruined it further; it was rebuilt in the 20th century. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibi-Khanym_Mosque
