context: Skara Brae had a drainage system running in stone-lined channels beneath the houses, and each little wall-cubicle was plumbed into it -- one main reason archaeologists read the recess as a toilet. If so, it gave Skara Brae indoor sanitation that most later Orcadians would not have again until the 20th century. (The reading as a toilet is likely but not certain.) Source: orkneyology.com/skara-brae.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.  (Legend.)

question: Skara Brae was only one corner of a vast Neolithic ritual landscape on Orkney. Nearby rose the Ness of Brodgar, a great temple complex whose largest hall, Structure Ten, was deliberately shut down and abandoned around 2400 to 2200 BC. Rather than quietly walking away from it, the Stone Age community marked the closing with one enormous ceremony -- and left unmistakable evidence of it heaped in the ruins. What did archaeologists find there, the remains of that great farewell?
answer: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
choices: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
the shards of thousands of smashed clay pots
a ring of carved stone balls set into the floor
the ashes of a huge timber roof burnt to the ground
context: The Ness of Brodgar, between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness, held 'Structure Ten,' one of the largest Neolithic buildings in northern Britain. Around 2400-2200 BC it was ceremonially closed with a vast feast: excavators found roughly 400 cattle tibias (shin-bones), the remains of hundreds of slaughtered animals. Skara Brae, Brodgar and Stenness together make up the UNESCO 'Heart of Neolithic Orkney.' (A closing feast is the leading interpretation of the bone deposit.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ness_of_Brodgar.  (Legend.)

question: For a few weeks around midsummer, St Petersburg never really goes dark: the sun barely dips below the horizon, and at midnight the sky still glows bright enough to stroll the embankments or read outdoors, so crowds fill the bridges past 1 a.m. What are these luminous summer nights called?
context: Near the solstice St Petersburg gets about 18 hours 50 minutes of daylight, and even the rest of the night stays in bright twilight, light enough to read outdoors. This isn't the true 'midnight sun' (where the sun never sets at all): here it slips just below the horizon, so the sky glows rather than shines. The season fills the embankments and bridges with crowds past midnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: St Petersburg is built across dozens of islands in the low, watery Neva delta, threaded by more than 60 rivers and canals and stitched together by over 300 bridges. What European nickname did this maze of water and islands earn the city?
context: Land reclamation trimmed the delta's original ~101 islands to about 42, and the city is crossed by 342 bridges over its rivers and canals, with some tallies running past 500. All that water threading between the islands is why St Petersburg is called the Venice of the North. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bridges_in_Saint_Petersburg; introducingsaintpetersburg.com/bridges

question: In 1703 Peter the Great decreed a brand-new capital into being on a cold, mist-shrouded marsh at the mouth of the Neva. Conscripted peasants and Swedish war prisoners drove countless wooden piles into the swamp, and so many tens of thousands died in the mud that St Petersburg earned which grim folk nickname?
choices: the city of a thousand sorrows
context: The founding date, 27 May 1703, is still marked as the city's birthday. Peter the Great forced his capital onto ground everyone called unbuildable; conscripted peasants and Swedish prisoners of war drained the swamp and drove countless wooden piles, and tens of thousands of forced laborers died, the real human cost behind the grim folk name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: Deep in the cellars beneath St Petersburg's Hermitage, one of the greatest art museums on Earth, a special staff has patrolled against rats for nearly 300 years, ever since Empress Elizabeth first brought them in to protect the imperial palace. What are these long-serving guardians of the Hermitage?
context: A resident population of cats has protected the Hermitage's cellars and courtyards from rats for centuries, a tradition dating back to imperial times: Empress Elizabeth first had cats brought in to guard the palace. They still work the basements today, though they are kept out of the galleries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: St Petersburg did not begin as grand palaces; it grew outward from the very first thing Peter the Great built here, on 27 May 1703, on tiny Hare Island in the Neva delta, the seed the whole imperial capital spread out from. Which landmark was it?
context: The Peter and Paul Fortress was laid down on 27 May 1703 on tiny Zayachy (Hare) Island in the Neva delta. The citadel came first, and the imperial capital grew outward from it across the marsh; it is the founding kernel of the whole city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: Behind the mint-green-and-white facade of St Petersburg's Winter Palace, the Hermitage holds around three million works of art and artifacts, a collection begun when Catherine the Great bought a batch of paintings in 1764. That staggering hoard makes the Hermitage exactly what, among the world's museums?
context: The single largest is the Louvre in Paris; the Hermitage ranks second by the size of its collection. It grew from Catherine the Great's 1764 purchase of about 225 paintings from the Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky, the batch that founded the imperial collection, now spread through the Winter Palace and its neighboring buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: On summer nights in St Petersburg, cross to the wrong side of the Neva after about 1 a.m. and you can be stranded until nearly dawn. For a few hours every night from spring to autumn, what do the Neva's great bridges do, cutting off all crossing until they close near sunrise?
answer: rise open to let ocean ships pass
choices: rise open to let ocean ships pass
lift to let spring ice floes through
close off for their nightly maintenance
swing shut against Gulf storm surges
context: St Petersburg is a working seaport, and ocean-going cargo ships can only move along the Neva when the bridges lift. In navigation season (roughly late April to November) the drawbridges open on a nightly schedule; the famous Palace Bridge splits open around 1:10 a.m. and lowers again near 4:55 a.m., so anyone caught on the wrong bank waits for dawn. Source: russiable.com/drawbridges-st-petersburg-schedules/; travelallrussia.com/blog/drawing-bridges

question: St Petersburg's Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood glitters inside with more than 7,500 square metres of mosaic, more than any other church on Earth. But its grim name comes from the very ground it covers: the exact spot where, in 1881, someone was killed. Who died there?
answer: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
choices: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
a grand duchess, lost in a fire
an army general, shot by an assassin
context: The victim was Tsar Alexander II, struck down by a bomb on this spot in 1881, the killing that gave the church its name, 'Savior on Spilled Blood.' Inside, over 7,500 square metres of mosaic cover the walls and vaults, more than in any other church in the world. Source: historyhit.com/locations/church-of-the-saviour-on-spilled-blood/

question: At Peterhof, Peter the Great's palace on the Gulf of Finland outside St Petersburg, more than 100 fountains, including the giant Grand Cascade, have played every summer since 1721, and the whole system runs on no machinery at all. What makes the water leap into those towering jets?
answer: gravity, from springs on higher ground
choices: gravity, from springs on higher ground
the daily rise and fall of Baltic tides
steady wind off the Gulf of Finland
context: The secret is elevation: water is gathered from natural springs in the Ropsha Heights about 22-24 km away and some 90 m higher, then channeled downhill. Arriving under its own weight, it has enough pressure to shoot skyward, no pumps needed. Engineered by Vasily Tuvolkov, the system has run this way since 1721, and the Grand Cascade alone feeds 64 fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace; unesco.ru/en/news/55-peterhof/

question: The golden centerpiece of Peterhof, its tallest fountain, fires a single jet some 20 metres straight up and celebrates Russia's crushing victory over Sweden. At its heart, a gilded strongman is locked in combat with a great beast. Which hero and beast does the statue show?
answer: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
choices: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
context: The Samson Fountain marks Russia's victory over Sweden: a lion is Sweden's heraldic emblem, and Samson, standing for Russia, rips its jaws apart. Its single vertical jet reaches about 20 metres (66 ft), the tallest of all Peterhof's fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace

question: St Petersburg's Bronze Horseman, a dramatic statue of Peter the Great rearing on horseback, stands on a single colossal slab of granite that once weighed about 1,500 tonnes, among the largest stones ever shifted by human hands. To move it, 400 men rolled it for months over a track of bronze balls. What is this famous rock called?
context: The Thunder Stone is a single granite boulder of roughly 1,500 tonnes (about 1,250 after carving), among the largest stones ever moved by people. Workers hauled it overland on a metal sled sliding over a track of bronze balls, 400 men over about nine months, with no animals or machines, then floated it the rest of the way by barge. The statue was sculpted by the Frenchman Etienne Maurice Falconet for Catherine the Great and unveiled in 1782; Alexander Pushkin's 1833 poem gave it the enduring name 'The Bronze Horseman.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Horseman

question: In St Petersburg the Neva River freezes solid for months every winter, yet around midsummer the sky never fully darkens and people linger outdoors at midnight. One single geographic fact about the city's position causes BOTH of these opposite extremes. Which fact?
choices: how low it sits above the sea
how far it lies inland from the sea
how mountainous the land around it is
context: At about 60 degrees north (59 degrees 57 minutes N), St Petersburg sits on the polar edge, far enough from the equator that the swing between summer and winter light is extreme. Near midsummer the sun barely dips below the horizon, giving the glowing White Nights; in deep winter it scarcely rises and the Neva locks in ice. Latitude alone sets the whole rhythm of the city's year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: Sweden's capital never settled onto a single shore. Stockholm grew up right where the fresh water of Lake Mälaren pours out into the salty Baltic Sea, spreading itself over the water instead of hugging one bank. How is the historic city laid out?
choices: A city raised on 14 wooden piers
A city split by 14 river channels
context: Stockholm sits on 14 islands at the outlet of Lake Mälaren into the Baltic, historically nicknamed 'the city between the bridges' (Staden mellan broarna) for the bridges stitching its islands together — Wikipedia counts about thirty bridges in the central city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Stockholm

question: In Gamla Stan — Stockholm's medieval old town, crowded onto one small island — the streets twist and narrow between tall ochre-gold houses. Tightest of them all is a stepped alley called Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, the narrowest street in the whole city. How wide is it where it pinches down the most?
answer: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
choices: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
About 3 meters — a single cart's width
About 6 meters — two carts side by side
context: Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, a stepped alley in Gamla Stan, is the narrowest street in Stockholm — about 90 cm at its tightest squeeze. Gamla Stan ('the Old Town'), crowded onto the island of Stadsholmen, dates to the 13th century and is one of the largest and best-preserved medieval city cores in Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_stan

question: Stockholm's historic center rests on 14 islands — but that is only the start. Sail east from the city and the coastline shatters into the Baltic as a vast scatter of islands, islets, and bare-rock skerries reaching far out to sea. Roughly how many islands make up the Stockholm Archipelago?
context: The Stockholm Archipelago scatters some 30,000 islands, islets, and skerries into the Baltic — a skerry being a small rocky islet too barren to build on. The exact total is genuinely uncertain: counts range from about 24,000 to over 30,000 depending on the source, so 'roughly 30,000' is the honest figure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago  (Legend.)

question: Ride the subway in Stockholm and the stations stop looking like a subway at all: instead of tiled walls, more than 90 of the roughly 100 stops open into caverns of raw, unfinished bedrock, their walls swirling with color — at T-Centralen, giant blue vines and leaves climb straight up the bare stone. What nickname has the Stockholm Metro earned?
context: The Stockholm Metro is called 'the world's longest art gallery': more than 90 of its ~100 stations are painted, sculpted, or blasted straight into the bare bedrock and decorated by over 150 artists along 105.7 km of track. At T-Centralen, the central hub, Per Olof Ultvedt painted cave-like blue vines and leaves across the raw rock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_metro  (Legend.)

question: In August 1628, crowds packed Stockholm's harbor to cheer the pride of the Swedish navy — the Vasa, the tallest, most heavily gunned warship the kingdom had ever built, glittering with hundreds of gilded carvings. For all that glory, the Vasa is remembered today for one humiliating fact. What is it?
answer: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
choices: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
She rotted at her moorings, never once putting to sea
She was captured by the Danish fleet within a year
She was lost with all hands in a storm off Poland
context: On 10 August 1628, the Vasa capsized and sank on her maiden voyage after sailing barely 1,300 m — going down only about 120 m from shore, as roughly 30 people drowned, in full view of the watching crowd. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: To make the Vasa a terror at sea, her builders crowded two full decks of heavy bronze cannon high in her hull — but left too little ballast down in her belly to steady all that weight up top. On her first voyage, a light breeze pushed on her sails and she heeled far over to one side. That single lean sank her. Why?
answer: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
choices: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
Her tall masts snapped and dragged her under
Her powder store caught fire deep in the hull
Her loose cannon smashed out through the deck
context: The Vasa's center of gravity sat too high over two gundecks of cannon, with too little ballast below; a light gust heeled her, and water flooded in through the open lower gunports until she went down. She carried 64 guns, mostly 48 heavy 24-pounder bronze cannon — the very weight, mounted high, that doomed her. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: For 333 years the sunken Vasa lay on the floor of Stockholm's harbor. In most of the world's seas, wood-boring shipworms would have eaten a wooden hull down to nothing — but the water here in the Baltic is so cold and so low in salt that shipworms cannot survive in it, so that particular destroyer never touched her. When she was finally raised in 1961, how much of the original 17th-century oak was still there?
context: Because the cold, brackish (low-salt) Baltic water excludes the wood-eating shipworm Teredo navalis, about 98% of the Vasa was still original oak when she was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom. She is the only almost-fully-intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged, now displayed whole in the Vasa Museum (opened 1990). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: The Stockholm Archipelago is not finished forming — it is still slowly emerging from the Baltic Sea, its islands standing a few millimeters higher above the water every year. Old shorelines creep inland, and new bare-rock skerries break the surface for the first time. All across Scandinavia the land is quietly climbing out of the sea. What keeps lifting these islands out of the water year after year?
choices: A slow fall in the sea level
Silt piling up from the rivers
context: As the kilometer-thick ice sheets of the last Ice Age melted, the enormous weight lifted off the crust, which is still slowly springing back — post-glacial (isostatic) rebound — raising the Stockholm region about 3 mm a year and lifting the archipelago's 'joint valley landscape' up out of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago

question: In Stone Town on Zanzibar island, tradition held that a family would build THIS part of the house first, before the walls even went up. Hundreds still survive along the maze of narrow, shaded alleys -- each a heavy dark slab worked with symbols that broadcast the owner's trade, faith, and wealth to everyone who passed. What is it?
context: Stone Town is famous for more than 500 hand-carved wooden doors. The door went up first when a house was built, and its carvings advertised the owner -- Qur'anic verses for the devout, a fish for a fisherman, lotus flowers and chains for prosperity. (Source: Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')

question: Stone Town gets its very name from its building material. While the surrounding coastal villages rose in mud and thatch, its merchants cut a local rock into blocks, bound them with lime mortar, and raised the tall multi-storey houses that still crowd the alleys today. Which of these is that local building stone?
context: The stone is coralline ragstone -- fossil coral quarried from the reef -- laced with mangrove-pole timber. Fusing Swahili, Arab, Indian and European styles, the old town became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. (Source: UNESCO WHC 'Stone Town of Zanzibar'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: The oldest doors of Stone Town bristle with rows of fat brass spikes jutting from the wood -- but Zanzibar never faced a siege in its life. The design was borrowed straight from India, where such heavy door-studs served one grim purpose: to blunt an attack that could otherwise batter a fortified gate right off its hinges. What were the studs first meant to stop?
context: Indian fort gates were studded to keep war elephants from battering them down. Zanzibar never fought such a war, so on the island the brass spikes became pure decoration -- a badge of a merchant's wealth during the spice-trade boom. (Source: TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Atlas Obscura 'The Doors of Stone Town'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')  (Legend.)

question: Under its Omani sultans, plantations spread across Zanzibar until the small island grew more of a single aromatic spice than anywhere else on Earth. Traders crossing the Indian Ocean stopped bothering with its real name and simply called it the 'Spice Island.' Which spice did Zanzibar come to grow more of than any other place in the world?
context: The Omani ruler pushed clove plantations across the island, and by the mid-1800s Zanzibar dominated the world clove trade -- the source of the 'Spice Island' name. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Capable Africa Tours 'History of Zanzibar'; BlackPast 'Sultanate of Zanzibar')

question: One of the twentieth century's most famous rock singers began life in 1946 in an ordinary house in Stone Town's alleys -- born Farrokh Bulsara to Parsi parents, before his family left the island while he was still a boy. His birthplace is now a small museum on the visitor trail. Which rock star was born there?
context: He was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town in 1946; the family later moved to England, where he became Freddie Mercury, frontman of the band Queen. The house where he lived is now a small museum. (Source: Machu Picchu 'Stone Town Zanzibar Guide 2026'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: Around 1840, the Omani sultan Said bin Sultan did something startling: he packed up his court and moved his capital from Muscat in Arabia across the ocean to Stone Town, on a small African island his family ruled. A ruler almost never abandons his ancestral seat. What had made this little island worth more to him than Oman itself?
choices: its fort on a sea strait
context: The wealth pouring out of his East African clove and trade empire had grown larger than Oman's own revenue, so Said bin Sultan moved his capital from Muscat to Stone Town around 1840. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Gulf News 'Zanzibar: A slice of Oman'; BlackPast 'Seyyid Said')

question: Stone Town once held East Africa's largest slave market, the hub through which traders bought and sold captives carried from deep in the African interior. After Britain forced the trade to close, workers raised a Christian cathedral on that exact ground -- and set its altar on the precise spot where one grim fixture of that market had stood. What had stood where the altar now sits?
context: The Anglican Christ Church Cathedral was begun on Christmas Day 1873 and opened in 1879 on the old slave-market site; its altar stands where the market's whipping post once stood. Below, the cramped underground cells where captives were packed to await sale are still preserved. (Source: Wikipedia 'Christ Church, Zanzibar'; Pongwe 'Christ Church Cathedral & the Old Slave Market')

question: In 1883 Sultan Barghash bin Said built a vast ceremonial palace on the Stone Town seafront, its marble floors and tall pillared verandas rising over the coral-stone alleys. People named it Beit-al-Ajaib -- the 'House of Wonders' -- for the marvels it was the first building in all of East Africa to contain. What made the palace so wondrous?
answer: it had electric light and an elevator
choices: it had electric light and an elevator
it had a rooftop garden and a zoo
it had gold walls and an ivory throne
it had a moat and a working drawbridge
context: The House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib), built by Sultan Barghash in 1883, was the first building in East Africa to have an elevator and the first in Zanzibar with electric light, running water and marble floors -- hence its name. A corner of it collapsed during a restoration in 2020, and Oman offered to help rebuild it. (Source: The National 'What is the House of Wonders?'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; Anadolu Agency)

question: Stonehenge's ring of standing sarsens is capped by a continuous circle of level stone lintels -- and they don't merely balance on top. To lock each lintel down, the Neolithic builders carved a joint borrowed straight from the carpenter's toolkit into solid, 25-ton stone about 4,500 years ago. What is this classic woodworking joint called?
context: A tenon -- a carved knob on top of each upright -- was dropped into a mortise, a hollow cut into the underside of the lintel, reproducing a woodworking joint in solid stone around 2500 BC. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: Stand at the centre of Stonehenge at dawn on one special morning each year, and the rising sun climbs up over a single outlying stone -- the Heel Stone -- and pours straight down the monument's main axis into the heart of the ring. This roughly 5,000-year-old alignment is keyed to which sunrise?
context: At midsummer the sun rises over the Heel Stone and runs along Stonehenge's axis, so the monument works as a roughly 5,000-year-old solar calendar marking the year's turning points. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Solstice_at_Stonehenge

question: The lintels crowning Stonehenge's outer ring do more than sit end to end. Each curved lintel is fixed to its neighbours with a second carpentry joint, so the whole capping circle knits into one continuous interlocking hoop -- something found at no other prehistoric stone monument on Earth. What joint links the lintels end to end?
context: A tongue carved on one lintel's end slotted into a groove in the next, so Stonehenge's sarsen lintels interlocked all the way around the ring like fitted timber -- unique among the world's ancient stone circles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: One of Stonehenge's stones carries a spooky old English legend. The story goes that the Devil, certain no one could ever count all the stones, caught a friar quietly tallying them and hurled a huge block to strike him down. According to the tale, what happened when the flung stone reached the friar?
answer: it bounced off the friar's heel
choices: it bounced off the friar's heel
it crushed him where he stood
it split in two as it fell
it sank deep into the soft ground
context: In the folk tale the stone struck the friar's heel so hard it dented the stone -- which is why the outlying block is nicknamed the 'Friar's Heel' or Heel Stone. This is legend, not history. Source: https://blog.stonehenge-stone-circle.co.uk/2011/03/16/stonehenge-folklore/

question: Stonehenge is built from two very different kinds of rock. The giant outer sarsens are local, but the smaller inner 'bluestones' -- just 2 to 4 tons each -- were dragged an astonishing 230 km (about 140 miles) to Salisbury Plain, one of the longest stone-hauls of the entire ancient world. Where did the bluestones come from?
context: The bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of west Wales and moved roughly 230 km to Stonehenge -- among the longest-distance transports of monument stone known anywhere in the ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: Lying at the very centre of Stonehenge is a single long slab, five metres of pale stone, so easy to overlook that visitors once strolled right over it -- the 'Altar Stone.' It lies flat rather than standing upright, and much of it is hidden from view today. What keeps so much of the Altar Stone out of sight?
answer: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
choices: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
deep soil that drifted over and buried it
a thick mat of turf grown across it
a heap of chalk rubble piled over it
context: The Altar Stone (Stone 80) lies flat near Stonehenge's centre, partly pinned beneath a toppled sarsen, Stone 55, that fell across it -- which is why much of the slab stays hidden and it is so easily missed today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_Stone_(Stonehenge)

question: For centuries the source of Stonehenge's biggest stones -- the 25-ton sarsens of the outer ring -- was a complete mystery. Then in 2020, scientists read the chemical fingerprint locked in the stone and matched it to one particular place. Where did the great sarsens come from?
context: A 2020 study led by geographer David Nash traced 50 of the 52 surviving sarsens to West Woods near Marlborough, only about 25 km north of Stonehenge, using portable X-ray fluorescence. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones-143564

question: Archaeologists digging at the Welsh quarries that gave Stonehenge its bluestones turned up a puzzle: the stones were cut there around 3400-3200 BC, yet they weren't standing at Stonehenge until roughly 2900 BC -- centuries later. What do many archaeologists now suspect happened in between?
answer: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
choices: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
the Welsh quarry kept cutting stone for other circles
the quarry dates were measured wrongly
the stones lay abandoned at the quarry for ages
context: The centuries-long gap hints the Preseli bluestones may have been raised in a stone circle in Wales first, then dismantled and carried to Salisbury Plain -- though this remains a hypothesis. Source: https://phys.org/news/2019-02-quarrying-stonehenge-bluestones-dated-bc.html

question: The flat Altar Stone at Stonehenge's centre was long assumed to be just another of the Welsh bluestones. Then in 2024, fresh laboratory tests delivered a shock: this six-tonne slab had not come from Wales at all, but from a source hundreds of kilometres away that no one had suspected. Where did the Altar Stone actually come from?
context: In 2024 researchers traced the Altar Stone to the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland -- over 700 km away and the longest journey known for any stone in any Neolithic monument. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: Tracing the Altar Stone to a source hundreds of kilometres from Salisbury Plain was only half the shock -- researchers were just as struck by how a six-tonne slab likely made that trip, long before the wheel is thought to have reached Britain. How do researchers think the Altar Stone reached Stonehenge?
answer: shipped by sea along the coast
choices: shipped by sea along the coast
floated down a chain of rivers
context: Because a 700 km overland haul of a six-tonne slab would have been extraordinary long before the wheel reached Britain, researchers think the Altar Stone most likely reached Salisbury Plain by sea, carried along Britain's coasts from northeast Scotland. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: The 2020 fingerprinting study matched 50 of Stonehenge's 52 surviving sarsens to the very same source at West Woods. But two of the giant stones -- numbered 26 and 160 -- stubbornly refused to match the rest. What does this tell archaeologists about those two sarsens?
answer: they came from a different, still-unknown source
choices: they came from a different, still-unknown source
they are natural boulders, never quarried at all
they were added by Victorian restorers
they are the oldest stones on the whole site
context: Stones 26 and 160 did not share West Woods' chemical signature, meaning at least two of Stonehenge's giant sarsens were hauled from a second source that has still not been identified. Source: https://blogs.bournemouth.ac.uk/research/2020/07/30/conversation-article-stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones/

question: Gangkhar Puensum rises 7,570 m on the border of Bhutan and Tibet, where the kingdom honors its peaks as homes of the gods. Among the world's great mountains, which distinction belongs to Gangkhar Puensum alone?
choices: The most remote of all great peaks
The last great peak to be mapped
context: Gangkhar Puensum (7,570 m / 24,836 ft) on the Bhutan-Tibet border is the highest mountain on Earth that has never been climbed; its Dzongkha name means 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers.' Four expeditions failed in 1985-86, Bhutan banned peaks over 6,000 m in 1994 and all mountaineering in 2003 out of respect for the peaks as homes of gods, and a 1998 Japanese permit was later revoked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangkhar_Puensum

question: Machapuchare, the 'Fish Tail' peak of 6,993 m rising over Nepal's Annapurna region, has been climbed by exactly one expedition. In 1957 a British team led by Jimmy Roberts reached a point only about 50 m below the top - and there they turned back. Why did they stop so close to the summit?
answer: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
choices: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
A sudden storm drove them back down the ridge
Their food and oxygen supplies had run out
A wall of unstable ice blocked the final climb
context: Machapuchare ('Fish Tail,' 6,993 m / 22,943 ft) in Nepal's Annapurna region was attempted only once, in 1957, by a British team under Jimmy Roberts; Wilfrid Noyce and A.D.M. Cox reached about 50 m below the top and stopped because King Mahendra had granted permission on one condition: no one set foot on the summit. The team kept the promise, no permit has been issued since, and the peak is sacred to the Gurung people as a home of Shiva. A rumored 1980s ascent by Bill Denz is unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machapuchare

question: Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on Earth, straddles the border of Nepal and Sikkim. When Joe Brown and George Band made its first ascent in 1955, they had promised Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal (ruler) of Sikkim, to honor the mountain's sacredness. What did that promise lead them to do at the very end of the climb?
answer: Stop a few steps below the true summit
choices: Stop a few steps below the true summit
Bury an offering at the true summit
Climb the last stretch only by night
context: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m / 28,169 ft), the world's third-highest mountain on the Nepal-Sikkim border, saw its first ascent in 1955 by Joe Brown and George Band, who stopped a few steps below the true summit to keep a promise to Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal of Sikkim, that the very top stay inviolate; Norman Hardie and Tony Streather did the same two days later, and many climbers still honor the custom. The name means 'the Five Treasures of the High Snow' - salt, gold, turquoise, sacred scriptures, and invincible armour - said to reveal themselves to the devout in times of peril. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga

question: Kawagarbo, at 6,740 m the highest peak in China's Yunnan province, has never been climbed. The Tibetans who live in its shadow believe standing on its summit would be a disaster for them all - and in 2001 the local government made that reverence law, permanently banning every climb. What do they believe reaching the top would cause?
answer: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
choices: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
The mountain's glaciers would flood the valleys
The winter snows would never melt again
The spirits of the dead would lose their way
context: Kawagarbo / Kawa Karpo (Meili Snow Mountain, 6,740 m / 22,113 ft), the highest peak in China's Yunnan province, has never been summited; Tibetans believe their guardian warrior god would abandon them if any human stood on top. On 3 January 1991 a nighttime avalanche killed all 17 members of a Sino-Japanese expedition, one of the deadliest mountaineering disasters in history, and in 2001 the local government permanently banned all climbing on religious grounds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawagarbo

question: Mount Kailash, a 6,638 m black pyramid rising alone above the western Tibetan plateau, is sacred at once to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and followers of Bon. Thousands of pilgrims walk the ancient path that circles its base. What is the mountaineering story of its summit?
answer: Its summit has never drawn a single expedition
choices: Its summit has never drawn a single expedition
Its summit turned back one team just short
Its summit ended one expedition in a deadly avalanche
Its summit draws pilgrims to a shrine each summer
context: Mount Kailash (6,638 m / 21,778 ft) in western Tibet has no recorded ascent at all - not stopped short like Kangchenjunga, but never attempted. It is sacred to four religions at once (Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Bon), pilgrims circle its base, and China prohibits all climbing; a 2001 Spanish permit request was refused. Reinhold Messner was reportedly offered a permit in the mid-1980s and declined, in a much-quoted but loosely worded remark suggesting climbers 'go and climb something a little harder' (treat as attributed legend). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 m, is an active volcano revered in Shinto belief as the home of the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, with shrines built at its very summit. Every summer, from July to early September, Fuji observes a tradition tied to its sacred peak. What is that tradition?
answer: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
choices: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
Its summit shrines are sealed against all visitors
Only the mountain's priests may ascend above the clouds
Fires are lit around its base but never its peak
context: Mount Fuji (3,776 m / 12,389 ft), Japan's highest peak and an active volcano, is sacred in Shinto to the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, with shrines at its summit. Rather than forbidding the top, it invites pilgrims up: an official season runs July to early September, and about 300,000 people climb each year as an act of devotion. Some sacred mountains you must not touch; others you climb to worship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji

question: High on a frozen mountainside above the Arctic town of Longyearbyen in northern Norway, a lone doorway in the snow drops into a chamber storing duplicate copies of the world's food crops — sent from gene banks in over 80 countries so farming could be restarted after a global catastrophe. What is this famous 'doomsday' backup called?
context: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, near Longyearbyen in Norway's high-Arctic Svalbard islands, opened in 2008 as a free backup for the world's roughly 1,700 other seed banks, holding duplicate samples from gene banks in over 80 countries — the Arctic World Archive, also on Svalbard, stores data rather than seeds. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was drilled 130 metres into a Longyearbyen mountainside whose rock has stayed frozen solid, year-round, for thousands of years — and that is the whole reason engineers chose this Arctic spot. Even if the electricity and every freezer broke down, the mountain itself would keep the seeds cold for free. What is this kind of frozen Arctic ground called?
context: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen year-round for years on end. Deep in the mountain the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even without power, while machines chill them further to −18°C; engineers estimate a total freezer failure would still take roughly 200 years to warm the chambers to 0°C. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: Longyearbyen, the tiny town beside the Svalbard vault, sits at about 78° North — no settled town on Earth lies closer to the North Pole. Step past the last houses and you are in true Arctic wilderness, so by old local rule every resident is urged to carry one particular thing whenever they leave town. What is it?
context: By long-standing Svalbard practice, people carry a rifle outside the settlements because of polar bears. Longyearbyen, at about 78° N, is the world's northernmost town with a permanent population over 1,000; nearby Ny-Ålesund lies even further north but is a research station, not a town. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: Everyone assumed the Svalbard Seed Vault would sit sealed until some far-off global apocalypse. But in 2015 its doors were opened for the very first withdrawal ever — 128 crates of wheat, barley, lentil and chickpea seeds were shipped out to be regrown elsewhere. What disaster had wiped out the original collection and forced the vault to prove itself?
context: The seeds belonged to the ICARDA gene bank in Aleppo, Syria, whose researchers had to abandon the city during the civil war. The vault's first-ever withdrawal — about 38,000 samples in 128 crates — was regrown at safe stations in Lebanon and Morocco, then re-deposited. The 'doomsday' vault had done its job for real. Source: https://www.seedvault.no/2019/09/11/withdrawal-of-icarda-aleppo-seeds-accomplished/

question: In 2017, alarming news reports announced that Svalbard's 'doomsday' Seed Vault had FLOODED: an unusually warm winter had thawed the frozen mountainside, and meltwater came seeping into the vault's entrance tunnel. Deep inside sat millions of irreplaceable seeds. What actually became of them?
answer: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
choices: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
about a third of the samples thawed and spoiled
a batch of the oldest wheat seeds was ruined
they were flown to the mainland as a precaution
context: The meltwater reached only about 15 m into the entrance tunnel and froze, touching some electrical gear but never getting near the seeds, which sit behind a second sealed door deeper in the mountain. No seeds were harmed. Norway later rebuilt the tunnel to be waterproof, at a cost of about $13 million. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/doomsday-seed-vault-flooded/

question: The Arctic town of Longyearbyen still has a small cemetery, but it stopped accepting new burials around 1950 — ever since, the dead have been flown south to mainland Norway instead. The reason lay underground: townsfolk had made an unsettling discovery about anyone laid to rest in the frozen soil there. What was it?
answer: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
choices: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
the shifting soil kept pushing the coffins back up to the surface
meltwater had flooded and collapsed the older graves
there was never soil soft enough to dig a proper grave
context: Burials stopped around 1950 after bodies of townsfolk who died in the 1918 flu pandemic were found still preserved in the permafrost, undecayed decades later — researchers later exhumed some hoping to study the 1918 virus. It isn't literally 'illegal to die' there; there are simply no burial options, so the dead are flown to mainland Norway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: On a point of land reaching into Sydney's harbor stands a building whose roof rises in a cluster of great white curved shells, leaning together like sails swelling in the wind above the water. Opened in 1973, which world-famous building is this?
context: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973 on Bennelong Point, its white 'shells' reading as sails over the water. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most recognized buildings on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: Beside the Opera House, a single giant steel arch leaps clear across Sydney's harbor -- opened in 1932, one of the world's widest steel-arch bridges. Struck by its shape, Sydneysiders nicknamed the Harbour Bridge after a common object. Which one?
context: The Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932, is one of the world's widest long-span steel-arch bridges. Sydneysiders looked at its great curved silhouette and dubbed it 'the Coathanger,' and the name stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: For years engineers were stumped by the Opera House's swooping roof shells: each seemed a different, impossible curve to cast in concrete. In 1961 the architect, Jorn Utzon, cracked it -- he saw that every shell could be cut from the surface of one and the same imaginary form, so all would share a single curve. What form?
context: Utzon's 1961 'spherical solution' let every shell be cut from the surface of one imaginary sphere (about 75 m radius), so all shared a single curve and could be mass-cast from common moulds -- the breakthrough that finally made the roof buildable. Source: sydneyoperahouse.com/our-story/the-spherical-solution

question: From across the harbor the Opera House roof gleams a smooth white, but up close it never looks flat or plain -- in changing light it seems to shimmer and shift. What actually covers the giant shells?
answer: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
choices: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
thousands of polished white marble slabs
hundreds of enameled white steel panels
many coats of specially mixed white paint
context: The shells wear about 1,056,006 tiles made in Sweden by Hoganas, in two finishes -- glossy white and matte cream -- laid in a chevron pattern so the roof shimmers and never looks flat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: The Opera House stands on a narrow tongue of land jutting into Sydney's harbor, where a fort and later a tram depot once stood before both were cleared away for it. What is this point called?
context: Bennelong Point honors Bennelong, an Aboriginal man who lived alongside the first British governor, Arthur Phillip. A fort and then a tram depot (Fort Macquarie) stood there before both were demolished for the Opera House. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: The Sydney Harbour Bridge is a single steel arch springing high over the water. Today, roped to a safety line, adventurous visitors can do something on it that almost no other great bridge in the world allows. What is it?
answer: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
choices: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
walk a glass floor hung beneath the road deck
ride a lift up a stone pylon to a lookout
abseil down a steel cable to the water below
context: On 'BridgeClimb,' visitors roped to a safety line ascend the steel arch to its summit -- 134 metres, more than 400 feet, above the harbor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Sailing into Sydney's great harbour, Port Jackson, you pass the rocky Heads at its mouth and the water fans out into a maze of deep coves branching inland for miles -- sheltered and deep enough for the greatest ships in the world to ride in safety. What do geographers call this kind of coastal feature?
context: A ria is a river valley drowned by rising seas -- here, Port Jackson's ancient valleys flooded as Ice Age ice melted, giving Sydney a shoreline that branches for miles and runs deep enough for the greatest ships. (A fjord, by contrast, is a drowned GLACIER-carved valley.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson

question: Governor Arthur Phillip steered the First Fleet into Sydney's harbor in 1788 and was stunned by its size and shelter. He wrote that here was 'the finest harbour in the world,' with room for a fleet so vast he fixed it in a single ringing phrase. What did he say could ride there in perfect safety?
answer: a thousand ships of the line
choices: a thousand ships of the line
a hundred ships of the line
every ship in the Southern seas
context: Arriving in Port Jackson in 1788, Phillip called it 'the finest Harbour in the World, in which a thousand Sail of the line may ride in the most perfect security.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson

question: At the grand opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge in 1932, huge crowds waited for Premier Jack Lang to cut the ceremonial ribbon. Suddenly a man in military uniform, Francis de Groot, spurred his horse forward and -- before Lang could act -- did something that stole the moment and got him arrested. What did de Groot do?
answer: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
choices: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
seized the scissors and hurled them into the harbor
chained his horse across the empty roadway
tore down the official banner overhead
context: Before Premier Lang could cut the ribbon, de Groot galloped up and slashed it with his cavalry sword, declaring the bridge open 'in the name of the people.' He was arrested and the ribbon retied for the official ceremony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Sydney's sea-cliffs, the rocky 'Heads' at its harbor mouth, and its grand old buildings all glow the same warm honey-gold, cut from the local stone the whole city rests on. Braided rivers laid down this sandstone grain by grain around 230 million years ago, back when the very first dinosaurs were appearing. In which geological period did that happen?
context: Sydney rests on Hawkesbury sandstone, laid down by braided rivers ~230-240 million years ago in the Triassic. Quarried for the city's cliffs, harbor 'Heads,' and grand old buildings, its warm color earned nicknames like 'yellowblock' and 'yellow gold.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkesbury_sandstone

question: Jorn Utzon, the Danish architect who dreamed up the Opera House's soaring shells, did not stay to complete them. In 1966, worn down by bitter fights over money and control, he resigned and left Australia, and a local team finished the building. Honored at last with architecture's Pritzker Prize in 2003, Utzon died in 2008 -- one quiet sorrow shadowing his triumph. What was it?
answer: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
choices: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
he had asked to have his name struck from it
he had spent his last years suing the government
he had never designed another major building
context: Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes over money and control; an Australian team finished the building. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but died in 2008 having never returned to Australia to see his masterpiece complete. Source: classical-music.com (Sydney Opera House history)

question: In the early 1900s the French conservators of the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient restored temple after temple across Angkor. At Ta Prohm -- where huge roots had poured over the walls and cracked the roofs apart -- they made a famous decision. What did they do with the temple?
answer: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
choices: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
They felled the trees and rebuilt the galleries stone by stone.
They dismantled the temple and moved it to safer ground.
They cleared the roots and laid a formal garden around it.
context: When the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient restored Angkor in the early 1900s, they deliberately left Ta Prohm tangled in forest 'as a concession to the general taste for the picturesque.' The conservator Maurice Glaize said it was chosen because it had 'best merged with the jungle, but not yet to the point of becoming a part of it' -- wild enough to be spectacular, sound enough not to collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Ta Prohm is now the most famous 'lost temple' in the world, and locals point tourists to it by a nickname borrowed from Hollywood. In 2001 an adventure blockbuster filmed its star sprinting through these root-choked galleries, and the temple has carried the movie's name ever since. Which film was it?
context: The 2001 film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider, starring Angelina Jolie, was shot among Ta Prohm's roots -- Lara picks a jasmine flower and falls through the earth into the ruins -- and the site has been the 'Tomb Raider temple' ever since, the world's most famous 'lost temple.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Enormous pale roots pour over Ta Prohm's walls and pry the stone blocks apart, and most of them belong to a single giant species that towers above the temple. What tree is it that holds this ruin in its grip?
context: The dominant giant is the silk-cotton tree (Tetrameles nudiflora, locally called 'spung'), joined by smaller strangler figs (Ficus gibbosa). The trees never grew up from the ground: birds dropped their seeds onto the temple's gallery roofs, the seedlings took hold high up, and their roots crept DOWN through the walls, splitting the stonework as they descended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Ta Prohm was not only a temple but a working monastery, and its own founding stele -- still standing at the site -- boasts of the workforce it took to keep this one complex running: hundreds of dancers, dozens of high priests, thousands living inside the walls, and many more in the villages that fed it. All told, how many people did the inscription say served Ta Prohm?
context: The figure comes from Ta Prohm's foundation stele (inscription K.273), which records that nearly 80,000 people were needed to maintain and serve the monastery -- including 615 dancers, 18 high priests, and 12,640 people living inside the temple walls. Its real name was Rajavihara, the 'Royal Monastery,' built by the Khmer king Jayavarman VII and consecrated in 1186; scholars suspect the stele's numbers were inflated to glorify the king. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm  (Legend.)

question: Agra's Taj Mahal is famous as a monument to love, but it is truly a tomb. Emperor Shah Jahan raised this vast white marble hall over the grave of one person he lost in 1631, mourning so deeply that he gave up music and fine clothes for two years. For whom was it built?
context: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. Shah Jahan's grief became a building project that ran for roughly two decades, turning a personal loss into the most beautiful tomb on earth. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The Taj Mahal's tomb gleams white because its brick core is entirely sheathed in one prized stone, quarried more than 300 km from Agra and dragged there by oxen and elephants. Masons chose it for a whiteness no nearer rock could match. Which stone sheaths the Taj Mahal?
context: The white marble came from the Makrana quarries in Rajasthan, still worked today, while the red sandstone of the surrounding complex came from Fatehpur Sikri. The other choices are famous white marbles too -- Carrara from Italy, Pentelic from Greece, Proconnesian from Turkey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Visitors to the Taj Mahal swear the tomb wears a different color at every hour -- blush pink at dawn, dazzling white at midday, and soft gold beneath a full moon. Photographers return year after year to catch each fresh shade. Why does the tomb seem to change color through the day?
choices: the dome is sheathed in gold leaf
colored glass fills the arched windows
river mist tints the stone at dawn
context: Nothing is ever painted or coated. The fine Makrana marble is faintly translucent and simply reflects whatever light falls on it, so the tomb glows pink at sunrise, white at noon, and gold under the moon. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Inside the Taj Mahal, two beautifully carved marble tombs sit at the center of the great domed hall, ringed by an inlaid screen, and thousands of visitors file past them each day believing they stand over the dead. But Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal are not there. Where do their bodies actually lie?
answer: in a plain vault one floor below
choices: in a plain vault one floor below
inside the hollow of the great dome
under the mosque beside the tomb
context: The ornate tombs on display are false cenotaphs. The real graves sit in a plain, undecorated lower chamber, laid north-south with the faces turned toward Mecca -- a Mughal convention that kept the actual resting place simple and hidden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The four slender minarets at the corners of the Taj Mahal's platform were not built standing straight up: each leans about two degrees outward, away from the great dome. Study of the tomb has shown this tilt was deliberate, worked in by its Mughal builders. What were they planning for?
context: The outward lean is an earthquake-safety trick centuries ahead of its time: if a quake ever toppled the towers, their built-in tilt would carry them falling away from the tomb rather than crashing down onto the dome. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: The Taj Mahal's white marble is scattered with flowers, vines, and leaves so finely shaded that visitors take them for paintings. They are not paint at all: look closely at a single blossom and you find it built from as many as 64 separate pieces. What are the Taj's flowers actually made of?
answer: cut gemstones set into the marble
choices: cut gemstones set into the marble
colored enamel fired onto the surface
context: The craft is pietra dura, called parchin kari here: chips of agate, jasper, carnelian, and lapis cut and polished flush into the marble so a whole garden of flowers glows in stone. A single cenotaph blossom can hold 64 inlaid pieces. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: A famous story says the grieving Shah Jahan meant to raise a second Taj Mahal in black marble on the far bank of the Yamuna -- a dark twin to hold his own tomb, joined to the white one by a bridge. Ruins of dark stone across the river seemed to prove it. When archaeologists excavated those ruins in the 1990s, what did they find?
answer: white marble blocks blackened by age
choices: white marble blocks blackened by age
the foundations of an unfinished black tomb
a buried cache of black marble slabs
a bridge footing pointing across the river
context: The 'Black Taj' is a legend. The 1990s excavation showed the dark ruins across the river were ordinary white marble stones darkened by centuries of weathering -- there was never a black twin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Tallinn's Old Town, the medieval heart of Estonia's capital, is all narrow cobbled lanes, red-tiled roofs and church spires, ringed by a stone wall with pointed watchtowers. Most such medieval town-centres are long gone -- bombed flat or made into museums. What is remarkable about Tallinn's?
answer: it is still a lived-in, working town
choices: it is still a lived-in, working town
it was rebuilt from rubble after the war
it is an open-air museum of moved houses
it is a modern replica built for tourists
context: Tallinn's Old Town is a rarity: a still-lived-in medieval city of cobbled lanes and red-tiled roofs, not a ruin or a museum but a working town. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1997 for its 'exceptionally intact 13th-century city plan' -- one of Europe's best-preserved medieval towns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town' (UNESCO 1997).

question: When Tallinn's town wall was finished it bristled with 46 defensive towers along a rampart up to 16 metres high. Most medieval walls have long since crumbled away to nothing -- but how many of Tallinn's towers still stand guard today?
answer: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
choices: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
all forty-six, every one still intact
just one lone surviving gate tower
none at all, only their foundations
context: In its 16th-century prime Tallinn's wall ran about 2.4 km, stood 14-16 m high and up to 3 m thick, and carried 46 towers -- one of the most fortified towns in northern Europe. About half survives today: nearly 2 km of wall and around two dozen towers still stand, one of the best-preserved medieval city walls in northern Europe. Source: inyourpocket.com 'Town Fortifications'; historyhit.com 'Tallinn City Walls'.

question: Tallinn is really two towns stacked together: down below sprawled the merchants' lower town, while up on the hilltop sat Toompea, the upper town of nobles, clergy and whoever ruled the land -- Danes, German knights, Swedes and Russians each held it in turn. The two stayed separate towns for centuries. What sits atop Toompea today?
context: Toompea, the upper town on the hill, was held in turn by Danes, the Livonian Order, Swedes and Russians; Estonia's parliament, the Riigikogu, meets in Toompea Castle today. The merchants' lower town spread below, and the two stayed separate towns until they were administratively united in 1878. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: Tallinn spent the Middle Ages as a rich merchant town on the Baltic, its harbour crowded with cargo ships and its guildhalls and spired churches raised on trading profits. Tallinn owed that wealth to membership in one great medieval alliance of northern European trading towns. Which league was it?
context: The Hanseatic League was the great medieval merchant network of the Baltic and North Seas. Tallinn's guildhalls and spired churches survive so nearly intact that UNESCO listed the whole Old Town in 1997 as a preserved town of 'medieval and Hanseatic origin'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town'.

question: Tallinn's St Olaf's Church has been rebuilt again and again: its towering spire has drawn lightning at least eight times and burned the whole church to the ground three times. Sailors far out in the Gulf of Finland still use it as a landmark. By old tradition, before the great fire of 1625 that spire had earned Tallinn one astonishing world record. What was it?
choices: the tallest lighthouse in the Baltic
the largest church in northern Europe
the northernmost cathedral in the world
context: By tradition St Olaf's spire soared to about 159 m and was the tallest building in the world from 1549 until lightning burned it in 1625 -- though historians reckon the true medieval height was more like 115-125 m, so the record is a claim, not a certainty. The steeple has been struck by lightning at least eight times and the church has burned down three times; it still stands about 124 m tall, a landmark visible far out at sea. Legend/claim flagged. Source: Wikipedia, 'St. Olaf's Church, Tallinn'; visitestonia.com.

question: Toompea's hill fooled attackers who took it for a man-made rampart -- but it is wholly natural. It is the tip of the Baltic Klint, a pale limestone cliff-line running for hundreds of kilometres along Estonia's coast, its 20-30-metre drop handing the upper town a ready-made wall of rock. What is the general geographic name for this kind of long, steep coastal cliff-line?
context: Toompea's hill is part of the North Estonian Klint, a subsection of the Baltic Klint -- a pale limestone escarpment that runs for hundreds of km along the coast. 'Klint' is the local name for this kind of long cliff-line; geographers call it an escarpment (a long steep face where higher ground drops to lower). Rising 20-30 m above the lower town, it gave the upper town a natural rampart before a single wall was built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: When Mount Tambora exploded on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa in April 1815, the blast was heard about 2,600 km away on the island of Sumatra. It sounded so exactly like heavy gunfire that the colonial troops there were sure a battle had begun. What did those soldiers on Sumatra do?
answer: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
choices: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
Fired their own cannons in reply to the distant booming
Rushed to load ships and evacuate the governor to safety
Fled far inland, certain that warships were shelling the coast
context: The eyewitness detail comes from Sir Stamford Raffles's memoir, which records that the noise was 'almost universally attributed to distant cannon.' Tambora's 1815 blast was the largest eruption in recorded human history, and its roar carried roughly 2,600 km (1,600 mi) to Sumatra. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora  (Legend.)

question: Mount Tambora's 1815 eruption on Sumbawa killed about 71,000 people -- more than any other eruption ever recorded. Yet only around 11,000 of them died from the eruption itself: the choking ash, the fiery flows, and the tsunamis it hurled ashore. What killed the far larger number in the weeks and months afterward?
answer: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
choices: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
Floods, as rivers dammed by falling debris burst downstream
Wildfires that spread from the still-glowing ash
Fresh eruptions from the crater the following spring
context: About 71,000 people died in all -- some 10,000-12,000 in the eruption itself (ash, pyroclastic flows, and 4-metre tsunamis), and tens of thousands more from the starvation and disease that followed once the ash smothered the fields of Sumbawa and nearby islands. It remains the deadliest eruption in recorded history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Tambora's 1815 eruption threw so much dust and haze around the globe that the following year, 1816, brought freakish cold to lands half a world away. In New England, snow fell in June and killing frosts returned in July and August; across Europe and North America the grain harvests failed. By what haunting name did people come to remember 1816?
context: Snow lay about 46 cm (18 in) deep at Cabot, Vermont on June 8, 1816, and Americans nicknamed the disaster 'Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.' The freakish cold was traced back to the dust and haze from Tambora's eruption the year before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: Beside Lake Geneva in the cold, storm-dark summer of 1816 -- its skies dimmed by Tambora's distant haze -- a group of English writers were trapped indoors for days. To pass the time, Lord Byron challenged each of them to write a ghost story. Eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley took up the dare and began a novel that would become one of the most famous horror stories ever written. What did she start writing that gloomy summer?
context: The gathering was at Byron's rented Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva. The same ghost-story contest produced John Polidori's 'The Vampyre' (an ancestor of Dracula), and Byron wrote his apocalyptic poem 'Darkness,' imagining a world where the sun goes out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: The failed harvests of 1816 sent oat prices soaring -- from about 12 cents to 92 cents a bushel -- and across Europe horses grew too costly to feed. Searching for a way to get around without a horse, the German inventor Karl Drais built and rode a wooden 'running machine' he unveiled in 1817. That strange contraption, born of a year of hunger, is remembered as the direct ancestor of what everyday machine?
context: With oats scarce and expensive, Karl Drais's pedal-less 'running machine,' or draisine, of 1817 is widely remembered as the direct ancestor of the bicycle -- a chain running from a volcano in Indonesia to the machine kids ride today. The famine is the commonly cited spur for his invention. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: The deepest wonder of Tambora is how a mountain in Indonesia could chill the entire planet. The eruption flung tens of millions of tonnes of sulfur gas far above the weather, into the stratosphere, where it turned into a fine haze of sulfate droplets that circled the globe and lingered for more than a year -- long enough to dim the sun and cool the whole planet by more than half a degree. What did this high haze physically do to the sunlight passing through it?
answer: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
choices: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
Absorbed it up high, warming the haze but not the ground
Bent it away from the equator and toward the poles
Scattered it into a red glow that carried no heat
context: Tambora lofted an estimated 60 megatons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed sulfate aerosols that reflected sunlight and cooled the globe by roughly 0.4-0.7 C for over a year. The eruption column reached about 43 km (27 mi) up; the resulting 'dry fog' dimmed the sun enough that people could see sunspots with the naked eye, and it tinted the lurid skies in J.M.W. Turner's paintings. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Tambora did not only bury villages -- it wiped out an entire small kingdom on Sumbawa, along with its people and their language, which vanished from the earth in 1815. Nearly two centuries later, in 2004, archaeologists dug down through 3 m of ash and uncovered a house frozen in that final moment: bronze bowls, iron tools, and two of the kingdom's people lying exactly where the eruption caught them. Because of finds like these, Tambora's lost kingdom earned a nickname borrowed from another famous lost city. What is it called?
context: In a 2004 dig, volcanologist Haraldur Sigurdsson uncovered the buried house under about 3 m of ash. The Tambora people's language, thought to be related to the Mon-Khmer tongues of mainland Southeast Asia, was wiped out with them. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambora_culture ; https://today.uri.edu/news/uri-volcanologist-discovers-lost-kingdom-of-tambora/  (Legend.)

question: In the Scottish Highlands, a tartan's whole criss-cross design comes from one small block of coloured stripes repeated over and over across the cloth — design that block and you've designed the tartan. What do weavers call it?
context: The repeating block is the 'sett' — fix the sett and the whole tartan follows, since the same sequence of stripes just repeats across the cloth. Warp and weft are the lengthwise and crosswise threads; twill is the diagonal 2/2 weave tartan is woven in. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartan

question: On a cold night out on the open hills of the Scottish Highlands, a clansman needed no bedroll: he unbelted the tartan he had worn all day, rolled himself in its folds like a blanket, and slept where he lay. Which Highland garment was this?
context: The feileadh mor, or 'great kilt' (belted plaid), really was a single four-to-six-yard length of tartan belted at the waist with the top draped over the shoulder. The image of a Highlander unbelting it to sleep rolled up inside like a blanket is the traditional picture of how handy the one-piece garment was. The tailored knee-length 'small kilt' came later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_kilt  (Legend.)

question: The oldest piece of tartan-like cloth ever found in Scotland — the 'Falkirk tartan,' woven around the 3rd century AD — survived because someone had jammed the scrap of checked wool into the mouth of a buried clay pot as a stopper. What was the little rag of tartan keeping sealed inside?
answer: a hoard of Roman silver coins
choices: a hoard of Roman silver coins
the ashes of a cremated chief
context: The 'Falkirk tartan,' from about the 3rd century AD, is the oldest tartan-like cloth found in Scotland. The checked scrap of undyed wool had been used to plug a pot holding almost 2,000 Roman coins — a humble rag stopping up a small fortune. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartan

question: After the 1745 Jacobite rising ended at Culloden in 1746, Britain's government turned on the everyday clothing of the Scottish Highlands. Its Dress Act of 1746 took direct aim at the kilt and tartan. What did the law do to Highland dress?
choices: required a licence to wear it
context: The Dress Act of 1746, part of the Act of Proscription after the Jacobite defeat at Culloden, outlawed the plaid, the little kilt, and tartan for men and boys across the Highlands — one of the rare times a government has banned a pattern of cloth outright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Under the Dress Act, a Highland man caught wearing the kilt for the first time was jailed for six months. A second offence brought a far harsher sentence — the same one courts handed to thieves and forgers. What was done to a repeat offender?
choices: branded on the cheek with hot iron
context: A first offence under the Dress Act meant six months in prison; a second meant being 'transported to any of His Majesty's plantations beyond the seas' for seven years — exile for the crime of wearing your own clan's cloth. The ban ran 36 years before its repeal in 1782. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Many Highland families treat their clan tartan as an ancient badge handed down for centuries. In fact the tidy rule that each clan owns one fixed pattern was cemented at a single spectacle, when the novelist Sir Walter Scott persuaded the chiefs to parade in matching setts. At which event did this 'invented tradition' take hold?
answer: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
choices: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
the Jacobite defeat at Culloden in 1746
the lifting of the tartan ban in 1782
Queen Victoria's move to Balmoral in the 1850s
context: When King George IV visited Edinburgh in 1822, Sir Walter Scott choreographed a tartan pageant so lavish it fixed the 'one clan, one tartan' image in the public mind — largely a romantic invention, not ancient law. The stout king even wore a Royal Stuart kilt cut so short he added pink tights to cover his knees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visit_of_George_IV_to_Scotland

question: Many of Scotland's 'official' clan tartans trace back to the Vestiarium Scoticum, an 1842 book that claimed to copy a lost ancient manuscript listing each clan's true sett — but scholars proved it a fake. Its two authors, Welsh-born brothers named Allen, propped up the hoax with a bold lie about their own ancestry. What did they claim to be?
choices: heirs of the executed Lord Lovat
context: The Vestiarium Scoticum (1842) claimed to reproduce a lost ancient manuscript giving each clan's true sett, and many 'official' clan tartans still trace to it — but it was exposed as a forgery. Its authors, the Welsh-born Allen brothers, styled themselves the 'Sobieski Stuarts' and falsely claimed to be grandsons of Bonnie Prince Charlie, dressing fake ancient tartans in fake royal glamour. Rob Roy MacGregor, Simon Fraser (Lord Lovat, beheaded after Culloden), and Flora MacDonald were all real Jacobite-era Highlanders, but the brothers claimed no descent from them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestiarium_Scoticum

question: On Washington's Olympic Peninsula, the Hoh Rain Forest is soaked by about 140 inches of rain a year -- the wettest forest in the lower 48 states -- and every trunk hangs heavy with moss and lichen. Yet it grows in a cool northern climate, not the steamy tropics. What do we call a rainforest like this, drenched and mossy but growing in the cool?
context: A cool, drenched, moss-hung forest like the Hoh is a TEMPERATE rainforest -- rainforest without the tropics. The North American rule of thumb: cool (mean temperature about 4-12 degC) and soaked with more than 140 cm (55 in) of rain a year, so a rainforest does not have to be hot. The Hoh's giants are Sitka spruce and western hemlock, draped in 'lettuce lichen.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoh_Rainforest and /wiki/Temperate_rainforest.

question: The tallest living thing on Earth is not an animal but a tree -- it stands over 116 metres (381 feet), taller than a 35-storey tower, in the cool, fog-drenched forests of northern California near the Pacific shore, where two climbers found and named it Hyperion in 2006. What kind of tree is Hyperion?
context: Hyperion is a coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens), measured at 116.22 m (381.3 ft) -- the tallest known living tree on Earth. Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor found it in Redwood National Park on 25 August 2006. In 2022 the National Park Service closed the area (fines up to $5,000) after visitors trampled the ferns at its base, and its exact spot is kept secret. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperion_(tree).

question: In Washington's Hoh Rain Forest, walk beneath the mossy giants and you may meet an eerie sight -- a row of young hemlocks and spruces standing in a dead-straight line, evenly spaced as if set out with a ruler. What lined the seedlings up in so perfect a row?
answer: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
choices: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
park rangers replanted that strip in rows after a wildfire
their seeds washed into a dead-straight crack in the bedrock
they followed the line of an old logging road through the grove
context: The rotting trunk was a 'nurse log' -- as it decays, moss, needles and soil fill it and seedlings take root along its length. When the log finally crumbles away, the young trees are left standing in a dead-straight 'colonnade' that traces exactly where the old giant fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nurse_log.

question: On the seaward side of Washington's Olympic Mountains the forest drinks over 140 inches of rain a year, yet a dry scrubland barely 15 miles east of the peaks gets only about 8 inches. What makes one side of the very same mountains a soaking rainforest and the other side almost a desert?
answer: moist ocean air is forced up the western slope, cools, and rains out before crossing the peaks
choices: moist ocean air is forced up the western slope, cools, and rains out before crossing the peaks
the cold ocean current offshore chills the eastern air until it can no longer hold rain
the eastern side sits under a belt of sinking dry air that rings the globe at that latitude
warm winds from the south drench the western slope and leave the eastern side dry
context: This is orographic rain: moist Pacific air is shoved up the windward slope, cools, and dumps its water before crossing the crest -- so the seaward side can get over 140 in a year while a rain-shadow desert 15 miles east gets about 8 in. The same recipe grows every temperate rainforest on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orographic_lift.

question: The Pacific Northwest has a mirror twin far to the south: on the coast of southern Chile, a cool, dripping forest is pinned on a narrow strip between the open Pacific and the wall of the Andes, drenched by up to 6,000 mm of rain a year. It is the second-largest temperate rainforest on Earth. What is this Chilean rainforest called?
context: It is the Valdivian rainforest, named for the Chilean city of Valdivia -- a cool, dripping forest getting 1,000 to over 6,000 mm of rain a year, the second-largest temperate rainforest on Earth after the Pacific Northwest. Its signature tree, the alerce (Fitzroya), is a cypress relative; one giant, the Gran Abuelo, was ring-counted at 3,622 years in 1993. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdivian_temperate_rainforest and /wiki/Fitzroya.

question: New Zealand's far southwest is one of the rainiest corners of the planet: westerly gales tear in off the Tasman Sea, and Milford Sound is soaked by about 8,000 mm (310 inches) of rain on roughly 200 days a year, feeding a dense rainforest of southern beech. What is this drenched southwest region of New Zealand called?
context: It is Fiordland. Westerlies off the Tasman Sea are forced straight up over the mountains, so Milford Sound catches about 8,000 mm (310 in) of rain on some 200 days a year -- among the wettest inhabited places on Earth. The rainforest is southern beech, wrapped around the glacier-carved fiords that give the region its name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiordland.

question: Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are the forests people name first as the planet's great carbon stores. Yet an Australian study weighed the carbon held in cool, wet temperate rainforests -- the mossy giants of places like Tasmania -- against tropical forest. Acre for acre, how does a temperate rainforest's carbon store compare?
answer: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
choices: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
it holds only a small fraction of a tropical rainforest's carbon
it holds almost exactly as much as a tropical rainforest
its stored carbon leaks back out faster than a tropical rainforest's
context: Acre for acre, temperate rainforest can out-store the tropics.
