An Australian National University study (Keith, Mackey & Lindenmayer, PNAS 2009) measured 377 tons of carbon per hectare above ground in temperate moist forest versus 171 tons in tropical rainforest; Australia's Mountain Ash forests reached up to 2,844 tons per hectare including roots. Being cool, they rot slowly, so the wood piles up -- among the densest carbon stores on land. Source: news.mongabay.com/2009/07/temperate-forests-store-more-carbon-than-tropical-forests-finds-study/.

question: The Aztec (Mexica) built their capital, Tenochtitlan, on an island with no farmland of its own — a city ringed entirely by shallow water, high in the mountains of central Mexico. On which lake did they raise it?
context: Tenochtitlan was founded on islands in shallow, salty Lake Texcoco, traditionally dated to about 1325. Lake Pátzcuaro and Lake Chapala are real lakes elsewhere in Mexico; Titicaca lies far to the south, high in the Andes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Mexica legend says their god Huitzilopochtli promised them a homeland and told them to settle where they saw a certain sign. On a nopal cactus in the marsh they finally spotted it — and there they founded Tenochtitlan. What did they see on the cactus?
context: The eagle-on-a-cactus omen is the Mexica founding legend — and that exact image sits at the centre of Mexico's flag and coat of arms today. (The modern flag adds a serpent in the eagle's beak; the oldest Aztec pictures show just the eagle on the cactus.) Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan' and 'Coat of arms of Mexico'.

question: Tenochtitlan had no fields of its own, so the Mexica staked out long rectangular beds in the shallow lakebed, piling up dredged mud and rotting plants and lashing them down with willow roots. So rich they cropped up to seven times a year, these lake-garden plots were called what?
context: Chinampas are often called 'floating gardens,' though they were rooted to the lakebed, not floating. Andenes are Inca terraces, waru waru are Andean raised fields, and a milpa is a maize-bean-squash plot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Tenochtitlan's garden plots were divided by a grid of canals, and its people moved about mostly by canoe, gliding between the houses on the water. The awestruck Spanish nicknamed the canal-laced island city after which European city?
context: The Spanish called Tenochtitlan 'the Venice of the New World.' Amsterdam, Bruges, and Stockholm are all famously threaded with canals too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Three broad raised roads carried travellers across the water to island Tenochtitlan — running north to Tepeyac, south to Iztapalapa, and west to Tlacopan, each broad enough for ten horsemen abreast. The Mexica gave these causeways a defence that could seal the city off from an attacking army. What was it?
context: The raised roads across the water are called causeways; gaps in them were spanned by wooden bridges the Mexica could pull up, cutting the island off. Cortés had to fight past exactly this defence in 1521. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Because Lake Texcoco was too salty to drink, the Mexica piped fresh water into Tenochtitlan from the springs of Chapultepec, a wooded hill to the west, through a stone aqueduct built with two parallel channels side by side. Why two channels instead of one?
answer: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
so one carried water and the other carried off sewage
so the second doubled the flow in the dry season
so a cracked channel could be swapped for the spare
context: Aztec rulers began the twin aqueduct around 1418; one channel carried water while the other was scrubbed clean, so the city never ran dry. Moctezuma reportedly bathed every day thanks to the fresh Chapultepec water. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chapultepec aqueduct'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: The Aztec way of farming on lake-bed plots did not die with Tenochtitlan. In the canals of one district in southern Mexico City, people still pole flat boats between the surviving old garden plots today, drawing visitors from all over the world. What is this 'floating-garden' district called?
context: Xochimilco, in southern Mexico City, still keeps working chinampas and canals — a living remnant of Tenochtitlan's farming, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: At the sacred heart of Tenochtitlan rose a great stepped pyramid crowned by two shrines standing side by side at its summit — one to Huitzilopochtli, god of war, the other to Tlaloc, god of rain. By what name is this twin-shrined pyramid known?
context: The Templo Mayor was the sacred centre of the Mexica world; its twin shrines honoured war and rain, the two forces the city lived by. The Pyramid of the Sun stands at Teotihuacan; El Castillo and the Caracol at Chichén Itzá. Source: Grokipedia, 'Templo Mayor'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Just north of Tenochtitlan lay a market so vast that Cortés claimed sixty thousand people came to trade there every single day — gold, obsidian blades, turkeys, medicinal herbs, and cotton cloth, all under one roar of haggling voices. In which neighbouring sister-city was this great market held?
context: The market of Tlatelolco, Tenochtitlan's twin city, astonished the Spanish; friar Sahagún and soldier Bernal Díaz put the daily crowd at 20,000–40,000, Cortés at 60,000. Texcoco and Tlacopan were Tenochtitlan's partners in the Triple Alliance; Azcapotzalco was an older rival city. Source: mexicolore.co.uk, 'The great market of Tlatelolco'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: After Spanish forces and their native allies razed Tenochtitlan in 1521, they built their colonial capital right on its ruins. The new city flooded again and again, so over the following centuries engineers did something drastic to Lake Texcoco itself. What was it?
choices: they dammed it into a reservoir
they dredged it into a harbour
context: The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 was both a real razing — Cortés and his allies besieged the island for over 90 days, cutting its aqueduct — and a real epidemic collapse, as smallpox swept the city beforehand. To end the floods afterward, the Spanish drained Lake Texcoco almost completely; it shrank by more than 95%, leaving modern Mexico City on the dry old lakebed. Source: Grokipedia, 'Lake Texcoco'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: In 1978, electricity workers digging a trench beneath the streets of downtown Mexico City struck the edge of a colossal carved stone disc more than three metres across — the find that led archaeologists straight to buried Tenochtitlan's holiest temple. Whose dismembered body was carved across the great disc?
context: The Coyolxauhqui Stone, over three metres wide, shows the Aztec moon goddess dismembered by her brother Huitzilopochtli in myth. Struck by chance on 21 February 1978, it triggered one of the largest urban digs in history, uncovering the Templo Mayor beneath modern Mexico City. Source: smarthistory.org, 'Templo Mayor: the Coyolxauhqui Stone'; Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'.

question: Modern Mexico City stands on the soft clay bed of Lake Texcoco, the Aztec lake the Spanish drained long ago. As that old lakebed dries and squeezes together, parts of the city drop by as much as 50 centimetres a year, and the great Metropolitan Cathedral visibly leans. What is the geologist's single word for this slow sinking of the land?
context: Subsidence — the gradual sinking of ground — has lowered parts of Mexico City more than 10 metres in a century as the drained lakebed compacts. Erosion wears land away, liquefaction turns soil to slurry in an earthquake, and subduction is one tectonic plate sliding beneath another. (Tenochtitlan's peak population, an estimated 200,000–400,000, is a modern estimate, not a census.) Source: ScienceAlert, 'How fast Mexico City is sinking'; Grokipedia, 'Sinking cities'.

question: Dead straight and about 40 m wide, a ceremonial road runs for over 2 km through the heart of the ruined city of Teotihuacan, lined with flat platforms. Long after the city was abandoned, the Aztecs decided those platforms must be the tombs of ancient lords, and named the road to match. What did they call it?
context: The Aztecs came upon Teotihuacan centuries after its fall and, certain the platforms flanking the great road were royal tombs, named it Miccaotli -- the Avenue of the Dead. They were wrong: the platforms are temple bases, not graves. The road runs about 40 m wide and some 4 km long. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'  (Legend.)

question: Rising beside the great avenue at Teotihuacan, one flat-topped mountain of stone and rubble climbs about 65 m, its square base nearly 230 m to a side. Which of Teotihuacan's pyramids is this?
choices: the Temple of the Feathered Serpent
context: The Pyramid of the Sun stands about 65.5 m (215 ft) high on a base roughly 230 m square -- the largest building at Teotihuacan and one of the biggest in ancient Mesoamerica. Its name, like the city's, was given by the much later Aztecs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Sun.'

question: Around 500 CE, Teotihuacan was among the largest cities on Earth, well over 100,000 people living in its stone compounds. For all the ruins archaeologists have unearthed, one basic fact about these people can no one recover. Which?
context: Teotihuacan's own people left no readable record of what they called themselves or their city; 'Teotihuacan' is a name the Aztecs coined centuries later, so scholars simply call them 'the Teotihuacanos.' Population estimates for its peak run from 100,000 to well above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Most families at Teotihuacan lived in broad single-story stone apartment compounds whose inner walls blazed with painted murals. The most famous, at a compound called Tepantitla, shows a great mountain pouring out streams of water, with dozens of tiny human figures scattered across the land below. What kind of place do scholars believe this mural portrays?
answer: a watery paradise of the afterlife
choices: a watery paradise of the afterlife
a great flood that drowned the valley
a map of the city's canals
the mountain where its stone was quarried
context: The Tepantitla mural, often called the Paradise of Tlaloc (Tlalocan), is usually read as a blissful, watery afterlife tied to the rain god -- the mountain gushes water while people swim, sing and gather flowers below. Teotihuacan's apartment walls were covered in such vivid paintings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan'; Tepantitla murals.

question: The name we use today, 'Teotihuacan,' did not belong to the people who built the city. It was coined much later by the Aztecs, who found ruins grander than anything they knew and gave them a Nahuatl name so lofty it is now the only name the city has. What does 'Teotihuacan' mean?
context: Awed by the abandoned city, the Aztecs named it Teotihuacan in their Nahuatl language -- usually glossed as 'birthplace of the gods' or 'the place where the gods were born.' It was to them a sacred site of creation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Teotihuacan's workshops held a near-monopoly on a prized material dug from the nearby Sierra de Pachuca: a fine volcanic glass called obsidian, razor-sharp when knapped and traded across Mesoamerica. Unlike the ordinary black glass everyone else used, Teotihuacan's obsidian had one unmistakable quality. What made it instantly recognizable?
context: The Sierra de Pachuca yielded a rare golden-green obsidian found almost nowhere else in Mesoamerica. Teotihuacan controlled its supply, working it into blades, mirrors and ornaments that traveled hundreds of miles in trade -- a signature of the city's reach. Source: Ponomarenko 2004; Tulane University research on Pachuca green obsidian.

question: When Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent was raised around 150-200 CE, its builders marked the dedication with a mass offering, and archaeologists have since dug up the pits beneath and around the pyramid. What did the builders bury there to consecrate the temple?
context: More than 200 people -- many with their hands bound, apparently war captives and soldiers -- were sacrificed and buried in pits beneath and around the Temple of the Feathered Serpent when it was dedicated about 150-200 CE, along with jade, obsidian and animal offerings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan.'

question: Teotihuacan was no isolated town but a metropolis that drew people from across Mesoamerica. In a district called Tlailotlacan, archaeologists found tombs, urns and carvings in a foreign style -- a whole neighborhood settled by migrants who kept the customs of their distant homeland. Which people made this quarter their home?
context: Teotihuacan was a genuine melting pot. Its Tlailotlacan barrio housed Zapotec migrants from the Oaxaca Valley, who kept their homeland's tomb styles and hieroglyphs; other quarters held Gulf-coast and Maya traders. Bone-isotope tests confirm many residents grew up hundreds of miles away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: In 2015, archaeologist Sergio Gomez finished tunnelling along a passage sealed beneath Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent for some 1,800 years. Among jade statues, carved shells and glittering pyrite spheres, his lamps lit up pools of a strange liquid glinting on the tunnel floor -- something no one expected in a shaft sealed since antiquity. What was this liquid?
context: Sergio Gomez of Mexico's INAH found pools of liquid mercury in the sealed chamber, along with jade statues, carved shells and pyrite spheres. He suspects the shimmering metal stood for an underworld river or lake -- and may mark the way to the first royal tomb ever found at Teotihuacan. Source: Archaeology Magazine, 27 April 2015.

question: At the north end of Teotihuacan's great avenue, the Pyramid of the Moon rises about 43 m, with the sacred mountain Cerro Gordo looming directly behind it. This was no accident: the builders deliberately tied the pyramid to the mountain at its back. In what way?
answer: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
choices: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
its stairway aims straight at the summit
it sits on the mountain's center line
its shadow reaches the peak at dawn
context: The 43 m Pyramid of the Moon was built to mimic the contours of Cerro Gordo, the mountain directly behind it, so that from the avenue the pyramid and peak read as one continuous silhouette -- binding the city's sacred architecture to the living landscape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Moon.'

question: The entire city of Teotihuacan -- its long avenue, its pyramids, its thousands of buildings -- is deliberately rotated about 15.5 degrees off true north, all on one giant grid. Astronomers found the tilt is no mistake: it lines the whole city up with something in the sky. What did the builders orient their city to?
answer: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
choices: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
context: Teotihuacan's grid is turned about 15.5° east of north, and the Pyramid of the Sun's orientation records sunrise on 11 February and 29 October and sunset on 30 April and 13 August -- dates that likely anchored the ritual calendar. The whole city was squared to the sky, not the compass. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: For centuries Teotihuacan was the greatest power in Mesoamerica; then around 550 CE its grand civic buildings were deliberately burned and the city collapsed. Archaeologists still debate the cause. What is the leading explanation today for what brought Teotihuacan down?
answer: a revolt from within the city
choices: a revolt from within the city
a war with a rival city
context: Because the burning around 550 CE targeted the elite civic buildings along the Avenue of the Dead rather than ordinary homes, most archaeologists now blame an internal uprising -- likely sharpened by drought and failed harvests -- instead of a foreign invasion. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: In the ancient Ethiopian city of Aksum stands a 24-metre stone pillar weighing about 160 tonnes. What amazes engineers is not its size but how it was shaped, for the entire giant obelisk was ___?
answer: carved from a single block of stone
choices: carved from a single block of stone
context: One solid piece of nepheline syenite, a hard granite-like rock, standing 24 m (79 ft) tall and weighing roughly 160 tonnes. Unlike Great Zimbabwe's mortarless dry-stacked walls or the stacked basalt logs of Nan Madol, the Obelisk of Axum is a single carved monolith. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The Obelisk of Axum is carved to look like a tall Aksumite tower-house, with false window-frames climbing all the way up its 24-metre height. At the very bottom the sculptors carved a false doorway, and into that stone door they cut one clever detail to make it seem like the entrance to a real home. What did they carve into the door?
context: The whole monolith imitates a nine-storey Aksumite tower-house laid out flat and stood upright, false windows and beams carved storey above storey. At the base its two false doors even carry carved false locks, as if the dead king's monument were a lived-in house. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/artifacts-other-artifacts/obelisk-axum-0011516

question: At the very top of the Obelisk of Axum the stone is carved not into a sharp point, like an Egyptian obelisk, but into a smooth rounded half-moon crown. Old fixings show that this crown once wore a decorative covering, long ago stripped away. What is thought to have capped the rounded top?
context: The moon-shaped crown was once fitted with metal frames or plates, thought to be bronze, so the grey stone skyscraper was capped in shining metal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The towering carved stones of Aksum stand together in a field on the edge of the city, and the tallest, most richly decorated of them were each deliberately raised over something specific hidden below the ground. What did the greatest stelae of Aksum stand over?
answer: the tomb of a king or noble
choices: the tomb of a king or noble
a temple to the sun god
a spring feeding the city's wells
context: Rock-cut burial chambers and vaults run beneath the stelae field; the giant carved stones were grave-markers, the biggest and most decorated standing over the tombs of Aksum's kings and nobles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: In 1937 the Obelisk of Axum was cut into three pieces, hauled by truck to the coast, and shipped overseas to be re-erected in a conqueror's capital as a towering war trophy. Which foreign power seized the Ethiopian obelisk, and in which city did it stand the stolen monument up?
context: Mussolini's Italy, having invaded Ethiopia, looted the obelisk in 1937, cut it into three sections, trucked it to the Red Sea port of Massawa, shipped it to Italy, and raised it in Rome near the Circus Maximus on 28 October 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: After standing far from its homeland for 68 years, the looted Obelisk of Axum finally returned to Ethiopia in 2005. Its three colossal stone sections made the journey back to Aksum by the most dramatic means the modern age could manage. How did the obelisk travel home?
answer: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
choices: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
hauled home by a convoy of trucks
context: The pieces were flown home in April 2005 aboard an Antonov An-124, one of the world's largest cargo aircraft and among the heaviest airfreight loads ever carried. The operation cost Italy about $7.7 million; the obelisk was re-erected at Aksum and unveiled on 4 September 2008, home after 68 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: While the looted Obelisk of Axum still stood abroad, a bolt of lightning struck its top in 2002 and cracked the ancient stone. Engineers blamed three steel bars that had been driven through it in 1937, which had turned the tall monument into a giant lightning rod. When Ethiopia later rebuilt the obelisk, what modern high-strength material did engineers use to bind its pieces together?
context: Italy's three steel bars had acted as a lightning rod, so when the obelisk was rebuilt at Aksum the steel was replaced with eight bars of Kevlar, the aramid fibre used in bulletproof vests, so it would no longer attract lightning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: In Aksum stands the Church of St Mary of Zion. Ethiopian Orthodox Christians hold that their church guards one of the most sacred relics in the whole Bible, said to have been carried to Ethiopia in ancient times and hidden ever since. According to this living tradition, which holy object rests inside the chapel at Aksum?
choices: a piece of the True Cross
context: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that the Ark of the Covenant rests in the Church of St Mary of Zion, guarded by a single monk chosen for life who alone may see it and never leaves the chapel. The Kebra Nagast tells that Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (Makeda), brought the Ark from Jerusalem. Presented here as a living sacred belief, held on its own terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Our_Lady_Mary_of_Zion  (Legend.)

question: The Great Stele of Aksum, about 33 metres long and over 500 tonnes, lies broken into massive fragments across the stelae field, likely the largest single stone any people ever cut to raise as a standing monument. How did this colossus come to lie shattered on the ground?
answer: it fell while being raised and never once stood
choices: it fell while being raised and never once stood
an earthquake toppled it a thousand years later
invaders pulled it down and smashed it apart
its own weight cracked it after centuries upright
context: The Great Stele probably collapsed during the very attempt to stand it up and never successfully stood; as it toppled it crushed a stone chamber beneath it called Nefas Mawcha, and it lies where it fell to this day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: The stelae were quarried at Gobo Dura, a hill about four kilometres west of Aksum, then dragged all the way to the stelae field with no river and no wheels to help. Local Aksumite tradition still names a powerful helper that, it is said, hauled the giant blocks into place. According to that tradition, what moved the megaliths?
context: The quarry at Gobo Dura (Gobedra) and the roughly 4 km drag are established fact; the elephant-haulers are local tradition, presented as such. Unlike Egypt's obelisks, cut at distant Aswan and floated down the Nile, Aksum's stones were quarried close to home and moved by organized manpower. Source: https://www.africanhistoryextra.com/p/megalithic-landscapes-of-ethiopia  (Legend.)

question: The stelae were raised by no small town but by a Red Sea empire whose ships reached Rome and India. Around AD 270, under King Endubis, Aksum achieved something no other state south of the Sahara ever had, a true mark of a world power. What did Aksum become the first sub-Saharan state to do?
answer: mint its own gold and silver coins
choices: mint its own gold and silver coins
build a fleet of ocean-going warships
cut a great canal to the Red Sea
context: From about AD 270 under King Endubis, Aksum struck its own coinage in gold, silver and bronze, the first state in sub-Saharan Africa to do so. Later, under the Christian king Ezana, its coins swapped a pagan disc-and-crescent for the cross, among the first coins anywhere to bear a Christian cross. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksumite_currency

question: So mighty was the Red Sea empire that raised these stelae that in the 3rd century AD the Persian prophet Mani counted it among only four truly great kingdoms on all the Earth, writing that none surpassed them. Mani placed Aksum in that highest rank of world powers. Which three empires did he name alongside it?
context: In his Kephalaia, Mani listed four great kingdoms: Babylon and Persia, Rome, the kingdom of the Aksumites, and Silis (China), 'there is none that surpasses them.' Tiny Aksum was ranked beside Rome, Persia and China. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-137-11786-1_2

question: The Alps arc about 1,200 km across the heart of Europe, and unlike most ranges they belong to no single nation — from tiny Monaco all the way to Slovenia, their snowy peaks are shared among a surprising number of countries. How many countries does the Alpine range touch?
context: The Alps run in a crescent through eight nations — Monaco, France, Switzerland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria, and Slovenia — one great mountain wall shared across the center of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: One dome of ice and rock towers over every other summit in the Alps, reaching 4,808 m — the highest point not only in the range but in all of Western Europe. Which peak is this rooftop of the West?
context: Mont Blanc — French for 'White Mountain' — rises 4,808 m on the French-Italian border, the highest summit in the Alps and Western Europe. Monte Rosa (4,634 m), the Matterhorn (4,478 m), and the Eiger (3,967 m) all fall short. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: On 8 August 1786, Dr. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and the crystal-hunter Jacques Balmat, both of Chamonix, clawed their way to the summit of Mont Blanc — the first humans ever to stand there. Their daring feat spread excitement across Europe and is remembered as the birth of a whole new sport. What is that sport called?
context: Dr. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat, both of Chamonix, made the first ascent of Mont Blanc on 8 August 1786 — a climb now seen as the birth of alpinism, the high-mountain sport that took its very name from the Alps. Bouldering (climbing low rocks), spelunking (cave exploring), and orienteering (cross-country navigation) are other outdoor pursuits. Source: 1786.travel

question: Climbers high on the Alps sometimes find fossil seashells in the rock beneath their boots — stone that once formed on an ocean floor, now lifted kilometers into the sky. The Alps rose when the African plate ground north into Europe and slammed shut the sea that had lain between them. What was that vanished ocean called?
context: As Africa drove into Eurasia, it closed the ancient Tethys Ocean and thrust its former sea floor skyward — which is why marine fossils and old seabed rock now sit atop Alpine peaks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: So much of Europe's water is born in the Alps — meltwater pouring off their snow and glaciers into rivers that reach four different seas — that the range is nicknamed the continent's 'water tower.' Which of these great European rivers rises high in the Alps?
context: The Rhine, the Rhône, the Po, and the Inn (a Danube tributary) all rise in the Alps, which supply up to about 90% of some lowland regions' water. The Rhine begins as Alpine meltwater in eastern Switzerland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: Ötzi, a prehistoric hunter whose frozen body emerged from an Alpine glacier, was found carrying a finely made axe with a gleaming metal blade. Its material rewrote the history books — proof that metalworking had reached the Alps centuries earlier than scholars believed. What was the blade of Ötzi's axe made of?
context: Ötzi's axe blade was nearly pure copper, showing metalworking had reached the Alps by about 3,300 BC — earlier than scholars thought — even though he still carried flint tools and a bow. Source: britannica.com/topic/Otzi

question: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure of Geneva had been obsessed with Mont Blanc for decades — years earlier he had even posted a cash prize for the first person to reach its summit. In 1787, the year after that prize was finally won, Saussure climbed the peak himself, spending more than four days high on the mountain while porters hauled a heavy load up the ice behind him. What did Saussure haul to the summit of Mont Blanc?
choices: chests of gold and silver coins
a carved altar of white marble
context: Saussure reached the summit of Mont Blanc on 3 August 1787 with porters and instruments, spending days taking scientific measurements on top. Decades earlier, in 1760, he had funded the cash prize whose lure helped spur the first ascent in 1786. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace-Benedict_de_Saussure

question: In September 1991, hikers crossing a high pass on the Italian-Austrian border spotted a brown, shriveled body half-melted out of the ice and assumed a climber had died there not long before. Then scientists dated the corpse — soon nicknamed 'Ötzi' — and got a shock. Roughly how long ago had this man actually died?
context: Hikers Erika and Helmut Simon found the body in the Ötztal Alps; dating showed 'Ötzi' died about 5,300 years ago — the oldest known intact human mummy, preserved on ice since the Stone Age. He is now displayed in Bolzano, Italy. Source: iceman.it

question: The force of Africa driving into Europe was so immense that whole slabs of rock slid tens of kilometers, stacking older layers on top of younger ones across the Alps — the reverse of nature's usual order. Geologists have a special name for these displaced masses of rock. What are they called?
context: A 'nappe' (French for 'tablecloth') is a large sheet of rock folded over and thrust far from where it formed; the Alps are the classic example, with older rock shoved atop younger. Synclines are downward folds, while horsts and grabens are up- and down-dropped fault blocks — all real tectonic structures, but not the far-traveled thrust sheets that define Alpine geology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: In 1837, after years of fieldwork in the high Alps, the naturalist Louis Agassiz stunned a gathering of Swiss scientists with a claim about Europe's deep past that most flatly refused to believe — yet time proved him right. What did Agassiz argue had once buried much of the continent?
context: Reading glacier tracks — moraines, out-of-place 'erratic' boulders, and polished bedrock — Agassiz told the Swiss Natural History Society at Neuchâtel on 24 October 1837 that ice sheets had once covered Europe: the birth of the Ice Age theory. Source: hgss.copernicus.org

question: One river carries roughly a fifth of all the fresh water that the world's rivers deliver to the oceans — more than the next seven biggest rivers put together. Which river is it?
context: The Amazon's average discharge is about 215,000–230,000 cubic metres per second — enough to make it the largest river on Earth by volume, though not the longest. (The Congo is a distant second by discharge.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: The Amazon pours out more water than any other river on Earth, so people often crown it the world's greatest river. Yet it usually loses one particular contest to a river on another continent — the race to be the LONGEST. Which river is generally counted longer?
context: By water volume the Amazon is unmatched, but the Nile is usually reckoned the longer river. The title is genuinely disputed: the Amazon's recognized length is about 6,400 km (some surveys report 6,575–7,062 km and, by following a different southern source, call the Amazon the longest). Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).  (Legend.)

question: Two reliable measurements of the same stretch of the Amazon disagree wildly: one records the river as about 11 km wide, the other so wide that the far bank cannot be seen at all. Neither is wrong. What accounts for the huge difference?
answer: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
choices: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
One counted the river's mid-stream islands, the other left them out.
One measured the deep central channel, the other the full surface.
One was recorded at high tide, the other at low tide.
context: In the dry season a broad stretch of the Amazon runs about 11 km across; at the height of the annual flood the same stretch can swell to over 48 km (about 30 miles) wide — more than four times as far — so a boat in the middle is out of sight of either bank, and at its mouth the estuary spans hundreds of kilometres. It is a river that changes size with the seasons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: The Amazon's main stem runs several thousand kilometres through the rainforest of Peru and Brazil, in flood over 20 km wide and passing river cities like Iquitos and Manaus. Along that whole vast course, how many bridges cross the main river?
choices: a dozen or so, across Brazil
dozens, up and down its length
context: Not one bridge crosses the Amazon's main stem. The only bridge over any part of the system is the Ponte Rio Negro (2011), linking Manaus and Iranduba — and it spans the Rio Negro tributary, not the Amazon's main stem, so 'no bridge over the Amazon' still holds. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: At Manaus the pale, sandy-brown Rio Solimões meets the coffee-black Rio Negro. The Solimões is milky because it carries fine sediment washed down from the Andes. But nothing muddy darkens the Rio Negro — so what stains its water almost black?
answer: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
choices: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
oils and resins washed from flooded rubber trees
a bloom of dark microscopic algae in the slow water
soot blown in from distant rainforest fires
context: The Rio Negro is a 'blackwater' river: almost sediment-free, its water is stained dark like strong tea by tannins from decaying leaves and plants draining off the forest. The Solimões is a sediment-rich 'whitewater' river carrying Andean silt. Where they meet at Manaus, the two run side by side as the Meeting of the Waters (Encontro das Águas). Source: Wikipedia, 'Meeting of Waters' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters).

question: Below Manaus the black Rio Negro and the pale Rio Solimões flow side by side in the same channel for about 6 km without blending into one colour. What keeps the two rivers apart for so long?
answer: they differ sharply in temperature and speed
choices: they differ sharply in temperature and speed
a submerged rock ridge runs between their channels
a strip of thick floating weeds divides them
the Solimões is far saltier than the Rio Negro
context: The Rio Negro is warm (about 28 °C) and slow (~2 km/h); the Solimões is cooler (about 22 °C) and fast (4–6 km/h). The mismatch in temperature, speed, and density keeps them from mixing for roughly 6 km before they finally merge into the lower Amazon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Meeting of Waters' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters).

question: Twice a year the Atlantic tide drives a roaring wall of water up to 4 m high hundreds of kilometres upstream against the Amazon's current — a tidal bore heard long before it is seen. What is this Amazon river-wave called?
context: This is the pororoca, a tidal bore: at the spring tides near the equinoxes (September and March) the Atlantic tide funnels into the shallow river mouth and rears up into a wave up to 4 m high that races as far as 800 km inland. The name comes from the indigenous Tupi language and is usually translated 'great roar.' (The mascaret, aegir, and benak are real tidal bores on other rivers.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: An ocean surfer counts a good ride in seconds. But the Amazon's pororoca is a single wave that keeps rolling upriver for kilometre after kilometre, and in 2003 the surfer Picuruta Salazar caught one and rode it without stopping. How long did that one ride last?
context: Riding the pororoca upstream, Picuruta Salazar stayed on one wave for about 37 minutes and 12.5 km (7.8 miles) in 2003 — a record ride. An annual pororoca surfing championship has been held since 1999 at São Domingos do Capim. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: Engineers could span the Amazon if they had to, yet not one bridge crosses its main stem. The biggest obstacle is not the width or the current but the ground itself along the banks. What makes the banks so hard to build on?
answer: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
choices: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
they are steep rock gorges too narrow to anchor a pier
they are honeycombed with deep limestone sinkholes
they are packed with hard clay that cracks in the heat
context: The Amazon's banks are soft, waterlogged wetland that shifts as the river rises and falls up to 10 m a year, so a bridge would need very deep foundations and miles of approach viaducts across the floodplain. There is also little reason to build one: the river runs through sparsely populated rainforest with few roads, and it is cheaper to move Manaus's factory goods to São Paulo by boat than by road. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: Each year the central Amazon does not just brim over — it rises and falls about 10 m between low water and high water, and the flood spreads far into the trees, drowning huge stretches of rainforest for months at a time. What is this seasonally flooded forest called?
context: This drowned floodplain forest is the várzea, flooded each year by sediment-rich whitewater. The annual 'flood pulse' of roughly 10 m (locally 9–14 m) shapes life along the whole river, and fish move among the tree trunks to feed while the forest is underwater. (The pantanal, cerrado, and caatinga are other Brazilian landscapes.) Source: seasonal flood-pulse research, PMC / US National Library of Medicine (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7612842/).

question: The mightiest river on Earth begins as a trickle of snowmelt high on the Peruvian peak Nevado Mismi. Astonishingly, its westernmost source lies only about 160 km from one ocean — yet the river runs the entire width of South America before reaching the sea. Which ocean does the Amazon's source lie so close to?
context: The Amazon rises on Nevado Mismi (about 5,597 m) in the Peruvian Andes. Its westernmost source is only about 160 km from the Pacific, yet the water turns east and crosses the whole continent — running downhill through the Apurímac, Ucayali, and Marañón headwaters before it becomes the Amazon — to empty into the Atlantic some 6,400 km away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: Where the Amazon finally meets the sea, its outflow is so enormous that its effect reaches far past the shoreline. More than 100 km out into the open Atlantic, sailors and satellites find the water strangely changed. What has the river done to the ocean that far from land?
answer: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
choices: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
warmed it into a band of unusually hot water
dyed it bright green with drifting algae
stilled its waves into a glassy calm
context: The Amazon's freshwater plume spreads a brownish, low-salinity layer across the open Atlantic — reaching well beyond 100 km from shore and covering nearly a million square kilometres of ocean surface, enough fresh water to measurably lower the sea's saltiness far from any coast. Source: Amazon–Orinoco plume literature review, SALINITY-PIMEP case studies (https://www.salinity-pimep.org/case-studies/river-plumes/amazon_orinoco/literature_review.html).

question: Cross most mountain ranges and you are through them in an hour or two of driving. But head inland from the coast of Chile into the central Andes, and the far edge can lie up to 700 km away -- for a range of such colossal length, none on Earth is broader. What gives the Andes this tremendous breadth?
answer: several parallel mountain chains side by side
choices: several parallel mountain chains side by side
a single broad dome of uplifted crust
a wide plain of stacked lava flows
a thick belt of tightly folded rock
context: The Andes are the widest mountain range on Earth for their enormous length, swelling from about 200 km to as much as 700 km across and staying 200-300 km wide along most of their run. That breadth comes not from a single wall of rock but from several parallel cordilleras -- mountain chains marching side by side -- with high basins and plateaus trapped between them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes.

question: More than fifty separate Andean summits stab above 6,000 m into the thin, freezing air -- a crowd of giants packed so tightly together that only one other mountain region anywhere on Earth can rival such a concentration of towering peaks. Which region is that?
choices: the Southern Alps of New Zealand
context: Outside the Himalaya-Karakoram belt of Asia -- home to every one of Earth's fourteen peaks above 8,000 m -- no place packs together as many 6,000 m summits as the Andes. The Alps top out near 4,800 m and the Rockies near 4,400 m, so neither comes close. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes; Guinness World Records ('Over fifty of the Andes peaks reach over 6,000 metres').

question: High on the Andean plateau at about 3,810 m, straddling the border between Bolivia and Peru, lies Lake Titicaca -- a cold, deep-blue lake held sacred by the Andean peoples who have lived and fished along its shores for thousands of years. Across the whole of South America, what distinction does Titicaca hold?
answer: the largest lake on the continent
choices: the largest lake on the continent
the deepest lake on the continent
the saltiest lake on the continent
the youngest lake on the continent
context: By surface area Titicaca is the biggest lake in South America, and it is also widely described as the highest large lake in the world that boats can still navigate, sitting some 3,810 m above the sea. Reed boats and even 19th-century steamships have crossed its waters. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the largest lake in South America'); navigable-lake claim widely reported.

question: Between the Andes' eastern and western chains the mountains draw apart to cradle the Altiplano, a bleak, wind-scoured tableland averaging about 3,750 m in height and sprawling across Bolivia, Peru, Chile, and Argentina. Only one plateau on Earth is both more extensive and higher. Which one?
choices: the Colorado Plateau of North America
context: The Altiplano is the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet, and the world's second-highest. Its wide, flat basins -- floored with salt pans, shallow lakes, and volcanic ash -- formed as crust piled up and downwarped between the two Andean mountain chains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet').

question: On the desolate frontier between Chile and Argentina, where the high Andes bristle with fire-built peaks, rises the immense cone of Ojos del Salado. Among all the volcanoes on Earth, what record does this Andean giant hold?
choices: the most active volcano on Earth
context: At 6,893 m, Ojos del Salado is the tallest volcano anywhere on Earth and the second-highest peak in the Americas, just behind Aconcagua. It is only rarely active. The world's largest volcano by bulk is Hawaii's Mauna Loa, a completely different kind of mountain. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado; britannica.com 'Mount Ojos del Salado'.

question: Everyone learns that Mount Everest is the highest point on Earth -- but 'highest' means highest above sea level. Because our planet bulges outward at the equator, a mountain sitting on that bulge can jut farther out into space than Everest while standing more than 2,500 m lower. One Andean peak in Ecuador, almost exactly on the equator, does just this: its summit is the single spot on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre. Which peak?
context: Chimborazo's summit stands 6,263 m above sea level -- 2,585 m lower than Everest -- yet because it sits on the equatorial bulge it reaches about 2.1 km (1.3 mi) farther from Earth's centre than Everest's peak does. That makes its summit the closest point on the planet's solid surface to outer space. Cotopaxi, Cayambe, and Antisana are its fellow Ecuadorian volcanoes, but Chimborazo is the tallest of them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimborazo.

question: Why should a titanic mountain range run the whole Pacific edge of South America? The answer lies just offshore on the seafloor: there a dense slab of ocean crust meets the continent and, being heavier, is dragged down beneath it into the hot mantle in what geologists call a subduction zone -- where the sinking rock melts and rises again to feed the Andes' volcanoes. Which ocean-floor plate is doing the diving beneath South America?
context: The Andes are built by subduction: the oceanic Nazca plate plunges beneath the South American plate, and the melting slab feeds the Andean Volcanic Belt while the grinding boundary still unleashes major earthquakes and eruptions today. Unlike the Himalayas (two continents in head-on collision), the Andes rise where ocean floor dives under a continent. The Cocos plate subducts off Central America, the Scotia plate lies to the far south, and the Caribbean plate to the north. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes.

question: Along the coast of northern Chile stretches the Atacama, a rust-red waste of salt crusts and bare stone where NASA test-drives its Mars rovers before sending them to other worlds. Setting the icy poles aside, among all the great deserts of the world, which superlative belongs to the Atacama?
answer: the driest desert outside the poles
choices: the driest desert outside the poles
the largest desert outside the poles
the hottest desert outside the poles
the coldest desert outside the poles
context: The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth. It is squeezed dry from two sides -- the Andes block moist air from the Atlantic while the coastal range blocks the Pacific -- and the cold, north-flowing Humboldt Current together with a permanent high-pressure zone overhead keep rain away. Average rainfall is around 15 mm a year, some spots get only 1-3 mm, certain weather stations have never recorded rain at all, and evidence suggests parts of the desert saw no significant rainfall between 1570 and 1971. This ladder only touches the Atacama; it earns its own desert ladder elsewhere. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert.

question: Fly over the Appalachians of eastern North America: mile after mile of low, rounded, tree-covered ridges — no bare rock spires or jagged snow-capped horns like the Alps or Rockies wear. In geology, what does a range's soft, rounded shape usually reveal about it?
answer: It is very old, worn down over immense time.
choices: It is very old, worn down over immense time.
It rose recently and is still growing taller.
It sits far from any tectonic plate boundary.
It was built by a single volcanic eruption.
context: Old ranges erode into smooth, low ridges; young ranges like the Himalaya and Rockies stay jagged because uplift still outpaces erosion. The Appalachians have been wearing down for over 240 million years — you are looking at the worn-down nubs of what were once towering peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: Nowhere in all of eastern North America — nowhere east of the Mississippi River — does the land rise higher than one forested 6,684-foot summit, its windswept top far colder than its modest height suggests. Which Appalachian peak is the highest of them all?
context: Mount Mitchell (6,684 ft / 2,037 m), in North Carolina's Black Mountains, is the highest point in North America east of the Mississippi. Clingmans Dome (6,643 ft, in the Great Smoky Mountains) is a close second, and Mount Washington is the Northeast's highest. The whole range runs about 2,050 miles, from Alabama up into Canada. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: The Appalachians first rose about 480 million years ago, onto a young Earth so ancient that something we now consider a timeless part of nature had not appeared anywhere in the world — and would not for another 100 million years. Which of these was completely absent from that early Earth?
context: The first true trees — like Archaeopteris, the earliest forest-builder — appeared around 385 million years ago, roughly 100 million years AFTER the Appalachians first rose. Rivers, rain, and sand are all far older. So these forested mountains are, quite literally, older than forests themselves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/385-million-year-old-fossils-reveal-worlds-oldest-forest-had-modern-tree-roots-180973810/

question: In 2023, scientists announced a stunner: one of the most spectacular sights in the entire solar system is far younger than anyone thought — perhaps just 100 to 400 million years old. That makes this dazzling feature of another planet younger than the gentle Appalachian Mountains, which rose about 480 million years ago. Which planetary showpiece turns out to be younger than a mountain range on Earth?
context: A 2023 study led by Sascha Kempf (University of Colorado Boulder), using dust measurements from NASA's Cassini probe, set an upper limit of about 400 million years on Saturn's rings — possibly as young as 100 million. The ring age is still debated, but even the oldest estimate is younger than the Appalachians: a range of hills on Earth predates a feature of another planet. Source: https://www.colorado.edu/today/2023/05/12/how-old-are-saturns-rings-far-younger-once-thought-according-new-study ; https://science.nasa.gov/missions/cassini/nasas-cassini-data-show-saturns-rings-relatively-new/  (Legend.)

question: Do not be fooled by the Appalachians' soft green ridges — they are the ground-down roots of a giant. About 300 million years ago the African plate slammed into North America and heaved the young Appalachians up into a wall of towering, snow-capped peaks. Geologists estimate that at their height these mountains stood as tall as one of today's mightiest ranges. Which one?
context: The final and greatest uplift — the Alleghanian orogeny (~325-260 Mya) — pushed the Appalachians to an estimated 15,000 feet or more, rivaling today's Himalayas. Every gentle ridge you see now is the eroded stump of that lost, colossal range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alleghanian_orogeny ; https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/

question: The same continental pile-up that once raised the Appalachians to Himalayan heights did something even grander: it crushed nearly all of Earth's land into a single vast supercontinent, with the Appalachians running down its center like a great spine. Which famous supercontinent did that collision help assemble?
context: As Laurussia and Gondwana crushed together (~300 Mya), the Appalachians formed the central spine of the enormous Central Pangean Mountains, and the collision helped weld the supercontinent Pangaea. Gondwana and Laurasia would later become its southern and northern halves; Rodinia was a far older supercontinent that had assembled and broken up long before. Source: https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Pangean_Mountains

question: The Appalachians hide the strangest secret of all: they are only ONE broken piece of a mountain range now scattered across an entire ocean. Long ago the chain ran unbroken through the heart of Pangaea. Then, starting about 200 million years ago, the Atlantic Ocean tore open right through it and rafted the fragments onto separate continents. Which two ranges are the Appalachians' long-lost other halves?
context: When Pangaea rifted and the Atlantic opened (~200-180 Mya, in the Jurassic), it split one ancient mountain belt across three continents. Geologists match the Appalachians' rocks to Scotland's Highlands (raised in the Caledonian orogeny) and Morocco's Anti-Atlas — once a single continuous chain. In a poetic twist, Scottish Highlanders who emigrated in the 1700s settled the Appalachians, unknowingly returning to a broken-off piece of their own homeland's mountains. Source: https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: Within living memory the Aral Sea, straddling Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the world's fourth-largest lake. Then more than 90% of its water drained away, and the exposed, salt-caked seabed became a desert the maps now call the Aralkum. What distinction do geographers give it?
context: Most of the old seabed is now the Aralkum -- a salt-and-sand desert that geographers call the newest desert on Earth, formed within a single human lifetime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea; geographyrealm.com/aralkum-desert-worlds-newest-desert/

question: The Aral Sea's name comes from an old Turkic word. It fit the place perfectly once -- but after the water drained away, the name turned painfully ironic. What does 'Aral' translate to in English?
context: 'Aral' is usually translated as 'Sea of Islands,' a nod to the more than 1,000 islands that once dotted its waters. Now that most of the sea is dry land, the old name reads like a sad joke. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: The Aral Sea did not die by accident. Beginning in the 1960s, Soviet central planners deliberately diverted its two great feeder rivers -- the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya -- into vast irrigation canals to raise one thirsty crop across the desert. Starved of inflow, the sea evaporated away. Which crop did the planners choose to grow?
context: Cotton -- nicknamed 'white gold' -- was the priority. The rivers that had filled the Aral for millennia were bled into the cotton fields, and by 1988 Uzbekistan was the world's largest cotton exporter, even as the sea behind it collapsed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: In July 2001, as the Aral Sea kept pulling back, archaeologists ventured onto a patch of Kazakh seabed that had lain roughly 20 metres underwater. There, on ground the water had hidden for centuries, they made a discovery now known as the Kerderi find. What did the retreating water lay bare?
context: The retreating Aral uncovered Kerderi -- a lost medieval town called Aral-Asar and a domed mausoleum, inhabited around the 14th century and found in July 2001 after lying about 20 metres underwater. It proved the Aral had grown and shrunk before: people once lived and were buried on ground that later became sea floor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerderi; advantour.com/uzbekistan/aralsea/history.htm

question: The Aral's exposed seabed is not clean sand -- decades of irrigated farming left it caked with salt, pesticides, and fertilizer. Each year the wind tears an estimated 80 to 100 million tons of this poisoned dust off the dry lakebed and hurls it across Central Asia. Tracing where the dust lands, scientists were startled to find it settling somewhere astonishingly far from the Aral. Where?
context: Aral dust has been traced onto distant glaciers, including Greenland's, and it settles on the snowpack that feeds Central Asia's rivers -- carrying the disaster far beyond the old shoreline. Source: geographyrealm.com/aralkum-desert-worlds-newest-desert/; eurekalert.org/news-releases/1041605

question: For decades a small island sat in the middle of the Aral Sea, unmarked on Soviet maps and ringed by water that kept everyone away. As the sea shrank, that island slowly grew into a peninsula joined to the mainland -- and the world grew deeply alarmed at what the Soviets had left buried on it. What had Vozrozhdeniya ('Rebirth') Island secretly been?
context: Vozrozhdeniya was a secret Soviet site where anthrax and plague agents were trialled. Isolated by water for years, it became reachable on foot around 2001-2008 as the sea receded, raising fears the buried pathogens could be reached. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: The Aral's story does not end in ruin. In 2005 Kazakhstan completed the Kokaral Dam, a long dyke that sealed off the sea's smaller northern lobe and trapped the Syr Darya's water inside instead of letting it drain south. The water rose more than 12 metres. Then something that had completely vanished from these waters came roaring back -- years ahead of every scientific forecast. What was it?
context: Behind the Kokaral Dam the North Aral rose over 12 metres by 2008 and its saltiness fell from about 30 back toward 8 grams per litre -- fresh enough for the native fish to breed again. The comeback outran every forecast: Kazakh fish were being exported as far as Ukraine by 2006. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_Kokaral; eros.usgs.gov/earthshots/kok-aral-dam

question: The world's smallest and shallowest ocean is so completely ringed by land — Eurasia and North America wrap almost the whole way around it — that it is the one ocean you could very nearly walk around the edge of. Which ocean is this?
context: The Arctic Ocean covers only about 14 million km² with an average depth near 1,038 m — smaller and shallower than the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, or Southern Ocean. Eurasia and North America wrap almost all the way around it, so it is nearly landlocked, the one ocean you could very nearly circle on foot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean

question: Picture standing at the exact geographic North Pole, the very top of the world, with ice stretching flat and white to every horizon. What lies directly beneath a person standing at that precise spot?
answer: drifting sea ice floating on deep ocean
choices: drifting sea ice floating on deep ocean
a mile-thick ice cap resting on bedrock
a small rocky island hidden by snow and ice
ground frozen solid for many kilometres down
context: This is the load-bearing surprise of the far north: the geographic North Pole is not land at all, but a raft of sea ice only a few metres thick drifting over about 4 km of water (measured at 4,261 m in 2007). The South Pole is its opposite — solid Antarctic rock under a deep ice cap. Nothing permanent can be built at the North Pole, because the ice beneath it is always moving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole

question: The nearly land-locked Arctic Ocean has only one narrow doorway to the Pacific — a channel just 82 km wide and only about 40–50 m deep, opening between Siberia and Alaska. What is this single Pacific gateway called?
context: The Bering Strait is the Arctic Ocean's only doorway to the Pacific — about 82 km wide and just 40–50 m deep, between Siberia and Alaska. Every other connection the Arctic has runs to the Atlantic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: During the Ice Age, sea levels dropped so far that the shallow strait between Siberia and Alaska dried out completely, becoming a cold grassland up to 1,000 km wide — a 'mammoth steppe' that animals and people could simply walk across from Asia into America. Rising seas drowned it about 11,000 years ago. What is this lost land bridge called?
context: Beringia (the Bering land bridge) appeared when Ice Age sea levels fell and drained the shallow strait, opening a cold 'mammoth steppe' grassland up to 1,000 km wide between Asia and America. Rising seas flooded it about 11,000 years ago, leaving the Bering Strait behind. The story of the people who crossed it belongs to history — here the answer is the place itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: Off the coast of Greenland, towering icebergs — some as tall as buildings — drift out into the sea. They look like sea ice, the frozen crust of the ocean itself, but they are something completely different: an iceberg is freshwater ice that reached the sea another way. How is one of these Greenland icebergs actually born?
answer: a chunk breaks off the end of a glacier and floats out to sea
choices: a chunk breaks off the end of a glacier and floats out to sea
a mountain snowbank slides downhill and freezes onto the waves
a frozen waterfall snaps off a coastal cliff and topples in
a river freezes solid and a slab floats free when spring arrives
context: Sea ice is frozen seawater — as the ocean freezes, most of its salt is squeezed out, so sea ice is far less salty than the water it came from. An iceberg is completely different: it is freshwater ice that calved (broke off) from a glacier or ice shelf that formed on land, like the glaciers that ring Greenland. Same-looking ice, opposite origins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_ice

question: At the geographic North Pole the sun does something it does nowhere else: once it climbs above the horizon in spring, it circles round and round without ever setting — a single unbroken day — and then it sinks and does not rise again for one long, continuous night. About how long does each of these, the endless day and the endless night, last at the Pole?
context: At the North Pole the sun essentially rises and sets just once a year: it climbs above the horizon around the March equinox and stays up for about six months (the midnight sun), then sinks around the September equinox for about six months of continuous polar night. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole

question: Sonar mapping of the Arctic seafloor revealed a hidden mountain range running about 1,800 km straight across the deep basin, from the New Siberian Islands to Ellesmere Island — rising more than 3,000 m off the seabed and splitting the deep Arctic into two separate basins. Russia, Canada, and Denmark all claim it, because owning it could redraw the seabed borders. What is this undersea range called?
context: The Lomonosov Ridge is a submarine mountain range about 1,800 km long, running from the New Siberian Islands to Ellesmere Island and rising 3,300–3,700 m above the roughly 4,200 m deep basin floor. It splits the deep Arctic into the Eurasian and Amerasian basins, and Russia, Canada, and Denmark all argue over it because it could decide where the seabed border runs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lomonosov_Ridge

question: Freeze a ship, a message in a bottle, or a crate of spilled cargo into the ice off the coast of Siberia, and years later it will travel the whole width of the Arctic Ocean and emerge in the North Atlantic through the Fram Strait — all carried by one great current of drifting ice. In 1893 the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen deliberately locked his ship, the Fram, into that ice to ride it, and came out about three years later right where he had predicted. What is this ice-carrying current called?
context: The Transpolar Drift is a current of moving ice that sweeps from the Siberian coast, past the North Pole, and out through the Fram Strait into the Atlantic over roughly two to four years. In 1893 Fridtjof Nansen let his ship Fram freeze into the ice to ride it; the Fram drifted for about three years and emerged near Svalbard, right where he had predicted, proving the current was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpolar_Drift_Stream  (Legend.)

question: One desert is so bone-dry that some of its weather stations have run for decades and never once recorded a single measurable drop of rain — the driest place on Earth outside the frozen poles. Which desert is it?
context: The Atacama, in northern Chile, is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth; at some stations, instruments have never recorded measurable rain. Antarctica is technically drier, but as a polar desert it stands in a class of its own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert'.

question: The Atacama almost never sees rain, yet its coast is not lifeless: nearly every day a thick grey fog rolls in off the cold Pacific, wetting the hills just enough for lichens, algae and cacti to cling to green 'fog oases.' By what name do Chileans know this life-giving fog?
context: The camanchaca is the marine fog that lets 'lomas' (fog oases) survive with almost no rain, feeding lichens, algae and Copiapoa cacti. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Camanchaca'; 'Atacama Desert'.

question: In the heart of the Atacama, near the village of Yungay, lies ground so utterly lifeless that NASA drove a prototype rover across it for four seasons — drilling the soil and feeding it to onboard life-detection instruments. The whole mission was a dress rehearsal for hunting life on which other world?
context: NASA's ARADS project (Atacama Rover Astrobiology Drilling Studies) ran four field seasons near Yungay because the core Atacama's soil holds so few microbes that it fools life-detection hardware the same way Mars would. Source: NASA, 'ARADS'.

question: Most deserts are dry for one reason; the Atacama stacks three at once. The high Andes wall off rain from the east, and the sinking air of the South Pacific high presses down from above. But the cause people most often forget works from the sea: a cold ocean current chills the coastal water so hard that barely any evaporates to fall as rain. Which current cools the Chilean coast?
context: Three forces make the Atacama hyper-arid: the Andes rain shadow, the sinking dry air of the South Pacific anticyclone (Hadley subsidence), and the cold, north-flowing Humboldt Current, which chills the sea so little moisture evaporates. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert'.

question: Some Atacama coastal villages have no river, almost no rain, and groundwater too salty to drink — yet families there still fill their jugs with fresh water every morning. How do they manage it?
answer: they string mesh nets to catch fog
choices: they string mesh nets to catch fog
they truck it in from the Andes
they seed the clouds for rain
context: Atacama villagers hang Raschel-mesh 'fog collectors' on the hills to catch the camanchaca; one roughly 40 m² net yields about 200 litres a day, and in the 1980s the village of Chungungo was supplied by around 100 of them. Source: Mongabay, 'Can fog harvesting help solve water scarcity in Chile's Atacama Desert?'

question: High on Cerro Paranal, a 2,635-metre peak rising straight out of the Atacama, sit four 8.2-metre telescopes that can be linked to work as a single eye — built here because this desert has some of the clearest, most cloudless night skies on Earth. Which observatory scans the southern sky from that ridge?
context: On Cerro Paranal (2,635 m) in the Atacama sits the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope: four 8.2-metre telescopes that can be combined into a single giant instrument, the largest optical/infrared observatory in the Southern Hemisphere, built here for the desert's exceptionally clear, cloudless night skies. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paranal Observatory'.

question: Every few years a single freak rainstorm soaks the Atacama and wakes seeds that have lain dormant in the ground for years. For a few weeks between September and November the bare sand disappears under a vast carpet of some 200 wildflower species — a spectacle so prized that Chile made a national park to protect it. What is this rare event called?
context: The 'desierto florido' (flowering desert) erupts after rare rains — big blooms hit in 2015 and 2017, splashing roughly 200 species like the yellow añañuca and pink-purple malvilla across the sand; Chile created the Desierto Florido National Park to protect them. Source: National Geographic, 'Chile's Atacama desierto florido'.

question: The Atacama's night sky is so dry and cloudless that astronomers built one of Earth's mightiest telescopes high on its freezing Chajnantor plateau, 5,000 metres up — 66 giant dish antennas moving as one to catch the faint radio glow of galaxies being born. Which of these observatories is it?
context: ALMA — the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array — has 66 antennas on the 5,059 m Chajnantor plateau; the thin, bone-dry air barely absorbs the millimetre-wave signals it hunts. Nearby on Cerro Paranal, ESO's Very Large Telescope enjoys some of Earth's clearest night skies. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Large Millimeter Array'; 'Paranal Observatory'.

question: Long before anyone in the region learned to embalm the dead, the Atacama itself was turning bodies into mummies. Along its coast, some human remains have survived — skin and all — for as long as 9,000 years, with no resin and no wrappings. Besides the rainless air, what feature of the ground preserves flesh so perfectly here?
context: The Atacama's rainless air plus salty, nitrate-rich soil mummifies flesh naturally; one naturally preserved body on this coast dates to about 7020 BC. The same chemistry preserved the region's later, deliberately made mummies. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinchorro mummies'.

question: Preserved by the Atacama's killer dryness, the oldest deliberately made mummies on Earth lie along its northern coast near Arica. Their makers began wrapping and remaking their dead around 5050 BC — roughly 2,000 years before the Egyptians mummified a single pharaoh. What are these mummies called?
context: The Chinchorro of the Atacama coast practised artificial mummification from about 5050 BC — some 2,000 years before Egypt. They mummified everyone, even infants; 'black mummies' were taken apart, cleaned and reassembled, later 'red mummies' painted with ochre. UNESCO named the sites a World Heritage Site in 2021. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinchorro mummies'.

question: Chile's Atacama Desert runs about 1,000 km down the Pacific coast — a vast land of bare rock, gravel, and dunes stretching to the horizon. Geographers award it one famous 'world's most' title. Which one does the Atacama hold?
choices: the highest desert in the world
context: Antarctica is technically Earth's driest desert of all, so the Atacama holds the 'nonpolar' crown. Some interior weather stations have gone more than a century with no rain in the record at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'

question: The Atacama is so dry that some weather stations have never logged a single drop of rain — and yet the desert is not lifeless. Most mornings a thick, cold fog drifts inland off the cold Pacific, and lichens and cacti drink that moisture straight out of the air. Local people have a name for this life-giving fog. What is it called?
context: The camanchaca rolls in off the cold Humboldt Current that runs up this coast. It is why the Atacama is called the 'driest' desert, not a desert with no water at all — the fog keeps hardy plants alive. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'

question: The Atacama is one of the emptiest, most remote places on Earth — hundreds of kilometres of bare rock where almost no one lives. Yet the world's wealthiest nations have hauled heavy equipment up onto its high plateaus and spent billions of dollars building here, in the middle of nowhere. What did they come to this desert to build?
context: The air above the Atacama is the clearest and driest of almost anywhere on Earth — over 200 cloudless nights a year, high up and far from any city's glow. With so little cloud or moisture to blur the view, the European Southern Observatory and others put their giant telescopes here rather than anywhere else on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert' (ESO).

question: Deserts everywhere have dry spells — a few weeks, sometimes a couple of years between rains. But when scientists studied the Atacama's parched core, they found signs that one part of this desert may have gone without a single real rainfall for one almost unimaginable, unbroken stretch. Roughly how long did that dry spell last?
context: The evidence points to roughly 1570 to 1971 — about four centuries — with no significant rain in that spot. It is an estimate from soil and climate clues, not a rain gauge, so scientists give it carefully. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'  (Legend.)

question: On the Atacama's Chajnantor plateau — 5,000 m up, where the air is so thin that workers carry bottled oxygen — 66 dish-antennas link together as a single telescope called ALMA. Sitting on the ground, ALMA ought to be no match for the Hubble Space Telescope orbiting far above, yet it can see the sky more sharply than Hubble does. Roughly how much sharper?
context: At 5,000 m, ALMA is the highest major observatory on Earth. Its 66 linked antennas cost about US$1.4 billion — the most expensive ground-based astronomy project ever built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Large Millimeter Array.'

question: Before NASA sends a rover to explore another world, its engineers first put it through its paces in the Atacama. The desert's soil is so dry and dead that scientists call it Earth's closest 'analog' — a stand-in — for the surface of one particular world. Which world does the Atacama double for?
context: In 2003 scientists ran the old Viking lander's life-detection tests on Atacama soil near Yungay and found almost no living microbes — the same near-empty result they would expect on Mars. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'

question: Near the oasis town of San Pedro de Atacama lies the Valle de la Luna — the 'Valley of the Moon' — a Mars-like world of wind-carved salt ridges and stone. In the deep silence, as the fierce daytime heat gives way to a freezing night, the salt-crusted ground makes a startling sound. What do people hear?
context: The salt crust crackles and pops as it expands and shrinks with the desert's huge day-to-night temperature swings. A neighbouring basin is grimly named Valle de la Muerte — 'Death Valley.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Valle de la Luna (Chile).'

question: The Salar de Atacama is a vast salt flat where pink flamingos wade in bright turquoise lagoons. Beneath its crust lies a briny soup of dissolved metals, and one of them is packed into this brine more richly than anywhere else on Earth — about a quarter of all the world's known reserves sit right here. Which metal is the Salar's great prize?
context: The Salar de Atacama holds the highest lithium concentration of any brine on Earth — roughly a quarter of the world's known reserves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salar de Atacama.'

question: Most years the Atacama stays bare and brown. But every few years a rare, freak rain soaks the sand and wakes seeds that have lain asleep underground for years — and within weeks the desert erupts into a horizon-to-horizon carpet of millions of wildflowers. Chileans have a name for this astonishing bloom. What is it called?
context: 'Desierto florido' means 'flowering desert.' The blooms include the pink añañuca and the mallow, sprung from seeds that can wait years underground for a single soaking rain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'

question: Carved into a lonely hillside on Cerro Unita stands the Atacama Giant — at about 86 metres, the largest ancient figure of a human etched into the earth anywhere in the world, made by desert people around 1000–1400 CE. Its true purpose is debated, but one leading idea is that this giant worked as a practical tool. What might it have been used as?
answer: a calendar to track the seasons
choices: a calendar to track the seasons
a burial tomb for a chieftain
context: By one leading theory, lines running from the giant's head line up with the moon to mark the seasons and predict when the rains would come. Its meaning is still disputed, and some sources put its height as high as 119 m. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Giant.'  (Legend.)

question: On the Atacama's Pacific coast, the Chinchorro people preserved their dead as mummies about 7,000 years ago — taking the bodies apart, drying them, and rebuilding them around sticks and reeds. When most people picture ancient mummies, they think of Egypt. How do the Chinchorro mummies compare with Egypt's?
context: The oldest known Chinchorro mummy is a child from the Camarones Valley, dated to about 5050 BC — the world's oldest artificial mummies, roughly two millennia before Egypt's. Everyone was mummified, even babies, not only the powerful; the salty, bone-dry coast preserved bodies so well it likely gave the Chinchorro the idea. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinchorro mummies.'

question: Everyone pictures the bagpipe as Scottish, yet it is far older than Scotland's fame with it. In ancient Rome, the historian Suetonius recorded that one emperor vowed to appear in public playing the bag-fed reed pipe the Romans called the 'tibia utricularis.' Which Roman emperor made that vow?
context: Long before the Highland pipes, the bag-and-pipe was already at home in the ancient Mediterranean. The Roman historian Suetonius wrote that the emperor Nero — a compulsive public performer — vowed to appear on stage as a 'tibia utricularis' player, a reed pipe fed from a bladder or bag squeezed under the arm, exactly like a bagpipe's air-bag. Every bagpipe works this way: a squeezed bag of air feeds a fingered melody pipe (the chanter) and one or more pipes that drone a single steady note beneath the tune. So although Scotland treats the Great Highland Bagpipe as its national symbol, the instrument itself has no single birthplace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Highland_bagpipe  (Legend.)

question: Centuries before Scotland's pipers, ancient Greek writers already describe the very same music machine: a melody pipe fitted into an inflated animal-skin bag, squeezed by the arm to sound one steady droning note. What did the Greeks call this instrument?
context: The bagpipe's roots reach deep into the ancient Mediterranean. Greek writers describe a bag-and-reed pipe they called the askaulos — a name built from askos ('wineskin') and aulos ('reed pipe'), so the word means, almost literally, 'wineskin-pipe.' Roman writers, too, tell of an emperor performing on a bladder-fed pipe. Long before any piper skirled in the Highlands, the bag-and-pipe was already at home around the Mediterranean and across Europe — which is why Scotland, though it made the Great Highland Bagpipe its national symbol, cannot claim to have invented the pipes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes  (Legend.)

question: The bagpipe isn't only a Scottish or Irish thing. In the green, rain-soaked northwest corner of Spain — Galicia and Asturias, Celtic-flavored lands of stone villages — the bagpipe is a proud badge of regional identity, as beloved there as the Highland pipes are in Scotland. What is this Spanish bagpipe called?
context: Galicia and Asturias, on Spain's rainy Atlantic northwest, wear their gaita as proudly as Scotland wears its pipes. Bagpipes were never only Celtic: cousins ring across Europe — Brittany's mouth-blown one-drone biniou, and Bulgaria and the Balkans' single-drone gaida, a near-cognate of the Spanish gaita. In modern times Pakistan even became the world's largest bagpipe manufacturer. Source: https://worldinstruments.org/instruments/gaita/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes

question: Scotland's Great Highland pipes are blown hard by the mouth and skirl loud enough for a battlefield. Ireland's own bagpipe is the gentle opposite — soft and sweet, played sitting down indoors, and never blown by the mouth at all: the seated piper feeds the bag dry air from a small bellows instead.
