Its Irish name, 'uilleann,' refers to which body part?
context: The uilleann ('elbow') pipes took shape in Ireland in the early 1700s. A bellows strapped to the waist and arm, pumped by the elbow, feeds the bag dry air — so unlike mouth-blown pipes the reeds stay dry and the tone stays sweet. Played seated, they reach a full two-octave range, and a full set adds keyed 'regulators' the piper's wrist can tap to sound chords. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uilleann_pipes

question: Twice a day, the sea in one great bay climbs and falls by about 16 metres — the height of a four-story building — the biggest tide swing measured anywhere on Earth, with the record set at a spot called Burntcoat Head. Which bay is this?
context: The Bay of Fundy sits between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Its mean spring tides average about 14.5 m, with an extreme range near 16.3 m recorded at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia — the figure Guinness recognized in 1975 as the greatest tides on Earth, measured by a Canadian Hydrographic Service tide gauge. (Wikipedia, 'Bay of Fundy' and 'Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia')

question: On the New Brunswick shore of the Bay of Fundy, the falling tide bares a cluster of towering sandstone pillars 12 to 21 metres tall — many wider at the top than the bottom, with shrubs and small trees growing on their crowns. At low tide you can walk the bare sea floor around them; hours later a kayak floats over the very same spot. What are these famous 'flowerpot' pillars called?
context: The Hopewell Rocks stand on the New Brunswick shore of the Bay of Fundy. The tide carves them by eating the softer base away faster than the top, leaving the wide-crowned 'flowerpot' shape — some 12 to 21 m tall, with shrubs and small trees rooted on their crowns. Visitors walk the exposed sea floor at low tide, and hours later the same ground lies deep enough to paddle over. (Wikipedia, 'Hopewell Rocks')

question: Twice a day the tide pushes an almost unimaginable amount of seawater into the Bay of Fundy and drags it back out — roughly 100 billion tonnes with every single tide. Just how much water is that?
answer: More than every river on Earth combined
choices: More than every river on Earth combined
About as much as the Amazon carries
Roughly the water in the five Great Lakes
More than all the rain that falls on Earth in a week
context: About 100 billion tonnes of water flood in and out of the Bay of Fundy with each tide — roughly twice the combined flow of all the freshwater rivers on Earth. Much of it squeezes through the narrow Minas Passage in the bay's upper reaches. (Wikipedia, 'Bay of Fundy'; bayoffundy.com)

question: As the giant Fundy tide turns and comes rushing back in, it can send a single wall of water surging up a river against its downstream current, refilling mudflats that lay drained minutes before. On New Brunswick's Petitcodiac River in 2013, surfers rode one such wave 29 kilometres upstream to Moncton — a North American record. What is this upstream wave called?
context: A tidal bore is a wave that runs upstream when a strong incoming tide overpowers a river's outflow. On the Petitcodiac the bore has topped 2 m; in July 2013 surfers rode a bore about 29 km upstream from Belliveau Village to Moncton, a North American continuous-surfing record. Rafters ride the Shubenacadie River bore in Nova Scotia. (Wikipedia, 'Tidal bore')

question: At Cape Split, a long finger of cliff reaching into the Bay of Fundy, the incoming tide races through the narrows at about 8 knots. The churning water grows so loud that a deep, hollow roar rises up and fills the forest on the clifftops — a sound local people have long called by one haunting name. What is it?
context: Cape Split reaches into the Bay of Fundy near the Minas Channel, where the tidal current can hit about 8 knots (15 km/h). Locals say the turbulence sends a deep hollow roar up into the clifftop forest, which they call the 'Voice of the Moon' — fitting, since the moon's pull drives the tides. (fundydiscovery.ca, 'Fundy Fun Facts')

question: Where the Saint John River empties into the Bay of Fundy at the city of Saint John, the water runs over a set of submerged rock ledges. Twice every day, as the enormous tide comes surging in, it overpowers the river entirely — and something startling happens to the rapids there, giving the spot the famous name locals use for it. What happens?
answer: The rapids reverse and churn upstream, uphill
choices: The rapids reverse and churn upstream, uphill
The rapids freeze into a standing sheet of ice
The river splits and pours down two channels
The fresh water turns salty in a matter of seconds
context: This is the Reversing Falls (or Reversing Rapids) at Saint John, New Brunswick. When the Fundy tide surges in, it overpowers the Saint John River and forces its rapids to churn backward, upstream over submerged ledges. At slack tide the flow pauses for a few minutes — the only safe window for boats to pass — before it turns and runs seaward again. (Wikipedia, 'Reversing Falls')

question: The Bay of Fundy's record tides come down to timing. Water sloshing from the bay's mouth to its head and back takes about 13 hours — almost exactly the rhythm of the incoming Atlantic tide, close to 12.5 hours. So each new pulse of tide arrives just in time to shove the sloshing water even higher, like a child kicking a swing higher at the top of every arc. What is this amplifying effect called?
context: This is tidal resonance. The bay's natural sloshing period (Garrett's 1972 study put it near 13.3 hours) nearly matches the ocean's main tide, the M2, which has a period of about 12.42 hours. Because the two are close, each incoming pulse arrives roughly in step and adds to the last, building the world's highest tides — not the funnel shape alone. (Garrett 1972, 'The resonant period of the Bay of Fundy')

question: The Bay of Fundy's ordinary record tide reaches about 16 metres. But the highest water ever measured there — roughly 21.6 metres at Burntcoat Head — came on a single night in October 1869, when a hurricane's storm surge piled on top of an already-extreme tide, bursting the dykes of the Minas Basin and drowning the marshes. By what name is that 1869 disaster remembered?
context: The Saxby Gale of October 4–5, 1869 drove Fundy's highest water on record, about 21.6 m (71 ft) at Burntcoat Head, when a hurricane's surge landed atop a perigean spring tide and burst the Minas Basin and Tantramar dykes. It is named for Lt. Stephen Saxby, a Royal Navy instructor who had warned nearly a year earlier that three lunar events falling within hours would drive extreme tides that day — he was mocked as an astrologer until the storm proved him right. (Wikipedia, 'Saxby Gale')  (Legend.)

question: During the Ice Ages, so much of the world's water froze into the great ice sheets that global sea level fell far below today's — as much as 120 metres at the coldest peak. The shallow strait between Siberia and Alaska drained, and its bared seabed rose as dry land, joining Asia to North America. Geographers gave this vanished country a name — what is it?
context: The lost land is BERINGIA, named in 1937 by the Swedish botanist Eric Hultén after Vitus Bering, the Danish-born explorer who sailed into the strait in 1728 (which is why the strait bears his name too). During the ice ages, enough of the planet's water was locked in ice sheets to drop the sea more than 50 metres — plenty to expose Beringia's floor — and up to about 120 metres at the peak of the Last Glacial Maximum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: The water gap between Asia and North America sounds as though it should be a deep ocean trench, a fitting barrier between two great continents. But the strait dividing Siberia from Alaska hides a surprise. On average, how deep is its seabed?
context: Only about 40–50 m (130–160 ft) deep on average, the Bering Strait's floor is so shallow that a fairly modest fall in sea level is enough to turn the whole strait into dry land — which is exactly what the ice ages did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia ; https://hakaimagazine.com/features/sunken-bridge-size-continent/

question: Picture the Ice-Age land bridge and you might imagine a frozen white wasteland. In fact this vast plain was a cold but surprisingly DRY world, where fierce, dust-laden winds swept the ground nearly free of snow. Scientists have a special name for the vanished Ice-Age ecosystem that stretched across it. What is it called?
context: Beringia was the 'mammoth steppe' — a cold, dry grassland of grasses and herbs rather than forest, named for the great Ice-Age beasts that grazed it. It was no narrow footpath either: at its greatest extent the land bridge stretched up to about 1,000 km (620 mi) from north to south — a whole grassy country between two continents. Source: https://home.nps.gov/subjects/beringia/nature.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: Beringia was no mere sliver of shore briefly bared by a falling tide. At the peak of the last Ice Age, when the world's seas stood at their lowest, the exposed floor between Siberia and Alaska spread wide into one great, open plain. At its greatest extent, roughly how large was this drowned land?
answer: as large as British Columbia and Alberta combined
choices: as large as British Columbia and Alberta combined
as large as Alaska and Yukon combined
as large as Texas and California combined
as large as France and Germany combined
context: At its greatest extent Beringia covered roughly 1.6 million square kilometres — an area comparable to the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Alberta combined. This was no bridge to be scurried across in a day but a broad, grassy world in its own right; the first peoples out of Asia crossed it on foot during the Ice Age, before the rising seas drowned it again around 11,000 years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: As the ice melted and the seas climbed once more, Beringia's plain flooded and split the two continents apart again. Almost the whole land bridge now lies drowned — but a handful of small islands still break the surface, the last high points of that lost country. Which islands are these surviving remnants of Beringia?
context: They are the Diomede Islands. Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (Alaska, USA) sit just 3.8 km (2.4 mi) apart — yet both the U.S.–Russia border and the International Date Line run between them, so Big Diomede is nicknamed 'Tomorrow Island' and Little Diomede 'Yesterday Island,' nearly a full day apart in time. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Diomede-Islands ; https://polarjournal.net/diomede-islands-only-3-8-kilometers-separate-the-usa-and-russia/

question: Beringia was not the only land the Ice Age opened and then swallowed. When the same worldwide drop in sea level bared the shallow floor of what is now the North Sea, a broad plain emerged that joined Britain to mainland Europe — a country of rivers and marshes where Mesolithic hunters lived and fished, until the returning sea drowned it for good. What do we call this lost North Sea land?
context: This drowned plain is Doggerland, now under the North Sea. Its end was violent as well as slow: around 6150 BC a giant undersea landslide off Norway, the Storegga Slide, sent a tsunami sweeping across the North Sea. The same worldwide sea-drop had also joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into one continent, Sahul — New Guinea split off about 8,000 years ago and Tasmania about 6,000 years ago. So Beringia was just one door among several the ice ages briefly opened. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doggerland ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/tiny-islands-survived-tsunami-almost-separated-britain-europe-study-finds-180976430/ ; https://www.britannica.com/place/Sahul

question: Delta blues guitars have one unmistakable sound - they seem to wail, moan, and 'cry' out like a grieving human voice, a tone unlike any other guitar music. That haunting, vocal cry became the signature of the whole Mississippi style. What is the hallmark Delta guitar technique that makes the strings 'cry' this way?
context: The tool is a 'slide' or 'bottleneck' - a smooth glass or metal tube (originally the broken-off neck of a real bottle, or even a pocketknife) worn on one finger and glided along the strings so the notes bend and 'cry' like a voice. Slide playing is the hallmark of Delta blues. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: Long before anyone in the Mississippi Delta picked up a guitar, the sound of singing already carried across the flat Delta country - one voice would call out a line and a whole crowd would answer it straight back, over and over. The blues grew directly out of this older Black music. What were these songs called?
context: The blues grew straight out of the field hollers and call-and-response work songs of Black laborers in the Delta's cotton fields - one voice cries a line and the others answer it back. That answering pattern carried right into the blues, where the guitar 'answers' the singer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: Near the town of Cleveland, Mississippi sprawls a giant cotton plantation where, around 1900, Charley Patton and a cluster of the first blues musicians lived, worked, and played. Standing on its grounds, B.B. King once declared, 'If you had to pick one single spot as the birthplace of the blues, you might say it all started right here.' What is this plantation, often called the cradle of the blues?
context: Dockery Farms, a huge cotton plantation near Cleveland, Mississippi, is often called the birthplace of the blues; Charley Patton and other founders lived and played there. B.B. King said, standing on the grounds, that 'it all started right here.' Source: https://msbluestrail.org/blues-trail-markers/birthplace-of-the-blues

question: Charley Patton, the small, gravel-voiced 'Father of the Delta Blues,' was as much a wild showman as a musician - his rough voice was said to carry 500 yards across the Delta cotton fields with no microphone. Decades before rock stars made the same antics famous, what crowd-pleasing trick did Patton perform with his guitar?
context: Patton - about five foot five - played guitar behind his head, down between his knees, and behind his back, clowning that showmen like Jimi Hendrix would echo decades later. His gravelly voice was said to carry 500 yards with no amplification. Source: https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/charley-patton/

question: Nearly every blues song born in the Mississippi Delta is built on the same simple skeleton: a verse of a fixed handful of measures riding on just three chords, repeating over and over so any player can jump in and join. What is this standard blues form called?
context: The '12-bar blues' runs twelve measures on just three chords (the I, IV, and V of the key) and usually carries an AAB lyric - the singer states a line, repeats it, then answers with a rhyming third line ('I woke up this morning...' twice, then the payoff). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-bar_blues

question: Outside Clarksdale, Mississippi, at a lonely spot where two country highways cross, blues fans still gather at the site behind the Delta's most famous tale. Legend says the guitarist Robert Johnson - a clumsy beginner who vanished for a season and returned uncannily brilliant - came to this crossroads alone at midnight, where an encounter supposedly explained his sudden genius. What does the legend claim happened here?
answer: he sold his soul to the devil
choices: he sold his soul to the devil
he was cursed by a hoodoo woman
he was blessed by a river spirit
he stole a rival's magic guitar
context: This is folklore, not fact. The crossroads sits where Highways 61 and 49 meet in Clarksdale, Mississippi; the legend of a midnight deal for supernatural talent lies behind Johnson songs like 'Cross Road Blues' and 'Hellhound on My Trail.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Johnson

question: The true story behind Robert Johnson's 'deal with the devil' is less spooky but just as telling. The older bluesman Son House recalled that Johnson left the Delta as a fumbling beginner and came back astonishingly good - and researchers later found that his mentor, Ike Zimmerman, knew a quiet local spot to drill Johnson after dark, where no one would disturb them. Where did the two actually go to practice at night?
context: Son House said Johnson simply vanished and returned brilliant. Modern research credits long night practice with mentor Ike Zimmerman in graveyards - quiet, with no one to disturb them. The soul-selling tale was actually first told about a different bluesman, Tommy Johnson. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Johnson

question: One two-lane U.S. highway runs like a spine up the entire story of the blues - starting in New Orleans, threading straight through the heart of the Mississippi Delta, and climbing north to Memphis and on toward Chicago, carrying bluesmen out of the cotton country as they moved north. Bob Dylan even borrowed its name for a landmark 1965 album. Which road is nicknamed 'The Blues Highway'?
context: U.S. Highway 61, 'The Blues Highway,' runs from New Orleans up through the Delta to Memphis and on north, carrying Delta bluesmen out of Mississippi during the Great Migration. Bob Dylan named his 1965 album 'Highway 61 Revisited.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: In 1903, the bandleader W.C. Handy sat stranded for nine hours waiting on a late train at the tiny depot in Tutwiler, Mississippi. A lean, ragged man settled beside him with a guitar and, to make it moan, pressed something hard against the strings and slid it as he sang a strange refrain - 'Goin' where the Southern cross the Dog.' Handy called it 'the weirdest music I ever heard,' the first blues he ever encountered. What was the man pressing against his strings to bend the notes?
context: Handy's nine-hour wait at Tutwiler gave him the first blues he ever heard - a knife pressed to the strings, 'the weirdest music,' he wrote. He noted the trick was done 'in a manner popularized by Hawaiian guitarists who used steel bars.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._C._Handy

question: In the Mississippi Delta, bandleader W.C. Handy chased down a haunting line he had heard sung - about the spot near Moorhead, Mississippi where two railroads cross. There the Southern Railroad met a smaller line, the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley Railroad, which local folks had given a colorful nickname - one Handy wove into his 1914 song. What was that little railroad nicknamed?
context: The Yazoo & Mississippi Valley Railroad was nicknamed the 'Yellow Dog' for its mustard-yellow cars painted with the initials 'YD.' At Moorhead it crossed the Southern Railroad - the spot behind the line 'Goin' where the Southern cross the Dog' - and Handy spun it into his 1914 'Yellow Dog Blues.' Source: https://msbluestrail.org/blues-trail-markers/w-c-handy

question: In the cotton country of the Mississippi Delta, the very first instrument of many a future bluesman was never bought in a store - it was a homemade thing a dirt-poor child could throw together for free from a scrap of wood and wire. Elmore James and plenty of others first taught themselves the blues on one, years before they could hold a real guitar. What was this homemade first instrument called?
context: The one-string 'diddley bow' - wire nailed to a porch or wall, plucked while a glass bottle slides along it to bend the pitch - taught many bluesmen (Elmore James among them) their first notes and shaped the slide sound. It traces back to single-string instruments of West Africa's Sahel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diddley_bow

question: The Camino Frances, the classic pilgrim road to Santiago, begins in the French village of Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. On the very first day walkers climb a high mountain wall to cross out of France into Spain, coming down to the monastery village of Roncesvalles on the far side. Which mountain range must they climb over?
context: The Pyrenees form the natural wall between France and Spain. The popular 'Route Napoleon' over them tops out at the Lepoeder pass (about 1,430 m) before dropping through beech forest to Roncesvalles at 945 m -- where, in AD 778, Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed and wiped out, the real battle behind the medieval epic 'The Song of Roland.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camino_de_Santiago; pilgrim.es french-way stage 1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Roland.

question: For a thousand years the Camino has needed no signposts. Pilgrims find the way by two humble marks repeated on walls, pavements, and stone posts all along the road: a painted yellow arrow, and a single seashell that nearly every walker wears clipped to their pack. Which shell is the age-old badge of the Camino?
context: Pilgrims have worn the scallop -- the vieira -- since the Middle Ages. Look closely and its grooves all fan out and meet at a single point: a picture of the many pilgrim roads across Europe all converging on the one tomb at Santiago. Source: caminoways.com/camino-markings; caminoways.com/the-scallop-shell-and-the-camino-de-santiago.

question: About a third of the way to Santiago, the Camino leaves the green mountains behind and strikes out across the burning heart of Castile: a high, flat, treeless tableland, 700 to 900 m up, where the horizon runs unbroken in every direction and a walker crosses for a week with no hill in sight. Many pilgrims dread this section most. By what Spanish name is this vast central tableland of Spain known?
context: The Meseta Central makes up much of interior Spain. On the Camino it runs roughly 220 km almost dead straight between the great cathedral cities of Burgos and Leon; the punishing leg out of Carrion de los Condes crosses about 17 km with no village, no shade, and no water in between. Source: caminoadventures.com/blog/meseta-camino-de-santiago; followthecamino.com/en/blog/the-meseta-on-the-camino-de-santiago.

question: The Camino's goal is the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, one of the very few churches on earth built directly over the tomb of an apostle -- here, St James the Great. Legend says the long-lost tomb was rediscovered in the 800s when a hermit was drawn to the exact spot in the Libredon woods, night after night, by the same wonder. What led him to it?
answer: a light in the night sky
choices: a light in the night sky
context: From this legend the place is read as Campus Stellae -- 'field of stars' -- the likely root of the name 'Compostela.' The cathedral was raised over the shrine of St James and became the end of every pilgrim road in Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_de_Compostela_Cathedral.

question: The whole 800 km Camino Frances is waymarked so simply that pilgrims say it needs no signposts, and nearly all of it is the work of one man. Don Elias Valina, the parish priest of the mountain village of O Cebreiro, set out in 1984 to mark the entire route from Roncesvalles to Santiago himself, so no walker could ever lose the way. With what unlikely kit did he do it?
answer: a bucket of leftover yellow road paint and his old Citroen 2CV
choices: a bucket of leftover yellow road paint and his old Citroen 2CV
a cart of carved granite waymark stones and a pack mule
a can of whitewash and a tall wooden painter's ladder
a surveyor's theodolite and a stack of printed maps
context: The colour stuck: those humble marks became the famous yellow arrows that now guide pilgrims not just along the Camino Frances but across the whole of Spain. Valina made the run from Roncesvalles to Santiago in that battered 2CV, dabbing an arrow at every turn from a bucket of leftover yellow road paint, and he did it in a single push in 1984. Source: vivecamino.com/en/elias-valina-and-the-yellow-arrows-of-the-camino-de-santiago-no-190; caminoways.com/camino-markings.

question: High on the last mountain before the road drops into green Galicia sits O Cebreiro, a tiny stone village wrapped in mist at 1,296 m. Among its lanes stand round houses with thick stone walls and steep straw roofs and no chimney -- a design lived in here since Celtic times and found almost nowhere else. What are these ancient round dwellings called?
context: Pallozas kept out the mountain cold with drystone walls and a thick thatch of rye straw, sheltering families and their animals under one roof; some were lived in at O Cebreiro into the 20th century. O Cebreiro is the gateway where the Camino climbs into Galicia, the last region before Santiago. Source: caminoways.com/o-cebreiro; vivecamino.com/en/o-cebreiro.

question: Reaching the cathedral is not the end for everyone. Many pilgrims keep walking for three more days, about 90 km on to the Atlantic coast, to a wild rocky headland the Romans believed was the very edge of the world -- the place where the land of Europe runs out and the sun drops straight into the ocean. What is this cape, the true finish of the walk for so many?
context: The Romans named it Finis Terrae -- 'the end of the earth.' It is not truly Iberia's westernmost point, though: Cabo da Roca in Portugal reaches about 16.5 km farther west, and even nearby Cabo Tourinan sticks out a little more. Pilgrims here watch the last sun of the day and, by old custom, burn a boot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Finisterre.

question: The Caspian Sea covers about 371,000 km2 -- a stretch of water wider than the whole of Germany -- and no channel links it to any ocean, so it lies landlocked between Europe and Asia. People have always called it a 'Sea' because of its sheer size, yet geographers file it under a very different title. What is the Caspian, really?
context: By both surface area (about 371,000 km2) and volume, the Caspian is the largest lake on Earth -- bigger than Germany, ringed by five nations (Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, and Turkmenistan), and holding roughly 40% of all the lake water on the planet. It is called a 'Sea' only for its size and its salt; with no link to the ocean, it is truly a lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: Several great rivers pour into the Caspian Sea from the plains of Russia and Central Asia. Yet the Caspian is strange among the world's great waters: not one river flows OUT of it toward the ocean. With water always rushing in and no outlet river, how does the Caspian keep from endlessly overflowing?
answer: it evaporates away into the air under the sun
choices: it evaporates away into the air under the sun
it drains through a hidden channel to the Black Sea
it spills over into the desert each spring
it flows back up the rivers each season
context: A lake fed by rivers but with no outlet to the sea is called ENDORHEIC -- a 'closed basin.' The Caspian loses water only to evaporation under the sun, so its size is a balance between the rivers pouring in and the sunshine drying it out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea; geographyrealm.com.

question: The Caspian Sea's water level depends almost entirely on the rivers feeding it, and one single river supplies about 80% of ALL that inflow -- so much that this one river's flow largely decides whether the whole sea rises or falls. Which river holds such power over the Caspian?
context: The Volga, the longest river in Europe, provides roughly 80% of the Caspian's inflow. Because the Caspian is a closed basin, its level then swings by whole metres over the decades -- it fell about 3 m from 1929 to 1977, then rose about 3 m by 1995 -- marching the shoreline at Baku in and out. The Ural also reaches the Caspian; the Danube flows to the Black Sea, and the Amu Darya once fed the Aral. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: On the Absheron Peninsula near Baku, on the Caspian's shore, a curtain of flame about 15 m long dances straight out of the bare hillside -- fed by natural gas seeping up through the sandstone, it has burned for centuries, and neither rain nor snow can smother it. Travellers have marveled at this ground-fire since ancient times. What is this ever-burning hillside called?
context: Yanar Dag means the 'Burning Mountain.' Ground-fires like it gave Azerbaijan its nickname Odlar Yurdu, the 'Land of Fire,' and long ago drew Zoroastrians, who revered fire as sacred; Marco Polo wrote of such eternal flames near Baku centuries before anyone drilled for oil. The other three are real eternal-flame sites too -- Baba Gurgur burns in Iraq, Mount Chimaera in Turkey, and Darvaza is Turkmenistan's fiery gas crater, the 'Door to Hell.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yanar_Dagh; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Land_of_Fire.

question: Scoop up Caspian water and it tastes faintly of the sea -- not fresh like a mountain lake, yet only about a third as salty as the open ocean. This landlocked lake carries salt because it is the shrunken remnant of a real ancient ocean, sealed off from the world's seas millions of years ago as the land slowly rose around it. What was that vanished ancient sea called?
context: The Paratethys was a vast sea across ancient Eurasia; tectonic uplift and falling sea level cut it off from the world ocean in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago. The Caspian, Black, and Aral seas are its surviving remnants -- which is why a landlocked lake is still brackish, about 1.2% salt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: Along the Caspian's eastern shore, in Turkmenistan, a wide but shallow gulf bakes under the desert sun so fiercely that it evaporates faster than any river could fill it. To make up the loss, Caspian water is drawn steadily IN through a narrow strait -- then bakes away, laying down blinding flats of salt and Glauber's salt, while the water left behind grows nearly as briny as the Dead Sea. What is this evaporating gulf called?
context: Kara-Bogaz-Gol reaches about 35% salinity -- as briny as the Dead Sea, far saltier than the Caspian's own 1.2%. In 1980 the Soviets dammed its strait to stop it draining the Caspian; the lagoon dried out by 1984 and wind blew poisonous salt dust across the land, until Turkmenistan removed the barrier in 1992 and Caspian water flowed back in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garabogazkol.

question: Near Baku on the Caspian shore stands the Ateshgah, a five-sided stone temple raised over natural gas vents so that its central altar-flame burned on its own -- needing no fuel and no keeper, an 'eternal' fire that drew pilgrims across Asia for centuries. Then in 1969, after years of gas being drawn from the ground nearby, the flame went out for the first time in memory. How is the Ateshgah's altar kept burning for visitors today?
answer: gas piped in from outside keeps it lit
choices: gas piped in from outside keeps it lit
a keeper relights it fresh each dawn
a newly found vent under the altar feeds it
oil drawn from the temple's own well fuels it
context: The Ateshgah drew Zoroastrian, Hindu, and Sikh pilgrims to its self-kindling altar. Decades of nearby gas extraction finally starved the natural vents, and the eternal flame went out in 1969; today the altar is kept alight with piped gas for visitors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ateshgah_of_Baku.

question: A packed Colosseum could seat around 50,000 people, yet the Romans could clear it in just a few minutes. Spectators streamed out down wide vaulted passages built through the stands, each feeding into the 80 numbered archways around the base. What were these fast-emptying exit tunnels called?
context: 'Vomitoria' comes from the Latin for 'to spew forth' -- the passages let the stands disgorge a huge crowd fast, exactly like the numbered gates and concourses of a modern stadium. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: The builders of Rome's great arena never actually called it the Colosseum. That famous nickname came from a towering neighbor -- a bronze giant about 30 metres tall that stood right beside the amphitheatre -- and medieval Romans began naming the arena after it around the year 1000. Whose enormous bronze statue was this giant?
context: The statue was the Colossus of Nero; 'Colosseum' really means 'the place by the Colossus,' not 'the colossal arena.' The giant bronze was later remodeled into a sun-god, but it began as Nero. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colossus_of_Nero  (Legend.)

question: Almost nobody knows the Colosseum's real name. The emperor Vespasian and his son Titus, who built the arena and opened it around AD 80, named it after their own ruling family dynasty rather than after its size. What was this amphitheatre's proper, official name?
context: Vespasian, Titus, and Titus's brother Domitian were the three Flavian emperors: Vespasian began the arena around AD 70-72, Titus dedicated it in AD 80, and Domitian later added the underground level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum

question: On scorching afternoons the Colosseum's velarium -- a colossal retractable awning -- was unfurled high over the seats to shade tens of thousands of spectators. Wrestling that much heavy canvas into place on ropes and masts, high above a packed crowd, took a crew with rare skill, so the emperor kept a specialist workforce permanently assigned to the arena. What was these men's ordinary trade?
context: The awning was worked by sailors brought from the Roman navy's base at Misenum on the Bay of Naples -- only crews used to a ship's rigging could manage the ropes, masts, and vast canvas overhead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velarium  (Legend.)

question: The Colosseum stands on land that once belonged to the hated emperor Nero -- the centerpiece of the sprawling private estate around his Golden House. When Vespasian took power he gave this ground back to the Roman people as a public arena, but first he had to undo the extravagant feature Nero had made the heart of the estate. What had Nero built there that Vespasian cleared away to lay the foundations?
context: Nero had flooded an ornamental lake, the stagnum, into the middle of Rome for his Golden House (Domus Aurea). Vespasian drained it and built the public Colosseum on the lakebed -- turning an emperor's private playground into a gift to the people. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Golden-House-of-Nero  (Legend.)

question: Beneath the Colosseum's sand-covered wooden floor ran the hypogeum -- a two-level labyrinth of tunnels and machinery that the emperor Domitian dug out and fitted with lifts, pulleys, and trap doors. To the thrilled crowd above, all this hidden apparatus produced one spectacular effect during the games. What did the hypogeum make suddenly appear in the arena?
context: Caged beasts and painted scenery rode the hidden lifts up their shafts; when a trap door in the floor sprang open, a lion or bear seemed to erupt out of nowhere. The sand on the floor was there partly to soak up blood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: Down in the hypogeum the caged animals rose to the arena floor with no engine at all -- the Romans had none. Each cage was cranked about 7 metres up its shaft by hand, hauled by a simple winch called a capstan. It sounds like plain muscle work for a few strong men, yet keeping every lift in the maze running at once, show after show, took a small army laboring unseen below the sand. About how many men did it take to run all the lifts together?
context: The hypogeum held roughly 24-28 lifts, each capstan cranked by as many as eight men -- so running them all at once took over 200 workers coordinating below the floor like a stage crew. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/how-ancient-romans-got-wild-animals-colosseum-180955580/

question: In 2014 a team of engineers rebuilt one of the Colosseum's long-vanished animal lifts, using only the materials and hand tools the ancient Romans had, then tested it in the arena itself. For the first time in more than 1,500 years, a live wild animal rode a Roman lift up onto the Colosseum floor. What animal did they raise?
context: The reconstruction was built for the PBS/NOVA documentary 'Colosseum: Roman Death Trap.' The wolf reached the arena floor calmly and was rewarded with a biscuit rather than a fight. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/how-ancient-romans-got-wild-animals-colosseum-180955580/

question: Ancient writers Cassius Dio and Martial claimed the Colosseum's very first games included a naumachia -- the whole arena flooded so boats could stage a mock sea-battle on the water. Historians are skeptical it ever really happened there, and they point to one later change to the building that would have made flooding flat-out impossible. What change ruled it out?
answer: a two-level maze of tunnels was dug out under the floor
choices: a two-level maze of tunnels was dug out under the floor
the sand floor was resurfaced with waterproof concrete
a deep drainage cistern was sunk at the arena's center
the foundations were driven far deeper into bedrock
context: Once Domitian excavated the stone hypogeum beneath the arena, there was no watertight basin left to fill. No physical proof of the early sea-battles survives, and skeptics add that a shallow one-metre pool couldn't float real warships -- so scholars still debate whether, or how, it was ever done. Source: https://www.througheternity.com/travel-guide/did-sea-battles-take-place-in-the-colosseum-a-history-of-roman-naumachiae  (Legend.)

question: The Colosseum's honey-colored travertine stone is pitted all over with thousands of small holes, as if a swarm of giant insects had bored into solid rock. These pockmarks aren't from weather or war -- they're scars from something people deliberately dug out of the walls in the Middle Ages, when the ruined arena was mined like a quarry. What were medieval scavengers prying out of the stone?
answer: the iron clamps binding the blocks
choices: the iron clamps binding the blocks
the bronze cramps sealing the joints
the copper ties joining the blocks
the iron dowels pinning the joints
context: The Romans set over 100,000 cubic metres of travertine largely without mortar, pinning the blocks together with roughly 300 tons of iron clamps. Medieval Romans chiselled the metal out to melt down and reuse, leaving the pockmarks that still scar the building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: Where the Congo River nears the Atlantic, its lower channel drops about 220 metres straight down — far enough to swallow a 70-story skyscraper, with the riverbed lost in blackness far below. What title does the Congo hold among all the world's rivers?
context: No other river comes close — and this is a river depth, not a lake. Scientists first grasped how deep the Lower Congo runs when fish hauled up from the bottom showed the 'bends,' the same decompression injury that strikes divers who rise too fast, proving the channel plunges far deeper than anyone had guessed. Sources: worldatlas.com, 'The Congo River — World's Deepest River'; livescience.com, 'Congo River.'

question: Most great rivers swell in the rainy months and shrink to a trickle in the dry season, but the Congo pours out an almost unchanging flood every month of the year and never runs low. What keeps its mighty flow so steady, season after season?
answer: it crosses the equator twice, so rain always falls somewhere in its basin
choices: it crosses the equator twice, so rain always falls somewhere in its basin
it is fed by high glaciers, so meltwater trickles in every season
it is dammed in stages, so stored water flows through the dry months
it sits in the monsoon belt, so heavy rain soaks it each month
context: The Congo is the only major river to cross the equator twice. Because its huge basin sits both north and south of the line, one part is always in a rainy season while the other is dry — so the river is fed all year and never fails. Source: livescience.com, 'Congo River.'

question: The Congo's name runs deep in the region's history — for a time in the 20th century the whole country on its southern bank was even renamed 'Zaire' after the river. That word came from the old Kikongo name 'nzadi,' which people living along the banks are said to have understood as an awe-struck phrase. What did that name for the river mean?
answer: the river that swallows all rivers
choices: the river that swallows all rivers
the mother of all the waters
the great serpent of the forest
the road that has no ending
context: The Kikongo root 'nzadi' or 'nzere' is popularly translated 'the river that swallows all rivers' — a fitting name for a torrent fed by countless tributaries. Some linguists caution the root may simply mean 'river,' so the poetic gloss is widely cited but debated. The nation of Zaire bore the name from 1971 to 1997. Source: Wikipedia, 'Zaire.'  (Legend.)

question: On opposite banks of the Lower Congo stand two national capitals: Brazzaville, capital of the Republic of the Congo, and, across the water, Kinshasa, capital of the far larger Democratic Republic of the Congo. What distinction do these two river cities share?
answer: they are the closest two capitals of any two countries on Earth
choices: they are the closest two capitals of any two countries on Earth
they are the two most populous cities in all of Africa
they are the two oldest capital cities in Africa
they are the two capitals lying nearest to the equator
context: Setting aside Vatican City, which sits inside Rome, Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the closest pair of capitals of two separate nations anywhere — near enough to face each other across the water. Both countries and cities carry the river's name, from the old Kingdom of Kongo. Source: Wikipedia, 'Congo River.'

question: As the Congo makes its final charge toward the Atlantic, the entire river funnels into a narrow gorge and crashes down a staircase of about 32 giant rapids — called 'cataracts' — dropping some 270 metres and hurling more water than any waterfall on Earth. By what name is this thundering staircase of whitewater known?
context: Livingstone Falls, named for the explorer David Livingstone, is a ~350 km staircase of cataracts carrying more water than any other waterfall on Earth. One stretch, the Inga rapids, drops 96 m and holds around 40 gigawatts of hydropower potential — one of the largest untapped power sites on the planet. Source: Wikipedia, 'Livingstone Falls.'

question: Every second, the Congo hurls about 41,000 cubic metres of water into the Atlantic — enough to fill roughly sixteen Olympic swimming pools each second. Only one river on Earth empties more water into the sea than the Congo does. Which river is it?
context: The Congo is the second-largest river on Earth by discharge, beaten only by the Amazon. It drains a basin of about 4 million km² — some 13% of Africa — feeding the world's second-largest rainforest. (Wikipedia ranks it third only if the joined Ganges–Brahmaputra delta is counted as a single river.) Sources: worldatlas.com; Wikipedia, 'Congo River.'

question: Most rivers finish their work at the coast, but the Congo does not stop there. Far out beneath the Atlantic, avalanche-like flows of sediment — the most violent underwater currents ever measured — race hundreds of kilometres across the seabed, still charged with the river's power. What do these tremendous currents do to the ocean floor?
answer: they carve a deep canyon across the seabed
choices: they carve a deep canyon across the seabed
they bury the seabed under a blanket of sand
they scour the seabed down to bare rock
they heap the seabed into a ridge of boulders
context: The Congo Canyon is a giant submarine gorge with V-shaped walls up to about 1,100 m tall, running roughly 500 km — up to about 800 km if the deep-sea fan is counted — out across the Atlantic floor from the river's mouth. Its turbidity currents are the strongest ever recorded, so the river keeps cutting even on the ocean bed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Congo Canyon.'

question: Seen from space, a hurricane over the Caribbean spins counterclockwise, but a cyclone off Australia spins the opposite way — clockwise, a perfect mirror image between the two halves of the globe. One single cause flips the spin direction from one hemisphere to the other. What is it?
context: It's the Coriolis effect. Because the whole planet spins beneath the moving air, storms only appear to curve — counterclockwise north of the equator, the mirror image clockwise to the south. Not wind, magnetism, or gravity flips them, but Earth's own rotation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (low-pressure systems rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in the Southern); Britannica, 'Coriolis force.'

question: In Sacramento, California, a marksman fires a rifle at a target a thousand yards downrange — yet the bullet lands a few inches to one side of the bull's-eye, quietly shoved off-line by the Coriolis effect, the sideways deflection Earth's spin gives to anything moving freely over the ground. That same push nudges every freely moving thing the same way all across the Northern Hemisphere. Which way does a moving object bend north of the equator?
context: In the Northern Hemisphere the Coriolis effect bends every freely moving thing — that Sacramento bullet, an ocean current, the winds of a hurricane — to the right of its path; in the Southern Hemisphere it bends everything to the left. For a 1,000-yard northward shot the drift is only about 2.8 inches (71 mm), tiny for a bullet — but spread across a storm hundreds of miles wide, that same rightward bend is what winds a Northern hurricane up counterclockwise. That single mirror rule is why the two hemispheres' storms spin in opposite directions. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (at the latitude of Sacramento, California a 1,000-yard northward shot is deflected about 2.8 inches to the right; moving objects deflect to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern).

question: Warm tropical seas breed typhoons that batter Southeast Asia, yet a city sitting right on the equator — like Pontianak in Indonesia — has almost never taken a direct hit from one. All around it storms whirl to life, but never on the line itself. What keeps a spinning storm from ever forming right at the equator?
answer: the Coriolis effect drops to zero there
choices: the Coriolis effect drops to zero there
the trade winds shear young storms apart
the calm doldrum belt starves them of wind
the overhead sun scatters the storm clouds
context: On the equator the Coriolis effect fades to exactly zero, and a storm needs that sideways push to wind itself into a spin — so a typhoon or hurricane practically never forms right on the line, which is why an equatorial city like Pontianak is spared. The effect is instead strongest near the poles, following the planet's rotation about the local vertical axis rather than the raw speed of the ground. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (greatest near the poles, decreasing to zero at the equator).

question: At the painted equator line outside Quito, Ecuador, guides love to show tourists a basin that seems to drain one way just north of the line and the other way just south — proof, they say, of the Coriolis effect that spins hurricanes. Careful experiments show it's a myth: the very same basin can swirl either way on different days. Why can't the Coriolis effect really steer a draining basin?
answer: it is far too weak at that tiny scale
choices: it is far too weak at that tiny scale
it acts only on saltwater, never fresh
it shuts off for water flowing downward
it needs an object moving very fast
context: Scientists who tested the claim found it a myth: the Coriolis force is real, but at the size of a sink it is fantastically weak — far too small to overcome the shape of the drain and whatever leftover swirl the water already had, which are what truly set the direction. That is why the same basin can drain either way on different days, and why the guide's equator-line demonstration proves nothing about Earth's spin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (its magnitude is negligible at this scale); Sciencing, 'the common toilet-swirl myth.'

question: In World War I, Germany's giant Paris Gun hurled shells about 75 miles to strike Paris, each one climbing so high and flying so far that it stayed airborne for nearly three minutes. Gunners knew Earth's rotation would nudge each shell sideways — but over that record distance the turning planet did one more thing to the shot that they had to build into the aim. What else did Earth's rotation do to the flight?
context: Aloft for about 177 seconds at record range, the shell flew long enough that Earth's rotation measurably lengthened its flight, adding several hundred meters — on top of shoving it sideways as the planet turned beneath it. Coriolis corrections were baked into the gun's firing tables. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paris Gun' (shelled Paris from 120 km / 75 mi); HistoryNet, 'Paris Under the Gun' (177-second flight; rotation added over 600 m to the range).

question: In northern Chile lies a desert so bone-dry that some of its weather stations have gone their entire working lives without recording a single drop of rain. Which desert is this — the driest nonpolar place on Earth?
context: The Atacama is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth; its cloudless, dust-free air also makes it the planet's clearest window on the stars — sites like Cerro Paranal enjoy more than 200 cloudless nights a year, which is why the world's great observatories crowd its peaks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert

question: The Atacama is starved of rain partly by a 'rain shadow' — moist air is shoved upward against a mountain wall and wrung dry before it can spill over onto the desert floor. Which great mountain range, rising along Chile's eastern edge, throws this rain shadow across the Atacama?
context: The Andes to the east and the lower Chilean Coast Range to the west trap the Atacama in a double rain shadow, blocking moisture from both the Amazon and the Pacific. A rain shadow is the dry zone a mountain range casts on its far side, where the descending air holds almost no water. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert

question: Along the Atacama's coast, years can pass with no rain at all, yet hardy plants and villagers still gather water — combing it straight out of a thick, cold sea fog that drifts in off the Pacific. What do locals call this life-giving coastal fog?
context: The camanchaca drifts in off the cold Pacific; people string up mesh 'fog nets' to harvest drinkable water straight out of the mist, and desert plants soak it up through their leaves. In many coastal spots it is the only water that ever arrives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert

question: The Atacama's dryness has a second engine out at sea: a cold ocean current, sweeping up the Chilean coast from the far south, chills the air above the water so it cannot rise, build clouds, and rain. Which cold current helps keep the desert parched?
context: The cold Humboldt Current wells up deep, chilly water along South America's Pacific coast. A fourth force piles on the drought: the permanent South Pacific anticyclone, a high-pressure zone that presses dry, sinking air down over the desert. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert

question: On the Chajnantor Plateau, more than 5,000 metres up in the thin Atacama air, 66 giant dish antennas stand together in the cold, tuning in to faint radio whispers from the frozen clouds of gas and dust where new stars and planets are being born. What is this array of listening dishes named?
context: ALMA is the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array — fifty 12-metre antennas plus a compact array of smaller ones. At millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths it sees the cold, dark clouds where stars and planets take shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array

question: The four huge telescopes of the Very Large Telescope at Cerro Paranal aren't numbered One through Four — each carries a name from an indigenous Chilean language for a light in the sky: Antu the Sun, Kueyen the Moon, Melipal the Southern Cross, and Yepun the evening star. Which of Chile's native peoples gave the telescopes these names?
context: The names come from the Mapuche language: Antu means Sun, Kueyen Moon, Melipal the Southern Cross, and Yepun the evening star. Each of the four 8.2-metre telescopes at Paranal carries one of these names. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_Large_Telescope

question: On Cerro Armazones, a peak neighboring Paranal, engineers are piecing together a single curved mirror nearly 39 metres wide from 798 hexagonal segments — set to become the largest telescope ever built on the ground. What is this giant instrument named?
context: The Extremely Large Telescope's single mirror spans 39.3 metres, assembled from 798 hexagonal segments — being built to become the world's biggest eye on the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremely_Large_Telescope

question: Far from every city glow — over the Atacama or a certified dark-sky reserve — the night reaches the blackest rating on the astronomers' scale. There the brightest reach of the Milky Way, toward Scorpius and Sagittarius, does something almost nobody alive has ever witnessed. Standing in the open, what can you watch it do?
answer: cast a shadow on the ground
choices: cast a shadow on the ground
context: This is a Bortle Class 1 sky — the darkest of the nine steps on the Bortle scale, devised by John E. Bortle in Sky & Telescope in 2001. Only there is the summer Milky Way bright enough to throw a faint but real shadow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bortle_scale

question: On the very blackest nights at these sites, a second, stranger shadow can appear — cast not by the Moon but by a single planet, blazing at magnitude -4.9, the brightest thing in the whole sky after the Sun and Moon. Which planet burns brightly enough to cast its own faint shadow?
context: At its brightest Venus reaches about magnitude -4.9. Almost no one ever catches its shadow, because almost no one lives somewhere dark enough to see it. Source: phys.org/news/2005-11-shadows-venus.html

question: In Namibia's vast NamibRand Nature Reserve the nearest neighbors sit about 100 km away and not one artificial light breaks the horizon. In 2012 it earned a title shared by only a handful of places on Earth — and it was the very first anywhere in Africa to hold it. What certification did NamibRand receive?
context: NamibRand holds the strictest 'Gold Tier' rating, marking one of the darkest skies ever measured, and in 2012 became Africa's first International Dark Sky Reserve. Source: spacenews.com/namibrand-becomes-africas-first-international-dark-sky-reserve/

question: From a truly dark site like New Zealand's Aoraki Mackenzie reserve, an hour before sunrise a faint triangle of light leans up from the horizon along the Sun's coming path — the glow of sunlight scattering off dust strung between the planets. It fooled old skywatchers into thinking day was breaking, earning the nickname 'the false dawn.' What is this glow properly called?
context: The zodiacal light traces the ecliptic, the plane of the planets, because that is where the Solar System's dust lies. Directly opposite the Sun the same dust makes a fainter oval called the gegenschein, or 'counterglow,' seen only from the very darkest places on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiacal_light

question: The Dead Sea lies in the desert between Israel and Jordan, its shore crusted white with drying salt. What geographic record has made the Dead Sea famous the world over?
answer: the lowest dry land anywhere on Earth
choices: the saltiest lake anywhere on Earth
the largest salt flat anywhere on Earth
the lowest dry land anywhere on Earth
the oldest desert anywhere on Earth
context: The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest dry land anywhere on Earth -- about 430 m below sea level, and its surface measured a record -439.78 m (-1,443 ft) in 2025. It is still dropping. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: You can wade into most lakes and easily duck your head under. A first-time visitor to the Dead Sea tries the same and gets a shock -- this water behaves like no other. What does the Dead Sea do to a swimmer who tries to duck below the surface?
answer: it shoves them straight back up to the top
choices: it drags them down with a strong current
it shoves them straight back up to the top
it stings their skin with sudden heat
it clouds around them with thick mud
context: The water is so heavy with dissolved salt (a density of about 1.24 kg per litre, far more than plain water) that it pushes a swimmer up instead of letting them sink. Bathers famously lie back on the surface and read a newspaper. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: The Dead Sea earns its grim name honestly: no fish swim in it, no weeds grow in it, nothing lives in its water at all. The reason is that it is astonishingly salty. Compared with ordinary seawater, how salty is the Dead Sea?
answer: almost ten times as salty as seawater
choices: roughly three times as salty as seawater
roughly five times as salty as seawater
almost ten times as salty as seawater
about twenty times as salty as seawater
context: The Dead Sea is about 34% salt -- roughly 9.6 times as salty as the ocean -- which is why no fish or plants can survive in it. (After unusually rainy winters, though, salt-loving bacteria and a red alga called Dunaliella can briefly bloom and even tint the water.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: The Dead Sea is vanishing. As Israel and Jordan divert the Jordan River that once fed it, the shoreline retreats about a metre every year, and the drying ground has turned deadly: more than 6,000 sinkholes now pit the old seabed, opening at over 400 a year, and one swallowed enough of Ein Gedi's beach to close it for good in 2015. Why does the retreating shore keep collapsing into sinkholes?
answer: fresh groundwater dissolves the buried salt and the ground caves in
choices: earthquakes shake the rift valley and the dry ground splits open
the salt crust bakes in the sun and crumbles away to dust
fresh groundwater dissolves the buried salt and the ground caves in
underground streams wash the loose sand out and the surface drops
context: Because Israel and Jordan divert the Jordan River (mainly via the National Water Carrier, completed in 1964), the surface drops about a metre a year and the sea shrank from about 1,050 km2 in 1930 to roughly 605 km2 by 2016. As the water retreats, fresh groundwater dissolves the buried salt and the emptied ground caves in -- over 6,000 sinkholes now pit the shore, about 400 opening a year. Source: https://www.timesofisrael.com/sinkholes-on-receding-dead-sea-shore-are-natures-revenge-not-easily-appeased/

question: The Jordan River pours into the Dead Sea, yet no river ever flows out of it again -- geographers call such a lake 'endorheic,' a basin with no river to drain it. Trapped in the desert, the water that arrives has to leave some other way. How does water actually escape a landlocked lake like the Dead Sea?
answer: it slowly evaporates away into the dry desert air
choices: it trickles out through hidden underground cracks
it slowly evaporates away into the dry desert air
it freezes into ice and is blown off each winter
it drains slowly underground toward the Red Sea
context: An endorheic basin has no river draining out of it, so incoming water can only leave by evaporating. The Jordan keeps delivering dissolved salt, but when the water evaporates the salt has nowhere to go and keeps concentrating -- which is exactly why the Dead Sea became so extraordinarily salty. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: On the Dead Sea's southwestern shore rises Mount Sodom, a bare ridge about 210 metres high. Astonishingly, that visible hill is only the tip -- the very same material plunges another 2.3 kilometres straight down beneath it. So what is Mount Sodom, from peak to buried root?
context: Mount Sodom is an entire hill of halite -- rock salt -- about 210 m tall, and it sits on a salt layer roughly 2.3 km thick. From its visible peak to its buried base, the whole ridge is essentially solid salt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: The Dead Sea's shore is studded with weird pillars and towers of white salt. One lone salt column on Mount Sodom has been pointed out for centuries as a person frozen in place. In the biblical legend set right here, this pillar is said to be Lot's wife, turned to salt as she and her family fled the doomed city of Sodom. According to the legend, what single act sealed her fate?
answer: she looked back at the burning city behind her
choices: she drank from a spring the angels had forbidden
she carried treasure out of the ruined city
she looked back at the burning city behind her
she spoke the doomed city's name out loud
context: The biblical account of Lot's wife turning into a pillar of salt is set at Sodom, by the Dead Sea, and has long been attached as a place-legend to the salt columns of Mount Sodom. It is told here as legend, not as established fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea

question: In Arnhem Land, in Australia's tropical north, Aboriginal players blow into one long instrument that hums out a single deep, unbroken note — no melody, just that vast rumble. It ranks among the world's oldest wind instruments still in use. What is it?
context: In Arnhem Land, in Australia's tropical north, the didgeridoo is a long wooden drone-pipe — you blow into one end and it pours out a single deep, unbroken hum. It is counted among the world's oldest wind instruments still in regular use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo

question: In Arnhem Land, a real didgeridoo isn't drilled or carved hollow by hand. Makers roam the eucalyptus bush hunting branches that are ALREADY hollow inside — the dead core gone, leaving a ready-made tube. What made the branch hollow?
context: Makers don't drill the bore — they hunt the bush for living eucalyptus branches that termites have eaten hollow from the inside. The termites strip only the DEAD heartwood at the center and leave the living outer wood standing, so the tree survives and the maker gets a ready-made tube. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo, https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Didgeridoo

question: In Arnhem Land, a finished didgeridoo's raw blowing end could scrape a player's lips, so the maker presses a smooth, molded rim around the mouthpiece for a soft, airtight seal. What is that rim made of?
context: The blowing end is finished with a rim of beeswax molded around the mouthpiece, giving the player's lips a soft, airtight seal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo

question: In Arnhem Land, a didgeridoo drone can run past 40 minutes without a single gap. The trick is 'circular breathing': the player breathes IN through the nose without letting the note die. What keeps air flowing into the pipe during that quick nose-breath?
context: In circular breathing the player snatches air in through the nose while, at the same instant, squeezing stored air out of the puffed cheeks — so the drone never breaks. Recordings document players holding one continuous note for more than 40 minutes. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Didgeridoo

question: To the Yolngu people of northeast Arnhem Land, the instrument is the 'yidaki,' one of dozens of local names across northern Australia. But the word most of the world uses — 'didgeridoo' — has a very different origin. Where does 'didgeridoo' come from?
answer: an English word echoing its droning sound
choices: an English word echoing its droning sound
an Aboriginal word for 'a hollow log'
a cattle rancher's name for his trade goods
a Dutch sailors' word from the coast
context: The Yolngu of northeast Arnhem Land call it the 'yidaki'; in West Arnhem Land it is the 'mako,' and there are at least 45 regional names across northern Australia. 'Didgeridoo' is an outsiders' word — an onomatopoeic English coinage imitating the burbling 'didge-ri-doo' sound, first appearing in print around 1908. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo

question: The didgeridoo is often called the world's oldest wind instrument — some say Aboriginal people have blown it for 40,000 years. But the hard proof is a dated rock painting at Ginga Wardelirrhmeng, high on the Arnhem Land plateau, showing a player among song men in a ceremony. How far back does that proof actually reach?
context: Rock art shows the didgeridoo has been played for well over a thousand years: a roughly 1,500-year-old painting at Ginga Wardelirrhmeng, on the Arnhem Land plateau, shows a player with song men in an Ubarr ceremony. There is no evidence for the popular '40,000 years / oldest instrument' claim — verified use goes back about 1,500 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo

question: Travelers cross Turkmenistan's Karakum Desert to camp beside a 70-meter pit of flame that locals nicknamed the 'Door to Hell,' its glow visible for miles across the night sand. Which of these is true of this fire?
answer: It has burned nonstop for more than 50 years.
choices: It has burned nonstop for more than 50 years.
It flares up only during desert sandstorms.
It burns for one week each year, then dies out.
It must be relit by hand every single morning.
context: The Darvaza gas crater has blazed without pause in the Karakum Desert for over half a century, so bright the flames can be seen for miles at night. The exact start is genuinely disputed: the standard account dates it to 1971, but some local geologists say the ground collapsed in the 1960s and the fire was only lit in the 1980s, since Soviet records are missing or classified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darvaza_gas_crater; discoverwildlife.com/environment/darvaza-gas-crater-turkmenistan  (Legend.)

question: The 'Door to Hell' looks like a natural volcano, but it isn't. In the Karakum Desert a Soviet drilling rig punched into a hidden underground cavern, the ground collapsed, and poisonous methane began venting into the air. What did the engineers do next?
answer: They set the escaping gas on fire to burn it off safely.
choices: They set the escaping gas on fire to burn it off safely.
They pumped concrete into the pit to seal off the leak.
They fenced off the site and left the gas to vent.
They flooded the collapsed pit with water to smother it.
context: The standard (though not fully documented) account: after the 1971 collapse, engineers torched the escaping methane rather than let the poisonous gas spread, expecting it to burn off within days. It never stopped. Both the exact date and even the deliberate-ignition story are disputed, because Soviet records were lost or classified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darvaza_gas_crater; popsci.com/environment/darvaza-gas-crater  (Legend.)

question: For decades the 'Door to Hell' was Turkmenistan's top tourist attraction, drawing thousands who camp in yurts beside the burning pit — yet the government keeps ordering the flames put out. Why do Turkmenistan's leaders want to extinguish their most famous landmark?
answer: The fire is burning off valuable natural gas the country could sell.
choices: The fire is burning off valuable natural gas the country could sell.
The crater is slowly spreading toward nearby desert villages.
Sandstorms keep pushing the flames toward the distant capital.
The constant smoke has begun to foul the air of nearby towns.
context: President Berdimuhamedow recommended limiting the fire in 2010 and announced plans to extinguish it in January 2022: half a century of burning wastes natural gas Turkmenistan could sell and leaks methane, a potent greenhouse gas. By 2025 the fire had shrunk nearly threefold as engineers drilled methane-capture wells nearby. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darvaza_gas_crater; popsci.com/environment/darvaza-gas-crater

question: The East African Rift is a giant crack, roughly 6,000 km long, where a whole continent is slowly splitting in two on dry land. Geologists have already named the two new plates it is carving: the larger western slab is the Nubian plate, and the smaller eastern slab is the ___ plate.
context: The rift runs some 6,000 km from the Afar Triangle down to Mozambique -- a divergent plate boundary caught in the act on dry land, prising the African plate into the Nubian plate (west) and the Somali plate (east). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift

question: As the East African Rift slowly widens, its two halves creep apart at only about 8 to 9 millimeters a year. To picture that incredibly slow crawl, geologists like to compare it to the growth rate of one everyday thing on your own body. Which?
context: At roughly fingernail speed, the plates drift apart so gradually that the rift has taken over 20 million years to open this far. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift

question: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, 12 km north of the city of Goma, the volcano Nyiragongo towers over the Western Rift. Nyiragongo is world-famous for a single feature in its summit crater -- one of the largest of its kind anywhere on Earth. What does Nyiragongo hold in its crater?
context: Nyiragongo (3,470 m) sits about 12 km north of Goma; before its 1977 drainage the molten pool was roughly 600 m deep, one of the largest lava lakes on Earth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Nyiragongo

question: The East African Rift doesn't run as a single line -- it branches into two great arms, and more than 50 volcanoes rise along them. The mightiest stands alone on the Tanzanian plains, an ice-capped giant and the highest mountain anywhere in Africa. Which volcano is it?
context: The rift's two branches -- the Eastern (Gregory) Rift and the Western (Albertine) Rift -- carry over 50 volcanoes, including Mount Kenya and Africa's highest peak, Kilimanjaro. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift

question: One January night in 1977, the lava lake inside Nyiragongo drained away through fissures low on the mountain's flanks, and molten rock reached the villages below. At least fifty people were killed. That 1977 flow entered the record books -- for what?
answer: being the fastest lava flow ever recorded
choices: being the fastest lava flow ever recorded
being the largest lava flow ever recorded
being the longest lava flow ever recorded
being the hottest lava flow ever recorded
context: Nyiragongo's lava is so low in silica and alkali-rich that it can race downhill at up to 100 km/h; the 1977 flow clocked about 60 km/h, the fastest lava flow ever recorded, killing at least 50 people. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Nyiragongo

question: At night, most lava glows a furious orange-red because it erupts at around 1,000 C or hotter. But the lava creeping down Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai, near Lake Natron, erupts at only about 540 to 590 C -- far too cool to glow orange like ordinary lava. Freshly erupted, what startling color does Ol Doinyo Lengai's lava appear?
context: At only ~540-593 C (versus ~1,000 C+ for ordinary lava), Ol Doinyo Lengai's flows are too cool to glow orange and run in thin black ribbons. It is the only volcano on Earth known to erupt carbonatite lava. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol_Doinyo_Lengai

question: In Ethiopia's blistering Danakil Depression sits Erta Ale, a low shield volcano whose name means 'smoking mountain.' In a pit at its summit churns a lake of lava that has never gone cold -- bubbling continuously since at least 1906, the longest-lived lava lake known on Earth. What ominous nickname have people given its restless southern pit?
context: Erta Ale ('smoking mountain') in the Danakil Depression holds the world's longest-lived lava lake, churning since at least 1906; its southern pit is nicknamed 'the gateway to hell.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erta_Ale  (Legend.)

question: Ol Doinyo Lengai's freshly erupted lava is a strange black. But it doesn't stay black for long: within hours to days, rain and volcanic gases chemically attack the fresh rock, weathering it into new minerals like trona and calcite that spread across the whole cone. What startling transformation does the black lava undergo?
choices: it turns deep green, like moss
context: Rain and volcanic gases weather Ol Doinyo Lengai's fresh black lava into pale sodium-carbonate minerals like trona and calcite within hours to days, coating the mountain white as snow. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol_Doinyo_Lengai

question: Where the Western Rift's floor cracked and dropped away, it opened a basin so deep it now cradles a sliver of water that plunges about 1,470 meters -- nearly a mile straight down. Only Siberia's Lake Baikal runs deeper. Which African lake is this, the second-deepest on Earth?
context: Lake Tanganyika reaches 1,470 m deep -- second only to Lake Baikal -- where the Western Rift floor dropped away. It is also the world's longest freshwater lake, holding about 16% of Earth's available fresh water. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika

question: Just downhill from Nyiragongo, on the border between the DR Congo and Rwanda, lies beautiful Lake Kivu, whose deep water hides roughly 65 cubic km of methane and 256 cubic km of carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure. Some 2 million people live along its shores. Geologists count Kivu as one of only three lakes on Earth of what rare and dangerous kind?
context: Lake Kivu traps roughly 65 cubic km of methane and 256 cubic km of carbon dioxide in its depths -- a 'limnic eruption' hazard to the ~2 million people on its shores, one of only three known exploding lakes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Kivu

question: At the mouth of the Catatumbo River, where it empties into Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, a storm flares in the sky night after night. To someone standing on the shore watching a Catatumbo storm at full strength, what does the sky look like?
answer: an almost unbroken strobe of lightning
choices: an almost unbroken strobe of lightning
a single blinding bolt near midnight
a faint flicker every few minutes
a soft glow with no visible bolts
context: Watched from the shore, the Catatumbo storm looks like an almost non-stop strobe — it fires 16 to 40 flashes a minute for about nine hours a night, mostly 7 p.m. to 5 a.m., and it returns to this one river mouth 140 to 160 nights a year. Few places on Earth pack so much lightning into a single spot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatumbo_lightning.

question: For three hundred years, sea captains feeling their way through a pitch-black Caribbean night toward the port of Maracaibo had one guide they could always trust: the Catatumbo storm, which flares over the same stretch of sky at the river's mouth almost every night of the year. What did generations of sailors treat this everlasting storm as?
context: Sailors called the glow the 'Faro de Maracaibo' — the Beacon (or Lighthouse) of Maracaibo — and an older name was the 'Lanterns of Saint Anthony.' Because the storm hangs over the same place almost every night, ships could steer straight toward it to find the port on the blackest nights. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatumbo_lightning.

question: Long before scientists studied it, the Barí people who lived beside Lake Maracaibo had their own story for the sky that flashed above them every night. In their telling, the nightly lightning was not a storm at all. What was it?
answer: clouds of fireflies gathered to honor the ancestors
choices: clouds of fireflies gathered to honor the ancestors
campfires of the spirits who guard the peaks
a serpent thrashing deep beneath the lake
sparks from the sky-god forging the dawn
context: The Barí saw the flashes as clouds of glowing fireflies gathering to honor the dead, while their neighbours the Wayuu saw the lightning as the spirits of the departed. Peoples around the lake wove the everlasting storm into their cosmology for thousands of years. Source: mentalfloss.com/science/weather/catatumbo-lightning-storm-facts; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatumbo_lightning.  (Legend.)

question: Ordinary thunderstorms drift across the land and burn out within hours, but the Catatumbo storm rebuilds over the very same corner of Lake Maracaibo almost every single night, as if bolted to that one spot. What keeps forcing it back there?
answer: warm lake air colliding with cool air off the Andes
choices: warm lake air colliding with cool air off the Andes
cold Pacific winds sweeping into the humid lowlands
salty sea water mixing with the fresh river flow
hot desert air rolling over a cool jungle canopy
context: Warm, wet air rising off the lake meets cool air spilling down off the Andes, the Perijá range, and the Mérida Cordillera, which wall the lake in on three sides. Those mountains funnel the winds together — a 'wind convergence' — so the storm keeps rebuilding over the same warm water. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatumbo_lightning.

question: In 2014, Guinness World Records crowned Lake Maracaibo the lightning capital of the world — about 250 flashes strike each square kilometre there every year, the densest anywhere on Earth. Maracaibo seized that crown from another place that had long held it. Which place did it dethrone?
answer: Kifuka, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
choices: Kifuka, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
the Lake Victoria basin, in East Africa
central Florida, in the United States
the island of Java, in Indonesia
context: Guinness recorded about 250 flashes per square kilometre a year at Lake Maracaibo — roughly 1.2 million strikes over the area annually. Kifuka in the DR Congo had long held the per-square-kilometre record; the Lake Victoria basin and central Florida are other real 'lightning capitals' Maracaibo now outdoes. Source: phys.org/news/2014-01-venezuelan-region-guinness-lightning.html; geology.com/records/lightning-hotspots/.

question: For years, tour guides explained the Catatumbo lightning by claiming that methane gas, seeping up from the oil-rich marshes below the lake, fed the endless storms. Scientists now doubt that tidy story. Which observation casts the most doubt on the methane explanation?
answer: the storms peak in the rainy season, when gas should matter least
choices: the storms peak in the rainy season, when gas should matter least
the rising gas turned out to be nitrogen, which cannot burn
the marsh gas proved far too thin to catch fire
the same gas seeps from many lakes that have no lightning
context: If rising gas were the fuel, the lightning should be strongest in the dry season — but it actually peaks in the wet months, so the methane idea is now disputed. The storm is better explained by the mountain-and-lake winds that keep colliding over the same water. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catatumbo_lightning.

question: In early 2010, something happened over Lake Maracaibo that no one had recorded before: for roughly six weeks the everlasting storm went completely dark — night after night with not a single flash — and frightened locals feared their lightning was gone for good. What had switched the storm off?
answer: a severe drought had dried out the whole region
choices: a severe drought had dried out the whole region
a strong earthquake had shifted the lakebed
an oil spill had spread across the lake surface
a thick cloud of volcanic ash had blocked the sky
