context: More cave-bear skulls lay scattered on the floor around the block. Many scholars read this careful arrangement as a sign that Chauvet was a sacred, ritual place, not merely an art gallery -- one of the eeriest hints of Ice-Age belief. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/ ; https://archive.archaeology.org/1103/features/werner_herzog_chauvet_cave_primer.html

question: In 1879, eight-year-old Maria de Sautuola wandered into Altamira cave in Spain, looked up, and -- as the story is told -- cried 'Look, Papa -- oxen!', having spotted the great bison herd painted across the ceiling. When her father presented the discovery to Europe's leading scholars, how did they treat his find?
answer: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
choices: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
They hailed him as Spain's greatest scholar.
They rushed to dig for more caves.
They shipped the ceiling off to a museum.
context: Europe's experts insisted that Ice-Age people could not possibly have painted so beautifully, and Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola died in 1888 still branded a fraud. Only after more painted caves turned up in France did the leading skeptic, Emile Cartailhac, publicly apologize in his 1902 article 'Mea culpa d'un sceptique' ('the apology of a skeptic'). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelino_Sanz_de_Sautuola  (Legend.)

question: In caves across Ice-Age Europe, from Lascaux to Altamira, prehistoric people left what scientists call some of the oldest 'signatures' on Earth. A person would press part of their own body flat against the wall, blow powdered pigment all around it, then lift it away -- leaving a pale stencil that has lasted 30,000 years. Which body part did they stencil this way, over and over, across Europe?
context: An artist pressed a hand flat to the wall and blew a mouthful of powdered pigment all around it -- sometimes through a hollow bone tube -- then lifted the hand away, leaving a pale outline. Found in caves across Europe, these handprints are among the oldest 'signatures' humans have left anywhere. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/

question: Europe's painted caves -- Chauvet, Lascaux, and Altamira -- are the most famous Ice-Age art on Earth, yet they are NOT the oldest. In 2021, archaeologists dated a life-size painting of a wild pig to at least 45,500 years ago -- older than any European cave -- deep in a limestone cave on a tropical island far from Europe. On which island did they find the world's oldest known animal painting?
context: The painting, in the Leang Tedongnge cave, shows a Sulawesi warty pig and is dated to at least 45,500 years old -- far older than France's Chauvet Cave. It is a reminder that Europe's caves are the most famous Ice-Age art, but not the first. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/45500-year-old-pig-painting-worlds-oldest-animal-art ; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.abd4648

question: On a bitter, clear morning over the frozen plains of North Dakota, the low Sun can appear flanked by two smaller bright suns — one burning to its left, one to its right, at the very same height. Farmers and old sailors had a homely name for this pair of false suns. What did they call them?
context: 'Parhelion' comes from Greek — para + helios, 'beside the sun.' The homely folk name 'sun dog' comes from the way the two false suns seem to follow the real Sun across the sky, the way a dog trails its master. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; sciencenotes.org/what-is-a-sun-dog)

question: High over the Canadian prairies in deep winter, a faint luminous ring can encircle the Sun, with the two sun dogs sitting right on it. This ring always stands exactly 22 degrees out from the Sun — a width you can check against the sky using nothing but your own body. How wide across does the ring look?
answer: the span of your outstretched hand at arm's length
choices: the width of one finger held up at arm's length
the span of your outstretched hand at arm's length
the spread of both arms flung out to the sides
the width of the full Moon's bright round disk
context: This is the 22-degree halo, the most common of all ice-crystal halos. A hand held out at arm's length spans roughly 20 degrees — almost exactly the halo's radius, so the ring seems to just fit inside your outstretched fingers. Inside the ring the sky looks darker, because ice prisms bend no sunlight to angles smaller than 22 degrees. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo)

question: Miles above the Rocky Mountains, in the highest, thinnest cirrus clouds, sunlight can bend into a pale 22-degree halo that shimmers with a faint hint of color, almost like a washed-out rainbow. Far overhead, millions of tiny prisms are bending that sunlight to make the ring. What are those prisms made of?
context: A rainbow is made by round droplets of liquid water; a halo is made by six-sided (hexagonal) ICE crystals high in cold cirrus — the same sunlight, split by different sky-stuff. The magic 22 degrees is simply the smallest angle a hexagonal ice prism can bend light: about 21.84 degrees. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog)

question: Around Fairbanks, Alaska, sun dogs and a 22-degree halo sometimes appear on a day with no clouds in the sky at all. On the bitterest mornings the freezing air right down at street level fills with countless tiny drifting crystals — enough to bend the sunlight and paint a halo without a single cloud. What do northerners call this ground-level ice haze?
context: Diamond dust is a ground-level haze of tiny ice crystals that forms in very cold, moist air — proof you don't need high cirrus to get sun dogs and halos. It's famous around Fairbanks and across the far north, where halos can hang right down at street level. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; carpenternaturecenter.org/sun-dogs-halos-and-diamond-dust)

question: On a still, bitterly cold night over the frozen streets of Montreal, a glowing shaft of light rises straight up above a bright streetlamp — a light pillar, stacked by column-shaped ice crystals hovering with their flat faces held level in the freezing air. What does a light pillar look like?
answer: a single glow the same color as the lamp
choices: a single glow the same color as the lamp
a soft silver-white glow, whatever the lamp's color
a glow that flickers between light and dark
a full spread of rainbow colors, like a halo's
context: Unlike a 22-degree halo or a sun dog, which split sunlight into a faint rainbow, a light pillar is made by REFLECTION — light bouncing off the level faces of column-shaped ice crystals like millions of tiny mirrors — not by refraction (prism-splitting). Because reflection doesn't separate colors, a pillar simply glows in the color of whatever light it reflects: orange above a sodium street lamp, white above a low winter Sun. Pillars can even stretch below the light as well as above it. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_pillar)

question: Over the winter skies of Finland, the loveliest of all the ice-optics sometimes appears when the Sun sits low: the circumzenithal arc, a short bright band curving like a smile — an 'upside-down rainbow' whose colors glow even purer than a true rainbow's. Scientists insist it isn't rare at all, yet hardly anyone ever spots one. Why is it so easily missed?
answer: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
choices: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
it needs the Sun sitting almost exactly 22 degrees high, a narrow window
it forms only in a small patch low near the horizon
it lasts only a few seconds before the crystals drift apart
context: The circumzenithal arc forms when horizontal plate crystals let sunlight enter through their flat TOP face and leave by a SIDE face — the reverse of the path that makes a halo. Its colors are purer than a rainbow's because they overlap far less: blue-violet on top, red toward the Sun. It appears only when the Sun is below 32.2 degrees and glows brightest when the Sun is 22 degrees up — yet it's missed so often simply because it rides high overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumzenithal_arc)

question: Over Stockholm on the morning of 20 April 1535, the sky filled for two hours with sun dogs and glowing rings of light. The uneasy city had the whole spectacle painted, and that picture — the Vadersolstavlan, or 'Sun Dog Painting' — still hangs in Stockholm's cathedral today. Besides being the oldest known image of sun dogs, the painting holds a second 'oldest' record as well. Which one is it?
answer: the oldest color view of Stockholm
choices: the oldest color view of Stockholm
the oldest royal portrait in Stockholm
the oldest color map of Stockholm
the oldest church mural in Stockholm
context: The Vadersolstavlan ('weather-sun painting') is the oldest surviving color depiction of Stockholm as well as the oldest known image of sun dogs. The reformer Olaus Petri read the eerie sky as a warning from God against King Gustav Vasa; the king took it as a jab at his rule and dismissed it. The version that hangs today in Storkyrkan cathedral is a 1636 copy by Jacob Heinrich Elbfas. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vadersolstavlan)  (Legend.)

question: From Cusco, high in the Andes, the Inca ran a mountain empire of millions -- royal roads, filled storehouses, a full census -- yet they never developed written words. How did Inca officials keep the accounts of the whole empire?
context: The Inca called these knotted-string records quipu (also spelled khipu). From Cusco they governed millions across the Andes with cords instead of writing -- the accounting of a whole empire hung on colored strings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: On an Inca quipu -- the Andes' knotted number-cords -- a knot can stand for a single unit or for a full hundred, and the two may be tied exactly alike. What decides whether a knot counts as one, ten, or a hundred?
answer: how high up the cord it is tied
choices: how high up the cord it is tied
what color the cord was dyed
how tightly the knot was pulled
which way the cord was twisted
context: The quipu is a base-10 place-value machine: knots low on a hanging cord count ones, higher up tens, higher still hundreds and thousands. You read the number by a knot's position -- with your fingers as much as your eyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: An Inca knot-keeper in the Andes must record 308 -- three hundreds, no tens, eight ones -- as clusters of knots along a single cord. The hundreds and the ones each get their knots, but the tens place is a zero. Reading the cord with your fingers, how does the quipu show that the tens row holds zero?
answer: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
choices: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
a special 'nothing' knot is tied there
that stretch of cord is dyed solid black
the cord is cut short just below there
context: Most striking of all: a bare gap with no knot is the Inca zero. They kept a place-holder for zero centuries before the idea reached much of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: A khipukamayuq -- a trained Inca 'knot-keeper' -- held an entire province's accounts in his cords and his memory: the tribute owed, the llama herds, the grain in every Andean storehouse. The Sapa Inca demanded these figures be flawless. By some colonial accounts, what could befall a knot-keeper who got the imperial accounts wrong?
answer: he could be put to death
choices: he could be put to death
he could be fined a herd of llamas
he could be sent to the fields
he could be made to retie it
context: The role of khipukamayuq was hereditary and demanded a prodigious memory -- a single error in a knot's color, shape, or position could change the record. The death penalty comes from colonial-era testimony, so it is reported as claim, not certainty. Sources: worldhistory.org/Quipu; machutravelperu.com/blog/quipu  (Legend.)

question: Hand a modern scholar an Inca quipu from the Andes and the numbers come through clearly -- herd counts, tribute totals, and storehouse tallies all readable. But the same cords carry colors, cord-orders, and knot-patterns that may hide names, words, even whole stories. Where do we stand with that non-number content today?
choices: only a few cords have been read
context: We can fully read the quipu's numbers, but its possible 'language' -- part ledger, part story -- is still unread. In 2005 Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine argued that three figure-eight knots on one cord spell the place-name Puruchuco, perhaps the first word ever read off a quipu. Sources: theconversation.com; artsandculture.google.com (the Puruchuco khipus)

question: After Spain conquered Peru, church officials decided the Inca knot-records were dangerous -- 'idols of the devil,' one called them, obstacles to converting the Andean people to Christianity. In 1583 the Third Council of Lima ordered the quipu destroyed. What became of thousands of them?
context: Thousands of quipu were burned as idolatrous, and only about 1,400 pre-Columbian quipu survive today, mostly in museums -- the conquered people's own records largely erased by the men who conquered them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: Four and a half thousand years ago, the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro — in today's Pakistan — was laid out on a neat brick grid with covered drains, as planned as a modern town. Its people also pressed a script of small signs onto stone seals. What is still true of that Indus script today?
answer: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
choices: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
It is still used to write Sindhi today.
It gave rise to the Arabic alphabet.
It was fully deciphered a century ago.
context: First unearthed at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the Indus Valley script has resisted every reader since: no scholar can say what a single seal says. Its people mastered covered drains and grid streets, yet left us a writing we still cannot open. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Most of what survives of the Mohenjo-daro script is carved on tiny stamp seals — polished stones about the size of a coin, each showing one animal above a line of signs. Among all these creatures, one appears far more often than the rest. Which animal turns up most on the Indus seals?
context: Scholars nickname it the 'unicorn,' but it is almost certainly a bull drawn side-on, the near horn simply hiding the far one. This one-horned figure stands above the signs on more Indus seals than any other creature. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)  (Legend.)

question: Other ancient peoples left long inscriptions — temple walls and clay tablets crowded with rows of signs. What is the longest text ever found in the entire Indus script — the record-holder, carved on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro?
context: The record-holder carries just 26 signs, on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro. There is no long text anywhere in the Indus world — no story, no law, no letter — leaving codebreakers with no paragraph to get a grip on. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script)

question: Iravatham Mahadevan's 1977 catalog of the Mohenjo-daro seals counted 417 different signs — and half a century later, scholars still cannot agree on one basic point about them. What have they never settled about the Indus signs?
answer: Whether its marks are truly writing at all
choices: Whether its marks are truly writing at all
Whether kings or traders carved the seals
Whether Harappa or Mohenjo-daro invented it
Whether it shaped later Indian scripts
context: Mahadevan's 1977 concordance counted 417 signs — too many for a 20-to-30-letter alphabet, yet far too few for a one-sign-per-word system that would need thousands. That maddening in-between has fueled a real scholarly fight over whether the Indus marks are true writing at all, or symbols that never recorded language. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Indus seals turn up far from home — in the Mesopotamian city of Ur, where merchants knew the distant Indus land as 'Meluhha.' On one Mesopotamian cylinder seal, a man named Shu-ilishu is labeled by his trade — a haunting reminder of how tightly Ur and the Indus cities were once bound by sea. What trade did Shu-ilishu practice?
choices: Scribe in the temple of Ur
context: The Akkadian cylinder seal names him 'Shu-ilishu, interpreter of the Meluhhan language' — proof that people once spoke and translated the Indus tongue. Yet even a named ancient interpreter cannot help us: the seals stay silent. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus-Mesopotamia_relations)

question: Egyptian hieroglyphs fell to the Rosetta Stone, and Greek's lost Linear B was eventually cracked too. Scholars fear the Indus script of Mohenjo-daro may NEVER join them — defeated by one wall those other scripts never faced. What is the deepest reason the Indus script resists every codebreaker?
choices: Its clay tablets have all crumbled away
Its signs were deliberately kept secret
Too few seals have ever been dug up
context: Egyptian hieroglyphs were cracked with the Rosetta Stone, and Greek's Linear B was eventually read too, because scholars could tie the signs to a language they already knew. The Indus script has no such bilingual key, and no one knows what language its people spoke — so it may stay silent forever. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Seven miles up over the North Atlantic, a narrow band of wind screams from west to east. A jet from New York to London rides it and lands more than an hour early, while the flight home against it drags. What is this fast, high-altitude river of wind?
context: The jet stream flows near the tropopause, about 30,000 feet up, always west to east. The classic mix-up is the Gulf Stream — that is a warm WATER current in the ocean, not a wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: In the 1920s a Japanese meteorologist, Wasaburo Oishi, ran the Tateno observatory near Mount Fuji. From 1923 to 1925 he logged 1,288 upper-air readings proving a fierce, permanent high wind blew over Japan — the first real record of the jet stream. What did he use to measure those winds seven miles up?
context: Oishi released small hydrogen 'pilot balloons' and followed them with a theodolite — a surveying telescope — reading the wind's speed and direction at each height as the balloon rose. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: Wasaburo Oishi had proved the jet stream existed over Japan in the 1920s, yet the world's scientists ignored his breakthrough for decades. The reason was strange: an idealist, he wrote all 19 of his observatory reports in a made-up international language almost no scientist could read. Which language was it?
context: Oishi was a devoted Esperantist. His 1926 report and 18 more through 1944 were all in Esperanto, so his jet-stream discovery sat unread until the West rediscovered the winds during World War II. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: In World War II, Japan built about 9,300 balloon bombs called 'fu-go' and launched them into the winter jet stream to drift 6,000 miles across the Pacific and strike North America — the first intercontinental weapon. What were these balloon envelopes made of?
context: Each fu-go was many sheets of washi (mulberry paper) glued with konnyaku, a paste made from konjac potato. About 300 reached North America in 30 to 100 hours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu-Go_balloon_bomb

question: The jet stream that drives the winter storms of Europe and North America is not equally strong all year — it howls in winter and slackens in summer. It rides a sloping boundary in the atmosphere, and the sharper the temperature difference across that boundary, the faster it blows. What is this boundary that the jet stream rides called?
context: The jet forms and speeds up along the polar front, the sloping boundary between cold polar and warm subtropical air. Winter's sharper cold-versus-warm contrast is why the jet stream is strongest then. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: The jet stream almost never runs straight. Instead it wanders in enormous north-and-south loops that snake around the whole hemisphere, and when one plunges far south it drags a lobe of frigid Arctic air down into places like Texas or Georgia — a sudden cold snap. What are these giant meanders in the jet called?
context: These planetary meanders, called Rossby waves, ripple along the jet. A deep southward dip pulls Arctic air far below its usual range; a northward bulge lets warm air push up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: In late June 2021 the jet stream buckled and locked in place over western North America, trapping a dome of scorching air that could not move on. Lytton, British Columbia hit 49.6°C — smashing Canada's heat record by almost 5 degrees — and over a thousand people died. Forecasters call this stuck, storm-stalling jet pattern a 'block,' and name its most common shape for a Greek letter. Which letter?
context: A ridge of high pressure that halts the eastward flow of weather is a 'blocking high'; the classic shape is the omega block, its loop mimicking Ω. The 2021 heat dome was one of the deadliest in North American history. Source: https://www.livescience.com/a-dangerous-omega-block-is-trapping-scorching-hot-air-over-the-us-and-canada

question: In February 2020 an unusually strong jet stream turbocharged flights across the Atlantic. A British Airways Boeing 747 crossed from New York to London in just 4 hours 56 minutes, reaching a ground speed of 825 mph — faster than the speed of sound at sea level. Yet no sonic boom ever thundered down. How can a plane race across the ground faster than sound without a sonic boom?
answer: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
choices: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
Its swept wings broke up the shock wave before it could form
The thin air seven miles up muffled the boom before it fell to earth
The tailwind blew the shock wave forward, far out of earshot
context: The plane's speed through the air stayed below the sound barrier — the whole river of air was racing east at hundreds of miles per hour and simply carried the jet along, setting a subsonic transatlantic record of 825 mph. A sonic boom depends on speed through the air, not speed over the ground. Source: https://www.flightradar24.com/blog/flight-tracking-news/special-event/british-airways-sets-new-transatlantic-speed-record/

question: High over the Arctic spins a vast ring of fast, jet-stream-like wind that normally bottles up the planet's coldest air, penning it near the pole. But when this ring weakens and wobbles, it can split apart, the jet stream buckles, and that trapped Arctic cold spills far south — as in the brutal February 2021 freeze that knocked out power across Texas. By what name do forecasters know this Arctic wind system?
context: When the stratospheric polar vortex is strong, it locks cold in the Arctic; a 'sudden stratospheric warming' can weaken and split it, sending the jet stream and Arctic air plunging south into North America and Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_vortex

question: The Kalahari's sand is about 90% quartz — a mineral that is naturally colourless — yet its dunes and plains glow a deep burnt red. Something incredibly thin, wrapped around every grain, gives it that colour. What coats the pale grains red?
answer: a thin coat of iron oxide
choices: a thin coat of iron oxide
a fine dust of windblown clay
a living crust of desert algae
a residue of dried mineral salts
context: Each grain of Kalahari sand is nearly pure quartz — colourless on its own — but wears a microscopically thin stain of iron oxide (the mineral hematite): iron that weathered out of the rock, was carried in by groundwater, and dried onto the grains. It is the same chemistry that turns iron rusty red. Source: USGS 'Iron oxide coatings give sand a red hue'; sandatlas.org/hematite; madsci.org 'Why is the sand of the Kalahari Desert red?'.

question: The Tswana people named this immense sweep of red sand across Botswana and Namibia after their word Kgala. Travellers who cross its 900,000 km² of dunes learn very quickly why the name fits. What does 'Kalahari' mean?
context: 'Kalahari' comes from the Tswana word Kgala, 'the great thirst' (or Kgalagadi, 'a waterless place'), for a vast land of sand with no permanent surface water, spreading about 900,000 km² across Botswana, Namibia and South Africa. Yet despite the name it is not a true desert but a semi-arid 'thirstland' that catches 110 to over 500 mm of rain a year — enough for grasses and camelthorn trees. Source: Wikipedia 'Kalahari Desert'.

question: The Okavango is one of Africa's great rivers, yet it never reaches the sea. It flows down into the Kalahari, fans out into a huge green wetland, and there every drop is lost — the whole delta is a dead end for water. Since none of it flows onward, by what route does nearly all of the Okavango's water leave?
answer: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
choices: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
it sinks away to refill hidden underground lakes
it hardens into vast sheets of white surface salt
it is drunk and carried off by huge animal herds
context: The Okavango flows in from the Angolan highlands and dies in the sand: an estimated 96–98% of its water vanishes as evaporation and plant transpiration or soaks away, and almost none escapes. Because it drains inward and never reaches the sea, the Okavango forms a rare inland delta in an 'endorheic' (closed) basin; in the June–August flood it swells to about three times its permanent size, drawing animals from kilometres around. In 2014 it became the 1000th site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Wikipedia 'Okavango Delta'.

question: The blinding-white Makgadikgadi salt pans — about 16,000 km² of dead-flat crust, among the largest salt flats on Earth — are the dried bed of a vast ancient lake that vanished around 10,000 years ago. When geologists traced how far its old shoreline once reached, the size of this long-gone Kalahari lake astonished them. How big was it?
choices: as large as the whole Sahara Desert
as vast as the Mediterranean Sea
context: The Makgadikgadi pans are the ghost of Lake Makgadikgadi, an ancient inland sea that covered roughly 80,000–275,000 km² — bigger than Switzerland, rivaling the United Kingdom or New Zealand — with an average depth around 30 m. Fed by the Okavango, Upper Zambezi and Cuando rivers, it existed from about 2 million until roughly 10,000 years ago. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi', 'Makgadikgadi Pan'.

question: Around 20,000 years ago, the great Kalahari lake — Lake Makgadikgadi — brimmed so full that it overflowed and spilled away to the northeast. Geologists believe that escaping flood of lake-water helped carve out one of Africa's mightiest waterfalls. Which waterfall did the vanished Kalahari lake help create?
context: Around 20,000 years ago the brimming lake overflowed to the northeast, and that outflow helped cut the gorge of Victoria Falls on the Zambezi. A drying climate plus the Gumare fault lowering the land then let the Okavango spread out and starve the lake, and by about 10,000 years ago it was gone. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi'.

question: Out on the blinding-white Makgadikgadi salt pan, a lone crescent of granite called Kubu Island rises barely ten metres above the flatness. Marooned there, kilometres from the nearest water, grows a grove of gnarled, ancient trees — some more than 2,000 years old — that once shaded the shore of the vanished lake. What kind of ancient tree crowns Kubu Island?
context: Kubu Island (Lekhubu) is a crescent of granite over two billion years old, about a kilometre long and 10 m high, crowned with baobabs some estimated at over 2,000 years old that once stood on the vanished lake's shore. A national monument and sacred site — 'Kubu' means hippopotamus in Setswana — it holds stone-age relics including a curving dry-stone wall about 1.25 m high and 344 circular stone cairns left by people who lived at the water's edge. Source: Wikipedia 'Kubu Island'; amusingplanet.com 'Kubu Island: A Desert Island of Baobabs'.

question: The San people have lived in the central Kalahari for tens of thousands of years and can find water where a stranger would die of thirst. In a dry riverbed they scrape down to damp sand, sink a long hollow grass stem, and patiently suck the moisture up through it. To carry that hard-won water, they blow it through a second straw into a container, then cork it and bury it in the sand as a hidden canteen. What is that buried canteen?
context: The San carry the water home in ostrich eggshells, corked and buried as hidden canteens; in the driest months a buried wild tsama melon (a wild watermelon, its seeds about 35% protein) can be the only water for people and animals alike. The central Kalahari is the San's ancestral land, and DNA studies suggest their ancestors began diverging from all other humans roughly 200,000 years ago — among Earth's oldest continuous cultures. Source: Wikipedia 'San people'.

question: The Karakoram bristles with the planet's deadliest 8,000-metre giants, yet its name is far older than any climber's map. Turkic traders first pinned the word on the high Karakoram Pass, for what they saw underfoot; Europeans later stretched it across the whole range. What does 'Karakoram' mean?
context: 'Kara' means black and 'korum' (koram) means gravel or rubble in Turkic. The name first belonged only to the Karakoram Pass, whose high route is floored with dark, broken scree; European surveyors later stretched it over the entire range of giants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Only fourteen mountains on Earth rise above 8,000 metres, and most crowd the Himalaya. But one small tangle of Karakoram valleys, on the Pakistan-China frontier, hoards four of these giants closer together than anywhere else on the planet. Which four crown the Karakoram?
answer: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
choices: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
context: The Karakoram packs four of Earth's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks -- K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, and Gasherbrum II -- into one small knot of valleys, more giants per square mile than anywhere else. The Everest region and the rest of the Himalaya hold the other ten. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Trek for days up a broad highway of ice to the frozen crossroads called Concordia, 4,600 metres high, and four of the Karakoram's mighty giants stand ringed around you at once. In 1975 the American photographer Galen Rowell stood there awestruck and gave the amphitheatre a name that stuck. What did he call it?
answer: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
choices: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
the Rooftop Hall of the Snow Kings
the Cathedral of the Frozen Giants
the Great Court of the Sky Gods
context: Galen Rowell coined 'the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods' during the 1975 American K2 expedition and made it the title of his 1977 book. From Concordia (~4,600 m), where the Baltoro and Godwin-Austen glaciers meet, all four of the range's 8,000-metre peaks can be seen at once. Source: Galen Rowell, In the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods (1977); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier  (Legend.)

question: Outside the Arctic and Antarctic, no place on Earth wears more ice than the Karakoram -- nearly a third of the whole range lies frozen. Down its heart grinds a single river of ice about 63 km long, spilling from the flanks of K2 to feed the Braldu River and, in time, the mighty Indus. What is the name of this great glacier?
context: The Baltoro Glacier runs about 63 km, one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, and its meltwater joins the Braldu and then the Indus. Outside the Arctic and Antarctic the Karakoram is the most heavily glaciated place on Earth -- roughly a third under ice, versus about 8-12% of the Himalaya and 2% of the Alps. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: As the climate warms, almost every mountain glacier on Earth is shrinking back -- but the Karakoram refuses to follow. When geographer Kenneth Hewitt surveyed its ice in the early 2000s, he found dozens of glaciers behaving so strangely that scientists named the whole puzzle the 'Karakoram anomaly.' What are these glaciers doing?
context: Geographer Kenneth Hewitt named the 'Karakoram anomaly' in a 2005 paper: between 1997 and 2002, 13 glaciers (10-20 km long) advanced and 9 larger ones thickened by 5-15 m, some rebuilding moraines that had been ice-free for over half a century -- while glaciers almost everywhere else retreated. Source: Kenneth Hewitt, Mountain Research and Development 25 (2005)

question: Everywhere else, hot summers melt mountain ice -- so why is the Karakoram's growing? The leading explanation is a rare local weather pattern: each summer a pool of cold, high-altitude air settles over the range, wrapping it in cloud and snow and keeping its summers cool while the Himalaya to the south bakes -- so the ice is fed, not starved. Newcastle University scientists named this the Karakoram ___. What is the missing word?
context: The leading explanation is the 'Karakoram vortex,' a swirl of cold air that in summer contracts to sit over the range, keeping its summers cool and snowy while the rest of the Himalaya warms -- so the ice is fed, not starved. Proposed by a Newcastle University team (Nathan Forsythe, Hayley Fowler), it remains an active area of study, not settled fact. Source: sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/08/170807112835.htm; nature.com/articles/s41561-019-0513-5  (Legend.)

question: The Kathmandu Valley grew up around three ancient royal cities — Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur — and at the heart of each, ringing the old king's palace, spreads a great open plaza packed with tiered, many-roofed wooden temples. What is this palace-plaza at the center of each royal city called?
context: Each of the three old capitals — Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur — kept its own royal court, so the valley has three Durbar ('palace') Squares, not one. Around each king's palace, generations of Newar craftsmen raised clusters of tiered, many-roofed temples, making the squares open-air museums of Nepali woodcarving. All three belong to the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site (WHC #121). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Valley

question: Swayambhunath's long stone stairways, high on a hill above Kathmandu, are famous for the bold animals that patrol them in noisy gangs and snatch offerings and snacks from pilgrims. From those unruly residents the hilltop stupa earned the affectionate nickname foreign visitors still use for it. What is that nickname?
context: Troops of rhesus macaques really do rule Swayambhunath's hill and its 365-step eastern stairway, so travelers have long called it the 'Monkey Temple.' A Buddhist legend explains them: the bodhisattva Manjushri, tending the hill, let his hair grow long, and the lice in it are said to have turned into the monkeys. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: On a green hill above the Kathmandu Valley rises Swayambhunath, a whitewashed, dome-shaped Buddhist shrine — a stupa — capped by a golden spire. Painted huge on all four sides of that spire is the same image, one of the most recognizable sights in all Nepal. What is painted there?
context: The great painted 'all-seeing eyes' of the Buddha look out from all four sides of Swayambhunath's spire, symbolizing a wisdom that watches every direction at once. Between them curls a squiggle that looks like a nose; it is really the Nepali numeral 1, standing for unity and the single path to enlightenment. A stupa is a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often holding relics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: Facing Kathmandu's Durbar Square stands the Kumari Ghar, a richly carved wooden palace. Its resident is chosen from among little girls after a rigorous search, then kept apart — her feet never touching the open street — appearing at a lattice window so crowds below may bow and be blessed by her gaze. What is this venerated child believed to be?
context: She is the Kumari — a young girl worshipped as the living embodiment of the goddess Durga (locally Taleju). Chosen as a small child and revered until adolescence, she lives in the Kumari Ghar in Kathmandu's Durbar Square and appears at its window on festival days; once, even the king came to receive her blessing. The tradition is centuries old and still observed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square

question: On the valley floor a short way east of Kathmandu swells a vast whitewashed dome, one of the largest Buddhist stupas on Earth, its base circled all day by a slow river of pilgrims walking clockwise and spinning long rows of prayer wheels. Which great stupa is this?
context: This is Boudhanath, rising about 36 m (118 ft) — among the biggest stupas in the world. Walking clockwise around it while spinning prayer wheels inscribed 'Om mani padme hum' is called doing kora. After the 1959 Tibetan uprising, thousands of Tibetan refugees settled around it and built more than 50 monasteries, making Boudhanath a great living center of Tibetan Buddhism on the old Tibet-to-India trade route. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boudhanath

question: Nepal's capital, Kathmandu, took its name from a single building in its Durbar Square: a broad open pavilion called Kasthamandap, one of the oldest structures in the whole valley. Local tradition claims the entire pavilion was built from one astonishing source. From what was the whole pavilion supposedly made?
answer: the timber of a single tree
choices: the timber of a single tree
the bones of a great serpent
context: The pavilion is Kasthamandap ('kastha' = wood, 'mandap' = pavilion), and the city of Kathmandu takes its very name from it. Tradition holds the whole rest-house was raised from the timber of a single great sal tree. Kasthamandap stood for centuries until it collapsed entirely in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake; it has since been rebuilt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square  (Legend.)

question: The Buddhist Swayambhu Purana says the Kathmandu Valley was once a single vast lake, with a lotus of light blazing at its center. To reach that light and open the land for cities, the bodhisattva Manjushri came to the valley's rim and struck it a single blow, splitting the rock into the deep Chobar gorge, through which the whole lake drained away. What did Manjushri strike the rim with?
context: In the legend Manjushri cleaves the gorge with his flaming sword of wisdom, and the self-arisen ('Swayambhu') lotus of light comes to rest on the hill where Swayambhunath now stands. Remarkably, geologists agree the valley really was a lake for much of its deep past, slowly drained through the Chobar gorge — so the legend preserves a memory of the land's true history. Source: https://sacredsites.com/asia/nepal/swayambhunath_stupa.html

question: In the 1270s a young architect from the Kathmandu Valley, Araniko, led eighty Nepali craftsmen over the Himalayas to serve Kublai Khan, raising a great white temple-tower in the Mongol emperor's Chinese capital. Historians credit Araniko and his Newar tradition with helping shape the temple form now seen as the very symbol of East Asia. Which building form is that?
context: The architect was Araniko (Arniko, 1245–1306). When his king hesitated to send so young a man abroad, the boy answered, 'My body is indeed young, but my mind is not.' In Kublai Khan's capital Dadu (modern Beijing) he built the White Stupa of the Miaoying Temple, over 50 m tall, around 1279–1288, and the Khan made him Duke of Liang and Director of All Artisan Classes. The Kathmandu Valley's tradition of stacked temple roofs thus helped shape the pagoda across China and Japan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araniko

question: A vanished seafaring people left no writing behind, yet archaeologists can still pinpoint exactly where they first landed across the Pacific, from the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea eastward to Fiji. Their unmistakable calling card, turning up island after island, is what?
context: That signature is called Lapita ware: reddish-brown clay stamped before firing with rows of tiny toothed ('dentate') geometric patterns, pressed in with a comb-like tool. Wherever a matching shard turns up, the first seafarers had reached that spot -- which is how we know who sailed into the empty Pacific first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The whole Lapita culture takes its name from one site on the island of New Caledonia, in the southwest Pacific. In 1952 an archaeologist there asked a local man what the spot was called and wrote it down as 'Lapita' -- but the Haveke word he half-heard actually meant roughly what?
context: The Haveke word was 'xapeta'a', meaning something like 'to dig a hole' -- so an entire ancient civilization ended up named, through an archaeologist's mishearing, after a word for digging (fittingly, exactly what archaeologists do). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The same distinctive Lapita pottery appears island by island from the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea eastward to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa -- an unbroken trail more than 4,000 km long across open ocean. To archaeologists, this pottery trail is the record of what?
answer: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
choices: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
the widest trade network of the ancient world
the first empire to rule the open Pacific
the oldest island religion ever found
context: That trail maps the peopling of Remote Oceania -- the first humans ever to reach these far-flung islands, crossing thousands of kilometres of empty sea. It is counted as the greatest ocean-going migration in all of prehistory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The Lapita were the leading edge of a vast seafaring expansion whose ancient roots lay far to the northwest -- DNA from the 3,000-year-old Teouma graves on Vanuatu links these first voyagers to indigenous peoples of Taiwan and the northern Philippines. These first Pacific voyagers became the direct ancestors of which people?
context: These first voyagers were the direct ancestors of the Polynesians -- the eastern leading edge of the great Austronesian expansion that began near Taiwan and the northern Philippines. Ancient DNA from the Teouma graves carries the classic 'Polynesian motif' (haplogroup B4a1a1a) and clusters the earliest settlers with indigenous Taiwanese and Philippine peoples rather than with the nearby Papuans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The Lapita set out from the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea in great ocean-going canoes, island-hopping ever deeper into a Pacific no one had sailed before. What did they carry aboard these canoes across the open sea?
context: Their canoes were floating farms: pigs, dogs and chickens plus taro, yam, coconut and breadfruit, all carried to seed each new island with food. It was a provisioned, planned colonisation of empty islands -- powerful evidence the Lapita were skilled voyagers who sailed out on purpose, not castaways drifting on the current. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: At the 3,000-year-old Teouma cemetery on Efate island, Vanuatu -- the oldest burial ground ever found in the Pacific -- many Lapita skeletons lay in the ground with no skulls at all. Once a body's flesh had rotted away, the living Lapita carefully lifted out its skull. Where did archaeologists find some of these missing skulls?
context: On one old man's chest lay three skulls set side by side, with three more placed between another person's legs; a seventh was tucked inside a decorated Lapita pot -- part of over 100 vessels found at Teouma, the largest single haul of Lapita pottery anywhere. The site was found by chance in 2003 when a bulldozer clearing land for a shrimp farm turned up red pottery shards. Source: https://humanities.org.au/power-of-the-humanities/lapita-cemetery-in-vanutu-thelps-solve-ancient-mystery/

question: On a clear, still evening over the Pacific off Hawaii, beachgoers keep their eyes on the Sun's very last rim as it slips into the sea. In the one second before that top edge vanishes underwater, watchers sometimes catch it doing something startling — a sight sailors have told tales about for centuries. What can the Sun's final rim do?
context: The classic 'green flash.' It's best seen over a clean, unobstructed ocean horizon on a clear, still evening — off Hawaii, the California coast, or Key West — and it's over in a blink, about one to two seconds. The Sun doesn't really turn green; only a thin rim of green light shows at its very top edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: As the Sun's disk touches the sea off the California coast, the low, thick air near the water bends and fans its light like a weak prism, tinting the very top rim. At that edge the Sun is really giving off blue and green light together — yet what beachgoers catch is a green rim, never a blue one. On its long, slanting path through the air, what happens to the blue light?
answer: the air scatters it out of the beam
choices: the air scatters it out of the beam
water vapor absorbs it near the sea
it bends down below the horizon first
the red light overpowers and hides it
context: It's the same reason the daytime sky is blue: air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light out of the beam (Rayleigh scattering). The low air over the horizon also bends and separates the Sun's colors like a weak prism (refraction and dispersion); with the blue scattered away and the red already set, a rim of green is the last light left at the Sun's edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: An ordinary green flash is a one-second blink, gone before you can point. But in October 1929, at Admiral Byrd's Antarctic base of Little America near the Bay of Whales, the Sun barely sank at all — it crawled sideways along the ice horizon. Byrd's men watched a brilliant green spot flash on and off, on and off, at the edge of the world. How long did that green flash keep flickering?
context: Byrd's own account: 'a tiny but brilliant green spot... no sooner disappeared than it flashed forth again... it remained on the horizon with short interruptions for thirty-five minutes.' Near the poles the Sun moves almost parallel to the horizon, so instead of a one-second blink the flash can wink on and off for many minutes; optics researchers reconstructed the 16 October 1929 event in a 2015 study. (Little America sat near the Bay of Whales at about 78 degrees S — not the geographic South Pole.) Sources: aaas.org/membership/scientia/catching-elusive-green-flash; opg.optica.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-54-4-B54.

question: In the coldest winters of the 'Little Ice Age' — roughly 1300 to 1850 — the River Thames in London froze hard enough to walk on. The name sounds apocalyptic, as if mile-high ice sheets had crushed the continents. In Europe and North America, how much colder than winters today were the coldest Little Ice Age winters?
context: Despite the fearsome name, the Little Ice Age (c.1300-1850) was a modest, patchy REGIONAL cooling — European and North American winters ran up to about 2°C colder than today's — not a true planet-wide glacial ice age with continental ice sheets. You read it not in mile-high ice but in frozen rivers, advancing glaciers, and the winter art people painted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age.

question: In the bitter winters of the Little Ice Age, the River Thames in London sometimes froze so solid that Londoners threw carnivals right on the ice — the famous 'frost fairs,' with rows of tents, shops, and taverns. At the very last one, in February 1814, they led a single large animal out onto the frozen river below Blackfriars Bridge to show how thick the ice was. What animal walked across the frozen Thames?
context: Londoners called these ice carnivals 'frost fairs' (the term dates to the fair of 1608), pitching tents, shops, taverns, and even printing presses on the frozen Thames. The February 1814 fair was the last great one, and the elephant led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge is its most famous — and most often-retold — image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.  (Legend.)

question: Londoners blamed the Little Ice Age cold for freezing the Thames, but the river's own shape did half the work. Before the 1800s the Thames ran broad, shallow, and slow, and one crowded medieval bridge spanning it on nineteen fat stone piers pinched the current into narrow arches — so at low tide, drifting ice jammed against it, held back the water like a dam, and the river froze solid. Which Thames bridge choked the river into a near-dam?
context: Old London Bridge's nineteen piers wore bulky timber 'starling' casings that squeezed the tide into narrow arches, damming the sluggish, shallow river until it froze. It was demolished in 1831 and replaced with wider arches, and through the 1800s the banks were walled with embankments — so the Thames ran narrower, deeper, and faster, and it has never frozen solid in London since. The frost fairs ended partly because the RIVER changed, not only because the climate warmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.

question: In the Alps above Chamonix, France, the Little Ice Age drove the Mont Blanc glaciers forward — the ice ground downhill and buried whole hamlets, until by 1616 one village had only six houses left standing at the ice front. Around 1645 the frightened villagers summoned the Bishop of Geneva, who climbed to the glacier's snout and performed a solemn church rite right there on the ice. What rite did the bishop carry out on the glacier?
context: The advancing ice between about 1600 and 1610 destroyed the hamlets of Le Chatelard (settled since the 1200s), La Bonnenuit, and La Bonneville. The exorcism didn't work — only the end of the Little Ice Age, two centuries later, finally halted the glaciers. Recorded tradition. Sources: chamonix.net history of Chamonix glaciers; academic.emporia.edu Late Holocene climate.  (Legend.)

question: As the Little Ice Age froze the canals of the Netherlands each winter, a Dutch painter named Hendrick Avercamp — deaf and unable to speak, and nicknamed 'the mute of Kampen' — turned the frozen waterways into art. His crowded 1608 canvases show entire towns swarming out onto the ice. What winter pastime, painted again and again by Avercamp and still a Dutch passion today, fills those frozen-canal scenes?
context: Avercamp's 'Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters' (1608) helped pioneer the Dutch winter-landscape genre — a whole art form born from the Little Ice Age's frozen canals, and a near-photographic record of those winters. Skating on the frozen waterways became a lasting Dutch passion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrick_Avercamp.

question: Around 985 Erik the Red led Norse settlers to Greenland, and through the milder centuries that followed they built a thriving farming colony — a few thousand people on some 500 farms, raising cattle and sheep at the edge of the habitable world. Then the Little Ice Age crept in, and by the late 1400s the colony had dwindled and vanished. Historians still debate the causes, but the central climate blow was straightforward. What did the deepening cold do that doomed the Greenland farms?
answer: left summers too short to grow winter hay
choices: left summers too short to grow winter hay
buried the farms under advancing glaciers
froze the soil into permanent permafrost
locked the fjords in ice all year round
context: The Western Settlement emptied around 1350 and the Eastern by the late 1400s. Cooling shortened the growing season and disrupted the seal hunt — but the colony had also funded itself by exporting walrus ivory to Europe, and that trade collapsed when African elephant ivory undercut it and the walrus were over-hunted. So climate was one thread among several, not the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America.

question: The Dasht-e Lut, a desert in southeastern Iran, is the hottest place anywhere on the planet's surface -- so remote and so blistering that its record heat was clocked not by a thermometer on the ground but by satellite from orbit. Out on the bare sand, you truly could fry an egg. What temperature did the satellites record?
context: That 80.8 C (177 F) reading, captured by NASA's MODIS satellite instrument in 2018, is the hottest land-SURFACE temperature ever recorded anywhere on Earth -- an earlier 2005 pass had already clocked 70.7 C. One thing worth remembering: this is the temperature of the GROUND, seen from space, not of the air. The world's hottest reliably-recorded AIR temperature is much lower -- 56.7 C (134 F), set at Furnace Creek in California's Death Valley on 10 July 1913. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (MODIS surface-temperature study); WMO Death Valley air-temperature record.

question: The Dasht-e Lut roasts hotter at ground level than any other desert on Earth -- hotter even than deserts that get more blazing sun. The secret lies in what the desert floor is made of, and its colour. Why does the Lut's ground heat up so ferociously?
answer: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
choices: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
Dark obsidian gravel sheets it, baking like a tray of broken glass
A red iron crust bakes it, hoarding the day's heat long past sundown
Fine volcanic ash blankets it, dark and soft as fireplace soot
context: More than half the Lut's surface is covered by dark volcanic rock, blackened by ancient lava -- and dark ground drinks in sunlight instead of bouncing it away, exactly like a black cast-iron pan left in the sun. A ring of mountains around the basin then traps that heat, with almost no wind to carry it off, so the surface bakes far past what the sunshine alone could explain. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (over half the surface covered by volcanic rock).

question: The single hottest patch of the whole Lut is a scorched plateau the locals call Gandom Beryan -- Persian for 'Toasted Wheat.' A local legend explains that curious name. According to the tale, how did the plateau earn it?
answer: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
choices: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
Traders roasted their wheat there by burying the sacks in the scalding sand
Bread left on the rock came out toasted golden by the heat of the ground alone
A caravan hauling wheat vanished on it, leaving only spilled, blackened grain
context: Gandom Beryan ('Toasted Wheat') is a dark plateau in the northern Lut, long reputed to be the desert's single hottest ground. The story that a stash of wheat, simply left on the surface, blackened within days is folk legend rather than measured fact -- but it fits a place whose bare ground is the hottest ever measured on the planet. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (Gandom Beryan); Adventure Iran, 'Gandom Beryan Lut Desert'.

question: For ages, fierce winds roaring in from the northwest have hurled sand against the Lut's bedrock, grinding it into 'kaluts' -- long parallel ridges that geologists call yardangs, running for tens of kilometres across the desert. Seen from high above, what do these ridges eerily resemble?
answer: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
choices: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
a single giant fingerprint pressed into the sand
the curved ribs of some enormous buried beast
a frozen sea of rolling, wind-worn stone waves
context: These corrugated ridges are yardangs -- rock and hard sediment carved by relentless, sand-laden wind. In the Lut, the winds sweep in from the northwest between June and October, sculpting yardangs up to 75 m tall that run for over 150 km. From high above, the endless ranks of ridges and hollows look so much like a ruined metropolis that the region is nicknamed the 'abandoned city of ghosts' -- and the Lut holds some of the finest yardangs found anywhere on Earth. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; UNESCO World Heritage Convention; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (yardangs to 75 m, over 150 km).

question: When UNESCO inscribed the Lut Desert in 2016, Iranians hailed it as a first. After decades of listing palaces, mosques, and ancient cities -- Persepolis, Isfahan's great square, Pasargadae -- Iran had finally added a World Heritage Site of an altogether new type. What type of site was the Lut?
answer: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
choices: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
an endangered site -- a treasure judged already at risk
a transboundary site -- one wonder split across two nations
a mixed site -- wild desert wrapped around ancient ruins
context: On 17 July 2016, at UNESCO's 40th session in Istanbul, the Lut Desert (World Heritage list no. 1505) became the first NATURAL site anywhere in Iran to earn World Heritage status, inscribed for its yardangs and vast sand seas under criteria vii and viii. Every Iranian site listed before it had honoured human culture; the Lut was the first chosen to protect the land itself. Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, list no. 1505; IFP News, 'Lut Desert inscribed... Iran's first natural site'.

question: The Maldives strings some 1,200 islands across the Indian Ocean, yet the land barely clears the water: it averages just 1.5 m above the sea, and its highest natural point, on Addu Atoll, reaches only about 2.4 m. Among the world's nations, what record does the Maldives hold?
context: No nation has a lower high point. The Maldives averages about 1.5 m (4.9 ft) above sea level, and even its natural summit on Addu Atoll is only about 2.4 m (7 ft 10 in). A resort on Villingili markets a 5.1 m landscaped mound as the 'highest peak in the Maldives,' but that is an artificial dune, not natural ground. Source: Wikipedia, 'Geography of the Maldives'; earthsky.org.

question: A ring of coral reef enclosing a shallow lagoon is called an atoll, and the Maldives -- built almost entirely of such ring-reefs -- gave the world that very word. 'Atoll' is one of only a handful of English words borrowed from the Maldivian people's own language. What is that language called?
context: English 'atoll' comes from the Dhivehi word 'atholhu.' Dhivehi is the language of the Maldives; Sinhala (Sri Lanka), Tamil, and Malayalam are neighboring South Asian languages, but the word 'atoll' came only from Dhivehi. Source: Wiktionary, 'atoll'; Wordnik.

question: Charles Darwin puzzled over atolls like those of the Maldives: a ring of living coral standing alone in the open ocean, with nothing but a lagoon in the middle and no island at all. In 1842 he gave a bold answer -- a volcanic island had once risen right there, and its reef had grown around the shore; then something happened to that island, leaving only the coral ring. In Darwin's theory, what became of the volcanic island?
answer: it slowly sank beneath the sea
choices: it slowly sank beneath the sea
it slowly eroded away in storms
it was buried under drifting sand
it split off on the moving seafloor
context: Darwin's 'subsidence theory,' published in 1842 in his first book, The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs: the volcano slowly sank while the reef-building coral kept growing upward toward the sunlight it needs, so when the island finally vanished under the sea, a ring of living coral marked where it had stood. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; Britannica, 'Darwinian subsidence theory.'

question: Standing on the Keeling atoll in the Indian Ocean in 1836, Charles Darwin was struck that this whole vast reef had been raised by tiny, soft coral animals, one grain at a time. In The Voyage of the Beagle he wrote that these 'mountains of stone' made humanity's grandest ancient ruins seem utterly insignificant -- and he named the single most famous of them. Which monument did Darwin say the coral dwarfed?
context: Darwin wrote: 'We feel surprise when travellers tell us of the vast dimensions of the Pyramids and other great ruins, but how utterly insignificant are the greatest of these, when compared to these mountains of stone accumulated by the agency of various minute and tender animals!' Source: Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 20; standardebooks.org.

question: Astonishingly, Charles Darwin worked out how atolls form before he had ever seen one. Sailing on HMS Beagle in November 1835, he studied the coral reef ringing one lush Pacific island and sketched his entire sinking-island theory on the spot; only months later did the Beagle reach a true atoll, the Keeling Islands, to test it. At which island did Darwin first dream up his theory?
context: Darwin first sketched the subsidence idea after visiting Tahiti in November 1835, then tested it against a real ring-reef when the Beagle surveyed the Keeling (Cocos) Islands in April 1836 -- six months before the voyage came home. He had the theory before he had the proof. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; darwinproject.ac.uk.

question: For over a century, Charles Darwin's atoll theory stayed unproven, because no drill could bore through the towering pile of coral to reach whatever lay at its base. Then in 1952, engineers on Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific drilled straight down through more than four thousand feet of coral, until the bit finally reached the floor beneath. What did the drillers find waiting at the very bottom?
context: At Enewetak in 1952, drills bored through roughly 4,200-4,600 ft (about 1,300-1,400 m) of coral and struck volcanic basalt -- the drowned volcano Darwin had predicted in 1842, confirmed more than a century later. Earlier holes fell short: Funafuti in the 1890s reached about 1,114 ft and Bikini in 1947 about 2,556 ft, both still in coral. Source: royalsociety.org; Britannica, 'atoll.'

question: The Maldives is so low that it lives on the front line of rising seas: a coral atoll is alive and can grow taller as the ocean climbs, but only so fast. In 2009, the country's president, Mohamed Nasheed, staged a dramatic first for any government to force the world's climate summit to pay attention. What did Nasheed do to sound the alarm?
choices: marched his ministers to the North Pole
chained himself to the summit gates
shut every airport in the country
context: In October 2009, President Mohamed Nasheed and his ministers, in scuba gear, held a cabinet meeting about 5 m (16 ft) underwater and signed a document to hand to the Copenhagen climate summit. Nasheed even floated buying higher land abroad (naming Sri Lanka, India, and Australia) as a possible new home for the population; his successor later dropped the idea. The UN's IPCC has warned the low atolls could become uninhabitable this century if seas rise faster than the coral can build. Source: CBC News; commondreams.org.

question: The Challenger Deep, at the bottom of the western Pacific's Mariana Trench, is the deepest spot on Earth — nearly 11 km straight down. Picture sinking all of Mount Everest, the planet's highest mountain, to the trench floor. How far beneath the ocean surface would the famous summit still lie?
context: Challenger Deep bottoms out around 10,935 m (about 6.8 miles) down — more than 2 km deeper than Everest is tall (8,849 m), so the whole mountain would vanish beneath the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench (2021 depth study; 'more than 2 km farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest').

question: The Challenger Deep, the deepest point anywhere on Earth, lies in the western Pacific only a few hundred kilometres from the nearest large inhabited island — the closest patch of land to the bottom of the world. Which island lies nearest?
context: Guam, the largest of the Mariana Islands, is the nearest sizeable inhabited land to the Challenger Deep, which lies roughly 300 km to the southwest in the western Pacific. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('about 200 km east of the Mariana Islands near Guam').

question: In 1875, a British sailing ship — a former warship refitted as a floating laboratory — was well into a four-year voyage around the world when it paused over the western Pacific and lowered a weighted rope nearly 8,000 m to the seafloor: the deepest sounding of the entire expedition. Which ship made that record reading?
context: HMS Challenger sounded 4,475 fathoms (about 8,184 m) here on 23 March 1875 during its 1872-76 round-the-world science voyage — the deepest reading of the whole trip — and the deepest point on Earth, the Challenger Deep, was later named for the ship. NASA named a space shuttle after the very same vessel. Sources: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml; ocean.si.edu (HMS Challenger expedition); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger.

question: The Mariana Trench is a vast but slender scar on the western Pacific seafloor near Guam — stretching about 2,550 km from end to end, yet nowhere more than about 70 km across. Traced on a map, what shape does this long, thin trench form?
context: The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped gash about 2,550 km long but only 69 km wide, curving across the western Pacific seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('crescent-shaped... about 2,550 km in length and 69 km in width').

question: For 85 years after it was discovered, no one had touched the bottom of the Challenger Deep. Then, on 23 January 1960, a tiny steel sphere slung beneath a fuel-filled float sank for nearly five hours into the black, and two men became the first ever to stand at the deepest point on Earth. Who were they?
context: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom on 23 January 1960 after a descent of nearly five hours — the first humans ever to reach the deepest point on Earth, and for 52 years the only ones. Sources: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml; earthmagazine.org (Benchmarks: 23 January 1960).

question: Deep into the Trieste's 1960 descent toward the Challenger Deep floor, the two-man crew suddenly heard a startling BANG echo through the cabin. Something on the craft had cracked under the monstrous pressure — yet they chose to keep sinking. What had cracked?
context: On the way down, the Trieste's outer Plexiglas viewport cracked under about 16,000 psi of pressure with a loud crack; Piccard and Walsh kept descending anyway, but the crack and stirred-up silt limited them to about 20 minutes on the bottom. Source: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml.

question: In 2012, more than half a century after the first descent, a lone pilot rode the sub Deepsea Challenger to the bottom of the Challenger Deep — the deepest solo dive in history. Astonishingly, the man sealed inside was far better known for directing blockbuster movies. Who made this record-breaking dive?
context: James Cameron, director of Titanic and Avatar, dived solo to about 10,908 m in the Deepsea Challenger on 26 March 2012 — the deepest solo dive ever. His descent took 2 hours 37 minutes and he spent about three hours on the bottom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepsea_Challenger.

question: At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 km of ocean bears down at over a thousand times the pressure you feel at sea level. Concentrated onto a spot the size of your thumbnail, that force is like balancing which of these on it?
context: At the bottom the water presses at about 1,086 bar (15,750 psi) — roughly 1,072 times sea-level pressure, or about 8 tons on every square inch, like balancing an elephant on your thumbnail. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('1,086 bar... approximately 1,071.8 times... eight tons per square inch').

question: No ray of sunlight ever reaches the floor of the Challenger Deep, so nothing there can grow by photosynthesis. Instead, the animals of the deep live on a constant, faint fall of dead plankton and scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. Scientists gave this endless food supply a poetic name — what is it called?
context: No sunlight reaches the pitch-black trench floor, so life there depends on 'marine snow' — a steady drift of dead plankton and organic scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. Sources: csmonitor.com (What James Cameron saw 6.8 miles deep); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench.

question: The Challenger Deep is not a simple crack in the seafloor. It marks the line where the old, cold Pacific Plate bends downward and slides beneath the smaller Mariana Plate, dragging ocean crust back down into Earth's hot mantle. Geologists call this plate-swallowing process by what name?
context: The Challenger Deep is a subduction zone: the old, cold Pacific Plate bends and dives beneath the smaller Mariana Plate, recycling ocean crust down into the mantle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('the Pacific plate is subducted beneath the smaller Mariana plate').

question: Along the edge of the Mariana Trench, at least 19 enormous mounds rise from the seafloor — among the biggest 'volcanoes' of their kind anywhere on Earth. Fluids wrung from the Pacific Plate as it dives beneath the Mariana Plate are forced up through cracks in the crust, building these giants. Surprisingly, what do they erupt?
context: At least 19 serpentinite 'mud volcanoes' rise along the Mariana forearc: fluids squeezed from the subducting Pacific Plate turn mantle rock into serpentine mud that oozes up through faults and feeds sunless chemosynthetic microbes at the edge of life. Sources: pnas.org/content/109/8/2831; publications.iodp.org (IODP Expedition 366).

question: The Matterhorn rises alone above the Swiss village of Zermatt as an almost perfect rock pyramid — the 'Toblerone' peak. Climbers noticed a tidy surprise about its four steep faces: what does each face line up with?
context: The four faces point almost exactly north, east, south, and west — three sit on the Swiss side, the south face on the Italian side. The lonely 4,478 m (14,692 ft) pyramid is so iconic it inspired the Toblerone chocolate logo. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Matterhorn; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn.

question: The Matterhorn looks like a stone spike shoved straight up out of the earth. Geologists say the truth is the opposite: the peak is only the hard core left standing after everything around it was slowly stripped away. What did the stripping?
choices: a river carving a canyon through it
context: Four glaciers gnawed bowl-shaped hollows (cirques) into four sides of the same peak at once, grinding the rock between them into knife-edge ridges that meet at a point. A summit carved to a spike this way is called a glacial 'horn' — and a four-faced one is textbook enough that geologists call it the 'Matterhorn type.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramidal_peak; britannica.com/science/horn-glacial-landform.

question: Stand on the very summit of the Matterhorn, in Switzerland, and the rock beneath your boots is not European at all. The mountain's top slice is a slab of crust that was shoved up and OVER Europe when another whole continent slammed into it and squeezed an ancient ocean shut. Which continent's rock forms that summit?
context: Only the top ~1,000 m is African: it is gneiss of the Dent Blanche nappe, a slice of the African (Adriatic) plate thrust up and over Europe when the two continents collided and closed the ancient Tethys Ocean. The rest of the mountain sits on European bedrock — so the very summit of a Swiss peak is a piece of Africa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dent_Blanche_nappe; earthlymission.com.

question: On 14 July 1865 Edward Whymper's team of seven became the first people ever to stand on the Matterhorn's summit — on Whymper's ninth attempt. Starting down, the least experienced climber, Douglas Hadow, slipped and pulled three companions off the ridge. The rope tying those four falling men to the three above them snapped, and all four plunged nearly 4,000 feet. What was damning about that particular rope?
answer: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
choices: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
it had frayed on the sharp rocks during the climb
it was the thinnest, lightest cord they carried
it had been nicked by a falling rock earlier
context: The snapped rope was the oldest and weakest the party carried, brought only as a reserve; the four fell about 4,000 ft down the north face. Whymper and the two Taugwalder guides survived. In 'Scrambles Amongst the Alps' (1871) Whymper wrote that he watched them slide 'downwards on their backs... endeavouring to save themselves,' and warned that courage and strength count for nothing without prudence. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Whymper; smithsonianmag.com.

question: High on the Matterhorn's Hörnli ridge in 2003, a block of rock the size of four houses suddenly broke loose without warning, and helicopters had to lift about 90 climbers off the peak to safety. Investigators discovered that the mountain's cracks had, for thousands of years, been held firmly shut by a hidden binder — until it finally gave way. What was that binder?
choices: natural mineral cement between the grains
compacted rubble wedged in its cracks
context: That ice is permafrost — frozen groundwater cementing the rock's cracks. In the 2003 heatwave it thawed and about 1,500 m3 of rock (roughly four houses' worth) broke off the Hörnli ridge, forcing helicopters to evacuate around 90 climbers. The scare launched the PermaSense project, which now monitors the crumbling ice inside the mountain. Source: news.uzh.ch (Matterhorn-Permasense); futurity.org.

question: Sensors bolted onto the Matterhorn reveal that its rocky summit is never truly still — it quivers up to 14 times more than its base. Some of that faint sway comes from distant earthquakes, but researchers were amazed to find the peak is also rocked, tremor by tiny tremor, by something hundreds of miles away with no quake involved. What keeps nudging it?
answer: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
choices: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
the roar of faraway mountain winds
the churn of a great distant river
context: The summit resonates like a slow tuning fork, swaying up to ~14 times more than its base. Much of it is 'microseism' — faint, ceaseless ground vibration made when ocean waves pound far-off coastlines and ripple through the Earth to the peak; nearby seismic tremors add more. A landlocked Alpine giant, gently rocked by the sea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Matterhorn.

question: On the lower Mississippi, the water on the outside of every bend races along and gnaws its bank away, while the inside slows down and drops a fresh load of sand. Bend after bend, this lopsided cut-here, fill-there action turns a straight channel into one that winds in great curves across the valley floor. Geographers have a name for one of these grand river bends — what is it?
context: The fast outer bank becomes a steep 'cut bank' (or river cliff); the sheltered inside builds a gentle 'point bar' of sand — erode on the outside, deposit on the inside, and the whole train of bends slowly crawls downstream. The word 'meander' itself comes from the Buyuk Menderes (ancient Maiandros) River in Turkey, whose bends were so famous that, so the story goes, the Greeks copied them into the repeating 'Greek key' fret carved on the Parthenon. Source: Grokipedia, 'Meander,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Meander.'

question: Follow one of the Mississippi's bends as it loops back on itself until only a thin sliver of land still separates the two arms of the river. One big flood then punches straight across that narrow neck; the river seizes the shortcut, and the stranded bend is sealed off from the current and left as a still lake all its own. What is this kind of lake — a whole river bend, cut off and left behind — called?
context: An oxbow lake is named for the oxbow, the U-shaped wooden collar that curved around an ox's neck in a plow yoke — the very shape of the abandoned loop. Australians call it a 'billabong,' Texans a 'resaca.' The Mississippi valley is freckled with them: Arkansas's Lake Chicot is the largest oxbow lake in North America, and Tennessee's Reelfoot Lake was born when the great 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes reshaped the ground. Source: Grokipedia, 'Oxbow lake,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Oxbow lake.'

question: Across the lower Mississippi's floodplain, a river bend cut off from the channel is doomed the moment the water leaves it. With no current to keep it clear, the still crescent pond fills in — first a reedy swamp choked with mud and plants, then, at last, it dries out for good. All that is left is a faint curved line printed on the valley floor, traced across farm fields and picked out from a passing plane. What is this last dry ghost of a vanished bend called?
context: Geographers call this dry, curved trace a 'meander scar' — the fossil footprint of a bend that no longer exists. The full sequence runs oxbow lake to marshy swamp to dry scar, sometimes over centuries. From the air the old scars stack in curved stripes, mapping every path the river once took across its floodplain. Source: Grokipedia, 'Oxbow lake,' corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Oxbow lake.'

question: At the Goosenecks of the San Juan River in Utah, the river coils back on itself in tight loops sunk about 300 m (1,000 ft) below the surrounding desert — winding more than 6 miles to advance barely 1.5 miles as the crow flies. Unlike the lowland Mississippi, which loops lazily across a soft, open valley, the San Juan is boxed inside sheer stone walls it carved straight downward as the whole region slowly rose. What do geologists call bends like these, sunk deep in solid rock?
context: These are 'entrenched' (or 'incised') meanders — bends sawn straight down into bedrock. Long ago the San Juan wandered near sea level; then the Monument Upwarp slowly lifted the whole region, and the trapped river cut downward to keep pace, engraving its old loops 300 m into stone. The Goosenecks are the finest example of entrenched meanders on Earth. Sources: Visit Utah, 'Rafting the San Juan River'; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Goosenecks State Park.'

question: At Horseshoe Bend near Page, Arizona, the emerald Colorado River sweeps almost a full circle around a lone butte of Navajo Sandstone, running 300 m (1,000 ft) below the overlook rim just downstream of Glen Canyon Dam. The loop is nearly closed — only a thin neck of rock still separates the incoming river from the outgoing river. Ages from now the Colorado will saw clean through that neck and desert the loop. What will it leave standing where the neck once stood?
context: Horseshoe Bend is a single incised meander.
