context: Guinness World Records recognizes the Sundarbans, at the mouth of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, as the largest mangrove forest on Earth -- about 10,000 sq km of trees rooted in salt water. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/507848-largest-mangrove-forest

question: The people of the Bengal delta named their vast tidal forest long ago in their own language: Sundarbans. In Bengali, what does that name mean?
context: In Bengali, sundar means 'beautiful' and ban means 'forest' -- Sundarbans, 'the beautiful forest.' The name is also tied to the sundari tree (Heritiera fomes), the dominant mangrove that once carpeted the delta. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; britannica.com/place/Sundarbans

question: The mud of the Sundarbans is so waterlogged that no oxygen reaches down into it, yet the mangrove trees rooted there must still breathe. How does a mangrove get air to the roots buried in that airless mud?
answer: it grows snorkel roots that poke up into the air
choices: it grows snorkel roots that poke up into the air
it stores a bubble of air inside its trunk
it soaks up air dissolved in the seawater
it opens tiny mouths on its bark at night
context: The airless delta mud has almost no oxygen, so mangroves grow 'breathing roots' (pneumatophores) that poke straight up out of the mud. Tiny pores called lenticels on these snorkel-roots let the tree take in air at low tide. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; britannica.com/place/Sundarbans

question: The Sundarbans is a shifting patchwork of about a hundred islands, laced by some four hundred tidal rivers and creeks. Twice a day the Bay of Bengal's tide floods in and drains back out. What does that daily tide do to the land itself?
answer: it drowns about a third of the land
choices: it drowns about a third of the land
it pushes the islands out to sea
it carries the topsoil off to the ocean
it slowly turns the fresh water salty
context: The Sundarbans is a patchwork of about 102 islands laced by roughly 400 tidal rivers, creeks and canals. The tide averages about 2 m and can reach 5.7 m, and about one-third of the land vanishes and reappears every single day. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Sundarbans,_The

question: When a 1999 super-cyclone drove a wall of seawater onto India's Odisha coast and killed nearly ten thousand people, researchers walked village by village afterward, asking why some places lost far fewer lives than others. They found that one thing about a village's mangroves mattered most of all. What was it?
answer: how wide the mangrove belt was
choices: how wide the mangrove belt was
how tall the mangrove trees were
how old the mangrove forest was
how dense the mangrove roots were
context: The tangled root-wall blunts storm surges. In a rigorous study of the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone -- which killed nearly 10,000 people, more than 70% of them drowned by the surge -- the WIDTH of the mangrove belt between a village and the sea best predicted survival: villages behind wider mangroves lost far fewer lives, and researchers estimated 1.72 more deaths per village would have occurred if the mangroves had been stripped to zero (Das & Vincent, PNAS 2009). After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, coasts with mangroves also suffered less damage than bare coasts (Danielsen et al., Science 2005), though the trees could not stop the very worst zones, and the PNAS authors caution their cyclone result may not fully carry over to tsunamis. Sources: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0810440106 ; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16254180/

question: A mangrove coast like the Sundarbans is one of the greatest carbon traps on Earth -- so effective that scientists gave the carbon it stores a name of its own: 'blue carbon.' Acre for acre it holds far more carbon than a tropical rainforest. Where does a mangrove lock most of that carbon away?
answer: in deep mud around its roots
choices: in deep mud around its roots
in the wood of its trunks
in the seawater at its roots
context: The answer is the mud. A mangrove buries most of its carbon in the deep, waterlogged mud around its roots -- roughly 3-5 times more carbon per acre than an ordinary tropical forest, and buried about ten times faster, locked in airless mud that piles up meters deep for centuries. Scientists call it 'blue carbon.' Sources: oceanservice.noaa.gov/ecosystems/coastal-blue-carbon/ ; thebluecarboninitiative.org/about-blue-carbon

question: Mangrove forests fringe warm coasts all around the globe -- in Florida, across Indonesia, along West Africa. Yet one big cat prowls a mangrove in only ONE place on Earth: the Sundarbans, where it swims the tidal channels from island to island to hunt. Which big cat is this?
context: The Sundarbans is the only mangrove forest on Earth where tigers live -- roughly 180-200 Royal Bengal tigers (estimates vary by census) that swim the tidal channels from island to island to hunt. No other tiger population lives in a mangrove; the tiger is the signature of this place. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; whc.unesco.org/en/list/798/

question: A single unbroken band of dark evergreen conifer forest wraps almost the whole way around the top of the world -- across northern Canada, Sweden, Finland and Russia -- and it is the largest land biome anywhere on Earth. What is this vast northern biome called?
context: The taiga, also called the boreal forest, forms one nearly unbroken ring of conifers across northern Canada, Scandinavia and Russia. It is the largest land biome on Earth -- by some reckonings only deserts and dry shrublands cover more ground overall, so the safe claim is 'largest land biome,' not 'largest biome of any kind.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga.

question: The taiga's second name traces straight back to Greek myth. The Greeks gave each of the four winds its own god, and one ruled the freezing northern gale that roared down each year to usher in winter. Which of these Greek wind-gods was he?
context: The answer is Boreas, Greek god of the north wind and of winter -- and the taiga's second name, the 'boreal forest,' was built straight from his. Boreas passed into Latin as borealis ('northern') and entered English in the late 1400s. The other three choices are the remaining Anemoi: Zephyrus (west wind), Notus (south) and Eurus (east). Sources: etymonline.com/word/boreal; theoi.com (Boreas).

question: Picture every tree on Earth -- the Amazon's jungle, and every forest, orchard and city park. It is tempting to assume most of them grow in the warm, crowded tropics. In truth a startling share stand in the cold boreal ring of conifers wrapping the far north. Roughly what fraction of all the world's trees grow in the boreal forest?
context: The boreal forest holds roughly a third of all the trees on Earth -- about 27-33% of the world's total forest cover -- which makes it the single largest forest belt on the planet, even though each tree grows slowly in the short, cold summers. Sources: onetreeplanted.org; forest-healing.co.uk.

question: Nearly every conifer on Earth stays green right through winter -- that is what makes an evergreen evergreen. But across Eastern Siberia the taiga is ruled by a strange exception: a cone-bearing tree that each autumn blazes gold, sheds every last needle and stands bare through winters near -60 C, then grows a whole new coat come spring. Which conifer is this?
context: The Eastern Siberian taiga is a vast forest of larch, a rare 'deciduous conifer' -- it bears cones like a pine but drops its needles each autumn, an adaptation that helps it endure winters colder than -60 C. The Dahurian larch is the most cold-hardy tree on Earth. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga; conifers.org (Larix gmelinii).

question: Across much of the taiga, a conifer's roots spread out sideways in a shallow mat rather than driving straight down. Below the thin skin of soil that softens each July lies a hard, unyielding layer that reaches down hundreds of metres and that no root can pierce. What do geologists call this deep layer beneath the taiga?
context: This year-round frozen ground is permafrost. Trees can root only in the thin 'active layer' of soil that thaws each summer, which is why shallow-rooted species like larch -- whose roots seldom reach deeper than about 20 cm -- dominate. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga; conifers.org (Larix gmelinii).

question: We usually picture the steamy tropical rainforest as the planet's greatest carbon store. But the boreal forest holds carbon as well -- in its conifers, in its cold soils, and in the peat of its bogs. Set against the world's tropical rainforests, how much carbon does the boreal forest and its soils lock away?
answer: more than the tropical forests hold
choices: more than the tropical forests hold
the same as the tropical forests hold
half what the tropical forests hold
less than the tropical forests hold
context: It holds more. Because the cold slows rot to a crawl, the boreal forest's trees, soils and peat bogs store nearly twice as much carbon per unit area as tropical rainforests. The northern permafrost zone alone holds an estimated 1,460-1,600 billion tonnes of frozen organic carbon -- roughly twice as much as is in the entire atmosphere. Sources: nrdc.org; onetreeplanted.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga.

question: Popularly, the Taklamakan's name is read as a warning to travelers: go in, and you don't come out. Caravans crossing this vast desert of shifting dunes in western China gave it a second, grimmer nickname. What was it?
context: The name 'Taklamakan' is popularly read as a warning — 'go in and you don't come out' — and its killing dryness and shifting dunes earned it the grim nickname the 'Sea of Death.' (Scholars actually debate the true etymology: it may come from an Arabic phrase for 'abandoned place' or a Turkic one for 'place of ruins' — but the folk meaning is the memorable one.) Sources: Grokipedia 'Taklamakan Desert'; Wikipedia 'Taklamakan Desert.'  (Legend.)

question: The Taklamakan is one of Earth's driest places partly because it lies trapped in a giant bowl, walled on nearly every side by some of the tallest mountain ranges in the world, whose icy 5,000-meter peaks strip the rain from passing clouds. Which range rises along the desert's northern edge?
context: The Taklamakan lies in a bowl walled by some of the highest ranges on Earth — the Tian Shan ('Celestial Mountains') to the north, the Kunlun to the south, and the Pamir to the west, many peaks topping 5,000 m. Those walls block nearly all rain, trapping the desert in one of the planet's deepest rain shadows. Source: Grokipedia 'Taklamakan Desert.'

question: Along the Taklamakan's edges once stood bustling Silk Road oasis towns like Loulan and Niya, full of houses, orchards, and written records. Then, one by one, they vanished from every map — lost for more than a thousand years before explorers stumbled on their remains in modern times. What had become of these towns?
choices: A great flood swept them away.
context: The dunes move so relentlessly that whole Silk Road oasis cities were buried and lost. Loulan — the 'Oriental Pompeii' — was abandoned around 330 CE after the Lop Nur lake dried up, then rediscovered by chance in 1900 by Sven Hedin; Niya was uncovered in 1901 by Aurel Stein, who dug out about a hundred wooden tablets in Kharosthi script, left where they fell when the sand took the town. Sources: China Daily 'Exploring the lost land of Loulan'; Silk Road Foundation 'The Most Important Findings of Niya.'

question: The Taklamakan's salt-dry sand mummifies its dead: bodies buried nearly 4,000 years ago still keep their skin, their reddish-fair hair, and their woven wool clothes. One of them, the 'Chärchän Man,' was buried in leggings whose bold woven pattern astonished archaeologists — it closely matched the cloth of the ancient Celtic peoples of far-off Europe. What is that distinctive Celtic-style weave called?
context: The salty, rainless sand naturally mummified the dead. The 'Tarim mummies' are up to about 4,000 years old (oldest ~1800 BCE) yet keep their skin, blond-to-red hair, and finely woven wool. The 'Chärchän Man' wore a red twill tunic and tartan-plaid leggings whose checked weave strikingly resembles the ancient Celtic Hallstatt cloth of Europe — an eerie echo across thousands of miles (the resemblance is real and observed; what it means for their origins is a separate, debated question). Source: Wikipedia 'Tarim mummies.'  (Legend.)

question: The fair-haired Tarim mummies, dressed in cloth that looked almost European, set off one of archaeology's great arguments: had these people wandered in from some faraway land, or had their ancestors always lived in this desert? In 2021, scientists finally sequenced the DNA of the oldest mummies. What did the genome reveal them to be?
context: The mummies' Western-looking features made their origins one of archaeology's great puzzles. A 2021 genome study found the earliest Tarim people were NOT migrants from the west but a genetically isolated LOCAL population — about 72% Ancient North Eurasian ancestry, a relic of Ice-Age hunter-gatherers — overturning the older 'European wanderers' idea. The preservation and fine cloth are settled fact; deeper questions about their culture and language remain open research. Source: Wikipedia 'Tarim mummies' (2021 Nature genome study).

question: Great rivers like the Tarim, the Hotan, and the Yarkand pour down out of the mountains ringing the Taklamakan, fan out across the desert floor — and then simply vanish, soaking away into the sand. Not one of them ever reaches an ocean. Geographers have a special word for a basin like this, whose waters never escape to the sea. What is it?
context: The Tarim Basin is endorheic (Greek endon 'within' + rhein 'to flow') — it has no outlet to any sea. The Tarim, Hotan, and Yarkand run down from the mountains, feed oasis farms, then soak away and evaporate in the sand rather than ever reaching an ocean, making it one of the world's great inland-drainage basins. Sources: New World Encyclopedia 'Takla Makan Desert'; WorldAtlas.

question: To reach oilfields hidden deep in the Taklamakan's heart, China drove a paved highway straight across hundreds of kilometers of live, shifting dunes — the longest road ever built over a moving-sand desert. But the restless dunes kept creeping over it, threatening to bury the road entirely. How did the engineers hold the sand back?
answer: They planted a living green belt along the road.
choices: They planted a living green belt along the road.
They paved a second road as a backup route.
They raised the road high on concrete stilts.
They lined both sides with tall steel walls.
context: The Tarim Desert Highway runs about 552 km, roughly 446 km of it over live shifting dunes — the world's longest road across a shifting-sand desert, built in 1993-1995 to reach oilfields in the basin's heart. To stop the marching dunes from burying it, engineers lined it with a living green shelterbelt about 436 km long, watered by more than 20,000 km of drip-irrigation pipe fed from salty groundwater and tended from well-houses every 4 km — over 20 million saplings. In 2024 China 'closed the loop,' finishing a roughly 3,050-km green belt that now rings the entire desert. Sources: Wikipedia 'Tarim Desert Highway'; Tianshannet; China Daily.

question: Tango was born in the 1880s in the crowded immigrant docklands of two rival port cities — Buenos Aires, Argentina and Montevideo, Uruguay — which is why both nations still claim it as their own. The two cities sit facing each other across the banks of which vast river?
context: Both cities grew up on opposite banks of the Río de la Plata — the wide estuary where the Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet the Atlantic. Tango emerged in the poor port neighborhoods on both shores in the 1880s, so Argentina and Uruguay have argued ever since over who 'owns' it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tango' — originated in the 1880s along the Río de la Plata in the impoverished port areas of Argentina and Uruguay.

question: On the street corners of tango's birthplace — the ragged Buenos Aires arrabal, the city's rough outskirts — young toughs called compadritos practiced the new dance night after night. Whom did these men most often dance with as they learned it?
context: The immigrant docklands had far more men than women, so young men practiced tango with each other — the dance almost a stylized mock duel between two rivals before either ever partnered a woman. Source: National Geographic, 'Sensual and scandalous: How tango took the world by storm'; Escuela de Tango de Buenos Aires — a severe shortage of women meant tango was often danced by two men, expressing symbolic combat.

question: Carried to the Río de la Plata docks around 1870 by immigrant sailors, one small, bellows-driven instrument with a deep, sobbing, heartbroken voice became the very soul of tango. What is it called?
context: The bandoneón — a square, button-covered relative of the accordion — gives tango its unmistakable mournful cry. German and Italian sailors and immigrants brought it to the Río de la Plata docks around 1870. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bandoneon' — brought to Argentina about 1870 by German and Italian emigrants and sailors.

question: In the milongas — the dance halls of Buenos Aires — the old milongueros, tango's grey-haired masters, boasted they could size up any dancer the instant the music began, from one thing alone. What was it?
context: Tango's defining feature is the abrazo, the close embrace danced chest to chest. From that first point of contact, the milongueros claimed to read a dancer's musicality, his respect, his whole character. Source: Tango Voice; Ultimate Tango School — the close-embrace (milonguero) style is danced chest-to-chest, and masters judged dancers by the embrace.

question: The bandoneón sounds so achingly Argentine that most people assume it was invented on the Río de la Plata. In truth, Heinrich Band built the first ones in 1840s Germany for a completely different, humble purpose. What was the bandoneón originally made to do?
answer: replace the pipe organ in poor churches
choices: replace the pipe organ in poor churches
play music for village folk dances
teach schoolchildren to sing in tune
context: Heinrich Band, a German instrument dealer, designed and named the bandoneón as a cheap, portable stand-in for the pipe organ or harmonium in small churches that couldn't afford one. Only later did emigrants carry it to the docks, where it became tango's heart. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bandoneon' — created and named by Heinrich Band, designed to replace organs/harmoniums.

question: Carlos Gardel, the golden-voiced singer who turned tango into song, is claimed as a native son by both Uruguay and Argentina — and in 1920 he filed papers swearing he was born in Tacuarembó, Uruguay. But the birth certificate confirmed in 2012 revealed his real birthplace lay in a whole other country. Where was Gardel actually born?
context: Gardel's true birthplace was a mystery he made himself. His French birth certificate — confirmed genuine in 2012 — records his birth in Toulouse, France, on 11 December 1890. Yet in 1920 he filed papers in Uruguay claiming he had been born in Tacuarembó, most likely to dodge French military registration — which is why Uruguayans and Argentines alike still claim him as their own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carlos Gardel' — birth certificate confirmed Toulouse, France, 11 Dec 1890 (verified 2012); filed false Uruguayan papers in 1920 claiming Tacuarembó.

question: The most famous tango melody in the world was written around 1917 by a 20-year-old Uruguayan architecture student, Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, in Montevideo. When Roberto Firpo's orchestra premiered it at the Café La Giralda, the crowd made them play it six times in a single night. What is this tango called?
context: 'La Cumparsita' premiered on 19 April 1917 at the Café La Giralda in Montevideo, played by Roberto Firpo's orchestra — and it was such a hit it was encored six times that night. Its young composer went on to become an architect. Source: revistapanorama.com, 'One Hundred Years of La Cumparsita'; notihoteles.com (Confitería La Giralda).

question: At a milonga in Buenos Aires you may invite a partner from clear across the crowded hall without speaking a single word: you catch their eye and give a tiny nod. Hold the gaze and it's yes; look away and it's a gentle no — so no one is ever publicly refused. What is this silent custom called?
context: The cabeceo (from cabeza, 'head') uses a shared glance — the mirada — then a small nod to invite a partner, sparing anyone the embarrassment of a public refusal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Milonga (dance event)' — the cabeceo uses mutual eye contact, a mirada then a nod, to invite partners and minimize embarrassment.

question: In the 1950s Ástor Piazzolla, a bandoneón virtuoso from the Río de la Plata, began fusing traditional tango with jazz and classical music into a startling sound all his own. Argentine purists were so enraged — some even sent him death threats — that they swore his creation was not tango at all. What did Piazzolla name this movement he founded?
context: Ástor Piazzolla called his style 'nuevo tango,' fusing jazz and classical music with the traditional form and outraging purists who swore it wasn't tango at all. His works include 'Libertango' (1974) and 'Adiós Nonino,' which he wrote in under an hour after learning his father had died. In Paris his teacher Nadia Boulanger urged him to stop imitating the Europeans and write tango. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ástor Piazzolla' — created nuevo tango blending jazz and classical, a controversial figure rejected by traditionalists.

question: For over a century, Buenos Aires and Montevideo argued over which city truly gave the world tango. In 2009 UNESCO added the dance to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. How did the honor fall between the two rival nations, Argentina and Uruguay?
answer: jointly, as one shared listing for both nations
choices: jointly, as one shared listing for both nations
solely under Argentina, the larger nation
solely under Uruguay, its true birthplace
as two rival entries, one from each nation
context: Argentina and Uruguay submitted tango together, and UNESCO inscribed it in 2009 as a single shared treasure of both nations — a rare joint listing that finally split the honor evenly between Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Tango' (ich.unesco.org/en/RL/tango-00258) — inscribed 2009, jointly submitted by Argentina and Uruguay.

question: One of the greatest finds in archaeology happened by accident in the spring of 1974. The First Emperor's buried army near Mount Li, in central China, was uncovered not by any expedition but by local farmers busy with an ordinary chore. What were they doing when they struck the first clay soldier?
answer: digging a well for water during a drought
choices: digging a well for water during a drought
plowing a new field for planting
quarrying stone to build a house
fishing along the banks of a river
context: On March 29, 1974, farmers led by Yang Zhifa were digging a well during a drought in Xiyang Village near Mount Li, outside Xi'an, when they hit the head of a terracotta soldier about a meter down and broke into a pit holding thousands more. The archaeologist Zhao Kangmin was called in and painstakingly reassembled the first warriors from fragments, some as small as a fingernail. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: When archaeologists finished mapping the pits beside the First Emperor's tomb, they had not found a handful of statues or a small honor guard. They found a whole army in battle formation, standing rank on rank in the underground chambers. Roughly how many life-size clay warriors are buried there?
context: More than 8,000 life-size warriors stand in the pits, alongside about 130 wooden chariots, 520 chariot horses, and 150 cavalry horses rendered in terracotta -- an entire buried army drawn up for battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: China's First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, had thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried in battle formation beside his tomb near Mount Li. Why would a dead ruler want a whole army sealed in the ground with him?
answer: to guard the emperor forever in the afterlife
choices: to guard the emperor forever in the afterlife
to carry his spirit up to the heavens
to serve as his laborers in the next world
to replace the live soldiers once buried with kings
context: The clay army was built to protect Qin Shi Huang -- who unified the warring states as China's first emperor in 221 BCE -- in the afterlife, an eternal bodyguard meant to keep him safe forever. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: Archaeologists studying the terracotta army found something that sets it apart from nearly every other monument of massed figures in the ancient world. Comparing the warriors one against another, what did they discover about their faces?
answer: each one has a different face
choices: each one has a different face
each one wears the same stern face
each one has no face at all
each one has the emperor's face
context: No two warriors share a face. Sculptors began from roughly ten base facial forms and then modified each by hand -- adding hair, ears, mustaches, and expressions -- so the army looks like a crowd of thousands of distinct, real men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: The terracotta soldiers stand today in the dull gray of bare baked clay, and most people picture them that way. But archaeologists who examined the freshly excavated figures found faint evidence that the army once looked utterly different. How did the warriors originally appear when they were first placed in the pits?
choices: covered head to toe in gold leaf
polished to a glossy black shine
context: The warriors were once brightly painted, including with a synthetic pigment scientists call 'Chinese purple' (barium copper silicate) that the Qin craftsmen manufactured. Exposed paint on newly dug figures can curl and flake within minutes of hitting the air, so most now look like bare clay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Buried in the pits beside the First Emperor's tomb near Xi'an, the terracotta soldiers were armed with real bronze weapons -- archaeologists have recovered over 40,000 arrowheads, spears, and swords. When they drew several of the bronze swords from the ground, more than 2,000 years after burial, what did they find about the blades?
answer: they were still sharp enough to cut
choices: they were still sharp enough to cut
they were plated in thin silver
they were etched with battle maps
they were snapped into short pieces
context: Over 40,000 bronze arrowheads, swords, spears, and crossbow triggers have been recovered. Some swords came out still sharp after 2,000 years underground, and several are inscribed with dates between 245 and 228 BCE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: The historian Sima Qian wrote that the First Emperor's sealed tomb held a model of his whole empire -- its hundred rivers and seas recreated in miniature, beneath a ceiling of painted stars and constellations. For 2,000 years scholars filed this under fairy tale. Then scientists tested the soil over the untouched tomb mound and found the old account was, chemically, telling the truth. What did the tests detect at strangely high levels?
context: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (c. 94 BCE) described rivers of flowing mercury, long dismissed as myth. In a 2020 study, scientists aimed a laser radar (lidar) at the air over the mound and measured mercury up to about 27 ng/m3, several times the local background of 5-10 ng/m3 -- physical corroboration of the 2,000-year-old account. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-67305-x

question: According to Sima Qian, the First Emperor's tomb was built to defend itself. He recorded that a hidden mechanism was set inside the burial chamber, ready to strike on its own at any robber who broke in. What did he say was waiting to strike intruders?
context: Sima Qian recorded that the tomb was rigged with automatic crossbows set to fire at anyone who broke in -- an ancient booby trap guarding the First Emperor's body. Whether any such mechanism survives is unknown, since no one has entered the chamber to check. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army  (Legend.)

question: The First Emperor's mausoleum was one of the largest building projects of the ancient world: Sima Qian says some 700,000 conscripted workers labored on it for roughly 38 years. Here is the surprise -- work on this colossal tomb began the very year its owner took the throne of the Qin state. How old was the future First Emperor when construction started?
context: Construction began in 246 BCE, when the future emperor was only about 13, and continued for roughly 38 years. Sima Qian recorded around 700,000 conscripted workers on the mausoleum. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: The terracotta pits have been excavated for fifty years and draw millions of visitors. But the First Emperor's actual burial chamber -- beneath the grassy pyramid-shaped mound at the center of the complex -- is treated completely differently by archaeologists. What is the status of that central chamber today?
choices: it was looted in ancient times
it was moved to a museum
context: Archaeologists deliberately leave the chamber sealed -- partly because exposed paint on excavated figures has flaked within minutes of hitting the air, and partly because of the mercury detected in the mound. What lies inside the First Emperor's tomb remains unseen. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/emperor-qin

question: The thousands of warriors in Pit 1 are not arranged as a random crowd. They stand in tight battle ranks, and every single row faces the exact same direction, gazing outward toward the horizon. The First Emperor lined them up this way on purpose. Which way does his whole army look?
context: The pits sit about 1.5 km east of the tomb mound, and the warriors face east -- toward the rival warring states the First Emperor had conquered and the direction his old enemies had once come from -- set as an eternal vanguard. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: In 1920, the Russian physicist Lev Termen unveiled an electronic instrument whose eerie, wavering wail would later become the ghostly voice of old flying-saucer and horror films. What was Termen's Russian invention called?
context: Lev Termen — known in the West as Leon Theremin — invented it in Russia in October 1920, the first musical instrument you play without ever touching it. One critic described its voice as 'a cello lost in a dense fog, crying because it does not know how to get home.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin

question: At Iceland's Thingvellir, a footpath leads down into Almannagja, a deep canyon where a cliff of the North American plate towers on one side and the Eurasian plate forms the far wall. Nowhere else on land can you walk between two continents in the open air. What type of plate boundary runs through Thingvellir?
context: At Thingvellir the two plates spread apart about 2 cm a year; over the 10,000 years since the lava flowed there, the ground has widened roughly 70 m and dropped some 40 m. This is a DIVERGENT boundary -- the one place on land where you can walk inside the seam between two continents. (thingvellir.is/en/education/nature/tectonic-movements)

question: At Silfra in Iceland, divers drop into a flooded crack in the earth filled with glacial meltwater so clear they can see almost 100 metres, the length of a football pitch. Floating down the narrow gorge, they reach out and do something possible in almost no other spot on Earth. What are they able to do?
answer: touch two tectonic plates at once
choices: touch two tectonic plates at once
swim through a flooded lava tube
float in water too salty to sink
glide beneath the edge of a glacier
context: The Silfra fissure runs right through the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates -- stretch out your arms and a hand rests on each side. Its water is glacial melt filtered through porous lava for decades, giving visibility of around 100 m. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silfra)

question: Off the Pacific coast of South America, a deep ocean trench plunges just offshore, and rising straight up behind it stand the Andes, their spine studded with towering volcanoes. What type of plate boundary produces a coastline like this?
context: Where the Nazca plate dives under the South American plate at the Peru-Chile Trench, melting rock feeds the Andes' volcanoes and lifts its great peaks. One plate diving beneath another is a CONVERGENT (subduction) boundary. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: Earth's ten tallest mountains all rise in Asia's Himalaya and Karakoram. Far away in the Andes stands the highest peak found anywhere outside Asia, reaching 6,961 metres. Name this mountain.
context: Aconcagua, in Argentina's Andes, reaches 6,961 m -- the highest summit outside Asia, and the tallest in both the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere. The Andes themselves run about 8,900 km, the longest continental mountain range on Earth. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: In California, the San Andreas Fault runs some 750 miles up the state. Where it crosses fences, roads, and dry creek beds, it has jogged them sideways out of line, and every so often the ground lurches free in a sudden earthquake. What type of plate boundary is the San Andreas?
context: Along a TRANSFORM boundary the plates neither build new crust nor swallow old -- they just grind sideways. The San Andreas runs about 750 miles through California; a slip on its northern reach caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault)

question: The Pacific plate is slowly hauling the western sliver of California toward the northwest along the San Andreas Fault. Los Angeles rides that moving plate; San Francisco, up the coast, sits mostly on the plate next door. Millions of years from now, what becomes of the two cities?
answer: Los Angeles will drift north to sit beside San Francisco
choices: Los Angeles will drift north to sit beside San Francisco
Los Angeles will sink beneath the deep Pacific Ocean
Los Angeles will crumple upward into new mountains
Los Angeles will stay locked in place, unmoving, forever
context: Because the Pacific plate creeps northwest, Los Angeles inches toward San Francisco by a few centimetres a year. In several million years the two cities are expected to end up side-by-side neighbours -- still separated by the grinding fault. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault)  (Legend.)

question: Earth's entire rocky shell -- every continent and all the ocean floors -- is cracked into only about seven or eight major slabs. One of them dwarfs the others, spanning some 103 million square kilometres, larger than any continent. Which is Earth's largest tectonic plate?
context: The Pacific plate covers about 103 million km2, flooring most of the Pacific Ocean -- the biggest of the roughly 7-8 major plates (plus about 15 minor ones) that tile the planet. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Plate)

question: At Iceland's Thingvellir the North American and Eurasian plates creep apart only about two centimetres a year -- steady and unstoppable, and just about as fast as what part of your own body grows?
context: Plates typically move a few centimetres a year -- about as fast as your fingernails grow (your hair actually grows several times faster). At Thingvellir the North American and Eurasian plates part at roughly 2 cm a year. (usgs.gov/faqs/how-fast-do-tectonic-plates-move)

question: Tectonic plates usually creep along only a few centimetres a year -- but in 2005, at the Dabbahu volcano in Ethiopia's Afar desert, the ground split open along a gash 60 kilometres long and up to 8 metres wide. How long did geologists say this enormous rip took to tear open?
context: The 2005 Dabbahu event opened a 60-km fissure in about two weeks, releasing an estimated 400 years of built-up crustal stress almost overnight. Afar is a rare triple junction, where the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African rifts all meet and pull apart. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Triangle)

question: Along the East African Rift, geologists expect that in roughly 10 million years a long strip of the continent will finish tearing away from the rest of Africa. As the two pieces pull apart, what will be born in the widening gap between them?
context: As the East African Rift widens, the sea is expected to flood in, splitting off a slab of Africa and creating a brand-new ocean basin in about 10 million years -- the same process that long ago opened the Red Sea. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Triangle)  (Legend.)

question: On the beaches of California, the Pacific climbs up the sand and slides back out again twice every day, like the slow breathing of the sea. What in the sky does most of the pulling that lifts these daily tides?
context: The Moon's gravity is the true master of the sea — its tide-raising pull is more than twice the Sun's (the Sun adds only about 46% as much). Twice a day the whole ocean answers the Moon and rises. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Along one funnel-shaped coast the sea climbs the height of a five-storey building — about 16 metres — then falls again, twice a day: the highest tides found anywhere on Earth. Which coast is it?
context: This is the Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in eastern Canada — a world-record tidal range near 16 m. Ungava Bay in northern Quebec runs so close that some call the record a tie. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: Every time the tide floods into Canada's Bay of Fundy, about 100 billion tonnes of seawater pour in — then pour out again hours later. That single half-day surge outmatches one astonishing benchmark. Which?
answer: more water than every river on Earth combined
choices: more water than every river on Earth combined
more water than a whole year of rain on Canada
more water than all five Great Lakes hold
more water than the Amazon moves in a month
context: Each half-tide moves roughly 100 billion tonnes of water in or out of the Bay of Fundy — about twice the combined flow of every river on Earth over the same time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: Far out in the open ocean the Moon lifts the sea only about half a metre — a swell so gentle a passing ship never feels it. Yet the same tide rears up 16 metres in the Bay of Fundy. What turns that gentle ocean swell into such a coastal giant?
answer: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
choices: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
the Moon pulling harder directly over Canada
cold northern seawater piling up denser and taller
the great depth of the bay multiplying the pull
context: Tides are born tiny in the open sea — the Moon lifts it only about 54 cm — and grow into giants only where the shape of the coastline funnels and stacks them. Fundy's tapering funnel is the world champion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: At Mont-Saint-Michel, the island abbey off the coast of Normandy in France, the tide can sweep across the flat sands so fast that an old warning — often credited to Victor Hugo — matches its speed to one alarming thing. To what?
context: The saying — often credited to Victor Hugo — is that the sea comes in 'as swiftly as a galloping horse.' Treat it as vivid lore, not a measured speed; the real danger at Mont-Saint-Michel (tidal range about 14 m) is fast-rising water and quicksand that can strand walkers on the flats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont-Saint-Michel; thegoodlifefrance.com.  (Legend.)

question: On the Bay of Fundy, as on most coasts worldwide, the sea rises to a high tide not once but twice a day, about twelve hours apart. What does the Moon actually raise on Earth to give two daily highs instead of one?
answer: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
choices: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
a single bulge the spinning Earth sweeps past twice
a bulge that sloshes back and forth across the ocean
a ring of raised water circling the whole equator
context: The Moon pulls hardest on the ocean facing it, raising a near-side bulge, and least on the far-side water, which is 'left behind' as a second bulge. Earth turns through both each day, so most coasts get two high tides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Twice a month — as tide-watchers on the Bay of Fundy know well — at the new Moon and again at the full Moon, the Sun and Moon line up in a straight row and heave the sea together, lifting the tides to their very highest. What are these highest twice-monthly tides called?
context: 'Spring' here means 'springing up' or bursting forth — the tide leaping to its peak — not the season. These highest tides come when the Sun and Moon pull in a straight line, at the new and full Moon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: The Bay of Fundy's everyday tides already top out near 16 metres. Yet in October 1869 the water at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia, surged to a staggering 21.6 metres — a world record never beaten since. What extra force heaped those final metres onto an already-towering tide?
answer: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
choices: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
a sudden snowmelt flood pouring down the rivers
the wave from an offshore undersea earthquake
a heavy, days-long downpour swelling the bay
context: The record came during the Saxby Gale of October 1869: fierce winds and abnormally low pressure drove a storm surge on top of a tide already running unusually high. Burntcoat Head's routine maximum is about 17 m — the 21.6 m mark was a storm-amplified one-off, not the everyday tide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burntcoat_Head,_Nova_Scotia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1869_Saxby_Gale.

question: The Rance, in Brittany, France, opened a landmark power station in 1966, inaugurated by President Charles de Gaulle; for the next 45 years no rival of its kind grew larger. What was this station the first in the world to do?
answer: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
choices: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
turn the ocean's waves into electricity
turn the ocean's heat into electricity
turn the ocean's currents into electricity
context: It was the Rance Tidal Power Station — the world's first tidal power plant, using 24 bulb turbines to harness the estuary's roughly 8 m (up to 13.5 m) tide. It stayed the largest tidal station on Earth for 45 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rance_Tidal_Power_Station.

question: The Sun and Moon are not always allies. About a week after the spring tides, at the quarter (half) Moon, they pull crossways to one another and partly cancel — so even the mighty Bay of Fundy runs slack, the sea barely rising and falling. What are these weakest tides called?
context: 'Neap' is an old Anglo-Saxon word meaning roughly 'without the power.' At the quarter Moon the Sun's pull works crossways to the Moon's, so the two partly cancel and the tides run slack. (In line, at new and full Moon, they give the towering spring tides.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Many bays around the world are funnel-shaped, yet the Bay of Fundy alone grows the planet's highest tides. What lucky coincidence makes Fundy the champion, and not just another funnel?
answer: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
choices: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
it faces straight into the Atlantic's fastest current
its rivers pour in more fresh water than any other bay
it lies at the one latitude where the tides peak
context: This lucky match is called tidal resonance: Fundy's water naturally sloshes back and forth on nearly the same ~12.5-hour rhythm as the tides, so each tide pushes at just the right moment — like timing shoves on a swing — building the water ever higher. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy.

question: At Saint John, New Brunswick, the Saint John River tumbles over a hidden rock ledge as a churning rapid on its way to the sea. Twice a day, when the giant Bay of Fundy tide floods in, something almost unbelievable happens to that rapid. What?
answer: the whole rapid flips and the river runs backward, uphill
choices: the whole rapid flips and the river runs backward, uphill
the rapid swells and doubles into a roaring waterfall
the rapid drowns beneath the flood into a deep whirlpool
the rapid falls calm, smoothing into a glassy stillwater
context: This is the Reversing Falls (Reversing Rapids) at Saint John: at high tide the Fundy flood overpowers the Saint John River and forces the rapid to run upstream, against its own current, over an underwater rock ledge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reversing_Falls.

question: As the Bay of Fundy tide charges up the Petitcodiac River near Moncton, it rears into a tidal bore — a moving wall of water rolling upstream against the current. In July 2013 two California surfers caught that wall and set a North American record. For what feat?
choices: the fastest surf ride ever clocked
the most surfers on one wave
the tallest bore wave ever ridden
context: Surfers Mark Whitbread and Colin Wessels rode the Petitcodiac bore about 29 km (18 miles) over two and a half hours — a North American record for the longest wave ever surfed. A tidal bore forms when a big incoming tide funnels into a narrowing river. Source: cbc.ca (Moncton tidal bore, July 2013).

question: For five centuries a ship leaving Europe rode one dependable thing across the tropical Atlantic: a broad belt of warm wind blowing steadily out of the northeast, day after day, carrying sail after sail westward to the Americas and never once turning against them. What are these reliable tropical winds called?
context: In the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds blow from the northeast; in the Southern, from the southeast, both curving toward the equator. This same reliable highway of wind carried immense wealth and the great Columbian exchange of crops, animals, and ideas between continents, and it also carried European colonization of the Americas and the ships of the transatlantic slave trade. The wind was neutral; what sailed on it was not. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds).

question: Across the tropical Atlantic, these winds carried England's merchant fleet for centuries, so everyone assumes the name 'trade winds' comes from that cargo and commerce. But 'trade' here is far older than its money-meaning; sailors used it long before, in the salty phrase 'the wind blows trade.' In that original sense, what did 'trade' actually mean?
context: 'Trade' here comes from a 14th-century sense meaning a track, course, or direction, from the nautical phrase 'to blow trade' (to blow steadily one way). Only later, because these winds were so vital to England's merchant fleet crossing the Atlantic, did the money-meaning of 'trade' attach itself and stick. An etymology twist: the name is older than the commerce it came to serve. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds); Wiktionary, 'trade wind' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/trade_wind).

question: In 1492 Columbus let the steady northeast wind carry him due west from the Canary Islands to the Americas, but that same wind at his back made going home impossible, for it would only shove him further west. So for the return he climbed north into the cooler middle latitudes to catch a different belt of wind, higher up, that blows back toward Europe. What are these homeward winds called?
context: Columbus began his return on 16 January 1493, looping north to ride the westerlies home. The outbound trades and the homebound westerlies together form a great clockwise wheel of wind across the North Atlantic, the gyre that made round-trip sailing possible. Source: Wikipedia, 'Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

question: Right at the equator the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet head-on, cancel each other out, and rise straight upward instead of blowing across the sea. What they leave behind is a belt of breathless, dead calm where a sailing ship, with wind its only engine, could sit motionless for weeks beneath a broiling sun as its water ran low. What is this becalmed equatorial belt called?
context: Scientists call this belt the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ); 18th-century sailors named it the 'doldrums' for its stagnant, spirit-sapping calm. Do not confuse it with the horse latitudes, the separate calm belts near 30 degrees where ships were also becalmed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone).

question: For 250 years, from 1565 to 1815, great Spanish treasure ships hauled Asian silk, porcelain, and Mexican silver back and forth across the whole Pacific twice a year, riding the trade winds outward and the warm Kuroshio current home, linking a Spanish port in the Philippines to Acapulco on Mexico's coast. It was one of the longest-lasting sea routes in all of history. By what name is this great Pacific crossing remembered?
context: The Manila galleons ran for 250 years (1565-1815), an early engine of globalization pouring American silver into Asia and Asian silk into the Americas and Europe. It was also a lifeline of Spanish colonial trade, and it ended as Mexico moved toward independence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Manila galleon' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon).

question: A Portuguese caravel beating back up the coast of West Africa faced a maddening trap: the coastal winds and currents ran steadily against it, so a straight dash home to Portugal was hopeless. The captains' escape was to sail deliberately the wrong way first, striking hundreds of miles out into the empty open ocean toward Brazil, away from home, because only far out there could they swing around and finally catch the westerlies back to Europe. What did the Portuguese call this counterintuitive looping detour?
context: 'Volta do mar' means 'turn of the sea.' Its Pacific cousin, the tornaviaje, was cracked by the friar Andres de Urdaneta in 1565. Historians hold that Europe's sea empires could not have arisen without this wind-gyre trick; a 13th-century Genoese expedition, the Vivaldi brothers, sailed south past the Canaries and likely perished, unable to beat back upwind for want of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Volta do mar' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_do_mar).

question: Here is the puzzle hidden inside the trade winds. Air is pulled toward the band of low pressure lying along the equator, so you would expect it to blow straight south in the north and straight north in the south. Instead, in BOTH hemispheres the wind arrives leaning firmly westward, the very slant that let sailing ships ride it clear across an ocean. What phenomenon, arising from the Earth's rotation, bends the equator-bound wind into that westward slant?
context: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, giving equator-bound wind its westward push. If the Earth ever stopped spinning, the slant would vanish and the winds would blow straight toward the equator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force); 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds).

question: The Lombok Strait is so narrow — barely 35 km — that from Bali you can look across the water to the island of Lombok. Yet step ashore and the wild animals have changed completely, as if you had crossed to another continent. What is this abrupt wildlife frontier called?
context: Cross the Lombok Strait and Asia's tigers and monkeys give way to Australia's marsupials and cockatoos. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace mapped this frontier in 1859; Thomas Henry Huxley named it 'Wallace's Line' in 1868, and it is also called the Wallace Line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: During the ice ages, the seas fell about 120 metres and dry land linked island to island across the region, joining many of them into vast peninsulas. Yet the animals of Bali and Lombok, close enough to see one another across the strait, still never mixed. Why did this one narrow gap never close into dry land?
answer: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
choices: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
the seas there never dropped as far as elsewhere
a swift current kept sweeping the sand away
its seabed kept sinking as fast as the seas fell
context: The Lombok Strait plunges to at least 250 metres — more than twice the ice-age sea drop — so its floor never surfaced as land. Everywhere else the falling seas welded islands into two giant landmasses; only across deep gaps like this one did the divide hold. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: West of the line, Bali, Java, Sumatra and Borneo all stand in shallow sea rarely deeper than 50 metres, on one broad drowned platform — a continental shelf. When ice-age seas fell, that whole platform surfaced and merged the islands into a single vast peninsula. Which shelf do these western islands sit on?
context: This is the Sunda Shelf, welded to the Asian mainland. At ice-age low sea it formed 'Sundaland,' a peninsula of Asia spanning roughly 1.85 million square kilometres, where water rarely exceeds 50 metres deep. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunda_Shelf

question: East of the line, a traveller could once have walked from Australia straight to New Guinea on dry land, because both rise from a single shallow platform that surfaced when ice-age seas fell. Which shelf joined Australia and New Guinea into one landmass?
context: This is the Sahul Shelf, the Australian continental shelf. At low sea it formed the landmass 'Sahul,' joined to New Guinea across the Arafura Shelf; ancient drowned shorelines here now lie 100-140 metres below today's sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf

question: Between the two great shelves lies a scatter of islands — Sulawesi, Lombok, Flores, Timor — that deep water kept apart from BOTH sides, so they were never joined to Asia or to Australia. Their wildlife is a strange half-and-half mix of the two. What do naturalists call this in-between zone?
context: This is Wallacea — about 347,000 square kilometres of islands, Sulawesi the largest — ringed by deep-water straits on every side, so its life is a blend of Asian and Australian types found nowhere else. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallacea

question: Where Asian and Australian wildlife blend together across the islands between the shelves, a single boundary was not enough, so mapmakers added others. One of them runs along the eastern rim of that blend zone, pressed tight against the Australian shelf, and was drawn in 1896. What is this eastern line called?
context: Richard Lydekker drew this line in 1896 along the edge of the Sahul Shelf, marking the eastern rim of Wallacea. Between it and Wallace's Line runs Weber's Line, the balance point where Asian and Australian life meet in equal measure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydekker%27s_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weber%27s_Line

question: Far north of Bali, a second great gap along the Wallace Line splits the huge islands of Borneo and Sulawesi. This one is vast — 130 to 370 km across, ten times wider than the narrow strait at Bali — yet it divides Asian and Australian wildlife just as sharply, and for the very same reason: it plunges to about 2,500 m deep. What is this wide, deep gap called?
context: This is the Makassar Strait, between Borneo and Sulawesi — 130 to 370 km across, far wider than the 35 km Lombok Strait, yet plunging to about 2,500 m in its northern basin. That proves the Wallace Line's real barrier is deep water, not mere distance. Source: britannica.com/place/Makassar-Strait

question: When the waltz reached Vienna's ballrooms in the early 1800s, newspapers branded it an 'indecent foreign dance' and chaperones were scandalized. Of all their complaints, what did critics single out as the real scandal?
answer: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
choices: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
Unmarried couples danced together with no chaperone between them
The women bared their arms and shoulders in daring ball gowns
Couples broke off to dance as pairs instead of in group sets
context: Earlier ballroom dances kept couples apart in group formations; the waltz's closed hold - man and woman face-to-face, his hand at her waist, turning together - was the shocking part. In July 1816 The Times of London denounced it as an 'indecent foreign dance,' warning of 'the voluptuous intertwining of the limbs.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz

question: The elegant Viennese waltz did not begin in grand ballrooms. It grew out of a rough, stomping folk dance in the same lilting three-beat time, danced by peasants in the villages of Austria and Bavaria and then cleaned up for the city. What was this peasant dance called?
context: The Ländler was a stomping Austrian and Bavarian peasant dance in 3/4 time; sped up and refined, it became the ballroom waltz. (Modern scholars increasingly treat the two as parallel 'sibling' dances rather than strict ancestor and descendant.) Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: The word 'waltz' comes from the German verb 'walzen' - to roll or turn - a nod to the dance's whirling spin. As the dance spread through Austria and southern Germany, the earliest known appearance of the word in print, in 1748, turned up in a single official document. What sort of document gave 'waltz' its written debut?
context: 'Waltz' comes from the German 'walzen,' to roll, turn, or revolve - for the dance's rolling rotation. The word first appears in print in 1748, in the text of a dance ban. Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: In 1863, Vienna's Habsburg emperor placed Johann Strauss the Younger on the imperial payroll with an official salaried post inside the royal court. What court title did the composer hold?
answer: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
choices: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
Music Director of the Imperial Court Opera
Music Director of the Court Chapel Choir
Music Director of the Emperor's Chamber
context: Johann Strauss II (1825-1899) wrote over 500 dance pieces, hundreds of them waltzes, and in 1863 was named KK Hofballmusikdirektor - Music Director of the Royal Court Balls. His father, Johann Strauss I, had forbidden a musical career, wanting the boy to become a banker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Strauss_II

question: Johann Strauss the Younger's 1866 waltz 'By the Beautiful Blue ___' became Vienna's unofficial anthem, the tune the city reaches for whenever it wants to feel most itself. He named it for the broad river that curls through the heart of Vienna. Which river fills the blank?
context: 'By the Beautiful Blue Danube' (An der schönen blauen Donau), composed 1866 and premiered in 1867, became Vienna's unofficial anthem. It began as a choral piece with satirical lyrics and only a mild success; the orchestral version at the 1867 Paris World's Fair made it a triumph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Danube

question: In 1814-15, the monarchs and diplomats of Europe gathered at the Congress of Vienna to redraw the continent's map after Napoleon's fall. Yet months passed with little settled, and Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne mocked that the Congress 'does not advance.' What had swallowed up the delegates' time and energy in the host city?
answer: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
choices: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
secret treaties argued in back rooms
long state banquets and royal hunts
context: At the Congress of Vienna (Sept 1814 - June 1815), the balls so filled the diplomacy that Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne quipped 'Le congrès danse beaucoup, mais il ne marche pas' - 'the Congress dances a lot, but does not advance.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna

question: One great river runs the 'wrong' way, south to north, and every summer its floods once spread rich black silt across the desert — the yearly gift that let the farms of ancient Egypt survive. Which river is this?
context: The Nile flows about 6,650 km from the highlands of central Africa north to the Mediterranean — long enough to rival the Amazon for the title of the world's longest river. Its yearly summer flood laid down fresh black silt (the Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land'), letting farms flourish in a desert. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: One river pours about a fifth of all the fresh water that the world's rivers deliver to the oceans — more, by itself, than the next seven biggest rivers combined. Which river is this?
context: The Amazon discharges roughly 215,000–230,000 cubic metres of water every second — about a fifth of all the fresh water Earth's rivers pour into the oceans, and more than the next seven largest rivers combined. Even where it first enters Brazil it already out-discharges every other river on the planet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River

question: Asia's longest river, about 6,300 km, tumbles down from the Tibetan Plateau and slices a chain of dramatic gorges through steep cliffs on its long journey to the sea. Which river is this?
context: The Yangtze runs about 6,300 km entirely within China — Asia's longest river and the third-longest on Earth. Where it carves the Three Gorges through Mount Wushan, engineers built the Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-electric power station in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze

question: North America's mightiest river begins as a shallow trickle out of little Lake Itasca in Minnesota, then gathers the waters of nearly half the United States on its long run south to the Gulf of Mexico. Which river is this?
context: The Mississippi rises at Lake Itasca and drains all or part of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces — a basin of about 3.2 million sq km, roughly 40% of the continental United States. Joined with the Missouri, it forms the fourth-longest river system on Earth (about 5,970 km), behind only the Nile, Amazon, and Yangtze. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River

question: One European river flows through or borders more countries than any other river on Earth — ten of them — winding from Germany's Black Forest all the way to the shores of the Black Sea. Which river is this?
context: The Danube touches ten countries — Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine — more than any other river on Earth. Europe's second-longest river (about 2,850 km, after the Volga), it is also the only river to flow past four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube

question: Each summer the main Nile suddenly swells into a great flood, and about 70% of that floodwater is delivered by a single tributary, the Blue Nile, which comes roaring down off one highland region after the heavy summer rains. From which highland region does the Blue Nile's flood come?
context: The Blue Nile pours out of Lake Tana on the Ethiopian Highlands. When the summer rains soak those highlands, the Blue Nile delivers about 70% of the flood racing down the main Nile (and roughly 54% of its flow across the whole year) — the surge that once flooded Egypt's fields on schedule. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: The White Nile carries far less water than the Blue Nile, yet it is the branch that gives the Nile its record-breaking length: its remotest sources trickle from the highlands around one enormous lake in the heart of East Africa. Around which great lake do the White Nile's farthest headwaters lie?
context: The White Nile's remotest headwaters gather around Lake Victoria in East Africa. Though it carries less water than the Blue Nile, this is the branch that gives the Nile its enormous length. The two branches then race north toward their meeting deep in the desert. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: At one great city, two rivers flow together and become the single Nile: the pale, sediment-milky White Nile and the darker, clay-stained Blue Nile, their waters meeting with a visible colour line. At which city do the Blue Nile and White Nile join?
context: Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, sits exactly where the two Niles join. The pale White Nile (milky with quartz and feldspar sediment) and the darker Blue Nile (stained with Ethiopian clay) meet with a visible boundary before merging into the single Nile that flows on to Egypt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: One African river cuts canyons so deep that its bed plunges about 220 m straight down into cold, pitch-black water — deeper than any other river anywhere on Earth. Which river runs the deepest in the world?
context: The Congo plunges to about 220 m (720 ft) in its dark canyons — the deepest river on Earth. It ranks only third by the volume of water it carries (behind the Amazon and the Ganges–Brahmaputra), but no river runs deeper. In its lightless depths a blind, colourless fish, Lamprologus lethops, evolved cut off from the world above. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River

question: The Congo winds in an enormous arc through the rainforests of central Africa, and somewhere along that curving course it pulls off a feat no other great river in the world can match. What is the Congo's one-of-a-kind feat?
choices: it empties into an inland sea
it reverses its flow each rainy season
context: The Congo is the only major river on Earth to cross the equator twice — its huge curving course dips south of the equator and swings back north again. Near its mouth it hurls itself toward the Atlantic through Livingstone Falls, a staircase of enormous rapids. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River

question: Near the Brazilian river-city of Manaus, two Amazon tributaries famously meet but refuse to blend, running side by side for about 6 km: the coffee-black Rio Negro and its pale partner. What is the pale partner river called?
context: The Rio Solimões is the name Brazilians give the pale, sediment-heavy upper Amazon — cool (~22°C), fast (4–6 km/h), and milky with silt washed down from the Andes. Beside it runs the coffee-black Rio Negro, warm and slow and stained dark by decayed leaves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: At the 'Meeting of the Waters' near Manaus, the coffee-black Rio Negro and its pale partner river flow side by side for about 6 km without blending into one stream. What keeps the two waters from mixing for so long?
answer: they differ in temperature, speed, and density
choices: they differ in temperature, speed, and density
a submerged rock ridge divides the channel
the Rio Negro's water is too oily to blend
opposing tides from the sea hold them apart
context: At the Meeting of the Waters (Encontro das Águas) by Manaus, the two rivers refuse to blend because they differ in temperature, speed, and density: the Rio Negro is warmer (~28°C), slow (~2 km/h), and nearly sediment-free, while the Rio Solimões is cooler (~22°C), fast (4–6 km/h), and heavy with Andean silt. They flow side by side for about 6 km before finally mixing into the Amazon. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: Sailing east down the Yangtze from the old riverside town of Baidicheng, boats thread nearly 200 miles of a corridor where the river narrows between sheer cliff walls that soar overhead before it finally reaches Yichang. What is this legendary run of Yangtze canyons called?
context: The Three Gorges — Qutang, Wu, and Xiling — run about 193 miles (311 km) down the Yangtze from Baidicheng in Chongqing to Yichang in Hubei. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Of all the canyons the Yangtze carves, one is loved above the rest for its beauty: a 45-km stretch of steep cliffs and twelve famous peaks crowned by the legendary Fairy Peak. Which gorge is this?
context: Of the three gorges, Qutang is the shortest (just 8 km) and Xiling the longest (66 km), but Wu Gorge (45 km) is the most celebrated, famed for its Fairy Peak and its row of twelve peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Near the city of Yichang, the Yangtze is blocked by a wall of concrete 185 metres tall and more than 2 kilometres wide; its 32 turbines out-generate every other power station on Earth. What is this record-breaking dam?
context: Built at Sandouping near Yichang and completed in 2012, the Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station on the planet — 22,500 MW from 32 main 700-MW generators, making over 100 terawatt-hours of electricity a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: The Three Gorges Dam holds back a reservoir stretching 600 km up the valley — some 40 billion tonnes of water raised high above the old riverbed. In 2005 NASA scientists calculated that lifting that much mass had a real, if almost unimaginably tiny, effect on the whole planet. What did all that raised water do to the Earth?
answer: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
choices: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
sped up its spin, shortening the day
context: In 2005, NASA geophysicist Benjamin Fong Chao and colleague Richard Gross calculated that raising about 40 billion cubic metres of water so high shifts enough of Earth's mass to lengthen the day by roughly 0.06 microseconds — 60 billionths of a second, far too small to feel. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: When the Three Gorges Dam sealed the Yangtze, the rising reservoir drowned whole towns and farmland up and down the valley, ancestral homes lost for good beneath the water. Clearing the flood zone in time meant not moving a village or two but resettling a major city's worth of people all at once. Roughly how many were forced from their homes?
context: Filling the reservoir forced about 1.3 million people from their homes to clear the valley before the water rose. Planning documents projected that 13 cities, 140 towns, and 1,350 villages would be partly or wholly flooded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: Scientists explain the Three Gorges reservoir's tiny slowing of Earth's spin with a trick every figure skater knows: a spinning skater can change her speed just by moving her arms, with no push at all. To slow her spin — the way the raised reservoir slows the planet — what does the skater do with her arms?
context: It is the moment of inertia: moving mass farther from the spin axis makes a turning body rotate slower, so the raised reservoir slows Earth just as a skater slows by spreading her arms. For scale, the natural 2004 magnitude-9.0 Indian Ocean earthquake shortened the day about 2.68 microseconds — dozens of times more than the dam. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: For 1,500 years the Yangtze's gorges were China's most poetic landscape, their cliffs carved with verse by passing travelers. The Tang master Li Bai caught them in one immortal line, written as his small boat shot downstream between the canyon walls: a sound followed him, echoing endlessly from both sides of the river even as ten thousand mountains flew past. In Li Bai's line, what was making that sound?
context: Li Bai wrote, 'While monkeys keep howling at both sides of the river, the boat has swiftly passed thousands of mountains.' Poets had carved verse into these cliffs since the Northern Wei dynasty, over 1,500 years ago — much of it now drowned beneath the reservoir. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Asia's longest river empties into the sea beside Shanghai, yet 6,000 km inland its very first trickle is glacier-melt seeping from the ice atop 6,621-metre Geladaindong Peak in the Tanggula Mountains. On which vast highland is the Yangtze born?
context: The Yangtze is born from glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau, the 'roof of the world.' Its traditional source is the ice atop 6,621-metre Geladaindong Peak, which feeds the Tuotuo headwater stream at the start of the river's 6,236-km journey east to the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geladaindong_Peak

question: The Yellow River runs a steady yellow-brown not for a short stretch but for most of its 5,464 km across northern China to the sea — the trait that named it. What actually turns the water that color?
answer: fine mud it carries in the water
choices: fine mud it carries in the water
golden algae blooming on the surface
context: The color comes from fine sediment: as the river cuts through soft, pale highland soil it picks up enormous amounts of suspended silt, and that mud tints the water yellow-brown for nearly its whole length. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: Through its middle course the Yellow River saws down through a vast upland of soft, pale earth piled over 90 m (300 ft) deep — soil so loose that summer rains wash it into the water by the ton. What upland is this?
context: That wind-blown dust is called loess — fine grit that winds carried off deserts like the Gobi and piled over roughly 2.6 million years into the Loess Plateau, 50–80 m thick on average and over 90 m in places. More than 90% of the river's silt is stripped from this one region as it slices through. (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: The Yellow River flows right past the old capital of Kaifeng in Henan, where families have farmed and traded along its banks for 2,000 years. Yet a visitor who climbs the city wall and looks toward the water gets a shock. Why?
answer: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
choices: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
the river plunges over a waterfall taller than the wall
the river splits into dozens of braided channels here
the river disappears into a canyon below the city
context: Two thousand years of silt piling up in the channel forced people to wall the Yellow River in with levees built ever higher, until at Kaifeng its bed climbed about 10 m (33 ft) above the streets — some surveys say 13–14 m — held in only by those man-made banks. Geographers call such a channel a 'suspended,' 'above-ground,' or 'hanging' river: it literally flows overhead behind its levees. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River'; MDPI Sustainability 2019)

question: The Loess Plateau is blanketed in soft, pale soil tens of meters deep. For many centuries, how did families across this region typically make their homes?
answer: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
choices: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
by weaving domed huts from reeds and mud
by raising timber houses up on tall stilts
by stacking bricks baked from river clay
context: These carved dwellings are called yaodong — homes dug straight into the soft loess cliffs, made from the very soil the river is busy washing away downstream. (National Geographic Education, 'Loess')

question: Because its silt-raised bed leaves it forever ready to burst free, the Yellow River has broken its banks and drowned the northern plains again and again — its 1931 flood is often ranked the deadliest in recorded history. For this, the Chinese gave the river a grim two-word name. Which is it?
context: Between about 595 BC and 1946 the Yellow River flooded some 1,500 times and changed its main course 26 times; the 1931 flood's death toll is estimated at 1–4 million and the 1887 flood's at 900,000–2 million — among the worst disasters ever recorded. For its floods the river is called 'China's Sorrow'; for the civilization it fed, it is also called 'China's Pride.' (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: Deadly floods were only half the Yellow River's story. Its silt also spread a soft, mineral-rich yellow soil across the floodplain — loose enough to till with the simplest tools and generous with grain year after year. Chinese tradition honors this yellow-earth valley with one famous title. Which is it?
choices: the granary of the northern plains
the heartland of the Bronze Age
the birthplace of the Silk Road
context: The soft, fertile loess soil was easy to farm, so China's earliest villages clustered along the Yellow River thousands of years ago; the Loess Plateau and this floodplain are together remembered as 'the cradle of Chinese civilization.' (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: The Yucatan Peninsula is a flat slab of porous limestone where rain soaks straight down through the rock, leaving almost no rivers or streams on the surface. Instead the groundwater shows through in thousands of round, water-filled pits scattered across the jungle -- for the ancient Maya, the only reliable source of drinking water. What are these natural wells called?
context: The name comes from the Yucatec Maya word ts'ono'ot (dzonot), meaning a well or place of reachable groundwater, and is often glossed 'sacred well.' An estimated 6,000 to 10,000 cenotes pockmark the peninsula. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Divers who slip into a Yucatan cenote float in water so glass-clear they seem to hang in midair, the cavern walls sharp far below them. Cenotes are famous the world over for this glassy clarity. Why is the water so clear?
answer: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
choices: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
sunlight kills the algae that would cloud the water
cold water keeps silt frozen at the bottom
ocean tides flush the sinkhole clean each day
context: Cenote water is rainwater that has filtered for years down through porous limestone, leaving its particles behind, so the pools glow a deep, transparent blue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Map every cenote across northwest Yucatan and something eerie appears: the densest ones line up in a single giant arc, curving across the peninsula for no reason you can see on the flat jungle floor. Geologists were stunned to realize what this 'Ring of Cenotes' sits directly above -- a structure completely buried, betrayed only by the sinkholes tracing its edge. What does the ring trace?
answer: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
choices: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
the fault line of an ancient earthquake zone
the shoreline of a long-vanished inland sea
the channel of a collapsed underground river
context: The ring is a belt only about 5 km wide with a radius near 90 km -- roughly 180 km across -- curving from Celestun on the west coast past Homun and Tekit and back north to Dzilam. It marks the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater; the sinkholes are the surface fingerprint of the impact that ended the age of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
