Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5784/

question: Where the Yucatan's Caribbean shore drops into warm, turquoise water, a living wall of coral -- the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef -- runs unbroken for more than 1,000 km past the shores of Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras. Among all the barrier reefs on Earth, how does this one rank?
answer: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
choices: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
the largest of all, ahead of Australia's Great Barrier Reef
second-largest, behind only New Caledonia's reef
second-largest, behind only the Red Sea's reef
context: The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef is the second-largest barrier reef on Earth, outstretched only by Australia's Great Barrier Reef. It runs more than 1,000 km along Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras -- where the Yucatan's underground rivers finally reach the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Barrier_Reef_System

question: The crater buried beneath the Ring of Cenotes has a name: Chicxulub. About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide -- the size of a small mountain -- slammed into this exact spot, blasting a crater 180 km across and throwing up enough rock and soot to darken the whole sky. What did this single impact bring to an end?
context: The Chicxulub impactor hit near the present town of Chicxulub Puerto with force millions of times greater than a nuclear bomb. The debris and darkness triggered the mass extinction that wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs and about three-quarters of all species -- the leading scientific explanation for the end of the Cretaceous. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicxulub

question: A cenote isn't dug -- it's dissolved. Slightly acidic rainwater trickles into the Yucatan limestone and, drop by drop over thousands of years, eats the rock hollow, carving out caverns until a roof finally caves in and opens a round window down to the water table. Geologists have one word for this whole kind of landscape, where water slowly dissolves the bedrock into caves and sinkholes. What is it called?
context: Karst is landscape shaped where water slowly dissolves soluble rock like limestone, riddling it with caves, sinkholes, and underground rivers. The Yucatan is one of the largest karst platforms on Earth, which is why its cenotes number in the thousands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: To the ancient Maya, cenotes were sacred openings into the spirit world, not ordinary wells. On this bone-dry peninsula, where every drop of water came up from underground, the Maya prayed at their cenotes to the one god who could refill them from the sky. Which Maya god were the cenotes dedicated to?
context: The Maya believed cenotes were gateways to Xibalba, the underworld -- and above all they belonged to Chaac, the hook-nosed god of rain and lightning. In a land whose only water hid underground, the god who filled the wells mattered more than any other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Cenote  (Legend.)

question: Dive into one Yucatan cenote and, with the right training, you could swim through drowned stone passages to reach cenotes far across the jungle -- beneath the surface they nearly all connect into one flooded maze. This hidden, water-filled network holds a world record. What record do the Yucatan's flooded caves hold?
answer: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
choices: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
the deepest underwater cave systems on Earth
the widest underwater cave systems on Earth
the clearest underwater cave systems on Earth
context: Sistema Sac Actun ('White Cave' in Maya) maps about 378 km of submerged passage; in 2018 divers found a channel linking it to the Dos Ojos ('Two Eyes') system. Nearby, Sistema Ox Bel Ha ('Three Paths of Water') has over 435 km mapped -- the two are rival claimants for the longest underwater cave on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: At Chichen Itza one giant cenote stood apart from the everyday wells, reached from the great temples by a raised stone road -- the Sacred Cenote. From 1904 to 1910 Edward Thompson dredged its muddy floor and dived it in a diving helmet, hauling up thousands of offerings the Maya had cast into the water: gold, jade, copal incense, copper bells. Mixed in with the treasure, what else did he bring up?
context: Edward Herbert Thompson recovered thousands of offerings along with human remains -- evidence of sacrifices to the rain god Chaac. The Sacred Cenote is about 60 m across, its water surface 27 m below the rim, and a 300 m raised stone road, a sacbe, once linked it to Chichen Itza's temples. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Cenote  (Legend.)

question: In 2007, cave divers dropped into a pitch-black flooded chamber deep beneath the Yucatan, a pit they named Hoyo Negro -- the 'Black Hole.' On a ledge far below the surface, scattered among the bones of Ice Age sabre-toothed cats and giant ground sloths, lay the nearly complete skeleton of a teenage girl. Why did this skeleton, later nicknamed 'Naia,' stun scientists?
answer: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
choices: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
she had been buried with a hoard of gold
she stood well over seven feet tall
she was a wholly unknown human species
context: Naia was a 15-to-16-year-old girl who fell into the then-dry cave around 12,000 to 13,000 years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age; rising seas later flooded the chamber. She is among the oldest and most complete humans ever found in the Americas, helping trace how the first people reached the continent. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/140515-skeleton-ice-age-mexico-cave-hoyo-negro-archaeology

question: On the open grasslands of Tuva, in southern Siberia, a lone herder opens his mouth and a single voice sounds two notes at once — a low steady drone with a bright shimmering pitch floating above it. What is this steppe vocal art called?
context: Across Tuva and neighboring Mongolia the art is called khöömei, a Turkic word meaning 'throat' or 'larynx.' A single herder, standing alone on the steppe, can sound like two singers at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: Ask a Tuvan or Mongolian throat-singer where the styles come from, and herders across the steppe give the same answer: the sounds are not composed but borrowed, turning one person's song into a portrait of home. Borrowed from what?
answer: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
choices: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
the melodies of old Mongol war songs
the cries of their own herds and dogs
context: Singers liken the deep growl to the howling winds of winter, and the rolling trill called borbangnadyr to a bubbling brook — so one person's song becomes a map of the homeland: wind, water, and open sky. The whole art grows from an animist belief that a place's spirits live in its sound as much as its shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing  (Legend.)

question: Among Tuvan throat-singers, each style carries its own name. The highest is a clear, piercing, flute-like whistle that seems to hover far above the low drone — the sound of a thin wind slicing across the steppe. What is this whistling style called?
context: Sygyt, the high whistle, is one of three main styles, alongside the deep growling kargyraa and khöömei used as its own style, said to sound like 'wind swirling among rocks.' Singers point the tongue against the gums to force the piercing tone out clear and bright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: A Tuvan throat-singer is often joined by a two-stringed fiddle whose neck rises into a carved horse's head above the tuning pegs, its low bowing meant to echo horses crossing the steppe. What is this Tuvan fiddle called?
context: The igil is Tuva's horsehead fiddle; Mongolia bows a larger cousin, the morin khuur. Played low and steady beneath the voice, its rhythm falls like hoofbeats under the singer's drone. Both fiddles are carved with a horse's head — fitting, for music made by a people who live on horseback. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igil

question: Tuva has a throat-singing style built on a steady rocking pulse, flicked out by the soft palate opening and closing as the singer drones. Riders recognize the motion at once: the style's name, ezengileer, is taken straight from a piece of a horseman's kit, and the song sways in time with it. Which piece gave the style its name?
context: Ezengileer takes its name from ezengi, the Tuvan word for a stirrup, and its bouncing pulse imitates the sway of a rider posting at a trot. It joins a whole gallery of styles — each one, singers say, a different piece of the moving steppe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: A Tuvan singer's second, whistling pitch sounds like sorcery, but it is pure physics. He holds one low droning note, slowly reshapes his mouth and throat, and a bright separate pitch rings out above the drone — yet it is not a second voice. What is that high pitch, really?
answer: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
choices: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
an echo of the drone bouncing off the hard palate
the drone itself sliding rapidly up to a high note
air forced into a thin whistle between the teeth
context: Acousticians call this biphonation from filtering: one sound source split into two pitches. The singer's mouth focuses a narrow band of overtones — roughly the 6th to 12th harmonics of the drone — into a single sharp peak while hushing the neighbors, so one faint harmonic rings out as a separate note. UNESCO calls it 'a melody of harmonics' riding a continuous drone. Sources: https://elifesciences.org/articles/50476 ; https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/mongolian-traditional-art-of-khoomei-00396

question: Twice a day on England's River Severn, the incoming Atlantic tide is funneled into the narrowing estuary until it rears up into a single wall of water — up to about 2 m tall — that races upstream, against the river's normal seaward flow. Surfers paddle out to ride it. What is this kind of upstream wave called?
context: On the Severn the bore rides one of the greatest tidal ranges on Earth — about 13 m between high and low water — which is why surfers can chase a single wave miles inland. A tidal bore forms only where a big flood tide is funneled into a shallow, narrowing river mouth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_bore

question: On the Amazon, the tidal bore arrives as a distant rumble heard long before it is seen — a wall of water up to 4 m high that surges as far as 800 km upstream, tearing at the banks as it goes. Its name in the local Tupi language means 'great roar.' What is the Amazon's tidal bore called?
context: 'Pororoca' may come from a Tupi word meaning 'great roar' — the wave is heard as a rumble before the wall of water appears. It can rush up to 800 km inland, ripping trees off the banks; surfers and kayakers chase it for miles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca  (Legend.)

question: An ocean surfer is lucky to ride one wave for twenty seconds before it collapses. But a tidal bore is a single wave that never breaks — it just keeps rolling upstream for miles. In 2003, Brazilian surfer Picuruta Salazar caught the Amazon's pororoca and rode it 12.5 km up the river without once falling off. For how long did he stay on that one wave?
context: Because a bore is one wave that keeps reforming as it climbs the river, a rider can stay on it far longer than any ocean wave allows. Salazar's 12.5 km, 37-minute ride on the Guama River in 2003 is remembered as one of the longest in surfing history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca  (Legend.)

question: The pororoca doesn't only rush inland — its pounding erosion reshapes the coast, tearing whole trees from the banks. Near the Amazon's mouth lies low, flat Caviana Island. Between 1845 and 1850, the relentless bore did to Caviana something few waves ever do to solid land. What happened to Caviana Island?
context: Between 1845 and 1850 the pororoca's erosion split Caviana Island, near the Amazon's mouth, into two parts — a wave rearranging the map. The same bore constantly tears trees and mud from the banks as it charges inland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca

question: China's Qiantang River, near Hangzhou, has the biggest tidal bore on Earth — a roaring wall of water up to 9 m tall that charges upstream at 40 km/h, three times the height of England's Severn bore. Crowds have lined its banks each autumn to watch for over a thousand years. What is this giant bore nicknamed?
context: The Qiantang bore, nicknamed the 'Silver Dragon,' is the world's largest. Tide-watching here is over a thousand years old: the Southern Song court set a Tide Watching Festival on the 18th day of the 8th lunar month, and the world's oldest known tide table (AD 1056) was made for this river. In 2013 Typhoon Trami doubled the bore's height and it broke over the barrier into the crowd. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiantang_River  (Legend.)

question: For centuries, boats on France's Seine had to reckon with the mascaret — a tidal bore the locals called 'la barre' that surged up from the sea. Then, by the 1960s, it simply vanished, and today the lower Seine has no bore at all. What made the Seine's mascaret disappear?
choices: the sea's tidal range slowly shrank
the river's course was rerouted inland
context: A tidal bore needs a shallow, narrowing, funneling estuary; deepening the Seine's channel for shipping erased that geometry and 'la barre' was gone — proof a bore can be engineered out of existence. The reverse can happen too: Canada's Petitcodiac bore, choked by a 1968 causeway, came back after the gates were reopened in 2010. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascaret

question: At Tikal in the flat lowlands of northern Guatemala, Temple IV rises about 70 metres — the giant of the city's pyramids. A climber who reaches its summit suddenly emerges into open sky, having risen clear above the one thing that hides every other ruin for miles around. What has the climber risen above?
context: Temple IV rises about 70 m (roughly 64.6 m from its own platform to the top of the roof-comb) — high enough to look out over an unbroken sea of treetops. Accuracy note: it is NOT the tallest pre-Columbian structure. It is roughly the second-tallest still standing, after the Great Pyramid of Tonina, and Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun may once have topped it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: Two great stone pyramids stand face to face across Tikal's Great Plaza. The Maya named the taller, eastern one — a steep royal tomb-pyramid — for a fierce predator of the Peten jungle. Which animal gives Temple I its name, the 'Temple of the Great ___'?
context: Temple I is the 'Temple of the Great Jaguar,' named for a carved lintel showing a king seated on a jaguar throne. Facing it across the plaza is its shorter twin, Temple II, the 'Temple of the Masks.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: A film crew once hauled their cameras up Temple IV at Tikal and shot the view out over the endless Guatemalan jungle. In the finished movie, that summit vista became the surface of a distant alien world in one of the most famous science-fiction sagas ever made. Which film borrowed Tikal as its alien planet?
context: In Star Wars: A New Hope (1977), the view from Temple IV's summit stands in for the rebel base on the forest moon Yavin 4. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: Around 900 CE the people of Tikal walked away from their great city, and the Peten rainforest swallowed the plazas and temples, hiding them for nearly a thousand years. Across the whole Maya lowlands, what do most researchers now blame for this collapse?
context: The leading explanation is decades of severe drought, worsened by the Maya's own deforestation and soil erosion, though the exact trigger is still debated. After the collapse, the jungle reclaimed Tikal for roughly a thousand years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: Temple I at Tikal climbs to its summit shrine in a staircase of nine great stepped terraces. The Maya architects chose the number nine on purpose, to echo a sacred nine that stood at the heart of their view of the world. What did the nine terraces stand for?
answer: The nine layers of the underworld
choices: The nine layers of the underworld
The nine tiers of the heavens
context: Temple I's nine stepped terraces are widely thought to represent the nine levels of the Maya underworld. Its roof-comb is built as two parallel stone walls with a hollow vault between them, cutting the weight while giving a huge surface to carve the king's image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I  (Legend.)

question: The ruined city we call 'Tikal' had a different name when its kings ruled it — probably 'Yax Mutal.' The name 'Tikal' itself is a much later Yucatec Maya word. What does 'Tikal' roughly mean?
context: 'Tikal' is a later Yucatec Maya name meaning roughly 'at the waterhole' — a fitting name for a city with no rivers or lakes that lived and died by its rain-fed reservoirs. Its Classic-era name was likely 'Yax Mutal.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: For centuries Tikal shared the Maya world with rival superpowers. Its fiercest enemy rose in the forest lowlands to the north — a city whose kings called their dynasty the 'Snake Kingdom' and stamped a snake-head glyph on every monument. Which city was Tikal's great northern rival?
context: Calakmul, in modern Campeche, Mexico, about 35 km north of the Guatemala border, was the seat of the Kaan ('Snake') dynasty — Tikal's great rival across the Classic Maya lowlands. Its emblem glyph was a snake head reading 'Kaan.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calakmul

question: In 1962, archaeologists tunneled deep into Temple I at Tikal and broke into the sealed tomb of King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I. On the burial bench, still resting on the royal skeleton, lay the richest treasure ever found at the city. What jewel-work adorned the dead king?
answer: A necklace of heavy jade beads
choices: A necklace of heavy jade beads
context: The necklace held 114 carved jade beads and weighed 3.9 kg (8.6 lb). Burial 116 also held a jade mosaic vessel carved with the king's own portrait, 37 inscribed human bones, jaguar pelts, spondylus shells, and pearls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I

question: Tikal drank only rainwater, caught off its wide plazas and held in huge lined reservoirs — water that, in a hot jungle, should have turned foul within weeks. A 2020 study showed the Corriental reservoir somehow stayed clean for centuries, making it the oldest known water-purification site in the Americas. How did the Maya keep it drinkable?
context: The Maya filtered the water through imported zeolite and coarse quartz sand — a natural molecular sieve that stripped out microbes and even toxins like mercury. It is the oldest known water-filtration system in the Western Hemisphere, about 2,000 years old, and the minerals were hauled roughly 30 km (18 miles) from ridges near the Bajo de Azucar. Sources: nature.com/articles/s41598-020-75023-7; uc.edu/news/articles/2020/10

question: The same reservoirs that once made Tikal possible may, in the end, have turned against it. Sediment laid down in the city's largest reservoirs as it declined is laced with a poison that had leached in from the brilliant red pigment the Maya painted across their walls and tombs. Which toxic metal fouled Tikal's water?
context: Sediment studies of Tikal's largest reservoirs found them fouled with mercury, leached from cinnabar — the red pigment the Maya prized — along with blooms of toxic blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). Together they would have made the water undrinkable as the city declined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: For centuries English speakers said 'from here to ___' — naming a real, dusty city in what is now Mali — to mean the most remote, unreachable place on earth. Which city's name became this byword for the middle of nowhere?
context: 'As far as Timbuktu' and 'from here to Timbuktu' became English shorthand for the ends of the earth — yet Timbuktu is a real, reachable city of about 85,000 people in modern Mali. In the 1800s Europeans imagined it as a place of mythical riches at the world's edge. Source: NPR/WLRN, 'From Here to Timbuktu'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.  (Legend.)

question: Timbuktu grew rich at a crossing point: on the southern rim of the Sahara, camel caravans staggering out of the desert unloaded their cargo onto boats waiting on a great river 20 km to the south. Which river carried Timbuktu's trade into the heart of West Africa?
context: Timbuktu sits on the southern edge of the Sahara about 20 km north of the Niger River — the exact point where desert camel caravans met the river boats. That meeting of sand and water is what made it a great trading city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: The lands south of Timbuktu overflowed with gold yet lacked one desert commodity so badly that, traders said, the two were swapped toward equal weight. Camels carried this cargo south out of the deep Sahara, from Taghaza and Taoudenni. What was it?
context: Slabs of salt cut at the Saharan mines of Taghaza and Taoudenni were hauled south by camel; salt was so scarce in the gold-rich south that it was famously said to trade toward its weight in gold — an exaggeration, but salt worth pennies in the desert could sell for gold at the Sahara's edge. The 'azalai' caravans ran several thousand camels at a time, each carrying four or five 30 kg slabs on the roughly three-week trip from Taoudenni, about 660 km north. Sources: worldhistory.org, 'The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azalai.  (Legend.)

question: Scattered through Timbuktu stand the domed shrines of Sufi holy men — the marabouts — whom the townsfolk honor as guardians watching over the city. A great many of these saints lie buried within its walls, giving Timbuktu which nickname?
choices: the City of a Thousand Saints
context: Timbuktu is nicknamed the 'City of 333 Saints' for the 333 Sufi marabouts buried in shrines across the town, whose tombs the people venerated as protectors of the city. In 2012 militants smashed several of these tombs; local masons later rebuilt them with UNESCO support. Timbuktu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988. Sources: newageislam.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: In private family libraries, the people of Timbuktu quietly preserved up to ~700,000 hand-written manuscripts — hard proof that this Saharan trading town was also a city of deep scholarship. Beyond the medicine, law and poetry they contain, for which pair of subjects are Timbuktu's manuscripts most celebrated?
context: European colonizers spread a myth that Africa kept no written records — yet Timbuktu's families had guarded, for centuries, up to an estimated ~700,000 hand-written manuscripts covering astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law and poetry. The city's astronomy manuscripts, with their star charts and planetary tables, are among the most celebrated: hard proof that pre-colonial West Africa had literate, scientific scholarship centuries before European colonies, directly against the false 'Africa had no written history' trope. (The count is an estimate — hence 'up to ~700,000.') Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu_Manuscripts.  (Legend.)

question: Timbuktu's three great mosques — Djinguereber, Sankoré and Sidi Yahya — were raised by medieval emperors and have drawn worshippers for some 700 years, their broad towers rising over the flat desert town. From what material were these famous mosques built?
context: All three mosques are built of mud and adobe, not stone. Djinguereber, the oldest, was built in 1327 on the order of the emperor Mansa Musa and designed by the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili; Sidi Yahya was founded around 1400 and completed about 1440. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; grokipedia.com/page/Djinguereber_Mosque.

question: Around 1510 the traveler Leo Africanus wandered Timbuktu's crowded markets and marveled at its trade. Of everything sold there, he wrote, one good brought its sellers 'more profit than all other merchandise' — worth more even than gold. What was it?
context: Leo Africanus wrote of Timbuktu that 'there is more profit made from this commerce than from all other merchandise' — hand-written books were the single most valuable trade good, worth more than a slave, and owning them was how the wealthy showed off their standing. Source: brians.wsu.edu, Leo Africanus, 'Description of Africa' (1526).  (Legend.)

question: Timbuktu's greatest scholar, Ahmed Baba, wrote more than forty books of his own and filled his home with a personal library of over 1,600 volumes — a treasure in a city where books were the most precious goods of all. Then in 1591 a Moroccan army stormed Timbuktu. What did the conquerors do to Ahmed Baba?
choices: held him for a heavy ransom
put him to death in the square
burned his house to the ground
context: Ahmed Baba (1556–1627) was Timbuktu's greatest scholar and a chancellor of the Sankoré madrasa — the heart of what is remembered as the University of Timbuktu, one of the world's oldest centers of higher learning, said to have taught as many as ~25,000 students at its height (a historical estimate). He wrote more than 40 books and kept a personal library of over 1,600 volumes, which he lost when Moroccan invaders exiled him from the city in 1591. Timbuktu's modern manuscript-research institute is named the Ahmed Baba Institute in his honor. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; muslimheritage.com, 'The University of Sankore, Timbuktu'; face2faceafrica.com.

question: For years European explorers died trying to reach Timbuktu, dreaming of a fabled city roofed in gold. When the Frenchman René Caillié finally walked in and out alive in 1828 to claim a 10,000-franc prize, what did he actually find there?
context: René Caillié (1828) was the first European to reach Timbuktu and return alive, collecting a 10,000-franc prize from the Geographical Society of Paris. Expecting gold, he found only 'a mass of ill-looking houses built of earth.' The Briton Alexander Gordon Laing had reached the city first, in August 1826, but was murdered by his escorts just after leaving. Leo Africanus's earlier tale of a single 970-pound gold ingot in the ruler's treasury had helped feed the golden-city legend. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/René_Caillié; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gordon_Laing; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Rows of palm-wood beams called toron jut straight out from the mud walls of Timbuktu's great mosques. They are no decoration: the builders left them as permanent scaffolding, so that once a year the whole town can carry out one essential task together. What is that yearly task?
context: The toron — projecting Rodier-palm beams — are permanent built-in scaffolding: the mud skin must be re-plastered by the whole town every year in a communal festival, the crépissage, or the seasonal rains would slowly dissolve the building. Sources: reviewofreligions.org, 'Places of Worship: Timbuktu Mosque'; grokipedia.com/page/Sudano-Sahelian_architecture.  (Legend.)

question: In 2012 armed militants seized Timbuktu and set about destroying whatever they judged un-Islamic, putting the city's priceless ancient manuscripts in mortal danger. A quiet local librarian, Abdel Kader Haidara, organized a secret rescue. How did he and his helpers save some 350,000 manuscripts?
answer: floating them downriver in metal trunks
choices: floating them downriver in metal trunks
burying them in jars under the desert
sealing them inside the mosque walls
context: Librarian Abdel Kader Haidara and a network of helpers secretly smuggled roughly 350,000 manuscripts out in metal trunks and footlockers, spirited past checkpoints and floated down the Niger River by boat to safety in Bamako. It was a race against real destruction: on 25 January 2013 the retreating militants swept about 4,200 manuscripts off the tables of the Ahmed Baba Institute and set them on fire — only a fraction, because most had already been smuggled out. Sources: nationalgeographic.com, 'The Badass Librarians of Timbuktu'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.  (Legend.)

question: The ruined stone city of Tiwanaku rises from a treeless Bolivian plain beside Lake Titicaca. Its builders raised these monuments, then vanished -- but when? Placed on a timeline of the great civilizations of the Americas, where does Tiwanaku belong?
choices: At the same time as the Aztec
context: Tiwanaku flourished roughly AD 500-1000 and had collapsed by about AD 1000 -- centuries before the Inca empire arose in the 1400s. The two are a common mix-up because both centered on the Andes near Lake Titicaca. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: Tiwanaku stands on a vast, treeless tableland beside Lake Titicaca, spreading across Bolivia and Peru -- flat ground that lies higher than the summits of most mountains in the Alps. Geographers know this immense Andean tableland by a Spanish name. What is it?
context: The altiplano is the widest high plateau on Earth outside Tibet. Tiwanaku sits on it at about 3,850 m (12,630 ft) above sea level, near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca -- a plain so lofty it rises above most European peaks. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: At Tiwanaku stands its most celebrated monument: a great doorway carved from a single block of stone about 3 m tall and weighing some 10 tons, its lintel crowned by a commanding figure who grips a staff in each raised hand. By what name is this famous gateway known?
context: The Gateway of the Sun is cut from a single 10-ton block. The commanding figure on its lintel -- holding a staff in each hand, its head ringed by rays -- is usually identified as the creator god Viracocha, though some scholars suggest the Aymara weather god Thunupa. Source: Wikipedia: Gateway of the Sun.

question: Beside Tiwanaku lies the temple of Pumapunku, where masons cut hard andesite into interlocking blocks so identical and sharp-edged they look mass-produced by machine. Every one of these signature stones was shaped to the same distinctive, letter-like form. What shape were the famous Pumapunku blocks cut into?
context: Pumapunku's H-blocks lock together like precise puzzle pieces, forming blind miniature gateways. Their machine-like precision has made the site a magnet for 'ancient aliens' claims -- but archaeologists credit skilled Tiwanaku masons. Alexei Vranich points to well-preserved earlier stonework at nearby Pukara and Chiripa as proof the skill grew among the Titicaca-basin peoples themselves, and Franco Rossi has criticized alien theorists for dismissing the Aymara as incapable builders. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Pumapunku's builders raised walls of enormous stones without a scrap of mortar, yet fitted them so tightly a knife blade won't slip between. In matching notches carved across each seam, they anchored every block to its neighbor with a technique that still amazes engineers. What held Pumapunku's giant stones together?
answer: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
choices: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
iron staples hammered across the joints
reed ropes lashed around the blocks
wooden pegs driven into the seams
context: In carved notches at the joints, Tiwanaku metalworkers poured molten metal that hardened in place into I-shaped cramps of a distinctive copper-arsenic-nickel bronze alloy -- casting the clamps directly at the stone to bind block to block without mortar. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Pumapunku's builders had no wheels, no draft animals strong enough, and no iron -- yet they quarried the temple's hardest blocks on a peninsula about 90 km off and moved them across Lake Titicaca. The largest single stone at the site, a red-sandstone slab, ranks among the heaviest worked stones in the ancient Americas. Roughly how much does that one slab weigh?
context: The red-sandstone slab weighs an estimated 131 tonnes -- a calculated estimate, not a measurement -- and came from a quarry about 10 km off. Pumapunku's harder andesite blocks travelled far farther still: quarried on the Copacabana Peninsula about 90 km away, they had to be moved across (or around) Lake Titicaca itself. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku; Grokipedia: Pumapunku.

question: The altiplano around Tiwanaku freezes hard on clear nights, which should have killed its crops. Instead the Tiwanaku fed a city of many thousands by building long raised planting beds divided by water-filled channels: the water soaked up the day's sun and released its warmth after dark, so cold air sank into the ditches instead of settling on the plants. What is this frost-beating raised-field system called?
context: These raised beds -- called waru waru (also suka kollus) -- were typically 4-10 m wide and up to 100 m long, raised about a meter high. By trapping the day's heat in the channel water they kept the soil roughly 1 degree C warmer at night, out-yielding ordinary fields and helping feed a Tiwanaku of an estimated 10,000-20,000 people around AD 800. The system faltered when a long drought gripped the altiplano around AD 1000, coinciding with the city's decline. Source: Wikipedia: Waru Waru; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: In the heart of Tokyo, the traffic lights at one intersection all turn red at the same moment, and a flood of people -- up to 3,000 in a single light -- pours across from every direction at once, cutting straight through the middle. Which Tokyo district is famous for this 'scramble crossing,' the busiest on Earth?
context: This is the famous Shibuya Scramble (Shibuya Crossing), which opened in 1973. When the lights change, pedestrians surge across from all sides at once -- up to about 3,000 people per green light. Surveys estimate around 260,000 people cross on a weekday and up to 500,000 on the busiest days, making it the most famous pedestrian crossing on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibuya_Crossing  (Legend.)

question: Greater Tokyo packs roughly 37 million people -- nearly as many as the entire state of California -- into one unbroken sprawl of streets and buildings that runs for miles in every direction. Among all the cities humans have ever built, where does that place Tokyo?
choices: the second most populous on Earth
context: Greater Tokyo (the Tokyo-Yokohama agglomeration) is home to roughly 37 million people -- the largest single urban area in human history, about the population of the whole state of California or the country of Poland. Rankings depend on where you draw the boundary: a narrower UN definition counts about 33 million, and fast-growing Delhi is projected to overtake Tokyo within about a decade. Source: Statista 2025 urban agglomerations; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Tokyo_Area  (Legend.)

question: Tokyo has not always carried that name. For more than 250 years it was the stronghold of the Tokugawa shoguns under a different name, until 1868, when the young Emperor Meiji moved his court there from Kyoto and renamed the city. What had it been called for those centuries?
context: For over 250 years the city was called Edo, capital of the Tokugawa shoguns. When the shogunate fell in 1868, the young Emperor Meiji moved his residence there from Kyoto and renamed it Tokyo (東京), meaning 'Eastern Capital' -- the capital to the east of the old one, Kyoto. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo; britannica.com/place/Tokyo

question: Rising 634 meters over Tokyo, a slender broadcasting spire opened in 2012 as the tallest tower on Earth -- taller than any free-standing broadcasting tower ever built. Which of these Japanese towers holds that record?
context: The Tokyo Skytree rises 634 m (2,080 ft) and opened on May 22, 2012 as a broadcasting tower -- the tallest tower in the world, beating China's Canton Tower (600 m). Some buildings are taller (Dubai's Burj Khalifa is 828 m, Kuala Lumpur's Merdeka 118 is 679 m), but a 'tower' has less than half its height as usable floor space, so the Skytree still holds the tower record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree

question: One of Tokyo's busiest commuter railways has no final stop at all. Instead it runs endlessly around the center of the city in a great ring, threading together the giant hubs of Shibuya, Shinjuku, and Ikebukuro before arriving back where it began. Which line is this?
context: The Yamanote Line is Tokyo's famous loop line, circling the city center in a continuous ring that connects its biggest hubs -- Tokyo, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ikebukuro and more. One full loop takes about an hour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamanote_Line

question: About 3.5 million passengers pour through a single Tokyo railway station every day -- nearly six times as many as its closest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord -- making it the Guinness-record holder for the busiest station on Earth. Which station is it?
context: Shinjuku Station holds the Guinness World Record as the busiest railway station on Earth -- about 3.5 million passengers a day before the pandemic, and still 2.7 million in 2022. Its nearest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord, handles only around 600,000. It has well over 200 exits. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/busiest-station; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku_Station

question: At the exact center of the world's biggest city, a wide moat and high stone ramparts wall off a vast island of forest and gardens -- the grounds of the old Edo Castle. What fills this green, guarded heart of Tokyo?
context: The Imperial Palace (Kokyo), residence of the Emperor of Japan, sits on the grounds of the former Edo Castle, ringed by wide moats and forest at the exact center of Tokyo -- so a great island of trees and water fills the heart of the world's biggest city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Imperial_Palace

question: Out in Tokyo Bay lies Odaiba, a district of shopping malls, a giant Ferris wheel, and a life-sized Gundam robot. It began in 1853 as a ring of cannon batteries built to fend off Commodore Perry's American warships. What kind of ground is this whole waterfront district built on?
context: Odaiba is built on reclaimed land -- one of many artificial islands in Tokyo Bay, where about 249 km2 of ground has been created from the sea. It began in 1853 as a ring of gun batteries ('daiba' means 'battery') to defend Edo against Commodore Perry's 'Black Ships,' and was rebuilt into a futuristic waterfront in the 1990s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odaiba; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Bay

question: Before an emperor ever lived at the center of Tokyo, that walled ground was Edo Castle, the fortress-capital of the Tokugawa shoguns for two and a half centuries. Among all the fortresses of its age, what distinction did Edo Castle once hold?
answer: the largest castle in the world
choices: the largest castle in the world
the tallest castle in the world
the oldest castle in the world
the strongest castle in the world
context: In its heyday Edo Castle was the largest castle in the world: its outer defenses ran about 16 km (10 miles) around and covered roughly 230 hectares -- more than double Osaka Castle's 106. Today's Imperial Palace grounds are only about a third of the original castle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_Castle; worldhistory.org/Edo_Castle  (Legend.)

question: Tokyo has been shaken to rubble and rebuilt more than once, because the Kanto plain sits in one of the most geologically violent settings on Earth. What is the underground reason the city is so dangerously earthquake-prone?
answer: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
choices: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
a single deep fault line splits it
a volcanic hotspot rises beneath it
its soft soil amplifies far-off quakes
context: The Kanto region sits on a rare triple plate boundary: the continental (North American/Okhotsk) plate is being pushed under by BOTH the Philippine Sea plate and the Pacific plate, which dive beneath it. (Older texts call the continental plate 'Eurasian.') This double subduction makes Tokyo one of the most seismically active cities on the planet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake; agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com (dual subduction under Tokyo)

question: At 11:58 on the morning of September 1, 1923, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama. About 105,000 people died -- yet remarkably few were killed by the shaking or by falling debris. What caused the overwhelming majority of the deaths in the Great Kanto earthquake?
answer: a firestorm that swept the city
choices: a firestorm that swept the city
context: The Great Kanto earthquake struck at 11:58 a.m. -- lunchtime, when thousands of charcoal cooking fires were burning across a city of wooden houses. Whipped by winds from a passing typhoon, the fires merged into firestorms (one 'fire tornado' at a former clothing depot killed tens of thousands alone), causing about 90% of the roughly 105,000 deaths. The quake was driven by the Philippine Sea plate slipping beneath the continental plate along the Sagami Trough. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake

question: The Tokyo Skytree stands exactly 634 meters tall, and that oddly precise number was no accident -- it was chosen as a hidden pun. Read as digits in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 sounds out a single Japanese word. What does '634' spell?
context: 634 metres was chosen as a pun: in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 reads 'mu-sa-shi' -- Musashi, the ancient name of the province and plain that Tokyo was built on. This kind of number-wordplay is called goroawase. The Skytree opened in 2012 as the world's tallest tower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree; britannica.com/topic/Tokyo-Sky-Tree

question: Across the plains of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska, spring afternoons can turn the sky an eerie green-black and spin down more twisters than anywhere else on Earth. What nickname do meteorologists give this violent belt of the Great Plains?
context: Tornado Alley isn't an official line on any map but a nickname for the central Great Plains, where cold, dry air off the Rocky Mountains collides with warm Gulf moisture to breed more twisters than anywhere on Earth. The Dust Bowl was the 1930s drought that scoured these same plains; Hail Alley is the High Plains belt battered by the nation's worst hail; Hoosier Alley is a smaller tornado zone around Indiana and the Ohio Valley. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Tornado Alley churns out more twisters than anywhere on Earth thanks to one unstable recipe of stacked air masses that erupts into rotating thunderstorms from April through June. Which clash of air masses fuels it?
answer: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
choices: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
cool marine air off the Pacific sliding under hot air from the Mojave Desert
monsoon moisture from the Gulf of California damming against the Sierra Madre
frigid Arctic air from Canada pouring down onto the humid Atlantic Seaboard
context: The setup is a layer cake of instability: dry, cool air spilling east off the Rockies rides up and over warm, wet air streaming north from the Gulf of Mexico. The trapped moist layer bursts upward into towering, rotating thunderstorms called supercells - the parent storms of most violent tornadoes. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Every spring over the Texas Panhandle, an invisible boundary separates scorching desert air to the west from humid air rolling in off the Gulf; step across it and the dew point can plunge tens of degrees within a mile as the wind swings around. Storm chasers stake it out because the towering rotating storms called supercells fire right along it. What do forecasters call this boundary?
context: A dryline marks where hot, dry desert air meets Gulf moisture, often draped over the Texas Panhandle and western Plains in spring. Counterintuitively, the dry air is denser and wedges underneath the moist air, helping shove it upward into storms. Cross a dryline and the humidity - not the temperature - drops off a cliff. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dryline

question: On May 31, 2013, a violent tornado ground across the open plains near El Reno, Oklahoma, and mobile radar clocked winds screaming past 300 mph deep inside it. Which record does the El Reno tornado hold?
context: El Reno's tornado spread 2.6 miles (4.2 km) from edge to edge - the widest ever measured on Earth. Its winds screamed past 300 mph on mobile radar, yet surveyors rated it only EF3: tornado ratings read the damage left on the ground, not the wind itself, and this giant churned mostly over open country. Its record is width, not strength. Eight people died, including veteran storm researcher Tim Samaras, his son Paul, and Carl Young of the TWISTEX team - the first professional tornado researchers ever killed while chasing. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/2013_El_Reno_tornado

question: Across Tornado Alley, forecasters rank each twister on a single damage scale that runs from a 0 - snapped branches and peeled shingles - up to a 5, which strips asphalt off the road and lifts an anchored, well-built house clean off its foundation. What is this tornado-damage scale called?
context: Ted Fujita of the University of Chicago introduced his F scale in 1971; the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale replaced it in the United States on February 1, 2007. An original F5 meant winds of roughly 261 to 318 mph - 'incredible damage.' Because the scale reads the wreckage on the ground rather than the wind directly, a ferociously fast tornado can still earn a middling rating if it stays over open country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale

question: The Great Plains see the most tornadoes, but a belt across the Deep South - Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Georgia - kills far more people per storm. Meteorologists nicknamed it 'Dixie Alley.' What makes Dixie Alley's tornadoes so much deadlier than the ones out on the Plains?
answer: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
choices: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
they pack far stronger winds than any tornado the Plains can muster
they linger on the ground for hours, not the usual few minutes
they hurl grapefruit-sized hail ahead of the funnel
context: Dixie Alley's twisters strike disproportionately at night - about 29% after dark versus 19% on the Plains - and they hide in rain and dense forest, so people never spot the funnel. Night tornadoes kill roughly 2.5 times as many people, catching families asleep. The meteorologist Allen Pearson coined the name 'Dixie Alley' in 1971. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Along the Li River around Guilin and Yangshuo in southern China, hundreds of steep gray hills rise straight out of flat green rice paddies like a crowd of stone thumbs, slowly shaped by water over millions of years. What is this kind of landscape called?
context: This is 'tower karst' — solid limestone slowly dissolved away by rainwater over millions of years, not pushed up by any volcano or earthquake. The word 'karst' itself comes from the Kras Plateau in Slovenia, the barren limestone country where these dissolving-rock features were first studied. Karst is no rare oddity: it covers roughly a fifth of the continental United States, and karst springs and aquifers supply about a quarter of the world's drinking water. Sources: Grokipedia 'Guilin' and 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Tower karst' and 'Karst'.

question: The most famous stretch of Li River scenery — a lone fisherman poling a bamboo raft past sharp karst peaks doubled in the mirror-still water — is printed on the back of China's 20-yuan banknote. Which real riverside spot is the view on the money?
context: The spot is Yellow Cloth Shoal (Huangbu), just downstream of Xingping. It is named for a big flat beige slab of rock lying on the clear riverbed that looks like a sheet of yellow cloth spread out underwater; seven karst hills of different sizes stand around it, and it is famed for the finest peak-reflections on the whole Li River. Sources: lirivercruises.com (Li River 20-yuan note); topchinatravel.com (Li River).

question: Guilin stands at the head of the Li River, ringed by the stone-thumb hills that the Song-dynasty poet Fan Chengda judged the finest scenery under heaven. What does the city's ancient name mean?
context: Guilin means 'forest of sweet osmanthus' — it was named for the fragrant osmanthus (cassia) trees that perfume the city each autumn. Its karst scenery was so admired that the Song-dynasty poet Fan Chengda praised it as the finest under heaven. Sources: Grokipedia 'Guilin'; Wikipedia 'Guilin' (Fan Chengda).

question: Along the Li River, Chinese geographers sort the stone towers two ways — fenglin, 'peak forests' of separate spires standing on a plain, and fengcong, 'peak clusters' of cones sharing one base. Both took millions of years to form. How did these towers come to stand so high above the flat land?
answer: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
choices: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
an ancient volcano pushed them up as plugs
an earthquake fault thrust them up from below
an ice-age glacier carved them from the plain
context: Both fenglin ('peak forest' of separate towers) and fengcong ('peak cluster' of cones on a shared base) are carved DOWN by dissolving water, never pushed UP by any earthquake or volcano — the towers are simply the hard rock left standing after the softer surrounding limestone dissolved away over millions of years. Sources: Waltham, 'Fengcong, fenglin, cone karst and tower karst'; corroborated ScienceDirect (S0169555X13003826).

question: On Slovenia's rugged Kras Plateau — the barren limestone country that gave 'karst' its very name — rainwater soaks up a gas from the air and soil and turns into a weak natural acid, the same acid that drips for millions of years to hollow out the deep caves and sinkholes below. Which acid does rainwater become?
context: The acid is carbonic acid: rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil to form it, and this weak acid slowly dissolves the calcium carbonate that limestone is made of — the single reaction behind every cave, sinkhole, spring and stone tower on Earth. Slovenia's Kras Plateau, where these dissolving-rock features were first studied, is the barren limestone country that gave 'karst' its name. Sources: Grokipedia 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Karst'.

question: In Vietnam's Gulf of Tonkin, roughly 1,600 islands crowd out of the emerald sea in a maze of quiet channels — a place so strange that its name means 'descending dragon.' Ha Long Bay is the world's grandest example of what?
context: Ha Long Bay is drowned tower karst — the very same limestone towers as Guilin, but here the sea rose after the last ice age and flooded the valleys between them, leaving about 1,600 islands in the Gulf of Tonkin. 'Ha Long' means 'descending dragon': legend says the gods sent a mother dragon and her young to defend Vietnam, and the jewels and jade they spat out turned into this wall of stone islands blocking invaders. Thailand has a smaller cousin — the lone limestone tower in Phang Nga Bay nicknamed 'James Bond Island' after the film The Man with the Golden Gun. Sources: Grokipedia 'Hạ Long Bay'; Wikipedia 'Ha Long Bay' and 'Tower karst'.

question: In Yunnan's Stone Forest (Shilin), rain dissolved the rock from the top down into a maze of tall grey blades and pinnacles — some 50 meters high — that you can wander between on foot. Stranger still is where all that stone began: more than 270 million years ago, long before the pinnacles existed, this ground lay somewhere very different. Where did it lie?
context: Shilin's limestone is over 270 million years old: it began as shell-and-seafloor mud when the region lay beneath an ancient sea, then hardened into limestone and was later dissolved from the surface down into these 50-meter blades — karst at ground level instead of towering river hills. The local Sani (Yi) people tell of Ashima, a girl forbidden to marry the man she loved, who turned to stone in the forest and gave it her name. With Guilin and dozens of other sites, Shilin is protected as the 'South China Karst' UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of Earth's largest karst regions at roughly 500,000 square kilometers. Sources: Grokipedia 'Stone Forest'; Wikipedia 'Stone Forest' (Ashima legend; 270-million-year age; Yi/Sani).

question: In Hunan province, Zhangjiajie's forest of thousands of sheer sky-pillars — the floating peaks that inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in the film Avatar — looks exactly like a field of giant tower karst. But no acid ever dissolved them, and they are not karst at all. What rock are these pillars actually made of?
context: Zhangjiajie's pillars are quartz sandstone, shaped by freeze-thaw ice and running water — not limestone dissolved by acid — so despite looking like giant tower karst, they are not karst at all. Their floating-peak silhouette inspired the Hallelujah Mountains of James Cameron's Avatar. It is the classic trap: not every stone tower is karst — the real test is whether acid slowly dissolving limestone made it. Source: Wikipedia 'Zhangjiajie National Forest Park' (quartz sandstone; 'not the product of chemical dissolution'; Avatar Hallelujah Mountain).

question: Most plate boundaries either crash together to build mountains or pull apart to leak lava. But one runs about 1,200 km up the length of California, where the Pacific plate carrying the coast grinds slowly northwest past the North American plate — sliding by without colliding or splitting. Which famous fault is this?
context: The San Andreas Fault is the flagship transform boundary, running roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) up California. Unlike a subduction zone, where one plate dives beneath another, or a spreading ridge, where plates pull apart and new crust wells up, a transform boundary makes no new crust and destroys none — the two plates simply grind sideways past each other. The Alpine (New Zealand), Denali (Alaska), and North Anatolian (Turkey) faults are other real transform faults. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: Standing on the San Andreas Fault, you would never feel it, yet the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other the whole time — only about 20 to 35 mm a year. Geologists love to compare that slow, steady creep to one familiar thing on your own body that grows at almost the same rate. What is it?
context: About 20-35 mm a year — a couple of centimetres, the pace a fingernail grows — is how fast California's greatest fault moves. It feels like nothing, yet kept up over millions of years it carries whole regions of the state northwest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault.

question: On California's dry, treeless Carrizo Plain, a stream called Wallace Creek runs toward the San Andreas Fault — then its downstream half is found again about 130 m (425 ft) to the northwest, sliced off and dragged along by the grinding plates. Most of that offset crept up over thousands of years, but about 23 feet of it jumped in one instant during a single great 1857 earthquake. Which earthquake gave Wallace Creek that sudden jolt?
context: Wallace Creek is a textbook 'offset stream': the San Andreas has sliced its channel and dragged the downstream half about 130 m (425 ft) northwest over thousands of years — but roughly 23 ft of that jump happened in a single instant during the 1857 Fort Tejon earthquake, the great quake that ruptured this southern stretch of the fault. On the treeless Carrizo Plain — under 9 inches of rain a year, so nothing overgrows the ground — you can still walk the dog-legged bend today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrizo_Plain.

question: In the great 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the San Andreas Fault didn't crack at a single point — in one violent instant it split open along a continuous seam, leaving roads and fences that crossed it jogged out of line. The whole San Andreas runs about 750 miles. How much of that entire fault tore open in this one rupture?
answer: more than a third of it
choices: more than a third of it
context: The 1906 rupture tore along roughly 477 km (296 mi) of the San Andreas at about magnitude 7.9 — more than a third of the fault's entire 750-mile length ripped open in a single instant. Along the way the two sides slid up to about 6 m (20 ft) past each other horizontally, leaving fences and roads with a clean 20-foot jog that became textbook evidence of how the fault moves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake.

question: Because everything west of the San Andreas Fault is riding slowly northwest, the city of Los Angeles sits on the Pacific plate and is creeping away from the rest of California at a couple of inches a year. Wind that same slow motion forward about 20 million years, and geologists say Los Angeles will end up somewhere startling. Where?
context: Los Angeles rides the Pacific plate; San Francisco sits on the North American plate; the two creep past each other at 1-2 inches a year. Project that steady slide forward about 20 million years and Los Angeles — today some 350 miles south — would draw right up alongside San Francisco. Not a collision, just two cities that end up neighbours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: The tiny town of Parkfield sits squarely astride the San Andreas Fault, and it has logged a magnitude-6 earthquake at almost clockwork intervals — in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934, 1966, and 2004, roughly one every 22 years. So reliably do its quakes arrive that Parkfield has given itself a nickname. What does the town call itself?
answer: the Earthquake Capital of the World
choices: the Earthquake Capital of the World
the Earthquake Capital of the West Coast
context: Parkfield, home to only a few dozen people, straddles the San Andreas and has produced a magnitude-6 quake about every 22 years since 1857 — so predictably that the USGS made it the site of a long-running earthquake-prediction experiment, wiring the ground with instruments. Its proud self-given title: 'the Earthquake Capital of the World.' Source: https://www.earthquaketracker.org/faults/san-andreas; USGS Parkfield experiment.

question: Turkey's North Anatolian Fault is the San Andreas's near-twin — a right-lateral transform where the Anatolian plate grinds steadily west past Eurasia. Since a devastating quake struck Erzincan in 1939, its great earthquakes have come in an orderly chain: each rupture loads stress onto the next segment, so the fault tears open piece by piece, like a zipper. Toward which great city has that chain of quakes been steadily working its way?
context: The 1939 Erzincan quake (magnitude ~7.9, over 32,000 dead) began a westward-marching sequence: each rupture transferred stress to the neighbouring segment, more than 1,000 km of the fault breaking over the century. The 1999 Izmit quake (magnitude 7.6, over 18,000 killed) struck less than 100 km east of Istanbul, loading the last unbroken 'Marmara gap' right beneath the city — the segment seismologists now watch most closely. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Anatolian_Fault.

question: A great strike-slip fault runs down the Jordan Rift Valley through the Levant, where the Arabian plate has ground about 105 km north past the African plate. Like the San Andreas, it mostly just slides sideways — but wherever its line steps to one side, the crust caught between the steps has pulled apart and dropped into a deep pit. Strung out along this one sliding fault, those dropped basins have filled with water to make a famous chain. Which three bodies of water sit in the pits this fault opened?
answer: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
choices: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and Lake Nasser
the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov
the Persian Gulf, the Tigris, and the Euphrates
context: Where a strike-slip fault steps sideways, the crust in between stretches and drops, opening what geologists call a 'pull-apart basin.' The Dead Sea Transform's left-stepping bends dropped the pits now filled by the Sea of Galilee, the Dead Sea, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Dead Sea's shore, about 430 m below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth — a record that exists only because two plates are sliding past each other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea_Transform.

question: The grassy hill of Hisarlik in northwest Turkey looks like the ruin of a single old town. But when archaeologists dug down, they found one city built on the flattened rubble of an older city, again and again, across about 3,000 years. How many separate cities are stacked inside this one mound?
context: Labelled Troy I to Troy IX from bottom to top, the nine cities span roughly 3000 BC to 500 AD -- each one raised on the levelled rubble of the last, piling ~15 metres of ruins into a single hill. (worldhistory.org, Discovery of Troy; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: At Hisarlik the stone ramparts and gateway of Troy still stand -- solid, real, and climbable today. Yet the single most famous object from the whole tale of Troy's fall was never once found in the ground, and belongs entirely to legend. Which fabled object was it?
context: Homer's Iliad set the Trojan War at this mound, and the stone walls are genuine -- but no horse was ever excavated. Oddly, the wooden horse isn't even in the Iliad: it turns up only later, in the Odyssey. (Wikipedia: Trojan Horse)  (Legend.)

question: Hisarlik rises about 15 metres above a flat plain in northwest Turkey, yet the hill is not natural. For three thousand years, mud-brick towns rose and fell on the very same spot, each collapse lifting the ground a little higher until a whole hill had formed. Archaeologists across the Near East have one short, specific name for an ancient mound built up like this. What is it?
context: A tell is a mound raised from the layered remains of successive settlements; Hisarlik, Jericho, and Megiddo are famous examples. A barrow and a kurgan are burial mounds, and a midden is an ancient rubbish heap. (worldhistory.org; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: Most of the nine Troys were built of humble mud-brick, which is why their collapse melted into a soft hill. But the great rampart of Troy VI, still standing at Hisarlik, was cut and fitted from a far harder rock quarried nearby -- which is exactly why it survives while the mud-brick around it has long since crumbled. What stone are Troy's mighty walls built from?
context: Troy VI's citadel walls -- mortarless cut blocks sloping inward -- still rise 9-10 m in places and stand up to 5 m thick, much of the horseshoe circuit and its gates surviving at Hisarlik today. The humbler mud-brick cities simply crumbled into the mound. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The showpieces of the gold hoard Heinrich Schliemann dug from Hisarlik were its glittering golden crowns, fit for royalty. Caught up in Homer's tale, Schliemann gave them a romantic nickname that has clung to them ever since. What did he call the gold diadems of 'Priam's Treasure'?
context: 'Priam's Treasure' held gold diadems nicknamed the 'Jewels of Helen,' along with about 8,750 tiny gold rings, gold goblets, silver vases, and copper weapons. Schliemann tied the crowns to Helen of Troy, the runaway queen of Homer's tale whose flight launched the war. The Mask of Agamemnon and the Cup of Nestor came from Mycenae, and the Ring of Minos from Crete. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure)

question: Slicing north-south through the Hisarlik mound is a colossal man-made gash, about 40 metres wide and dug clear down to bedrock. It was torn out in the 1870s by a treasure-hunting excavator in his impatient rush to reach Homer's Troy, wrecking priceless layers on the way down. Visitors still call this great scar by its digger's name -- which is it?
context: Heinrich Schliemann's Trench -- about 40 m wide and cut to bedrock -- sliced straight through the Late Bronze Age citadel, the very layer now thought to be Homer's Troy, destroying much of what he was hunting for. Blegen, Korfmann, and Dorpfeld were later, more careful excavators of the mound. (Wikipedia: Schliemann's Trench; worldhistory.org)

question: Troy is one of the most dug-over archaeological sites on Earth -- Schliemann, Blegen, and Korfmann all spent years tearing into the Hisarlik mound across 150 years of work. You might assume the whole place has been uncovered by now. In fact, as of 2013, how much of Troy's sprawling lower city had actually been excavated?
context: As of 2013 only about 2-3% of Troy's lower city had been excavated, and roughly 2 m of the mound's surface has eroded away over the centuries, carrying buried evidence with it. Most of Troy still lies underground, waiting. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The gold hoard from Hisarlik became world-famous as 'Priam's Treasure,' named for the Trojan king of Homer's war. The gold is real -- but when archaeologists finally dated the layer it lay in, the royal label collapsed. Set against the true war-era Troy of King Priam, how far off is this treasure's age?
context: The hoard came from the Troy II layer, roughly 2400-2200 BC, while Priam's war-era city is Troy VI/VIIa, around 1250 BC -- so the gold predates any King Priam by about a thousand years. The treasure is real; the 'Priam' label is wrong. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure; worldhistory.org)

question: For a century everyone pictured Troy as just the small stone citadel crowning the mound at Hisarlik. Then, in the late 1980s, Manfred Korfmann's team traced a whole hidden lower town spreading around it, ringed by a defensive ditch cut into the bedrock. Once that lower town is counted, how much bigger is the real Troy than the citadel everyone assumed?
context: Korfmann's lower town covered about 30 hectares, ringed by a defensive ditch cut into the bedrock -- proof that Troy was over sixteen times the size of the citadel-only ruin everyone had pictured. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: The Troy VIIa houses at Hisarlik were crammed with stores for hard times: sunk deep into their clay floors stood colossal jars, some taller than a grown man, for hoarding grain, oil, and water. Greek archaeology has a specific name for storage jars of this giant, floor-sunk kind. What are they called?
context: Pithoi are giant storage jars; sunk into the Troy VIIa floors alongside rooms subdivided into cramped quarters, they read like a town packing in people and hoarding food -- bracing for a siege. Amphorae carried wine and oil, kraters mixed wine, and kylikes were drinking cups. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: One layer in the Hisarlik stack reads like a 3,000-year-old crime scene: sealed beneath a black burn line, its lanes strewn with sling-stones and Greek-style bronze arrowheads, its dead left lying unburied where they fell. Fire, weapons, and slaughter -- this is the storming and sack that best fits Homer's tale of a city put to the torch. Which of Troy's nine stacked cities is this, the layer archaeologists call the closest match to Homer's sacked Troy?
context: Fire, embedded weapons, and unburied dead mark a violent sack rather than a natural disaster or slow decline, making Troy VIIa (~1300-1180 BC) the best archaeological match for the sacked Troy of Homer's tale. Carl Blegen led its excavation. Troy II was Schliemann's early treasure layer, the grander Troy VI just below fell instead to a natural disaster, and Troy IX was the late Roman-era city. (worldhistory.org; Wikipedia: Troy)

question: A wall of water thrown across the sea by an undersea earthquake was once called a 'tidal wave,' but scientists reject that name — such a wave has nothing to do with the Moon-pulled tides. The correct term, the Japanese word 'tsunami,' literally means what?
context: 'Tsunami' (津波) joins tsu, 'harbour,' and nami, 'wave' — named because the swell that seemed slight far out at sea reared up to wreck Japan's harbours. Calling it a 'tidal wave' is wrong: tides are the gentle Moon-and-Sun pull on the whole ocean, while a tsunami is the water column shoved upward when a quake heaves the seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: Out in the deep open Pacific a tsunami is barely a ripple on the surface, and a ship sailing right over it would hardly feel a bump — yet beneath it the whole ocean is surging along at more than 800 km/h. Roughly as fast as which of these?
context: A tsunami is not a wind-blown surface wave — an undersea quake sets the entire depth of the ocean moving at once, so it carries immense energy while barely rising above the swell. In deep water it can race at over 800 km/h (about 500 mph), roughly a jet's cruising speed, crossing an entire ocean in hours; a passing ship feels almost nothing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On 26 December 2004 a magnitude ~9.1 quake ruptured the seafloor off Sumatra and sent tsunamis sweeping across the whole Indian Ocean, killing about 228,000 people in 14 countries — the deadliest tsunami ever recorded. Afterward, one stark reason the toll ran so high stood out above the rest. What was it?
answer: the region had no tsunami warning system
choices: the region had no tsunami warning system
the tremor felt too small to fear
the waves struck in the dead of night
the earthquake had cut every phone line
context: In 2004 the Indian Ocean had no tsunami buoys and no alert network at all, unlike the Pacific — so the coasts got no warning whatsoever. The waves were still noticed ~8,500 km away at Struisbaai, South Africa. Worst hit were Aceh in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Tamil Nadu in India, and Khao Lak in Thailand. The disaster spurred the world to build an Indian Ocean warning system. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: The giant tsunami-spawning earthquakes cluster in the same places again and again — Alaska, Japan, Chile, the Cascadia coast — all strung along one great belt around the Pacific, which is why the world's oldest tsunami warning centre keeps watch from Hawaii at the ocean's heart. What is this earthquake belt commonly called?
context: The 'Ring of Fire' is the horseshoe of subduction-zone trenches and volcanoes rimming the Pacific, where oceanic plates dive beneath others and unleash the megaquakes that shove up tsunamis — off Alaska, Japan, Chile, and Cascadia. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center, the world's oldest, was set up in Hawaii to watch it; the Indian Ocean had no such guard in 2004. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On All Saints' morning, 1 November 1755, a tremendous quake shook Lisbon for minutes; then the harbour sea drained away, stranding ships on the bare mud as crowds walked out to gawk — until, forty minutes later, a tsunami roared back over them. Why does the sea sometimes pull back like that before a tsunami strikes?
answer: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
choices: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
the quake drops the seabed and drains the bay
the wave draws the water up into its crest
the falling tide happens to meet the wave
context: The Lisbon quake (~M7.7+) shook for up to six minutes on All Saints' Day; the sea then drew back, luring the curious onto the mud before the tsunami engulfed the harbour ~40 minutes after the shock; a firestorm then burned for days, and ~40,000–50,000 died. The sea withdraws only when the wave's trough leads its crest — so it happens often, not always. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake.

question: Racing across deep water the 2004 tsunami stood only about a metre tall, but as it swept into the shallows at Banda Aceh in Sumatra the front slowed, the water behind piled into it, and it reared up 15 to 30 metres high. What is this piling-up of a wave's height in shallow water called?
context: In deep water a tsunami's crests can be 200 km apart yet only ~1 m tall; nearing shore, 'shoaling' slams on the brakes — speed falls from ~800 to under 80 km/h and the wavelength shrinks, so the trailing water piles the wave up into a towering wall. At Banda Aceh in 2004 it rose 15–30 m, with a maximum around 51 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On Maikhao Beach in Phuket, Thailand, on 26 December 2004, ten-year-old Tilly Smith watched the sea suddenly froth and pull far back and — unlike the curious adults wandering onto the wet sand — screamed for everyone to run, because she had recognized the danger. Where had she learned those exact warning signs just two weeks before?
choices: from a survivor of an earlier wave
context: Tilly Smith's teacher, Andrew Kearney at Danes Hill School, had shown the class the warning signs just two weeks earlier — the sea pulling back, the water frothing, waves that go out but don't return — using footage of the 1946 Aleutian Islands tsunami. Recognizing all three at Maikhao, she got the beach and hotel evacuated, and about 100 people were saved. A geography lesson literally saved lives. Source: International Tsunami Information Center (itic.ioc-unesco.org).

question: When the volcano Krakatoa blew itself apart in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra in 1883, the explosion was one of the loudest sounds ever recorded — heard thousands of kilometres away. Yet of the roughly 36,000 people it killed, the blast itself claimed only a fraction. What killed the vast majority?
context: Of the roughly 36,000 people killed by Krakatoa's 1883 eruption in the Sunda Strait, more than 34,000 died not from the explosion but from the tsunamis it raised — waves some 30–37 m high that crashed onto the coasts of Java and Sumatra. The blast itself was heard about 4,500 km away in Perth, Australia, one of the loudest sounds ever recorded. Volcanoes, not only earthquakes, can raise killer waves. Source: ncei.noaa.gov, 'On This Day: Historic Krakatau Eruption of 1883.'

question: High above the hamlet of Aneyoshi in Miyako, Japan, a stone slab carved by ancestors generations ago bears a stark command: 'Do not build any homes below this point. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis.' Then, in 2011, the greatest tsunami in living memory surged up the valley toward the village. What became of every household that had obeyed the ancient stone and built above its line?
context: The Aneyoshi stone reads in full: 'High dwellings are the peace and harmony of our descendants. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis. Do not build any homes below this point.' In 2011 the wave climbed the valley and halted about 100 m below the stone — and every household that had stayed above it survived. Japan has hundreds of such tsunami stones, some over 600 years old, many placed after an 1896 tsunami killed ~22,000 — ancestral knowledge carved to outlast living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami_stone; nbcnews.com.

question: On 9 July 1958 an earthquake dropped 30 million cubic metres of rock off a cliff into the narrow inlet of Lituya Bay, in Alaska. The splash surged 524 metres up the far mountainside — higher than the Empire State Building — and tore away the whole forest. This was the tallest wave ever recorded on Earth, yet how many people did it kill?
context: This was a landslide megatsunami, not an ocean-crossing tsunami: the rockfall's splash surged 524 m (1,719 ft) up the far slope — taller than the Empire State Building — the tallest wave ever recorded. Because Lituya Bay is a remote Alaskan inlet, only about five people died, on fishing boats caught in the bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Lituya_Bay_earthquake_and_megatsunami.

question: On 11 March 2011 a magnitude ~9.0 quake struck off Japan's Oshika Peninsula; the tsunami ran up to 40 metres high, pushed 10 km inland at Sendai, and overwhelmed one coastal site whose failure turned a natural disaster into a nuclear one. Which site did the wave overwhelm?
context: The magnitude ~9.0 quake struck 72 km off the Oshika Peninsula; the tsunami killed about 19,759 people, ran up to 40.5 m at Miyako, and pushed 10 km inland at Sendai, where people had only 8–10 minutes' warning. It flooded the Fukushima Daiichi plant and caused three reactor meltdowns — a natural disaster that became a nuclear one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tōhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: Almost every great Maya city was hidden deep inland beneath thick jungle canopy -- but one was built right on the lip of a low cliff, its stone temples looking straight out over open water. Tulum, on the Yucatan coast of Mexico, is the only major Maya city set on the sea. Which sea meets the cliffs below it?
context: Tulum stands on a cliff about 12 metres (39 ft) high on the east coast of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula -- the only major Maya city built on the coast, while almost all the others hide inland in the jungle. Below its temples the Caribbean glows famously turquoise. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.

question: The Maya called their clifftop city Zama long before anyone renamed it Tulum. Its temples stand on a low cliff on the Yucatan coast, looking straight out across the open Caribbean. What does that older Maya name, 'Zama', mean?
context: Zama means 'dawn' or 'sunrise' -- fitting, because the cliff faces due east, so the temples catch the very first light coming up over the Caribbean each morning. The name we use today, 'Tulum', is different and much newer: it comes from the Yucatec Maya word for 'wall', pointing to the great rampart that ringed the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'; Ancient Origins.

question: El Castillo, the tallest temple crowning Tulum's clifftop, looks out over the Caribbean cove where the city's traders once beached canoes loaded with obsidian, jade and salt. Archaeologists think this seaside temple quietly did a second job beyond worship. What do they think it doubled as?
context: This beacon role is an interpretation, not a proven fact. Because El Castillo lines up with the one natural break in the offshore reef, researchers think lights placed in its windows could have been lined up to guide trading canoes safely through that channel into the sheltered cove. Tulum was a busy Postclassic port trading obsidian, jade and salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.  (Legend.)

question: Across the far north — the tundra of Siberia, Alaska, and northern Canada — the trees give out completely, and beneath the thin skin of moss the deeper soil never thaws, staying locked solid all year, every year. What is this permanently frozen ground called?
context: 'Permafrost' means ground that stays at or below 0 C (32 F) for at least two years straight. Only a thin top 'active layer' — averaging about 1.5 m — thaws each summer; below that the freeze runs deep, reaching roughly 1,493 m down in Siberia's Lena and Yana river basins. About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's land sits on permafrost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost
